For a game like
, the question is less "is it good?" and more "does it hold up?"  As someone who played HL1 last century but never played this game till recently, I think it does.  A few grey hairs are showing, but
is still a fun and excellently-designed game worthy of your time.
The most obvious sign of ageing is, of course, the graphics.  However, while modern games may look better
still looks good enough.  NPCs look sufficiently human for suspension of disbelief, the backgrounds are convincingly sell the world and it's always clear what's going on.
Second, some modern players may be unhappy with the lack of regenerating health.  Ultimately that's a matter of taste, but
was clearly balanced around this, and medpacks are plentiful.  Unless you're playing on hard, this shouldn't be a problem for anyone who's played an FPS.
Lastly, there are some weaknesses on the narrative side.  One moment that I think was intended as a shock was so strongly telegraphed, the only surprise was that it
a red herring.  The fact that you need to do the same stupid action
to proceed in the Citadel casts a shadow on an otherwise excellent final level.  And most disappointingly, the story does not so much end as just stop.  These are only minor blemishes on otherwise strong storytelling, however.  The use of environmental cues and "show, don't tell" is excellent.  The named NPCs are all nicely fleshed out, and the interactions between them are particularly believable.  These factors ensure that while the plot may not win awards, it is well-told.
Aside from the story, the gameplay of
is great fun.  The core shooting mechanics work well, with enemies that can still provide a few surprises.  These are presented in a number of different yet exciting set-pieces.  Notable highlights include running Combine over in the airboat; the pseudo-horror section of Ravenholm, and the fear that poison headcrabs offer; crossing the bridge in Highway 17; getting antlion allies, even if they do tend to get in the way; and the assault on the Citadel.
That last point nicely leads into the Gravity Gun, still one of the most fun FPS weapons ever.  It's the kind of brilliant idea that's simple and obvious in hindsight.  The basic fun of throwing things around is complemented by the tricks available with skill and practice.  In a sense, you haven't really played
till you get it.  The rest of the weapon selection is pretty decent, too, balanced if not so remarkable.
deserves its praise.  Though it cannot have the same impact now as on release, time has not made its gameplay any less fun.  I'm certainly glad that I was finally able to play it.

I'll try to keep my review short and simple.
Let's start off with the things that are good about BDO.
There are a lot of things to do in Black desert, more than you can imagine. Best graphics to date in an mmorpg. Beautiful and immersive, realistic even. Combat, although it does get a bit repetitive, is fun and powerful. The character creation is insanely good! Full control over everything down to the smallet detail. Might be the best character creator in any game. For the first 10-25 levels you'll be having and fun and exploring, learning new things and enjoying yourself.
BUT... I cannot explain in words how frustrating this game is.
Black Desert is a grindfest. Until level 56 and after level 56. All you're going to be doing is grinding until you get sick of it so you pay real money to make things easier. This game is designed to make you pay money so you enjoy the game more. Something like a pay2enjoy. Sooner or later you will hit a paywall. Be it the pets that auto loot for you, the fancy outfits, and weight limits, the inventory slots... there is so much that will make you sigh out loud. But of course you can make all your tourbles dissapear with a little bit of $$$!
The thing that completely kills the game for me and makes me want to kms is how unatractive and stale your character looks. There's no real gear in the game; it's all just numbers. There is little to no difference between the gear you equip. There is absolutely no difference in appearance between a character that's level 1 and a character that's level 56. You'll be almost identical. If you want to look fancy, you gotta pay sucker. Oh sure people will tell you you can get any outfix from the marketplace. Well, good luck considering it's RNG and the pearl items in the market place are sold in the same second they get put on there. And people don't even want silver for these outfits considering how low the amount is.
I didn't do much PvP but from what I can tell it's unbalanced and Witch & Wizard are the most dominant.
Also there is no 'end game' in Black Desert. It's non-existant. No raids, no dungeons, nothing. At no point during leveling up will you need to team up with other players. It's almost as if it's a single player game that's always online.
Everything in this game feels like a chore. Afk farming everyday for 5-6 hours, killing mobs, cooking, farming. Only fun thing in this game is making a character. You can literally put the game in a tray and let it do it's thing over night while you sleep. This is BDO's end game. You play the game by being afk.
Do not waste your money on this, it's not worth it at all. Find something else and save yourself the trouble.

Review for Black Desert Online from the perspective of someone who genuinely enjoys the game.
I might have written one review before, so please forgive me if mine is not as detailed and flowing as some of the better game reviewers here on Steam.
The game is beautiful, with a unique atmosphere as you travel from place to place. Land or Sea.
You can catch wild horses, bread them to get better tier horses, with faster speeds, and better skills. You can build Wagons to haul your trade items around.  ( of varying quality, and varying quality parts) You also have Camels, Donkeys, and Elephants.
You can also build rafts, fishing boats, and even huge Sailboats with Cannons to traverse a massive ocean. Just like on land there are Bosses on the ocean and of course normal mobs to farm.
The combat and skill combos are also unique and engaging.
The gear you spend lots of hours of blood sweat and silver to get leveled up. Then later decide to use a different set, or got that BIS boss piece you wanted. No worries, you can sell it on the market because gear doesn't bind to your character.  Example: After I got my BIS pieces ( and got them upgraded), I sold off my old  Tet ( +19) gear I had been using for months for 155 to 322 million each ( depending on the piece)
The most surprising thing that hooked me on this game though was not the PvE, PvP combat you see in every game.  Even though I still really enjoy it.
It was the empire building, my huge worker empire of (Goblins, Humans, Giants) that gathered, and craft stuff for me (passively ie I just had to keep them fed), that I then sold.
The Trading system is amazing and way to complex to briefly explain. But if you enjoy it I think it is still one of the best wealth revenues in the game. I was shocked at how much I enjoyed figuring it out, and how much silver I made. Wealth helps you get that gear upgraded.
Off the wall stuff I had fun doing:
Building my Sailboat
Building better cannons. sails, prow, hull for my sailboat.
You can make a ton of silver however you feel like that day. If you want to grind mobs, no problem great money and exp. If you want to trade, fish, process cause you are not in the mood to grind mobs, you can make tons of silver that way too, all while leveling life skills. If you have a busy week, you can afk fish, process, etc check in every few hours when you have time and don't sweat that you will fall behind because you couldn't sit at your PC 8 hours a day and active grind.
There are dozens and dozens of other things you can do that would take me forever to talk about them all. Houses, Farming ( yes you can actually grow your own crops, cows ) Node/Siege wars that generate tax revenue for everyone in the guild,
Even do nothing but catch, tame, bread, and level horses and sell them for a few thousand silver to a few hundred million silver. Which is what my wife ended up falling in love with. There is no telling what you might enjoy. There's an insane amount of things to do in this game.
It's also great to break from the typical cookie cutter hack and slash, Clear same instance dungeons 1000 times to get everyone in the group their loot. Then rinse and repeat when next update adds new instances with new better gear.
I should mention, there is no required month to month charge to log in and play. But if you enjoy the game and play a lot, you will end up spending money on cash shop items. I spent about 250 over a year and my wife spent 50.  For me, I ended up spending less this year than I did the past few years. Paying Subs for WoW and FF. And a few vanity items here and there.
The big difference is I can spend the money when and how I want. I'm not forced to pay a monthly fee to log in.  And let's be real, there is no such thing as a free game. I assume the employee's that work on the game expect a paycheck just like you and me when we show up for work. I guess each model has it's positive and negatives, but for me, I prefer the pay at my convenience model.
Also, there are a lot of cash shop items you can buy for silver from the market. They sell fast and are highly sought, and you will lose more bids than you win, but eventually, you will win some.
I really enjoy the game. It takes a while to learn everything, but those that do will surely find their  niche. This is a sandbox type mmo, you make your own path and story as you see fit.
If you liked Diablo then buy this game.

Grim Dawn is a fantastic ARPG with easy-to-learn, hard-to-master game mechanics. The dual-class mode, augmented by the devotion system really brings a lot of variety to the builds that you can create. There are practically an infinite number of builds you can do that can really fit your playstyle. Be warned, this game restricts you to Normal for a reason; it can kick your♥♥♥♥♥at times... however, despite this the pacing is fantastic - it doesn't feel like a chore to go through a lot of the side quests and dungeons that are offered to you in the base game and personally, I recommend doing them as you get lots of good loot(tm) that later in the game (early-mid, mid game) helps you define what build you want for yourself. In terms of game mechanics, I kind of felt that the rep system was pretty grindy for some factions, especially Devil's Crossing but the rewards are very worth it.
The lore and interactions are also very in depth. There are lore entries that explore the universe that your character lives and fights in. There are also very minor side encounters that actually, to some extent influence some other interaction in the world. For instance, you can recruit characters that will show up later. Another example is you can influence an NPC reaction to either be hostile or friendly towards you.
The co-op in the game is fantastic, with only a few quests that gave my friend and I issues. For example, some quests that require some resources to hand in would only complete for the person who handed it in. Another example is when there are two warring factions, the host will determine the presence of which faction will appear. One faction will cease to talk to you if the host is on the opposite faction, so you have to do some of their missions solo.
There are a few issues I had with the game itself, notably some stuttering every now and again. This could apparently be fixed by disabling Steam saving, but I don't care enough to lose that feature so I left it on.
In all despite the minor issues I listed, I strongly recommend getting this game if you are a fan of Diablo, Path of Exile, Torchlight 1/2. Get it on sale or not, it is worth it either way and I can guarantee many hours of enjoyment from this game

The first "rogue-like" game I've played, and it's damn brilliant and got me hooked to the genre. Basically, in a "rogue-like" you try to survive as long as possible - when you die, it's over. In this game, you control a lone space-ship navigating through different galaxies as you try not to die and ultimately take down the Federation ship that threatens the universe. The story is never really that important in "rogue-likes". What matters is the sense of tension and urgency as you navigate a harsh and cruel world in your the never-ending fight to survive. Each time you die, you learn, and try to get just a little bit further next time.
Because that's the core essence of a "rogue-like". Death. As hard as you will try to avoid it, you will die, and you will die a lot. The hope is that every time you do - you learn something from it. You learn what works, what doesn't. Is it better to upgrade your shields to block more attacks, or upgrade your engines to increase your evasion chance? Should you use lasers, ion cannons, missiles, or attack droids? You try one thing, then another, until you find a way that works for you. In a good rogue-like, (like this one, especially with the free Advanced Content patch), there are multiple ways that work, but there are still luck based events that can throw a wrench into your plans. So even if you get down a strategy that works, not every game will be the same.
So if all of that seems interesting to you, I'll get to the mechanics. You control a space-ship, with anywhere from 1-10(?) crew members. You can assign each member to boost one of the ships systems - be it the shields, weapons, engine, and of course you'll need a pilot. You travel throughout various galaxies, one space-jump at a time, where you'll encounter many events, good and bad, that will keep you on your toes and keep you constantly adjusting your tactics. Some events will reward you with new crew-members, weapons, or special items, Other events will force you to forfeit scrap, damage your ship, or even kill one of your crew-members. As you defeat enemy ships, or help out civilians, you get scrap, which is used to upgrade your ship and buy various weapons, crew members, as well as fuel, missiles, and droid parts. So you really have to balance what you use your precious scrap on.
In battle, you can control your weapons to shoot specific parts of the enemies ship - to disable the shields to inflict maximum damage, or disabling the engines to prevent them from getting away. You can pause whenever you want in battle giving you ample time to plan and execute your strategies. Obviously, the aim is to take down enemy ships while trying to minimize your own casualties. There are various ways to do this, whether it be disabling their weapons system via ion cannon, using missile launchers that bypass their shields, or activating droids that shoot down enemy projectiles, Again, you have to find out what works for you, but more importantly, you have to learn to work with what you got. Sometimes you have the choice of letting enemies surrender for a chance at getting more fuel or missiles, or blast them into space dust for more scraps.
Just as a word of warning, "rogue-likes" are usually pretty difficult, at least at first. It'll take you some time to get accustomed to the world, and probably even more time before you defeat the last boss. But that just makes victory so much sweeter. Each time you play, you get a little bit further, or at least learn something to get you a little further next time. If you like the idea of going through trial and error as you adapt to survive in a cruel, unforgiving world until you achieve victory, the final culmination of the sum of your experiences, then look no further, and pick up FTL today.

For starters, I have played two Telltale games with similar mechanics(Walking Dead 1 and Tales of the Borderlands), I have also watched Game of Thrones for 4 seasons but have not read the books. I enjoyed both TT-game but felt constantly let down by the TV-show.
I'm torn in my opinion but mostly leaning towards "do not buy untill they have actually made few sequels". For me this cost about 4 euros(telltale bundle), but essentially felt that the story alone wasn't enough satisfactory for the time spent. So essentially if you get this cheap, it's in my opinion still not worth the time you're going to spend. This is a somwhat of a rant rather than a serious review.
I honestly haven't liked many of the GoT characters and bringing them into this game was a huge mistake. They should've taken some other time and even another place in the plot or completely ignore the most famous characters. I shared many peoples feeling that when a famous character from a show arrives in screen, I know I cannot harm that character or even win should we have an argument or a fight. Also the voice acting, while mostly quite good, felt lackluster coming from the actors. Like they didn't give much of an effort for the game.
In a sense, this game feels too much like Game of Thrones in smaller scale. It tries too much to copy all aspects of the plot, Forresters are Starks, a bunch of "goodies" we're supposed to care but we don't.  Garret is Jon, trying to make the plot seem more grander by adding snow zombies and talks about destiny.  Mira is Sansa, hanging around in Kings Landing being a pawn of "evilgenious plotters". Asher... well asher is there so you can interact with  Daenarys and spend  one third of the playing time in the desert environment doing nothing substantial, just like in the TV-show.
But the biggest let down is that the game lacks Telltale immersion. While TT games have said that the game adapts to my decisions(doesn't mean the game changes radically), this felt that whatever I do, it ends the same way. What I mean is that even if I chosed something, even the lines and reactions of other characters didn't change that much, or were just a random reaction. Combined with the plain awful facial expressions of TT-games, the conversations felt weird. Sure Borderlands act in a way the same way, after completing that, I felt I could achieve something different with other choices. In this case I felt that almost nothing would change and there is no reason to play this again, ever. There were times when the game just seems to bypass what you chose and instead offer you the main course, enemy soldiers suddenly appearing inside your closed fort and you killing someone you don't want to. The game didn't even bother to explain why my choice was irrelevant this time, it just skipped like I didn't make the choice.
During Ep4 I felt that I wanted to see the ending of this, but at the time I already felt that the game isn't going to end properly, some of the characters were too far away, still doing irrelevant stuff to actually make a difference in the plot. So during ep5 I started to have a feeling that was confirmed in the last episode, this was just a prelude to some other season that actually tries to tie everything up. This could also be summarised "non-happyending story of a random family in a fantasy environment with some loose ends".
Gameplay is similar to other TT-games. I think someone calculated how many clicks they had to do to actually complete 5 eps of Borderlands and it was around 130. So yea, these are more or less interactive stories, only this time there was barely any interaction. Most of the time the game acts a bit wonky, characters appear out of thin air objects missing each other or going through and already mentioned facial expression that goes pretty much like this: :) :(  >:( :O, and that is the basic reaction from characters to anything. "I love you" says the NPC. >:) =O :) :( says your characters face in 3 seconds.

Black Desert Online is, if not the best, one of the best MMORPGs available in 2017. However, you have to know that this game is probably not for you, as it requires a lot of time and investment to progress through it.
There are many "kinds" of MMORPGs available nowadays, and BDO falls into the "Korean" category, which means you will need to grind a lot in order to progress.
If you are not interested in PVP, I would suggest you not to buy it. There is (almost) no dungeon nor raids in BDO. Instead, we have world bosses whose drops the best gear of the game.
The rest of the PVE content is about grinding monsters, which means you might (actually, will) have to kill the same species of monsters a lot of times (hundred of thousands) in order to earn silvers and then gear up. Don't be scared, it goes fairly fast, as you can usually kill two or three thousands monsters of your level with an average gear.
If it does not scares you, fine, let's continue.
Black Desert Online is a game that relies A LOT on RNG. When I mean a lot, I mean that features like : Enhancing gear, Loot (what a surprise), PVP and even your characters base stats are influenced by it. Of course, almost any feature influenced by RNG can have its chances of success be increased in some ways. It's either you are lucky or not.
You can end up upgrading your gear with 4 millions (which is NOTHING, removesfrom your mind the fact that 1M is a lot, you will get billions of silver during your play time fairly early) or spending 2 billions and keep failing.
This games have a lot of "cons" (I don't really think RNG is a con) which can be kind of scary, but has a lot of good aspects. The gameplay is insane. There is content for everyone (You can make money either by killing monsters, chopping wood, making silver ingots, breeding horses...). Fights looks amazing, and the game is beautiful. Yes, if your computer is bad, the game will run bad. How is that surprising ? A 1060 can run the game is high graphics, it's 2017 guys, gear up ...
As I don't want this review to be too hard/long to read, I'll skip some aspects of the game, but I recommend you to watch youtubes videos about the game before buying it. But if you start playing, I advice you not to judge the game before level 57/58, as the game really starts at level 56, which you can reach fairly fast (I level up my alts in less than 10 hours, which really isn't fast, I know people going 0-56 in 5 hours).
This review was more a kind of "warning" review, just to make you know that the game is different, and you might not like it. If you don't really care about the cons I said, just buy it, you will discover all the best aspect of the game by yourself.
Oh, and, don't trust the "bla bla bla the game is pay to win" ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. Most of the interesting items from the cash shop can be purchased from the market place. For example, the Value Pack (subscribers bonuses), which cost 15 euros for 3 days, can be purchases for 15 millions of silver on the market place. 15 millions are made in less than 4 hours of grinding, and can be done in 1 hour if you are lucky. You can even make it by AFK processing overnight. The game will give you 2 or 3 times more from your "beginner rewards". Keep in mind that 1 euros = 1 million of silver when browsing the cash shop.

As someone who adores Tropico 3, I felt skeptical about playing this game, since most of the assets are ripped straight from its predescessor, and the mechanics are very similar, although distinctly improved.
What I discovered when I finally got around to playing it, however, is a beautifully silly game. Where Tropico 3 had tossed out puns and occasional tongue-in-cheek exclamations over the radio, Tropico 4 has mostly-voiced campaigns, a suite of comedic characters with hilarious interactions, a genuinely funny radio announcement for a lot of the buildings (which does not play as frustratingly frequently as in 3), and a distinct sense of absurdity in the very structure of the campaign. For instance, one of the campaign missions has a series of voice clips which are direct spoofs of "the most interesting man in the world," which left me giggling to myself.

A really cool concept and awesome aesthetic are mired by the experience of actually trying to play. BDO in practise combines the worst of both the worlds of mobile gaming and korean styled MMO grindfests. Controls are convoluted, the UI is a cheap looking mess and the much touted character customization feels very superficial and overhyped. In the game world, body customization only shows in cash shop outfits. Many mechanics rely on leaving the game on in the background to 'afk farm' as it is called, it is an intensely passive, sedentary system only sped up by spending money. Beware buying any items of the traveler and explorer pack as the majority are single use, character bound items. Also runs the XIngcode 3 spyware, which is hell to remove. If you like the Musou (dynasty warriors) style combat it can be fun to blast through groups of mobs, though for how cool the animations all look, the combat system is very shallow and repetitive. If you can get used to the afk farming based systems, enjoy the combat system and have enough cash to burn it might suit your tastes. Despite my personal disapointment in it, BDO does offer a niche experience that people fond of Korean style MMO's and micro-management of workers and crafting facilities will enjoy. I would not call it pay to win at all, but I would call it pay to get anywhere in a remotely reasonable amount of time. Basic quality of life stuff such as inventory and auto-loot are also cash shop bound, as is the norm with these kinds of MMO's.

Overcooked is one of the most fun multiplayer experiences I have had in a very long time.
It's chaotic, it's stressful, it's slippery, it's everything you can imagine when you wonder how it's like to work as a top chef (that of course includes doing such everyday tasks as feeding the spaghetti monster to prevent the apocalypse from happening). And it is so darn funny, my brothers and I haven't laughed this hard with a game in a long time. Simple tasks as cooking soup grow increasingly difficult as you are suddenly forced to travel from van to van and teamwork is the key to victory.
The single player is very minimal, so multiplayer is a must to fully enjoy Overcooked.
One of the cool things about Overcooked is that due to the simple controls, only one controller is required for two players to play, since they can share one controller. This means that with just one controller and the keyboard, you already got 3 players.
Overall, I recommend Overcooked for everyone who can gather a group of people for some hilarious co-op. The controls are so simple and fluid, everyone can pick the game up and play, and oh boy are you gonna have some very fun times!

After recently getting into racing games and wanting to try out a bike racing game, I picked up MotoGP 15 Compact after reading a review from another user. I was excited to try the game and was looking forward to riding a motorbike for the first time.

The graphics are beautiful, sound is on point and everything is top notch but those controls are extremely unforgiving, even with all the assists turn on. From a newbie's prespective I would definitely recommend avoiding this one as it is clearly catered to people who have experience with racing games.
I could barely keep my bike on the road and couldn't get out of last place no matter how hard I tried due to the extremely difficult learning curve. This is not a game for newbies and definitely not for people just starting out with racing games. Unfrortunately I can't really recommend any other alternatives so if you do want to put in the effort to learning the mechanics and controls in this game just understand that it will take a very long time to master.

This game....is freaking awesome!
I'm only familiar with the first entry of the series but this one is totally different: for starters, no guns in here, only bows, clubs, spears which gives way to a melee-based gameplay that completely fits the overall idea of this game: SURVIVAL.
Now to fully enjoy the survival idea, I would advise to play a few hours the way the game is, i.e. console oriented with ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s of on-screen indicators, minimap, icons of all sorts then, turn those off according to your liking but the less on-screen icons, the better the immersion and that's what this game is all about!
Immersion, feeling like you are 10 000 years ago, feeling like any encounter with a predator can be lethal, and I mean lethal, you're not on top of the food chain in FarCry; unless you are extremely careful, you can't just rush in otherwise you'll get ambushed by either a wolf pack, a bear or a random encounter with a sabretooth tiger, and you won't survive those encounters, unless you are really prepared. And even so...
You'll also need to gather food and stuff to survive. Otherwise you won't be able to experience FarCry Primal the good way. That is if you play the game in Survivor Mode which is mandatory.
Be on the edge at all time, listening to your surroundings, be one with nature, engage or not, measure the risks, flee or die.
The sound, the absence of ambient music and the gorgeousness of the environment alone is enough to make you think you are in a Europen forest 10.000 years ago.
There's a team of linguists that worked to make the Wenja language plausible, on a side note.
Taming the beasts that aid you in your adventure is awesome, i mean who never dreamt of hunting deers alongside with a jaguar?! or charge an ennemy camp with a bear at your side? while your owl drops stingbees bombs on a group of flesh-eaters? and you impale them with spears you throw at them?
Now, there is a lot of resource gathering which can be tedious toward the end but that is part of the immerison. You use arrows, spears, so you need to craft them out of something which means gathering wood and stuff.
In survival mode, you must manage your hunger and fatigue, which can be tricky at times, stopping you from fast travelling and stuff. But it all makes sense in terms of survival and immersion.
I've tried permadeath mode which is the best experience ever for this game, and something you can't experience in any other game, you really fear for your life, especially during the beginning of the game but I died so many times from a surprise attack by a jaguar, a bear or sabretooth tiger that I gave up on that mode for hardcore, survival mode. Only because I got sick of seeing the game intro and all. Some dude completed permadeath mode, kudos to him, i don't think i ever can.
To sum up, roaming the land of Ouros with no on-screen icons, no cursor to aim, the fear of crossing paths with a powerful predator is something I had never experienced before in a video-game. And that is what gaming is all about!
If this game was VR compatible, I think i would have♥♥♥♥♥♥bricks on multiple occasions.
For instance, a jaguar won't attack you from the front or if you are with a more powerful predator, it would sneak up on you silently, from behind when you least expect it most likely killing you before you can even react, or flee if overpowered.
That is how good the AI is in this game. Wolves, dhoves attack in groups or flee, that is how good the AI in this game is.
If you attack a mammoth, the other ones will come and defend it and stomp you to death, that is how good the AI in this game is.
Now the human AI, well they either charge at you mindlessly or snipe you from afar and they really are sharp-shooters and they detect you easily from a distance if you're not careful.
Overall, well-balanced human AI, again, in hardcore mode with no on-screen help or it becomes easy if you're not a total noob. Tag ennemies? common! console kids use it, not "real"gamers.
If you are capable if immersing yourself into a game and if you like animals and melee combat, and survival, this game IS for you. It runs well, it's polished you can rebind keys however you want.
I insist on the fact that on-screen icons kill immersion so get rid of as many as you can, it's all costumizable in the menus, thanks developpers, you did a great job!

I bought this game after seeing Nerdcubed's video on it because it looked so fun! And it is...to begin with.
The sense of humour and the whole design of the game is imbeccable, it's great fun, strangely immersive even though it's ridiculous, I can't fault the design of the game in that sense at all. And the first league is great fun to play through, but this is where things change, and why I wouldn't be willing to recommend the game just yet.
The difficulty curve, if we can call it that, suddenly takes an enormous jump. Aside from the ocassional glitches that are still in the game, the AI suddenly remembers it is a computer and can kick your sorry meat♥♥♥♥♥♥without even trying if it wants to. And it does! Quite suddenly the ball is being passed around the pitch from player to player at such an incredible rate you'll be lucky to know where on the pitch you even are any more. A bit of speedy silly play does fit in with the theme of this game, but it reaches such an insane speed it is literally untouchable, borderline un-seeable. At present as well, you have to get used to successful tackles somehow resulting in their player not losing the ball, your defenders refusing to ever be behind the halfway line in some games, the auto-select of players (for you may not do this yourself) is often very unhelpful, either not selecting anyone near the opposition with the ball, or randomly changing your selection when you want to tackle to someone who is not in a useful position, and then the game won't let you try and tackle again for quite some time.
This game will be brilliant, I don't doubt that, as long as it keeps being updated and improved. I just don't know how long we will have to wait for these things to be improved on, because at the moment they are taking the silly fun this games offers and turning it into an infuriating affair that is best described more as a video than a game, because all you can do it watch, and feel just a bit humiliated as the AI keeps passing the ball across your goal at 200mph because none of your team are even in your own half...
I'm looking forward to changing my recommendation to yes, because I feel confident it will happen, it's all there! It's just not meshing right yet :)

Needless to say, this is a great game to play. It's a challenging Turn-Based and Tactical Strategy game, where you try to stop the aliens from destroying Earth, whereas it's the main storyline.
Pros:
+Storyline is interesting in a way.
+You can customize your squad. By that, I mean the skills they should choose to have.
+The game teaches you to plan carefully, instead of just rushing in to find the enemy.
Cons:
-When you "spot" the enemy, they get a free turn, allowing them to run away and take cover. This is one of the big problems people do not like about this game.
-Well-known bugs in the games.
-Sometimes the hit percentage is inaccurate, even if you are just close enough to the enemy.
-When you have an abduction site taken place, you either have 2 or 3 places you choose to help. You can't help all 3, and you must choose one country to help. Not helping the other or 2 other countries causes their panic level to increase. If it's full, they will threaten to leave the Council, and once they leave, there's no way to get that country back in. It's a done-deal decision.
Basically, this review consists of half positive and almost most negatives. Still a good game though.

As someone who absolutely loves football, I thought I'd try this - a football game made by an accomplished indie developer who admits he couldn't give a stuff about the sport. Here's my take on it.
PROS

+ The 'three strikes (fouls) and you're out' rule is a cool addition, as is 'doing' more than one goal if you score from a longer distance.
+ Dan Marshall got the offside rule absolutely spot on, in my opinion.
+ It's cheap. I'd recommend spending a few spare quid on this, with the proviso that you know exactly what you'll be getting into.
CONS
- Much like with the 'Dan & Ben' games, I found the humour to be VERY hit-and-miss. Indeed, the good stuff can start to grate after a couple of hours.
- The storyline is somewhat naff, even by FIFA 17 'The Journey' standards. And if you want to complete it, set the number of enemy teams as low as possible to avoid monotonous repetition of the same old matches. I stupidly went in the opposite direction, as I thought at first that I'd still be playing this game weeks later.
- The rubber-band difficulty setting. The enemy team is either unplayable (when losing) or just incapable of playing (when winning). There's no middle ground. While dynamic difficulty is a nice concept on paper, it's not exactly enjoyable when you squander a six-goal lead because the AI start playing on fast-forward and do a couple of lucky goals from distance.
- Why can't you alter the direction of your tackles? Unless I was breathing down the enemy's neck, 80% of my tackles would end with my 'kickman' sliding literally anywhere other than towards the opponent.
- And don't get me started on the goalkeepers, erm I mean 'gold-keepers'. I wasn't expecting Buffon-like gold-keeping in this game, but I was hoping that they'd be somewhat competent. A lot of matches seem to come down to which team has the least inept gold-keeper.
- Did Skrillex do the music for this? The EDM is so loud and migraine-inducing, even at half volume.
- You need a mouse to navigate the menus, but also a keyboard/controller for the gameplay itself. For some users, that's not ideal.
- No multiplayer, therefore not much playability once you've completed the story.
I got about two hours' enjoyment out of this game before the novelty wore off. Behold The Kickmen is NOT a terrible game, and I don't regret buying it (certainly not at such a low price), but it just hasn't grabbed my imagination. Sorry about that.

I've seen a lot of negative reviews for this game lately and while I think some of them make some valid points, I don't think they're necessarily entirely fair. I want to make some counterpoints as to why I (and some other people with similar taste) might actually enjoy the game so everyone isn't immediately turned off to it when they might actually like it:
1). The actual game mechanics are absolutely a little clunky sometimes. My controller stopped working half way through the game and the keyboard/mouse aiming system sometimes was a huge pain. That being said, it never ruined any major decisions, I just had to redo a few of the fights which, whatever. Those weren't my favorite part anyway.
2). There’s definitely some plot frustrations (you are at a disadvantage a
), but I honestly think anyone who knows anything about Game of Thrones (and the obvious parallels between this family and the Stark family) probably could have seen that coming. There is always a lot of ‘losing’ in that show before there is any ‘winning’, and I think what the developers were doing was building a platform for future seasons where ‘winning’ will feel so much more satisfying after how poorly you’re treated this season. I know that’s not for everyone, but I know that for me, personally, it got me more into the narrative than it might have if there really was some perfect ‘path’ to take where you immediately come out on top.
3). The graphics are a little funky, but I enjoyed the watercolor style sometimes. And when I didn’t (a lot of the violence looks kind of strange in this style) I was into the story so I didn’t really care that much.
Ultimately, I get why this game isn’t for everyone, and I would have probably been a little iffier on it if I’d paid full price (I waited for a sale and got the whole season for about six dollars), but I liked it and if you can find it on sale somewhere I’d recommend giving it a try.

Game of Thrones Season 1 from Telltale is a lot better than I expected. My experience with Telltale was limited to the great walking dead season 1 and I can honestly say that I enjoyed them at the end in about the same amount. It is true, that Game of Thrones is more of a film/series in which you press every few minutes some buttons than a real game. But once you are ready to accept this term you will enjoy this game a lot, IF you like GoT. If you have watched the show and didn`t like it, than this game is not likely to change your opinion. But as a Fan it feels like an extra season to the great series.
The Story itself begins at the end of season 3, when you start to create the destiny of House Forrester. You take control over various characters linked to the house and switch in every episode multiple times between them. In my opinion that was a really smart thing since you never get tired and experience many different views on the power games in Westeros. As mentioned above because of this constant switch of characters and place within an episode you immediately feel reminded to the show.
The first 4 episodes last for approximately 2 hours, while I got through the last two in about 1,5 hours each. A lot of people complain that your decisions do not really matter and up to a point that is kind of true. But you also got to mention that while the ending of the story is not gonna change so much a lot of the smaller details will. So your decisions will have a great impact on the relationships between the characters and whether this persons dies or that. It is true that it doesn't matter how you decide, at the end you will always feel like you made the wrong choice, but in the shady world of Westeros this seems quite fitting to me.
Pro:
-Great Story
-Making Decisions
-Strong GoT atmosphere
-Great Voice Acting
Contra:
-Decisions do not really influence the ending
-More a movie than a game
Result: I recommend this game to every Telltale Games or Game of Thrones Fan. The story alone is totally worth playing.

For some reason Steam has insituted a character limit on their reviews, so I have had to scale down my review to the first two sections and the conclusion. You can read my full critique here:
_____________
This will be focused on the story of the game, and how it fits in with the wider A Song of Ice and Fire/Game of Thrones world, but I will touch on the rest briefly on the rest in this opening paragraph. The engine is still awful, the game stutters through all seven hells when changing scenes, and the illusion of choice is more apparent than ever before. Anyway, let's get to the meat of any Telltale game - the story.
House Forrester - They are what I'd call a forth-rung House (like how House Tollett is sworn to House Royce is sworn to House Arryn is sworn to House Baratheon, House Forrester is sworn to House Glover is sworn to House Stark is sworn to House Baratheon). Then why does this incredibly minor House have sole ownership to the ability to construct the defensive equivalent of Valyrian Steel swords? According to the game, this incredibly rare and valuable resource apparently only grows in two places south of the Wall (both places conveniently obey the contours of the political regions of two minor forth-rung Houses), and House Forrester are the only ones who can work it - why then aren't they richer than the Lannisters, or the Starks, or at very least the Whitehills? If there was a minor House that uncovered the art of re-forging Valyrian Steel they would make enough money to buy and sell the Iron Bank of Braavos. Why is this House so seemingly poor? Is the only reason they are so poor despite their huge deposit of natural resources due to the need to shoehorn in a sense of urgency and foreboding into the plot? Every problem this House runs into throughout the course of the game could be solved if they reached their hand into Ironrath's treasury (which should be overflowing due to the demand of the products of the miracle wood that grows only in their backyard) and hired a sellsword company. Also, why aren't they rushing to the defence of House Glover? This game takes place at the tail end of season three, and throughout season four of the show. During this entire time House Glover's seat of Deapwood Motte is under the control of the invading Ironborn. Why aren't we helping to free our liege lords? More to the point, why haven't the Ironborn invaded Ironrath, considering how valuable Ironwood is?
House Whitehill - My biggest gripe with this House is that when you take their location and their religion into account they make zero sense. Ask yourself this: how did a House, sworn to the Boltons, situated north of Winterfell, end up following the Faith of the Seven, the religion of the south? Telltale's decision with House Whitehill just baffles me. The only thing we knew about House Whitehill before this game is that they followed the Faith of the Seven, and every decision Telltale made with them doesn't take this one fact into account. I liked the design of their seat, Highpoint, and I felt it really fit their status, but House Whitehill would make much more sense being sworn to House Manderly (a powerful third rung House in the North that follows the Faith of the Seven, and has numerous vassal forth-rung Houses sworn to it), and having nothing at all to do with this game.
Also, where does this House make their money? It's repeatedly pointed out how House Whitehill can't work Ironwood, so it's not like they're trading that valuable resource - how then are they able to afford hundreds of Sellswords when House Forrester (which is literally surrounded by valuable natural resources only they can use) cannot also do the same?
If I had the ability to alter only minor things within this game, I would remove House Whitehill. Have a rival House, by all means, but make it one of the other Houses sworn to House Glover (e.g. House Branch, House Bole, or House Woods -  all of which were introduced in the same sentence in 'A Dance with Dragons' alongside House Forrester). This would also handily explain why House Glover couldn't interfere in defence of the Forresters - they didn't want to pick sides in a skirmish between their vassals. It would also help to make the spread of Ironwood trees more believable, as it would be one large patch of Ironwood trees within the Wolfswood, as opposed to two separate patches spread out on opposite sides of the North. This in turn helps make the fight for resources more believable, whereas the Forrester vs. Whitehill feud displayed in the game is the equivalent of a border dispute between Alaska and Florida.
Conclusion - From the day this game was announced I kept going over and over the possibilities for this game. My first thought was a Recruiter from the Night's Watch, going from peasant villages, to market towns, to cities across all seven kingdoms, recruiting boys and men alike to take the black, and having some adventures along the way. Then I thought it could be similar to the Ser Duncan the Tall novella series, and have you play as a Hedge Knight, going from keep to keep to sell your sword, and maybe take part in a few notable battles and lesser known skirmishes. I thought it could take place during Aegon's conquering, or the Dance of Dragons, or the War of the Ninepenny Kings, or Robert's Rebellion, or the Greyjoy Rebellion. But Telltale chose to force themselves into a corner by picking the exact period of the show and books, having us play as a minor House, and yet somehow having these minor characters regularly having meetings the most important people alive at the time to the extend where I spent most of the game waiting for a character called Gump Forrester to appear. This game feels like such a waste of a great licence, with so much squandered potential. Take the Greyjoy Rebellion as an alternative setting. We could have played both sides of the War, such as one of Balon's sons who died during their father's war (or maybe Balon's brother, Victarion Greyjoy, and have him die at some point, which would serve to both explain his absence from the television series and keeping both book readers and show watchers in suspense whilst playing), a member of House Mallister at Seaguard, a member of House Lannister at Lannisport. We could have seen the coronation of Balon, the burning of the Lannister fleet, the siege of Pyke, the Tourney of Lannisport. We could've seen many show characters like Tywin Lannister, Ned Stark, Stannis Baratheon, Robert Baratheon, Balon Greyjoy, Jorah Mormont, etc, with none of the character interactions or appearances feeling as inconsistent or forced within the wider story as what Telltale gave us. This game could have fit in so succinctly with the wider story of both the show and the books, but every baffling decision made by Telltale just has everything stick out like a sore thumb.
Would I recommend the game? Only in a 75% off sale. And even then if you're very - VERY - hungry for some adventures in Westeros and you don't feel like reading the books, watching the show, or playing the Crusader Kings II mod.

My only true gripe with the game is that you can't replay missions. Missions are the most fun thing do in the game and once you beat them things get dull fast. Making missions replayable would be amazing for co-op and add so much to the replay value as a whole.
Overall, I'd say I went into playing this game not necessarily wanting to like it, but it won me over. The AI is so simple that combat is never really a challenge.  MICROTRANSACTIONS that are necessary to be the cool guy that the game borderline forces you to be.  A loot system that is far behind most modern games.  And to top it all off, the co-op is unbearable.  It is the soul reason that I haven't played the game in 3 months.  The game has the normal party system, but there's so much travelling that losing your friend is garunteed.  And when you lose your friend, you will likely waste 15 minutes trying to find them again.

Summary:
People will ardently defend the changes made to Quake Live, claiming they're for the better, they're breathing new life into the game, they're not affecting the difficulty etc. These claims are by & large, absurd; Putting the Game on Steam brought the majority of these new Players to QL. The rest of them are returning "veterans" who couldn't handle Q3/QL as it was before, so they welcome this watered-down crutch-filled version of it. The changes are not for the better, as these new Players will be unable to easily accustom themselves to the "Classic" Mode of play, so they'll switch back to "Standard" & never learn to play Quake Live as it was meant to be. Finally, regarding claims that the changes "don't actually affect the actual Gameplay/Difficulty" - No.
Quake Live now feels like you're playing in God Mode (cheats on), against people/bots also using God Mode, but even looking at it from that point of view, it still feels watered down, since nobody is actually Immortal, resulting in some cheesy ripoff that fails to have any real reason to exist. Extremely disappointing.
----------------------------------------
For those of you who don't know Quake Live (QL), QL is a HD "remake" of Quake 3, with some adjustmens, alterations, modifications, & tweaks. Weapon Balancing is improved for example, there's a new HUD, there's a lovely new "Pre-Match Warmup" feature which I actually enjoyed, & while there's also a handful of new Maps & Modes, there's also a lot of missing Features. Gore is gone (completely), the infamous Defrag Mod is missing, & many popular Maps, Modes & Mods have yet to make an appearance in this watered-down (content-wise) Mod-free HD remake of Quake 3.
But that there is the old Quake Live; Quake Live as it was before it received the recent "2.0 Overhaul" Patch, alongside its Steam Re-Release.
For those of you who haven't played Quake 3 before, the rest of this won't make much sense to you. For those of you who have, prepare yourselves, you're going to have a very bad combination of Niagra Falls & Head-to-Keyboard the likes of which you haven't had since Daikatana.
What follows, is a summarized list of the biggest Gameplay changes in the 2.0 Overhaul/Steam Re-Release;
- Loadouts have been introduced; Basically, much like in CoD & Battlefield, you can, before spawning, choose two Weapons that you will Spawn with, Ammo included. For example, I can spawn with a charged up Rocket Launcher & Plasma Combo. Gone are the days of tediously running towards a Weapon Spawn Point upon Spawning!
- Ammo Packs are no longer exclusive to each Weapon. Running low on Rocket Ammo? No problem, because you no longer need to look for that small floating Red Rocket Ammo Box, now you just need to look for any of those Silver-Grey Boxes situated anywhere around the Map to get yourself some more Rockets.
- Heavy Machinegun: Since you no longer spawn with an MG (unless you choose the new Heavy MG from the Loadout Menu), you can pickup both the HMG, & the MG on the Map, like any other Weapon.
- 3D Countdown Icons now show you in intervals of 5 seconds exactly how much time is remaining until important Pickups respawn. Gone are the years of counting down seconds until that Quad Damage respawns, now you've got a 3D Timer over the spawn location which does the job for you!
- 3D Combat Text: Ever wondered how much you actually hit that opposing Player for? How much Damage you actually dealt him, specifically? Well, fear not, because now, you don't need to, the Game takes the liberty of telling you!
- Bunny-Hopping: You remember when you used to get those bad twitches in your thumb from extensive "Whack-Whack-Whack-ing" your Space Key? Good news! You don't have to worry about that anymore either, because those days are now long gone. Now you can just press Space, & Bunny-Hop away! Whee!
- Announcer: There's a brand new announcer that sounds nothing like the deep, dark spooky voice that once permeated the halls of Quake Live, & still does so in Quake 3. Definitely another improvement.
There's so much more to get into & detail, but to be honest, I'd rather not waste more of your, or my own time, I'll just jump straight to the best part of it all instead; Classic Mode still exists, so long as you queue up for the "Official Duel Servers", or if you buy a Subscription plan (minimal fee - 4.99 USD per-month), & Customize your own Server with Classic Mode.*
In short: a Game that was well worth the Subscription Fee several times over before, has now come to deserve it even more than ever before! Why are you still here? Go! Go on already! Go!
So, folks, you sold yet? Good. While you're at it, don't forget to salivate all over yourselves at the thought of pre-ordering that upcoming Doom Game!
*Footnote: Since I have yet to actually try this so-called "Classic Mode", I cannot definitively state at this time whether or not the amazing feature of 3D Combat Text will be carried over or not. I for one do definitely hope for the 3D Spawn TImers however, I can only imagine how much the Pros will love those!
---------------------------
Seriously now, (assuming you got the sarcasm above), before this, I actually never thought that I'd ever come across a Game that would negatively benefit from Steam (& while sure, one has technically nothing to do with the other, this "version 2.0 overhaul" came with the Steam Re-Release, so yeah). It is seriously amazing how ridiculously low ZeniMax-Bethesda has sunk. I can't wait to see how much worse the upcoming Doom Game is going to be. I really find myself wondering when I play this - has id Software truly sunk this low, or are they this badly cash-strapped that they'd reduce themselves to doing stuff like this? I wonder.
As far as I can see, the only thing left for us to do is to put up those big "IN EPIC WE TRUST" Banners, & hope they don't bend us over & ♥♥♥♥ us up the♥♥♥♥♥as well. Though to be entirely honest, they'd have to actually actively seriously try in order to beat out the horrorshow that id Software has unleashed upon Steam, & the World at large with this. It saddens me to see so many people Recommending the Game to others, either because they know nothing of what came before it, or because they simply couldn't fully grasp the entirety of Quake in its true "Classic" Form as they call it now, & welcome this watered down, crutch-filled version of it where they think they'll be able to compete on a more equal level with others.

First off, this is my first Far Cry Game and I was drawn to it because I love survival and story based games like this. I am also an avid fan of history and minored in anthropology in college.  I have always loved ancient and pre-history and the fact that a gaming company was willing to go the extra mile to create such an interactive world involving people of the stone age is a feat unto itself. For that I commend ubisoft.  Now to the actual review.
PC specs: Windows 10 Ultimate, FX-8350 @4.5ghz, R290x stock, 32gb ram, SS HD
Pros
Starting from the ground up, the world is absoultely gorgeous.  I was able to run the game with a mix of very high and ultimate settings with my aging rig at an FPS rate of between 45-70 on a 27 inch monitor.  It was very engrossing and I found it hard to stop playing due to the wonderful atmosphere.
Moving on, combat. Contrary to what people say, the combat was good but not stellar. I wish there were more otpions when it came to hand to hand combat but the array of pre-historic weapons was rewarding and fun for me.  With all the upgrades, your short bow felt like a machine gun against your enemies.  The death sequences from sneak attacks and kill steaks were also wonderfully gory and realistic.
I am also going to throw hunting in here. I am a hunter in real life and always dreamed of hunting mammoth.  Getting to hunt mammoth in the game, especially helping your tribe bring down the Elder Mammoth quest and the blood tusk mammoth, was some of the most memorable parts of the game.  I also enjoyed the quest challenges hunting the dangerous blood fangs and wolf pack.  Deffinitly a strong part of this game.
Story line. The story was also good enough to like.  People cite that it was shallow but we must remember that these were simple times and simple stories about hunting beasts, slaying enemies and praying to the gods. Culture and technology were in its infancy and the world was very brutal, bloody, and life was short.  The game drives that home with the ample amounts of blood, guts, human and animal sacrifice and death.  None of that is boring. The game also did not shy away from some nudity and women were topless in the game, which added to the realism of the era it was set in. Towards the end of the game, when I finally conquered all of the other tribes, I did feel a sense of peace and love for the tribe I was fighing for because of the engrossing nature of parts of the story.
Cons
These are personal gripes.  The game was set in Europe during the ending ice age, yet we see multiple tribes of different humaniods that never existed at the time period, which would be some time around 10000 BCE.  They decided on that date I am sure because farming was mentioned several times in the game and this would be right around the Neolithic Revolution (invetntion of farming). Neanderthals never existed at this time and the traits of a few of the tribe also exibit bits of African culture but I find that a hard buy. However, for the sake of game diversity, it was acceptable.  This is a very mintor gripe.
Combat. I stated before that combat was a pro but we also see cons.  The game could have implemented blocking of some sort for hand to hand combat, even taken a few more aspects from Assassins Creed but decided that simple swing mechanics were good enough.  During combat, I also found that certain weapons were much better than others, which means that the game was imo a little imba.  I found myself defaulting to the short bow and after researching steady hands, could snipe from some pretty extreme distances, landing headshots with ease.  The spear was also, a very strong weapon in the game and uttery destroyed chiefs with one to two shots once upraded.  Other weapons like the club were only really useful exploring caves as a torch. The owl was also laughable when dropping bombs on ememies and to me, took away from parts of the realism.
Story line.  I loved the human aspects of the game, but found the animals storys while high off of blood soup and shrooms to be annoying and tedious.  While some may have found it to be fun, I did not and tried to push past it as quick as possible.
Crafting. Crafting was meh. You collected stuff and put it together. Not much to it but you had a lot of things to choose from. It could have been more in depth but that might have become tedious.
Final Verdict.  Good, memorable game, brave for trying something new but not stellar in a few ways.  I am glad I bought the ultimate version with all DLC while it was on sale during the winter.  I would not have paid full price for this game, but I never like paying full price.  Get it when it is 50% off or over and it will truly be a great experience.

I wanted to like this game. I really did. I was in the middle of my Game of Thrones craze and this seemed like a good addition to my library.
Boy was I wrong.
I ended up ditching the game after episode 1. Or was it halfway through episode 2? I don't even remember. It's been a while.
The good:
+ Excellent voice acting, with all the wonderful actors from the show and great work from the newcomers who voiced the rest.
+ Dialogue and storyline feels very much in-tune with GoT/ASOIAF.
+ Beautifully designed world, although be warned that high-res graphics are not the selling point of this game. It is very stylized, but beautifully so, almost like a painting.
The bad:
- Your playable characters are essentially a poor man's Stark family, only less dimensional. By the end of the first episode I did not care enough about any of them to see me to end of this game.
- Side characters are even worse, with a few exceptions. By the end of episode 1 I uttered the words that no one should ever have to say about any piece of entertainment: I do not care what happens to any of these people.
- There are zero gameplay mechanics beyond picking dialogue choices and the occasional QTE. I was warned about this before playing (having never played a Telltale game before), but even despite my severally lowered expectations it got really, really boring really fast (and this coming from a casual gamer who doesn't need or want 5000 moves or action combinations to be happy).
- While it seems at first like your choices matter, they don't. At least not in the long run. It makes the entire journey seem painfully pointless. That wouldn't be a problem if the characters were interesting, but sadly, they are not.
The ugly:
- The music and sound design was utterly forgettable, which is a shame since GoT has some of the best music in television. I honestly don't know what went wrong here.
- I bought this game when the first episode came out and paid the full price for all episodes up front, even though the episodes were released separately. In the end, having been so severely disappointed, I just felt kind of cheated out of my money. Lesson learned, I guess. No more buying on release day.

With Battlefront coming out from EA in Open Beta, I reinstalled this because my potato computer couldn't hope to run the newest installment of this franchise. Luckily, I could run this on decently high graphics without my laptop exploding in front of me. So, let's get the review out of the way!
BF2 has a few different versions of single player (just like in BF), so let's start off with the campaign. It pits you as a clone trooper of the 501st, and gives a semi-detailed description of what those clones went through. While I'm not going to spoil too much for those who haven't played/seen a player do the campaign, it's sort of a tear jerker when you REALLY think about it.
For the second sort of SP, instant action, it doesn't come off as lacking. Each map you do has a  ton of variation, and even switching eras in the menu can somewhat alter how the game goes. Droids and Rebels have two of the most OP classes, but still easily countered so there's not really any bias because of the very limited numbers of them allowed at once. The most overpowered normal class is easily the Engineer, where you can end up killing half the enemy reinforcements with a single life if you're good enough. And prominent characters from each faction can be set to appear at different times/not at all once you kill or do enough, so that's a bit of a bonus.
The third type of SP is a glactic conquest thing that returns from the first game. Instead of just picking a planet to fight on, in here you have to manually send a fleet over to each enemy controlled planet and defeat all the forces on there. If you lose, you lose a fleet. If you win, you get the planet. That simple. With the addition of space battles, you can now have skirmishes in 'deep space' between planets, or battles for the planet in the space around it. Should you win those space battles, you then take the fight to the surface.
With Galactic Conquest, like the first game, you can chose a bonus when you fight. Unlike the first game, you have to buy them. And your troops. Until you do that, you're running around with a Pilot (for space battles) and a normal trooper. You could really win campaigns with just those two, but your enemy AI certainly won't stick to them. The consumables range from better blasters and armor, to being able to tote along a Hero/Villian for the duration of the battle. Certain ones won't work in space, so you can't play as General Grevious in a battle for the space above Naboo.
Now, on to the Multiplayer. For MP, it's basically just Instant Action. Except everyone only plays Hero Battles. So you can't really find any populated servers over, say 5 players, on any other map.
Overall, the game's a good game, but the AI could've REALLY used some more work. They do ridiculous things at the best of times, and it can be infuriating if you're playing a CTF game on Tatooine and a Jawa picks the flag up. When you don't have friendly fire enabled. I'd give it a 8/10, because it has a slight feeling of being a very late beta instead of a true game. That's just with instant action games, of course.

It’s somewhat ironic that a series I have never once thought of after years of a hiatus after the hundreds of hours I’ve spent on PC (disc copy) and consoles would be the day where an itch to replay it would make it relevant once again. This coincidence also occurred with System Shock, Wolfenstein: The New Order and The Evil Within, so if this trend is something more than mere chance then the next time I have a craving for BioShock will be when the next title is announced. In all seriousness, though I am not exaggerating the odd timing on my part, it’s nice to finally have closure to a long-awaited finale with the series as now it’s a perfect time to reflect about how a MIT graduate would become one of the most venerated names not only of modern FPSs but of modern video-games.
As far as discussing the leaked information of Half Life 2: Episode 3, I will not discuss it until the very end of Half-Life 2: Episode 2 as that is when it will be the most relevant after reliving the series from beginning to end. This review will mainly focus on the merits and issues with Half-Life 2 itself. However, what I want to stress to those who desire to burn away Gordon Freeman’s legacy out of spite is to consider if those memories are worth destroying after all the time, the thrills and the heartaches they have brought without closure, and now we can carry on with peace of mind and the end of the Half-Life 3 memes. (We still have “Where is Xen?” to keep us occupied for Black Mesa.)
When it comes to the gameplay of Half-Life 2 itself it’s not the FPS mechanics themselves that have withstood the test of time; instead, it’s the immersion and the thoughtfulness of the Source Engine to create a focused, well-paced and seemingly freeform campaign that does all it can to disguise its linearity. The first-person perspective itself is merely the catalyst for the innerworkings of HL2 that have made its campaign so venerated as it was on release as it is nowadays, and it’s how this information is conveyed to the player for the sake of immersion. Where series like The Elder Scrolls and Bethesda’s Fallout games attempt to accomplish this feat with the worlds of the Creation Engine, HL2 and the Source engine manage to create as seemingly real of a place in the small-scale with as much depth behind the smoke and mirrors. These tricks have often been referred to as the “invisible tutorials” and level-design structure that guides the player without waypoint markers for direction.
However, one thing that has made Half-Life 2 dated more so than its episodic sequels is not the usage of its quiet-time moments that might as well be cutscenes but rather a consequence of these invisible tutorials of HL2. Similar to the problem of invisible walls in open-worlds, once the illusion of player agency and the tutorials become more blatant on repeated playthroughs the illusion makes the artificiality of these moments harder to ignore. This wouldn’t be nearly as much of a problem if it wasn’t for the fact that the game has these moments from beginning to end littered throughout the campaign with invisible, audio and simple gameplay tutorials that seem more present than the actual gameplay. The worst offenders are the blatant tech-demo puzzles meant to show off the Source engine rather than being interesting set-pieces driven by the player feedback with the environment that appear as potholes on the overall pacing of the gameplay such as the many seesaw/weight puzzles.
Probably the one touted mark of excellence that has been untouched for over ten years is the overall pacing and level-design itself that keeps the simplified FPS mechanics from becoming tiresome. Environments like scripted, intense thrills of Ravenholm and Nova Prospekt are contrasted with the immense scale of the speeder-boat of the Water Hazard chapter as well as the adventure alongside Highway 17 that possess optional landmarks for exploration. Combined with the moments to reflect on the journey with NPCs or peaceful environments to the next location these breathers act as momentary pauses between the highs and lows of the campaign that has made HL2 unparalleled with its quality of excellence from beginning to end despite having issues of its own gameplay and its series’ continuity.
It’s uncommon for me ever to play a series out of order unless it’s a reboot with more modern mechanics to become invested into the franchise first, but with the Half Life series Half Life 2 was my first experience into this world. This is perhaps why the issues with the continuity across HL1 and HL2 have little to any bearing on my view of the game other than being inconsistent across the series even if we excuse the expansions of HL1 as being non-canonical. However, it’s mainly the lackluster narrative driven by a pointless silent protagonist along with characters that have aged poorly with time.
As was the case with Jack from BioShock, the absence of the protagonist’s voice adds little, if anything, to the experience beyond what HL1 attempted to convey as the growth of Gordon Freeman from a scientist to super-soldier with the player’s skill in a meta-sense. HL2 assumes this pinnacle of Gordon Freeman has become this world’s second coming of Christ for some reason as he was one of many survivors of the Black Mesa incident that would idolize Freeman fora resistance group against new alien overlords on the Earth. Besides the obvious retcons of the series, the narrative itself is serviceable at best that really has little going for it other than the journey itself through the Source engine that enhances the simple resistance fighter storyline into an epic of its own.
Where the game really shows its age is the characterization of Gordon Freeman and other characters with clear, distinct personalities with mainly superficial differences when it comes to the plot. Gordon himself is a reclusive, silent type jokingly referred to as a man of few words; Alyx Vance is an endearing character on her own with little to say about her personality other than upbeat; Gordon’s friends, Barny, Dr. Kleiner and Eli all retain some semblance of their past selves with quirks of their own such as Dr. Kleiner’s infatuation with his new pet, Lamar; and the villains of the games have simplified motives and clear personalities that designate them as villains. It may be harsh to criticize these caricatures as being simple but given how the game is mainly character focused when it comes to the narrative the issues with their overall simplicity highlight their issues with time.
Time, of all Half Life’s antagonists, is mainly the one entity that has left its mark on the legacy as the technical issues of the Source Engine can be forgiven yet the game designs and characters themselves will only show their wear with further age. Where Half-Life 1 will be benefited from its lack of series’ baggage and a simplified, timeless conflict for a game, Half-Life 2 and its sequels will show its dated nature because of its legacy. While Half-Life 2 is by no means a bad game for a first playthrough or the hundredth, the acclaim in which it has become venerated is mainly due to its nostalgia behind its name more so than the merits of its games.  However, unlike the original, the episodic sequels would improve on the flaws of the original by focusing more on the gameplay than their storytelling merits.

Raywin wants  to be perceived as  a throwback to old-school 2D RPGs but this claim is built upon a very flimsy structure. I really wanted to find some redeeming points to this game. Whenever I read about a title’s negative rating on Steam, I still try to find some good aspect to cling on to. None to be found. I had my modest share of 2D RPGs here on Steam and found several gems which I won’t mention here out of respect for them. I really don’t wish to associate their name with Raywin, even by comparison. In front of your eyes (if you payed what has to be, a ridiculous sum given the case) you have an almost highschool project-like level of RPG Maker use of assets. And even that was somehow botched by bad grammar, constant use of the same textures/sprites, bland storyline with an even worse game map and last but not least glitches and bugs that will surely break your game or at the very least, crash to desktop. Truly, the only thing the developer had right is the presence of Achievements and Cards, but even those should not be considered sufficient to warrant a purchase. I usually try to understand some of the issues mentioned above, if this was a title released recently. Sadly it’s not, since more than one year has passed since Raywin has become available on Steam. The developer has no other published project and the fact that they didn’t bother in so many months, to release even a measly patch or update, speaks volumes regarding their respect for any potential buyers of their game. And I cannot stand for it.

Company of Heroes 2 is one of the more successful sequels of the RTS world. It lives up to its predecessor, despite the overwhelming criticism by butt-hurt Russians, who claim that Relic is full of a Nazi cast. Nonetheless, I will jump into the review by using Pros and Cons.
Pros
-Excellent graphics
-Great story telling in single player, shows the reality of the war
-The new commander feature is absolutley amazing. Each is unique and a player can find one that will fit their niche.
-Units are very detailed. Even explosions rip limbs apart.
-Things like Dynamite to blow up bridges, mine fields, and bunkers allow for excellent defenses if deployed correctly.
-The tanks are sexy to use. One may find themselves slightly aroused when using a Panther or a KV-2
-Winter attrition, mud and heavy snow create that "feel alive" atmosphere
-Terrains are detailed. Tanks run over trees, shells create craters in the ground that not only stay for the whole game duration, but your units can go in them for cover.
-Building munition or fuel caches on what would other wise be useless points. Allowing you to stockpile supplies and gain more income.
-Things like suppression allow you to halt an enemy advance, and pounce on them when they are overwhelmingly superior.
-Over all a great game.
Cons
-Want to buy some pretty OP commanders? Put in the extra dollars and get a Tiger Ace.
-DLC skins are pretty dumb.
-DLC faceplates.....really?
-The maps get boring after a while, and once you toggle them off, it takes a lot longer to find a game.
-More of a cinematic RTS experience than a realistic (don't let that discourage you)
Rating: 8.5/10
Conclusion:
One of the best RTS games out there. While it has adopted the DLC cash game, you can still be a very good player without the OP commanders. I highly recommend this game to any friend, and you will find yourself playing this for hours at a time.
