It's a really cool game, but I think the majority of people are playing it wrong, and that's why they don't like it. They play all Far Cry games breezing through the main-quest, taking minimal time to study stuff like syringes, collectibles, and understanding stealth. I'll elaborate at the bottom. You can play like that if you want, but Primal is a game that requires you to enjoy side-quests - for you to not play for the big scripted moments. I love this, however the reviewers and fan-base are a little sour that there is no driving down a mountain with an infinite ammo rocketlauncher. That and an unpleasant 60€ release. Far Cry Primal has no real big missions, and a lot of the experience (dare I say the whole experience) is you running around, hunting and taming animals, capturing camps, and completing the side-quests. Do the side-quests man! Some provide a decent challenge, and they show you chunks of the terrain that you wouldn't fully explore otherwise.
Ubisoft tends to have these 'in-betweener' games, where they reuse a lot of assets to make a game similar (in resources) to a previous game, and instead saving their budget for a bigger release, and don't get me wrong, this is definitely an in-betweener. But with what they had at their disposal; with their mind set on making an early-neolithic era game, I actually really like it.  And I know that in spite of the team probably feeling like this was their worst work yet, I know they learned a lot while making it, and Ubisoft is definitely in the lead if any dev-team would feel like making another stone-age game.
So, if you want the full Far Cry experience, make sure you take a look at the syringes (foods in this game). If you're tired of every tiger jumping you, make the animal repellent. If you're tired of reapplying it all the time, make it your default healing item - it isn't expensive. They are there to make up for the fact that the environment is otherwise pretty unforgiving.
Try to take all the camps silently, you get sometimes FOUR times exp bonus for not getting detected, and that really is a challenge sometimes. You have to distract enemies, utilize that your takedowns are (somehow) quiet, making sure you spot as many people are you can with the owl, and taking into account that there could be people in the houses and caves that your owl couldn't spot. Using your animal well, as it won't count as you being discovered, but the sight of the animal will cause the neanderthals to panic. Remembering that there are 'civilians' in each village (in the shape of washerwomen and slaves - sorry gals) who can spot you, but won't fight you. They also don't need to be killed for the camp to be captured. There's so much depth to taking a camp, and it's ALWAYS very possible with a lot of planning, with just about any amount of skillpoints.
Lastly, don't forget about collectibles. They are challenging to get to, and in turn give you experience. It's no secret that one of the most exciting aspects of Far Cry games are the skilltrees, acquiring the insane takedowns and buffs.
So while Far Cry may be kind of unappealing at first, there definitely is a fun and unique game. It just requires you to let go of that fear of side-quests you got from GTA and Witcher and the rest. Enjoy the beautiful scenery, and don't be a pessimist!
Also don't mind my low playtime, I refunded it on Steam and played it elsewhere. Wink.

Gone are the good storyline (although there are some fun bits in this one), suspense, atmosphere and detailed locations of the original, this is a shooting fest for few hours set in the same world, and expanding the lore/plot of the original.
The combat itself is fluid, they seemed to concentrate on that mostly, which is understandable, but still the levels feel very empty. I loved the game when I started playing it, but as stupid as this complaint sounds, the game needs a way better tutorial.
It is a well made game, visually looks wonderfull, solid mechanics, but the combat can get really repetative and just frustrating.
Save games
There should be no save game option in any game mode, but the easyest, as this just makes the game pointless, as soon as you lose somebody, you are going to load the game. That would have made the game more challenginig and fun, but also rage inducing, but in a more fair way.
Aiming
It works on a percentage based accurecy system, where the higher percentage gives you the higher chance of hitting a target and that is where most of my frustration comes from.
Even with a 95%, I had 3 people miss in a row and caused my entire team to die because of this.
Also, how far is close, medium or long range, iIm just guessing.
Enemy movement
Ground units, cool, they work normaly, but flying units, those are horrible. I get that they can move around in a space without issues, but being in a building and instantly be on the roof, ignoring walls and such... that is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. Obstructions
You have your high walls and low walls, simple and they protect you depending on there the enemy is fireing at you, sure.... but when you or the enemy just straight shoot through the walls, no... thats not how cover works.
Some times, the cover explodes, sometimes bullets ignore cover, most of the times, when you think you have a safe shot, you dont and it just breaks the logic of how things should work. Walls cant be trusted, especially when some walls explode and some dont.
If the tutorial was made to give more than a few examples on how players interract with the enviroment, so that I can learn the mechanics better, I would be happy and call my failures my fault, but when I legit dont understand how things work, I rather give up.

- They just recently announced a sequel, Lethal League Blaze, to come out in 2018. The game looks to be essentially an upgrade to this game, meaning if you might as well wait for the sequel to come out rather than spend money on this game.

Writing a review for the game is tricky because it does a lot of what made its predecessor interesting. The light based gameplay and weaponry is back, as is the meta-narrative and badass music when its time to kick♥♥♥♥♥
Still, it feels like its missing something. My best guess as to what is the enviroments that the previous game had. While the setting of the first game was a rural, heavily forrested mountain town, it provided a few interesting areas to explore. The sequel features three areas which are each revisited twice with minimal changes to their arrangement.
Another weak spot for me came from the story. The manuscript pages, which lended themselves to giving the player context regarding events outside of his awareness are a bit more limited this time. It focuses the story more but doesn't really deepen it. The story itself is okay, again, the meta-narrative component is worth talking about and expands on some ideas from the first game about fate and storytelling. The antagonist doesn't feel mysterious or dangerous to either the player or the character so it was a little difficult to feel a true sense of danger from him. On a related note, the game came off as much more actiony than the first. It didn't quite qualify as horror in the same way the first did. I felt very much in control throughout the game, almost never low on ammo or other resources.
Gameplay is still nice. Successfull dodges feel nice and the usage of flares and flashbangs as weapons for dealing damage remains a cool way of dealing with darkness based enemies. I was a little thrown by the various weapons you can acquire. The first game was reasonably limited to conventional weapons like a revolver and a hunting shotgun with a flare gun and flashbangs being the most outlandish items you acquired. In this game, military grade weaponry shows up very quickly. It felt a bit odd, hauling around an automatic shotgun or a crossbow. Enemies are a bit more diverse this time which is nice. The animated objects of the first game are present, but much less prevalent. Overall, individual enemies feel much more threatening and groups of enemies are much more effective at grouping around you.
If you enjoy the combat, the arcade mode seems like its worth checking out, especially if the 5 or so hours to complete the main story leave you wanting more.
All in all, while its not a bad game, I was left a little dissapointed. That said, at $10, its a reasonable price. Especially if you like the replayability of horde modes.

If you're diligent in what you choose to do in this game, pretty much everything can be used as a source of funds for gear or resources. Horse breeding, fishing, trading, gathering, alchemy, standard old grinding, everything can be used for profit if you keep going to a level where the output outweighs the input. Most of these are boring, yes, and usually the more boring it is, the more rewarding it is at the end (Trading being the prime example of this, being the highest profit of all of them.)

Use Contribution Points to connect nodes. Some of these nodes will have resource nodes on them. Hire workers at cities connected to these nodes, and have them work the resource nodes. You now have a steady stream of resources coming in. Sure, there are resources that you can only get from the market or gathering them yourself, but free stuff is always nice. You'll only ever have to pay these guys in beer (which you can make with the wheat, barley or corn they bring in massive piles of from nodes near Velia, Heidel or Calpheon). Later on, you can use these resources and workers in workshops to build things, just don't go building an Epheria Sailboat until you know what you're getting into.

Yes, the combat
is a pro, but the simplicity is a certain con. PvE kock-ups, stuns, knockback, etc. are only useful up until 56, when everything suddenly becomes immune to them, and PvP is a mess of "knockdown or stun an enemy so you can get behind them for bonus back-attack damage". There are no status effects like bleed, poison, freeze, blind, confuse, etc. only incapacitating or slowing your opponent and hoping they don't do it for you first. This is the same across all classes. The classes only dictate wether you want mobility or survivability, range or melee, magic or physical. There's no way to "outplay" your opponent, merely react the fastest and hope RNG is on your side (or hope they've only got the base resist against stuns, knockdown, etc). Certain classes are also useless. Don't let anyone tell you that every class has a use and are balanced. Sorc is terible and Striker is current flavour of the month. The only reason at high level they have a chance against each other is that the sorc has learned their class to a tee just to make it viable, and will play to their limit. The striker presses his buttons and attempts to grapple his enemy over and over until they're stunlocked to death or one of them dies IRL from old age because of how long it takes.

You're gonna want all of your gear you spent months getting up to "TRI" enhancement at least (Enhancement goes from +1 -> +15, then "PRI", "DUO", "TRI", "TET", "PEN" with more expensive enhancement). That sounds fine, until you realise that from DUO onwards, if you fail to enhance (which you'll fail a lot, even knowing how to failstack) it will return to the previous enhancement. They call it TET Roulette for a reason. Most people give up at TET because of how rediculous getting a PEN can be. Oh, and if that sounded bad enough, accessories (Rings, Earrings, Belts, Necklaces) follow the same enhancement rules except if you fail, the item is destroyed.

I've often wondered to myself why I even chopped all thsoe trees, mined all those rocks, killed the millions of mobs I did and even bothered showing up to world bosses. There will always be an event going on that has a chance to get boss gear and accessories. The past 4 events gave me gear every day that I'd been previously grinding for.

Previous KMMOs I've played at least felt like you could cheat a little by fighting above your level, or at least group up with friends and take down some harder enemies for better exp. This falls off completely in BDO because enemies here are designed to give you very little, because you'll be killing so many of them. Enemy drops are often generic, being a mob-type-specific trash item you collect 1,000 of to hand in to some npc for a gold bar or similar. Yes, they drop gear or enhancement items, but rarely, and you'll be needing to bank or vendor way before filling your inventory because of how the weight system works.

Everything in this game is designed to frustrate you until you pay cash to relieve some pain. Increase weight capacity, inventory space, pets for auto-looting, outfits for marginal boosts to combat exp or costumes for afk stuff (Fishing outfit, Maid outfit for processing, Chef outfit for cooking, all of which will only knock a few seconds off or give a little success chance). Remember how enchanting is a ♥♥♥♥♥? Well, failing enhancement reduces max durability on items, which si repaired with another of the same item or memory fragments. This is expensive lategame, so you can use Artisan's Memory (for 400 Lotalty points each, which is 4 days of logging in, OR, buy 1/10/100 for up to $40). None of this is cheap. Pets to auto-loot are at least $10 each. Costumes can be up to $60. All optional.
The Value Packs, however, are basically not optional. People will argue it's the same as a sub to WoW or etc, as for ~$15 you get a pack that lasts a whole month. This makes it so that the 40% tax on everything you sell on the marketplace comes down to about 20% (no, I'm not joking), extra 10% EXP in everything but Combat, extra inventory and storage space, extra weight limit, and unlimited gear dyte/character customising. Oh, and with a value pack active, you can manage your node connections without moving an inch, as you can spend energy to connect to them, managing your worker empire as you afk a skill. You could say it's not optional, but they give you 3 of them in your first month just to see how "value" they really are - and how essential they are for wanting to get anywhere.

Boxes, chests, packs, night vendors, drop tables - you'll always be playing against that 0.001% chance to get something of worth. Work your♥♥♥♥♥off for 2 hours to get a chest with a chance at a Dandelion awakening weapon, but you're probably getting a cheap enhancement item instead.
Even on the marketplace, when something is posted, it has a 50% chance to go either to bid or pre-order (Pre-order is an actual bid system - whoever bids highest wins). Bid system is basically "everyone clicks 'bid' and someone is chosen to be able to buy the item". If they don't, it goes up so anyone can buy it, so long as it's the cheapest one posted.

As soon as you invest money into it, you're ♥♥♥♥ing done. It has its claws in you, and you'll play it simply because you've sunk funds into it. Don't buy it, don't gift it to people, don't recommend it. Go play GW2, or something. The combat and graphics aren't worth putting yourself through hell for.

There are a lot of frivolous "football" games out there, but as something of a football afficionado myself (or "soccer", as it's called by those in the know), I was very pleased to hear that a serious developer was finally willing to put in the work and create a proper football game.
Most football games use a vocabulary that's "dumbed down" to cater to people who are more familiar with simple sports like cricket or rugby, but Behold the Kickmen isn't afraid to use the correct terminology while you're doing goals – including the fabled three-pointers – out there in the arena.
The same dedication to proper football rules can be found in the use of red cards, and I have to say that the treatment of the offside rule in this game is the most faithful and true-to-life that I've ever seen in a computer game.
My only complaint is that the enemy soldiers sometimes go a bit crazy and start passing the ball at lightning speed and in seemingly random directions, occasionally leading to them doing an own 3 goals. However, I'm prepared to let this one go through to the goldkeeper because I've often seen real footballers play like this when I watch them on the telly.
This game is great fun and absolutely hilarious. I'm so glad to finally be out there trading goals with my heroes in the Brazil United Football Club.
Congratulations, Dan Marshall, you've done a good football game!

Saw all the negative reviews and thought, "Oh, it can't be
bad. People are probably just being harsh because it's an RPGMaker game."
Got the game in a bundle.
Started it up.
First room, immediately climbed up the wall.
-_-
Short version: it is that bad. Like, if other bad RPGMaker games are
bad,
is
bad.
There's no intro or tutorial or anything, the game just starts with you standing in a room. I know what the default RPGMaker controls are, so I'm not going to complain about that. I will complain about not being able to interact with anything in the room. Trying to talk to your father does nothing. You have to try to leave the house for his scripted dialogue to pop up. (And of course all the dialogue in the game is full of typos and poor comprehension of how English works.)
Oh, and you can walk up the walls. This isn't a one-off thing; it happens in every room and dungeon. Consider it a feature, I guess. The prophecy foretold of the one with magic wall-walking powers. It makes as much sense as your random ability to turn into a rock later on.
Second town map, "The door is locked," you're told upon trying to enter a house that has no door. And you pick vegetables by walking over them and pressing Z, and why did I even bother because it's just some random filler side quest?
Then I realized the main quest and story has about as much depth. Like, you're the chosen one of prophecy (the game helpfully informs you in a brief text scroll) because you're a fighter traveling with a mage, which has somehow never happened before in RPG Cliche Land. And... that's it.
The maps are all poorly designed, particularly the stores and houses, which are big, awkward empty spaces apparently designed by someone who's never seen the inside of a building. The best/worst is one store that's literally just a full screen of empty wooden floor and a counter, with a bed in the top corner. When the storekeeper goes to give your Healing Macguffin to the girl in bed, he's so far up the screen that his head is cut off.
Oh, and the bed with the girl just disappears. "Oh, who cares," I thought at this point. "At least I can just continue with the game." Except the quest reward was only one half of what you need to continue -- apparently you can't open the plot door with your locksmith tools unless you have a pouch to put them in. (And you can't walk around the door, either, even though it's just a regular house-sized door lying in the middle of an open gate that's three spaces wide.)
So I wandered around trying to find a locksmith tools pouch and got attacked by eye beasts. One at a time, because I guess programming more than one enemy sprite on the battle screen was too difficult?
And why eye beasts? If you're going to face hordes of enemies that have no special abilities, do negligible damage, and go down in like three hits, why something that looks so alien and dangerous? (Why am I trying to apply logic to
?)
If you get past those, you have to guess your way past a riddle, go into a labyrinth (which is actually just a room) and rescue a "Preist," who gives you the locksmith tools pouch, and blah blah blah, you get on a ship, you have to catch stowaways from the Clan of Stowaways, who show up and join your party before you actually receive the quest to find them. I was going to say at least the game doesn't bug out completely, but then I was told to take off my stowaway disguise that I had to put on to infiltrate the secret stowaway meeting, and the game just froze, and this is the point where I just give up and idle the game for cards.
The fact that someone looked at
and thought, "Yes, I deserve money for my efforts," is ludicrous. Either they're straight up delusional, or they're just taking the p*ss.

And the series end with this
only a story.
Thank you Marc Laidlaw for giving this community a closure.

Raywin is a 2D JRPG made on RPG Maker. Just as the name of the game suggests, the story is focused on the hero Raywin who according to a prophecy must defeat Salemsun. The game is just bad, even if it is the first game that the developers made.
Heck, one of the game's selling points is having "★ Over 40 items" which isn't even that much compared to other RPG Maker games or RPGs in general. Blantly, the game is incredibly short and overall not a fun experience.
Now for the headaches, where do I start with the flaws of this game.... First of all the game has tons of noclip/wall glitches, the first one being on the first room, yes, you read right, the first room. I know it’s the first game they "attempted" to make and they used floor tiles to give the walls effect but still they should have play tested it before release. One bug that I encountered is that you need to press space to enter the museum.
Uh.... the quests which maybe the worst part about the game. The quests involve you going to some place maybe two to four screens away to rescue a random person or get an item for someone and maybe fighting a monster along the way. These quests just serve as a device to move the game foward with no coherence at all.
Graphics wise the game is mediocre at best, the sprites are basic and what you would expect from an RPG Maker game, nothing special but dear god.... the dialogue character portraits and overworld monster sprites look horrendous. If a game has its entire overworld pixelated then keep the graphics the same. There isn't a need for 3D CGI images, though this is entirely my opinion or maybe you are one specimen that enjoys this no effort CGI along with the ranks of "A Car's Life".
This game like any other standard RPG Maker game or RPGs in general has item drops after battles but the item descriptions and the mundane items themselves are awful. To expand upon this - Here is a scenario : Oh great! a monster dropped an orange (real creativity there, potions didn't cut the mark? Better use a tomato next time! Remember to eat healthy kids and you need not a complete stranger to tell you that) maybe I could use it to heal one of my characters. Oh! But wait! It doesn't tell you how much it will heal, same goes with the monsters whose health you cannot see so you don't know when to heal or attack. However, you won't ever need to strategize because every encounter is a cakewalk.
Moreover, I had to fight like what? 8 monsters, including the bosses might I add, throughout the entire game! (Monsters not encounters). On a sidenote the game is barren with bland surroundings followed by a couple of NPCs as an attempt to breathe life into an already dead game.
Before I end the review I would like to mention that the story is generic even for RPG Maker games, following the same old trope of the chosen one story which has been outdated since the dawn of the fourth generation of gaming consoles.
This game though being the developers first try to make an actual game is just an unfinished, sloppy RPG Maker test project which they tried to pass of as a complete game. The only good thing about this game is that you can get an extra perfect game to add to your collection because all the achievements in this game can be earned throughout the game which is about 1 hour long at most.
Without any innovative mechanics or a fresh story, Raywin fails to separate itself from the generic RPG Maker games. It is not at all worth the buy.

This is a game that does everything right gameplaywise in the sense that your mistakes are (usually) the only reason you lost health/died, your choices are the only things getting you into sticky situations, and your knowledge and skill at and of the game is the only determining factor in how far you get. You're going to die quickly your first few times, and that's okay. This game is what many NES games were/should have been in the sense that it's not made to be beaten in a day, the same reason Castlevania is such a great game. You have to play it, fail, find out what you did wrong and learn from it, and you'll find yourself improving with every run. This never gets repetitive, as every run is different, with millions upon millions of different sets of events you could find your party going through, and more wagons being unlocked. Which wagon you choose out of your arsenal is up to you, you may choose a faster wagon to dodge projectiles, you may choose a wagon with a better weapon to fight off more enemies, or you may just go with the standard wagon because it's what works best for you. This is a game that lets you play it your way, choosing the path your party takes as you travel through a noticeably stranger 1830-1870's America, bobbing your head to the beat of the excellent soundtrack and giving a satisfied sigh at the NES-era graphics through this game, a game that gets my 10 out of 10.

The best local co-op game of the year! The concept is simple: grab ingredients, cook them up, put them on a plate, and send the dish out the door. But the challenge is is the curve balls that the levels throw at you! You might be in a kitchen that is broken in half by an earthquake. You might be on in a kitchen that split between multiple moving trucks. You may go into a level having a game plan; maybe you and your 3 friends each assign a role to yourselves, like dishwashing, or chopping. But those plans will likely get quickly dashed as the levels get more complex. And that's where the game really shines! It’s just hard enough where you’ll likely fail the first time you play some of the more complex levels, but just approachable enough that you’ll be able to figure out the correct “rhythm” to take when you play the level a 2nd time. Beyond all of that, the art and style are unique and fun, and the story is silly and absurd. Go grab 3 friends and play it now!

Overcooked is, quite honestly, one of the most fun games we’ve played in a long time. I’ve sat alongside the wife spending many an hour dashing around Overcooked‘s kitchens, giggling and yelling at each other in our remarkably bad attempts at conquering the game’s crazy environments. We were bombarded by food orders, kept falling off maps, and failed often — and we loved it.
Sitting down with a friends to play Overcooked is a blast. It nails the fine line between difficulty and derpiness in such a way that you can’t help but play just a few more levels. The simple controls and concept make it easy for anyone to grab a controller and jump into the action, and the more challenging levels will keep aficionados coming back to get those three-star ratings.
If you have a friend or three coming over, this is an amazing way to spend an evening. Overcooked is one of the most fun titles we've played in months, and one we revisit often. Try it for yourself.

It was not his face - as red as it was - or his ginger hair, that separated him from his fellow recruits. It was not his absurdly large arms or his fondness to guns bigger than himself. It was not his courage to always strike first when the battle was hardest. It was the simple fact, that unlike any other recruit of his whole class -
Atleast for a while.
He began his journey as any other new rookie in the XCOM initiative. Fresh out of barracks and prepared to die. Of course, for Machete it was his duty. He never questioned why. Just like no recruit should.
It was on his third mission - as a freshly forged corporal - when his squad got flanked by an alien ambush. Against all odds the squad managed to outflank the aliens. Despite taking heavy casualties the remaining members of the squad managed to neutralize the threat - and once again - save the World. This was the time the XCOM commander figured Machete might be more than just another ginger without a soul. He might be the one.
Operations went and passed and Machete ranked more kills than any other member of XCOM. He started to gain reputation amongst the scientists and the engineers, yet not so much amongst the new recruits. For he was known to be often the sole survivor of daring missions. But Machete didn't care about peoples opinions. He had once had a friend, but just like everyone else, he died when the aliens attacked. That was when Machete decided to never get fond of anyone again. It would be easier that way.
Then finally came the day when XCOM decided it was time to assault the alien base. It was no guess who would lead the charge. For them - he was the chosen one.
Amongst the people of the World he was known simply as "Cowboy" - mainly due his tendency to handle everything himself. It was only reasonable to name him as the Colonel of the XCOM and  lead the charge to the alien base. Together with the commander they chose the best squad XCOM had ever seen. Sergeant Richard "Freedom" Mason, the close-combat master, Corporal Omar "Yo" Watermelon, known for his preferance of rocket launchers, Squaddie Eddie "Nuggett" Teddie, supporter in charge of medikits, Squaddie Selina "Mad Dog" Kyle, the sniper and a new hot-shot rookie Donald Trump. And of course - the leader of the company - Colonel Cowboy.
"The attack of the heroes" - as the historians later called it - was not a complete success after all. The squad got flanked, cornered and outnumbered by the aliens. It was up to Colonel Machete Moleman - once again - to save the day. He shot bullets, threw grenades and blew lasers. Eventually it was just him against the alien leader. He had outmaneuvered and cornered him. The alien had to reload his weapon. That's when Machete stepped up behind the desk he had used for cover and walked in front of the alien. The sad little creature seemed pathetic for him. Yet he felt no sympathy as he pulled the trigger. He knew he would hit him. He would hit from this distance 99% of times. He had tested it many times at the practice range.
But it had to be this time. Machete Molemans plasma-gun had missed the target. With a shock of disbelief he looked at the alien. The alien pulled up his gun and pointed it towards him. The time seemed to slow down and the moment last for a thousand lifetimes. Last thing Machete "Cowboy" Moleman saw in his life was the aliens smug grin and a flash of bright light as the gun blazed.

Let me start off by saying that this game is incredibly subjective. You can just read the other reviews to see how many people hate this game and declaim it as the "definition of wasted potential" while others have 2000 hours on it and tell you all about how immersive and expansive the game experience can be. This is an extremely polarizing game for several reasons, most of which I'll be describing below.
The first polarizing aspect is how unique BDO is overall--this can be a good thing or a bad thing. Whereas most of the MMOs you encounter have raids, dungeons, etc. this game eschews all that in favour of massive PvP and intense grinding in certain locations. This grinding mentality and divergence from the typical "theme park" style of MMO with vertical progress and dungeons/raids means the game is extremely polarizing. Some people, like myself, love this enormous aspect of the game. Others find it overwhelming and others find it rather bland as they don't feel like they're ever really making progress. It all comes back to what you enjoy doing in an MMO. If you hate grinding and difficult progress in MMOs, you will hate BDO. If you enjoy the feeling of working hard at something to eventually overcome the odds and accomplish something that was very difficult to accomplish, then you'll probably love BDO.
The second aspect is the cash shop. Yes, this game has microtransactions. I could offer a million arguments as to why this game isn't pay-to-win and others will give you the same amount as to why it is pay-to-win. At the end of the day, I think that's fairly subjective. There are clear advantages to using the cash shop, i.e. pets that pick up loot for you and outfits that slightly increase your exp gain, but you can't get any game-breaking items like super powerful equipment, easy enhancements or amazing mounts that you would have to grind eternally to get in-game. That being said, many people consider this to be pay-to-win anyway. Despite thinking that this mostly seems to be a knee-jerk reaction to other games that certainly ARE pay-to-win (Blade and Soul, Heroes and Generals, Dragon's Nest, the list goes on) I definitely see where they're coming from, and although I disagree I do think that many people will take it that way and it has driven people away from the game. It's ultimately up to you how you choose to see this.
The third thing about this game is that it's very PvP oriented. No dungeons (although those are being implemented slowly), no raids, none of that. The PvE in this game is mostly focused on helping you get enough money and experience to gear up (which in itself is very long, difficult, and oftentimes infuriating, but I'll get to that later) so that you can eventually join a guild and participate in large-scale PvP like Node Wars and Sieges. These are incredibly fun and unique as you fight other guilds for control of the map for various morale and monetary bonuses, and the scale of these battles is exciting and always fresh. That being said, working up to this point takes a long, long time, and for many people this is just not worth their time. And that's ok! BDO is a time sink, and although this is true for pretty much any MMO, this is particularly true for BDO.
Now for the points most people generally tend to appreciate about the game:
1) Worker system; this is essentially a form of Diet Slavery where you pay goblins, giants, and humans in beer to gather resources for you around the map. Once you get this really well established, you can make some serious bank. As far as I know, it's something completely unique to BDO.
2) Guilds; this game is heavily community-oriented and joining a guild has a bunch of benefits from a daily payout (yes, you get paid for being in a guild) to various buffs that the guild gives its members as it becomes stronger. It's the sort of bond-forming guild system that I haven't seen since WoW.
3) Crafting; this game has an in-depth and rewarding crafting system that pays off really well. Whereas in many MMOs crafting feels relatively useless, in BDO it's something that is worthwhile to invest your time into as the goods you can produce over time can rake you in lots of money. Starting off from brewing simple alchemical reagents and ramping up to making Alchemical Stones is incredibly satisfying and makes you some phat stacks in the long run.
4) ENORMOUS GAME. This game has so much content and after almost 1000 hours of gameplay I have not yet reached the maximum potential of my main character and I have not yet explored the entire map, completed every quest, or gained even half the available knowledge in this game. It's wild, the map is enormous, and overall you never feel like there's nothing to do. There's always more money to be made, always more xp to be earned, and always a new place to explore, and this will only keep going as the game is updated and more content is added.
Now for the negative points (and lemme tell ya these are some really negative points lol):
1) The playerbase; probably the most immature playerbase I've come across in an MMO. It obviously isn't 100% bad, but many of the top guilds and high-level PvPers are essentialy keyboard warriors who will grief you for looking at them wrong. It's upsetting and just generally silly to see how they lord their in-game power over others and how seriously they take a Korean video game.
2) Enhancement. Holy♥♥♥♥♥♥the enhancement system. It's constant gambling with the durability of your equipment (and at higher levels even its enhancement level) and your money as you invest millions of silvers into black stones to get very little out of it as the enhancement system is entirely RNG based. Getting yourself to a maximum level of enhancement on your gear is essentially a question of pure luck and you can either spend very little on a piece of equipment or a mind-numbing amount, and this is completely random. It sends much of your hard work to waste. Fortunately, you can buy pre-enhanced equipment on the marketplace, but these don't come buy often and they cost a LOT of silvers.
3) RNG; kinda running off what I said in the last point, many aspects of this game rely entirely on RNG. The bargaining minigame lets you earn more money for trade goods (essentially special items that you can transport to various parts of the map and make phat stacks off of trading with specific NPCs) but the success or failure of your bargaining is entirely based on RNG. As far as I know, your Trading skill does not affect its success, and neither does you level of amity (friendship, essentially) with the NPC (although it does increase the amount of times you can attempt to bargain). There is also, of course, the aspect that enhancing your gear is based entirely on RNG. Success or failure and whether or not your money goes to waste is based on pure luck.
Overall, this is certainly a niche game. Many people hate this game, and many people love it intensely (as I do). The complaints against this game are valid, as are its praises. It's not perfect, but it's good for me and for many, many other players, and personally it's one of my favourite games of all time and right up there with Runescape as for my favourite MMOs.
I can't give this game any real x/10 score because it's ultimately what you make of it. You get out of this game what you put into it, and it's neither an inherently good or bad game. It's a niche game, and therefore it appeals highly to a certain playerbase and pushes away others. If you don't like this game, that's ok! And if you love it as much as I do, I hope to see you in-game and

TLDR: Boring AF.  Immediatley dated.
(-) GD is a tiny setting.  Evil has invaded the world, supposedly, but your adventure spans a few villages on the banks of a river, their surrounding hillsides, local crypts, what have you.  It's impossible to care.  The singular reason one requires hours for travel, a portal system, or even a map is:
(-) the crappy level design.  Every zone, regardless of tile, shares the same series of corridors, switchbacks, and dead ends.  As a veteran of countless skirmishes, why do I have to run endlessly between the hedgerows where children clamber when the undead aren't about?  Why can my enormous warhammer, custom grenade, or fireball not take down this wooden door?  Every game manages the same thematic challenges but its's been a long time since I've seen such a poor solution.  Impassable fences or closed doors are best placed at zone boundaries implying the edge of giving a damn.  In GD, a hedgerow is the obstacle between yourself and glorious battle yet you have to find a way around.
(-) Hence, there's no action.  The hero spends far more time running between narrow terrain features than actually fighting.  When a wide space does occassionally open up, there's maybe one or two monster groups inside.  There's no way to pull a truly satisfying mob behind you upon which to unleash your skills.
(-) Did I say skills?  I meant skill.  One.  At level five, I started focusing skill points into smashwave or something, tied it to my left mouse button, and haven't needed anything else for thirty more levels.  It's not even a top skill.  There are no builds in the current GD forum compendium using it.  It probably could be any skill.  Focus on any attack tree, add defense passives, and you're set.
(-) There are plenty of class combinations but every build is the exact same.  There's a left mouse skill, right mouse skill, something on 1, and your potions.  Buffs don't matter.  Debuffs don't matter.  Teleports, counters, interupts, snares, none of them matter.
(+) I'm just going to stop.  What a letdown.
Come to think of it, every (-) I listed is something Torchlight 2 did better.  Damn, that game was ahead of its time; someone please refresh TL2!  Grim Dawn is the Titan Quest rehash we didn't need.

I'm probably one of the first to finish the game. It took me a while longer than it should have because I had to contact the dev to figure out a bug. A regular play through would probably take 45 minutes at the most. First things first, the dev is very helpful and great. Unfortunately the game has a ways to go before it's worth buying.
There are some glaring problems, and I'll try to make this review as constructive as possible so hopefully Raywin 2 addresses these problems.
1. There is no tutorial to learn the controls. They are easy enough but you first need to try all your keys to see if they do anything.
2. Items don't tell you what they do. You have a healing potion? Great! But it doesn't tell you how much it will heal you. Vegatables? Fun! What are they even used for? I didn't use an item throughout the entire game.
3. You can't see the HP of the enemy. How am I supposed to know when to heal/attack? So far I just attack and eventually win, and have some NPC heal me. Not much strategy.
4. Wall/noclip glitches everywhere. Doesn't feel like a complete game. Not to mention, 95% of every shop screen is empty space. There is no decoration, and on the off-chance there is decoration, half the time you can walk right through it.
5. Can't go back to places already visited. Found that out too late, so I think I missed some content.
6. The "quests" are as simple as "walk 5 spaces and click 'space' 8 times then come back". Another quest you literally turn into a rock, for no good reason, to sneak by some guards. That's the only time you turn into a rock in the whole game. I would understand if it the game was introducing a new mechanic, but it's not. I just don't get it.
One nice part about the game is the leveling system. It seems really cool, but since you only defeat maybe 5 enemies (you can avoid the rest without problem) you don't really get to try it out. At the end, each of my characters levelled one.. to level 2. I feel like this would have been a fun part of the game, I just wish I was able to take advantage of it!
Overall, not a very gripping game. Needs a lot of work fixing some bugs. I don't recommend it in its current state.
**To get into the museum, you need to press space to enter. This is a confirmed bug so may not be relevant if the dev fixes the bug before you read this review.

An overall qualifier for this recommendation: Squad and base-building games are something I adore, and this rather skews my predisposition to XCOM towards the positive.
That said, it's one of the finest examples of these genres and turn-based combat and tactics games in general that's out there, in my opinion.  Your squad is deep and varied, tech and research provides gear that changes up your options and approaches, and the presentation and story are done in a compelling and involving way; it's not hard for me to develop attachments to my individual soldiers, especially with campaign options that allow each to have a unique skill tree.
All of the things I like about this game are further enhanced by the Long War mod for it-- more equipment, more challenge, more character builds with more compelling and balanced options, and more varied technology to uncover.  If you're a fan of base building strategy and turn-based tactics, this one deserves a look-- buy it with Enemy Within, its fully featured expansion pack that greatly improves the campaign experience and lets you train psychic humans using alien tech, among other things.  Defend Earth.  Purge xenos.  Good times.

Behold the Kickmen is a magic thing that succeeds brilliantly at something it doesn't even seem to care about. It sets its stage as a silly parody of football and football games, and acts on it with such an effortless swag that you won't question the rules of this little universe for a second. But the real magic is inside: the actual football game is a blast.
It has all the rules hilariously wrong, yes. The goldkeepers. The 2-goals and 3-goals shots. The oval field, and of course the offside. But at its heart, this plays like a honest-to-god descendant of Sensible Soccer and Speedball. The gameplay is straightforward, fast and addictive. The tackling implementation is wonderful. There's an actual learning curve behind the jokes, and it's handled with sweet delicacy.
Overall, Behold the Kickmen brings fun, simplicity, and unabashed silliness to the super-serious football game world, and it was about time someone did. Don't miss out.
And please, please, go for stamina. You'll thank me later.

Me and my friend both feel like we've hit a "wall" in the game. Had a blast starting out, learning combos, messing with AFK fishers (you can literally shanghai them)--building a boat was particularly rewarding and fun. Like everything else, trading and building a wagon was fun at first, but you eventually hit that wall where there's no advancement but doing the same things over and over and over. And not in a fun way: just hit auto travel and tab into your browser to ignore the grind or leave your PC on overnight. I didn't bother with combat grind after awakening because it only takes ~30 mins of spamming the same combos on mobs to make your brain go numb (and 30 mins is literally no advancement at all; expect to spend 2 or more hours on the same mob, even longer at higher levels, which eventually turns into days spent on the same mobs).
On the aspect of nodes and worker empires, they are fun features as they give you something to manage to break up the monotony. Once again though, you are going to have to grind your workers up to artisan level for them to be useful. And guess what? It takes 24 hours to complete the promotion test! And they can fail their worker promotion test! And not only that, but you have to level that worker 10 more levels to try again... And only one worker can test at a time... And you'll have 10-20 workers... Heh.
If you want to play BDO, be prepared to make it a second job. I've tried toning down my hours per day playing to become more casual toward the game, but it just deosn't work. You'll end the day's playtime feeling like nothing was completed or advanced.
All this considered, the game is relatively cheap, so if you want to spend ~200 hours advancing to the wall I mentioned, you'll have a good time. Just don't expect it to last.

Despite some issues with the matter of whether or not choices matter, Telltale's take on the Game of Thrones universe proves to be the first game to tackle it well enough, having just the right amount of politics, violence, and story development. My biggest complaints are on the technical side of things.
Lets start with the story, though. I came to really like the story. I think the Forrester family and household would fit nicely in the books or the show, albeit they'd be much more of a background subject. Just like most things in Westeros, their story is quite tragic. The game starts with the Lord of the House, Gregor, being murdered during the Red Wedding. But you're playing the squire, Gared. Gared's story is sad because of how vindicated he becomes and how everyone tries to put him down. Ultimately, though, I think he'll have a huge impact in Season 2. There are several other Forrester's you get to play as, but, ultimately, the story is about their downfall as they keep their integrity. The Whitehills don't like them and they feel like they can do as they please. The only character whose story I would consider a comeback is Asher, as he works to travel back to Westeros from Essos. WARNING: While I recommend this game to fans of A Song of Fire and Ice (a.k.a Game of Thrones), I feel like you should still read this warning before buying!
The game offers an interesting side story that expands and explores the lore of Westeros, which is welcomed.  It does a decent job of capturing the feeling of the GoT universe as well. However, your decisions in this game DO NOT matter as they have ZERO influence on the outcome of the story. - The characters in this game that appear on the show are voiced by the actual actors/actresses on the show. For example, Lena Headey voices Cersei Lannister in this game. Others include: Iwan Rheon as Ramsay Bolton, Kit Harrington as Jon Snow, Emilia Clarke as Daenerys Targaryen, Peter Dinklage as Tyrion Lannister, and Natalie Dormer as Margaery Tyrell. This nice touch plays as a positive for immersion but also the frustration of lack of real decisions. You obviously cannot kill Ramsay or betray Tyrion as this would change their respective plotlines. This game is technically lore-friendly and can be considered canon.
- This Telltale game seems to have more graphical bugs and slightlly longer load times than other Telltale games, however outside of this performance the rest of the game is fine for the most part.
- There are 6 episodes rather than the usual 5 episodes in this season and you play as multiple protagonists rather than the usual solo hero.

Quick Summary: An interactive movie full of quick time events, including the dialogue options. You only have about 5 seconds to choose what you want to say, or the conversation will continue without your input. Don’t worry too much about making the wrong decisions though, since the story is going to march on one way or another. You only “lose” if you fail a quick time event during battle scenarios (for example, press down to dodge or you get chopped in the head). This is Game of Thrones after all, people are dying left and right.
*Spoilers ahead*
The game’s story starts just before the Red Wedding, and continues on through several seasons’ worth of the HBO television series, but following a different set of characters. I’ve never read the books but the story fits right alongside the television show, including the having some of the show’s actors voice their characters in the game and even using the TV show’s title sequence for each game episode. While you “control” a number of different characters throughout the game’s six episodes (each episode is about 2 hours), most of the time you will be playing members of House Forrester, who were banner men (sworn allegiance) to the Stark family. After the events of the Red Wedding, the Stark house is basically destroyed, and as a result things aren’t looking very good for House Forrester. There are Forrester family members in various places around the world though, working together to save your house. The game’s story is not complete, by the way. There’s probably another “season” coming up some time in the future, kind of like the Walking Dead.
As I mentioned before, the game is sort of a movie for about 2/3 of the time. At key points in conversation you will be given options on how to speak or act. It’s similar to the Mass Effect conversation system, except that in this game you only have a short window of time to choose your answers, and some “key” decisions can vastly affect the future. There’s no “good” or “evil” though, the consequences are generally in how your companions view you. In the game’s combat sequences, you need to navigate simple quick time events to avoid dying since some of the characters you control aren’t really fighters for the most part. At the end of each game episode, a list of the major decisions is displayed for you, letting you know how your choices compared to other players in the world. For example “You and 90% of other players chose to kill this dude.” If you’re like me you’ll probably end up allying yourself with characters you know from the TV show to be “good guys,” but just remember that even good guys lose once in a while, and if you’re allied too closely with them, they can drag you down.
Pros:
+Interesting and compelling story. Even if you read the books or watch the television series, you won’t know what’s in store for the Forresters since they’re just a minor house. No plot armor for you.
+The game is pretty easy, so you’re just playing for the plot and to slap the sass out of some ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ characters.
Cons:
-The game’s graphics are a bit of a disappointment the first time you run the game, looking like a lot of the art is painted or “water colored” even at 1920x1080. You’re not playing a game like this for the graphics though, and you’ll get used to it pretty fast.
-Unskippable cutscenes, including the long title sequences. The game uses an auto save system and usually saves between “scenes” so if you have to quit fast for whatever reason, you may have to sit through 5-10 minutes of talking to get back to where you were.
-This is a minor gripe, but in the very beginning of the game, you can use the mouse for quick time events, and then suddenly in the first action sequence only the keyboard works. The problem is they don’t give a warning, and I was pin cushioned by crossbows half a dozen times before I realized I was supposed to be pressing a key rather than swiping with the mouse.
Overall, Game of Thrones is a pretty good game, and worth your time to play. I tried to set up a Telltale account but wasn’t able to get it working properly (verification emails took about an hour to come and then the account activation code didn’t work). It’s not like Uplay though, so not having a functioning Telltale account did not hinder the experience.  Also, the only other Telltale game I’ve played is The Walking Dead, which had more “puzzle solving” to do. In Game of Thrones you do a lot less searching for clues or wondering what you’re supposed to do next.

Auralux: Constellations is for those of us that love RTS on a pure level. Its simplistic design can be found in all facets of the game. Graphics are beautiful, controls are easy to learn but tough to master in the more difficult scenarios and the whole experience is rounded off with a beautiful sound scenery. I have always been a fan of simplistic games as they are the hardest to master (if done right) but this one easily makes a top 3 entry together with Eufloria and Osmos.
The game challenges your overview and spacial awareness at its finest! The gameplay in a nutshell? You start with a planet that produces a certain amount of drones per second and your goal is to eradicate all other factions. Some planets you can upgrade to produce more. Sometimes you will be facing just one enemy and in other sceneries you got multiple of them coming at you and each other. All constellations (featuring multiple planet-milestones one needs to master) give the player a fresh challenge every single time and with challenge I mean challenge! Each constellation also has a specific theme. I just got through one with minefields that help defend planets but also make it hard to attack them and now I am dealing with slowly advancing shockwaves...the surprises never end and I mean that in a very positive way. In some levels you have to think out of the box or you won't manage to beat the AI which is very well done!
Some scenarios are about speed, sometimes you have to be patient, in others you need to evade or trick your enemies into fighting each other until you are strong enough to beat them all and more...
On top of that you have multiplayer!! A dream come true for those of us who made it through the single player experience or those who are more competitive in general.
If you want an easy to learn but challenging game that will keep you busy for many, many hours then this is cash well spent!
To the Devs: Well done folks, well done! I am having a blast!

I was hoping for more of Alan Wake's suspensful atmosphere. I didn't get that, but in retrospect I am glad that was the case.
This is undoubtedly an Alan Wake game. There is a well written story, interesting characters and more of the panic-inducing combat;  but there far less suspense, mystery and horror than before. As a result, American Nightmare feels much more like an action game.
The big win vs. its predecessor is sharper combat mechanics: encounters are less chancy, less clunky and more satisfying. There are a few different enemies which make life more interesting too. Battles are more fun in American Nightmare.
The story is pretty good too. It's shorter than the first game, and unfolds well, but personally I didn't enjoy it quite as much this time around. Mr Scratch is a cool bad guy, and given quite a bit of airtime via the TV broadcasts. Quite fun to watch, although some could drag on a little.
Graphics are better technically but, in terms of overall art design, not as good as the first game. The cinematics now feature live action rather than rendered cut scenes for characters, which is a bit hit and miss in terms of quality. This is also buggier than the first game (which was a very solid port), but is better optimised in terms of graphics performance.
It's a good game. Not as enjoyable as it's predecessor, but worth trying if you want to reenter the great game universe Remedy have created.

If you liked the story of the first, I wouldn't get my hopes up. This is truly an arcade expansion, there's very little story but more things you have to do to give you some fun gameplay moments. There are only three small maps that are reused three times, but given the pricing of this game it's somewhat excusable.
The game also adds a fun horde/zombies type mode. I really enjoyed the gameplay during the story so I went to try the survival mode, but it's not as engaging as I anticipated it to be, which makes me believe the fun gameplay is reliant more on the level design than the actual combat.
All in all, if you liked the first game I'd pick this up. It's not a full sequel, but it's a fun little 4-5 experience with fun combat and a servicable story.

Alan Wake's American Nightmare features the titular protagonist whisked away from the original Alan Wake's setting of the American northwest to Arizona. As Alan, you fight off dark enemies using flashlight and guns.
Whereas the original game had a mysterious and original main storyline, this game's story is convoluted and short. There is a lot of combat which features  new enemies, but it lacks the atmosphere and scares of the original.
There are three different areas which you end up exploring three different times. It is repetitive. I did not bother with the arcade feature, but if your complaint with the original game is that you didn't get enough flash light and guns, you can go nuts.
If you can get this very discounted and are a huge fan of the original, I would recommend it. Otherwise, I think it is a pass.

Anche se le due storie non sono collegate consiglio a tutti di giocare il titolo originale e poi di buttarsi su American Nightmare :)
Noi vestiremo i panni del famoso scrittore Alan Wake che dovrà affrontare e distruggere la sua altra personalità. In poche parole ci sarà un altro Wake però malvagio che farà di tutto per impedirci di ucciderlo e così ci lancerà contro orde di nemici che cercheranno di farci fuori. Mi sono divertito molto a giocarlo e l'ho finito circa in un giorno. Anche questo è a tratti monotono e ripetitivo come il primo ma forse scorre meglio visto la breve durata.
La grafica mi piace molto e mi sembra un pochino migliorata rispetto all'originale ma questo forse è solo una mia impressione.
Le ambientazioni mi sono piaciute moltissimo. Adoro queste tipo di location in mezzo al deserto, dentro e nei dintorni di un motel, dentro e fuori un osservatorio astronomico che si trova su una montagna che si affaccia sul deserto. Secondo me la cosa che aiuta a migliorare ulteriormente l'atmosfera è sicuramente che il gioco è interamente ambientato di notte.
Durante il gioco troveremo una torcia, una carabina, un fucile a pompa, una revolver e una mitraglietta. Poi troveremo bengala e granate accecanti. Se non vado errato queste sono le armi.
Il gioco dura 2 ore e mezza circa.
Il gioco è sottotitolato in italiano ma per il resto è in inglese.
Comunque questo gioco mi è piaciuto ma non posso darli un voto molto alto visto che andando avanti sarà ripetitivo (poi appena lo giocherete capirete di cosa sto parlando XD) e anche il Boss finale sarà molto deludente.
VOTO FINALE 73/100

Star Wars Battlefront II.  If you enjoy Star Wars, play this. If you enjoy classic FPS games, play this.
Star Wars Battlefront was the game based on a movie that made us all believe that it could actually be done right.  Star Wars Battlefront II is the sequel that expands on the original in all the necessary departments.
This game is by no means perfect.  It has it's bugs and general issues, but you won't find a better Star Wars game that takes place in canon locations and with canon characters at your will.
The GameSpy set-up originally dispersed with this title has been disbanded, and as such, the multiplayer was considered dead, but the community still loves and enjoys this title, and through some easy Googling skills, you too can join in on the multiplayer fun.
The game has a very fun and great story mode, allowing you to play on both sides of the story, Empire or Rebels, as well as quick play matches in single player or with friends, and my personal favorite, a strategy-type game-mode called Galactic Conquest.  This mode allows you to slowly but surely take over the galaxy as the dark or light side as you wish.  Space battles, land battles, card-based match boosters and different game objectives galore, this is the game mode that really makes this game unique for me.
In short, Battlefront II may be aged, but it's aged well and still has the great community it always had.  A must-play for Star Wars fans for sure, a great game and a staple of my childhood.

GRIM DAWN is what DIABLO 3 should have been, but never even got close to: the best hack'n'slash ARPG: it thrives where Diablo 3 just sucked:
+ the grim setting with the mutilated corpses is atmospheric and not watered down, unlike D3 one can actually FEEL the (post-)apocalypse
+ the map is a hand-crafted,  believable world instead of generic mega-dungeon after generic mega-dungeon
+ melancholic score fits the setting
+ beautiful and HUGE open world to explore
+ very long campaign (60+ hours), top value for your $
+ character customization!!!!!! I can use all weapons with all characters, unlike D3 (try giving a witch doctor a sword)
+ excellent, well-balanced character classes, two classes can be chosen per character which results in a special dual-class
+ passive skill system ("constellations") adds depth without being as overwhelming as PATH OF EXILE
+ an original and refreshing setting and world. D3 just clones D1 and D2 worlds, characters and events (yawn)
+ factions
+ simply the best Hack n' slash game since the original DIABLO!
Sure there are issues:
- not a lot of voice acting
- no cinematics to write home about
- one male and one female character (no customization of hair, body, skin, etc.)
- story is rather poor
Overall, just forget DIABLO 3 exists, GRIM DAWN is my personal favorite in the ARPG Hack and Slash genre. It isn't as complex as PATH OF EXILE and beginners will  be able to enjoy this as well. The DLC "ASHES OF MELMOUTH" also is a must!

AURALUX: CONSTELLATIONS, developed and published by War Drum Studios, is the sequel to the indie classic Auralux. This is the Steam debut for the franchise which has gotten a cult following from both the PC and mobile audience.
In each round the player begins with a single planet. The task is to then upgrade, expand and take over the enemies planets for sole power of the solar system. That may sound simple and it is at the easier levels. However, once the game reaches normal and harder modes the challenge becomes increasingly difficult. It’s a case of minimalist RTS elements being executed perfectly. The more you play the more elements are added.
The biggest upgrade from the original game to Auralux: Constellations is the addition of multiplayer which can take place in a local and online format. This addition gives the game significant playability if you have a friend or family member that can play at home or online. It’s been a feature that the game’s community has been begging for a long time.
The graphical presentation does not deviate away from the minimalism that is the main drawcard of the game. In fact, I would suggest that it takes it a level further. The graphics are simple enough that it allows the player to focus on the core focus of the gameplay. The music does the same only it helps raise the intensity to the next level. Although the developers claim to have designed it to provide a ‘relaxing, cerebral experience’ I would argue that the intensity and the intelligent gameplay forces the player to think and act quickly.
I cannot really fault it. The game achieves what it sets out to do at a high level and although I am yet to experience the multiplayer – holler at me if you’d like to play against me – I can only imagine that it is a wonderful addition.

Normally, I would quote "You get what you pay for," since I bought this game for $0.99 during the Summer Sale.  However, since I bought Half-Life on Steam during a sale for $1.99, I think I am entitled to complain.
This game is something you would normally see on a flash games website, good for maybe a half-hour of entertainment before it gets boring.  To make matters worse, all of the wagons need to be unlocked through achievements save for the default one.  It also provides little real challenge other than twitch response in terms of gameplay.  The gameplay consists of being flashed a "random" message, then being thrown into a scenario that usually involves shooting animals, people, or dodging obstacles.  However, after a half-hour of play, I was seeing the same events every other run.  It turns out that the game isn't procedurally generated in the traditional sense, other than the random location of enemy spawns.  There are certain events that are fixed, such as crossing rivers, where the player is presented with a choice on how to do so.  However, most events that have a chance occur are linked to other events that is required to immediately follow, such as burning buffalo during a prairie fire only happens if there was a prarie fire, which only happens if there was a herd of buffalo, which happens every time upon entering the Great Plains level.  So there is actually not much variety in gameplay, since the event generation seems to only be based on two possible outcomes, often y/n, if a --> b ?, or based on player choice.

I am surprised by how poorly received this game has been. It isn't perfect, but damn is it fun! With a full-fledged parkour system, fun and engaging melee combat, and plenty of weapons/looting/crafting, this one is a must have for those who enjoyed games like Borderlands, Dishonored, and Dead Island. Here's my summary.
Gameplay: Excellent. Aside from some slightly awkward parkour animations, everything is highly responsive and generally feels good, with a fine sense of "weight." Parkour is precise and exhilarating - you really can go anywhere, and eventually you get the best grappling hook I've ever seen in an FPS. Combat is also smooth and responsive, with plenty of options - dodging, jumping over people, tackling, slide kicks, jump kicks, heavy/light attacks, throwing weapons, guns, air attacks, stealth takedowns, shields - it's all here. Zombies react realistically to getting hit, with a pretty extensive damage system. You can see the physics react to every hit, and it honestly feels better than most melee FPS games. Also, did I mention how many weapons there are? Well, there are tons, and you can augment them. Seriously, I haven't had this much fun looting since the original Borderlands. As for stealth, there are some options, but no silenced guns. You are limited to melee takedowns. AI is pretty damn finicky. All in all, it is passable - stealth can be employed with some enjoyment, but it's often more fun to cause mayhem in this one.
Story: Meh. Did you actually buy this for the story? Go watch The Walking Dead
Graphics/sound: Fantastic, aside from the occasional low-res texture. It can look almost photorealistic at times. Sounds are right on. Music ranges from excellent to cliche. Voice acting is good - not great, just good.
Ultimately, 8/10. I rated higher to boost this games reputation. Take note, there are minor performance issues on the PC, which are slowly getting worked out. Oh, and mod tools are coming.
Buy this for the gameplay if you like parkour, melee combat, and looting. You will not be disappointed.

Star Wars Battlefront II.  If you enjoy Star Wars, play this. If you enjoy classic FPS games, play this.
Star Wars Battlefront was the game based on a movie that made us all believe that it could actually be done right.  Star Wars Battlefront II is the sequel that expands on the original in all the necessary departments.
This game is by no means perfect.  It has it's bugs and general issues, but you won't find a better Star Wars game that takes place in canon locations and with canon characters at your will.
The GameSpy set-up originally dispersed with this title has been disbanded, and as such, the multiplayer was considered dead, but the community still loves and enjoys this title, and through some easy Googling skills, you too can join in on the multiplayer fun.
The game has a very fun and great story mode, allowing you to play on both sides of the story, Empire or Rebels, as well as quick play matches in single player or with friends, and my personal favorite, a strategy-type game-mode called Galactic Conquest.  This mode allows you to slowly but surely take over the galaxy as the dark or light side as you wish.  Space battles, land battles, card-based match boosters and different game objectives galore, this is the game mode that really makes this game unique for me.
In short, Battlefront II may be aged, but it's aged well and still has the great community it always had.  A must-play for Star Wars fans for sure, a great game and a staple of my childhood.

(This is for the NA server, I have never played on any other servers, mainly because I live in the NA place, and because it's hard enough to figure out things without trying to learn korean on the fly on top of that)
Is Black Desert more confusing than trying to watch an episode of Twin Peaks without knowing anything about it? - Yes
Is is a PvP centered game? - It can be, but I would say you need to be in a guild that does a lot of node wars.  If not, the PvP is minimal.  You'll get as much PvP as you want, from nearly zero to omgzorz why are these guards killing me why why.
Do you have to spend money beyond the initial game?  Absolutly not.  However, $100 for the largest pearl pack certainly makes a big difference.  Save your money for special sales, they happen all the time.  For instance, there is usually a big pet pack at halloween, and the black friday sale after thanksgiving.  Pets will vastly improve your play experience as there are only a token few free ones here and there (you want 4, at a minimum)  Wait for sales, patience is a virtue.
If you don't like crafting, you can purchase almost everything off the auction house.  The game is designed for crafting though, and it's not bad at all once you figure out what the heck you're doing.  You can have an army of peons scratching in the dirt for everything from wood to pumpkins, while only having to throw them vast quantities of beer.  So much beer.    It could be called Beer Distribution Online.
If you are AFK for long periods, you can still be playing BDO the entire time.  You can fish afk, you can turn raw metal into melted raw metal, you can drive horses around until they get stuck on a rock because you failed to make sure the path you chose was rock free.
Item upgrading - probably the biggest source of frustration in this game.  You will fail at upgrades ALL THE TIME.  You will curse the people at Pearl Abyss, you will call them terrible things.  You may possibly rage quit.  Upgrading is the source of all that is evil in the world.  Your friend will upgrade with no effort and shove the results in your face.  Don your tinfoil cone of shame, you'll need it.
In summation - this is the most single player MMO I've ever played.  You can pretty much look at other players as computer AI with a penchant for occasionally killing you for no good reason (only after level 49, and you should level beyond that, there's almost no reason not too).  You can't trade with anyone for the most part.  You can join guilds (definitly worth doing for the perks) and group up but there are not really any "dungeons" per se, and the boss raids are a huge ffa, where you'll die a lot if you don't know how any particular world boss operates (they smash in your face, for free).
All in all I really like BDO.  I get far more out of it than I ever did playing WoW, I get more satisfaction than I ever did playing Everquest.  It is not the game for everyone.  If you do not enjoy extreme tedium at times, or RNGesus slapping you about the face-head-chest-neck you won't get much enjoyment from BDO.
Buy it, watch lots of videos (there is a ton of outdated info out there, things have vastly changed, become an internet Sherlock Holmes to get current info, you'll be glad you did) and give it a good hundred or so hours, then you can decide if it's for you.  You will be completely lost for a while.  It gets better, knowledge is power, reading is fundamental, the more you know, reading rainbow, g.i.joe, porkchop sandwiches.
