EDIT: By some miracle, the game suddenly decided to work a second for me, so I have since been able to play the full game in one go, since I wasn't going to risk this game not running for me a second time.
Having beaten the whole game, I can now say what I think about it as a whole rather than just one episode. Parts of my original review will remain, but they have been amended in light of having played through it all.
I will say, though I can give a more detailed review, my overall points haven't changed much.
***SPOILER ALERT: DO NOT READ A MARKED SECTION OF THE CONS IF YOU DO NOT WANT TO BE SPOILED ON CERTAIN STORY ELEMENTS****
Pros:
-Decent writing that makes for a gripping story (I won't say amazing, as I'll explain in cons there are a few things that detract from the writing quality). My favourite sections of the story were those involving the characters of Asher, Rodrik, and Gared in that order, Mira has some good ones too, but as I'll explain in the cons hers is severely hamstrung by canon.
-Excellent use of Actors and Actresses from the TV series for their roles, unlike some games where they use different people for iconic characters of certain franchises. Though the fact that some particularly important characters from King's Landing especially are conspicuously absent at Court was noticeable (Namely, every Lannister with the exception of Cersei and Tyrion, even though Tywin's supposed to be running the show in King's Landing by this point in the story and Jaime since they're using the show's canon. And Littlefinger and Varys), but they also aren't the characters who we would be likely to meet openly anyway.
-Doesn't break Canon! (This may be a very small thing, but I cannot say the same for other games of this type of genre.)
Cons
-Art style (This could be my settings, but I actually think this is one of the few times where the Telltale Art style DOESN'T fit well with the game. Tons of graphics and textures end up looking muddy or low-res around edges, including character textures at times and its really jarring considering how sharp The Wolf Among Us's art design was or even The Walking Dead's. Especially since the most well-known content of GoT is in very well-done live action, it leaves me wishing for better visuals. The backgrounds especially can look like♥♥♥♥♥♥ especially when you have dialogue between a couple characters in some places since the camera seems to like to blurr out even more of the background when talking, making it look like the sharper characters are talking in front of a matte painting than an actual place.)
-Impacts of Choices, or lack thereof ****SPOILERS BEYOND HERE**** (I have played through this whole game, and I can safely say that this game sucks as an RPG when it comes to meaningful choices. Sure, you can make dramatically different choices in this game, but NONE OF THEM MATTER. The conclusions all feel the same in each episode, and the ultimate conclusion of the whole series feels almost completely unchangeable. No choice you make throughout this whole game, for any of the characters, will have any bearing on the ultimate points of the ending. Ironrath falls, almost all of the Forrester Family dies with maybe 3 survivors if you're lucky, you're completely ♥♥♥♥ed from the start of the game to the end by more powerful families and forces that you stand no chance against.
The only times I enjoyed the story and felt I was making meaningful choices were when I was with Asher, since his story arch from beginning to end you feel dynamic and feel like you can crawl up from the bottom and take what's yours with enough skill, brains, and power. Probably helps a lot that his arch, though it crosses paths with Dany, deals with the least number of canon characters. From the first time I played as him, I got hooked on Asher.
Close second is Rodrik's arch, and then Gared. But even so, these were just moments when I FELT I was making meaningful choices. Looking back on it, almost none of them are.
Mira's choices especially feel meaningless because you're dealing very much with a lot of characters whose actions are dictated by canon. Margarery, Cersei, Tyrion, all of them act exactly as they would in the show, which is both great and bad for a game like this specifically because they all have power over Mira. Mira is literally next to nothing without support from at least one of them, and this is made VERY clear at the end of her arch when she's basically abandoned by all 3 for one reason or another. And while it certainly feels accurate to a GoT side-story, that doesn't make for a very compelling RPG where you can feel like your choices mean anything.
It all just culminates in a lackluster game that doesn't compare to previous Telltale games where at least you not only felt like you made a dynamic choice, but you could actually see the results of that dynamic choice on several ocassions.
For example: TWD Season 1, episode 1 whether you save Carly or Doug feels noticeably different and you're left thinking that there will be a big difference to come depending on which choice you made, even if the overall end of the episode is the same regardless of who you picked. In episode 2 alone you can see the differences if you play it differently both times based on that single choice.
The Wolf Among Us, episode 1 is full of choices you can make that you know will lead to drastically different outcomes, ripping off Grendel's arm or not, arresting Tweedle or Woody, saving or letting Lawrence die (and hence picking which place to go to first beforehand) its full of choices that you can feel in that moment have major impact or potential consqeuence later on.
But here in this, the choices feel meaningless since there are very few whose outcomes are left hanging and feel drastically different, really, at least that's what I felt. It left me feeling railroaded for a lot of the game outside of a handful of choices. I do not feel as if any significant events in this game could be avoided or significantly changed at all from any choice in this game. The outcomes are always the same, by and large.
-Stupid choices. This is different from meaningless choices, and it can probably be backed up by statistics gathered from this game. What I mean is that there are more than a few moments in this game where even though it presents you with a choice, the choice is between a completely moronic or pathetic move and one which is obviously the better choice given what you have already done previously. This is especially true late in the game, but there are a few moments where its apparent as early as episode 2. It felt as some choices were expecting us to just forget what happened not even 20 minutes ago for it to actually be a choice you wouldn't think about for more than a few seconds.
-Absolutely ridiculous moments in the writing. Though I praised the writing earlier, there are a few glaring problems I noticed while playing that just felt so unrealistic to me. I cannot list them all here, but they really didn't help the railroad feeling.
-Meaningless Extra Items. Though I was wrong about some of the items not carrying over, I was completely right about them having no meaning later on in the game. Kept the Ironwood Royal Decree? Meaningless. Kept the dagger? Meaningless. Kept the bandage materials? Placebo effect is all we get, the result is still the same as if you didn't even get them. Unless you're using the items immediately, NONE of them matter even if they carry over, not in any significant way. This is a problem I know a lot of Telltale games have, so its not limited to this game, but if they're going to let us keep items in an inventory across multiple episodes, then make us able to use them or get rid of them!
-Terrible lip-syncing at times.
Overall, not a very good game by Telltale. Play it if you're a GoT fan more than an RPG fan, because this game sucks as an RPG.

I read some other (negative) reviews. Some of them are quite right. I just wished they were told in a more objective manner. One thing I got a little angry about was the impact of your choices but it got me also thinking. Any game needs "plot nodes" (a point in the plot where story lines come together for a major event, which sometimes might be delayed but will always happen no matter what). Do not mistake this for "your choices having no impact". Your choices along the way to a minor or major event is what makes your stance towards the next event. Whether your took your axe with you to be armed for a fight or you menaged to talk someone out of it usually makes harder or easier to deal with that event. If that event did not happen because of diplomacy it still means that it was a plot node.
That said, yeah this game is kinda tight. The impact of your choices in this game is limited. Ofcourse it's limited because you cannot influence the main story of the tv show, but it would have been nice if there were actually more ways to play through the game, and better influence characters, than it currently is.
And ofcourse you get a major cliffhanger at the end, it's the Game of Thrones. But I enjoyed the story, which is the most important part of the game. And I still believe I made an impact in the story which (hopefully) come back a little stronger in TTG's Game of Thrones.

Whether looking to expand and explore the vibrant world of Game of Thrones beyond the books and the hit show on HBO or delving into the realm the very first time, this isn't too bad of a place to start and will certainly make you have the feels one way or another.
Making decisions and later on accepting what you have done to your poor characters is certainly Telltale Games; mostly dialoge, button mashing and dodging are as well. While lacking in the action department they make up for in gripping story arcs, compelling characters and well done voice acting.
You play as one of several members of your family or close family in a war-torn country trying to save it from ruin in a episodic setting. From politics to sword fighting you better carve out a future for your family and hold on tight because it's one emotional ride.
Without spoiling anything I couldn’t stop playing the game. I wanted to know what happened to everyone and was very attached to my characters. Knowing the universe of Game of Thrones just made it more thrilling to lose myself in it and I very much enjoyed how true it stayed to the TV show adaptation. The graphics could have been a bit better, but all in all it’s not that bad yet time will tell how they hold up. Overall for a game that is episodic it’s what I expected. Since they have to stay true to the story and can’t really give any spoilers for future books or the HBO series at the time of release.
That said unless you can’t wait to buy it after this review pay full price, for everyone else this is a great game to pick up during a sale. Though you can play it multiple times, I’m pretty sure most people would max at two play throughs. I’m on my third.

A worthy continuation/spin-off of Alan Wake franchise.
I am not sure as the game is presented as a... well, if you want to know just finish it, it's not long and it's more action oriented than Alan Wake:)
Pros:
- more action packed than Alan Wake - now we have more of a shooter than action thriller/horror
- reworked torch mechanics - now it's replenishing its power quickly but standard pointint at enemies does nothing, you need to focus your beam
- plot is really good - we have a time loop where Alan needs to beat Mr. S*%@^!# plan to entrap him into endless loop of events
- more guns that really pack some serious punch - we have automatic shotgun, assault rifle, hunting rifle, uzi, nail gun, etc. Nothing explosive besides standard grenade and flare gun though.
- ending is really cool but leaves a question mark whether this is a continuation of Alan Wake or just some spin-off. That's great ambiguity by the way
- stories written on pages that lie here and there are really great, same for TV broadcasts from Mr.S*%@^!# and radio auditions
Cons:
- there are not many locations in this game but this is connected heavily to the plot and loop that traps Alan in those locations
- no meaningful NPCs here, no one like Barry, Thomas Zane aka retro Swimsuit Guy or Old Gods of Asgard, just some poorly written and bland characters that take the weird things going on as something normal. Imagine something like that - you go to the store to buy some milk or soft drinks or whatever and suddenly you see a guy running with an axe or some chainsaw usually used to cut pavement bricks. Pretty normal, huh?
- graphics are slightly worse than in Alan Wake, everything is brighter, almost no brilliant light-shadow play as in the first game
- this game is so action oriented that it seems that the main idea why to produce such game was to make Alan shoot more weird shadow men aka The Taken. This shooting is quickly dominating the game.
- locations are really small and you will feel it during your playthrough
- the main plot is not really pushed forward, we've got some details here and there but nothing really major
Overall I really like this game. Those cons I've listed are really minor to me as the game as a whole is really fun. I would really like to see Alan Wake 2 or whatever they want to call it.
As to American Nightmare - if you see it on sale you can give it a shot. It lasts for about 5 hours of pretty casual play. It's a shooter with Alan Wake theme but still fun and likeable.

If I ran UBISoft and someone came to me with the idea of taking one of their top franchises and sending it to paleolithic time periods, I'd expect that person's desk to be cleaned out by the end of the day.  Yet - they pulled it off!!!  FC Primal is the BEST Far Cry yet, and since FC3 was one of my all time favorite games, that is saying a lot from me.  They hit on almost every aspect perfectly.  I was a very harsh critic of FC4 and this took all the best from that game, all the best from 3 and made an awesome cave baby.
Is it perfect?   There are some things that bothered me, but for the most part I give it a 10/10.
Pros -
Combat is simply a blast.  It is equally fun to stay hidden and take out everyone without their knowledge as it is to run in club swinging, knocking some sense in to your enemy
Wildlife is absolutly everywhere- you feel like you are in a time period where you are equal to every animal that is walking around.
Wildlife is balanced perfectly.  I never felt like I was constantly being attacked, yet I had that cautious feeling the entire time that I need to be looking over my shoulder and I had to keep my guard up.  There are numerous animals that WILL kill you even later in the game.  This was something that FC3 and 4 never got 100% correct.  3 was pretty close though.
Snakes are actually dangerous in this game.  Not in that they will kill you, but that they are now not just strategically placed like 3 and 4 felt.  You can be running full speed through a field and get hit by a snake.  But it isn't too frequent.  Happened 3 or 4 times.
Eagles attack - but not every time you turn to take a p*ss.  Again - balanced perfectly.
Fire is incredible!!!  I always liked how 3 used fire, probably better than any other game that I played, however, in FC-P they take it to another level.  It is entirely possible to burn a village to the ground by starting 1 fire.  It is done very, very well.  I expect actual building damage next game though.  Looking at you UBI.
Caves are back!!!  And better than ever.  The caves in 3 were great.  4 was a HUGE dissapointment.  FC-P caves make FC3 caves feel like small holes in the ground and FC4 caves like the ditch outside the front of your house.  They are massive and you can/will get lost if you do not pay attention.  Plus - they are darker.  Torch is recommended!
The grappling hook is back - works great as expected.  Pretty much the same as 4
The throwing knives, called shards, are back.  They work the same too, however I didn't feel the need to use them.  If I was that close, I was already in hand to hand combat.  Any further and I was striking from a distance.
Enemy AI seemed pretty good.  On harder levels it gets smarter.
Crafting is well balanced and the need to find the rare plants and animals was a good touch.
There is animal training - absolutely awesome.  I'll miss my rare sabertooth and owl team of death.
Cons -
Wow - not much....
At times it played like a powerpoint presentation but I can't really blame the game for that - Just my underpowered crap gaming PC.  I7 4720HQ 2.6 Ghz, 8 Gig mem, Nvidia 950M, slow A** 5400 RPM HD.
Someimtes my animal would get in the way - a simple command to move him is all it took, but they could have taken a note from some of the Skyrim followers mods.
I ran in to a bug in the Izila final mission where the tribesmen that were there to help me out were just terrfied of my tiger.  All they did was cower in fear shouting TIGRI and not pushing the stone like I needed them too.  So after blowing through most of my supplies, I ended up clubbing them like baby seals in hopes that I could get more that were a little more brave.  I did.  They moved the rock like they were supposed to, but now I had no weapons to kill fire chick.  That made that mission EXTREMELY difficult even with the supplies on the other side.
That's about all there is bad about the game.  And it is VERY minor.  It was relatively bug free otherwise.
There is no sniper rifle!  I mean - of course right?  But I thought they could add a blow gun or something.  The owl in a sense is your sniper rifle that never misses, but has a 45 second reload time, so, very slow.  Still, this isn't a complaint...  I see why they did it.  Stealth is still very fun, albet a little slow.
You see actors from FC3 (maybe 4 too) that appear in the game. Batari acted and sounded very similar to Citra and even Hurk has several missions as Urki.  At first I was disappointed they did this, then I just made the leap to the idea that these were their ancetors.  You can tell it was done on purpose (at least with Urki) and not just because they were cheap/short on new talent.  Urki is no where near as funny as Hurk was though.
TL:DR
All in all this is an excellent game.  It is my favorite FC now and one of the best game I played in the last year. Def worth the money. Rated PG in my opinion as there is nothing really bad in it.

Rogue Starship: Faster Than Light (review)
The roguelike subgenre has experienced a tremendous surge in popularity over the last few years. Blending heavy RPG elements with the constant threat of permanent death and success often at the mercy of a random number generator, the appeal of roguelikes rests in fast gameplay and the player accepting that victory is anything but assured. While I have not personally explored the roguelike genre heavily, the space opera setting of FTL, developed by Subset Games, was enough to finally bring me over. Today I provide my (belated) review for FTL.
The Short
+challenging but (mostly) fair
+surprisingly deep gameplay
+fast paced and genuinely entertaining
-sub-par graphics and sound
-final boss is a bit cheap
8.5/10
The Long
Gameplay
Because a complete game in the roguelike genre seldom takes more than an hour, it is imperative that gameplay be compelling from start to finish; the structure simply doesn't allow for a meaty exposition or plodding middle. From the get go, FTL instills a sense of urgency. The plot revolves around the crew of the space ship Kestrel escaping from a looming rebel fleet to bring vital information to the home world to defeat said fleet. Through a series of sectors, comprised of about 20 points of interest, the player is tasked with rapidly making progress to an exit point before the pursuing fleet catches up. The rub here is that each successive sector ramps up the difficulty and the only way for the Kestrel to increase in power is to make diversions from the main route salvaging scrap parts (currency) to exchange for upgraded systems. Consequently, each sector is a balancing act between quickly reaching the exit while deviating to points of interest. The game can be paused at any moment which expertly allows the player to focus on each agonizingly tense decision without ever feeling like they were rushed into it.
Upon arriving at a point of interest, the player is effectively subjected to a dice-roll event. Sometimes the Kestrel is thrust into combat, other times a choice is presented to intervene in an ongoing conflict, and, still others, the player is offered a the option to purchase items from a shop. The majority of challenges are combat based which demands the player to assign crew members to various tasks such as manning weapons systems, fixing hull breaches, and defending against boarding parties. At the same time, the player must manage weapon systems and choose targets on the enemy ship. Solid strategy usually revolves around using missiles to take out an opponents shield system and following up with energy beams to cut through the hull. Conflict usually takes a few minutes to resolve and, after some repairs, the player moves to the next point of interest on the map. This pacing provides for little downtime and the overall experience benefits greatly from it.
Decisions Decisions
One of the difficulties of the roguelike genre is in offering up a wide variety of decisions without inundating the player. Here, FTL performs admirably. With limited scrap, the player must decide which of numerous ship systems to upgrade (all of which have a tangible impact on play style) and which weapons to equip (which are varied but all useful). Depending on what the shops offer, one play through may see the Kestrel outfitted with a cloaking device and relying on boarding parties to incapacitate enemies and the next might warrant the outfitting of heavy pulse lasers to obliterate the opposition. In this way, there are multiple paths to victory and each new game provides a bevy of experiences and challenges.
Random Number Generator vs Strategy
Roguelikes are often criticized for success being primarily through lucky dice rolls over all else. While FTL ultimately requires the rolls to go right to achieve victory, I seldom found myself encountering insurmountable encounters until at least the mid-game. This is simultaneously a positive and a negative. It is heart-wrenching to see your perfectly constructed ship fall to ruin through the simultaneous bad luck of an ion blast knocking out shields, a solar flare setting fires everywhere, and a boarding party taking out your best engineer. On the other hand, most games develop to the point where some attachment is made with the Kestrel and her crew and victory often feels tantalizingly close to the players' grasp. In fairness, most failures are rarely due to a single catastrophic string of bad rolls as opposed to poor or inefficient decision making by the player.
The major exception to the above is the final fight against the mothership which takes place in three consecutive stages with each representing, by far and away, the most difficult fights in the game. Breezing to the end game to only be dramatically outmatched by an opponent is infuriating the first few times but also teaches the value of properly upgrading the Kestrel along the way. Indeed, while each sector is an increased challenge, the final battle is a true test to see if the player became complacent in upgrading along the way. Given that the process, instead of victory, is the major draw of roguelikes (failures can often feel nearly as satisfying as victory), a cheap final boss isn't a major issue and barely detracts from the overall experience. Also, it is important to note that the final boss is certainly far from impossible; it just requires solid planning from start to finish.
Graphics and Sound
Graphically, FTL is serviceable in a faux-retro style but not particularly memorable. Everything is somewhat cartoonish but fails to convey much personality. On screen action is easy to understand but nothing really pops. For example, ship fires are handled through a basic sprite animation; it serves the mechanical purpose of letting the player know that they have an issue to attend to but nothing more. Compared to other recent indie titles which have found innovative ways to present otherwise simplistic graphics, FTL is a bit of a letdown. The same criticisms for graphics also apply to sound. The elevator music fades to the background and laser/missile effects are distinct enough to register hits and misses but little more. All told, the presentation is unfortunate because it might be off-putting enough to cause some players to miss out on the fabulous gameplay.
Priced at $10, FTL offers a ton of value. Fans of the roguelike genre should absolutely not miss it. For those, like myself, who are curious about this style of game, FTL represents an excellent starting point. Personally, I have been inspired to pick up a few more roguelikes based on my experience with FTL. Don't let the mediocre graphics and sound deter you, the gameplay is compelling enough that you won't even notice after the first 15 minutes. Only those who absolutely detest roguelikes should avoid this one.

As far as Korean MMO's go, this one's aight.  Straight up just alright, compared to "God awful" and "Please kill me now so I don't have to play this" like some of the Korean grindfests can be.  It has amazing customization, it has pretty solid economy aspects to it, and also has -really- good combat.  The combat is one of the most fun I've had in an MMO like this, it feels fluid and just---good.  Housing is a nice implement, but good luck competing in that (Which gets you daily money based on your rank) because your neighbors likely have better stuff than you... from the cash shop.
Ahh, cash shops.  It wouldn't be an MMO without it.  And this definitely has that.  Mounts, underwear, pets.  Buffs.  Your standard fare.  If that's not your kinda thing---well, there you have it, skip this game entirely.
Dress your waifu---er, character in outfits, because armor has very little variation and honestly comes in about ...maybe ten to twelve different sets which have various degrees of differentish looks, some showing no discernable or outstanding differences from the next.
The good news is, most things you can get from the cash shop -can be bought- from the AH.  Gold isn't super hard to get, just you have to know how the economy works, and be willing to take the time to get the gold to get the panties---er, I mean armor.
I should mention classes are restricted by gender.  Wanna play a female "Striker", the fist-fighting monk character?  Too bad!  Wanna play a male beast tamer?  Too bad. Telltale's stab at Game of Thrones is a very frustrating experience. The characters you play are almost exclusively in a position where every choice is a wrong one, and characters around you beat you down and laugh in your face. I get that this is A) because that's supposed to mirror the moral realism of the Game of Thrones books and TV show and B) it allows the story to happen in-universe without making any waves in the canon. But the simple fact of the matter is that it doesn't make for an enjoyable game.
Having played the game and watched others play through it, it's clear that your choices don't really matter - the game will get railroaded along the same path, just with little bits cut out or included. It includes Telltale's stock method of introducing two equally sympathetic and equally unreasonable friendly characters between whom you'll be forced to choose. The game can appear very lifeless due to an oddly bare soundscape - music is unremarkable (in stark contrast to the TV show) and many scenes seem to lack sound effects. A few of the show's actors have been recruited to reprise their roles in the game, but most of them perform as if either they or the voice acting director was half asleep. Lastly, the story builds up to absolutely nothing aside from a vague promise of a sequel.
If you've played a few Telltale games then the formula has become very obvious, and much as I enjoyed their earlier works, it's made me very wary of buying new titles from them. This one just wasn't any fun.

Grim Dawn looks like a great game, in fact I am sure that it is. So why am I not recommending it? Well, clearly this game has a great following of people who all like it very much. But that isn't to say that the game is not without its downsides. It is for these downsides that I personally didn't find the game fun. I feel that Grim Dawn lacks a few crucially important features that make other ARPGs much more easy to pick up and play. Firstly I think that the inventory, stash and UI are a complete mess. There is simply just too much going on, items in your inventory and stash just feel smashed together in a mess of pixels and tooltips are very hard to read. Now my eyesight is fine, but the 1-dimensional icons for
make it hard to easily distinguish their differences. Add that together with 'components' that need to be pieced together and attached to items.
For a loot based game, this is a fatal problem.
Secondly, with the lack of explanation as to how you can build your character. I had to spend a couple of hours lurking the forums and watching videos just to get an understanding of the levelling process because the game didn't bother explaining anything. Even after probably 5 hours of watching videos and reading, I was still pretty confused as to what each build offered me. When it came to actual combat and killing enemies I felt like the combat system is just
There is just such an underwhelming amount of physics in this game.
or
across the room or even over railings and down into chasms below. Combat in Grim Dawn just feels very 1-dimensional and there are a lack of dynamic animations that give your character a sense of 'power' and 'awe'. This is even more obvious when watching end-game players killing enemies and bosses with huge AoE spells. It just doesn't seem satisfying at all. Finally, I think with the buffs and AoE spells the animations are again, just so ridiculously simple and either you or your enemy are often
green or red light
Like I said, I'm sure that this is a great ARPG but I feel that certain very simple gameplay elements (UI, combat, lack of walkthrough, lack of impactful physics, huge colour blobs) resulted in the game venturing too far from established norms that make other ARPGs much easier to just pick up and play. Grim Dawn definitely does have its charm. The story looks very interesting, the build options look great, the loot of course looks awesome and the graphics are pretty good; not amazing but pretty good. I just don't feel like there is enough substance there to make me feel like swinging my axe at an enemy. A lot of people will disagree with me, but Grim Dawn just didn't tick the important boxes that I needed it to so I felt forced to keep my playtime under an hour in order to still be able to get a refund. Sorry fans, but I feel like the developers really could have done better with the UI, physics and 1-dimensional AoE spells and buffs just for a start.

I bought this during the summer sale, and finally decided to play it when the expansion came out.  I just played it for about 12 hours straight because I couldn't stop.
This is a really good game.
The art is top notch, although the character does feel a little floaty when they run across the landscape.
The sound is mixed for me.  The music is pretty good, but some of the character battle taunts can get a bit loopy.  For example, I got pretty sick of enemies telling me they were going to cut my face off when searching for Cronley.
Gameplay is very satisfying to me.  The combat feels good, some other ARPGs I've played get to the point where combat gets to the point that it doesn't matter what's on the screen, because you're always just doing the same thing.  I've found myself taking a more strategic view when encountering groups of enemies.
I really like the character advancement in the game.  Having dual classes and the additional devotions makes for a ton of possibilities.  Being able to reroll all of that stuff makes it a lot less intimidating.  I haven't looked at a build guide yet because when I feel like I've made a mistake in my build, I can just pay a bit to undo it.  I know some people don't necessarily enjoy that, but I do.
I'm enjoying the story.   They've done a good job of making the story simple enough that it's not overbearing but giving me enough that I don't just fast click through every conversation I come across, and I've even been reading the lore drops.  I don't think I've ever done that in an ARPG.
Overall, this game was a steal at the sale price.  I'm a fanatic for ARPGs and this game is satisfying as PoE without the anxiety of totally ruining my character through bad build choices or having to research builds for every character.

Poker Night at the Inventory is a fun and surprisingly complex poker simulation. As someone who has pretty much no real experience with poker before playing this game, it's good at explaining the rules and immersing you into the game quickly and simply. There's that addictive quality of "just one more round", hoping to increase your balance, or to get the varied achievements or new items, that's a mark of quality in a turn-based game.
But of course the real draw of Poker Night at the Inventory is the characters. If you're a fan of Homestar Runner, Team Fortress 2, Penny Arcade, or Sam & Max, or even if you aren't, the characters are going to make you laugh and come back for more. The dialogue is pretty fantastic, with all kinds of fun and dark humor (wait until you hear The Heavy's story about the Engineer). All of the characters fit well into their canon personalities, and even have playing styles that reflect them (e.g. Strong Bad likes to bluff and act all macho with large bets, so he can be vulnerable to called bluffs but is unpredictable about how good his hand really is). This is what really brings the immersion into the game.
I would recommend this game to anyone who's interested in poker and/or the IPs involved in the game. It can give you hours of fun, laughs, and a decent challenge for a pretty low price.

Rogue Starship: Faster Than Light (review)
The roguelike subgenre has experienced a tremendous surge in popularity over the last few years. Blending heavy RPG elements with the constant threat of permanent death and success often at the mercy of a random number generator, the appeal of roguelikes rests in fast gameplay and the player accepting that victory is anything but assured. While I have not personally explored the roguelike genre heavily, the space opera setting of FTL, developed by Subset Games, was enough to finally bring me over. Today I provide my (belated) review for FTL.
The Short
+challenging but (mostly) fair
+surprisingly deep gameplay
+fast paced and genuinely entertaining
-sub-par graphics and sound
-final boss is a bit cheap
8.5/10
The Long
Gameplay
Because a complete game in the roguelike genre seldom takes more than an hour, it is imperative that gameplay be compelling from start to finish; the structure simply doesn't allow for a meaty exposition or plodding middle. From the get go, FTL instills a sense of urgency. The plot revolves around the crew of the space ship Kestrel escaping from a looming rebel fleet to bring vital information to the home world to defeat said fleet. Through a series of sectors, comprised of about 20 points of interest, the player is tasked with rapidly making progress to an exit point before the pursuing fleet catches up. The rub here is that each successive sector ramps up the difficulty and the only way for the Kestrel to increase in power is to make diversions from the main route salvaging scrap parts (currency) to exchange for upgraded systems. Consequently, each sector is a balancing act between quickly reaching the exit while deviating to points of interest. The game can be paused at any moment which expertly allows the player to focus on each agonizingly tense decision without ever feeling like they were rushed into it.
Upon arriving at a point of interest, the player is effectively subjected to a dice-roll event. Sometimes the Kestrel is thrust into combat, other times a choice is presented to intervene in an ongoing conflict, and, still others, the player is offered a the option to purchase items from a shop. The majority of challenges are combat based which demands the player to assign crew members to various tasks such as manning weapons systems, fixing hull breaches, and defending against boarding parties. At the same time, the player must manage weapon systems and choose targets on the enemy ship. Solid strategy usually revolves around using missiles to take out an opponents shield system and following up with energy beams to cut through the hull. Conflict usually takes a few minutes to resolve and, after some repairs, the player moves to the next point of interest on the map. This pacing provides for little downtime and the overall experience benefits greatly from it.
Decisions Decisions
One of the difficulties of the roguelike genre is in offering up a wide variety of decisions without inundating the player. Here, FTL performs admirably. With limited scrap, the player must decide which of numerous ship systems to upgrade (all of which have a tangible impact on play style) and which weapons to equip (which are varied but all useful). Depending on what the shops offer, one play through may see the Kestrel outfitted with a cloaking device and relying on boarding parties to incapacitate enemies and the next might warrant the outfitting of heavy pulse lasers to obliterate the opposition. In this way, there are multiple paths to victory and each new game provides a bevy of experiences and challenges.
Random Number Generator vs Strategy
Roguelikes are often criticized for success being primarily through lucky dice rolls over all else. While FTL ultimately requires the rolls to go right to achieve victory, I seldom found myself encountering insurmountable encounters until at least the mid-game. This is simultaneously a positive and a negative. It is heart-wrenching to see your perfectly constructed ship fall to ruin through the simultaneous bad luck of an ion blast knocking out shields, a solar flare setting fires everywhere, and a boarding party taking out your best engineer. On the other hand, most games develop to the point where some attachment is made with the Kestrel and her crew and victory often feels tantalizingly close to the players' grasp. In fairness, most failures are rarely due to a single catastrophic string of bad rolls as opposed to poor or inefficient decision making by the player.
The major exception to the above is the final fight against the mothership which takes place in three consecutive stages with each representing, by far and away, the most difficult fights in the game. Breezing to the end game to only be dramatically outmatched by an opponent is infuriating the first few times but also teaches the value of properly upgrading the Kestrel along the way. Indeed, while each sector is an increased challenge, the final battle is a true test to see if the player became complacent in upgrading along the way. Given that the process, instead of victory, is the major draw of roguelikes (failures can often feel nearly as satisfying as victory), a cheap final boss isn't a major issue and barely detracts from the overall experience. Also, it is important to note that the final boss is certainly far from impossible; it just requires solid planning from start to finish.
Graphics and Sound
Graphically, FTL is serviceable in a faux-retro style but not particularly memorable. Everything is somewhat cartoonish but fails to convey much personality. On screen action is easy to understand but nothing really pops. For example, ship fires are handled through a basic sprite animation; it serves the mechanical purpose of letting the player know that they have an issue to attend to but nothing more. Compared to other recent indie titles which have found innovative ways to present otherwise simplistic graphics, FTL is a bit of a letdown. The same criticisms for graphics also apply to sound. The elevator music fades to the background and laser/missile effects are distinct enough to register hits and misses but little more. All told, the presentation is unfortunate because it might be off-putting enough to cause some players to miss out on the fabulous gameplay.
Priced at $10, FTL offers a ton of value. Fans of the roguelike genre should absolutely not miss it. For those, like myself, who are curious about this style of game, FTL represents an excellent starting point. Personally, I have been inspired to pick up a few more roguelikes based on my experience with FTL. Don't let the mediocre graphics and sound deter you, the gameplay is compelling enough that you won't even notice after the first 15 minutes. Only those who absolutely detest roguelikes should avoid this one.

This is my first experience with a Far Cry game, and overall I haven't been disappointed.
I will say that after about 15-20 hours it does start to get very repetitive, grinding for resources, taking over camps, saving Wenja etc. If you are like me and love to fully complete a game and fill collections, this will definitely take a lot of time and patience.
On the plus side, I like the feeling of a large scale world, filled with danger around every corner and I recommend not to let your guard down at all. I quite like the range of weapons and tameable beasts, which get stronger as you progress further into the game. The stronger the beasts, the less likely you are to be attacked by wild creatures.
If you are the type that loves a challenge, I recommend this game for it's epic boss fights. They are very rewarding.
With almost 30 hours up my sleeve, I am currently only around 26% complete with the game (but that's mostly because I went and spent a lot of time trying to tame all the beasts and collecting items rather than progressing in the story) so that is just an example of how much content is available. In other words, it's gonna take a long time to complete the story, it's not something you can do overnight, and that's what I like most.
Overall, I'm pleased. As repetitive as it is at my current point, I do enjoy finding new areas and know it will all be worth it in the end. Man this game is gonna feel great when it's completed!

Techland is back at it again but under a new publisher and a new IP, Dying Light. [SPOILERS!]
You play as a man named Kyle Crane, a GRE operative undercover on a island named Harran, that has been infected with a plauge which you guessed it, turned majorty of the folk there into meat-eating maniacs or zombies. So Crane parachutes of a plane and lands only to be halted by 3 raiders in yellow clothing (cough cough Rais Men cough cough) and you some how disarm one of them of there handgun and put one between the eyes, you intimidate the others and take them out in a little cutscene and pass out somehow....I guess. Whatever let's skip ahead to when you wake up all confused on a bed in a huge hotel that where some good people took charge over. You get tasked a job to clear the upper floor, too many infected come you escape somehow and you see "Dying Light" like any game would after a introductive mission they would show the title with sweet music. Anyways I won't explain the whole entire story but if your looking for a good story, click next on your zombie genre quere, the story is awful and is filled to the brim with cliches and being called a ♥♥♥♥♥ by a evil insane cliche villian named Rais atleast 5 times, a strange out of place drug mission and a crappy QTE (Quicktime Event) Final Boss.
However, the best part of the game is it's amazing gameplay, you got the Mirror's Edge parkour, the amazing combat of Dead Island and Dead Island Riptide, a Grappling Hook (Which is my best friend BTW in this game) and Drop kicks. You have an amazing collection of weapons here, as of the 1.12 update, I went through the files to find out there are 453 melee weapons, 40+ firearms, and 200+ Throwing weapons! These all are Sickles to Machetes, to Baseball bats to Katanas there are so many weapons that I couldn't play with every single one! Then like Dead Island, you get Weapon Modifications, but sadly they aren't for Firearms and they aren't as creative as I wish they were but the descriptions are somewhat of a chuckle. But the real fun in the blueprints are the Developer blueprints that are hidden all over the city, like the EXPcalibur or the SICK bomb or the right hand of GLOVa. There is way too much fun to be had here.
The Following: This is where I think Techland lost there minds and just said "♥♥♥♥ it" and took that 10/10 fun scale and just broke it and put it up to 1000/10.  The Following is where improvments are with the Story aspect, gameplay (even though I was perfectly fine with it's gameplay they made it 100x better) and more. The story goes of a man with a fever was telling Lena and Crane about a Countyside and where they can find a cure to the plaque that spread. So Crane goes out there and starts out jumping off a 100ft cliff and going to a farm to meet up with a guy named Jasir, he is a follower of "The Mother" with many others, you try your best to go get some answers but somewhat like the main story you are a errand boy for a while but not too long (Thank god) and yeah won't spoil much but the Ending is so much better, no QTE at all, you use your bare hands to defeat the final boss and there are 2 endings you can go for (3 if you count the secret one) and it is just so much better than the main story and I really think Techland understood there fanbase here (unlike 95% of the developers in this world) So let's get to the gameplay. The new feature they really showed off almost throws the parkour aspect of the game out the window into the public dumpster ready to be collected by a truck. That's not a bad thing though and it makes sense as well, it's a Countryside, not a run down city with 50ft buildings to jump on. They added dune buggys, and holy♥♥♥♥♥♥♥are they fun, you start off with lvl.1 white parts (which are trash) but you get blueprints to upgrade up to Military-Grade lvl.6 platinum parts (which make the damn thing go as fast as a SR-71 Blackbird or atleast that's what it feels like) and as you travel the huge map you get bobbleheads, paintjobs, etc to customize your go to travel machine. Something else that gives me a Walking Dead Dayrl Dixon vibe is the new crossbows, as you rank in the cult from the story you get rewards and the crossbow is one of them, you start off with default bolts and the normal crossbow already fun just with that but it get's better, you will get a upgraded variant you can craft later with elemental bolts (impact, stun, toxic) and it makes it triple the fun.
What can I give the game? I give the basegame a 9/10, a must own for the zombie genre lovers and even ones like me who ignored it for a while, it could of been a perfect 10/10 but for it's terrible story it did have to downgrade positive thoughts of the game, but it's flawless gameplay really kept it up there.
As for The Following I give it a 10/10, a your stupid if you don't buy it rating. Techland improved the gameplay and the story and it is just so amazing I couldn't find any flaw here.
Vinal Verdict:
Dying Light Base Game: 9/10 a Must Own.
The Following expansion: 10/10 a Masterpiece that should be legally required to buy.

Like most story modes, you start by creating your team including your name, color and other important options. Right away, the games humor shows as every team name MUST end in the word “United.” There are many little touches like this that true football fans will appreciate, and everyone else will just assume, like Dan did, that this is how the game actually is.
To set-up the action, there are various cutscenes where you interact with the “best player,” as well as your coach and I assume other characters as well. There are decisions to make, and relationships appear to build in these scenes, but I have no idea what effect this has on the game.
In story mode, you can spend money you earn from games on boosting abilities and every win unlocks an advanced ability. There’s also an option to move your players’ starting points on the field, but as you’ll see, at the beginning, it looks like your watching teams of eight-year-olds play the sport.
At this level, the players just bash into each other and are so horribly skilled that they can’t do much of anything. The only two advanced abilities you start with is shooting and tackling. I was a little dissapointed that even passing was locked out of this part of the game. The only thing that made these early matches bearable was that it is extremely easy. I won this first game 7 - 0. While there is a tutorial mode, I wish this part of the game was included there too and that I could skip to the point where I at least have the major game play elements unlocked.
Since I haven’t dived too deeply into the story mode yet, my favorite mode is simply the quickplay. In-fact, the game itself feels a little slow so I crank up the speed 25%. I am by no means an “expert” gamer and I will almost always choose “normal” difficulty, but something about this game just feels a little handicapped.
In quickplay, all the major game elements are present. There is passing which is simple enough, tackling which now includes a “timing mechanic” and if you press tackle, again, at the right moment, your player will continue with the ball instead of it being knocked away randomly. Shooting can be held for more power, but less accuracy, and also spun to curve left or right. There is also a dodge left or right ability that can only be used by a player once a possession, and it is great for dodging tackles. Altogether, these abilities make a fun and rewarding arcade soccer experience. When you land a perfect tackle, a huge pass and inevitably, a goal, it feels great.
Some quirks to the regular soccer formula that you are sure to notice is that sometimes, when you make a goal you get two instead of one. Extra time just randomly happens and offsides brings up a huge warning on the screen and you have to leave before you get penalized. There may be other “fake” rules and these are what make Kickmen unique.
Overall, this is a hard game to review. It’s based on soccer, but you have to call it an arcade soccer game. The rules are changed, so that reminds me of NFL Blitz, Mutant League and NBA Jam style games. Depending on how much you enjoy the humor, I believe this game could be fun to play through the story mode once and if it sells enough copies and receives a free multi-player one day, it will definitely be worth the money. I mean, it’s under $5.
I would definitely like to see this game on a mobile platform or portable console, because that’s what it feels like. Play a game of fast, arcade soccer action then put it down. If it ever comes out on Switch I may buy it myself.

I would recommend this game with some reservations: it gets one shell out of two.
(Video has more details.)
Assault on Arnhem (AoA) is a entry-level wargame (read: quite simple) set inside of the Operation Market Garden airborne invasion of German-occupied Netherlands during WWII. The game is hex-based and leans heavily on RNG elements.
The simplicity of the game lends itself well to tablet, but that also means that the game is extremely simple to pick up and learn.
The tablet-port aspect of the game makes little attempt to appeal to gamers on the PC, and I am sensitive to this in the fear that future games will follow in its path. The tutorial retains the words "tap the screen" and "pinch in or out", and there is a lack of any PC-focused interface (e.g. everything is done with left-click, right-click doesn't work).
I personally am not a fan of largely RNG-based games (like Risk or Monopoly), and AoA rewards chance more than solid tactics. You can replay the same mission dozens of times with the same strategy/tactics, and get wildly different results, which is to say that the tactics only give you a chance at winning, but you have to wait for the dice to roll in your favor to win.

For an operation that had very few chances to succeed in the first place, surely Market Garden has been overly popular among wargames. I think there are about 20 boardgames of old on the same theme.
This tiny video game version draws its inspiration and style directly from those SPI’s an Avolon Hill’s versions of the ill-conceived airborne assault on Arnhem: hex grid, NATO counters, command points, brutally simple map.
This should be considered as an introductory-level wargame: only 4 kinds of units (tanks, infantry, anti-tanks, artillery), three scenarios (one for each key bridge) and one campaign (pretty much the aforementioned three scenarios in a row), very basic terrain effects.
As such, it’s effective.
PROS:
+ Simple, yet somehow realistic (playing as the Axis is much easier)
+ Interesting supply system that some majors should learn something from (do you hear me, Paradox?)
+ The command points / activation system, while somehow obscure in its mechanics, makes it challenging to “prevent” historical events.
CONS:
-	Little appeal for expert players, due its raw simplicity
-	The way anti-tanks work is, well, odd
-	Very short (10 hours if you play all scenarios and campaigns, on both sides of… the bridge)
-	Lacks single-player replayability
OVERALL: 6/10

It is not a bad game overall, but I didn’t enjoy the writing as well – it is not as good as in the other Telltale games I’ve played. I found particularly ridiculous the motivation of one strong supportive character, which turned traitor – it was simply illogical – he might be unsatisfied by the ruler, but being so devoted to this house and hating the enemy so much – how could this result in joining the enemy?
Finally, as a game-designer I should note this - Telltale should realize that there is a difference between a movie and a game. When the player is the main character and his death and failure are inevitable, this is not as cool as in a movie, since this means his choices were pretty much meaningless. The failures are felt as a punishment, the constant humiliation also reflects over the character as well. As this is well done and a nice surprise in the first acts, its continuation and no possibility for victory, revenge or justice in the end leads to quite unsatisfactory feeling of the game.
I know that TT have taken their conclusions of the relatively negative feedback (considering this is a Game of Thrones Telltale game) and they will make much better sequel. Any day now…

This game is really good, I mean it's REALLY good.  I typically don't play city builders but this game made me think twice.  In short, this is a city builder with a healthy dose of politics thrown in.  You have to keep foreign relations high and keep the factions happy (except Environmentalist because screw Environmentalist).  There's so much to consider when you're playing a game, how is my housing doing?  How much do the communists hate me?  Why do I find Sunny so annoying?  It sounds complicated but the game is full of hints if you know where to look.  The game does a great job of introducing core concepts and leaving the rest up to you.  This game is also long.  It's really long. If you have the collecter's edition it's even longer.  I've logged 5 hours completing the first 3 missions.  I've got 17 more to go in the main campaign, however many are in the Modern Times campaign, and a sandbox mode.  It may sound like quantity over quality but from what I've played each mission is very different from the last.  My one complaint is that the Environmentalist faction is completely broken.  In a game about managing resources I don't need to be penalized for managing my %&@*ing resources.
I am having a lot of fun with Tropico 4 and I hope you will too.

FTL: Overall a pretty damn good game.  If all you want to know is whether it is worth the 10 bucks, then you can stop reading here; it definately is.  Keep reading below if you want the good, the bad, and the ugly about the game.
The good:
(1) Rougelike elements, (always fun) so if your given the option to be a good guy or take the easy way out, it actually matters.  Personally i never risk my crew and rarely risk my ship, but that's just me.
(2) lots of different weapons systems, play styles, etc.  You will usually mix and match systems to find an adeal combo.
(3):  A fair amount of unlockable ships, each with different strengths and weaknesses.
(4) the way your ship's systems and repairs are set up.  Micro'ing your people into the most efficient ship possible is always fun.
(5) customizable ship names/crew names.  This was recently updated, and while its only a cosmetic, i really appreciated it.
The Bad:
(1) Randomized Stores: If you ever thought to yourself, hey wouldn't it be cool to do ____ + _____ and see how it works out?  If so, your out of luck.  The chances of you running into those two specific systems/weapons before the game ends pretty unlikely.  Usually the type of ship you build is a hodgepodge of whatever is avaliable and you can afford, even if it isn't what you want.
(2) One type of official game mode:  The race against the rebel fleet is fun, but after a while it gets old, especially if you just want to explore the galaxy.  After you beat the boss at the end, the game comes to a sudden hault as well, so there's that.
The Ugly: (minor complaints)
(1) The AI isn't the best:  I'm not saying its bad, and there are certainly times where the AI will give you a major run for your money.  But this is mostly due to overwealming strength and numbers, not smart play on their part.  After a few games you will begin to learn how to exploit the AI in ways that you couldn't if you were against a player or a better AI.  Heres a few things the AI wont do:  Target specific systems, Turn off systems (like oxygen) that can be used against them), Vent compartments, fire in vollies if you desyncronize them (they will usually have the same reset timer, but if you knock one out when it comes back on it will fire asap, and not wait for the other one).  Target specific systems while boarding, etc.
(2) Ship names can't be changed in mid flight: nothing too serious, just a cosmetic problem
(3) sometimes my game crashes: it used to be a real problem but not so much anymore.  They initiated an auto save function so now i don't loose my ship if my game decideds to shut down on me.

I set off with myself, my adopted Jamaican uncle JoJo, and my platonic female friend Sexjoke.
We realize we need food, meat specifically, to keep our spirits hardy during the long journey. We kill countless animals and store their corpses in our wagon, we will eat well...
My company and I come across a legendary beast of old. The magestic yet misleading unicorn. Our feast for flesh knows no limits, so I consider killing the beast for food. I, being the leader, decide otherwise. "No!" I tell my companions. "We shall follow this beast, and see will it takes us!"
Ah unicorns are shifty beasts are they not? The magestic animal had led us into an ambush, and its brothers and sisters charged at us, their horns thirsting for blood. We fend them off and pick up their corpses for meat.
We thought it was over, but suddenly a ferocious cross between a snake, a bird of prey, and a big cat comes out of nowhere to send us to meet our maker. A dragon! It breathes flaming hot fire onto our wagon, burning JoJo and I to death.
Haunting the cart, I watch as Sexjoke valiantly defeats the vile creature. I've never been more proud.
Mourning our deaths, she came across a roaring river, she could ford it, but she could attempt to jump over it.
She chooses the latter, but miraculously survives, only to land in a family of bears, waking them from their slumber.
One of them runs up to Sexjoke and hugs her, the force of said hug causes the poor lady to explode.
Our journey is over, but we unlocked Fiona's wagon from Shrek.
(10/10) Would die again...

I was very on board with this game during it's run. As I had been for every Telltale light adventure slash ineractive tv show game up until this point. I shed tears at the end of The Walking Dead and I anxiously awaited every delayed episode of The Wolf Among Us. Now believe me when I say that, after playing the last episode and reflecting on the series as a whole, Game of Thrones - A Telltale Games Series is utter garbage and indicative of the larger problem of the Telltale machine. It has turned into a meat grinder. Feed in successful property and churn out a Telltale game.
People will rail against this game for it's obvious lack of choice and they should. You can't seem to affect the story no matter how hard you try this time around. It runs on pure inertia. it keeps going because it has to. It doesn't care if you care or not, but the best Telltale games don't succeed because of their choices. The best Telltale games get by on pure heart. They make you care about the characters. The lack of choice isn't so frustrating when you are willing to go on the ride the story has invited you along for. You are willing to believe you can make things better for the characters you care about and you are anxious for them when they fail, but when you are actively trying to make a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ story better through a perceived branching narrative yet are still always forced to watch the same ♥♥♥♥♥♥ story you become frustrated.
That's the problem here. Game of Thrones - A Telltale Games Series just has a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ boring story with ♥♥♥♥♥♥ boring characters. It knocks you around with a few shocking twists, but ultimately that's all it is. As a game, as a piece of the larger ASOIAF universe, as an excercise in fiction, it just has no reason to be. Popular property goes in the meat grinder and this is what came out.
What I like:
-Plenty of wacky twists like in the first season of Breaking Bad when Jesse melts the guy in the bathtub.♥♥♥♥♥♥like that.
-Good voice over performances. Good music. Areas where Telltale always shines.
What I don't like:
-Story is boring
-Characters are boring.
-Choices are pointless.
-Nothing matters because the main characters, their house, and the concept of Ironwood around which the entire story revolves do not exist in the show or books.
-Inclusion of HBO characters is pointless, poorly executed and they look weird. On top of looking weird they look completely different from the style of all the other character models.
-The filter that tries to make it look like a painting really just makes it look ♥♥♥♥♥♥ and bad.
Telltale has made and still can make, from time to time, amazing games. I'm still looking forward to Walking Dead season 3 and Tales From The Borderlands took a so-so license and crafted an all-time great science fiction serial adventure, but this game does not live up to the standard they set. I can't recommend it. Google the plot synopsis and I'm sure you'll be just as entertained.

If you want to enter the world of classical wargaming and to be a groghead, here is where you should start.
Get this game, it is cheap and not like other wargames on the market which are very costly and only hardcore fans of wargaming will buy it, because they know exactly what they are getting.
Assault on Arnhem is not only affordable wargame, it is also very accessible and easy to understand and play.
It is simplified comparing to the big names of WW2 wargames, but it is still a true wargame with all supplies, moral, HQ, terrains and order of battle system and mechanism are just there.
The interface and tool tips are clear and easy to understand, the mission are just clear and have a lot of strategy to do.
Unlike most of WW2 wargames where you play mostly on divisions level, here you play on lower scale (battalions), where also each turn consist of 2 hours, you have also night battles.
Each mission have certain objective and must achieved within a certain time.
You can play either allies as an attackers with mostly paratroopers units, or as an axis to defend certain location.
If you like this game, you can later look for something similar but more complex like Slithering/ Matrix games such as Decisive Campaigns or War in the East.
If you are already a wargamer, it is nice to add this game to you collection which you can play interesting scenarios of operation Market Garden.

Grim Dawn is a third person action game in the vein of Diablo and Torchlight. The greatest draw it has fis character creation, since it's all live: choose a class after you start playing the game. Like the pistol you just found? Invest some points in Cunning and start firing away! Now that you've found a weapon you like what do you want to do with it? Dual-wield pistols? There's a class for that. Want to throw grenades to keep your enemies at bay? You can do that? What about summoning hellhounds and carrion birds? Time to double-class!
The maps are linear, at least so far as I've played, with little room repeated exploration. This could lead to the game becoming a slog after a few runs but it doesn't because the maps and the story are merely window-dressing for the excellent gameplay: freeform baddie smashing in whatever style you could want.

If you like Torchlight and want something grittier, give this a go.
Edit: If the game is bricked after the latest patch, go into 'Libraries>Documents>my games>Grim Dawn' and delete the Options file.  Right click on Grim Dawn in your Steam library and verify the games files. This worked on a Win 7x64 machine.

Operational-level simulation of Operation Market-Garden in 1944 with hexagon map, battalion-sized units, ranged attack for artillery and anti-tank units, supply, fog of war, and most importantly limited command points which forces players to prioritize some moves and combat over others.  This is the same operation that the book and film A Bridge Too Far is about, and this little game reminds me of a paper-and-dice game published by SPI in their magazine Fire & Movement in the early 1980s.  So far the AI at medium has been fairly easy for me to defeat, playing both Axis and Allies, but this can be played with up to four people and several AI levels.  Very good playability, with the full campaign lasting 4-6 hours in single player mode.  I only wish the AI came in crazy aggressive mode because so far it has been a competent but sedate opponent.  Recommended.

Tropico 4: Steam Special Edition is the first game from Tropico series I have played. Here are my likes and dislikes:
Pros:
- Great sense of humor (no matter if you are interested in politic related issues or not the humor is great! building descriptions, radio messages, advisors, missions all are really funny - even for an adult player).
- A decent graphic with a very detailed zoom-in option
- 3-scale game speed up option - I usualy play in the fastest game mode
- a wide variety of buildings - a lot of industrial buildings, tourist attractions, housing and social facilities and governmental institutions
- interesting economy and political mechanisms -> as the el-presidente you make very important decisions (concerning economy, defence, external or interial policy, education etc.) and you can see what are the effects of your choices
- factions - citizens in your island are diveded into a few major factions (religious, nationalists, communist etc.). Your job is to make them happy... or make them be quit :)
- a lot of ways you can deal with unhappy citizens - you can bribe one, arrest him/her, arrange accident :) etc.
- Music -> you can't hold your feet calm while playing to this caribbean music :)
Cons:
- a little bit similar development pattern - as the objectives in every mission are different, there is a very similar pattern to complete them. You need a lot of money. You can either develop your industry or invest in tourism. However, once you will find the pattern you like the most you do the same thing in every mission. All over again.
- Bugged mission 18 (however bug doesn't occur always)
- music - at the beginning you really like it... but after some time you discover that there are just 3 or 4 songs.... for hours of playing way too little.
- it is difficult to lose the game - I am in mission 19 and so far I haven't lost one single game (although I needed to restart one mission :P )
Finally, my opinion is... you definately should buy this game. If you enjoy strategy games based on economy and political grounds it is something for you. After hours of playing there is always something new you haven't seen yet. And after all, it is so fun to be El Presidente :P

FTL: Overall a pretty damn good game.  If all you want to know is whether it is worth the 10 bucks, then you can stop reading here; it definately is.  Keep reading below if you want the good, the bad, and the ugly about the game.
The good:
(1) Rougelike elements, (always fun) so if your given the option to be a good guy or take the easy way out, it actually matters.  Personally i never risk my crew and rarely risk my ship, but that's just me.
(2) lots of different weapons systems, play styles, etc.  You will usually mix and match systems to find an adeal combo.
(3):  A fair amount of unlockable ships, each with different strengths and weaknesses.
(4) the way your ship's systems and repairs are set up.  Micro'ing your people into the most efficient ship possible is always fun.
(5) customizable ship names/crew names.  This was recently updated, and while its only a cosmetic, i really appreciated it.
The Bad:
(1) Randomized Stores: If you ever thought to yourself, hey wouldn't it be cool to do ____ + _____ and see how it works out?  If so, your out of luck.  The chances of you running into those two specific systems/weapons before the game ends pretty unlikely.  Usually the type of ship you build is a hodgepodge of whatever is avaliable and you can afford, even if it isn't what you want.
(2) One type of official game mode:  The race against the rebel fleet is fun, but after a while it gets old, especially if you just want to explore the galaxy.  After you beat the boss at the end, the game comes to a sudden hault as well, so there's that.
The Ugly: (minor complaints)
(1) The AI isn't the best:  I'm not saying its bad, and there are certainly times where the AI will give you a major run for your money.  But this is mostly due to overwealming strength and numbers, not smart play on their part.  After a few games you will begin to learn how to exploit the AI in ways that you couldn't if you were against a player or a better AI.  Heres a few things the AI wont do:  Target specific systems, Turn off systems (like oxygen) that can be used against them), Vent compartments, fire in vollies if you desyncronize them (they will usually have the same reset timer, but if you knock one out when it comes back on it will fire asap, and not wait for the other one).  Target specific systems while boarding, etc.
(2) Ship names can't be changed in mid flight: nothing too serious, just a cosmetic problem
(3) sometimes my game crashes: it used to be a real problem but not so much anymore.  They initiated an auto save function so now i don't loose my ship if my game decideds to shut down on me.

Sadly, Steam does not allow a "neutral" review, because this game might deserve that, but since I can only choose "yes" or "no" I'll have to go with the latter.
Alright, do you remember the great atmosphere and story of the original Alan Wake as well as the 2 DLC episodes? No? Then play those. If you already did that, you may kindly skip American Nightmare if you're into the game for those reasons.
Story spoilers if you have not played the original Alan Wake and bonus episodes:
The game takes place at 3 locations, which you will each visit three times, because time loop. Yay. Each time the story adapts to what you previously did. No, this does not mean player freedom, it's strictly linear. On your journy you will battle Taken (some new and cool enemies, which sadly don't change the combat system at all) with new weaponry (yes, assault rifles, yawn), save damsels in distress and collect almost unmissable manuscript pages.
Combat: Like I said it's just more of the same, no real new stuff.
Setting: Arizona. Desert. Boring as ♥♥♥♥. It's just an action slasher setting instead of a claustrophibic "omg I'm going to die" one. Not feeling it.
Collectibles: The manuscript pages are utterly boring. Most aren't even related to actual events in the game. They're just wasted money for the voice actor to speak these lines. The TVs are also back. Unfortunately what was a really great feature in Alan Wake has turned into an egocentric♥♥♥♥♥♥show of Mr. Scratch taunting you every time. The first TV was already boring, but omg it gets worse...
And some radio stations are also back again...and equally boring. They're only about the Old Gods of Asgard and Barry Wheeler as well as Alice Wake's movie. So 2 interviews in fact and some random callers in between. Jesus, how can you mess something like this up?
Story: Don't even get me started here. The little actual dialogue there is in the game is terrible and inconsequential. The narrator does an "ok" job, but the story itself is so badly written you don't care about that anyway. You just wish you could skip the ♥♥♥♥ing cutscenes instead of watching the same oil derrick get smashed 3 times in exactly the same way. ♥♥♥♥ that.
Overall AN offers nothing that would really add to the universe. You will complete the story on "normal" (only 2 difficulties this time around) in about 4 hours at most without dying. Ammunition and supplies are plenty, only health can be an issue if you take a surprise attack and can't regenerate a complete health bubble (once it's gone it's gone and you need a light source). When you're done with the "story" you can play arcade battles. Yay. This is not what Alan Wake is or should be about imho, but ok...you may pick it up during a sale. 10 bucks is still too expensive imho.
I dearly hope we will actually get a good AW successor at some point...or none at all, I was ok with the original ending.

What it's NOT, is a fully formed soccer game. That should be obvious from the title alone.
What it IS though, is a very fun and humourous sports game based loosely on football/soccer, sort of like Sensible World of Soccer meets Rocket League (kinda?). It's not meant to be taken seriously. It is to the FIFA games what a kickabout in the playground is to the Champion's League. Basic, simple, innocent fun for half an hour or so at a time.
There are a few things I'd consider 'missing' (the ability to customise your squad's player names, individual player stats (such as goals scored/tackle percentage/pass percentage, etc. Little things to get you more invested in your team). But for £2.50 it's hard to argue that these are sorely missed.

I generally like to get a dollar an hour out of playing a game, if possible. At that rate, I consider a game a wondrous success for raw entertainment value, alone.
This game has 6 hours on it from me, as of writing this, At 3 dollars, that's $.50 an hour for that entertainment.
It's funny, raw and just exactly what it is meant to be. Buy it, enjoy it, spread the word!

Presenting itself as an episode of a Twilight Zone-esque television show called "Night Springs," complete with a Rod Serling soundalike narrator, Alan Wake's American Nightmare sees the titular hero facing off against an evil manifestation of himself, called Mr. Scratch. Scratch has taken up residence in a small Arizona town, and has turned most of the population into zombie-like hostiles called "the taken." Much of Alan Wake's American Nightmare's gameplay involves dealing with the taken, who attack Wake at regular intervals. The taken are usually protected by a cloak of shadows, which must be "burned" away using Wake's flashlight beam before he can then employ firearms to permanently put them on the other side of the dirt. Dodging enemy melee attacks is a heavily emphasized element of the gameplay: successfully doing it both slows down time and lets Wake get some distance from bad guys.
It's funny and fun, and lays a very solid foundation for the inevitable GotY 2018 "Kickmen 2"

P2W = Yes
Horrible class balancing = Yes
Beautiful but garbage engine = Yes
RNG mechanics ruining the game = Yes
I have around 300 hours played (as of this post), and 200 of them are probably pure gameplay. It took me about 50 hours to realize that all this game is, is a money grabbing machine - that's it. The texture pop-in is horrendous, the enchanting system is absolutely stupid, there's zero class balancing in this game. You can buy superior gear with real money, so yes, it is pay-to-win, and people saying otherwise are just blindly defending their precious little game. You can use your VISA card to obtain in-game currency to buy superior gear, that's just facts.
This game would have been great if they weren't promoting "AFK gameplay", to get your character stronger/richer etc. This game would have been great if they took time to balance the classes. The game would have been great if they got rid of the absolutely stupid RNG mechanics. If they would get rid of the P2W features this game would be great.
It had potential, but they ruined it. That's pretty much it.
And to the all the angry BDO fans out there going "WHAT DO YOU MEAN P2W!?!?!?":
You can use your VISA card to purchase cosmetics in the pearl shop. For example, you can purchase the Blazing Inferno costume (striker costume) that you then sell in the in-game auction house for silver.
And considering that all the gear you need in the game can be obtained with silver, then if you can sell enough pearl shop items for silver, it's P2W, by definition.
So you can literally sell costume after costume after costume to get silver and buy, for example, a TET Gardbrace. Yes, there is a cooldown on how many items you can sell like that, but that does not matter. You can still obtain good gear by using your VISA card.
This is by definition P2W, aboslutely and undoubtedly.
VISA card -> Pearls -> Buy costume -> Sell costume @ in-game auction house -> Obtain silver -> Buy superior gear using the silver you just got from using your VISA card.
That's the truth.
