Chase me, chase me!  I’ve always told my kids ‘you can’t be chased if you don’t run’...but in Dying Light there’s nothing quite like the feral scream of newly minted zombies racing toward you, arms flailing as they rapidly zero-in on your position – or a nighttime cuddle from a volatile as you fumble for your UV light....soooo RUN it is!
I haven’t felt that thrill of being chased for years; where you can almost feel the hands reaching for your shoulder as you sprint up and over obstacles, and then the immense relief landing in a safe house.  Ahhh bliss.  There is real sense of terror when it gets dark and it’s pretty frightening.  Shortly after playing one night, I stepped out on my deck and felt an eerie sense of something lurking just beyond the light.  I admit I was a bit freaked out by the volatiles am still reluctant to go into their nests.
During those intense swarms, flight is sometimes the best course of action but is also preferable when the weapons crap out mid-scuffle, which happens a lot.  Grappling with parkour is a really fun way to get around and avoid those baddies and to explore.  However I found the over-abundance of weapon changes, along with multiple menus for upgrading, blueprinting, creating, repairing, okaying, entering, confirming, extremely time-consuming and frustrating.   Even 80 hours in, the process of crafting, sorting, and equipping is tiresome and takes you out of the game, forcing decisions about things you don’t necessarily care about.  I usually stuck with a few effective favs just to avoid leaving gameplay for extended periods of time.
I was pleasantly surprised at how seamless co-op worked; where we could join/drop on a whim with no disruption to the other.  The two of us enjoyed completing the various fetch and carry tasks while watching each other’s backs while picking locks.  I had hoped for a later skill that would simplify some tasks, such as the lock-picking, automatically crafting medical kits, providing an ability to pick up and throw any object, obtaining goodies without opening each and every cupboard, locker, basket, etc. -- but no such luck.   We could spend hours just ransacking an area, then crafting, shuffling backpacks, changing inventories, etc. before actually moving ahead with the game; I can’t stress how monotonous it became later in the story.
Other than the cumbersome menus, Dying Light has so much more to offer than Dead Island; the zombie NPCs are scary, the open environment is pretty spectacular, and the story is more immersive.  There are times when the fetch/carry and looting seems formulaic but overall the story moves enough to keep things fresh. Even though the main protagonist seems wooden at times, his character works because he’s in a multicultural crazy world where the NPCs provide more richness to the story.
The Following expansion has the added element of driving a tricked out buggy throughout the open countryside.  It’s a fun addition but there are times I miss the rooftop excursions, especially at night.  The quests and storyline in the Following didn’t hold my interest much; I lost track of what was actually going on and didn’t really care.  I just didn’t enjoy the expansion despite the cool buggy, but was eager to go back to the Slums and Old Town to finish some of the missed achievements, and maybe craft something extra special for the occasion.

Hello!
This is my review for All You Can Eat! Looking over it I think my review is not so much a review to encourage/discourage people from buying the game as it is an in depth analysis of what I thought about the game, what I liked and didn't like and why I liked and didn't like things. If that's your thing, stick around, if not... well......
Overview And Quick Review!
The game's description and many reviewers have already give great briefs of what this game is all about so I'll keep mine short:
All You Can Eat is a short 20-30 minute point and click adventure game hand drawn and laid out in the style of a comic book in which you play as unnamed guy who has managed to live in an All You Can Eat Diner for ten years due to a crazy loophole in an All You Can Eat coupon he bought that lets him eat as much food as he wants as long as he stays in the diner! Sadly, one day he discovers his life is about to fall apart as the diner is about to close down due to a local corporation buying it out! This pushes nameless guy to travel around the city and talk to people, collect items and solve some puzzles classic point and click adventure style as he tries to find some way of stopping the corporation in order to keep the Diner around! Because what will he do otherwise? Get a job? NEVER!
+ You can print off your play-through of the game after you have completed it.
My Overall Positives:
0 The aesthetic
0 It’s not strictly linear
0 Small nuances and attention to detail.
0 Charming characters and charming dialogue: My favourite line was when the MC tell the secretary         he is the boss’ mistress and she says “No, that’s me.”
0 Color/Colour Blind mode! More games should have this! I know this game probably wasn’t that hard to make a Color/Colour blind mode for but still!
0 Still Camera Mode!
0 It’s in Russian too
0 You can print it out
My Overall Negatives:
0 Weak plot!
0 The humour wasn’t always my cup of tea!
0 The story, characters and dialogue are not anything too spectacular
0 Printing it out has some issues – the game prints out EVERYTHING you have done in the game, which can cause the comic to not flow well; if you viewed the pizza roll 5 times in a row it will show up in your printed comic five times in a row. And due to fact that I click on things multiple times throughout out a play-through when I play games, the PDF file of my first play-through, if printed out, would be 300+ A4 pages!!!
I would consider this game worth a buy, it’s charming, it is dirt cheap and I think the concept of a point and click comic book adventure game has potential! Buy it as a small gift for a friend, for your kid (although I would consider the dialogue in this game to be at least PG). And this game is developer’s first I think! The purpose of this game is to see if people are interested in playing a larger, more fleshed out game of this style. So if you’re interested in critiquing new developers buy the game and write a review! Or if you want to support this new developer, buy the game!
If you like comic books give this game a shot too!
Analysis
My Introduction To The Game
Back in July I was scrolling through the videos of a youtuber I had only recently discovered: TheJessaChannel, and I noticed one of her recent videos had the word GIVEAWAY in it so of course I clicked on it. It turned out she was giving away two Steam keys for a game she had recently let's played (Which I hadn't watched) which was, wait for it, All You Can Eat! So I entered the giveaway and... I won a key! So without her video I probably wouldn't have discovered this game so soon! And honestly, I also probably would not have gotten around to buying it anytime soon if she hadn't gifted it to me. So thank you Jessa! Of course, I didn't get around to playing it until September, which I feel bad about, but now that I have I've got a few things to say about it!
My Thoughts On Story, Characters And Dialogue
All You Can Eat's story is definitely strange, goofy and dare I say original. But the plot definitely takes a back seat to the dialogue. It's incredibly simple as most 10-30 minute games are, which is not a bad thing by itself, but due to finding the story uninteresting and un-intriguing, its simplicity ended up making it a bit difficult for me to sometimes fully appreciate the characters and all of the dialogue since I didn't really care about the outcome of the story. And I found the ending managed to be anti-climactic for me despite already finding the plot lack-luster.
The characters and dialogue are definitely the focus of the game compared to the plot. The characters and dialogue are definitely charming and your interactions with them along with the MC's observations and inner thoughts actually manage to mostly distract you from the lack of plot! But at times I wasn't really a fan of some of the humour and the three panel layout of dialogue, I found it a bit too casual for my tastes but then again I also don't read comic books so it's possible this type of story-telling just isn't for me.
Overall, I personally found the story to be un-intriguing, nothing about it made me interested in how it was all going to end. I definitely think the characters and dialogue are much better, but I think the plot lets it down, and again, I found it to be a bit too casual for my tastes, and just not my kind of story-telling.
This game's story, plot and dialogue were like a straight line for me. It is nothing horrible by a long shot but, also nothing that great or memorable. I care about the story and characters at the end of the game almost the same amount as I did at the start. If you are looking for a great story in a video game, I would recommend many other games before this one.
But if you like comics I recommend trying this game since it is extremely cheap and I think the developers would be particularly interested in knowing what a comic lover thinks of this especially since the purpose of this game existing is partly for them to see if this type of game is what people would like to see more of.
One last thing, I have heard some people say this game is more suited for children because of its length and casualness ("young" children I'm guessing since I myself am 16), and I agree somewhat, although I found some of the dialogue to be what some would consider to be a bit unsuitable for children but I don’t think it’s too bad, I’d say PG.

I love ASOIAF and i love telltale games, so the Reeses Cup theorm lead me to believe i would really enjoy this game.  However what could be a fun experience is hamstrung almost immediately by a series of huge problems on a conceptual level
The first and most egregious of these problems is that rather than trying to build its' own version of continuity like the relationship between the books and the show; the game instead feels weirdly beholden to the cannon of the show. None of the characters you play as will have appeared in either the books or the show. And you quickly realize that even though you may encounter familliar characters dring the course of the game, you can't really impact on them in any sort of meaningful way.  The ergeious amounts of plot armor wouldn't be so frustrating on their own. But it leads to a series of pivitol choices where you know whatever you decide will be completely meaningless because it's sucess or failure wouldn't align with the show.  This design ends up negating choice in a game where that is literally all you do.
This leads me to my second issue with the game, choice. Telltale games have always talked a bigger game than they've delivered when it comes to choice. No matter what you do you're going to end up on one side of a series of binary set pieces. In a stark and post apocalyptic world like The Walking Dead, these kind of decisions make sense. Every choice is for survival and the wrong ones will kill. However this forulma doesn't really work in the more nuanced world of GOT, particularly with the amount the game trys to push the political intrigue angle. Yes, both worlds are brutal and bleak- but the GOT world is built not on mere survival but a complicated tapestry of relationships and alliances. An element that completely disappears when exposed to the kind of predictable dichotomy that is intrinsic to the TellTale games format.
Finally, lets talk about twists. This game treats twists like Lenny from of Mice and Men treats rabbits, taking something fun and cool and abusing it to death. I played the game through in its entirity and i felt like every 15 minutes some new horrible thing happened that i was supposed to feel bad about but i couldnt be bothered to give a♥♥♥♥♥♥because they were so random and outside of my control that i just decided not to get invested in any of the characters. Seriously, after the second or third surprise the gimmick ( and that's what it is a gimmick) lost all signifigance. The frequency and intensity with which these dramatic moments are applied to the lackluster story are not only detrimental to good story telling, they're anathema to it. This can be seen in the plot holes and mcguffins that plauge the games' story, and a cast of characters you couldn't get invested in even if they weren't all about to die at any moment for no reason.
All in all, the main problem with the game is that it's trying to be a Pg-13 version of the show. This remake of the 1993 X-COM: UFO Defense, an obtuse and painful but ultimately satisfying game, attempts to bring UFO Defense into the 21st century while also improving on the original game's intentions. Sadly, (or happily depending on your faith in such an endeavor) all of these changes present a double-edged sword. For every system Enemy Unknown improves - and they are solid improvements - something of the freedom or atmosphere of the original is lost. Some sacrifices are small but expected, such as the way you've built your base not having an effect on base invasions (a feature that itself was only added to the remake with the Enemy Within expansion). Others are a bit more surprising, such as the total change in atmosphere brought about by taking the original troop limit of 14 down to the much smaller squad of 6. Limiting the number of soldiers on the field at a time means that each individual is more valuable and stands out more readily which is also bolstered by an increased level of customization. I found myself even more attached to my Enemy Unknown soldiers than my UFO Defense regulars and as that attachment was one of the biggest joys of the original, it's hard not to consider that a successful change. However, with only 6 soldiers gaining battle experience at a time, any casualty is devastating, meaning you can no longer afford to send a group of bright-eyed red shirted rookies into a situation as you, an experienced commander, know it is unlikely they will survive. So that sense of constant Pyrrhic victories, of losing three men to breach a downed UFO and eliminate the final alien, are lost to gain a more beloved solider with a richer player-made story. This difference encapsulates the transition between the two games. While UFO Defense focused on the greater conflict, with individual soldiers representing little more than a resource, Enemy Unknown focuses on those called to fight and how this conflict affects them. The overarching narrative hasn't changed much, but the change in perspective makes for a unique, fresh experience.
That being said, Enemy Unknown can stand (and fall) on its own as well. The terror of a completely unknown threat and the slow unveiling of what it is you're fighting and why it's fighting you is satisfying without depending on the crutch of name dropping the original's enemies. The unlikelihood of any one shot being 100% certain in accuracy or damage forces the player to come up with backup plans and to deal with the unexpected, keeping the player on his or her toes. Sometimes, however, the unexpected comes not from an intended monkey wrench, but from an obtuseness in the game's mechanics. After completing two full games on two different difficulties, I still have a very poor idea of what a soldier will or will not be able to see and where. This disastrous flaw could have easily been corrected if I had the option to see from the soldier's point of view. Graphical glitches are also relatively common leading to a rushed and unfinished feel which is only compounded by the expansion, Enemy Within. Meld - a resource introduced in the expansion to fuel the new gene modifying and MEC trooper initiatives - both adds a new time element to missions and sticks out as completely artificial. Again this issue seems like it could be simply resolved with a bit more story relevance and/or more logical placements. The 'abduction' mission type seems equally artificial in that they always occur in threes, leaving the commander to choose only one site to defend while leaving the others to their fate and causing panic across those continents. The player is left with no solution to this 'one step forward two steps back' situation nor is there any explanation for why that's so. Which leads me to my biggest complaint about Enemy Unknown: The whole experience feels like it's on rails. Not only doesn't the alien invasion operate on its own independent timescale (a theme which is repeated with the aliens I meet in the field), but it doesn't even seem like anything I as the player do has an affect on how the invasion plays out, past the basic win-lose proposition. Due to this design direction, some story elements can't reach a satisfying conclusion. For instance, the comparison between the alien's situation and XCOM's current trajectory never pays off. The aliens seem to have undergone some great cruelty which is played up from the beginning as being both inhumane and the reason they're so effective, but there is little to no consequence for the XCOM project visiting the same cruelty on its own soldiers to match the enemy's results. This is possibly the most interesting story this setting has to tell and yet it's simply pushed aside once the situation is realized.
Stumbling blocks like these keep this exciting, ensnaring game from achieving the greatness it seems to be aiming for. But if you're prepared for a little (or a lot) of that 'what could have been' frustration, it's not the worst way to spend a good chunk of your time.

Tropico 4, for lack of a better definition, is kind of like SimCity. But where SimCity stands as placing you as the mayor of a common, modern American city, Tropico puts you in the position of "El Presidente", the leader of a small Caribbean island nation at the height of the Cold War.
Tropico 4 is a delightful game, and carries a number of excellent qualities. It exhibits a long, engaging campaign and offers moderate replay value for fans of city-building simulations. However, the true shine to Tropico is the tongue-in-cheek humor that underlies all gameplay and all story elements. The game has a relatively realistic basis to itself, but doesn't hesitate to recognize itself as what it essentially is - a Caribbean Dictator SimCity. And it does it
. Not only does the game make a couple of cheeky references, but it takes the mickey out of nearly everything within itself and keeps the mood lighthearted.
In terms of gameplay, Tropico 4 maintains a solid city-building mechanic, but tacks on the added difficulty of managing and keeping the numerous factions and foreign countries in and around your island happy. There are the profit-obsessed Capitalists, the overzealous Communists, the hippy-heavy Environmentalists, and even skinhead Nationalists. Paired with the United States and the USSR breathing down your neck, it makes for interesting and suprisingly difficult gameplay. However, you will be rewarded graciously for dealing with each of the factions and nations as you grow your legacy as "El Presidente".
I would recommend this game to most people, but this is a DEFINITE BUY for fans of city-builders.
Also - to all you soon-to-be Presidentes, heres a few helpful tips:
1. Set up your economy first.
2. Clinics and Churches are more necessary than you may think.
3. I learned this late in my play sessions: Media is suprisingly helpful. You'd be suprised what a single newspaper can do.
4. You DON'T need the DLC to play and have fun.
5. In Vanilla Tropico 4 - power is for ♥♥♥♥♥es. Only make power plants if you are rich or really need them.
6. In Modern Times Tropico 4 - power is for pros. Power is... well, power.
7. Industry will always make you more money than agriculture.
8. Agriculture is always more stable than industry.
9.
This will eventually come to you in time.
10. Don't be an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. Social Security is the best thing you can have if you know what you're doing.
Have fun, Presidente!

Despite the overwhelming negative reviews on the Steam page, I still think this game is quite fun when play casually with friends.  The campaign itself is alright, but not to the quality one can find in games such as StarCraft 2.  I do, however, find the the Theater of War game mode quite enjoyable.  The Theater of War features many single player challenge modes and multiplayer co-op modes on unique maps or unique settings.  Some I think are more interesting than the campaign.  Most Theater of War scenarios are DLC, but it is really fun for those seeking more single player or co-op missions to play.
Other DLC, on the other hand, are where the negative reviews are targeted.  The vehicle camouflage patterns and faceplates offers nothing more than cosmetic changes.  Yet they are quite expensive.  One vehicle pattern is $1.99 for one type (light, medium, or heavy) of vehicle, which is not really a fair business strategy in my opinion.  Commander DLC however, is really essential to the game because of the strategies they can offer.  At the time this review is written, the game includes about 9 commanders for both Soviet and German.  All others are DLC; which range from $2.99 to $3.99.  Really quite pricey.  But these are what really changes the tactic and strategies for the game.  I really think the game should come with more free commanders when purchased.
Some DLC commanders were once overpowered, but they have been addressed by the developer and balanced out.  If you really want to have the most out of this game, you might really have to invest in some DLC.  But the game itself is still very fun to play without all the extra DLC.  The system where units’ vision can be block by walls and smoke is really unique in a way where one can easily set up ambush behind obstacle to surprise the enemies.  Blowing holes on frozen river and watch enemy tanks slowly sink into the freezing water is also amusing.
I still recommend anyone who are interested in the WWII era and enjoy strategy games to give this game a try.  I do sincerely hope that the developer can learn from all the other negative feedbacks of the overpriced DLC and make changes to the DLC business model in the future.

I really want to give this game a thumbs up.
I love the setting: ice age Europe, teaming with (now extinct) life and other human species - like Neanderthals!
There is so much potential there. Like, for instance, this could be a moral tale about how humans (esp. homo sapiens) have a penchant for making other things extinct. You know... anything that isn't us.
Did we kill the Neanderthals? Probably. Did we kill all of the big ice age animals that roamed the plains of Europe and the Americas? Probably. Are any of these themes explored in the story of Far Cry Primal? No.
And that's the problem with this game: the game world is so beautifully realized, and the game mechanics are nice (although basically a copy-paste of the classic Ubisoft formula)... BUT THERE IS NO STORY. THERE IS ABSOLUTELY NO STORY.
Let me say that again: THIS GAME'S FATAL FLAW IS A LACK OF ANY COMPELLING STORYLINE OR COMPELLING CHARACTERS.
What a shame, too. What a waste. Maybe the next iteration will have a worthwhile narrative to keep things going.

Adoro este juego.
Empece a jugar este verano y madre mía, ¿Cuán profundo puede llegar a ser?
Este es un juego para disfrutar a fuego lento, hay tanto que hacer y experimentar... Mucha gente se satura al principio, quieren ser los mejores en cuestión de un mes o dos y acaban quemandose. Tomatelo con calma, se humilde en tus comienzos, encuentra una buena guild que te guie y disfruta el viaje.
Elige tu modo de juego, PVP, PVE o Life Skiller, no importa que decidas, el juego te ayudara y sentirás que el progreso vale la pena, bien sea cocinando, pescando, matando monstruos sin parar, criando caballos en tu establo, haciendo de leñador, minero, matando bosses, haciendo arenas de combate, cosechando en tu granja agricola o navegando los grandes mares, no hay fin a lo que puedes hacer en este juego.
Además, el juego cuenta con un montón de mecánicas AFK, para aquellos que no disponen de mucho tiempo para jugar, pero aún así desean mejorar las características de sus personajes o hacer dinero.
Otro gran punto fuerte de este juego es cuan controlado esta el flujo monetario, para prevenir la tipica inflación asesina de MMORPGs. El sistema es justo y hace lo mejor que puede para mantener los precios en ciertos rangos para que no se disparen. Además previenen que se cree demasiado dinero, aun cuando la sensación para el jugador es que es facil reunirlo.
Veo que los desarrolladores le han puesto mucho cariño a este juego, de verdad quieren que dure mucho tiempo y sea disfrutable, siendo este lo más balanceado posible (Evidentemente nadie es perfecto, algunos problemillas siempre hay que ajustar, peor nada que rompa el juego).
En fin, esa es mi experiencia y reseña, me encanta este juego, he estado buscando esta experiencia durante años y no la encontre hasta que BDO se cruzo en mi vida jugona este verano de 2017. Lo recomiendo al 100% para jugadores hardcore de MMORPGs.

So this game is a big load of fun, but I am not so sure everyone will appreciate it. Anyone who has played the GTA and SR franchises over the years knows that Saints Row has been the goofier, more slapstick of the two. But this one takes that factor and amps it up to 11.
There are a few things that make this game feel a little bland at times. The environment, characters and tone from SR3 has not changed much, and the city itself is a copy paste with some editing thrown in. If you drive cars and shoot guns, playing this in the more traditional GTA style, then you will most likely become very bored. In fact, very few missions or story aspects really depend on you even having guns or cars. The Super Power aspect of the game seriously side-lines what a lot of traditional GTA gamers might be there to enjoy.
The story is outright weird. While the last game changed the tone of the series from Gang Banger to Tech Spy Mobster, it still essentially was all about guns, gangs, cars. This game however starts you off in the seat of the President, to begin your term of success..... right as aliens invade. Through the story, you acquire Super Powers to fight these new overlords, each power making you more capable of taking on the bigger badder enemies that gradually surface.
The super powers are the real star of the show in this game. Strangely enough, it does a better job with powers and execution of their mechanics than a lot of super hero games out there. And the way they come by the powers is fun, albeit not at all original.
While the game feels a little short and out of place at times with it's hokey jokes and constant throwbacks to the previous games, it definitely tells a new and, if nothing else, interesting story driven by outrageous game mechanics. If you want the cool design and rigid controls of the GTA or earlier SR series, don't buy this game. But if you are open minded to a new experience surrounding the slapstick goofball story SR3 took on, then buy with confidence and enjoy!

This wasn't bad but it certainly wasn't one of TellTale's better games. The biggest issue with this game is that it features quite a few characters from the TV series in prominent positions in relation to your character. What worked well with The Walking Dead was that your story was separate from the comic/TV characters for the most part you were experiencing their world but there was room for unique situations and a different perspective on the world.
While I think cameo appearances in moderation is alright you were far too close to canon characters to think your actions would make a difference. I like the Margery from far away but being in direct contact with her, and various Lannister characters made me play with preconceived notions. For example giving me an option to attack Ramsey, who we know wouldn't die was a waste of time. I altered my decisions to how I knew certain characters would react.
This takes away from "your choices matter" gameplay to "here's two choices that don't matter". There was only one or two times where I felt I was making a real decision but one time in five episodes is pretty lacking for choice.
Despite those things I would still recommend this game on story alone. It was a highly entertaining adventure game that didn't get boring, featured various locations in the Game of Thrones world, the voice acting and story were pretty good. If you haven't experienced the books or the TV show I think you'd enjoy this game. If you are an avid watcher or reader of the series you might feel it a bit lackluster and obvious. If there is a season two of this I hope TT would take a page from TWD series and separate their story from the canon characters for a more unique experience. And with a world as robust and diverse as GoT is there's no reason it couldn't.

We were promised a much needed overhaul of Cricket Captain for 2014, but sadly the superficial and inconsistent changes fail to remedy the series' regular failings. The interface has been modernized, which is nice, but the new interface is poorly executed. Columns don't always line up when looking at stats, numbers have bits chopped off, letter spacing is irregular, ect. It has never been a pretty game, but the new interface is seriously ugly to look at, and if you have a decent size monitor you'll find yourself playing it in a window to make it bearable visually. The only positive is the inclusion of a "hawkeye" style ball tracker, which is useful when bowling in T20.
The "new" match engine is identical to previous years - the tweaks have been to graphics rather than game play, and even that hasn't really worked, as there is now an irritating lag when skipping through a highlight. Batting in T20 is still impossibly hard if you don't have a couple of star names, and T20 matches generally are still as boring and formulaic as before. The better side wins nine times out of ten, which completely negates the point of playing a management sim. 50 over and four day cricket allow you to have more of an effect on the result, but the flaws remain. The same plans work every time when bowling, and if you deviate from the steady progression of aggression when batting you invariably fail. There is zero opportunity to try something different, and the game is crying out for the kind of specific instructions that a real cricket captain would issue.
The reviewer who compared this game to Football Manager must be joking. Football Manager has an almost infinite number of formations/tactical instructions/player instructions, whilst this has one slider to control batting and two to control bowling. Even if you're desperate to use an updated database then Cricket Captain 2014 is overpriced for such a basic simulation. Buy Don Bradman Cricket or Football Manager 2014 instead.

ZeniMax can suck it; the company took a free-to-play game (which was a scaled-down version of Quake III - a game from the late 90s) and started charging for it. Here's my original review of Quake Live (from when the game was free-to-play, as it was always intended to be):
----------------------------------------
As a free, scaled-down version of Quake III Gold, Quake Live is a fun game that's worth playing for times when you grow tired of single-player games and feel like interacting with real opponents (as opposed to AI). The game still looks and plays great, but as with any online multiplayer mode, the quality of your experience will depend at least partly on who you play with.
I first played Quake Live not long after it was officially hosted as an ad-sponsored, web browser-based game. For some reason, I could not log into the Steam port of Quake Live with the profile I created for playing the game within web browsers. However, my main complaint is that the Steam Port freezes regularly on my machine.
The Steam port of Quake Live freezes every time I play the game for more than 15 minutes on my Phenom II rig that is more than capable of playing it. I have deleted and re-downloaded the game, but the problem does not go away. Before a fatal freeze occurs, I can have Steam validate the integrity of the game's cache and it will turn up fine. After a freeze, that same check will produce this result: "1 file failed to validate and will be reacquired." What gives?
The only game that freezes on me with the same regularity as Quake Live is Duke Nukem Forever. Given that Quake Live is a free game (and, unlike Duke Nukem Forever, isn't a letdown in the gameplay department), I recommend this game to anyone craving some online arena action.
------------------------
Back to the present: I can't possibly recommend this game to anyone. ZeniMax will never get another penny from me again. (I bought games published by Bethesda in the past, but will no longer do so.)

At the end of Alan Wake, we were promised that “Alan Wake’s journey through the night will continue.” Naturally, I believed that meant a sequel somewhere in the near future, so when Alan Wake’s American Nightmare was announced, I assumed it was that sequel. Rather than being a sequel, however, American Nightmare is more of an Alan Wake 1.5, a DLC-like expansion (think Red Dead Redemption’s Undead Nightmare or Infamous: Second Son’s First Light) that slightly continues the plot of the original, while still managing to ask more questions than give answers.
That in itself doesn’t sound very impressive, except perhaps for the die-hard Alan Wake cultists. However, in some important ways, American Nightmare is better than the original.
One of my biggest complaints of the original game was the dodge button, which rarely ever worked for me. In American Nightmare, it works almost flawlessly. Also, batteries recharge almost instantly. I don’t think I changed the battery more than twice in my entire play through, including all the challenges. With such a large focus placed on mobility in fights, these are extremely useful and welcome changes.
The areas to explore are much smaller than in Alan Wake, but I like how they still have a very large feel to them. Once again, there are manuscript pages to find, but locating them is much easier: Instead of solely hunting for glowing sheets of paper, when you get close enough to one, it appears on the mini-map as a circled question mark. Like in the previous entry, collecting manuscript pages give deeper insight to the story, but now they also allow you to unlock cases with high powered weapons in both the story and challenges. Thanks to being more convenient to find, players don’t have to worry about feeling outmatched by the more powerful Taken.
What makes this game really shine, however, are the challenges (and the new Poets of the Fall songs). You spawn in one of multiple areas, none of which are directly from the story, and are tasked with fighting back the Taken until the sun comes up (ten minutes). Defeating Taken in rapid succession increases your score multiplier, and getting hit by them resets it. The trick is balancing picking up finite ammo, weapons, flares, and flashbangs while blasting unlimited (and strengthening) waves of Taken. I had an absolute blast with this mode—the maps all feel different but fun and even more inspired than the areas in the story. There’s not much sweeter than the adrenaline rush of having a map-full of Taken and your score multiplier maxed at 9x when the sun finally comes up and blows them all away. I would not be surprised at all if people unfamiliar with Alan Wake were drawn into the franchise by this mode alone.
That all being said, I’m not a huge fan of the way the main story treads over the same/similar ground for three acts. Without spoiling anything, there are three areas in the game, and you visit them each three times throughout the story, completing almost identical objectives every time. Granted, it could have been handled far, far worse—there are enough changes each time to keep things from getting redundant and stale—but this design choice borders on development limitation, not plotline necessity. Fortunately, this would probably be something avoided in a true sequel.
At the end of American Nightmare we are, once again, promised that “Alan Wake’s journey through the night will continue.” While American Nightmare is a worthy appetizer for fans of the original, we are still hungry for that promise to be fulfilled once again. Honestly, this game is great, both out of my personal opinion as well as objectively speaking.
It is a roguelike game, has a neat combat system that allows for incredibly fast paced battle as well as well thought through strategic approaches. It is incredibly hard and punishing. Dying is one the most common outcomes of later on battles because one has missed to upgrade his/her ship in matters needed to go face to face against increasingly harder enemies.
The game holds a lot of different types of species all of which could possibly be part of your crew or part of the enemy's. Each of them holds special abilities and traits which can be beneficial for your ship or devastating for your enemy (four mantis crewmembers as a boarding party is by far the most gruesome thing to do or to receive).
The graphical aspects are very basic and simplistic, no huss no fuss. But it is the neat and perfectly optimised game mechanic that captures the player. It builds a lot on micromanaging your own ship, by distributing power to various parts of your ship, thus boosting your shields, or charging your weapons, or even basic things as providing your crew with oxygen. Battles are not only won by raw firing power but also by strategic placement of crew and energy throughout the battle. Moving the right crewmember in the nick of time from one place of the ship to the other can tip the scales in battle.
By now there are about ten different cruisers that can be unlocked through various methods and can help you play through the game in a different way:
Although the story is always the same and once you played it to the end, you have basically beaten the game, it will hardly feel as if you just completed something but rather just scratches the surface. The game builds upon it’s replayability and at this point I must honestly say, that whoever managed to play through this game in advanced mode on the hardest difficulty, deserves my deepest respect. Because you Sir or Madam, are a true

Just as a FYI, I got this game on the 5th of May, 2015 and I've played 395 hours.
This game caught my eye when it was still pay to play and in the beginning I enjoyed playing it quite a lot.
The tutorials are great, although I think they should actually be somehow enforced to avoid completely unaware players of diving into PvP without any knowledge of the game's or heroes's mechanics.
The maps were plenty and new ones were being introduced with updates. They were symmetrical so there were no balance issues.
The ORIGINAL heroes are well thought of and relatively well balanced. The ninja was only OP if the enemy team doesn't actually play as a team, which happens very often.
The graphics have that cartoonish look which to be honest I don't mind that much, not every game needs to have outstanding textures and special effects to be good and I think this one did that.
The control and movement does need some work, sometimes it feels like you're playing on ice and it often ends in you falling, sometimes into lava.
But then the bigger problems started appearing...
The player base was small, which was expected since the game had not been released for too long, and as a consequence joining a game sometimes took longer than 45 minutes.
Barely anyone talked during a game and there was rarely any sort of communication as a team.
The matchmaking algorithm is absolute trash, placing someone who just finished the tutorial against players with level 60.
Only one region for all of Europe, which generated huge amounts of lag and made many players go crazy because of shots not being registered, being disconnected, not being able to move, etc etc. You obviously can't expect someone from Amsterdam and someone from Portugal to be playing and everything going smoothly, it just won't happen.
New heroes started being introduced, and although I welcome new content with open arms for a game that I've paid money to purchase, I HOWEVER do not welcome new content that allows players to exploit lame tactics with new heroes or new content that allows players to be overpowered because they paid to be able to use an overpowered hero (two major issues here, one is allowing the game to be exploited by the use of lame tactics, the other is P2W).
Cheaters (not many) ingame. Imagine a Cogwheel shooting his minigun and only doing headshots... Yeah, not much fun to play against that one.
And then ranked was introduced...
And it was actually introduced correctly, there was a queue for normal games and there was a queue for rankeds, which is great!
Players just looking for a relaxed and fun game can just go for normals and players looking for a more competitive edge can go for rankeds.
BUT, they screwed it up. They made it all into a single queue. There is no more normals queue and no more rankeds queue. Now you just press Play and the ranking system is forced upon you.
And with a ranking system forced upon you, you can either be playing with someone who's just there for the hell of it or you can be playing with someone who's actually there to play as a teammate.
Now, if you're into normals, you're fine, you'll just play your game and you'll enjoy yourself.
But if you're into competitive, well, you're not going to enjoy it very much when that guy that just joined for a normal does absolutely nothing the entire game to help the team but instead spends his time building a tunnel under your own base.
Matchmaking remained trashy, placing 1 or more players in the top100 against people with Gold 3.
Even more new heroes came out, and again, more P2W heroes that were overpowered.
And now they've gone one step further (and in my opinion, downhill) and made the game free to play.
Probably hoping that this will expand the player base considerably.
Not only have they completely disregarded the many people that have paid for this game and just told them "Thanks for your money but now that we already have what we want, screw you" but they've opened the gates to every player with a half decent PC.
While I find it great that the queue has diminished, I absolutely hate the fact that now anyone can just install, cheat and even if banned, just install again and cheat again.
And obviously the amount of normal players will increase dramatically since it's another game you can just have for free in your library and play whenever you want.
This was the final drop and what made me stop playing the game, and I consider it unplayable at this point unless you're just going for normal.
It has clearly changed a lot from what I purchased and Jagex have ruined it.

Yes, this game is cheap and - as you might expect - it's short. But if you like old fashioned newspaper style comics and old fashioned point-and-click games it's worth your time. After you finish the game you'll be asked if you want to print your comic and if you do, the game will generate a pdf file containing all the panels of your play through.
It took me about half an hour for the first play through where I read every dialogue option and looked at every item description and then I spend another half hour or so in order to get all of the achievements. It was a short, but fun experience. My first play through resulted in a 320+ page pdf file because of all the dialogue options and item descriptions. But at heart it's a short game that can be finished within three minutes.
Once you've finished the game you can play a new game+ which features developer commentary. This is also worth listening to; I always find it fascinating to get an insight into the development process and you do indeed get an interesting look behind the scenes. The developers mention that they decided on a number of simple rules in order for the game to work well (like a simple interface and mostly three panel responses) and in my opinion they've succeeded.
Despite it's short length I was impressed by the game. The art style isn't stellar, but it's well done and fits the story and narrative style. I actually like the fact that you can sometimes see the left over lines from the penciled sketches and there's a coffee stain on one of the panels. The plot is kinda thin and the puzzles are simple but the developers state in their commentary that this is mostly a proof of concept. If enough people buy and like their game, they might create more and longer games with the same concept.
As far as I'm aware this is indeed the first interactive comic ever created. There have been some games with a comic book like aesthatic, inspired by comics or with comic book style cut scenes (Comic Jumper, Comix zone, Noctropolis and Max Payne come to mind) but none of those games were interactive comic books quite like this game is.
And as one of the other reviewers mentions it makes for a great (cheap) gift if you have friends that enjoy comics and/or point-and-click adventure games.

Oh would it be a dream for a restaurant to have a special all you can eat coupon where it only expires when you walk out of the door. Man you can probably even just hand it off to someone else to make it infinite! Though of course they would go out of business depending on how much the coupon is and if loopholes like this would be possible.
In this situation our protagonist bought an all you can eat coupon that does not expire as long as you stay in the establishment. Due to this he became a freeloader, living in that same diner for 10 years straight before the fated foreclosure sign appeared. If this diner closes his whole life will be turned upside down considering he has nothing from his old life. So he has to go out, sadly making his coupon expire, to save the diner.
The art is kind of what you’d see in what your school would give you or an illustration you’d see in a textbook. This also opens up to everything being easily readable, which is probably why a lot of people forget about being able to inspect something, and the characters being able to look unique. I also see this as a way to somewhat save ink if you want to print this so your printer would not have to worry about filling in the intricate details. With this you also have to wonder about how movement will go. Usually you would guess they would do a little animation in the panel itself but they skipped through this easily. Having the natural flow of a comic be the animation itself and  by pushing the panel away for new ones.
This is a pretty short game, around 30 minutes for your first playthrough, and is linear throughout. There would really just be one part you would be stuck on but everything else is very easy to put together. I do recommend talking to everyone as much as you can at first so you can get all the joke comments and some information you can easily skip over.

If you can't tell by the list above, I don't have much negative to say about the game.  As of this writing, it is $1.50, and it will take you quite a bit longer to beat/read this than it does a normal $2.99+ comic book you may pull from your comic shop of choice.  So, honestly, even though it is quite short for a video game, it's not necessarily a bad value, given the medium it is trying to emulate.  So, with that out of the way, I actually want to talk about the game.
I loved it.  I thought it was witty and fun.  Nothing dour or somber to be found.  Every character has a really distinct personality, and each one is enjoyable to see and interact with.  The plot is very simple, but it moves along nicely, and I enjoyed the story overall.  There's no major themes here that will leave you scratching your head.  It's a simple story of a guy trying to save his all you can eat buffet from closing down.  It's very charming.
The art is simple, clean, and easy on the eyes.  It looks exactly like a Sunday comic, and I love that.  As with dialog, each character has a unique design that is very expressive.  There isn't a lot to say about the game's style, but I enjoyed it.
As for playing the game, it's straightforward point-and-click.  Talking to characters, choosing all the possible conversation options, checking out your environment, using all the possible item combinations, and, ultimately, figuring out the correct combination of the above to move the story forward.  If you don't enjoy point and clicks, this won't change your mind; however, with the shorter format, you can easily check all those things within 30 minutes.  So even if this isn't a genre you traditionally enjoy, you can at least rest assured that the tedious part of those games isn't very prevelant here.  Brevity may just be this genre's friend.
So, in conclusion, I loved the game.  Is the best?  No, of course not.  But it's a charming, silly story, that you can experience over you lunch break, and I appreciate that.  It's got a fun cast of characters, witty dialog, and it's just engaging throughout it's short time on your screen.
P.S.  Printing out your comic after your first playthrough is also a neat feature.  I don't think it is something to be swayed by, and as such, I didn't mention it in my review, but I do think it's pretty cool to have.

It is truly a great and flawless game, I personally love every single aspect of it, be it gameplay, story, graphics, visuals, mechanics and etc. What I especially like is that, at the beginning it's much more of a survival so you'll have to avoid zombies as much as you can, as you level up and progress towards story, you'll unlock many various items/skills/gadgets that it may even turn the game into piece of cake on normal difficulty, of course if you invest some time and enjoy the game instead of rushing quests. You can also change difficulty anytime.
Gameplay heavily adapts on your skills, weapons and story progression. It's really interesting how you level up, unlock game changing skills and slowly develop your character by finding better weapons, upgrading and crafting with even more deadly upgrades.
Dying Light sometimes reminds me of Skyrim, and all that huge amount of fun I had from it. If you've played and liked Skyrim, you're most likely to enjoy the Dying Light.
You have total of 5 skill trees. From the beginning you'll have three, Survivor, which you gain by completing quests, saving survivors, delivering air drop packages and etc. Agility which you gain by running, jumping, climbing and harder the obstance more experience you earn. And power, you gain power experience by killing zombies with any weapons. Fourth skill tree would be Legend which I've explained below, fifth skill tree is a Driver which is only accessible in The Following DLC.
Dying Light has a decent and serious plot. It is a very interesting, memorable and enjoyable, there might be some plot twists and sad moments. The ending is very exciting and satisfying.
But be warned, story isn't the best side of Dying Light, it's gameplay.
Saving system is simple but there's no manual saving. Though almost on everything you do, auto save is triggered, as well upon quitting. I've never lost anything due to saving. Big missions have their own checkpoints. Upon dying or reloading save, you'll spawn in area depending on which quest you have selected or in safe zone.
There's huge weapons choice. Axes, machetes, knives, swords, scythes, katana, great axes/swords and etc. Throwable weapons such as shuriken, want to be ninja? well you can. As well as ranged weapons, pistols, revolvers, SMGs, assault rifles, shotguns, bows and crossbows. Each kind of weapons have quality tiers. Melee weapons have durability and repairs, that means you cannot keep repairing single melee weapon infinitely, it'll eventually downgrade and break.
It is the bows and crossbows, and their awesome and smooth mechanics. Also the fact that you can pickup and reuse the arrows/bolts which is really fun. You'll never run out of arrows this way, unless you're forced to flee from the area being unable to retrieve arrows.
Bows and Crossbows never downgrade and since you can pickup arrows/bolts, you can always use them if you run out of firearm ammo or your melee weapon breaks. You can also craft arrows, even elemental arrows, also buy them from merchants.
Over 1,000+ hours so far, and not even a single game breaking bug, of course I've encountered some minor glitches but they weren't really worth much of a trouble, in fact I can't even remember any of it now. Actually it was fun.
Legend skill tree is a great addition to the Dying Light, it came with Enhanced Edition. Once you max out one of your Survivor/Agility/Power skill trees, you'll unlock a Legend skill tree, all the experience gained from that skill-tree then goes towards the Legend, which adds 250 extra levels and a great opportunity to invest some more time in Harran. Legend skills are greatly useful in Nightmare difficulty.
And I mean it, I've started The Following DLC after 700+ hours, beaten the base game multiple times, still going for more.
They've upgraded the game to the Enhanced Edition totally for free. And if you purchase the game now you also get ALL the DLC to date, except Harran Ranger, Gun Psycho and Volatile Hunter bundles, though these 3 are very cheap and not really necessary to enjoy the game. You also get everything that's included in season pass.
My score would be 10+/10.

If you're familiar with the Telltale Games Series then you'll know that there is an inherent story that will happen somewhat regardless of your choices. I don't find that to be a bad thing but other people might. With that in mind here are my thoughts on the game:
The story starts off as the Red Wedding is happening. You play as various family members of the House Forrester who are loyal bannerman to the Starks. Even though you're playing on the peripheral of the story we all know and love you still feel like you are a part of the larger picture. I personally found it to be highly immersive and my first play through surprised me at how often I interacted with the main characters like Ramsey Snow, Cersei, Tyrion, Margaery, Jon Snow, and Daenerys. I played through the game again trying to alter my responses to what I thought would result in a better outcome for my family and it was even more enjoyable the second time as a felt I had a better handle on who these people were and how they would react to what was going on in the world. Because of that I would definitely say it has replay value.
The best way to play the game (I found) was to decide early on how I wanted my characters to interact to what was happening around them and to form my choices of dialogue and behavior around that. Sometimes for better and sometimes for worse. All 6 chapters kept me interested in what was going to happen to my family and by holding my interest I genuinely cared what happened to them. Out of all the characters I got to play, Mira (the oldest sister who is a handmainden at Kings Landing) was my absolute favorite and I wish she had had a little more play time as I feel her dealings with the Lannisters was some of the most interesting parts of the story.
Overall I give this game a big thumbs up and recommend it for anyone who likes story-rich games with a little bit of combat and a whole lot of tact.

I almost never write Steam reviews but I felt a special need to write one for Lethal League. I picked this game up in a game bundle a while back not knowing anything about it, and thought it was least exciting part of the games I got. But now that I've played several hours of it, I can wholeheartedly reccomend this game at full price.
It's hard to explain what exactly Lethal League is, but what I can call it is one of the most fun games I've ever played with friends, period. It's frantic, it's colorful, and it's extreme. Even playing it by myself in Challenge mode (basically singleplayer Arcade mode for those familair with fighting games like Street Fighter), it's an absolute blast and a great way to burn some free time.
The one big complaint I have with the game is that online multiplayer is a real pain, especially trying to find other players online. Simply put, there's almost never anyone trying to play on public servers which might be a bad thing to some players. Playing with friends is a decent experience over the internet, but I'd highly recommend local play if you can, as playing over the internet can cause some real issues with how well the game runs and can lead to some embarrasing defeats because of input lag.
Besides this issue, the game is a load of fun even though it sports a fairly limited amount of characters, the simple to learn but hard to master gameplay and unique abilities of each individual character means that it's content that will last you a while, and I'd consider Lethal League well worth the buy.

This is by far one of my favourite games of all time.
The real time strategy can feel intense sometimes but you can always pause if you start feeling overwhelmed or want to fire all of your weapons at the same time.
The combat system is satisfying to use and makes up the bulk of the game which is good. The weapons are what make this game feel futuristic, none are overpowered but it feels so good to disable enemy shield with an ion cannon you just bought from a randomly generated shop and then damage the enemy crew directly with an anti-personnel laser leaving the ship intact for a bigger salvage reward at the end of the combat.
FTL has random encounters that can make every play through feel different with random outcomes. I especially like the events that you get given another option if you have a certain piece of equipment; one time I came across a station with an automated defence system and I had the option to disable it from a distance with my ion cannon.
Although these encounters are great they do get repetitive over a lot of runs because of the limited number of them, this negative is reduced by the random outcomes.
The game features eight ships (with two special ships) which you have to unlock with objectives/events in previous play throughs. (or if this isn't to your liking, because some seem impossible, you can just download the save file will all the ships unlocked.) Each ship has its own play style and challenges the player to take a different strategy into the game. Example: the engi ship focuses on drone combat whereas the mantis ship focuses on crew teleportation and boarding combat.
Each ship has multiple variants, so although there is only eight ships because of the A B and C variants they actually come to a grand total of 24 + the two special ships having an A and B variant = 28.
28! - this is a huge number of ships to replay the game with.
The soundtrack in this game is by far the best soundtrack I have ever heard (edit: I have now played Stardew Valley and can say it comes close but still FTL stands strong), it creates the perfect setting for the game mysterious and quiet yet frightening and atmospheric.
Mods
Although this game has no steamworkshop it does/did have a huge modding scene. You can get mods like the famous captain's edition that adds in a load more weapons, events, background art and equipment.
This game is so good. I imagine whenever you are looking at this review the game will be below £10; if this is the case it is a steal for the base game, let alone the free update of advanced edition. I would even say this game is worth up to £20 because of the amount of time I have spent on it (I first got the game off of steam so have more hours than this).

It's alright, pretty much what you would expect from a Korean MMO. The classes are all gender locked which isn't terrible I guess but I would prefer to see more customization, they generally have parallel classes for each gender though, e.i. Witch and Wizard. The models are all the Korean MMO type of attractive which is alright but it just limits your customization options more. Graphics are really good which makes what customization there is in the game really nice to do.
The story is absolute nonsense, I don't know if it's a localization problem or what but I only have half an idea of what's going on. The main companion that kind of acts like a Legend of Zelda style Navi speaks either in gibberish or Korean, I can't tell, he also has a bunch of sayings that don't really make any sense which makes me think that they just literally translated some Korean sayings that don't work in English. The voice acting is honestly really bad, I don't know where they got these voice actors but it seems like 90% have gotten this job as their first step into the industry and don't know what they're doing.
There are some really interesting concepts like Horse Breeding. The weapons upgrade system is a pain to use and in higher levels I have heard that it is just a terrible grind, I don't really know what I expected from a Korean MMO, lower levels come really easy though. Your mounts level up as you ride them more which I think is pretty cool and there are a good amount of non-combat skills like fishing and crafting that you can work on.
Combat is really fun and fast paced, very similar to Tera Online which I use as a compliment. None of that click on enemy, click on skill and then watch style of combat, you actually have to aim the skills if you want them to hit. The combat plays like The Witcher now that I think about it.
It does have sandbox elements, kind of similar to ArcheAge, you can build small outposts and control areas of land that give you money through tax. Then you can fight for control of those areas of land amongst other players who want the land for the money.
The cash shop is pretty standard, you can buy costumes and outfits which make your character look good or shows more skin and things like more effective mounts. Some people might say jiggle physics on the boobs and butts is dumb but outfitting my character in lingerie and skimpy clothes and then panning around to watch everything shake around wasn't an... unenjoyable waste of time, I guess.
Overall, I give it an 8/10.

This wonderful little gem, All You Can Eat, is a perfect blend of comic and game. The gameplay is just like any adventure title, complete with inventory, and simple point and click. It centers on our intrepid, but very lazy, main character. He is without a name in the game but in my playthrough, I called him "Bob." He just seemed like a Bob. He needs to save his favorite all-you-can-eat diner from foreclosure and is forced into the wide world of his neighborhood to do so. The humor is corny and mostly clean (just a few curse words).
As I mentioned, it is simple gameplay, even as young as five could enjoy the game if an adult read it to him/her. But here is the neat thing. After you play, a comic book PDF appears on your desktop in the EXACT order you played the game! So each time you can choose a different order and get a different book. The outcome is always the same, but I saw a few panels from the developer that I did not see in my playthrough. So there is some variety.

Faster Than Light. What to say....
First off, I'll probably say that it is a RogueLike. If that doesn't at least hint at the fact that you will get owned a lot, I don't know what would. FTL is a game where you aren't actually any on-screen character. You are looking over your ship and it's rooms, and you can see your little people in them, usually three at the beginning.
There's the engine room, weapons room, the pilot's seat, the shield room and the medical bay. When you put a person in a room, it boosts the thing that the room is connected to (you put a guy in the engine room, your engine gets a little boost). You have to have a guy in the pilot's seat, and usually you would usually put people in the weapons room, then the engine room, then the shield room if you get another crew member.
This game is very difficult, and you will die multiple times before you get very far. You start out in a civilian sector, and there are about 20 beacons on your map. You have to "Jump", which means you go "faster than light" to the next sector (get it?). Almost every beacon will have something at it. Usually one or two per sector are a shop, one or two are people that need an escort, but usually it's someone who needs help fighting or just a plain ol' enemy.
There are eight sectors to go through total, and there are different types, including Nebula, Civilian, Hostile and so on. The first seven are just gathering supplies, weapons, upgrading, and getting a little extra fuel. There's a power system of what you can power and how much you can power it and how many power bars you have total. It's pretty easy to get the hang of though.
So yeah, this game is very, very enjoyable. I moved to Indiana from Colorado, and when I went to Colorado to visit family there, including my uncle (about five years older than me, we skype and play a lot), he showed me this game. I pulled out my laptop, and about three nights in a row while I was there I sat on the futon until about two in the morning playing it. Steam, with it's silly "Hours Played" system screwed it up, and says I've only played a couple hours. I have actually played this for a very long amount of time, including a two hour video on YouTube with said uncle (Squish92 on Steam). He has 70-some hours in it, and we both are big lovers of this game.
Highly Recommended, even if you don't like Rogue-Likes, but especially if you DO like Rogue-Likes

So, I realise that at this point civilization VI is out. However, some people are unable to play due to haveing a weak computer. And besides, that game hasn't been fully patched and balanced, unlike civ V. But back to this game. It is a massive time sucker, but not in a bad way. You may find yourself lost in this game for 8 hours straight, and feel like it's only been half an hour, because it's just so addicting. I can't fully express to you how much fun it is to crush a technologically inferior enemy still using warriors with your armies of riflemen and cannons. The joy found in a strategy game can't simply be written down, you either know exactly what I'm talking about and would love this, or would hate this/get bored of it immediatly. Now, it may take a couple of games for you to fully understand the games numerous machanics, but there's plenty on the internet to help with that, something else civ VI is lacking, as people continue to try and find all the exploits of the game. So for the time being, I would recommend this game over civ VI, which I personally can't play without upgrading my computer. But make sure you get the full expansions and have friends to play it with, otherwise you'll grow bored of this quite quickly.

Game of Thrones : A Telltale Games Series isn't bad... it just isn't good.
The game itself offers pretty meh gameplay, a pretty meh story, and pretty meh characters. The story is just like you'd expect from Game of Thrones, where you have main characters constantly dying left and right. The blend of the characters doesn't really maintain composure and sort of falls apart towards the end. The one thing that kept me going was Asher's storyline and Rodriks. I feel that the story line of the "North Grove" was terribly boring and turns out to be pointless, and i wanted to stop playing every time i got to Mira's storyline. The characters who coincide with the main characters (Such as Rodriks mother, sister, and sentinal) are all useless to the character himself. The story doesn't lead anywhere and is downright one of the worst endings i've seen in a video game. Don't even get me started on the decision making of this game either. The decisions you make are of utmost minimal importance and don't make a change to the end of the story at all (*SPOILER SPOILER SPOILER) unless you count the death of rodrik / asher, for whomever you choose, they both have almost identical endings.
If you're a fan of the Telltale Games, i'd give this a shot, but if you haven't played any of the Telltale Games yet, don't let this one spoiler the batch for you, they're all amazing, this one... not so much.

Tropico 4 is a great city builder where you are a dictator of an island in the Caribbean.  the campaign offers a variety of challenges with each mission so it stays fresh. There is also a sandbox mode where you are basically set free to do as you wish, wish a variety of options to set before the game starts such as how often disasters happen.

to get that last 1%?  you have to hire ninja's of course! to do this you send a trade mission to the USSR then pay for ninjas and the mission is over.
as a city builder the game isn't too bad either. every citizen has needs, and each citizen will have some needs mean more to them, such as housing or entertainment.
one annoying thing though is how hard the planning of the city can be. some islands have little build space, and traffic can be a big issue that is nearly impossible to fix in the game. the expansion pack "modern times" helps to fix this with "metro systems" which let people teleport from  one hub to any other you build. but that is it.
even with that issue though the game is still a blast to play and well worth any of the numerous sale prices steam has the game for.

I almost never write Steam reviews but I felt a special need to write one for Lethal League. I picked this game up in a game bundle a while back not knowing anything about it, and thought it was least exciting part of the games I got. But now that I've played several hours of it, I can wholeheartedly reccomend this game at full price.
It's hard to explain what exactly Lethal League is, but what I can call it is one of the most fun games I've ever played with friends, period. It's frantic, it's colorful, and it's extreme. Even playing it by myself in Challenge mode (basically singleplayer Arcade mode for those familair with fighting games like Street Fighter), it's an absolute blast and a great way to burn some free time.
The one big complaint I have with the game is that online multiplayer is a real pain, especially trying to find other players online. Simply put, there's almost never anyone trying to play on public servers which might be a bad thing to some players. Playing with friends is a decent experience over the internet, but I'd highly recommend local play if you can, as playing over the internet can cause some real issues with how well the game runs and can lead to some embarrasing defeats because of input lag.
Besides this issue, the game is a load of fun even though it sports a fairly limited amount of characters, the simple to learn but hard to master gameplay and unique abilities of each individual character means that it's content that will last you a while, and I'd consider Lethal League well worth the buy.

First, let's cover what Black Desert Online (BDO) is.  This game is a sandbox RPG in an online shared world where PVP and occasional cooperative PVE happen.
[[ Note: One of the bigger draws of the game is the ability of a guild to control a node and defend this ownership through nodewars.  Since I didn't participate in that system this review does not cover that topic.]]
BDO is not a typical MMORPG in the vein of WoW -- there is no instanced group content (save for "savage rift" which is a tower defense mode recently added).  There is no ability to trade items (other than food and potions, which then bind to the receiving player) between players, so your lifeskills are mainly useful for what they can provide you.  There is no way, for instance, for you to make and gift an item to your friends or guildmates in the game.  Market prices in game are regulated by the developers and only move up and down through a proscribed range for the item over time.  This has the effect of making some items overpriced and, the more common effect, of useful items being sold out on the market as the people producing them don't feel the market price adequately rewards them for the time to create or farm the item.    This does have the effect of eliminating "Gold Selling" like you see in the more traditional market systems, but mostly just serves as frustration.
THE GOOD:
1. BDO is a very nice looking game.
2. The Combat system is beautiful and fluid.
3. The life skills systems are varied and distinct, but ultimately pretty shallow.
4. The classes actually "feel" different for the most part (exception being opposite gendered classes witch/wizard, kuno/ninja)
5. Gear can be moved and shared between characters on your account, so you only have to collect and level a single set if you're willing to move it around.
6. You get tons of content for the $10 asking price
THE BAD:
1. The game has a really neat "empire building" system where you have workers all over the map gathering resources which you can process or craft into things worth selling on the marketplace (or just sell the raw materials for others to use for these purposes).  Unfortunately the workers only work when you are logged into the game, which means you'll want to leave your computer on 24/7 to get the most benefit from this system.
2. The game also encourages you to leave your character logged in to process or fish or do some other afk crafting activity to make the most of those resources your workers are gathering.
3.  As stated above, the game is gorgeous, however, the engine was developed in house by the team that made the game.  This means that issues such as pop-in that are issues even on advanced and well funded engines by other developers are *extreme* here.   This is made even worse as you get better horses and move through the terrain faster.  In addition, the PVP is hindered by constant de-sync which makes your timing sensitive grabs and knockbacks miss because the server doesn't agree that the enemy was where it appeared on your screen.
4. RNG inside RNG inside RNG.  What do I mean? -- drops/loot tables are random, once you have an item you can upgrade without issue to 5 or 7 levels, after which you have a chance of failure which lowers max item durability which you have to repair before you can level further (there are ways to fail stack and minimize this loss on valuable items but the entire system is a huge pain).  Once you finally get the gear to +15, you then get to use a more expensive item which can also fail to upgrade (and cause a larger loss of item durability) to get to PRI (+16) and DUO (+17).  From this point on, not only can you fail an upgrade, but the item which fails to upgrade will actually go down in quality.  That is if you are going from DUO to TRI (+18) and fail, your item actually goes back down to PRI (+16) in addition to eating your upgrade mats and durability.  The entire system is designed to make you hate life.  (Again as stated above, some view this as a positive, as you only have to do it once and can then move the equips (other than weapons) among your characters.)
5. More RNG -- one of the cooler life skills is Training whereby you capture wild horses and level them up to breed or sell to other players.  Here you have RNG on the capture (including what level the horse you've tamed is).  Then as you level the horses further the skills which the horse learns are random from a pool that varies based on the tier or quality of the horse.  There's no in-game method to change these skills other than getting a new horse and trying again.  (but there's a cash shop item that will let you swap one skill for another random one -- you could literally use hundreds of these items at about $2.50 a pop to get a Courser, or a horse which happens to have all the correct skills to get this coveted status.)  You need a T8 courser to *try* for the new super horses like the Pegasus -- it's yet another layer of RNG on whether it upgrades.  And even if it does, you lose your T8 Courser you probably spent hundreds of dollars making because it "Awakens" into the pegasus.  By the way you then get to level the pegasus from 1 to 30 again without the guarantee that it will relearn the skills it had before you awakened it.
6. Cash Shop Prices -- I'm not a huge fan of the proliferation of this business model -- but it seems it is the new normal, where even subscription based games like WoW have them.  With the $10 asking price of this game I don't fault the developers for having another revenue stream.  I do fault them for the insane pricing of the items though.  One thing every player will need is pets -- pets run around behind your character and loot items for you -- everyone will need 4 and they cost $10 each, so basically the game starts at $50.  The other items on the store consist of $30 outfits for a single character on your account which might enable crafting from the town bank or just give a 10% exp boost to your character.  These are bound to your character so even if you create another character of that same class the outfit cannot be moved once you've equipped it once.  There's also the typical storage space increases and bag space increases for the packrats and you can get by without those if you don't focus on certain lifeskills.  That also goes along with the horse training items (including costumes for both the player ($20+) and horses($20), skill resets ($2-3), appearance change ($9), and breeding and death counter resets for horses in the $5 range).  Maybe you think these prices are okay -- I certainly don't and even after spending around $200 total on the game between pets and maid and storage space increases I still don't feel I got my money's worth from the purchases.
TLDR: BDO could be an excellent game, but it is undone by the blatant cash grabs in the shop, questionable design choices and finicky engine.
