This is by far one of my favourite games of all time.
The real time strategy can feel intense sometimes but you can always pause if you start feeling overwhelmed or want to fire all of your weapons at the same time.
The combat system is satisfying to use and makes up the bulk of the game which is good. The weapons are what make this game feel futuristic, none are overpowered but it feels so good to disable enemy shield with an ion cannon you just bought from a randomly generated shop and then damage the enemy crew directly with an anti-personnel laser leaving the ship intact for a bigger salvage reward at the end of the combat.
FTL has random encounters that can make every play through feel different with random outcomes. I especially like the events that you get given another option if you have a certain piece of equipment; one time I came across a station with an automated defence system and I had the option to disable it from a distance with my ion cannon.
Although these encounters are great they do get repetitive over a lot of runs because of the limited number of them, this negative is reduced by the random outcomes.
The game features eight ships (with two special ships) which you have to unlock with objectives/events in previous play throughs. (or if this isn't to your liking, because some seem impossible, you can just download the save file will all the ships unlocked.) Each ship has its own play style and challenges the player to take a different strategy into the game. Example: the engi ship focuses on drone combat whereas the mantis ship focuses on crew teleportation and boarding combat.
Each ship has multiple variants, so although there is only eight ships because of the A B and C variants they actually come to a grand total of 24 + the two special ships having an A and B variant = 28.
28! - this is a huge number of ships to replay the game with.
The soundtrack in this game is by far the best soundtrack I have ever heard (edit: I have now played Stardew Valley and can say it comes close but still FTL stands strong), it creates the perfect setting for the game mysterious and quiet yet frightening and atmospheric.
Mods
Although this game has no steamworkshop it does/did have a huge modding scene. You can get mods like the famous captain's edition that adds in a load more weapons, events, background art and equipment.
This game is so good. I imagine whenever you are looking at this review the game will be below £10; if this is the case it is a steal for the base game, let alone the free update of advanced edition. I would even say this game is worth up to £20 because of the amount of time I have spent on it (I first got the game off of steam so have more hours than this).

Faster Than Light. What to say....
First off, I'll probably say that it is a RogueLike. If that doesn't at least hint at the fact that you will get owned a lot, I don't know what would. FTL is a game where you aren't actually any on-screen character. You are looking over your ship and it's rooms, and you can see your little people in them, usually three at the beginning.
There's the engine room, weapons room, the pilot's seat, the shield room and the medical bay. When you put a person in a room, it boosts the thing that the room is connected to (you put a guy in the engine room, your engine gets a little boost). You have to have a guy in the pilot's seat, and usually you would usually put people in the weapons room, then the engine room, then the shield room if you get another crew member.
This game is very difficult, and you will die multiple times before you get very far. You start out in a civilian sector, and there are about 20 beacons on your map. You have to "Jump", which means you go "faster than light" to the next sector (get it?). Almost every beacon will have something at it. Usually one or two per sector are a shop, one or two are people that need an escort, but usually it's someone who needs help fighting or just a plain ol' enemy.
There are eight sectors to go through total, and there are different types, including Nebula, Civilian, Hostile and so on. The first seven are just gathering supplies, weapons, upgrading, and getting a little extra fuel. There's a power system of what you can power and how much you can power it and how many power bars you have total. It's pretty easy to get the hang of though.
So yeah, this game is very, very enjoyable. I moved to Indiana from Colorado, and when I went to Colorado to visit family there, including my uncle (about five years older than me, we skype and play a lot), he showed me this game. I pulled out my laptop, and about three nights in a row while I was there I sat on the futon until about two in the morning playing it. Steam, with it's silly "Hours Played" system screwed it up, and says I've only played a couple hours. I have actually played this for a very long amount of time, including a two hour video on YouTube with said uncle (Squish92 on Steam). He has 70-some hours in it, and we both are big lovers of this game.
Highly Recommended, even if you don't like Rogue-Likes, but especially if you DO like Rogue-Likes

There's a lot of negative reviews on here, and I do not understand why. This is a Telltale Game which means it is more of a movie then a game. The story branching is not as extensive as other adventure games, but the amount of actual Game of Thrones voice actors and quality of the level design would preclude the custom gameplay you'd see with a more text driven adventure game.
The only place the game really went wrong was trying to shoehorn as many original Game of Throne characters in there as they could. It brought believability down quite a bit, if these characters were so central to the main story line, why haven't we heard of them? I realize that this is a fictional spinoff of a fictional series, but the illusion is shattered when you once again stumble upon a major plot point of the show/novel.
The expansiveness of the show is also lost by the limitations of a computer game. While the graphics are stunning, and some of the set pieces feel like you're visiting them ... the Wall in paticular, other times when it takes a character seasons to get some place, you're suddenly there and back in two different scenes. Similarly, when ever armies are mentioned you do not get the massive armies we're accustomed to, but like 8 guys. You're left wondering if you only needed 8 guys to defeat an army why did I travel around the world?
There are some plot points, and without spoiling anything, that are like polar bears from "Lost." Lets make a big deal about something then, lets not actually ever explain it. I don't think it really detracts from the overall experience as long as one doesn't think about it too much.

Alright, so I have just calmed myself down over this game by drinking some nice tea and playing some lego batman. It is a nice game. Not this, but lego batman, and I will now tell you why.
First off, the story. This is really the big selling point of any telltale game, we all know that. And trust me, I love me a good telltale game. I fell in love with the walking dead and I think that it is a much better game featuring a father figure protecting a young orphan girl through a zombie apocalypse than other games under that description, that is to say the last of us. The wolf among us also held me engaged and i thought it was okay. But game of thrones just do not meet any of the requirements i want in a good story. I like the characters even though i suspect most of them were made up. While only having watched the show, I cannot say if every character has been in the book since a song of ice and fire, but I doubt it. It just features a lot of bullies punching you about, unlike a good game like lego batman, where you beat the bullies.
Second of all, the ending. I normally do not give a♥♥♥♥♥♥about my choices not mattering in these telltale games, as long as I am engaged it works, cause it is an illusion of choice. But when your game ends on a very dissatisfying cliffhanger, where while not spoiling anything, everything has turned to♥♥♥♥♥♥ it seems like the game makes me want to think it as my fault. It just feels like a big sequel hook without any really good ending, unlike lego batman that lets you see some effort after your hard work in the end.
Let us talk gameplay for a minute instead then, and I know that is controversial, but I have seen telltale games can make some fine enough puzzles. The walking dead had some alright and sensible puzzles and that served the overall experience. After all, we like to do stuff in an interactive medium. But here any action performed by the player is a tiny little stump, compared to what i know it could do. Why even keep the inventory system telltale games, if there is no more than two places where it could be useful? So puzzles are an absolute♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ and it cannot even compare to the likes of lego batman, a game where the puzzles are made so small children will figure them out quickly.
And then there are the action sequences, i sighed with discontent. Quick time events, that is it. If people ever get retrospective about your games telltale games, then they will say how they don't hold up because of these. Even lego batman has only one button for combat and it is still more free flowing and fun and exciting than this excuse.
Then there is a seriously big concern I have with this. I normally would not say this to a telltale game since they can look pretty nice, but this looks like♥♥♥♥♥♥ It has a stylised artform to make it all look like an oil painting. An idea i could get behind, if it was not because of all the blurry textures. When the camera moves i can just see the low pixel amount and blurry textures try to keep the facade and it really kills my immersion. I would have thought that impossible, but no, telltale improve these graphics before you try such an artstyle again. And it is really inconsistent too. Most oil paintings just have smeered things in the background cause they are far away and the foreground needs the fine details. But here fore-middle and the bloody background all do this and it looks like♥♥♥♥♥ Take some inspiration from a game like lego batman that also has a low pixel count but a charming and consistent artstyle in comparison to what you tried to do here, telltale games.
Most of the problems I have with this game probably comes from it being a tie-in to the show. It cannot overshine it like the walking dead did to the show, because we know what they would say at HBO then. But still, this is not what game of thrones is about. It is about having a big shock factor compared to Hitchcock and Kubrick and showing off our worst in the society we have built. It is not shy from backing away from these things. This may hit some of the notes, but it is still not able to create the anti-war symphony that we see in the show. Unlike this, lego batman can actually show you how to be an alright tie-in. By making a completely new story out of it and having small parts of humour that makes the overserious batman into a funny laughing figure. It holds up.
And last but not least, there are not♥♥♥♥♥♥in this game? Why? I would have thought that would be obvious to include, cause it is one of the things people remember. It is such a big deal in the show, cause it shows we can at last have some sexual liberation on tv, and also it makes people want to take a quick google search with parents' lock off, leaving the viewer satisfied. Even poison ivy's literally flat chested figure is more showing than any here, so again you are beaten by lego batman.

I love Quake. I'm sure mine is a familiar story - I've been playing this game since childhood.
If you're looking for a game that is so satisfying, but also not easy for anyone to master, Quake Live is the game for you. This is by far, the most difficult game to get good at. And I mean that in every possible good way.
There are other more casual modes that are easier to pick up and play, like instagib freeze tag, Clan Arena, etc. But some of the other, more classic modes, are incredibly difficult but SO satisfying once you get good enough to put up a fight.
For me, it's all about competitive pick up CTF - and of course DUEL.
Duel is where a large chunk of the difficulty comes into play. In order to win a match, you must control your opponent. You do that by timing item pickup times. Red armor and Yellow armor respawn every 25 seconds, Mega Health is every 35 seconds. Getting a stack so that you're able to attack or defend against your opponent - or getting enough of a stack so you can fight for other resources and positions on the map, is exactly what makes Quake so skill based and tactics based.
People might look at Quake and think it's just a shooter. But it's a thinking game. And I honestly believe that because I'm an AVERAGE-skilled player in Quake, that is why I do so well in other shooters. Because other shooters just can't compare to the sheer speed of everything in Quake. You have to react so quickly, think quickly, know where your opponent currently is or is going to be, and be accurate and position yourself intelligently when you fight.
This game is all about preparation for each encounter. And how to react if you're not prepared. And the skill of the other player FORCES that upon you.
I love this game. Not because it is easy, but because it is hard.

How are people liking this!? I mean, it started out pretty decently... until the "game" stopped becoming a game. It is literally a huge, tedious collect-a- thon where you go through the same levels, doing the same stuff that you already did, over and over again. I get it, the whole "plot" is that (SPOILERS) Mr.Wake is stuck in a time loop and is trying to make things right so that he may finally put an end to all the crap happening. Okay, yeah... that's fitting and that's okay. However, it is not okay when your so called "game" consists of (like I've said before) going through the same thing, again and again. It was interesting the first time but now, it's just getting on my nerves. It's boring, repetitive (literally), and just down right unenjoyable to have to go through. It's clear, at least to me that the developers did not put much thought into this and they sure seem to have run out of ideas half way through making this. To make things even worse, there is no variety. They try to switch it up with the tasks but, it's obviously the same ones that you just did but, in a different order... seriously, that's it. However, that's not really the worst thing about this. I think that the worst thing about this so calle "game" is the fights and the enemies. Since when was it okay to surround the player with more than twenty enemies!? Or so, it seems. There are way too many enemies during a fight and to amp up the unfairness even further, they are stronger, faster, very resilliant to your flashlight (or any ligh for that matter), and just close to impossible to kill, dodge, or runaway from. By the time you're even able to pull up your gun, you're surrounded and are being beaten within an inch of your life. You'll be trying your hardest to break the darkness off of them and shoot them but of course, while you're in the middle of doing this, there will be multiple enemies allready surrounding you. Nevermind the fact that your flashlight charge barely lasts long enough to even break the darkness on one enemy! You only have enough charge to even do one enemy at a time which obviously, doesn't work and just slows you down. And then finally, it really does seem like not that much thought was given to the programming. What I mean is that, you'll out run the enemy and be more than safe distance away from him but, it doesn't matter because somehow, he can still hit you. Enemy attacks are also very diffivult to get out of and so, if you get hit even once, then you might as well give up becasue you'll just get stuck into an enemy's combo and killed instantly. There is so much more that I could probablty complain about here but, I've already taken up enough space and I just can't think of anything else at the moment. Besides, trying to think about this game at all is slightly infuriating me. That's the key word here, "infuriating".,, that's all this will ever be, so much to the point where I flat out quit playing.

Behold the Kickmen is not only funny, which was pretty much a given after watching its development unfold on developer Dan Marshall's
. It's also really fun to play.
After playing through the Tutorial (or feeling really bad for not doing so), you start at the bottom of the league with a team of guys that pretty much can't do anything. However, as you start doing goals and winning games, you start unlocking abilities and earning money to upgrade your players.
The abilities you unlock include passing (which is extremely well implemented and pleasing to use), giving effect to the ball after a big kick, and others like better tackling (also a really cool mechanic), sprinting and dashing to avoid enemy players.
The difficulty curve seems pretty fair: the first match is quite easy, and after that you'll find lots of teams that will literally give you a run for your money.
And on top of that, the story mode is filled with hilarious dialogue and fun characters.
All in all, a really recommended purchase, even more so at the ridiculous price tag it's set. If you're even mildly curious about it, give it a go, it's certainly worth your time.

Half-Life 2 is one of the best games ever. What Valve did with HL2 was to create a masterpiece that revolutionized an industry and influenced the games that came later, becoming a pop culture object.
In Half-Life 2 they control Gordon Freeman, the scientist who survived the incident in Black Mesa, which arrives in City 17, a city controlled by Combine, an alien race that established an authoritarian regime in the city. Gordon is soon engaging in the struggle between a human strength and a Combine and a roller coaster of events that follow in one of the most memorable histories ever.
Half-Life 2 was developed for gaming and accounting. There are no cutscenes, a story unfolds around the protagonist and retains control over a character throughout the game.
It features memorable characters such as Alyx Vance, Barney, Dr Kleiner and of course the mysterious G-Man.
Visually the game is amazing. The game engine Fonte manages to create some of the most amazing animations and environments ever seen and a physics of objects corresponding to real life. The gameplay is fluid, and there are several weapons to use, with clear highlight for a Gravity Gun that allow manipulating objects or use them as projectiles. In certain sections there are vehicles to control, which varies the gameplay and there are also some puzzles that use the physics engine itself to the resolver during the advance in the game.
The AI ​​of the enemies is also excellent, they look for cover and prcuram flanquear the player, except for the zombies that like any zombie that prears so advances towards the player to kill it.
In short, Half-Life 2 is a milestone in the video game industry and a must-have for anyone considering a gamer.

As a writer, I consider the first Alan Wake a great game for its metalinguistic. The story within the story, the topic of what makes a writer a writer, the symbolism of the dark force as the market and the stupid corporate suits who twist and turn the will of an artist to make raw money... The fact that the story unfolded in two fronts (the game and the pages you collected) was specially fascinating.
As a gamer, the first Alan wake was interesting, nothing special beyond the light mechanic but fun on its own way, I ended up annoyed because even in the nightmare, the enemies were merely annoying and there was too much ammo (and with my hoarder mentality from games like Resident Evil and Dead Space, I ended having lots of moments where I left crates of ammo behind because I was full).
But this... unfortunately... feels like a shoddy and lazy filler. There is no story, it's just Alan hunting his doppleganger that it's in his place because story reasons that aren't really explained, the same places are used over and over and over. The city that the developers made with care to look alive and real is replaced by three patches of boring desert with three female characters that are awfully and lazily voiced. The combat has been dumbed down (amazingly), even if there are more guns for you to use, you can only carry two: A main arm, and a sidearm.
"But sir! Alan Wake was supposed to be realistic! The devs said so! You don't see a guy carrying fifteen weapons on his pockets!" Yeah, the devs also said that this game is more action-packed and inspired in americana action series. It's specially grieving since now ammo is universal. Black and red boxes will fill ammo for your side arm, and orange boxes will give ammo for your main weapon. Regardless if you're using an uzi, a nail gun, a rifle or a shotgun. It mostly boils to the fact that they wanted to port it from the consoles to the computers as fast as they could and couldn't be bothered with changing.
And to make things 'worse', the 'realistic' excuse can't be used anymore, since Alan now fights weird enemies that turn into birds or that split in half when shown bright light. While in the first game the dark presence merely took possession of people and objects, now it... mutates them? It gives an excuse that since the antagonist is different, it does different stuff but... again, within the own meta-linguistic, the story gives no reason WHY the antagonist could do it.
Speaking of meta-linguistic, all the pages that explained what happened to npcs and about the story that is unfolding were, again, severely dumbed down. With only three girls to talk to and three scenarios, and with most of the surprises being gone, most pages are just filler, annoying filler, needless filler.
While I didn't had high expectations about this game (with the company acknowledging that they wanted their time to make Alan Wake 2 and didn't wanted to rush things) I at least expected that they would do an enjoyable work, like the DLCs from the first game.
The only way I could reccomend this game is if you liked the combat mechanics from the first Alan Wake and wanted to play a dumbed down, arcade version of it.

Recycled gameplay from FarCry3, blocky graphics and chunky user interface, made for consoles. Buy it for consoles because thats what it's designed and intended for, its a PC port of a console game, stating the obvious but this is not a next generation game.
FarCry 1 release = 2004 (Original)
FarCry 2 release = 2008 (4 year gap ^)
FarCry 3 release = 2012 (4 year gap ^)
FarCry 4 release = 2014 (2 year gap ^)
FarCry 5 release = 2016 (2 year gap ^)
What made FarCry 3 stand out was that it was rewritten around a real person who personified a character in his own acting talent. That person was Michael Mando aka Vaas. Intially Vaas didn't exist. The original antagonist was 6'6, 280lbs, sociopathic and unemotional. When Michael Mando auditioned he didn't get the part, they called him back later and rewrote the script and story around him, which is what single handedly saved FarCry 3 and made it iconic.
Michael Mando is the real MVP. FarCry 3 set the bar too high and the recycled gameplay and sounds doesn't cut it anymore no matter the theme or story, it all feels the same. Which is what happened with Crysis 3. Grab a copy of FarCry 3 instead if you haven't already. Especially if you are new to the series.
If you want to play a story rich game that could move you in the way FarCry 3's story did, pick up a copy of Call Of Juarez: Gunslinger - they don't make games like this anymore.

Dying Light is the best Socialist Simulator on the market! Do you want to live in a dystopia where you have to fight warlords for basic food and medicine? Do you want to run with fear after dark? Do you want to fashion weapons from discarded saw blades and string? Do you want to risk your life trying to find insulin for a dying child only to be thwarted by faceless government agencies?
You don't need to fly to Venezuela. Load up Dying Light for hours of socialist fun!
What makes Dying Light different and fun are:
1)
. The running, jumping, grabbing, climbing and falling are done well. With practice you can become fast and fluid. The best early advice I got was to "Follow the terrain." If you see a ledge with a rope, grab it. If you see a ramp, take a blind leap. Something will always catch you. The designers put a lot of thought into flow to make sure you won't leap into a pitfall or blind alley. Trust your instincts and run!
2)
. We all love guns. Guns are great, but guns are loud. Noise brings the zombies so melee is your friend. "Get gud" with melee. The melee weapons and gameplay are solid and satisfying. Timing that swing to get an instant-kill decapitation never gets old.
3)
. Finally a shooter in this FPS. Guns are noisy but situational. When you need them, the gun play is good and satisfying.
4)
. The main story is compelling enough to make you want to push forward. Some say the ending is a bit of a let down (I would agree) and the side quests are very good (I would agree again.) I wish there was a dynamic story arc letting me make some major decisions, but that's okay. The length is good. I play very methodically, exploring all the areas and playing all the side missions and I got about 50+ hours out of the base game. Add the DLC and you can extend that another 20+ hours.
5)
. There are some light RPG elements to Dying Light. It isn't too risky because eventually you can get all the upgrades and become a flying tornado of zombie slaying, but it does add to the sense of progression and growth. You start huddled in a corner, clutching your rusty nail-board, praying for the night to end and become a real master of the night, leaping from buildings with little fear.
6)
. That leads me to the sense of progression in the game. Even though become a zombie meat-grinder, there is still a sense of dread. Become too complacent and you become dead from a missed jump or overwhelmed by zombies. But the game rewards ingenuity and cleverness. Play smart and you will thrive.
7)
. Check other reviews if you are interested in multiplayer. I only played solo, but I can see how co-op and the multiplayer options would put Dying Light over the top for fun. As a solo-only player I had great fun for many hours, so you fellow misanthropes will have no problems.
I was getting burned out on zombies, but I held my nose and jumped into Dying Light anyway. I'm glad I did. Even if you are not a big fan of zombie games, it is a unique experience for any FPS fan looking for something different. Getting the base game and all the DLC for a low price is a great value.

If you are looking for a Diablo 2 replacement look no further than Grim Dawn.
It is perhaps through all the game who have came and gone through the years the closest to it in feel, story and general gamelay feel. While PoE is a great game (more than 3000 hours on it) Grim Dawn captures the Diablo 2 feel in a much better way, While also giving a far superior single player experience if you are disillusioned by the trading and player interaction in the other ARPG games.
But not only Grim Dawn emulates what we so like about the old ARPG systems, it improves upon them greatly, the devotion system, the dual mastery system and the hectic gameplay are something never seen before in the ARPG landscape.
I think this is the only ARPG game where i felt i had more than 12 buttons to press on certain charcters, and the game UI also encourages you to get as many skills as you like and experiment with them to generate "combos" using the devotion tree.
This gives the game a hectic gameplay feel and actually make you feel immersed in your surroundings during combat, while at the same time compared to other ARPG's the gameplay feels slower and more refined, you dont rush through the game holding 1 "I WIN BUTTON" you go slowly and take your time to kill mobs or to use your skills.
If you are looking for a game that can suck you in for a month or two, give this a try!

Alan Wake’s American Nightmare is the unofficial sequel to the original Alan Wake.
As a fan of the original game, I would highly recommend playing this one after you’ve gone through the original. While it can be played as a standalone, there are many references to characters and stories from the original that help to enrich the story throughout the game.
No longer is Alan Wake in the beautiful rustic backdrop of the pacific northwest, this time he finds himself in the arid deserts of Arizona. With a new western theme, the game remains true to itself by using the same fighting techniques and graphic qualities as the first game, but with slight tweaks and updates that breathe a new life into the game. Collecting manuscripts to unlock weapons, more dialogue options for NPCs, and containers that give max ammo/batteries, for example.
Like the first game, this game has many interesting cut scenes that really add to the story, and the use of real actors is a nice touch as well. Television recordings and radio broadcasts help create a backdrop for the other characters in Alan’s old life, telling their current stories alongside his own.
There is also an Arcade Mode for those who wish to challenge themselves, or for those who just want to bash in some taken skulls.
For a short(er) game, I found the story to be intriguing and unique.  However, as I progressed further into the game I felt like the gameplay got a little repetitive and the enemies became more annoying than challenging. The fact that there are only three locations to explore, and that you return to them repeatedly, was disappointing. I was expecting more unique and exciting locations much like the original had offered.
My overall score for the game: 7/10. Recommended for any fans of the series or anyone looking for a short supernatural shooter with both mystery and intrigue.

Alan Wake's American Nightmare follows the adventures of Alan Wake as he attempts to chase down and thwart the schemes of his mysterious double by rewriting reality. As interesting as this may sound, the premise is ultimately let down by shallow combat and uninspired environments. In a story which seems so incredibly bizarre at first glance, it is a shame that the game which surrounds it is so average.
Alan Wake's American Nightmare markets itself as a third person horror game, but fails to differentiate its self from other games in its genre. It's combat, While not bad, will seem very familiar to anyone who has spent any amount of time playing similar games. Ammo is plentiful and combat is relatively easy as a result. Most of the weapons available feel familiar as well, with basic pistols, rifles and shotguns making up the bulk of your arsenal. Only the occasional power tool manages to change up the stagnant weapon variety, but such weapons are too few and far between. Another minor way in which Alan Wake's American Nightmare tries to differentiate itself from its peers is through its use of the flashlight. Before an enemy will be vulnerable to attacks, they must be exposed to light for a period of time, either with a flashlight or other means. This creates some welcome tension, as the player tries to juggle foes with their flashlight, all while watching their batteries slowly drain. Unfortunately, doing so can become cumbersome in later sections of the game as the quantity of enemies being thrown at the player increases.
I was also alarmed to discover that despite Alan Wake's American Nightmare's short length, it still managed to recycle most of it's environments multiple times. I don't believe that recycling environments is always a bad thing as long as they are sufficiently altered to create new and unique game-play experiences, but in this case I just felt as though the recycled spaces were their to serve as padding.
While by no means a terrible game, Alan Wake's American Nightmare feels far too familiar. Throughout the experience I couldn't help but feel that my time would be better spent elsewhere. For people who are interested it may still be worth giving a shot, but don't expect anything amazing.

Double Action Boogaloo like if you combined The Matrix and Face/Off into a single video game.
GAMEPLAY:
It's mainly a third-person shooter, although you can toggle first-person if you set a key for it. You start off by picking your guns, style skill and character, and then you jump straight into the fast-paced action. Basically, the game involves lots of crazy stunts and flips. Your goal is to kill people in the coolest way possible, and gain style points. Punching somone while diving, for example, will give you extra style points. Through style points, or melee you can gain slow-motion abilities, and activate it by pressing the "C" button. The gunplay is simple, which is good since there's usually a lot of things going on at once. Just load, point, and shoot. You have unlimited ammo, but you still have to reload. There's no iron sights, although certain weapons let you zoom in by pressing shift. Overall, very fun.
PRESENTATION:
The graphics aren't a whole lot better than the base Half-Life 2 graphics. It has some fancy effects but the texture detail is about the same. I don't really expect a whole lot in this regard when it comes to mods. Though Double Action isn't going to turn heads, it looks decent for a mod. However, the in-game HUD looks pretty good and fitting for the art style, and the level design looks nice most of the time.
Definitely a very good mod, and although the graphics aren't amazing, the gameplay is very strong. I'd reccomend this for sure, especially since it's 100% free - no advertisements or in-game purchases. You can't go wrong by downloading this one.

Admitedly, I have grown tired of the Telltale games, so take this with a grain of salt if you may.  The way Telltale sort of gives you this "decisions matter" jargon you quickly realize after playing through several titles that there are truly only a handful (if that) of important choices that impact that overall arc of the story.  There is not much gameplay here, but again it is not meant to be this type of game.  But, I will make this argument:  I can watch an Telltale series on Youtube or Twitch, and NOT be inticed to play the game because watching it is a "good enough" experience, I don't need to go back and do the action sequences where you tap a button to dodge at the right moment, and honestly after one playthrough you may not feel compelled to try out the other dialogue choices after you've experienced the climax and know what will happen despite your choice.  On the other hand, watching someone play something like Witcher 3, yes, the story is there, but at the end of the day I feel like I would get my moneys worth playing Witcher 3 after watching it.
TLDR:  This is more of one giant long cutscene with button mashing mini-games here and there.  The story tends to suffer and has a lousy start, isn't as good as some of the material were acustomed to from GRRM and there were a LOT of missed opportunities here.  I know Telltale games aren't based on action gameplay, but I can't agree with Telltale on their pushing this big "decision-making" mechanic when it isn't a big deal and doesn't really effect gameplay (if you can even call it that)

To start, I should say that I knew nothing about Game of Thrones going into this game, and picked it up solely due to my enjoyment of Telltale's story-driven adventure games.  I'd heard mixed things on it going in, but I was left surprised by how well this game stood alongside Telltale's best,
If you've played any of Telltale's games since The Walking Dead, you'll know exactly what to expect.  The glut of the game is making split-second decisions that could potentially have long-term consequences.  Actual "adventure-gaming" where you walk around solving puzzles to progress is almost non-existent.  This is disappointing, but understandable, as this is a game that holds you by the consistent progression of the story. But in their future endeavors, I hope to see some sort of a challenge that isn't something that weighs on your conscience and instead makes you think.  Maybe take a note from the new King's Quest series, which allows for players to make choices organically through their puzzle-solving. So in short, if decision-making is your thing, this should be essential.
The game's "combat" consists mostly of choreographed fight scenes where the player executes quicktime events.  The efforts of The Wolf Among Us to make this system more dynamic and interesting is completely gone, so it does feel like a bit of a step backwards. But again, if you're picking these games up for the combat, saying you'll be disappointed is a severe understatement. That's not the focus, so if you don't care about getting past some tedious combat sequences and enjoy poweful storylines, don't let the weak combat stop you.
If the goal of each of these kinds of games is to make it feel like each decision holds true weight, then Game of Thrones is a resounding victory.  I held my breath almost the entirety of my playthrough, as the stakes always feel high and you can actually fail some of the set out objectives in the game.  This was sorely missing from Tales From the Borderlands, which was funny, but it felt like you were more along for the ride than actually making an impact.  Telltale has a habit of making these complex stories that eventually lead to one outcome, and although this game suffers from the same
ending, there are some major differences that will undoubtedly affect the inevitable second season.
But in the end, how could decisions hold any weight if you don't care about any of the characters?  The game performs a juggling act between characters, and it for the most part is successful.  This mechanic allows for Telltale to break some longstanding rules in their games, and you learn quickly that
of the characters could die in an instant.  While this was an interesting hook, I hope they take it a step further with future releases.  The writing is still superb, so it makes every loss and defeat much more meangingful.
Don't worry, I'm not going to spoil anything, but the ending does need to be discussed.  To put it simply, it wasn't satisfying, clearly paving the way for the next season.  I'd assume it's to make room for further developments in the show that can affect the situation in the game, but it doesn't make it less of a punch to the face.  After becoming so engrossed in these characters, it hurts that this season's story couldn't stand on its own two feet.  Nonetheless, I'm excited for what's coming and will be there when it finally comes out.
While I have high praise for the game, it's not quite as good as The Walking Dead Season 1 or The Wolf Among Us, so I'd recommend picking up either of those first if you want to see if this genre interests you.  And even if it does, you may be more satisfied waiting for Season 2 to come out to help with the ending.  Yet, this is still a great game for those looking for a narrative-driven experience.

TL;DR: this game might've been a landmark in gaming 13 years ago, but a lot has happened in 13 years and HL2 is showing some serious crow's feet.
I had heard this game was supposed to rival the second coming of christ in terms of quality, so i picked it up on sale.
For anyone who hasn't played this game yet, it's honestly not worth getting at full price. sure it showcases a physics engine and looks and animates great for a 2004 game, but it's not 2004 anymore.
Storywise, it's nothing special. some foreign militant force has taken over earth, you get picked up and taken into a resistance force but there's a traitor working for the enemy among you, you rescue somebody important to the resistance from jail, and then you return to destroy the enemy's big doom tower. It's not awful but it's certainly not the heartrending masterpiece i was lead to believe it was.
The gameplay doesn't make up for it either. Combat doesn't evolve at all beyond "shoot a gun at a man", which can work for games with different enemy types or fast-paced gameplay, but every enemy in the game is just a slight variation of a man with a full-head helmet and hitscan weapons.
While there are quite a few weapons on display, none of them feel great to use. the two automatic weapons you get are wildly inaccurate beyond 20 metres and do a pathetic amount of damage, the crossbow and magnum are decent long-range high-damage weapons but you never get ammo for them so you'll rarely use them, the grenades don't go where you aim them so trying to bounce them off a windowsill to kill someone in cover is needlessly complicated, and the rocket launcher is only slightly more effective against vehicles than blowing kisses. Possibly the only decent weapon is the shotgun, which has just enough range to almost make the SMG obsolete and enough damage with the secondary fire to kill most enemies with a single headshot. There's also gun that you can use to toss loose physics objects at things but that's only really particularly useful in one level where the game basically decorates the walls with sawblades and explosive barrels.
The level design seems intent on showcasing the game's physics engine, and it gets old fast. Often you'll have to stop some high-octane action to solve a physics puzzle, using the word "puzzle" as loosely as possible.  9 times out of 10 it just involves putting a physics object somewhere either as a platform or as a weight, or using the above mentioned gravity gun to move a bunch of heavy objects out of your path. sometimes the levels can be big and sprawling but they're more often than not entirely linear with little side areas that might hold a few supply crates.
As an aside: for a game all about its physics engine it has some of the most mediocre vehicle physics i've ever seen. A high-powered assault buggy handles like a homemade go-cart powered by an electric toothbrush motor and a fanboat seems to handle almost exactly the same over water. It's not the tech limitations either; halo came out in 2001 and made its jeep feel like a real car. I'm pretty sure it even lost traction on icy surfaces. beyond good and evil came out in 2003 and had a water vehicle that actually felt like it was going through water. both of these games had plenty of other content on top of vehicle sections that didn't control like an RC car on low battery.
What finally got me to give a negative review was a bug in the second last level where the game relied on a scripted event to blow up a wall to let me progress, but it never happened. I spent half an hour shooting the infinitely respawning enemies (which hadn't occurred up until that point - if you killed all the enemies in an area they were gone for good) and dying over and over again looking for the way forward. After checking a walkthrough and seeing that an event wasn't triggering i had a look for solutions, where i was told to restart the level and hope the event worked this time. Given the level was if not the longest then certainly the most tedious thus far, i decided i had played enough.
If you want a decent shooter made by valve, get team fortress or counter strike. If you want a good puzzle game from valve, get portal. If you want a shooter with a good story, get spec ops. This game does all three fairly blandly and i can't recommend it unless your PC can't run anything else.

I recommend this game for the combat and the setting. It's worth playing through once.

If you are looking for a Diablo 2 replacement look no further than Grim Dawn.
It is perhaps through all the game who have came and gone through the years the closest to it in feel, story and general gamelay feel. While PoE is a great game (more than 3000 hours on it) Grim Dawn captures the Diablo 2 feel in a much better way, While also giving a far superior single player experience if you are disillusioned by the trading and player interaction in the other ARPG games.
But not only Grim Dawn emulates what we so like about the old ARPG systems, it improves upon them greatly, the devotion system, the dual mastery system and the hectic gameplay are something never seen before in the ARPG landscape.
I think this is the only ARPG game where i felt i had more than 12 buttons to press on certain charcters, and the game UI also encourages you to get as many skills as you like and experiment with them to generate "combos" using the devotion tree.
This gives the game a hectic gameplay feel and actually make you feel immersed in your surroundings during combat, while at the same time compared to other ARPG's the gameplay feels slower and more refined, you dont rush through the game holding 1 "I WIN BUTTON" you go slowly and take your time to kill mobs or to use your skills.
If you are looking for a game that can suck you in for a month or two, give this a try!

War is hell. War never changes.
This was my entry into the XCOM series, and I made it reluctantly. I have always been a fan of turn-based strategy, but of the 4x variety. The turn-based tactical shooter is brand new territory for me, but a family member recommended that I try this game. So, after months of deliberation, I downloaded and installed EU.
Lord have mercy, I haven't seen the sun since.
This is one of those rare games that I absolutely love... that I am also absolutely terrible at. And, this game will make you feel like you suck at it 9 times out of 10. After all the hours that I've put into this, I've only beat the campaign once. All the other hours are either me losing, or me starting over because I could no longer bear the pain of being such a failure as a commander.
I started with the randomized squad member names. But, being a real-life combat vet, I thought I'd spice it up a little. I named all of my soldiers after soldiers that I have served with over the years. I thought this would give me a little more motivation to keep these troops alive, up the immersion factor a bit. After I lost the entire platoon that I served with in Ramadi in 2006, I decided to go back to randomizing.
But, that's a big part of the beauty of XCOM: EU: it makes you care about your wins, and your losses. Did you manage to make it through a large UFO assault without a single fatality? Breathe a sigh of relief, crack open a beer, and live to fight another day. Did you get your rookies killed on their first mission? Go cry in a corner, and write letters to their imaginary families. Or, shrug your shoulders, beef up your roster to replace the losses, and remind yourself that in war, soldiers are tools to be used and thrown away.
I thought that the game alone would be enough. But, within a  few days of all-day playing, I heard about a mod called "Long War." I read a little about the mod, and downloaded it.
Beware the Long War, Commander.
I'm losing more than ever. I haven't completed a single Long War campaign. I have uninstalled it and re-installed it. I KEEP COMING BACK. I am slowly learning to shake off the inevitable losses, to abort the missions that are just too tough, to curse the sudden but inevitable betrayals of countries that I was sure were solid allies.
The Base Building game is challenging, without being impossible. Prepare to draw out a grid on a piece of paper before you build anything. You will want to fire your chief scientist within a month, and the voice of your tactical advisor will grate on your nerves. You'll learn new curses, and combine known curses to surprising new effect. You'll celebrate your victories and wail at your losses. And, with XCOM 2 around the corner, you'll want to get started right away.
Good luck, Commander.

Playing FTL is alot like watching Star Trek. You do dumb stuff. A lot. Your crew will suffocate, burn to death, explode, and get eaten by alien Spiders. A lot. You will learn to despise human beings. All the while coveting your enemy's mantis. You will become ruthless. Killing an enemy simply because his offer didn't please you, or because you know you can get more. You will have to make hard decisions. Such as: Should I upgrade my shields or buy that cool looking attack drone. You will spend half an hour staring at the paused image of your crew struggling to survive, deciding what to do. You will forget to name your ship a cool name and regret it as that very ship tops your current high score. You will want to throw your computer out the window, because you forgot to do the obvious and it ultimately ended up with your demise. You will probably kill the dread Pirate Tuco. You will most definitly name one of your humans "Red Shirt" and then send him out the airlock, because humans are common and uninterusting.  I had to take a second look at the game after I got it. I decided I was glad I got the game. It is a blast to play on the Ipad or the pc. It is fun alone or with friends. It is funny and Horribly Frustrating. It can even get dull at times, but it gets better the farther you get into it. The only con that I can see is that it only has one saved game at a time. That and the Huge pest problem of giant alien spiders that literally every backwater space station seems to have.
The bottom line? Buy this game. It is worth it.

What a great game! My favorite of 2013. Even bought it on iOS (and it's awesome).
Yes, the game is hard. It's meant to be that way. The unlockable ships and layouts, the randomness, the permadeath.  It is, after all, a rogue-like.
You gotta play three or five times before you figure out a few strategies:
Try to jump to as many locations as possible, especially in the first two sectors.
Pause often!
Time your weapon strikes - fire when you've worn down the shields.
Sometimes putting fires out by opening the outer doors works best. Also good for suffocating intruders.
I really like Cloak, Weapon Pre-igniter, and Crew Teleporter. Drone recovery arm if you use drones.
Beating the final boss is really tough. And when you do beat him for the very first time you feel so awesome! The sense of accomplishment is huge, as is the adrenaline rush.
This is a game you can play for 2 minutes, or two hours.
A must buy!

Alan Wake's American Nightmare is a standalone 'DLC' and is a sort of continuation from Remedy's Alan Wake, and I have to say, it's mostly the same as the first game, only shorter... much shorter
Alan Wake wakes up in a place known only as Night Springs, he meets up with his evil counterpart known as Mr. Scratch as he terrorizes the lives of many innocent people. Alan has to try and stop him while going through a continous loop
Throughout the game you will visit three maps which are a motel, an observatory and a drive-in theatre and you will visit these places three times with mostly the same mission objectives, this kind of bored me after the second time and I could tell that the writers had no idea what they were going to write for in this "American Nightmare". The gameplay is mostly the same and will be familiar to people who played Alan Wake
The music was interesting and I liked that the game took a sci-fi route this time rather than a psychological horror route Alan Wake took. The voice acting was the weakest part, Alan's voice actor returns from Alan Wake and is the strongest in the game, the other side characters apart from Alan's wife Alice, were all played poorly, plus there is hardly any character development and I hardly know or care about any of the characters I met along the way
I like the references to the classic TV show, The Twilight Zone, from the opening of the TV series in the game known as Night Springs and the amazing narrator resembling the narrator from The Twilight Zone. A thumbs up to Remedy on that. The game is extremely short and you will complete the game in roughly 2-3 hours, if you only look for a few manuscripts and don't play the boring arcade mode
Overall, Alan Wake's American Nightmare is a mixed bag, the sort of short games such as Wolfenstein: The Old Blood are good and fun to play, but Alan Wake's American Nightmare does suffer on some of its supports, I'd only recommend this to people who have previously played Alan Wake or for a very low price during a sale or in a price drop

This has to be one of the better remastered games out there on Steam today. I understand that some people may think that this game is boring and repetitive, however I disagree. I want to address this first before I get into the nitty gritty of this game. I understand that some levels (i.e. the helicopter and mech missions) people find repetitive, but repetetive level ideas happen in ALL games. Dishonored was assassin simulator, GTA is drive to this location and shoot people, and then there's Banjo Kazooie (Which I feel is very similar to Ty) which is collect random items and finish a level. Most games have the same level formulae.
Now that rant is out of the way, I think it's time we get into what makes Ty 2 good/bad depending on perception and preferences. I'm going to start off with the negatives first. I do agree that some of the controls (I.e. the mechs) control a bit bad along with the forubie. But considering that the game was released in 2004, I think that we can let it slide.
To be absolutely honest, I don't really have any other negative opinions about this game. The positives on the other hand expand far beyond the negatives. The voice acting in this game seems much better than the first (I know, controversial opinion), but it is, Ty seems more mature along with the other characters they don't sound like 10 year old Aussie kids hyped up on Pepsi. The variety of rangs is far better as well and their uses are soemtimes vital for some missions, which gives more meaning to collecting opals until you have all of the rangs and bunyips. The story and free-roam was appealing to me as a child and it still does now. The issue with the first game for me was that the missions were too cloase to each other and it made the game feel too short. The music in Ty 2 feels far more upbeat and joyful with the addition of more guitars and such whilst still retaining the Australian style. One of the greatest things I find about this remaster however is the care and love the developers have for it. Most devs would rip the original and port it to PC with no change. Not Krome. Krome have added to this game extensively and made it what it was intended to be. They have fixed bugs that existed in the original games, added features not available on console due to memory limitations and have good contact with the community and fanbase.
Personally I find that this release has only improved on the experience that Ty gave me as a lad. I can't wait for 2018 when Krome release Ty 3 and then improvge on that. I would rate this game a solid 8.2/10, only downfalling on some wonky PS2/Xbox/Gamecube controls and a tad repetitiveness in some levels (Only the helicopter ones really).

Alan Wake's American Nightmare takes place after the events of the original Game and DLCs. Now Alan must confront himself with the Psychotic Mr Scratch, which is trying to bring the darkness out and spread it in the world... Between a murder and a torture.
The premise is solid and the gameplay seems improved, but this is all a mask on a product which seems made with short time, minor inspiration and different purposes. This leads to a "sequel" which is not a sequel (remedy stated this is more like a spinoff), with a lack of atmosphere as in the original title, underdeveloped valid ideas and a gameplay improved and ruined at the same time.
The atmosphere and the gameplay are two elements really close as even though the story takes place always by night in unpopulated areas, with bad or no illumination the locations are not... interesting. They have nothing to do with the charm of Bright Falls, the landscapes, the detailed ambiences. Of course few places or elements are very interesting and detailed, but in its entirety it doesn't even compare with Alan Wake.
The Gameplay doesn't help much. They Have added more weapons unlockable with collectible manuscripts, but the worst part is the Ammo Box... A self regenerating ammo box. This seems like the same evolution that affected the Resident Evil Saga, so you had to survive with few bullets and a bunch of weapons with a character that can barely run, and now Alan Wake can Magically Run three times longer before spitting a lung, he can easily get his hands on an arsenal and the game almost throws ammo box at him... Nope. Even though I'm quite glad Alan Can Run longer (It was really frustrating in the Original Game), and I'm glad they've replaced the six-shoots revolver with an automatic gun... I mean, seriously? A gun with six bullets to be reloaded one by one? Come on... (Don't misunderstand me, I understand it was meant to give the game a Survival gameplay, it's just me hating that kind of guns...).
And once again For both the atmosphere and the gameplay, you will visit three relatively small locations for three times... And every time it will take you less to complete each locations. It took me 4 hours and I was even looking for collectibles...
There's also an arcade mode which is nothing more than an arena with hordes of takensattacking you. I don't even know why I'm bothering to mention it...
The only positive note is the idea behind the game and the character of Mr Scratch. Just look at the TVs you can find around the locations, you'll see his "messages" for Alan. Not to mention the Trailers With Mr Scratch, Ilkka Villi has done a really great interpretation. Too bad the character wasn't developed further than what you see in those videos, which is a serious waste...
The other and last positive note in the game is the music... Nevermind, I eat it back, because it features a new track from the "old Gods of Asgard", from Poets of The Fall (Actually the same Guys XD) and another track, "Club Foot" from Kasabian... And Even though I adore them that's everything good the soundtrack has to offer, which for me is not enough. There's no ominous music, the good tracks are wasted in Climaxing Action scenes which actually lasted 10 seconds on top and there's no credit song worth listening as in the Original Title.
What can I say, Alan Wake's American Nightmare isn't a very bad game, it had some good potential but some gameplay choices altered the spirit of the Original Alan Wake and the game itself looks rushed without any detailed developing in locations, characters or story. So all in all it's not a bad game actually, but a sequel/spinoff, call it whatever you want, which unfortunately doesn't really compare to the Original Alan Wake, and really this is a pity as I really loved it.

Back in 90's one of the few games I played on the NES was Nintendo World Cup, an arcade-y football game with a both co-op and vs modes, cartooney feel and most important of all, I could play it without knowing anything about football as the real sport does not interest me in the slightest. I believe my cousin owned it and frequently brought it with him when his family was over at ours, and we played it a bunch over the years.
Eventually he got bored of it, I forgot the game and the football games got more and more serious. That game ended up being the only football video game I played during the first 25 years of my life. Perhaps there have been more arcade football games over the years but either they haven't scratched the same itch or I've missed the good ones, either way it looked like I might never play a football game again...
...until I ran into the dev tweeting about this happy little accident. Forget your fifas and pesses, they got it all wrong: This game is what they should thrive to be. Psyonix proved it with Rocket League (Disclaimer: which, according to a statement by Size Five Games, is not a football game), Size Five Games echoes it with Kickmen: You can't directly copy a sport to make a sports game. Sports are not fun, as proven by studies. Thus, a realistic game about sports can not be fun.
Maybe there isn't a real study that proves what I said but the point is, this game is basically a game that happens to be football themed, not a football theme that's been made into a game.
The menus kinda suck though so I'm torn between giving this game 6 or 7 points out of ten, but at least I can whole heartedly say that this is the very second best football game I've ever played.

This review is more of a comparison to the original release.
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Many of the issues that made this game average during the original release have been fixed in this port.
-Driving the car, for instance, no longer has road blocks or mud to keep you slow enough to let the game load in. Infact, driving is actually faster in this port, making traveling the outback fun.
-Kart racing, for those who cared, has also been touched up and feels better.
-One can now use all boomerangs, upgraded rangs no longer replace your starter rangs. The biggest issue in the original release, the kaboomerang replacing the smashering, is not an issue anymore.
-Missions that were a one time only play through, are now replayable. This means all bosses are replayable.
- A new addition, skins for the car and Ty himself, can be earned or bought in game.
- More scenic models are present as the game is no longer constrained by PS2 era memory. The game as a whole looks more lively because of this.

-Tons of controls in general were update. The doomerang, for instance, controls much better and has a far better range of movement now.
- Tons of UI updates and much much more
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Realisticly speaking, I have never seen a port get as much love and care as this one has. If you were a fan of the original game, you will love this definitive version of the game.

After playing the game significantly more, this is a re-review of this game, as my opinions have changed since my initial review.
Lethal League is basically Dragonball Z Death Ping Pong Dodge Ball. And it's an absolute blast. It's such a unique idea, and it's executed brilliantly. Up to 4 players, with 6 characters to choose from, are plopped in one of many stages with varying height and width (which matters for reasons I'll get to in a moment). There is a small ball, and you hit the ball to tag it as yours - making you invulnerable to it while it's still tagged by you, and deadly to any others it hits. That's the core of the game.
Now there are various ways to hit the ball. A neutral hit (any hit made while not moving sideways in the air) can hit the ball up, forward, or down. It can also be charged, and if you hit the ball fully charged, it reduces the hit lag, more on that in a moment, and also doubles the speed of the ball. You can also SMASH the ball - which happens if you are moving sideways in the air while you swing. This hits the ball downwards and doubles the speed of the ball. Lastly, you can bunt the ball upwards or downwards, completely fixing the speed of the ball to a slow pace until it's either hit, or hits a wall. Hitting a bunted ball adds 2 bars to the Special Meter, which is filled at 4 bars. Bunting removes most of the hitlag off of any swing, no matter what speed.
As the ball gets faster, the hitlag increases. The Hitlag is basically the amount of time freeze there is when you hit the ball.Hitlag is generally bad - as when the hitlag is high, you're stuck hitting a ball while the opponent can set up a counter swing, if they can predict the angle. This makes SMASHing dangerous, as it only goes in one direction. As such, Bunting and Charge Swings are essential to give your opponent no time to react to the ball.
One more thing. While in hitlag, you can use your entire special meter to produce a small shield around the ball for a split second. If the enemy hits this shield, they are stunned and sent in the direction your ball will go - it's almost always a confirmed kill. This is helpful if you can predict an enemy is going to try to hit the ball as soon as it leaves your swing. It's also possible to use it on a ball you're both about to hit at the same time - if you hit it first and parry at the same time, they will probably hit the shield and die.
Characters:
There are 6 characters, all of which have unique characteristics and one unique special ability. Special Abilities can be activated by swinging while in hitlag. Some are better than others, but I don't think any are bad. For example, Raptors special hits the ball a second time, removes most hitlag, and allows you to change to any of six directions for the ball, even in a Smash. Candymans special sends the ball through a portal in the nearest wall, coming out the opposite side of the stage.
Every character also just plays slightly differently. Each character sends the ball at different angles for every type of swing, and have different movement speeds and mobility abilities. Latch can climb up walls and stick onto them, Sonata has a double jump, and Candyman just has a very very high jump. This can possibly give you an edge depending on the stage.
My Actual Critical Opinion
Lethal League is well made. It's mechanics work exactly as they intended, and it all fits together very well, creating a very well balanced game that is consistently fun. However, that fun is somewhat ruined if you're trying to play online, sometimes. The game's playerbase is very small now. It will take long queue times to find matches, 5 minutes if you're very lucky. I've waited 15 minutes many times. If you get in a game, it's likely with someone with high ping, or if not that, someone who is very dedicated to this game and infinitely better than you. Still, I think it's worth playing online if you can contend with the more medium-level players.
If you have friends who are also interested in this game, I recommend you get it. It's a very fun party game, or off game to play a few rounds in.
If I have ANY criticism for the mechanics, it's the parry system. Namingly, it's a little too powerful. There's very little inscentive to approach someone if they are ready to parry at a moments notice - thus it's almost always a better option to just predict the angle and hope for the best. This is being fixed in the sequel game, Lethal League Blaze - in which there is a counter to the parry, but that game is not out yet. So for now, you have to deal with parry's kinda ruining the fun sometimes. But that is a minor gripe.
Conclusion:
Lethal League is a great game. Amazing, in fact. You should play it. I wouldn't personally buy it at full price, but if it goes on sale, I'd buy it again in a heartbeat. The game got me to love it enough to confirm I will buy the sequel, whenever that comes out. It's worth the money.

Odds are, if you're looking at this game and debating purchasing it, you are already interested or have played through Hyperdimension Neptunia Re;Birth1. However, do note that is NOT necessary to play Re;Birth1 first (although it is recommended), as this game takes place in a different timeline/continuity than the first one.
Hyperdimension Neptunia Re;Birth2: Sisters Generation, like its predecessor Re;Birth1, is a comedic parody of JRPGs and the game industry itself revolving around the CPUs (goddesses of the world of Gamindustri) and their sisters, the CPU candidates. It is a turn-based game with a simple combat system that offers a lot of variety, a unique (if sometimes one-dimensional) cast of characters, and a grand total of nine endings to pursue. Notable changes from Re;Birth1 include upping the party size from three to four and the introduction of Stella's★Dungeon, which will be discussed later on.
This game, as it takes place in a different timeline than Re;Birth1, starts with the nurse-in-training IF and Compa venturing into the Gamindustri Graveyard to rescue the CPUs from captivity by the officers of ASIC, an organization intent on reviving the Deity of Sin, Arfoire, and creating a new world order. They succeed in rescuing Nepgear, CPU candidate of Planeptune and younger sister of Neptune, but cannot do any more before they are forced to flee the graveyard. Upon returning to Gamindustri, Nepgear, IF, and Compa set off gather the other three CPU candidates to thwart ASIC's plans and rescue their sisters.
Musically, Re;Birth2 has very little deviation from Re;Birth1. Aside from the battle themes and a few cutscene tracks, most of the OST is the same as Re;Birth1. I personally prefer the battle themes from this one, though, but that's just me. Graphically, it has the same issue as Re;Birth1 does in that it reuses a large amount of assets. However, Re;Birth2 not only does this less, but the assets it does reuse are higher-quality than those in Re;Birth1. The dungeons are actually very aesthetically pleasing, with the only complaint being repetition of a few dungeon designs.
The most unique mechanic added to Re;Birth2 is that of Stella's★Dungeon, which is a "minigame" of sorts in which you gear up a character named Stella and send her off to explore dungeons, which you can do simultaneously while you adventure in dungeons yourself. It acts almost like a cell phone game in that exploring dungeons takes a certain amount of time (for example, 30 minutes to explore Virtua Forest) and, depending on whether her exploration finishes or she is knocked out early, will bring you back treasures and spoils of battle. It's an interesting concept, but can become very obnoxious quickly, as getting gear proves to be a hassle - you lose it all upon a failed dungeon run. This, of course, can be remedied with purchasing the Felis Insurance DLC, but still remains a chore at absolute best.
One thing I cannot go without mentioning that is unique to Re;Birth2 is its Conquest ending. This ending, while hated by a number of Neptunia fans, I found to be one of the most memorable endings in any RPG I've played, simply because of its drastic change in tone. The Conquest ending, in contrast to the comedic and lighthearted nature of the rest of the game, is rather dark and depressing, and almost feels out-of-place, were it not for the fact that it was written very well. If you do decide to shoot for the Conquest ending, be forewarned: the contrast is jarring, and you might wish you hadn't played through it after all is said and done.
Neptunia Re;Birth2 is a fun little game that fixes a number of the problems that Re;Birth1 had while still maintaining its core features: comedy, simple combat/story, grindy nature, and fanservice CGs. If you liked Re;Birth1 or don't mind the grinding and fanservice, I'd recommend picking it up (maybe not at full price, but on a sale certainly). It proves to be an excellent time-killer, and worth the sale price for how many hours of entertainment you get from it.

Welcome to the bleak world of Grim Dawn. Humanity is close to extingtion, and holding out in small fortifications. The supplies are running low. You wakes up after being possessed by a rather nasty spirit. You find yourself in a place you do not know, and you can't remember a thing of your past. The people of the encampment are suspicious about you too, so you have to earn your keep... by doing what comes naturally to you - slaying undead and hideous beasts threatening your new home, using swords, shields, ranged weapons and magic.
This game is a worthy spiritual successor for Diablo 2, but I would hesitate to call it a clone. No, it is more. The character customisation options are nearly endless, and you can distribute your stats and skills yourself. This game will not hold your hand. The enemies won't be holding back, and neither should you. The difficulty level is finely tuned for ARPG veterans who want a challenge. However it doesn't mean it is for hardcore players only. The difficulty level ramps gradually, and you either learn to play better and prevail, or get stuck with a bloody nose until you learn how to deal with enemies. But you should know that some of your choices have long-term consequences. Sometimes you find an NPC and you are given a few dialog options. The resulting reaction can make your life more difficult, but the choice is usually obvious.
You can redistribute your skill points for a fee and the skill tree is very versatile. You can have up to two professions, and they all have their distinct skill trees. Want to play an engineer who can also use dark magic? Sure, go ahead. A warrior-witch? Sure, go ahead. An elementalist-assassin? Be my guest. Some professions mesh better than others, but nothing will stop you from playing the game the way you like. You can complement and improve your skills with enchanted equipment too.
This game is a game made with love for the genre, and it shows.
If you find Diablo 3 too cheerful and colourful, try this one out.

My first real foray into the ARPG genre, at time of writing I have done two play-throughs of the main campaign on different class characters and played a whole lot of crucible ... I'll be getting Ashes of Malmouth on release!
tl:dr: great environments, well paced campaign, (1) huge variety with unique class definition system, plenty to explore (or not), (2) fun instances, well written (dark) fluff, (3) crucible is ace if you have friends. Strong replayability (1 2 3). in-game dps calculation is awful.
Characters:
Classes feel nicely unique, the three pronged approach (skill, devotion, attributes) to character development gives huge flexibility allowing you really mess with class boundaries, limited only by where you can find common ground between skill-trees and there's quite a bit! One really nice thing is the ability to completely respec if / when you get bored with one set-up or just pick up a cool weapon that you'd like to build around for the next 10 levels or so. That said, mixing and matching takes a decent amount of thought and planning, especially when it comes to devotions (which are kinda like the skill constellations in skyrim). Only criticism here is that attribute points could be a bit more relevant, so far it seems like just maxing physique and any cunning / spirit required is covered by the gear for you desired class.
Environment:
Relatively linear, well paced progression through a series of distinct areas, which on the whole transition smoothly, but are plenty varied. Dungeons & caves are a little less varied (Everybody seems to have a MONSTER cellar for some reason ... :D) but different enough to keep things feeling fresh. There are lots of secret places for those that like to delve but not so many that those who just want to burn through the campaign are lacking gear. The ingenious personal and static portal system saves you lots of time running through parts of the map that you've already cleared - mobs only respawn in an area when you leave a session. Finally there are instances where the stakes are raised - an entry fee, no portals, scaled difficulty, which have really good items in them. Overall really, really good and by the end you wish there was more!
Story (spoiler free):
On your first play through DON'T just blitz through, read the fluff, it's well written and some of it is really, properly dark. if you get a feel for the world you'll enjoy the game much more, lending a *grim* atmosphere to the proceedings!
Crucible:
Excellent implementation of a "Last Stand" type battle where you can actually get useful stuff for the main campaign and your character's development. Adds huge replayability and a different set of tactics from the and campaign.
Grind reduction:
ARPGs are necessarily grindy, there's a reason why I havent stuck to them before. GD does a very good job of keeping things fun. If you find and learn a recipe on one character, all your other characters get it. Once you have lots of reputation with one faction you can give your other characters a huge boost to rep generation with that faction (+100%).  At the higher difficulty levels, more mini-bosses spawn this speeds up your rep gain massively and gets you good gear faster. You can store items / consumables / crafting mats and transfer them between characters - "this gun would be perfect for a two handed ranged demolitionist, i'll keep that for when I make him".
Gripes:
I want there to be more campaign, waiting for expansions is hard!(!).
DPS calculation in-game is terrible, please fix this.
(minor) Difficult to keep track of allies / pets and enemies once the explosions start.
(minor) Secondary classes are a little too secondary, it would be really good to access more of the skills in the secondary class without a huge base skill-point investment - perhaps this is just good balancing though.
(minor) No pet action bar, could do with some extra on-screen space.
(minor) managing equipment swapping with attribute point buffs is tedious if you've decided to change build direction.

I really wanted to like this game. But I have a real problem with how the choice system pans out. Essentially, when you are allowed choices in a game, you want the consequences which flow from those choices to be logical. But what this game does is allow you to make good, intelligent choices for the characters, which result in just as terrible consequences that would have happened if you'd picked the rash or less diplomatic choices.
SPOILERS AHEAD
For example, playing as Mira, there is NO way to go through the game and have Margaery not hate you or help you out. Which is really, really strange given that it makes Mira's plotline entirely useless. Early on, it is established that you, Mira, are in King's Landing in order to establish yourself at court and help your family. Nothing happens. You're either married off or executed, an ending which the game didn't really set up and basically forces you into.
Another problem I have with this game is that it suggests something will happen based on certain decisions - but nothing happens. It's just trying to build suspense and failing miserably. For example, if the guard is stabbed, Mira will decide whether or not to keep the knife. It seems to be a decision of importance. But regardless, nothing happens to Mira. Interestingly enough, without warning you will suddenly be held up on charges for killing the guard, with NO prior warning and no opportunity to defend yourself. It's ridiculous.
I wouldn't mind if the game had different ways to get to the same ending if those endings made sense based on my choices. But they don't. What happens can be entirely contrary to your decisions and that's why I wouldn't recommend this game.
