Your soldiers WILL die. That is an ironclad rule of XCom. If you're looking for a (as much as a game about fighting off an alien invasion could be) realistic turn based tactical game, this is your game. You arn't using some ragtag group of people who just happen to be semi-immortal elite warriors, but soldiers. They can level up, and they will die, sometimes after one lucky shot from a sectoid while they were in full cover, sometimes after taking on an army of aliens. One of the fun parts of this game is your ability to make up stories about your troops. During a routine UFO landing I had most of my team in the craft, with the sniper, Andres, providing fire support from outside. When the assault team was getting surrounded one of them launched a short range rocket to try and takeout a group of Muton. Instead it took out several of the team, and left them vulnerable. Andres had to listen as his team, his friends, were dying. The one survivor of the massacre tried to make it to the evac zone, but was shot in the back as she tried to run. Fighting despair, he managed to end the last of aliens at the site, and completed his mission.
XCom's gameplay allows for stories like this. ITs great!. Also you know fighting aliens and outfitting elite soldiers with more and more advanced tech. Like armor? There're ones that turn your soldiers into tanks (and the ability to turn them into robot tanks), jetpack ones, and ones that turn them invisible.
Don't worry if a game starts to look bleak, or you can't win missions because you have no soldiers strong enough to fight later aliens. End the game, and start a new one. You can't win them all. One last tip, as tempting as it is to name all of your soldiers after your friends and family, but wait till you at least get a few games (or at least successful battles) under you. Unless you want to watch the soldier you named after your girl/boyfriend, and spent longer than you should making them look as much like them as you could, get killed in the first fight.

Welcome to the bleak world of Grim Dawn. Humanity is close to extingtion, and holding out in small fortifications. The supplies are running low. You wakes up after being possessed by a rather nasty spirit. You find yourself in a place you do not know, and you can't remember a thing of your past. The people of the encampment are suspicious about you too, so you have to earn your keep... by doing what comes naturally to you - slaying undead and hideous beasts threatening your new home, using swords, shields, ranged weapons and magic.
This game is a worthy spiritual successor for Diablo 2, but I would hesitate to call it a clone. No, it is more. The character customisation options are nearly endless, and you can distribute your stats and skills yourself. This game will not hold your hand. The enemies won't be holding back, and neither should you. The difficulty level is finely tuned for ARPG veterans who want a challenge. However it doesn't mean it is for hardcore players only. The difficulty level ramps gradually, and you either learn to play better and prevail, or get stuck with a bloody nose until you learn how to deal with enemies. But you should know that some of your choices have long-term consequences. Sometimes you find an NPC and you are given a few dialog options. The resulting reaction can make your life more difficult, but the choice is usually obvious.
You can redistribute your skill points for a fee and the skill tree is very versatile. You can have up to two professions, and they all have their distinct skill trees. Want to play an engineer who can also use dark magic? Sure, go ahead. A warrior-witch? Sure, go ahead. An elementalist-assassin? Be my guest. Some professions mesh better than others, but nothing will stop you from playing the game the way you like. You can complement and improve your skills with enchanted equipment too.
This game is a game made with love for the genre, and it shows.
If you find Diablo 3 too cheerful and colourful, try this one out.

I really enjoyed this game, and I think it's well worth the money if you know what you're looking for. Unfortunately, the campaign isn't as fun or interesting as vCoh. It holds your hand for far too long and doesn't offer much strategic challenge. I really shouldn't be able to beat the whole thing on normal without failing once, but that's just how it is. The Theatre of War section has quite a few fun challenges, but it isn't something that kept  me hooked for any long amount of time. Playing with friends could be a fun way to enjoy it though.
All that said, however, multiplayer is where this game really shines. The implementation of the battle servers recently has pretty much wiped out the lag issues that this game once experienced, which should satisfy many people's chief concern. Also, the balance has been getting better and better and the most recent patch is no exception. People who still complain about being beaten unfairly by this or that just haven't learned how to counter certian strategies or play to their factions strength. While many long time vCoh fans may find the lack of commander trees startling, the new system really isn't all that bad. The overlap in commanders allows you to find strategies and playstyles that fit you best, instead of locking yourself into a tree that you may end up regreting choosing. The many commanders available to you for free aren't any worse than the dlc ones. It's all about how you play them. Multiplayer in general is fast and fluid, with a great counter system that rewards micro and skill (and luck, this is Coh ofc).
Overall, if you plan on playing multiplayer online against other people, I think that this game is well worth it for any world war 2 geek or rts gamer. If you just want to play the campaign, challenges, and then move on, you may end up getting less than you expect. For me, definitely one of my favorite games!

Time to do a proper review ^_^   170 hours almost so i think its fair by this point.
Pros
-The best character Creation i have ever seen in gaming, i spent 10 hours alon making characters at this point.
-Decent graphics, compared to most MMO's i've played.
-Action combat is ok, this one is biased i usually prefer less action combat in mmo's and more hotbar, atb like systems. but this is a nice change of pace from what im used too, so its a pro for the people out there who enjoy this type
-Decent storyline/quest, its still in the category of "GO here, kill that, grab these" which isnt exactly a good thing, but here in there are some quests that require specifics to reach, and compliment as a tutorial to some of the games systems(Crating, nodes. ets...)
-Nice Crafting/Node system. The crafting is actually nice, you purchase nodes/buildings hire workers, then have those workers work in the nodes/buildings, crafting what you need them too craft. (Boats, Gear, CLothes, More gear)
-Sandbox. This one is a 50/50 if you like sandbox open worlds, then you will love this one, its truly giant spanning a entire contenent, an ocea, another continent in development and then some. there is no fast travel really, so you walk everywhere. (Get them Running shoes on, and Hold "B")
-PVP/PVE. I generally dont like PVP in these types of games, Gear, and Lv. carry your character, as long as your numbersa re bigger your most likely to win, but the node wars are actually really cool, so i let that pass in exchange for it. PVE is nice, but there isnt enough CO-OP content currently,
-The price tag, This game is $10 standard, i bought it for $5 on sale not long ago, i also played it back at launch for a bit, but had to quit for unavoidable reasons :(   if you have a few bucks to spend, and you enjoy action oriented MMO's then i reccomend it.
Cons
-Grinding. The game has a very, very large grind, if not combat, you will grind life skills half of the time, while it is rewarding, (Grinding for Boat/Gear mats, Grinding to get stronger)
-PVE/PVP-This part is back ^_^ while the combat can be fun at times it really comes down to "Dodge, Hit, Skill, Evade, Repeat, especially during PVP combat, where everyone becomes a acrobat of death, sliding and dodging all over the place XD  Still fun though.
I will be adding more to this list as i progress through the game, Keep in mind it is standardized everything on it is part of my opinion, and mine alone. we will see how this game progresses in time ^_^    until next time have a good one!!

Company of Heroes 2 is a real-time strategy video game developed by Relic Entertainment and published by Sega for the Microsoft Windows platform. It is the sequel to the critically acclaimed 2006 game Company of Heroes.
As with the original Company of Heroes, the game is set in World War II but with the focus on the Eastern Front, with players going primarily on the side of the Soviet Red Army on various stages of the campaign, from Operation Barbarossa to the Battle of Berlin. Company of Heroes 2 runs on Relic Entertainment's proprietary Essence 3.0 game engine, which THQ claims allowed the developer to bring "new technological advancements" to the game. In January 2013, Sega acquired Relic Entertainment and along with it the Company of Heroes intellectual property from THQ. The game was released on June 25, 2013 in North America and Europe. The game caused a strong negative reaction from the Russian speaking players and was subsequently withdrawn from distribution by the Russian game publisher 1C-Softclub.

My first real foray into the ARPG genre, at time of writing I have done two play-throughs of the main campaign on different class characters and played a whole lot of crucible ... I'll be getting Ashes of Malmouth on release!
tl:dr: great environments, well paced campaign, (1) huge variety with unique class definition system, plenty to explore (or not), (2) fun instances, well written (dark) fluff, (3) crucible is ace if you have friends. Strong replayability (1 2 3). in-game dps calculation is awful.
Characters:
Classes feel nicely unique, the three pronged approach (skill, devotion, attributes) to character development gives huge flexibility allowing you really mess with class boundaries, limited only by where you can find common ground between skill-trees and there's quite a bit! One really nice thing is the ability to completely respec if / when you get bored with one set-up or just pick up a cool weapon that you'd like to build around for the next 10 levels or so. That said, mixing and matching takes a decent amount of thought and planning, especially when it comes to devotions (which are kinda like the skill constellations in skyrim). Only criticism here is that attribute points could be a bit more relevant, so far it seems like just maxing physique and any cunning / spirit required is covered by the gear for you desired class.
Environment:
Relatively linear, well paced progression through a series of distinct areas, which on the whole transition smoothly, but are plenty varied. Dungeons & caves are a little less varied (Everybody seems to have a MONSTER cellar for some reason ... :D) but different enough to keep things feeling fresh. There are lots of secret places for those that like to delve but not so many that those who just want to burn through the campaign are lacking gear. The ingenious personal and static portal system saves you lots of time running through parts of the map that you've already cleared - mobs only respawn in an area when you leave a session. Finally there are instances where the stakes are raised - an entry fee, no portals, scaled difficulty, which have really good items in them. Overall really, really good and by the end you wish there was more!
Story (spoiler free):
On your first play through DON'T just blitz through, read the fluff, it's well written and some of it is really, properly dark. if you get a feel for the world you'll enjoy the game much more, lending a *grim* atmosphere to the proceedings!
Crucible:
Excellent implementation of a "Last Stand" type battle where you can actually get useful stuff for the main campaign and your character's development. Adds huge replayability and a different set of tactics from the and campaign.
Grind reduction:
ARPGs are necessarily grindy, there's a reason why I havent stuck to them before. GD does a very good job of keeping things fun. If you find and learn a recipe on one character, all your other characters get it. Once you have lots of reputation with one faction you can give your other characters a huge boost to rep generation with that faction (+100%).  At the higher difficulty levels, more mini-bosses spawn this speeds up your rep gain massively and gets you good gear faster. You can store items / consumables / crafting mats and transfer them between characters - "this gun would be perfect for a two handed ranged demolitionist, i'll keep that for when I make him".
Gripes:
I want there to be more campaign, waiting for expansions is hard!(!).
DPS calculation in-game is terrible, please fix this.
(minor) Difficult to keep track of allies / pets and enemies once the explosions start.
(minor) Secondary classes are a little too secondary, it would be really good to access more of the skills in the secondary class without a huge base skill-point investment - perhaps this is just good balancing though.
(minor) No pet action bar, could do with some extra on-screen space.
(minor) managing equipment swapping with attribute point buffs is tedious if you've decided to change build direction.

Dawn is a short and sweet platformer made by a student team. A little bit of collecting and exploring accompany the platforming gameplay and make for a nice, bite-sized game with soothing music in a solitary place.
Visually, Dawn presents a colourful, natural world on rocks floating in the air. Consisting of one continuous and rather linear level, the world offers side paths here and there that invite the player to explore and discover little secrets. Encouraging exploration are the realisations of finding and activating the beautifully blooming flowers and small mysterious ruins. The level design makes pathing very intuitive and gives the impression that a lot of thought was put into it.
Together with the intuitive pathing, straightforward controls enable the player to fly through the level in a quick and flowing manner. Except for emitting a gust of wind to activate vines and stones, nothing else out of the ordinary running and jumping mechanics is needed to navigate through the world. All fine and dandy, apart from the camera position, which is too high up so that it can become difficult to execute close jumps on smaller platforms.
Overall though, Dawn is a well made game worth a try.

Your soldiers WILL die. That is an ironclad rule of XCom. If you're looking for a (as much as a game about fighting off an alien invasion could be) realistic turn based tactical game, this is your game. You arn't using some ragtag group of people who just happen to be semi-immortal elite warriors, but soldiers. They can level up, and they will die, sometimes after one lucky shot from a sectoid while they were in full cover, sometimes after taking on an army of aliens. One of the fun parts of this game is your ability to make up stories about your troops. During a routine UFO landing I had most of my team in the craft, with the sniper, Andres, providing fire support from outside. When the assault team was getting surrounded one of them launched a short range rocket to try and takeout a group of Muton. Instead it took out several of the team, and left them vulnerable. Andres had to listen as his team, his friends, were dying. The one survivor of the massacre tried to make it to the evac zone, but was shot in the back as she tried to run. Fighting despair, he managed to end the last of aliens at the site, and completed his mission.
XCom's gameplay allows for stories like this. ITs great!. Also you know fighting aliens and outfitting elite soldiers with more and more advanced tech. Like armor? There're ones that turn your soldiers into tanks (and the ability to turn them into robot tanks), jetpack ones, and ones that turn them invisible.
Don't worry if a game starts to look bleak, or you can't win missions because you have no soldiers strong enough to fight later aliens. End the game, and start a new one. You can't win them all. One last tip, as tempting as it is to name all of your soldiers after your friends and family, but wait till you at least get a few games (or at least successful battles) under you. Unless you want to watch the soldier you named after your girl/boyfriend, and spent longer than you should making them look as much like them as you could, get killed in the first fight.

Telltale are masters of the illusion of choice, and this game is a prime example.
No major spoilers here.
The bulk of the gameplay is simply clicking dialogue options and watching the fireworks. However, there are quick-time events which almost always suck and feel like an attempt to keep you paying attention. There are many times these QTEs don't matter because if you fail to do them, you're forced to retry. If the story won't advance until I succeed, just omit the QTE entirely and get on with the story! Now, there are some QTEs that actually do matter if you fail or succeed, but they are very few and far between. Even then, all they do is add some dialogue or one small scene.
This game is worthy of the title "Game of Thrones." You witness the lives of House Forrester, who are vassals to the Warden of the North, Roose Bolton at this time, and the crown. They're basically House Stark 2.0, as each character you'll find is quite honorable and brave, always willing to do what they must for family. This being Game of Thrones, they suffer for that.
Everything else about the atmosphere is spot on. The lore, feudalism, languages, characters, names, houses, locations, intrigue, everything just feels like it was ripped straight from the show. The music is masterful. The voice acting is the best part. Many of the original cast from the show are the voice actors of our favorite characters.
Many people complain about "storyline." No, no. It's all about the storytelling. Even a bland and dull story in the hands of Stephen King can be made interesting. This game does quite well with its story. The most well-written parts of the story take place in Ironrath and King's Landing. These parts are so masterfully written and acted out that you can't help but fear for your characters. The two other branches of the story take place at the Wall and north thereof with Gared, and in Essos with another character. Both of these stories drag on and on, and Gared's storyline is quite useless unless they plan on making a sequel.
My main gripe with the storytelling: illusion of choice. Now, this game does it right. You will, for the most part, feel like your decisions matter. Many of them do. Most of them don't. This game is not really replayable, but the first playthrough is really quite entertaining, especially if you're a fan of the show. Heed this warning: your favorite character is doomed.
I must add, kudos to the writers for making a character whom I hate even more than Joffrey and Ramsay.
Fans of the show and books will most likely enjoy this game. This is not Telltale's best work, but it's really quite good. There was really only one or two deaths that touched me, and there are a few areas that just feel dragged out. But as an experience overall, it's worth it.
7/10

DISCLAIMER: I played this game when I was younger, around 5 years old, younger. I have a heavy set of nostalgia for this game. That, however, does not give it the right to stay exactly the same, this is supposed to be an HD Remake, and with that I will treat it almost as if it came out within this generation.
Ty the Tasmanian Tiger 2: Bush Rescue, a game Krome Studios have remade from 2004 and brought back to life this year. So, what happened since then? Krome Studios sort of "fell out" somewhere after the mid-2000s, creators of great games like the Ty series right here, as well as helped develop some side games for the Spyro series, as well as developed Star Wars: The Force Unleashed. In 2010 they made a sort of small reappearance with Blade Kitten, then fell out again, and seemed to be missing for years, until lately. Before now, they also developed some mobile games, many of which you probably have never heard of.
Krome came back to life in 2015, when Ty the Tasmanian Tiger 1 was released for Early Access on Steam. Praised for it's re-release, Krome announced that they would be updating the game constantly, making it feel smoother, look nicer, and feel more "up to date". Being a fan of the series, I was skeptical of this, Early Access games tend to not leave it's Early Access state, either due to time constraints or lack of money. They, however, pushed through, the game looks beautiful for being an astonishingly 15 years old, released on the sixth generation of consoles (Gamecube, PlayStation 2, and Xbox), yet somehow looks like it was made in the last few years.
Ty the Tasmanian Tiger 2  was originally released in 2004, and it's been 13 years since. Being released on the computer earlier in 2017, it definitely deserved the Early Access title, multiple bugs and issues, frame drops every few minutes, as well as hundreds, if not thousands of areas where the camera would try to make the game unplayable. 8 months later, there are very few bugs, but still some, the frame drops have been more or less dealt with, and the camera no longer tempts you to jump off a cliff.
On to gameplay, there's two big things you're going to do in this game, walking and driving. Walking is as great as it's going to get, however, with the ability to glide, you have far more mobility than most games give. There is, however, some side minigames, the biggest one being Kart racing. Kart racing has a very,
odd way of moving around, the ability to drift feels like you're losing speed but doesn't at the same time, there's powerups that can ruin your amazing run, AI that seems to pass mach 3 the moment you pass them, just all sorts of iffy things. Another minigame, which is not as big, is one where you, the player, get to pilot and shoot as a helicopter. Adding these minigames in the original game was not the best idea, however it did offer something new to do other than run around. There were multiple things off with them that seem to have been more or less fixed, if not feel much nicer than before, thanks for community feedback. There still needs to be work done on the game, though the UI feels better, the menus work better, there's support for multiple languages, online leaderboards, and achievements. Multiple new ideas have been implimented into the game that the community has suggested, including shops that make you want to go for more collectables, and a 'rang wheel that was added quickly from community feedback.
Speaking of, the Dev team for this game is outstanding, they clearly care for this game and heavily rely on it's amazing community for feedback. Something wrong? Tell them, they'll fix it, think of a cool new idea? Tell them, they'll think about it, something annoying you? Tell them, they could help. The team heavily uses the discussions page on Steam, far more than any other team I've seen before, they have a thread for bugs, a thread for suggestions, a thread for achievement ideas, they have a thread for almost anything, and if you don't see it there, make your own.
With a game this old, you'd expect it to look it's age, you'd expect the team to more or less run away, you'd expect a lot of bad things to happen, but with this game, the team didn't run, they came back to it. The game is still iffy, and that's not something to look past, the team wants to show they care for it, and they're trying to show so. There's still bugs, issues, errors, etc. and those will always be in games, no matter how old it is. However, this game has a wonderful community, it has a wonderful team, and it has wonderful gameplay.
Ty the Tasmanian Tiger 2: Bush Rescue is a great game, it has great controls and an amazing development team. There are issues here and there, but they can be, and more than likely will be fixed. I would suggest getting this game and helping the team make it even better, and if we're lucky, they might even release the third game on Steam as well.

Buy Alan Wake, but you can readily give this one a pass.

Super Amazing Wagon Adventure is Oregon Trail meets WarioWare as a scrolling shoot 'em up. Essentially you are thrown into a variety of bizzare scenarios where you shoot and dodge stuff for about 30 seconds or less, and then there's a short transition and you're suddenly somewhere else shooting and/or dodging other stuff. For example, you might be crossing a river dodging boulders, and then you'll make it across the river and into the prairie where you'll gun down some buffalo. The general order of events never changes (forest-->river-->plains-->desert/second river-->mountain-->freefall-->rapids/present day) but there are special random events that can occur, including everything from unicorns to time travel to pirates, many of which will unlock new wagons.
SAWA is really fun, but also difficult. I've only completed it once, and I had to use the invisible wagon, which has a super tiny hitbox. Thankfully it has a good sense of humor and charming visuals and music to ease the pain of my many, many deaths.

Time to do a proper review ^_^   170 hours almost so i think its fair by this point.
Pros
-The best character Creation i have ever seen in gaming, i spent 10 hours alon making characters at this point.
-Decent graphics, compared to most MMO's i've played.
-Action combat is ok, this one is biased i usually prefer less action combat in mmo's and more hotbar, atb like systems. but this is a nice change of pace from what im used too, so its a pro for the people out there who enjoy this type
-Decent storyline/quest, its still in the category of "GO here, kill that, grab these" which isnt exactly a good thing, but here in there are some quests that require specifics to reach, and compliment as a tutorial to some of the games systems(Crating, nodes. ets...)
-Nice Crafting/Node system. The crafting is actually nice, you purchase nodes/buildings hire workers, then have those workers work in the nodes/buildings, crafting what you need them too craft. (Boats, Gear, CLothes, More gear)
-Sandbox. This one is a 50/50 if you like sandbox open worlds, then you will love this one, its truly giant spanning a entire contenent, an ocea, another continent in development and then some. there is no fast travel really, so you walk everywhere. (Get them Running shoes on, and Hold "B")
-PVP/PVE. I generally dont like PVP in these types of games, Gear, and Lv. carry your character, as long as your numbersa re bigger your most likely to win, but the node wars are actually really cool, so i let that pass in exchange for it. PVE is nice, but there isnt enough CO-OP content currently,
-The price tag, This game is $10 standard, i bought it for $5 on sale not long ago, i also played it back at launch for a bit, but had to quit for unavoidable reasons :(   if you have a few bucks to spend, and you enjoy action oriented MMO's then i reccomend it.
Cons
-Grinding. The game has a very, very large grind, if not combat, you will grind life skills half of the time, while it is rewarding, (Grinding for Boat/Gear mats, Grinding to get stronger)

I really enjoyed this game, and I think it's well worth the money if you know what you're looking for. Unfortunately, the campaign isn't as fun or interesting as vCoh. It holds your hand for far too long and doesn't offer much strategic challenge. I really shouldn't be able to beat the whole thing on normal without failing once, but that's just how it is. The Theatre of War section has quite a few fun challenges, but it isn't something that kept  me hooked for any long amount of time. Playing with friends could be a fun way to enjoy it though.
All that said, however, multiplayer is where this game really shines. The implementation of the battle servers recently has pretty much wiped out the lag issues that this game once experienced, which should satisfy many people's chief concern. Also, the balance has been getting better and better and the most recent patch is no exception. People who still complain about being beaten unfairly by this or that just haven't learned how to counter certian strategies or play to their factions strength. While many long time vCoh fans may find the lack of commander trees startling, the new system really isn't all that bad. The overlap in commanders allows you to find strategies and playstyles that fit you best, instead of locking yourself into a tree that you may end up regreting choosing. The many commanders available to you for free aren't any worse than the dlc ones. It's all about how you play them. Multiplayer in general is fast and fluid, with a great counter system that rewards micro and skill (and luck, this is Coh ofc).
Overall, if you plan on playing multiplayer online against other people, I think that this game is well worth it for any world war 2 geek or rts gamer. If you just want to play the campaign, challenges, and then move on, you may end up getting less than you expect. For me, definitely one of my favorite games!

Company of Heroes 2 is a real-time strategy video game developed by Relic Entertainment and published by Sega for the Microsoft Windows platform. It is the sequel to the critically acclaimed 2006 game Company of Heroes.
As with the original Company of Heroes, the game is set in World War II but with the focus on the Eastern Front, with players going primarily on the side of the Soviet Red Army on various stages of the campaign, from Operation Barbarossa to the Battle of Berlin. Company of Heroes 2 runs on Relic Entertainment's proprietary Essence 3.0 game engine, which THQ claims allowed the developer to bring "new technological advancements" to the game. In January 2013, Sega acquired Relic Entertainment and along with it the Company of Heroes intellectual property from THQ. The game was released on June 25, 2013 in North America and Europe. The game caused a strong negative reaction from the Russian speaking players and was subsequently withdrawn from distribution by the Russian game publisher 1C-Softclub.

Action RPG very similar to Diablo and PoE. Grim Dawn does some things better, and some things worse... thats how games work. Now a lot of reviews are based on comparison to PoE or Diablo series because lets face it, players of those games are bored as well with the titles and crave new adventure. Yes this game isnt free compared to PoE, but it doesnt cost what D3 does. May change with the upcoming xpac, who knows.
Grim Dawn in a nutshell is your base Action RPG, but with unique elements that you dont normally find in Action RPG dungeon crawl, hack n slash, loot fest games. There are only 6 classes right now, so the variety may seem small, but thats where playing through the game will always introduce something new you werent really expecting unless someone told you beforehand. I was expected a dull game, spinoff of all the Action RPGs trying to be D2, since many D2 players disliked 3. (Some people dont like change) But it kept me excited everytime I thought I was about to lose interest.
First level up you get to look through classes and their skills available. Seeing an actual skill tree again was exciting to me after PoE and D3. You get 3 skill points per level, which you use on whatever you want in the chosen classes. Now like D2, some skills are locked by level, merely because outside of leveling skills, there is a general skill point area for each class that allows you to access skills further down the tree, and give basic stat upgrades so you dont feel its a complete waste skipping a skill to put a couple points into the tree itself. This concept was new and intriguing to me anyways. At level 10 suddenly you get access to another class skill tree... and from there mix and match your playstyle. Think D2 skills tree, but dual class... sick. Kept me entertained for the first 20 levels or so. Then when the trees seem to grow less exciting with the need to push further into the classes with points...
suddenly your hit with a celestial tree that kinda reminds me of PoE tree. These celestial points only go up to 50, but this in itself, is another skill tree available to EVERYONE, not just one class. These points have a large impact on the playstyle you are building, and can continue tailoring. Adding 50% more DoT fire damage, or increasing all pet damage by 40%. Big impacts imo based on other games trees/point system. Not only does this celestial tree offer better customization to how you build your classes, but then allows you to access even more skills... that get this... STACK ontop of current abilities you have. Dual spell, one click... thats new to me in how they apply it. Instead of my pyromancer shooting just fire/explosive shells from his base skill (that still has more upgrades to go on it own), it also steals life and shoots out extra "projectiles" that pierce enemies and heal me... cool. How about a burning molotov, then mixed with the celestial tree, create mini fissures/volcanoes that erupt and do damage ontop of the skills original damage... or put a cold storm attached to the molotov... The skill customization is the best ive seen, to build a character how you want to play them. (imo fanboys). If playing through 3 difficulties like D2 isnt that exciting to you, you can always level up doing their DLC arena, which is a survival mode that still provides XP, Celestial Points, and Loot.
The game always uses a reputation system, which is different for this style of game, and they definitely tried to make it fit in. Did it work? Not how I see the usual reputation put into a game, but then again, ive never seen it in an action rpg period (that ive played). This is covered by giving random bounties to players for that faction, to improve the reputation with them. Or on a small scale, who you kill will change the rep as well.
There are some long term choices players can make, that will in a small way affect what rep rewards are avilable or crafting patterns.
Crafting exists like D3, just not developed as D3's crafting system is. Componets exist kinda of like PoE, but instead of trading them, they are used for crafting or on the gear itself.
Hidden areas with Shrines and other rare loot/bosses exist in Grim Dawn, that will make you want to revist areas youve been, because you found the method to open it (scrap, dynamite, etc) and see what was inside.
The map doesnt reset and randomize like Diablo, the campaign is very straight forward. The mobs do reset after leaving a game and reentering, but locations are all the same and the map is explored where you have been still.
The gameplay is definitely not as smooth flowing as Diablo 3, but was better than when I last played PoE. Environment is fitting to the name of the game, but you can see they did well making it seem somewhat realistic, but its not as clear as say looking at objects or foliage in D3. I still enjoyed the setting, in each area. Act 2 in both D2 and D3 I hated, I didnt have that feeling with this game, since the area blends without having a transition between acts like diablo does.
Overall, I find it was one of the few games ive played lately that was worth the cost. If your a hard fanboy of Diablo or PoE, nothing is ever going to satisfy as much as them. If the genre is your main focus as to trying more, give this a chance, it will be rewarding.
I have not hit max level on any character yet, so I can not vouch for the end game content, but I have enjoyed the hell out of leveling in this, more so than Diablo 3 or PoE. Turn on Veteran difficulty for a slow, more strategic approach, than the burn through mob grind that has always been Diablos style.
I tried Veteran Coop... most fun on an action rpg ive had in a long time. If coop is your style, snag this with a friend for sure.
Has some replayability depending on your interest to explore other classes and synergies from the celestial skill choices. Has kept me from ever hitting cap because I like trying different styles and seeing what is fun or not for me.
I have been a long time fan of Diablo since D2's release. Diablo 3 was not my thing versus D2 because variety died, and there became a 1 skill/armor set to rule them all, on each class. Skills were forced, not chosen. Skill tree's disappeared in diablo. The levels up to the max felt very dull with having to wait for a skill you wanted, since skill unlock at levels and not through skill points. Like an extra box set of Game of Thrones
This is an interactive novel, not a game.  You interact with the story and have some influence over how it unfolds, but largely you are immersed in a story that plays out with the Game of Thrones (as told in the TV series) saga as a backdrop.
If you like Game of Thrones you will like this game.  Featuring voice overs by the HBO cast the story feels true to the books in general and the TV series in particular.
The graphics seem a bit dated and the 'gameplay' is poor (but remember this is not a game it's an interactive novel).
However the storytelling is very well done, and true to the feel of the Game of Thrones Saga.  Expect lots of people to die, and expect that you won't be able to do very much about it.
As in the books and the TV series the story is divided between different characters and you will 'guide' each of the main protagonists for their scenes.  This works well, and is again in keeping with the feel of Game of Thrones.
Don't expect to be able to change the storyline significantly
Don't expect to 'win' - you are experiencing the story, not writing a new one
Don't expect this to be an RPG
Do expect an immersive plot with plenty of detail tying parts together as well as into the wider Game of Thrones Saga
Do expect to want to start the next episode as soon as you've completed the previous one
Do expect to face some difficult choices
Recommended for Game of Thrones fans.

The graphics are disgusting and terrible. I can see what they were trying to do and hide the low resolution textures and smear it with a painting look but it's very distracting and shows the respect and effort that went into this game. There are games that are 15 years old such as Max Payne that look better than this.
Modern Telltale games pride themselves on giving you choice in a 'choose your own adventure' sort of narrative and that your choices matter. With Game of Thrones its very apparent no matter what choice you make, you are led to outcomes that are unavoidable more so than previous Telltale games.  Lady Miras whole storyline is not only worthless in comparison to the other characters but is made worse when you realise the situation it always ends up in. While I appreciate the actors from the show lending their voices, I felt their inclusion was shoehorned in with the exception of Ramsey Snow in an attempt to lure people that watch the show to buy the game.
I did enjoy the game for the original story it told but it’s not one I can recommend due to worthless choices, barely any gameplay and its terrible graphics.

Livy writes of a meeting in 193 BC, as Rome prepared for war with the Seleucid Empire and generals from both sides met at the court of Antiochus the Great. There Scipio Africanus, the savior of Rome in the darkest days of the Punic Wars, found Hannibal Barca. The latter had left Carthage in exile when the Romans demanded his surrender seven years after his defeat at the hands of the former, lest he rebuilt the broken city to its former glory.
It is not often such great generals meet outside the blood and gore of the battlefield and thus the conversation between them fell to whom they ranked as the greatest generals of antiquity. Hannibal answered Alexander ranked highest and though Scipio was dismayed, they could all agree that Alexander was without equal. When asked who ranked second, Hannibal answered Pyrrhus, the Greek general who was the first to bring the young Roman republic to its knees. Scipio then asked whom he ranked third and Hannibal, without hesitation answered that it was himself who ranked third.
Scipio, hurt in his pride that the victim in his greatest success would rank themselves above their victor, asked where then would Hannibal place himself if he had won at the Battle of Zama? And Hannibal answered that beyond doubt, then he would place himself before even Alexander.
Scipio didn’t answer again, instead kicking a pig bladder at Hannibal, through his legs and in between two vases standing in the corner of the gymnasium. He pulled his toga over his head and galloped to the crowd with his hands in the air.
And so, the game of football was born, though it wouldn’t be rediscovered until the 1990’s in England, where some rich people decided they could be a lot richer still by asking people a lot of money to watch other people play. Soon, instead of playing football, people decided that they could make a game that was like football, but played on computers instead, so they didn’t have to go outside and get dirty.
You can kick the ball, run around with the ball, pass the ball, tackle other people who have the ball and if you want to pull your shirt over your head and run around yelling “goal, goal, goal”, you can do that while playing Behold the Kickmen on your computer. You can even play as United!

Okay, this game is fun and for the most part well-executed, but there are several caveats (bear in mind that I played the original on Xbox 360 so any judgments I make comparing 'American Nightmare' to the original will be biased accordingly).  Firstly, although the same gameplay mechanics that made the first game so perfectly clumsy and frantic are still present, the ♥♥♥♥ing unreal abundance of ammo and batteries makes combat a complete and utter joke.  There's only one part at the end of the game that's even remotely hard.
Secondly, the addition of new weapons is very much a double-edged sword.  On one had, it's cool to lay waste to an entire horde of enemies with an M-16, but since there's no influx in the volume of enemies to account for Alan's increased firepower, most of the skirmishes are just too easy, and while I'm as big a fan as any of judging every game individually on its own merits, the original is just so much better.  In the original game, the best weapon you can get is a bolt action rifle, and once you're out of ammo you have to reload each shell individually, same as the revolver and the shotguns.  This makes the enemies you face much more lethal in numbers, and a very gruesome death is usually no more than 6 shots away.
Thirdly, the live action cutscenes in this game are so unbelievably corny and redundant that I'm amazed someone as artistically savvy as the creator of the original Alan Wake would even think to put such trash in this game to begin with.  I don't know who directed these scenes, but he or she makes 'Sharknado' look like 'Gone with the Wind'.  The only thing that could possibly make them any worse would be having Alan dress up as a clown and slow dance with Philip Seymour Hoffman's corpse just before the credits roll.  SERIOUSLY, I cannot stress enough how insanely terrible these cutscenes are.
Lastly, although it's still pretty fun, it somehow leaves you wanting more and less at the same time.  It's ♥♥♥♥ing prolifically repetitive (I can't really reveal exactly how without spoiling the game, but this is much more than just your garden variety reptitiveness).  It's all for the sake of a plot device of course, but it looks more like laziness to me.  Yet, the creator would have you believe this is more than an expansion, but I don't buy that either.  It clocks in at only a couple hours, and even with the addition of the horde-style arcade mode, it's hardly worth the price of ten dollars.  Either wait for a sale, or buy it as a part of the Alan Wake package deal.  The original game is amazing, and you won't regret it.  'American Nightmare' is fun, but for hardcore fans of the game, the dumbed down feel and lack of any kind of narrative momentum will leave you a bit disappointed, if still relatively entertained.  7/10.

A review after 233 hours! So read some reviews and most aren't complete enough to be fair. So here it is a honost review:
1. It's a free game so you can't complain a lot about it.
2. Its is fun. The quality of this game is high especially considering it is free.
3. Unlike what most people say, it is not pay to win. I never payed a dime, got all the heroes. You will earn a lot of money, but you got to play to earn it. Some heroes are cheap some are more expensive.
4. There is no best hero. It is more important how you play with you hero. This game is not a FPS where you goal is to kill as many players as you can. You need to be smart. Every hero has a weakness and a strentgh. It will take a few hours to find them. So once again, you just need to play. When a hero is to strong, the developers will make him weaker within weeks after release.
5. Amount of players is a real problem. On average you need to wait 2min before every game. Not a huge problem, but you would think that given the quality and fun there aren't wait times.
6. Great support! We get new heroes and updates all the time! In terms of support it is the same as ARK, so just awesome.
7. I noticed that most players whom are complaining are actually the players who are just not that good. They fight hard but not smart. Like you will notice.
8. Strong learning curve. The game is easy, but it will take some hours for beginners to understand it. After that, with every new hero you will need some hours to master his skills. This game does not only depends on skills but also tactics.
9 One huge problem is that people will during the match. The problem is, when a player leaves there is no side effect for the other team. Meaning they got a extra guy. Also people will leave when your on the loosing side, while a game can change within seconds.
Conclusion: I think this is a must have game. It is fun, free and has great support. You would be stupid not to try it out. Is it perfect no... But how many EA games did you buy that last year that were unplayable, XD.

This review is SPOILER FREE.
I give Grim Dawn a rating of 9/10.
To fully understand why it gets this please read the COMPREHENSIVE review. [Unable to do summary this time, sorry ;) ]
For those unfamiliar with my reviews I tend to do reviews slightly different to most. For my overall rating I look at several features of a game which is nothing special but I rate them individually and the overall rating is an average of these. This allows anyone to fully understand the main positives and negatives in terms of scale.
For this review I am going to look at the story, audio & graphics, gameplay and performance.
1. STORY
Grim Dawn is set in a world in which humans are fighting for survival against an unknown ancient spirit-like foe. These spirits have the ability to possess humans, the undead, nature etc hence are extremely powerful. You begin the story as a human who was possessed but managed to break the binding spirit with the help of a mage/witch. You forget everything and basically start anew with the aim to defeat this spirit army. This is more or less the main objective but as you progress through the story you come across a lot of evil beings along the way. This includes bandits, monsters, evil cults etc. So there is a lot of substance to this game.
As you would expect throughout the game there are vast amounts of letters/notes, books and other resources which give a detailed look into the lives of the people of Grim Dawn which can show the change from a pleasant afternoon to a chaotic bloodbath. This is great lore telling and really gives a good understanding of the world. In some instances it is very funny such as someone noticing someone else acting strange but you already know why.
Throughout the game you will come across factions/clans which you can either become friends or foes with. Whilst I like this idea I did not believe it went far enough as most factions can either only like you or hate you but by how much is the question.
The story is built around an act structure. Were you come across a new area and monsters in a new act. Currently the game is not finished as the story only goes so far but add ons will add more acts. Such an add on is coming out very soon in the form of the Ashes of Malmoth.
The story recieves a rating of 9/10.
2. GRAPHICS/DESIGN AND AUDIO
This game is rather stunning when it comes to the design. It sets an evil undertone to all the surroundings, almost satanic in some areas. It really tries to present a world which was once beautiful that has been just destroyed with all law and civilisation being set back to the equivalent of the dark ages. The colours and imagery are great as well as the lighting and shadows. There are lots of enemies with their own unique designs. There are lots of different environments such as caves, crypts, mountains which will continue to amaze you of the great work done by the developers. But one thing which that bugged me was the lack of an intermediate environment, i.e. going from one major environment to another.
With the environments aside, there is the character design; in terms of the equipment, there is a lot of loot with emphasis on A LOT. A great deal of effort was clearly but into this as each has its own detailing. It is quite the mystery what loot you will end up recieving and to see the purple drop outline which equals a lengendary puts an excited grin on your face.
Lastly for design is the UI which at the start is a bit tricky to understand as there is a lot of it but I can assure you that with time you will understand it. The game makes you start on normal difficulty then you can restart the campaign on harder difficulties. This is somewhat telling you not to worry about not understanding things at first since everyone had their awful starting character. I cannot speak much of the UI as I would need a visual aid so I recommend just looking up pictures/videos to see it but do not worry about it.
The audio is another well done feature. You have a varying soundtrack which can be somewhat eerie and slow and then in another area you can come across a more soft rock adventurous theme. I must say I am suprised with it but in a good way. The noise effects are good such as enemy mumurs, magic/attacking and environmental. It is good quality in terms of what I listened to on my headphones.
The Graphics/design and audio get a rating of 9.5/10.
3. GAMEPLAY
To simply put the gameplay is fast paced especially at higher difficulties. You will need to act quick at different scenarios whether it be to use a certain spell to combat individuals/groups or to move your character about the map to avoid getting hit etc. The game is very strategic and somewhat complex in the way it is made through character customisation. There are several tiers of customisation. There is the first tier choice of class which determines what special abilities you will have such as magic or melee based. You can choose a second class at lvl10 which makes things interesting. The next tier is attribute points. There are 3 categories to put these points in which basically improve stats for either magic, shooting or strength. Tier 3 of custimsation is the distrubution of points into the abilities choosen at tier 1. Tier 4 of customisation is a star chart were you distrubute points which can improve anything, even giving you an extra sub-ability which tags on to an existing ability. A lot of customisation to get your head around. But like I said in the UI discussion do NOT worry about it.
The game is very much loot based were the loot comes in the form of common, uncommon, magic, rare, lengendary. There is so much loot it must have taken forever to design. It feels great to find something good but then again it can be frustrating later in the game.
I would recommend to look up videos of actual gameplay on youtube as I feel the videos on the steam store do not give it justice and somewhat makes it look like a wave based game which it is not. Though a DLC does have a wave based competition.
There is so much you can do in this game you will have hundreds of hours of play time though if you want to do well at higher difficulties you really need to have a perfected character which is difficult as all characters will have their strengths but also their weaknesses. Makes it fun.
The gameplay gets a rating of 8.5/10.
4. PERFORMANCE
For me this game had no issues in terms of compatibility, famerate or bugs. The devs clearly put an emphasis on making the game and any add ons perform well before releasing it which is rare nowadays since companies put out half finished games. In terms of what to expect in terms of requirements, I have what I would say as an average-decent laptop and a good custom built pc. I found that my laptop struggled to perform at max settings but did fine/ok at low settings. My pc on the otherhand worked fine at max settings. It is the type of game you do not expect to need good equipment but I found you do especially if you want to see it in all its glory. So keep that in mind. They have given requirements and you should make sure you go by them.
For performance It gets a rating of 8.5/10.
Note; The crucible add on basically adds a colleseum and a wave based gamemode which will give you prizes for successfully completing the waves. The higher the wave count you reach the better the prizes but if you die you get worse prizes. So it is a game of risk also, as you can determine when to stop. It is a nice extra but in the end it is only an extra. You will not miss out in anything as it has no relation to the story etc.
To finish, I 100% recommend this game. The dev team are what devs of a bygone age used to do and make a game that performs well which looks good and is fun to play. Whilst I would usually look for a bargain I would buy this game at any price as it is worth it and it supports the team.
Overall rating of 9/10.

Far Cry Primal isn't a bad game, but it has lots of unfulfilled potential, and unless you're a specific type of gamer, is either going to be an alright experience or a moderate amount of torture.  How did you feel about the gathering, hunting and crafting systems of the previous two games?  Those feelings will tell you EXACTLY how much you'll like Far Cry Primal.
You play as Takkar, a beast tamer out to defend his people from the onslaught of the cannibalistic Udam tribe, and the pyromanic Izila tribe.  Annnnnndddd that's pretty much it.  Now, I think writing a story that takes place in 10,000 B.C. is a tough sell.  You don't have a lot to work with, as these are essentially pre-tribal conditions.  Complicated social concepts CAN'T exist.  I knew this going in and was prepared for a simplistic plot, but I was surprised to learn that several linchpins of the plot are conveyed entirely through drug trips.  Now, I know that drug use has somehow become a theme in the last two Far Cry games, but using it as a plot mechanic creates a problem as it injects an element of pure fantasy into an otherwise entirely realistic game.  It draws attention to the fact that the game is neither as realistic as it should have been, nor as entertainingly fantastic as it could have been.
Most of the game's quests revolve around recruiting half a dozen specialists for the tribe and doing their bidding, as well as growing the tribe by doing things like saving tribe members (Wenja) in trouble and taking outposts from the enemy.  Almost all of the rest of the game is hunting, gathering and crafting.
In theory, this could have worked.  If you're going to have those systems dominate your game, go deep.  Hunting could have added real elements of tracking to the game, at the very least.  Instead, you hit V to see things through some magical Hunter Vision that is never explained.  Takkar's primitive arsenal is somewhat impressive, if redundant on certain items, but it could have been more complex.  I would have liked to have seen a flint-napping skill to increase the quality of your weapons over time.  Instead, we're left with the generic "gather these items and magically make your stuff better", which every Far Cry game has done.  Many of the game's unlockable skills have no purpose other than to craft or gather more than one thing at a time, but if you do every MEANINGFUL quest and gear/skill upgrade in the game, there's only about 25 hours here.
There are the typical side-quest/collectible/explore-area routines that every Far Cry game has, but every single one of them gives you either XP, a skill point, materials, or adds to the tribe's population.  The only conceivable benefit to growing the tribe (besides unlocking certain upgrades) is that they will gather certain types of materials FOR you and drop them into a bag you can access from almost anywhere in the world.  I don't think I completed half the game's content, and it was all rewards such as these.  While the world itself is savagely beautiful, there's just no point in going sight-seeing for such meager things.
Many quests are locked off unless you develop certain buildings within the tribal home, using quite a lot of resources.  I would have liked to have seen a much more extensive building mechanic since the game is so focused on gathering and hunting.
Being a beast tamer, you can tame 17 animals, but mostly they just have permutations of each other's abilities.  Outside of role-playing, you will use three or so, tops.  You can also ride certain ones, like the brown bear or either of the sabretooth cats, but not the largest bear.  Should you find one, you can also ride a young mammoth, but not the big ones, which I suppose is fine since it's stupidly overpowered anyway.  Most of the animals you just toss bait at to tame, but three of them (the most powerful) have their own legimitately exciting quest chains.  It's a real shame that they aren't nearly as durable AFTER you tame them, but I suppose nerfing their health was the only way to balance them out.
You can access any summoned animal from within the menu, and send them back just as fast.  If they go down in a fight (which even the toughest ones will with unfortunate regularity) you can feed them meat to get them back up.  If they die outright, you'll need red leaves to bring them back to life.  Sending them away before they die makes them invincible, and they regain health when not summoned.  Commands are limited to "go here, come back, go kill this."  There's also an owl you unlock in the beginning who can scout and tag enemies for you, but also kill a selected enemy outright or drop some of your bombs on them.  How did you unlock this stupendous ability to command the beasts?  A drug trip, of course.
Through a combination of a fully upgraded owl, and stealthy pets, it's possible to take out an entire base without lifting a finger or being discovered, however it is far more fun to fight alongside your beast, or simply run everyone over with a mammoth.  The combat system is a bit clunky.  Sometimes hitboxes are questionable, as are lines of sight, and melee combat has no crosshair and is pure guesswork where you're going to hit.  Takkar has vastly superior technology compared to his enemies, even without the beasts.
Pay no more than 30 dollars even if you're a fan of the systems I've outlined.  Even I was hard put not to get bored to some extent, and I happen to like the game's themes.

This classic PS2 title has made the transition to PC almost flawlessly. There are a few very minor cosmetic bugs on some textures, but other than that, all is well. And out of 7 hours playing, I only had 1 CTD.
The game itself retains the 'collect all the things' sidequest from the first game, with more uses for the objects than just for getting 100% completion. It does this very well, and takes the player in some new directions with a Mission system to make progress.
Some flaws: the Fourbie's handling is a little hard to deal with (leastways with a controller), and occasionally there's a lack of precision platforming. The minimap is difficult to follow at times, particularly in the larger zones - which are also awkward to navigate and frustrating if you lack patience.
All in all, this should tick every box you have for a game of this type.

Lethal League consists of hitting a ball back and forth in order to (hopefully) hit and kill your opponent. Now, it gets much more complex than just this, with parries, clashes, bunts, smashes, and even specials being thrown into the mix, but the basic premise is always the same; hit the ball. You can play with up to 4 people, online or on local, and that's where this game really shines. It's extremely fun to play with friends, due to the easy-to-learn nature of the game, and how hectic and intense the matches can be. If you have a few friends that are willing to play, you're going to have a great time. Even with only a single friend, this game can be a blast. Most people complain about the online multiplayer, as it can be pretty difficult to find a match, with wait times of 5+ minutes just to find one. Don't let this discourage you, however, because the weekends usually boost the playerbase and if you find a match with someone, they'll usually play with you 20 games in a row, so you don't have to go looking for another player again. Sometimes you'll get matched up with a really laggy player, but this is as simple as quitting out and looking for another match. It does happen, but when it does, it's not that big of a deal.
The gameplay itself is very enjoyable, and I can see myself playing this for hundreds of hours. Contrary to what it looks like at first, every single character is unique and different. Even something as simple as the angles they hit the ball at or their hitbox size is different. Every single one of them is properly balanced, with none of them being "the best." The only thing that determines their worth is the person playing them. Any character can beat any character. One of the main turnoffs is the lack of characters, with there only being 6 total to play as (excluding doombox.) But unlike most games, I see this as a good thing. This is due to the fact that all the characters have completely different feels to them, and with only 6 to choose, it allows players to actually learn their moves and develop strategies for each. More than 10 characters would be terrible for this game, because then it would be impossible to memorize all of their moves. And, unlike most other fighting games, there really aren't any "combos" that can be abused over and over again. Any ball can be hit if you're smart enough to know where to stand, or you know how to counter it. There are a few advanced concepts, as I mentioned above, but once you learn those, it's just getting to learn the ball and develop better strategies. If you ever want to switch things up, they do have a few things you can change, including a points mode, different types of balls, and even the ability to turn off ball tagging (making it so you can kill yourself with your own ball,) but generally the default mode is fun enough to not need anything added to it, and it's the most commonly accepted mode online. One of my favorite things about this game is how fast you can get playing, instead of waiting. Within 30 seconds, you can start a match, and within 4 minutes you can be done with one. If you are strapped for time, this will have you covered. Conclusion; you will not get bored of this game if you care enough to learn how to play.
The soundtrack is awesome. It sounds great and perfectly fits the exciting, fast paced action that usually occurs. It isn't just background music either; most of the tracks are pretty active, and can help build up the excitement. Unfortunately, there is only a very small selection of songs, with there only being one for each stage and then a few extras.
The perfomance is the downfall of this game. Everything about this game is perfectly fine, but the performance is absolutely god-awful. It actually isn't a demanding game at all; all of the art is somewhat pixellated, and barely anything warrants lag in any way. If you're worried about your older machine not being able to handle it, don't. It will work. The issue lies in the online aspect of the game. The game experiences no perfomance drops when doing local games or bots, but everything else has severe issues. For one, the game can randomly lag in the middle of games that have pretty decent ping. This is unacceptable in a game that has such a focus on timing and precision. There is also a severe issue with games of more than 2 players. When you look online for match, it automatically pairs you up with one other person, so all online matches you play (that I've come across, at least) are 1v1's. Any lag in a 1v1 is usually the result of the other person, not the game. However, this is not the same with a 3 player or 4 player match. Since Lethal League uses P2P connections, any players that lag the game slow down everybody else. This means that one person can slow down the entire game. There is also a crippling bug as of 6/18/17 that still hasn't been fixed for almost 9 months. When playing 3 or 4 player matches, the game can disconnect and prevent the match from starting. After this happens, every single person that has disconnected has to reload the entire game all over again. If you don't, the disconnection will continue to happen until you reload. This happens roughly once every third match for my friends and I, and it completely ruins the game. Just to play around 10 matches you have to reload 3 times. I really don't know why this hasn't been patched yet.
All in all, this game is pretty awesome. It requires a lot of skill, and it really stresses the importance of timing and precision. However, the frequent lag, crashes, and overall issues this game has can ruin the experience. If you have friends that are willing to buy it, or if you frequently play games on a local machine, I would definitely recommend it. A word of advice, though; wait for a sale. $14 is a lot for a game that only really consists of a small amount of content. So, yes, I would recommend this game to a friend.

The game features a career mode (where all the team names end in “United”) where you spend money, earned by scoring goals after making passes and tackles, on team-wide upgrades in skill. Quick custom games against the AI are also possible, though there is no multiplayer. Controls are performed better with a gamepad. Players move significantly slower with the ball, placing an emphasis on passing (though players can sprint for a limited time). Both kicks and tackles can be aimed, and tapping the tackle button again when near the ball will take possession. Dashing left or right is also available, though you are not able to manually switch players (which makes the game more challenging and exciting overall). This is not a serious depiction of the sport: there are no throw-ins, goalies barely get in the way, you score more points by kicking further out, extra time is added by running over clocks scattered on the field, and offsides penalties are given randomly (well, that part is realistic). The AI is just good enough to provide a decent opponent while adhering to the silly nature of the game. Although Behold the Kickmen is not the best arcade soccer game available, it does offer good gameplay mechanics befitting of its casual approach to the sport.

Ty the Tasmanian Tiger 2: Bush Rescue was my first Ty the Tasmania Tiger game. Originally played it as a young child on the Original Xbox console. I already had a soft spot for the game, and when it got re-released on steam I just had to grab it.
Ty 2 start off shortly after where Ty 1 left off… the Reptile forces are trying to break Boss Cass free from Currawong Jail. The prison where boss Cass got locked up following the event of ty 1. Ty and his friends do their very best to keep him locked up. But their efforts are not enough. Boss Cass breaks free with the help of his lead henchwoman Fluffy…
Following their failed attempt to keep Cass locked up the heroes form Bush Rescue. This strike team will allow them to better respond to distress calls all over the outback. Boss Cass his whereabouts are known but due to diplomatic immunity the heroes cannot arrest him. This is because Cass has setup his own country called Cassopolis.
Soon after the first mission you get dropped in to the open world, here you can do mission that become available to you. Once you've done enough mission within the outback the game will progress its story. This goes in the form of a boss battle or special mission. Just like the opening mission these are very scripted, But most importantly very fun!
Ty 2 is a platformer in heart. The core gameplay is solid and fun. Ty feels good to control, And jumping feels responsive and fast. Two attack types are available: his Boomerangs and a Bite Attack, he is a Tiger after all.
The boomerangs come in many types, like Fire, Ice and rope Boomerangs. You can get them in shops in town and upgrade at Sly’s tree house. You use the Red Coins you collect all over the outback to pay for them. These 'Rangs make combat and platforming easier and will allow ty to reach places he couldn’t reach before.
Other than 'Rangs you can also buy Bunyip license. Bunyip’s are mech suits used for combat, exploration or clearing a path.
Having the licenses is required to do some missions, same goes for the Boomerangs. This is a very annoying aspect of the design, because you're not always told what license or 'Rang you will need to do the mission. (Get them as soon as you can!)
Within the world of Ty2 you can collect many things. Of course the currency is all over the place, but you can also get Cogs, Chromium Orbs and Bilbies. The Chromium Orbs can be used to buy maps, they will show you the location of the other items to collect, they are required to get 100%. Also one of the best things to find is a guy called goo-boo (lost) Steve.
You might also have noticed I have not mentioned the cart racing mini game, they are scattered around the open world for you to do, luckily they are not required for the main plot to go forward because they (‘’Suuuuuuuuuck’’) are very bad. I’m pretty sure some people find them enjoyable but I can't get in to them. That's why I didn’t include them in this review.

First off.  If you're a fan of either Game of Thrones or Telltale, you're going to love this game.  Both?  You're in for a treat.
Telltale takes their type of gameplay and fine tunes it to the situation.  For those that don't like quick time events, unfortunately, you still have to put up with them.  That being said they are placed at the perfect moments where you'd expect them.  In combat, avoid someone trying to stab you in the neck, and trying to grab something to catch yourself as you're falling...etc.  They are used well and not over done like they might have been in previous titles.
In the world, you play the role of several members of a noble house that is loyal to House Stark.  The story starts you off a little before the Red Wedding.  I'm only saying that much about the story to be helpful to people for timeframe reference if you were/are following the show or the books.  Just as in the world of the show and books, the world is very dangerous.  Unlike previous Telltale titles where you can feel the climax coming as you progress through the chapters, the story here feels as though your whole house can be destroyed at any moment and by the actions of any of the characters you play if you make one wrong move or irritate the wrong noble.  Cersei is especially terrifying when your playing the role of a character and in her crosshairs as opposed to just watching her on the screen destroying someone else.  The story keeps you on the edge of your seat for almost the entire time.
Overall, Telltale is perfecting their craft as they go and a marriage between them and the world of George R.R. Martin is a suspenseful, terrifying, and extremely fun kind of evil.

So... Telltale's 'The Walking Dead' Season 2.6667(?) is paradoxically both an overly familiar, and a radical departure, from the established 'The Walking Dead' series. The most notable changes in this season of 'The Walking Dead' is that none of the characters from previous seasons of 'The Walking Dead' make appearances, while a number of actors/actresses from HBO's 'Game of Thrones' inexplicably lend their voices in wooden imitations (cameos?) of the characters they play from that series (It's been said before, but I dare say it again: actors good on stage and screen don't necessarily make good voice actors.)
Also, except for a little bit towards the end, the zombies have largely been replaced with fully alive sociopaths running around with swords and axes.
Anyway, when I bought this, I was hoping that with all these surface changes, that the core mechanics of 'The Walking Dead' would be changed up as well, but no they're still intact.  Like other seasons of TWD, this one consists of a mix of overly simplistic point-and-click adventure puzzles (the most common soluion being: find the thing in this very limited view space that we've highlighted for you, and click on it), a series of QTEs (that come out of nowhere and have little relation to what's happening on screen), and a series of 'choices', or rather a series of illusions of the player having any kind of effect on this universe at all (the only real consequence to the story being which character model or voice actor appears to say the lines that funnels the player down the preset story that Telltale had planned.)
While it was nice to get a TWD story that shakes things up by taking place in the North Pole and in a Sahara at the same time, it ultimately wasn't all that compelling a TWD story.  I wouldn't even say it was a very good GoT story either, despite all those really unsubtle GoT cameos thrown in there.
Summing up, this whole thing was BORING. The only real enjoyment I got from this... ehh, it's a stretch to call it a game.. ummm... happening?... is when given a dialogue choice, I just chose not to say anything everytime. Most of the time, it didn't matter at all, and I got a perverse enjoyment out of seeing the main characters just standing there in awkward silence while the supporting characters would bend over backwards just to keep the plot moving forward.

This game is plain awesome. The developers of this game are brilliant. They have come up with simple mechanics that deliver hours upon hours of gameplay.
A word of caution though: this game contains significant random elements. And I stress that because I know some people hate even minimal randomness in games. That doesn't mean that skill and experience don't account for anything though. Learning how to manage that randomness and your resources, as well as exploring the synergies between different kinds of weapons and their application to different strategies, does improve your performance in the game.
Furthermore, there are no save slots. The game saves automatically so that you can continue your playthrough were you left off, but you can't go back in order to correct a bad decision. That might put some people off, but the random events, coupled with the fact that every decision is final, is what makes this game interesting (it's akin to playing XCOM: enemy unknown in Ironman mode). It forces you to move out of your confort zone and just learn how to make the most out of every situation.
It is also worth mentioning that this is a difficult game. You will probably need a few trials before making it to the Flagship on easy difficulty, and probably a couple more trials (if not more) to actually defeat the Flagship. And even with a few tens of hours of experience in your back, it's not unlikely to have bad runs on easy.
I've heard some complaints about the graphics. There's no discussion that the visuals are simple. All I will say about this is that the simplicity of the graphics does not get in the way of the gamplay (which can't be said of other indie games that go for simple graphics), and in fact I like the art direction and the overall visual aesthetic of the game. The soundtrack is excellent too. It is an excellent companion to the game and, in fact, I think it's good even outside the game.
So, to wrap it up, unless you have an aversion to randomness and a low tolerance to a bit of frustration every now and then, this is a game I would definitely recommend.

ARPGs are fickle friends. They encourage us to do the same thing repeatedly for hours on end, often with little reward.
Grim Dawn does this. It lures you in. Subtly at first, as so many ARPGs do - and before long the loot-lust takes over and minutes turn into hours, hours into days, and so on.
Where Grim Dawn excels is that rather than slowly chew you up before spitting you out bitter and broken, it always leaves you wanting more - not more grinding, but more fun. The game is just fun to play and for me that's the sole requirement for a good game.
Pros & cons time:
Pros:
- 6 classes (masteries) all with viable skill sets endgame (2 more coming in the expansion this month)
- secondary class selection at level 10 further varying the customisation of characters and allowing for dozens of viable builds
- large 4 act campaign with many secrets and sidequests (once again, more coming in the expansion soon)
- massive loot variety with non-legendary items viable BIS for many builds
- extra character customisation skills from gear, augments, devotion shrines and slotted items.
- 4 player co-op
- Faction reputation system tied to various items (ally factions) and enemy bosses (nemeses from enemy factions)
- huge crafting system that co-exists with the loot table happily
- hardcore mode
- sweet soundtrack
- varied enemies
- replayability plus - see my hours played
Cons:
- Time sink (where is my life?)
- Have to fight constant urge to re-roll new character when finding sweet gear that supports an off-class character.
- character creation doesn't allow any visual customising beyond male/female.
- Faction system is a little grindy on first character but improves once mandates become available
Conclusion - best ARPG on the market at present. Play it. It's great.
