This is imo the worst entry to the Far Cry franchise. The story revolves around you building up your village and increase it's population and basically eradicate the other two factions.
It seems the game took inspiration from other survival games popular on pc but implemented a way to simple and boring crafting system to appeal to the console masses. The game is way to easy aswell, I played on normal and I recomend anyone looking to play this game to start on hard. And playing it on the hardest difficulty still doesn't make it a "survival game".
First things first when playing this game is unchecking the gathering animation as it does nothing but waste time and annoy you. You will be stopping and detouring on your way to your destinations ALOT.
Traversing this world is not as fun as in FC3 and 4 with the lack of a wing suit. And what they did add, the ability to have a pet beast, some even ridable does not make up for that. I found the beasts useless and annoying for the most part.
You also have very few weapon and attack variety making the action bland long term.
It is a huge game though with alot to do, all the ubisoft standard side activities are here but there is still no replay value to this game and there is no multiplayer to extend it's life beyond finishing it once. Imo the main value of this game is potentially mildly entertaining you for long periods of time IF you absolutely have nothing better to do or play

Well, this was an enjoyable experience, for what I paid for it. ($25) I played Far Cry 3 and 4 a lot more than what I played this one, so I definitely liked them more, but at 29 hours this was a pretty good, somewhat unique experience to the series. Other than the whole Beastmaster aspect of the game, and ancient weapons, the mechanics of this one are almost identicalt to the last 2 games... but commanding beasts really does add an interesting aspect to the strategy of the game. Collecting them, and utilizing them in the best way was a fun experience.
Even the ancient weapons lost their uniqueness by the end of the game though. The club is you melee, the spear is your shotgun, and the bows are your SMG, assault rifle and sniper rifle. They bring a new look to a tried and true system. I say tried and true, because it really does work well... but it's still the same system in practically every other Far Cry game.
The story of this game was ok, but, I dunno... lacking. Maybe it's the use of make-believe primitive languages, but it didn't pull me in at all. The bad guys didn't have the menice or cunning of 3 or 4, and the good guys mostly lacked in any charm. If you like Far Cry games for their gameplay mechanics, and want to try something slightly different, definitely give this one a go. If you played Far Cry 3 or 4 primarily for the story... you probably won't like this one so much.
So I'll close how I started. For $25, this was a great game. I am recommending the game at this price, give or take $5. If I had payed full release price, I would probably be disappointed overall. But at half off, it was a fun enough diversion from real life... even if it did turn out to be a little short.

I didn't like this game at first, I really didn't. It felt so slow compared to Dead Island which on console, I played over 1000 hours on. When I started this game I was running out of stamina in a matter of seconds, I could barely kill any zombies, I could barely explore the Parkour that this game mainly offered.
The campaign started off amazing however, I was engaged in the story so much. Once you get to the "Tower", you'll get to meet new survivors, learn peoples stories and take on totally different missions. Every mission I played is different to the other, no grinding or repetetive tasks.
Once I unlocked extra skills within my characters Parkour Skill Tree, the game started to feel alot more fun. I was able to have fun in fights with zombies, I was running around drop kicking zombies then smashing their heads by kicking their heads. It was extremely fun and got alot more simple for me to play. I was also able to sprint around as much as I wanted without running out of stamina as easily, making parkour alot more extensive and enjoyable.
Even now that I'm Max Power, Agility, Survivor, Legendary Rank. I still find some fights with the infected difficult, I can one hit kill zombies with crossbows however I can still be killed easily if I get swarmed. The game is extremely immersive and doesn't feel like a task to complete, but feels like a movie with extremely fun gameplay.
Some reviews are saying the protagonist isn't "enjoyable" or "likeable" however I really enjoyed his sarcastic/arrogant attitude and heroic actions he performed throughout the game, it's enjoyable to play as a hero in such a broken world however is extremely defensive against other people. Seeing/hearing him go from a strong man to a broken man after the death of a friend/loved one made the game even more immersive for me.
I'd recommend this game to any zombie game lover. I will definitely be pre-ordering Dying Light 2.

On the surface, Lethal League might seem really simple. You just hit a ball until it goes so fast that your opponent gets hit by it and you win. While that’s the jist of it, there’s a lot more to it that makes it fun to play as you make plays (or other people make plays on you). The bunt is an ability that stops the ball dead no matter the speed and pops it up, giving you the opportunity to hit it. With its big hitbox, it’s how you’re gonna turn an enemy’s 2000 mph ball into YOUR 2000 mph ball if you can hit it. When you hit a fast ball, there’s a pause before the ball launches off again and your opponent can time it to hit the ball right as it “unpauses.” At the same time, you can flash a little shield that blocks their hit during the pause if you time it right. And finally, each character has their own special ability that messes with the movement of the ball and makes it less predicable, especially at higher speeds. With all of these little things in place, it makes a weird “Pong fighter” into a chaotic and fun game to play with friends.
There’s one thing to watch out for. This game sometimes has connection issues, so you’ll probably need to pause every few games to remake a lobby because the netcode acted up.

Neptunia has really grown on me in the time I've taken to get familiar with it. Everything from the world to its characters oozes with that weird Japanese charm. Helps that I'm a big fan of console history and analyzing all the little things about each console. In general, you should expect some clunky but interesting gameplay mechanics, and compelling stories with a swiss-cheese fourth wall from all the lampshading. But let's go a bit more into detail about this remake of the second game in particular.
It's true that of all the Neptunia games, the second one has some of the darkest tones in the series. A lot of fans dislike this because Neptunia is more well-known as a lighthearted anime parody of the console wars, but me? I
this. Dramedies are arguably my favourite story genre; I love it when a story can put me at both extremes while still having a natural feel. I didn't exactly have any knee-slappers or sobs, but I found myself having a lot of trouble holding back giggles at a witty lampshade, or not wanting to hug a more tsundere character when she reveals her hidden insecurities. The plot sounds straightforward enough: Neptune, Noire, Blanc, and Vert; the four CPUs of Gamindustri, have been held captive by software pirates for three years, and with the rescue of CPU Candidate Nepgear, a quest begins to save the them all and defeat the pirates. At least, it sounds easy, but with a lot of branching paths (including one particularly infamous bad ending that rivals Undertale's Genocide route), and given how every character in the game is at the very least a little genre savvy, you'll find that things are not quite as simple as you think. With regard to cutscenes, they're all quite lively through the game's animation-rigged character portraits, and out-of-character moments are few and far between. One thing about the game's storyboarding that I really do have to call out, however, is the trademark Idea Factory practice of "wedge in a fanservice scene even if it makes no ♥♥♥♥ing sense". A particularly egregious example in this game is a scene where the party is...frankly, sexually assaulted by Dogoos (dog slimes) which come completely out of nowhere in an underground dungeon where Dogoos don't even appear in to begin with. This happens in the middle of an intense chase scene, by the way. Yeah. Dunno what the folks at IF were smoking when they thought that was a good idea. All in all however, story is solid dramedy, filled to the brim with self-referential humour, lampshades, and fourth-wall breaking; but also balanced by some touching monologues, heartwarming reunions, and one of the most horrific game endings ever published to date. But yes, do beware of forced fanservice.
Gameplay is rough at the edges and suffers from forced grinding, but it's nowhere near as bad as Neptunia Re;Birth 1. As it is mostly the same compared to the rest of the series, I'll just explain the general gameplay of the whole series. Some unique mechanics the Neptunia series brings to the table as a turn-based RPG are free movement on the battlefield (which also matters, as individual weapons and skills have different areas of effect). This is a great mechanic, although you will find yourself getting annoyed when you repeatedly flick the analog stick to try and line up an attack
right so you can get multiple enemies in one go. Normal attacks are put into special chains, where you assign individual attacks to different buttons based on a point budget. There are three different attack types, split up across these three buttons: Rush, which is pretty much the only one you need; Power, which is kind of useless except for Tera D-Drive; and Break, which has its utilities in decreasing guard gauge, but typically Rush is more efficient anyway. Despite its obvious balancing issues, this system feels really good to play with--freely swapping attack types at the press of a button feels pretty cool. Speaking of the guard gauge, that's something all enemies have. Effectively, when it hits zero (causing a Guard Break), the enemy's defense drops to zero. The gauge does partially restore on their turn however, so you need to time guard breaks correctly for maximum effect. The EXE Drive gauge is another unique mechanic; as you deal and take damage while in a dungeon, the gauge fills up. It's split into four segments; however, all four segments are not available immediately. Having segments filled will allow you to append EXE Finishes to your normal attacks for an extra kick; or spend a segment or more to perform an EXE Drive attack, which are the most extreme of all skills, complete with ludicrous attack animations and obscene damage. It feels rewarding to let loose with a full EXE gauge after turns of playing conservatively, and again, it feels good. All in all, the unique mechanics offered by Neptunia are pretty fun to play with, but they tend to have some issues with streamlining, and the concepts can be kind of alien at first. Also, don't use a keyboard and mouse. Keyboard and mouse control is awful with every Neptunia game; just grab your Xbox controller.
All in all, Neptunia Re;Birth 2 is the perfect entry point into the series. While its more serious tone compared to the other games can give new players the wrong idea about the series' theme and tone, it gives players a far better idea of what to expect of Neptunia games than the slow, grindy, and poorly-aged Neptunia Re;Birth 1--which I feel would actually turn players off because of its clunkiness. It's totally cool to skip the first game if you want to do a complete playthrough; you're not missing much, especially considering Re;Birth 1 takes place in another dimension entirely. And if you're not here because you've heard of Neptunia from the grapevine, this is a very strange and quite niche JRPG that can be quite the beast to tame, but you'll find yourself being a loyal fan in no time if it resonates with you. Pick it up if you're a hardcore JRPG fan, and see what the fuss is about.

Disclaimer: review will contain spoilers.
Before playing I saw some reviews stating that the choices you make in GoT do not matter. While that is a feeling I generally have with most Telltale games, I found it hard to believe playing through the game. What GoT does incredibly well is give you choices that you think will matter; you feel like a major part of the story and it feels like your story (or stories, as you play a family and thus multiple characters). These choises feel so important that I felt like going through the game again, something that has never happened to me before with a Telltale game and I'm not even a GoT fan (I've only seen a few eps since the Red Wedding.)
The sad part is, playing GoT the second time I realized how right other gamers had been. In GoT you're given a story to live through, not one to play through. Every time the game gives you the option of going in one of two or three directions, there is really only one way to go. Choose the wrong direction, and the game will immediately (or after a few minutes) force you in the direction it had always intended for you. The result is that my second playthrough basically ruined the game, because you realize that you're not creating your own story – as Telltale so boldly claims – you live a story that was completely planned out. It's like going through an adventure book where the end is always the same, only the pages you get to see are different, and then not even very much.
Does that mean that you have absolutely no impact on the story? No. And while the impact you have is in a sense major, it does not alter the story in any meaningful way. Sure it is important when you get to decide which brother dies, but the world is not affected by your choice. Even worse, when you do exactly what the game suggests you need to do to get a certain ending, it still finds a way not to give you that ending. The result is that the plot starts to feel ridiculous at some points, even in the world of GoT. The characters sometimes have absolutely no motivation to act in the way they need to act for the plot to develop in the way the writers want it to develop. Every episode is like a Family Guy episode: some weird♥♥♥♥♥♥may happen, but nothing matters in the end.
So should you play GoT? On the one hand: yes. I really enjoyed my first playthrough and I'm not even a GoT fan. Sure the plot is even more cynical than the books/tv show, and the Forresters have it worse than the Starks, but by now we know that's how the world works and so it's fine. On the other hand – and this is the recommendation I'm going with: no. The problem with GoT is that it is a lazy product. By that I mean that the writers created one plot line, with some minor tweaks. They want to tell you a story, while giving you the illusion that it's your story. If a developer promises before the game starts that your choices will influence how the game plays out (and that silence can be a valid response), it needs to keep those promises. GoT does not. So since the developers were lazy, I say gamers be lazy: buy this game when it is very cheap in a Steam Sale (I got it as a gift, so I'm happy) and play it only once.

FORGET EVERYTHING YOU’VE HEARD!!!!!!!
When I decided to play BDO I went on every single gaming website you can imagine to look up reviews. While most were mixed, a lot were very negative. Some even calling it a big mess. Boy am i glad i did not listen. What BDO is, in basics terms, is non other then Video Game Cocaine. You will be hooked before you learn everything, and once you do learn everything, forget life as you know it! The games core system is designed around Playing. Yep, the more hours you log, the better the game gets. I heavily suggest setting time aside before deciding to jump into BDO.
With that said, let me tell you what this game is, and is not:
IS:
1. Open world MMO where everything you do, even breathing, nets advancement of your character
2. A PvP system designed around open world sieges and overtaking of lands. The minute you join one of these combat scenarios, you will be hooked for life!
3. Real world farming system designed around a structured economy and time investment. Meaning, the more you put in, the more you get out.
4. Combat system the likes you’ve never seen. Everything Tera online has, but, also everything Tera Online SHOULD have had as well. The way the combat system works will make mob grinding actually fun. And thing die quick. Very quick. So you will not be stuck hitting a NPC or Boar for endless hours with Spell Fire III. You will simply wack the S*** out of it, and move on.
5. A true leveling system. What i mean by true is that you will not spend endless hours grinding XP, hit max level, and watch the que timer for dungeons and raids to pop. Then, hit max level on your gear and watch the calendar for the next content patch. Leveling in BDO actually stand for something. Time invested, resources invested, and continuous play. Meaning someone walking around level 70 will have a-lot more prestige and recognition then a level 50 player.
6. A no rush, no worries MMO. No need to rush ANYTHING. You will play at your pace, at your time, and at your level of time investment. No matter the hour you log on, there will ALWAYS be something to do which can advance your character.
Now, what it is NOT:
1. Traditional MMO. Everything in BDO is open world and community created. And, because its not a sub base mmo, there are MILLIONS logged on at all times.
2. Endgame is all there is type of MMO. You will never be done. There is no ending. Your contributions are endless, and your character’s progression is endless as well. Play this game for 5 years, and your character will have EXACTLY 5 years of experience and advancement on him/her. While that may sound stupid, scary, maybe even ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥......JUST TRY IT OUT! Believe me, one hour in, and i was hooked!
3. Graphically Light Weight MMO. While you may be able to play WoW on a toaster, this game will not. You dont need a 3k rig to play it, but anything less then a GTX 980 will struggle. You can tone the graphics down alot. And when i say alot, i mean even the wind can be adjusted in the options pane. However, the main thing this game banks on is the photo realistic graphics. No matter the review this game got, EVERYONE raves about its graphical display. Best ive seen in a MMO PERIOD!
4. Anything like ANY OTHER mmo out there. This game is exactly the opposite of anything you’ve ever played. There is so much to do in BDO, that no matter how much time you invest in it, you are never truly done. The open area content is 24/7 and the rewards are well worth the effort.
5. Boring. Ask yourself this: How many times have you been caught staring at a que timer, waiting for that dungeon/raid to pop, join a group, and then be lead by a bad tank or heals which ultimately nets you ZERO experience/gear/currency/ for time invested? How often have you logged in to your current MMO and wonder, “Whats next?”. BDO is the exact opposite. No matter what your cup of tea is, this game can serve it. Any day. Any time.
My suggestion is download the game. Open your mind to what it truly offers, and forget about what it cannot offer. This game’s exact comparison is the following all mixed into one game:
A. The adventuring and exploring fun of GW2
B. The tactical combat of Tera Online, but with actual mechanics that are fun to execute
C. The questing of FFXIV
D. The population of WoW
E. The leveling of SWTOR
F. ALL of the above with the SAME exact graphics of Shadows of Mordor. (Even the climbing and stealth)
See you all ingame.......

This game is plain awesome. The developers of this game are brilliant. They have come up with simple mechanics that deliver hours upon hours of gameplay.
A word of caution though: this game contains significant random elements. And I stress that because I know some people hate even minimal randomness in games. That doesn't mean that skill and experience don't account for anything though. Learning how to manage that randomness and your resources, as well as exploring the synergies between different kinds of weapons and their application to different strategies, does improve your performance in the game.
Furthermore, there are no save slots. The game saves automatically so that you can continue your playthrough were you left off, but you can't go back in order to correct a bad decision. That might put some people off, but the random events, coupled with the fact that every decision is final, is what makes this game interesting (it's akin to playing XCOM: enemy unknown in Ironman mode). It forces you to move out of your confort zone and just learn how to make the most out of every situation.
It is also worth mentioning that this is a difficult game. You will probably need a few trials before making it to the Flagship on easy difficulty, and probably a couple more trials (if not more) to actually defeat the Flagship. And even with a few tens of hours of experience in your back, it's not unlikely to have bad runs on easy.
I've heard some complaints about the graphics. There's no discussion that the visuals are simple. All I will say about this is that the simplicity of the graphics does not get in the way of the gamplay (which can't be said of other indie games that go for simple graphics), and in fact I like the art direction and the overall visual aesthetic of the game. The soundtrack is excellent too. It is an excellent companion to the game and, in fact, I think it's good even outside the game.
So, to wrap it up, unless you have an aversion to randomness and a low tolerance to a bit of frustration every now and then, this is a game I would definitely recommend.

Welcome to Grim Dawn; where I have to fight the urge to make Warhammer Fantasy references at every corner!
A delightful little A-RPG with heavy Titan Quest vibes. I -think- you play as an inquisitor; but the main thing to concern yourself with are the undead, cultists and lovecraftian horrors populating the hillsides. Six classes with the option of dual classing allows for some variety in class building; but I found I stuck with a single class (Nightblade). One thing to note, Veteran Normal is the highest difficulty available with two more being locked until you beat the base difficulty - frustrating to say the least for those of us who always crank difficulty.
Gameplay is quite standard for any who are familiar with Diablo, Titan Quest or Torchlight. Various classes are present focusing on tanking, summoning, buffs/debuffs, crits, casting, etc. giving variety for players seeking more than one playthrough or varity in skillsets. Areas don't take terribly long to fully explore, leveling is a speedy process and equipment changes up often enough that you won't be using one weapon set the entire game.
The lore and story of grim dawn seems to be told in journal entries you find scattered and NPCs. Truth be told I couldn't be bothered to read it all; hence my cluelessness as to my profession or initial driving purpose in this title other than to slash and murder things that are not human or share my point of view.
Audio and voice acting are average but nothing to really complain about considering the genre.
All in all; if Titan Quest tickled your fancy then Grim Dawn will provide the same entertainment in a new setting.

Like the details say this is a simple to pickup game but pretty hard to master.  To me personally, it is not enough in the core gameplay to keep playing over and over. I admit that I was very skeptial when I saw this game initially being advertised.  I mean, how many Far Crys (Cries?) can they make with what is now becoming a tired, old formula.  Well, with nothing else better to play, I held my nose and dove in on this one.
If you have played either FC3 or 4, then the mechanics of this game will be very familiar.  The only difference here is that all of the crafting, hunting, etc make much more sense and work far better in this game instead of FC3 or 4 because of the ancient time period that it takes place in.
At first, I wasn't sure how much fun this would be without guns and explosives, but I found it very satisfying to club the living crap out of primitive enemies or picking them off with a bow from a distance. Hunting animals is also better played out here as well, and actually a core function of the game play.

But the real fun comes with having a beast companion - once you learn the skill to tame the animals, you can pick any one of them to fight by your side and rip your foes to pieces.  It's a very satisfying way to play, and I wish more games had this feature.  There is also an owl that you can use to spy over a limited area and either mark items and enemies, or even attack them.  And when it's all done, you can either pet or heal your beast and move on to the next task at hand.
In terms of graphics, this game is nothing short of beautiful.  The scenery is really something and sometimes I just stop and look around because it's amazing to look at.    The sound is also spectacular - the sounds of all the nature and wildlife around you very much make the game feel like a living environment.
The only negatives are that the dialogue between you and the other NPCs sometimes goes on a bit much.  Stealth seems more difficult in this game for some reason, and attacking the harder camps can become very painful (and repetitive) if you are not leveled up.  There was also a sidequest with a character who was speaking in the game's native language with a modern southern USA accent (huh??).  All that and the boss battles pretty much suck.  Besides that, pretty much all of the other Far Cry gameplay elements that become repetitive, annoying, etc are all pretty much there.
Overall I like it, but I just wish it was a little more than what it is.  Regardless if you like FC3 or 4 you will probably like this one as well.

Re;Birth 2 is so, so similar to Re;Birth 1. Seriously, from a gameplay perspective, they are basically the exact same game. Toss in another character slot, shuffle some movesets around, and BAM. You've made Re;Birth 1 into Re;Birth 2. However, the design decisions regarding the gameplay and especially the story just...somehow manage to break the experience. But first...
Wow. This game is full of framerate issues. I've got what's a pretty decent rig; an AyyMD RX 470 with an AyyMD FX-6300 with 8GB RAM. Good enough to run DOOM '16 at 1080p with an average 80-90 FPS, and definitely able to run Re;Birth 1 with a (capped) 60FPS. Framerate dips in Re;Birth 1 were brief, almost unnoticeable and rarely happened. Re;Birth 2 however, would constantly drop to sub-30 while in some areas that are just...empty.
And don't get me started on the ♥♥♥♥ing guard breaks that would make the game grind to an immediate 0 FPS halt.
The story was just...boring. It never went anywhere for any logical reason, and contradicts the events of Re;Birth 1.
Yes, the Neptunia games aren't ones that you should play for story. I came into here knowing that, prepared to embrace stupidity, only to be hit with something that took itself unnecessarily seriously. There's no real payoff for anything that happens, events just kind of occur without any real reason, and just wasn't toying with the gamindustri as much as it should have.
With a lackluster story also comes some lackluster characters. Nep Nep and the other CPUs are gone, replaced with their little sisters. So...they don't work as main characters. The characters are the main highlight of this series. (Well, aside from the meta 4th wall gaming references.) And for the most part, they work. Amazingly well, despite being cliche as hell. Nepgear however, makes me want to yell. Interesting in the anime due to the way they stood opposite to the CPUs, but whiny and tedious here since there are no CPUs for them to support and be supported by.
One thing that makes itself apparent damn near immediately was the abundance of obvious filler quests. I’m not going to act like Re;Birth 1 didn’t have its share of filler quests, because it did. But at least there, they were backed by a plot that did feel like it was going somewhere, and felt like they were somewhat necessary to the events going on. In Re;Birth 2, the characters will literally go “Ah man, a completely pointless fetch quest? I don’t want to do that”, only to immediately make the player do the fetch quest. A recurring villain will pop up, they go “Hey, you going to bring out the mid boss fight of the chapter that always happens when you show up?” “Yeah, I’m going to bring out the big boss fight of the chapter that always happens when I show up.”
Without any hook to keep you going, the constant enemy battles feel really, really tedious. Re;Birth 1 got around this because...well, it was interesting. I wanted to battle the enemies to get their drops and make some items. Wanted to grind my♥♥♥♥♥off to see the characters deal tens of hundreds of thousands of damage. Here, since the story was just a slag, there’s no real motivation that I had to do anything.
Ignoring the motivations, grinding here is abysmal compared to Re;Birth 1. There’s less spikes overall, so good on you for that, but when they occur, they happen one after the ♥♥♥♥ing other, and are ♥♥♥♥ing steep. Once you’re done using a blatantly overpowered DLC item to skip what would be hours of grinding, you scrape by a boss battle using Compa with way too many SP boosters, only to move on to the next boss battle and find out that you need to do that again. And once you’re done with that boss battle, you’re now blatantly overpowered for the filler quests and just tirelessly wait for the enemies to spawn so you can get their drops.
It's so similar to Re;Birth 1, yet is just...off. It's off because of the lack of interesting and fun characters to mess around in a story that just barely flows together without poking fun at the gamindustri. It's off because of the filler quests that just make themselves known without any attempt at masking them. Off because of the lack of interesting things to do. Off because of the grinding that basically requires what would otherwise be an overpowered DLC item.
The NepNep games are by no means masterpieces. But they are mostly good, maybe great if you’re into moe ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. However, comparing how much less wit, humor and just fun I had with this one, it’s not one I can recommend.

This review will be spoiler free. I'll keep short bulletpoints of what you can read in other reviews and put my biggest criticism - historical accuracy - at the end.
Technical details
============
+ The game didn't have any bugs.
+ The graphics are good.
+ The sound is good.
+ Acting and voice acting are good.
- The gamepad implementation is substandard so x360ce wouldn't work and I had to block gamepad detection with a custom directx file to play with joytokey.
Atmosphere
=========
- There are no relaxing nice moments for any of the characters. You are just fed shock scene after shock scene. This kills the atmosphere since it makes you indifferent as viewer.
- Every character has just one facial expression: Worried frown.
+ In one episode a girl sings a song (sad one of course), but this is executed very well and results in a great atmosphere.
- No sex or nudity or drugs, only violence. The books have a lot of the former, which is interwoven with the plot and presented as important part of human nature. The TV show usually has nudity every 10min and sex at least once an episode again used to advance the plot.
This game has none! Probably due to bad experiences with "The wolf among us" and the iOS release, but this should not be a problem for me as PC gamer.
Story
====
Big minus here. I liked the Telltale stories from "Tales from the Borderlands" and "The wolf among us" very much.
- Very bad writing.
- No dark humor.
- A lot of choices you are offered or which the NPCs make do not make any sense.
- Most of the NPCs are very one dimensional (in strong contrast to the book).
- Most of the point of view characters are not very likable.
- Most of the NPCs are omniscient. As writer you can do this once or twice in a story, if you do not know how to continue (and granted a lot of other Telltale games have this as well at some times) but in this game it happens at every decision.
Historical accuracy
=============
"Fantasy, anything goes" you might say, but stay with me for a moment.
George RR Martin did his research very well. His books make the mindset of people living in a western Feudal society come very much to life. The books are very low on magic and fantasy effects. Most disputes are solved using conventional means.
The TV series tried to stay true to the authenticity of the books although it took a few historical liberties from time to time.
This game on the other hand:
The authors don't know jack-sh.. of history. Sorry to say it that blunt, but the missing skill of the writers clearly ruined what could have been a good game.
Some examples:
- Crossbows are used like modern day shotguns. In one scene one character fires a crossbow with a delay of maybe 2 seconds.
- Executions are done with bows or crossbows like modern day firing squads.
- Lords walk around without guards. In one scene in particular they make a big choice of going to the stronghold of your enemy either alone or with a detachement of a few guards. Your diplomacy councelor actually tells you to leave your guards at home. This is so stupid and historically wrong.
You would never be denied your honor guard otherwise any invitation to an enemy stronghold would just be seen as outright murder and an open declaration of war.
- The system of feudal tenure is not done right. In the books it is always a balance of your "name", your "current supporters" and the "strength of your allies".
In the TV series, they usually downplay the role of the "supporters" a bit and present them as given by your "name" (due to budgetary and time constraints, I would believe). But since the writers clearly only have watched a few episodes of the TV series and no other knowledge of historical events they don't get it at all.
So in this game it is mostly "name" alone. Which also goes along with the theme of walking around without guards, since your "name" will somehow magically protect you.

A lot of people said that you'd realize how none of your choices matter if you play the game more than once, but that's not true. I always play a single playthrough of Telltale games, because I like to keep "my" story moving forward. However, even if you play this only once you will see that your choices don't matter.
The game starts of great - big twists, touching moments and great characters and voice-acting. While the last three episodes have their moments, the first ones are what you should be looking forward to if you plan on buying this game. Before I go into spoiler territory, venting my frustration with this game, I would just say that Telltale tried to present you with a good, shocking, GoT story, but in that failed to make a game where your decision matter and don't just alter a few lines of dialogue. If you want to, basically, watch an extension of GoT - get it, if you want a good narrative-driven, choice-based GAME - don't.

Tldr: Microcosm of the macrocosm in pretty much every way. Designed to incenerate your effort, and maintained by staff who are powerless to fix anything. You will likely end up finding a small niche somewhere in the game where you can squeeze out a tiny bit of fun in a world designed to prevent enjoyment.
The good:
I really enjoyed striker combat. This is perhaps the one thing that keeps me coming back to this game.
AFK mechanics are worth experiencing. It is refreshing to be able to maximize the use of my time. I do not think it would be needed if some of the mechanics were not so ridiculously weighted toward consuming time (see horse breeding).
Lifeskills (crafting, etc) are pretty awesome and the complexity is deep enough to spend lots of time on. The economy will not let you make any profit but you can certainly save alot.
Events, this game has the best and most frequent events I have come across. Though they probably would not have to do so much to please their community if their game did not so heavily defecate on it.
Graphics and sound. Worth it, but only until you can see through the illusion.
The bad:
Exp decay on death. Really? Yup, beyond lvl 50 (i didnt notice it till 56) somewhere in the levels exp decay becomes a thing when you die, also gear enhancements usually break too. They arent cheap.
Broken world. Almost every time I have died on any toon it is because i get hung up on the environment or fall through the world. Combined with exp decay this is pretty awful. Boats get stuck in the harbor, wagons hang up on bushes and fences, etc... This is perhaps the most unrefined aspect of the game imo.
Horses are interesting but suffer unfortunate design. Being able to breed a mount with better speed is important and somewhat fun in concept. Each tier horse has better skills available than the last tier, though how many your horse learns and how often is RNG. It requires riding that horse for about 20-60 hours of earth time to level the horse for better breeding percentages. You will need to level two to breed them and the breeding is RNG such that the horse has about a 20% chance to stay the same tier or fall down one tier. The only upside to all this is that you can auto path your horses while AFK to level them, provided you can stay connected (typically a problem on weekends)
No fast travel, huge world.
Highly regulated economy. No player trading and all prices in the marketplace are set by the game world. Price fluctuations are not player based. You typically cannot buy, craft, and sell to any gain other than levelling crafting.
Money cannot be accessed unless you are in the town you have it stored in. This means every time you are not currently carrying the money you need, you will have to go get it from across the world or wait for it to be shipped between cities (takes awhile)
Inventory weight includes money so you can not just carry all your cash around. Having enough money to actually buy things you need means you have to carry less items. Money cannot be stored on a wagon, boat, or horse unless you convert it to gold bars which are still pretty heavy. While grinding it is typical to hit the  weight limit with low-value items that you have to either micro-manage or run to town to sell off.
Levelling beyond 55 is only practical through grinding out levels, and is amazingly bad past lvl 56. 200 monsters for 1% xp? That sounds about right, and it will only get worse with each level. No level cap but it will take you literally days for each level perhaps weeks beyond 60, provided you do not die and have your xp decay. In order to grind faster you need to get better gear via failstacking.
Failstacking is covered elsewhere pretty well at this point. I can only add that this concept seems to stem from a lack of gear diversity. There appears to be about 10 or so pieces of gear for each slot total. Every once in awhile gear gets added in small amounts. Is this a subtle nudge toward the player learning to embrace failure and overcome adversity? I could not care less, I came for entertainment not life coaching from a horrible demon that mocks me lmao.
Some or all of this above combines to create perhaps the most toxic player base I have found in dozens of mmo's. It makes sense, i figure most of the players are aggro from getting constantly violated by the rng or broken game design. Players kill eachother over tree resources when there is a whole forest around them. Grinding spots required to level are usually overpopulated by people with better gear willing to kill other players so they can get their 0.01% xp from the three mobs they would have stolen.
I find myself wondering if I left anything out. It probably doesnt matter because you will inevitably find something else that you hate about bdo specific to your own existence. The question is whether or not you can find enough things you enjoy in order to convince yourself that it is still worth playing.

Welcome to Grim Dawn; where I have to fight the urge to make Warhammer Fantasy references at every corner!
A delightful little A-RPG with heavy Titan Quest vibes. I -think- you play as an inquisitor; but the main thing to concern yourself with are the undead, cultists and lovecraftian horrors populating the hillsides. Six classes with the option of dual classing allows for some variety in class building; but I found I stuck with a single class (Nightblade). One thing to note, Veteran Normal is the highest difficulty available with two more being locked until you beat the base difficulty - frustrating to say the least for those of us who always crank difficulty.
Gameplay is quite standard for any who are familiar with Diablo, Titan Quest or Torchlight. Various classes are present focusing on tanking, summoning, buffs/debuffs, crits, casting, etc. giving variety for players seeking more than one playthrough or varity in skillsets. Areas don't take terribly long to fully explore, leveling is a speedy process and equipment changes up often enough that you won't be using one weapon set the entire game.
The lore and story of grim dawn seems to be told in journal entries you find scattered and NPCs. Truth be told I couldn't be bothered to read it all; hence my cluelessness as to my profession or initial driving purpose in this title other than to slash and murder things that are not human or share my point of view.
Audio and voice acting are average but nothing to really complain about considering the genre.
All in all; if Titan Quest tickled your fancy then Grim Dawn will provide the same entertainment in a new setting.

It would be a dramatic understatement to say that there are a lot of Diablo-style games that have come and gone through the gaming market over the years.  I tend to go with the general conscensus on Diablo 2 being the best for a very, very long time though it had a handful of flaws that irritated me (enemy immunities would top that list, rendering a lot of builds non-viable).
Where am I going with this? There is one thing that Grim Dawn does -extraordinarily- well.  It empowers the player to make the character they want to make.  You can focus on nearly any damage type or playstyle you like, so long as you do so by building your character in a way that maximizes whatever you're focusing on. You can go back to the well of character design over and over and over and still come away with something that feels unique and interesting.  There's no "this is the current flavor of the month build for this class" as there is with Diablo 3 where whatever gearset has been tweaked for the current ladder season is clearly the best option for end game success.  That doesn't mean Grim Dawn doesn't have some balance issues (it does) or that everything is viable (if you try to build around 4 damage types you're in for a bad experience).
The main draw of any ARPG in my experience is replayability.  You're functionally going to be doing the same thing over and over and over again regardless of which game you decide to invest your time in so it really comes down to how much fun that repetition is.  For me, Grim Dawn is by far the best option on the market.  Every character I've built feels unique to some degree and the content the game offers continues to be enjoyable for me nearly 700 hours in.  With the impending expansion pack right around the corner I fully expect to invest even more time in this relatively inexpensive gem.  If you want to play an ARPG masquerading as an MMO, you're better suited to play Path of Exile or, if you like spandex, grinding the same zone for endless hours, and pay to win you can go with Marvel Heroes.
Grim Dawn, however, is easily the best option in my estimation for anyone looking to play solo or with a friend or two.

This is my first time writing a review, so please forgive me if it's not quite up to snuff.
I'll start by saying that I'm a huge fan of Diablo style games. When Titan Quest came out, I played the crap out of that game for years. So when Grim Dawn popped up on my radar, I couldn't wait to sink my teeth into it.
I've been playing Grim Dawn since the early days of it's development. Even when the game barely had any content to it at all, I found there was more than enough to satisfy my hunger. As the game has grown, and developed into the wonderful product it is today, I found myself more and more amazed by just how much thought was put into it.
The designs for the world, characters, monsters, and equipment, are unique. Unlike most games you've seen on the market. Yes it does have some of the typical  features of a lot of fantasy-esque games, but it has it's own flavor to it.
It says I only have 28.3 hours on record, but it is FAR more than that. I just play a lot offline on my laptop when I'm out and about. I probably have hundreds of hours sunk into this game, and I don't regret a single minute of that time.
If what you're looking for is a Diablo style game, then this is the one you've been waiting for.
One of my favorite aspects of this game is the talent and attribute system. They obviously used a lot of the ideas from Titan Quest, in the sense that there are attribute points to increase your stats, and there is an extensive talent tree. You can choose to focus on just one class, or you can mix it up between two talent trees. In addition to this, they also added a sub talent tree of sorts, this adds an additional level of depth to how you want to develop your character.
With the talent system they have developed, there are near endless possiblities to how you can build your character. Of course with most games, some builds become the "go to" if you look on the forums. But I prefer to carve my own path and do my own thing.
As for comparison to Diablo 3, it's hard to even compare it. They're like apples and oranges. One thing I do find more rewarding about Grim Dawn as opposed to Diablo 3, is that it is much harder to get the best gear in the game. It's not like great gear drops all the time. It's in fact very few and far between, but to me it makes it all that more rewarding when you do get a great piece of gear. It's also not as easy to level up in Grim Dawn as it is in Diablo 3, and the content is far more challenging.
So if you're looking for a welcome change from playing too many hours of Diablo 3, and you want to really sink your teeth into something new, but familiar, then I highly recommend you play this game.

Remember how Dead Island was a dumb frustrating pile a crap that occasionally broke out into a few minutes of fun? Imagine that, but just change nothing. It's a shame because the fun moments are really fun, but so many gameplay choices that were made are just bad. A few examples
- Playing solo and die during a mission after killing 2/4 guys? Meh, there's still only those 2 left, just keep throwing your corpse at the problem until it goes away.
- On that note, death really has no meaning in this game. I set the game to the hardest difficulty because I was hoping for some intense zombie action, but like with Bioshock, it doesn't matter how hard the enemy is, when you get infinite respawns with minimal penalties (only losing Surivor XP, which is incredibly easy to get back) nothing has any threat anymore.
- Playing 'Be the Zombie' for the first time? Enjoy fighting 4 people with auto shotguns! Not sure if this mode ever has more than one zombie player in the match, but if not I have no idea how one would deal with being perma-stunned by 4 shotguns/UV lights
- Zombies are attracted to sound, right? That's why when you shoot a gun, runners will start coming after you. So why is it that if there's an explosion way in the distance, the runners still come after me? Shouldn't they be heading to the big bang a mile away?
*Spoilers* I think the prime example of how the devs didn't things through was the fight against the first Demolisher. Now, I understand that this was supposed to be a tough fight. You've lost your gear, your identity is blown, your ♥♥♥♥ed, and now here's this big♥♥♥♥♥beast covered in armor that you need to kill. I loved it. Until I died. As usual, I lost an insignificant amount of exp, then respawn. Now here's the problem: the Demolisher's health was restored, which is fine, but the machete, the only weapon worth a damn I have available to me still hasn't had it's durability restored, which is not fine. I had to run around, grab one of the♥♥♥♥♥♥♥pipes laying around, quickly disassemble it and repair my machete. Playing on the hardest difficulty, it was pretty easy to get one hit by the bugger, and I get that it's my fault for choosing that, but I beat him with probably under 10 hits left on the machete and 0 repairs left, and had I not won then, I'd essentially be getting punished for trying too many times by being forced to use weapons that deal a fifth of the damage of the machete. I could write another paragraph about how dumb the escape sequence was after the pit, but I think my point is across.
All in all, I've had some fun with this game. I enjoy sneaking around shooting arrows at zombies, and if you can get the game cheap or find a friend willing to play it with you, go for it. Other than that, skip it. There are a thousand other shooters out there, and plenty of them are zombie games more worthwhile than Dyling Light.

Short version: This is a damn good game but not quite the first one.
Long version:
HDN Rebirth 2 suffers from some issues that pull it behind the legacy of the first game. Most notable it is criticized for being a little too serious for the lighthearted tone of the series. But it also has some good changes.
In my opinion it also seriously suffers from poor level design, with a lot of the detail that made the levels in the first game interesting, gone. The "Stella's Dungeon" minigame is a huge waste of time, particularly for people like me who did an all achievement run. The random people popping up across the map to chat with you is extremely annoying, unlike the first game more then 90% of the people you talk too don't have anything for you. And you don't dare skip them unless they have something of huge importance. And the villains are repetitive.
But there ARE a lot of positive changes that caught my eye. The soundtrack is better in this game then the first, in my opinion. The characters and their character development is as good if not better then the original. There are 8 possible endings rather then 2. And in my opinion there is more and better end-game content for us crazy people who wanted to play the game after we had already beaten it several times. And the achievements are better set up for having fun trying to get them.
But above all else my favorite change was the Conquest Ending. HDN is light-hearted in nature but that doesn't mean it should always be flowers and sunshine. I had fun and I'm glad it was added to the game.

Taking off the nostaliga goggles now.
This game game out originally when I was a kid, so back then I wasn't aware of what a good ps2 game really was. Looking back, I can say that this game, while not particularly a pioneer of the system, was very well made for the system and its time. The game takes the parts of its predecessor that worked very well (the rang variation, story, setting, characters, and physics, among many other things) and fleshs them out to a much fuller extent.
The voice actors (some of whom are different from the first) did a much better job with their voicing of the characters. The new "home area", Bush rescue HQ along with the city of Burramudgee serve as a much improved replacement to the hub world of rainbow cliffs from the first game. Rather than being big and bland, this new area is home to lost of things to do, from getting collectibles to even some missions. As mentioned before, Ty 1's hub world was how you accessed missions. Ty 2, however, has you driving in a somewhat open world, choosing what missions you do in the various areas available. This areas are rather pretty too.
More than just pretty, however, they are populated, with enemies, npcs and missions. and while each area is surrounded by a large fence on the outside, within the areas there exist very few if any invisible walls, meaning you're allowed rather free movement throughout them. Something other platformers often suffer from that Ty 2 doesnt is weapon restriction. Ty 2, rather than relying on limited power ups or loadout slots, can carry any rang he owns with him, wherever he goes, meaning you can use any weapon you want at your pleasure.
What does Ty 2 do wrong however? No game is perfect, and certainly Ty 2 does not break free from that. Ty 2 on the ps2 suffered from a multitude of lock up issues and performance issues, however those issues were largely corrected in this port (as well were the graphics. It's rather pretty now). In my opinion, the only real thing that hurts Ty 2 is the cart racing minigame.
Obviously inspired by mario kart, its a shame work on the real game was diverted to it. It's not all that bad. Especially with the port's recent updates to it. But it does feel rather like a ripoff of mario kart, and it's not really fun. Requiring it to 100% the game is rather annoying as well.
But overall, I say the base game stands the test of time, and the HD remaster port of it updates it to be on level with other games released in this generation. If you like platformers, you'll love this game. If you like stylized games, you'll love this game. And if you liked the ps2, gamecube or xbox versions of this game, well duh youll especially love this game. I'd rate this game Great out of Great

For a while, I worked as a web designer in a small ad agency serving a very niche industry. Previously, the design team had no creative lead, and were all sort of operating independently across varying clients. We decided to hire a creative director to fill that gap, and I was given the task of sorting through and giving first round interviews to find the person who would later become my supervisor. Two candidates in particular stood out from the rest for very different reasons. One was exceptionally talented, an all around nice guy, and somebody who generally would have been great for the role. The other, let's call him John, had mediocre talent, came across as an insufferable, arrogant prick, but had previous experience working within the niche industry that we serviced. He also had contacts within that industry that could lead to new business. Despite my strong recommendation to not hire John, his relationships in the industry were too compelling to our agency's leadership to pass up, and they hired him.
It didn't take long before the entire company started to realize John was a huge burden. He had virtually zero experience in anything related to digital design. Design for apps, websites, mobile, etc., were all completely and utterly beyond his grasp, but he used his position of relative power to make decisions on those projects that the entire design team refused to support, most of which came back to bite the company in the♥♥♥♥♥later. The design team hated him, because fixing and working around his screw-ups became part of our daily routine. The sales team hated him, because he'd claim it took him unbelievably exaggerated amounts of time to complete even the most trivial of tasks (ex: 4 days to design a business card template), so they wouldn't even assign him projects anymore. Work that was clearly his responsibility started to rapidly trickle down to the rest of the design team. We'd be working late nights 4 out of 5 days a week, because all of his projects that were in danger of missing deadlines would be re-assigned to us. Meanwhile he'd be the first to walk out the door every day, right at 5PM, without fail. On top of all that, the guy was absolutely, without a doubt, the biggest tool I've ever met. Always right about everything, completely unbending on his idiotic opinions, and completely clueless that literally every person in the building wished he would get hit by a truck.
I genuinely tried to work with him for about a year, until I decided that the job had become intolerable because of him, and wasn't going to change any time soon, so I turned in my two week notice. About a month after I left, I heard that he had been let go from the job. Shortly after that, I noticed that he had changed his LinkedIn status to show that he was working for a new agency I had never heard of, also servicing that same niche industry. I looked them up, and quickly figured out that he had started his own agency... a primarily digital agency... when he had NO experience in digital or interactive design, and had literally ♥♥♥♥ed up every digital/interactive project he'd ever been on (I know, because most of them were reassigned to me when he proved incapable of doing them himself). I looked at the portfolio on his website, and found literally project after project of my work. He was using my work from the ad agency as examples of the work his agency could produce.
I briefly considered contacting him and requesting he remove my work from his portfolio for ethical reasons. But I could already hear his reply in my head. "As creative lead, all work done by my team is an extension of my creative direction." He'd used similar lines in the past to insert himself into receiving credit on successful projects he'd had zero involvement on.
So instead I sent an email to one of the partners of the agency we both had worked for, saying something along the lines of "hey, not sure if you've noticed this, but it looks like John is using your company's intellectual property to directly compete against you... if I had to guess, I'd assume his next step would be to make a move at your client list."

Re;birth 2's story is written like it should be more epic than the first Re;birth, but it's presentation never quite comes across nearly as grand in scale. There are multiple endings for the game, and some are better than others, but they all fall a little flat for me with how much of an impact they leave. With the one exception maybe being

One final complaint I have is I was never very crazy about the Underling character. It would be a dramatic understatement to say that there are a lot of Diablo-style games that have come and gone through the gaming market over the years.  I tend to go with the general conscensus on Diablo 2 being the best for a very, very long time though it had a handful of flaws that irritated me (enemy immunities would top that list, rendering a lot of builds non-viable).
Where am I going with this? There is one thing that Grim Dawn does -extraordinarily- well.  It empowers the player to make the character they want to make.  You can focus on nearly any damage type or playstyle you like, so long as you do so by building your character in a way that maximizes whatever you're focusing on. You can go back to the well of character design over and over and over and still come away with something that feels unique and interesting.  There's no "this is the current flavor of the month build for this class" as there is with Diablo 3 where whatever gearset has been tweaked for the current ladder season is clearly the best option for end game success.  That doesn't mean Grim Dawn doesn't have some balance issues (it does) or that everything is viable (if you try to build around 4 damage types you're in for a bad experience).
The main draw of any ARPG in my experience is replayability.  You're functionally going to be doing the same thing over and over and over again regardless of which game you decide to invest your time in so it really comes down to how much fun that repetition is.  For me, Grim Dawn is by far the best option on the market.  Every character I've built feels unique to some degree and the content the game offers continues to be enjoyable for me nearly 700 hours in.  With the impending expansion pack right around the corner I fully expect to invest even more time in this relatively inexpensive gem.  If you want to play an ARPG masquerading as an MMO, you're better suited to play Path of Exile or, if you like spandex, grinding the same zone for endless hours, and pay to win you can go with Marvel Heroes.
Grim Dawn, however, is easily the best option in my estimation for anyone looking to play solo or with a friend or two.

XCOM is a great slow-paced strategy game. I emphasize the slow part since, like the Civilization games that Firaxis puts out, gameplay is very much on a unit-by-unit basis. It's highly recommended to follow a wiki or a guide on your first playthrough and to defeintely select easy mode. The game holds up remarkably well for being 4+ years old since its launch. It's a very nice change of pace from the frantic madness that can be other AAA titles these days. The game feels a bit too slow to power through a couple missions in any time less than an hour, but it's an hour well spent and a good way to relax.

A reboot of what could be called a genre unto itself. XCOM, like many games from the '80s and '90s, were known for their brutal difficulty, but this one stood out because it was immutable - the setting was infamously stuck at "Superhuman" due to a bug. The modernised version thankfully does not have this problem, but is in keeping with series tradition still fairly hard despite loads of streamlining. Indeed, it's as hard as it sounds: you're leading a team of Kevlar-and-M4 redshirts against aliens with plasma rifles. Your troops will get better (as well as your tech), but not if they die - and some of them will die, I guarantee it.
For those who want a real challenge, installing the esteemed Long War mod (which requires the Enemy Unknown expansion) cranks the difficulty up to eleven. The alien AI gets a massive upgrade, to the point where it's almost
genre-savvy, and so do the aliens themselves. Base-building and tech also become noticeably more complex. In exchange for all this, you get more boots on the ground and a greater variety of stuff to equip them with.
Overall, the game is extremely engaging and stimulating, if not necessarily realistic (e.g. the "Lightning Reflexes" ability allows thus-trained soldiers to effectively go into bullet time). Pick it up and join the war effort, but prepare yourself for the inevitable casualties that will ensue.
Good luck, Commander. You're gonna need it.

This is my first time writing a review, so please forgive me if it's not quite up to snuff.
I'll start by saying that I'm a huge fan of Diablo style games. When Titan Quest came out, I played the crap out of that game for years. So when Grim Dawn popped up on my radar, I couldn't wait to sink my teeth into it.
I've been playing Grim Dawn since the early days of it's development. Even when the game barely had any content to it at all, I found there was more than enough to satisfy my hunger. As the game has grown, and developed into the wonderful product it is today, I found myself more and more amazed by just how much thought was put into it.
The designs for the world, characters, monsters, and equipment, are unique. Unlike most games you've seen on the market. Yes it does have some of the typical  features of a lot of fantasy-esque games, but it has it's own flavor to it.
It says I only have 28.3 hours on record, but it is FAR more than that. I just play a lot offline on my laptop when I'm out and about. I probably have hundreds of hours sunk into this game, and I don't regret a single minute of that time.
If what you're looking for is a Diablo style game, then this is the one you've been waiting for.
One of my favorite aspects of this game is the talent and attribute system. They obviously used a lot of the ideas from Titan Quest, in the sense that there are attribute points to increase your stats, and there is an extensive talent tree. You can choose to focus on just one class, or you can mix it up between two talent trees. In addition to this, they also added a sub talent tree of sorts, this adds an additional level of depth to how you want to develop your character.
With the talent system they have developed, there are near endless possiblities to how you can build your character. Of course with most games, some builds become the "go to" if you look on the forums. But I prefer to carve my own path and do my own thing.
As for comparison to Diablo 3, it's hard to even compare it. They're like apples and oranges. One thing I do find more rewarding about Grim Dawn as opposed to Diablo 3, is that it is much harder to get the best gear in the game. It's not like great gear drops all the time. It's in fact very few and far between, but to me it makes it all that more rewarding when you do get a great piece of gear. It's also not as easy to level up in Grim Dawn as it is in Diablo 3, and the content is far more challenging.
So if you're looking for a welcome change from playing too many hours of Diablo 3, and you want to really sink your teeth into something new, but familiar, then I highly recommend you play this game.

This game was great in the beta but subsequent patches really turned this game into a waste of your money. Unit balance has gotten better over time but this game was ruined whtn the vehicle caps were drastically reduced. Playing with lots of infantry wouldn't be so bad if squads that took 10+ minutes to become veterans could survive late game insta-gib attakcs.  The addition of later generals were a cash grab and put the nail in the coffin for this game as it became pay to win.
If you can get it for under $10 I'd say it would be a good pick if you are a WWII period fan or just love to collect RTS games. So now that you can get the game for 10$... I am not sure that you should. They completely ruined the OKW with the december 2017 patch.  Company of Allies would be a better fitting title.
On the bright side they did finally remove a few cheap tricks (soviet demo charges cant be placed in cap zones for easy mode squad kills) but after 2 years? I think it was a bit late.
Relic came out with a balance patch this month that makes the Axis into a complete joke faction. The reasoning for such nerfs were things like " The Elephant is too effective." To make a long story short (too late?) the design of the game balance for a very long time was that the Allied infantry push back the Axis early game and that Axis armor pushes back the Allies late game.
Catch phrases like this are really quite troublesome. The problem with this type of statement is that the Elephant is designed to hard counter one of most favorite soviet tactics: SU-85 spam.
You are damn right the Elephant ruins that tactic! That's the point of that doctrine unit. The problem overall is that CoH2 had a really neat idealistic asymetrical balance. But rather than using a different tactic people just cried until the other side's units got nerfed (so that they could blindly run their favorite build order with no variation).
The Elephant gets utterly hosed by guards/AT guns. It is one of the few heavily armored units that is weak against an infantry rush. It also has trouble vs super heavy mortars.... if only there were a soviet doctrine for those.
What I loved about CoH2 was that the doctrine system they gave us allowed for extremely tactical and intelligent play (assuming you had most of the good commanders- but that is another story). You were shooting yourself in the foot if you spam SU-85s when you load into a game and see the enemy has an Elephant commander available.
What you are supposed to do is push the enemy hard as the soviets (allied strategy really) in the early part of the game so that he thinks he wont ever reach the Elephant.... so he will pick another commander. You might even be required (/gasp) to pick an early general to push the German player so hard that he cannot wait and must pick a commander who can help him now.
What I see overall is that many people never learned how to push their enemy into making that kind of decision. And that lazy style of play is why Relic nerfed the Elephant.

Dawn is a very pretty game with lovely level design, a cohesive atmosphere, and beautiful animations.
Playing through the game the first time I found the menus simple and easy to navigate, and after getting into the actual game (after sitting through the long loading screen) I was enjoying the music and finding the little flowers scattered about. I soon finished the game for the first time having missed a flower, and upon reloading the game I was pleased to find that all the flowers I had already found had been saved. I found the last flower and got newgame+. After playing through a few times here are my full thoughts:
The level design in Dawn is great for many reasons and not so stellar with others. The collectibles were fun to find because they were hidden in ways that were inventive, but not too difficult. Many flowers being hidden right behind a rock, or with just a turn of the camera to see the path leading to them encouraged me to explore the entirety of the level just to find them all. On the other hand, there is no challenge to the game. The level design doesn't have any gaps that are difficult to jump, or areas that are hard to navigate. Depending on the goal of the developers and the type of person playing a lack of challenge could be a good thing, but I feel Dawn would have benefitted greatly from having more engaging platforming to match the engaging treasure hunting aspect.
The level design is great for exploring and seeing a pretty place, but they don't agree with some of the mechanics of the character. For instance, Double jumping is an unneccessary ability for the character to have. There is only one gap and only one vertical jump in the entire game that requires the double jump to clear. The vertical jump can even be bypassed by backtracking a short distance and using an alternate path, the gap is only to get to one of the optional stone monoliths that the character can activate. This game is a platformer, but there is no challenge in the platforming at all. On my second playthrough through Dawn I beat the game only using single-jump to verify it could be done, and still ended up beating the game with ease, having accessed all of the collectible areas even. Another mechanic that seemed out of place was the inability to activate while jumping. I feel a great bit more depth could have been added to the game if some areas on the main path were only accessable with double jumping, and some collectibles could only be accessed if the character activated toward them while in mid jump. The penalty for messing up is so minimal the game could have had a much higher difficulty in the platforming in general without being offputting to more casual players.
As for the control scheme, playing on a gamepad(Xbox 360 Controller) handled well but there were some small issues. using two different buttons for the same jump and two different buttons for the same activate made it confusing at first as I was trying to find the difference between the two. I feel it would have been better if B and Y were left blank and only X and A were used as input. The camera controls were a bit slow with the thumbstick, but perfect with the triggers. However, due to the way I hold my controller using the triggers to turn the camera was more of a hindrance than just using the slower thumbstick. A good fix could be adding a sensativity option for the thumbstick so that the camera could be sped up to the player's liking. In addition, playing through the game I was unaware that the bumpers did anything, and only after looking ion the settings did I discover that they were used to adjust the orientation of the camera.
The plot of Dawn was nice and simple, you are the last living piece of a grand old tree and you want to bring life to the rest of it. The plot is simple, gets the point across what is important to your character (the tree is like your characters momma) and works with the level design to guide the player to the objective (Follow the path to the tree, bringing life along with you). You know where to go because the path is designed in a way that moves you forward, and your motivation to follow the path is established because of the brief cutscene at the start of the game showing your objective.
There were some fun little things in Dawn that I enjoyed. The musical vileplumes, for one. I hopped on one for a bit listening to it perform a muscial scale, and was pleasantly surprised to have unlocked an achievement by the end of it. Another thing I enjoyed was "Windowed" mode was default borderless windowed mode, although adding another option for regular windowed mode wouldn't be looked down on. I enjoyed the twirl the character performed while double jumping. I enjoyed the way the game looked. activating all the flowers and getting the achievements was fun and never felt like a grind. I enjoyed the music, at first.
There were some nagging little issues with Dawn that I noticed. The music got kind of repetitive and uninteresting after a bit of playing. Having to stop part way through a run of the game means you have to start over from the beginning of the run. Unlocking all the collectibles and getting new game+ only allowed for a pallette swapped character which seemed like a poor reward.
I understand that most of the problems with the game probably stemmed from a deadline to finish and not an actual problem in the design process, so I'm willing to give most of them a pass. I'd rate this game a solid 4/10 for what it is.

I can see why a lot of people got turned off. Primal is less of a Far Cry game more of a survival and crafting game, and to ask for it the same price as for the previous Far Cry games, which already contained many of the mechanics of Primal, isn't right. Having said that, once this thing drops down in price to an acceptable level and you judge it on its own merit, there is plenty to enjoy:
The content:
One of the things to enjoy is exactly the fact that it is not burdened with all the weight of the content of the last two Far Cry games, which I have not played for that very reason. If something about the story or the setting pushed you away from playing those last few Far Cry games (as it did me) then Far Cry Primal may be a breath of fresh air you were looking for. There are no guns, there are no annoying teenagers and no urgent overbearing main storyline with an underused yet omnipresent antagonist. This is a much more custom and relaxing experience. Your tribe has been pushed to the brink of extinction and you have to rebuild and survive against the other tribes that try to destroy you. You hunt animals and gather resources as you craft and build up your village. You can tame different animals and have them attack enemies. I...I have a pet wolf I  can feed and pet. The game was almost worth the price just for that.
The graphics and performance:
The game looks good. The atmospheric haze is too strong and bright so that it becomes blinding, but just walking through the forest with the snowy peaks in the background feels great and brings memories of Elder Scrolls: Skyrim, (which is maybe not the best thing to bring up, considering all the things you can do in a modded version of Skyrim). The beauty is also well-optimized. My graphics card has not been meeting recommended requirements of games for a while now, but I can run Primal smoothly with most settings on max.
Issues:
The main problem with this game is that it didn't go all the way towards the survival aspect and did not make the game challenging enough. When I picked survival mode, the game's difficulty setting (a separate setting from survival mode) jumped to high, which I then switched back to normal because I thought that the survival mode will make the game difficult enough already. But it didn't. You can easily kill multiple enemies by yourself and it gets even easier if you have a beast you can send to attack them. You have a stamina meter, but running out of stamina does not kill you. You use meat and herbs to heal yourself, but if you do not have any meat on you, you can still heal yourself. I am personally glad there is no hunger or thirst meters because I find those annoying, but unfortunately that is yet another thing that you don't have to worry about, which makes the game easy.
Also, my manual saves don't get created for some reason, despite there being a menu where you can load manual saves instead of the auto-save. My wolf decided to commit suicide by running off the cliff and I reloaded the game and had to redo a lot because the game didn't save where I saved.
Conclusion:
Primal is survival game light. It is also story light. If you put those two together, is there enough content in this game? For the right price, I believe yes. It has just enough story to give you a reason to partake in its fun open-world activities, but the game is definitely more for those who enjoy atmosphere and exploration rather than challenge and story.
