I absolutely loved the original Alan Wake. The first game had an addicting combat system, excellent writing, and an engaging storyline that made me not want to put the controller down. It was the first game that got me hooked on singleplayer story-driven games.
So, naturally, I had to buy American Nightmare when it was on sale, and I have to say: had I played this first, I wouldn't have felt the same way.
The great combat system is still there, and Arcade Mode utilizes it very well. However, story mode is severely lacking. It's boringly easy (ammo is everywhere) and intentionally repetitive. Literally, the same three locations and the exact objectives are copied and pasted three times to lengthen the game.
And don't expect the same enthralling story, either. American Nightmare brings nothing to the table that the original game didn't already do. Unlike in the original, I just didn't care for the characters or the situation they were in. There was nothing particularly memorable that got me hooked.
I love Alan Wake, and American Nightmare's Arcade Mode is nice, but I can't help but think this expansion is a blatant cash-in. If you're an Alan Wake fan, just watch a Let's Play of this game and wait for the real sequel.

This is a port of the Gamecube/Playstation 2/Xbox game released in 2004 by the same software studio, Krome, which is now it's own publisher for this IP.
This game really brings me back. It was already a very good game back then, and 13 years later, it still holds the same level of polish and fun it used to. This is a collectathon platformer, though the collectables are not completely required to comeplete it unlike others. There are the Krome coins and silver cogs, which are hidden around or require hard platforming to reach, and there are also "billibies," which require rescuing. Unlike Ty 1, there is often only 1 to save in each level, compared to the 5 in the predecessor.
Also unlike the original, the game takes place in an "open world" connected by driving a jeep around to each stopping point. Some are full levels, others are side missions. Some are even racetracks, which have a similar feel to Crash Team Racing, while being a bit more... loose in some regards. This is required for 100%, so meh.
Rather than using guns or other weapons, Ty's gimmick is throwing twin boomerangs, which have various effects tied to them. From being able to see hidden boxes, to melting ice, and grappling onto rings, there is more than enough variety, even over the original to keep changing it up for yourself. This time around, Ty gets to use large mechs called "Bunyips," that allow you to extinguish flames, lift impossibly heavy objects, and dish out massive physical damage. The segments are laid out perfectly to introduce new stronger enemies, or explore some areas more effectively.
Unlocking new Rangs', more health, and the keys needed to control the Bunyips require the game's currency, Opals. They can be found floating around, but the majority of them are gained by completing missions, collecting the collectables, and finding bags of them around the game world.
Overall, this is a really good game. It's what I think Spyro could have been post S3, and far, far more. Getting this game on console would be good, and I would recommend the Gamecube release over the others from my own experience with all the controllers/console specs.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Now, to my review of this port:
The most notible thing is that the game runs 60 FPS over the original 30. Wow what a difference this makes to this game. It runs so well, even on ageing hardware. But the real fun is how the enhancements are. The game has options for resolutions of 1920x1080 and up, anti-aliesing of up to 8x, better texture/bumpmapping, and more to be added by the developers in the coming months. For even the max of the max, my GTX860M could more than keep up with everything, and still deliver buttery smooth performance.
The only issue, is how the effects of some rangs' and far off objects, such as the oil platform at the beach wouldnt render properly. This is more than likely an error of the new camera system, but it is still an issue affecting me with this review.
This is the most excellent port of any game I have seen on Steam so far, how it hasn't caught enough traction yet is beyond me. Absolutely pick this up on sale, and I would still pick it up full price.

A fun little game from the 2000's. If your coming to this from the original game then don't expect it to be structured the same way. It is no longer a collectathon but rather a GTA styled platformer with missions you can complete to get opals (currency) which let you purchase bunyip vehicles and different boomerangs. The vehicles are cool but barely get used each one getting 2 to 3 uses before never touching them again. Getting different boomerangs will allow you to explore little sections of each area, complete small puzzles to get extra collectables which usually end up awarding you with more opals, and can just be applied to combat. On top of this you can purchase upgraded versions of boomerangs you already own, ranging from the multirang which allows you to throw large heaps of basic boomerangs at once to the deadlyrang which grants remote control and explodes. These upgraded 'rangs are necessary to defeat the bigger enemies so you should at least get one of these to handle those.
All in all this game is fun and filled with the same platforming the original had just in a different structure and a slightly larger emphasis on combat.

Please excuse my foul swearing, I very rarely do so both in real life and online, but seriously, this game played with my emotions, thank you for understanding.
First of all, f*** conquest ending, but if you are planning on playing this game, assuming you finished Re;birth 1, I would strongly recommend doing conquest ending first.  That is, if you have the guts to do it.

GENERAL
-Nepgear is the protagonist in this game, although yes she's adorable, one can get tired of her "I don't know if I can do this" vibe. +++Side characters didn't always have to say generic lines as much as in Re;birth 1
CONS -

About f***ing conquest ending.  I love when shows make me cry, but jesus the christ, there should be a limit.  Why it's not on cons is because the ending really showed me how much I love the characters.  That and because the ending had an insanely clever plot twist. It is the epithymy of bad endings, yet it's so eye opening.  When I say insanely clever, I'm exaggerating. This is a genre of game I like to call the "Choose your own adventure movie" genre. I call it that because to me comparing this to a videogame is like comparing a chose your own adventure book to a tabletop roleplaying game; technically you could make the argument, but it feels far from what it claims to be.
As such, I always recommend you do not buy these games but rather watch your favorite Youtuber play them. They're more enjoyable as movies than games. However, since these are sold as games and it is a given they are better off watched than played, I'll review it compared to other choose your own adventure movies.
Telltale's Game of Thrones is about the tragic tale of House Forrester, a small family from the North that is unimportant enough to grant creative freedom for the story. House Forrester is allied to the Starks and the story begins at the time of the Red Wedding, so as one might expect things go very wrong and you have to try to survive.
It should be a given that you need to be a fan of Game of Thrones to enjoy this properly. If you aren't, you will have absolutely no idea what is going on and it will be altogether pointless for you. The story starts at the same time as the Red Wedding, which is the end of Season 3, so if you are a fan of the show you'll need to be caught up with Season 3 to avoid spoilers.
Several of the major characters from the show, such as Jon Snow and Tyrion Lannister, are featured in the story with their actors voicing them. It is a nice moment to see one of your playable characters interact with a major character from the show, but the novelty fades quickly.
While we're on the topic of characters, it is worth mentioning that you have quite a few. You get Mira Forrester in King's Landing, Ethan Forrester home in Ironrath, Gared Tutle at the Wall, and Rodrik Forrester in Mereen to play as and the story cycles through the characters on a regular basis. The problem with this is that it makes the story feel very unfocused and it's difficult to grow attached to characters. There is no one story and character arc for you to follow as in other itterations of the genre but rather several loosely connected stories each with their own main characters, antagonists, and conflicts. The end result is several mediocre stories as opposed to a single strong story. The lack of attachment you feel towards the characters also removes much of the gut punch when main characters die, which is historically a selling point for both Game of Thrones and Telltale's previous choose your own adventure movies.
The greatest problem with this choose your own adventure movie is that choices seem to have little impact. The story more or less plays out the same no matter what you say or do and there are several instances of the illusion of choice; that is, either your decisions all lead to the same outcome or there is only one right choice and the rest get you killed. The largest decision in the story is a binary one at the end of the story that has almost no impact because it's at the very end of the story. Speaking of the ending, the game ends in a blatant beg for a sequel which it will probably never get and leaves the story completely unfinished and with more loose ends than the show. The worst part is that the little story arc for House Forrester was at a point where it could have been wrapped up quite nicely, but the game went for a twist ending that left the story unfinished and unfulfilling.
So as with all choose your own adventure movies I highly recommend you watch it rather than buy it, but even if you do enjoy playing these games this one is still not worth buying. The story is very weak in comparison to other choose your own adventure movies and many of your choices virtually don't matter.

Hack and slash your way through hordes of enemies and try not to wear out your mouse buttons in Grim Dawn, a Diablo-style combat RPG. True to the genre, this game features frantic attacking, potion guzzling, spell button mashing, loot finding, quest-solving action. This time around it’s about stopping some mysterious invading force known as the Aetherials as your standard unwilling unassuming hero-to-be. Throughout the game you will also meet various factions struggling against the invading threat and choosing to assist them will open up new quests, items, and other rewards.
Grim Dawn stands out from other Diablo clones in that it has a great amount of class and build variety. Not only can you choose a single starting class, but you gain the option to expand into a second, dual class which changes your title depending on the combination. For example, I chose the occultist and nightblade classes, which granted me the combine class of witch hunter. Advancing in each class and unlocking new skills requires spending points in its mastery tree at the bottom of the screen. You can further expand on your repertoire by restoring shrines scattered across the game for devotion points used in the constellation system where star systems are completed to grant the player new passive abilities and statistic increases. Of course you also have 3 core stats (physique, cunning, spirit) that you can raise by one point every level (skills by 3) and they have their own effects on player statistics and armor/weapon requirements. Finally, the game allows you to re-allocate points for everything except your core stats and mastery points for a very nominal fee.
The overall story, graphics, and music of Grim dawn are fairly simple, as they should be, and the challenge is good enough for your typical sword and board or caster-spam builds. In fact, this game may be a bit on the easy side unless you pick a paper-tiger style build focusing on high damage with low health and resistance. Speaking of resistance, the game features ten (10!) different types of damage! Consequently, until you have reached higher levels and factional reputations and received certain augmentations and other gear, it will be impossible to have a loadout that gives you wide enough resistance coverage to significantly reduce all damage types. Basically, there will be areas of the game that you will breeze through, followed by areas where you will die over and over again before making any progress. Thankfully there is the handy portal button that allows you to drop a town-portal wherever you want at no cost, which remains even if you use it multiple times (e.x. after dying).
So is Grim Dawn worth playing? If you enjoyed Diablo 2, were bored by 1, and hated 3, you’ll probably like this game a lot. If you’re more into simplicity, a la Diablo 3, you may be turned off by all the extra resistance and point allocation systems. Either way, it’s worth a look-see for anyone craving some dungeon crawling, mouse mashing action.

Pretty altogether solid.
If you've played both Skyrim and LoTR Shadow of Morder, imagine more the latter than the former. There's not a great deal of depth in weapons/skills/etc., there's not a ton of variety of enemies (frightfully little, really!) and several other things that, perhaps, could have made it better.
But with that said, for what it has, it was the right length. Much longer and I woulda grown a bit bored, so that's good maybe. There's only a few nagging annoyances - some of the weapons just felt junky - the various enhanced bows never felt as good as the basic one, and there are several enemies that will knock you on your♥♥♥♥♥for 3-5 seconds, doing 2-3 bars of health in damage (6 is the max, period) and can be pretty jarring since there's NO block/dodge or any way to recover quicker, plus healing is a several-second-long animation, so it can be easy to be a little frustrated.
But with that said, those issues were altogether few and far between. I can't say this one will have a special place in my heart or anything, but the setting was good, unique, and well done, the characters were remarkable and I totally loved the way they did voice-overs in an ancient language, the game LOOKED visually splendid, and the combat controls and such all seemed to work fairly well save a few annoyances. I did use a bow 99% of the time as it just felt downright stellar compared to hacking away with clubs or poking with spears, when you can just headshot foes down in one go over and over.
But, really, all in all.. rock solid, pun slightly intended based on the setting. A little on the pricy side given todays realm of games and playtimes and such, but ultimately it's a good offering that's frankly worth it. The story isn't especially deep, and most all of the 'side' content is just.. kill these guys, save those two guys, take over this place, so if you don't *REALLY* dig the combat and feel of the game you'll probably stick mostly to the main story stuff, but it's still fairly worth it even then. I got about 50% completion of all the POIs and random junk and finished the story and feel pretty happy with it overall.

XCOM is a great slow-paced strategy game. I emphasize the slow part since, like the Civilization games that Firaxis puts out, gameplay is very much on a unit-by-unit basis. That might mean waiting for decent chunks of time while enemy movements are processed and displayed, when you would rather just have them finish their turn already.
That being said, the gameplay for XCOM is very deep, almost to the detriment of new players. It's highly recommended to follow a wiki or a guide on your first playthrough and to defeintely select easy mode. I've played a lot of Civ 5, but the discipline required for how methodical you have to be in XCOM is on a whole other level.
I like the general flow of the gameplay, although it seems like the story tends to take a back seat to all the alien invasions and you managing panicking countries with super soliders. The game holds up remarkably well for being 4+ years old since its launch. It's a very nice change of pace from the frantic madness that can be other AAA titles these days. The game feels a bit too slow to power through a couple missions in any time less than an hour, but it's an hour well spent and a good way to relax.

A reboot of what could be called a genre unto itself. XCOM, like many games from the '80s and '90s, were known for their brutal difficulty, but this one stood out because it was immutable - the setting was infamously stuck at "Superhuman" due to a bug. The modernised version thankfully does not have this problem, but is in keeping with series tradition still fairly hard despite loads of streamlining. Indeed, it's as hard as it sounds: you're leading a team of Kevlar-and-M4 redshirts against aliens with plasma rifles. Your troops will get better (as well as your tech), but not if they die - and some of them will die, I guarantee it.
For those who want a real challenge, installing the esteemed Long War mod (which requires the Enemy Unknown expansion) cranks the difficulty up to eleven. The alien AI gets a massive upgrade, to the point where it's almost
genre-savvy, and so do the aliens themselves. Base-building and tech also become noticeably more complex. In exchange for all this, you get more boots on the ground and a greater variety of stuff to equip them with.
Overall, the game is extremely engaging and stimulating, if not necessarily realistic (e.g. the "Lightning Reflexes" ability allows thus-trained soldiers to effectively go into bullet time). Pick it up and join the war effort, but prepare yourself for the inevitable casualties that will ensue.
Good luck, Commander. You're gonna need it.

This game was great in the beta but subsequent patches really turned this game into a waste of your money. Unit balance has gotten better over time but this game was ruined whtn the vehicle caps were drastically reduced. Playing with lots of infantry wouldn't be so bad if squads that took 10+ minutes to become veterans could survive late game insta-gib attakcs.  The addition of later generals were a cash grab and put the nail in the coffin for this game as it became pay to win.
If you can get it for under $10 I'd say it would be a good pick if you are a WWII period fan or just love to collect RTS games. So now that you can get the game for 10$... I am not sure that you should. They completely ruined the OKW with the december 2017 patch.  Company of Allies would be a better fitting title.
On the bright side they did finally remove a few cheap tricks (soviet demo charges cant be placed in cap zones for easy mode squad kills) but after 2 years? I think it was a bit late.
Relic came out with a balance patch this month that makes the Axis into a complete joke faction. The reasoning for such nerfs were things like " The Elephant is too effective." To make a long story short (too late?) the design of the game balance for a very long time was that the Allied infantry push back the Axis early game and that Axis armor pushes back the Allies late game.
Catch phrases like this are really quite troublesome. The problem with this type of statement is that the Elephant is designed to hard counter one of most favorite soviet tactics: SU-85 spam.
You are damn right the Elephant ruins that tactic! That's the point of that doctrine unit. The problem overall is that CoH2 had a really neat idealistic asymetrical balance. But rather than using a different tactic people just cried until the other side's units got nerfed (so that they could blindly run their favorite build order with no variation).
The Elephant gets utterly hosed by guards/AT guns. It is one of the few heavily armored units that is weak against an infantry rush. It also has trouble vs super heavy mortars.... if only there were a soviet doctrine for those.
What I loved about CoH2 was that the doctrine system they gave us allowed for extremely tactical and intelligent play (assuming you had most of the good commanders- but that is another story). You were shooting yourself in the foot if you spam SU-85s when you load into a game and see the enemy has an Elephant commander available.
What you are supposed to do is push the enemy hard as the soviets (allied strategy really) in the early part of the game so that he thinks he wont ever reach the Elephant.... so he will pick another commander. You might even be required (/gasp) to pick an early general to push the German player so hard that he cannot wait and must pick a commander who can help him now.
What I see overall is that many people never learned how to push their enemy into making that kind of decision. And that lazy style of play is why Relic nerfed the Elephant.

Having never played a Far Cry game before, I found this game refreshingly entertaining. The most noticeable downside of the game itself is it's repetitiveness. Fights against wildlife and humans may at times be too many, becoming a little overwhelming, but for the most part, smart use of the game mechanics can make every battle feel different. From a stealthy approach, to a more violent and less subtle charge, topped with each tameable animal's special abilities and your own weapons, it only takes creativity to craft your experience. The map is big enough to make it interesting, and small enough to avoid "fatigue", and it's diversity in landscapes make it unique anywhere where you are, in other words, it's easy to get lost.
The storyline is good, from an entertaining standpoint, and while some may find it generic, it's well executed.
Overall it's a good game, with more pros than cons.

One thing special about Dawn is that unlike many video games of its kind (3D university indie), it actually is complete, though small.
Unusually, it has a good offering of settings where you can actually tone things up and down to your computer's capabilities, instead of accept laggy conditions.
It also has a well designed set of achievements. This would normally be rather annoying to collect, but with the game's generous allowal of skipping scenes even from the start of the game, provision of a double jump even though it was never needed, as well as the ability to move back and forth across the map (no bridges burned as you move), it was far more pleasant.
Though the character's animation makes a player suspicious that the game was a crude product from a 3D engine, pretty much everything else in the game feels well designed. I personally like how the stones were used as level walls.
I personally can't identify a depth of meaning in this game, but I can see the depth of artwork and mood. There are no boring, sparse stretches of land, every island is topped with a selection of flowers and grasses, along with a few surprises.
By really living up to the 'Casual' tag and having a relieving relative lack of bad game design, this game provides a good hour of enjoyment.
Is it a must-play? No. But if you want to look at something new, and have some time to kill, I think you'll like this.
That aside, looking at the devs' social media, it seems that this is their first work, and they are very proud of it. It's too short to be a flagship, though; I'll be waiting for their next game, and I expect it to be bigger. And I think they know that.

This is a direct sequel to the first game. It attempts to explain events directly after the conclusion of the first game and then takes place two years after the events in Bright Falls. To simplify without spoiling too much, Alan is in a sort of limbo ("The Dark Place"), and is desperately trying to get back to the real world (which has written him off for dead), his wife, his friends, and his job.
However, the Dark Presence (the bad thing) has taken on Alan's skin and can travel to the real world; it is also actively keeping Alan stuck in the Dark Place while he attempts to ruin Alan's life in the real world by being a massive psychotic ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ (think serial killer / torturer). You have to get out of the Dark Place, kill the Dark Presence that is imitating you, and get back to life.
The only problem is: The Dark Presence can send you back in time to repeat the same thing over and over again, so this experience becomes basically a very, very dark Groundhog Day. Each time you go through the time loop, the people you interact with remember bits and pieces of your last visit, so you slowly untangle the mess.
This game is much more action-oriented than the first. There is no danger of running out of ammo, and there are lots more weapons (including heavy stuff like a combat shotgun, all kinds of rifles, automatic weapons, and even a sweet crossbow and nail gun). It's a lot more run-and-gun and much more satisfying in terms of killing bad guys.
The story is just as convoluted as the first game, so if you liked the story of the first one, this is a great follow-up to the game. It's much shorter than the first game so it's a fun little 1-2 night wrap-up of the story.
There's also an arcade mode with leaderboards where you just get to survive a certain number of waves of Taken while using ammo and weapons scattered around the level. Unlocking weapons in Story mode gets you better gear in Arcade mode.

If you are going into this game expecting a story and atmosphere on par with the original Alan Wake then you are going to be a little let down.  The story I feel is simply there for some decent filler (it has its moments).  What this game more than makes up for is the arcade mode (which is how the idea of American Nightmare came about, as a score-attack game).
How do you balance out the larger arsenal of weapons and more action?  Plop the player into an arena and throw more enemies at them.
While the arenas themselves are timed (and eventually end if you don't die) the real challenge is getting a good score.  The interesting bit about this is to get a higher score you want to be evading danger more often than dispatching enemies.
Pick it up if you want a little bit of extra story on top of a solid score-attack gamemode.

Background: This game came out during the Wave of Zombie Games riding on the push the walking Dead and that Brad Pitt movie. Anyways I have always enjoyed a good Zombie survival game and when you mix it with RPG elements I can't pass up a game like this.
Combat Mechanics: The game mixes the usual cast of cobbled together survival melee weapons like baseball bats, axes, and police batons, with the ranged option of guns and homemade explosives. You also have skill tress to increase your ability to survive and even hide from enemies. Now lets add in Parkour. Instead of having to rely on dead sprinting for doors and jumping around mindlessly the game blends in a set of basic to advanced parkour techniques that gives the game a certain verticality (excuse the pun). It makes navigation fluid and more realistic than not being able to climb onto a building to run away.
Social Mechanics: Slim to None. Story is straight forward. Most enemies are scripted to engage you in combat without conversation. Usual Evil dude quips over the handheld radio, standard survival dialog.
Final Thoughts: It is a breath of fresh air in the mass arrival of zombie games. It blends open world with crafting, parkour, co-op challenges, and cliche enemy bosses into a game worth playing for the freedom of Survial.

I love games that compliment a friendly and competitive style of gameplay. It's incredibly hard to find that on the Steam archives anymore, as games become easier to produce and too many greedy people attempt to swindle those who have adopted the number one pass time activity in the entire world. If you're tired of relating finances/money to video gaming and weighing the chances that the $60  you just spent on a new released AAA title is going to be well spent or a big flop, then welcome to Double Action.
I think this is the only game I've seen on the market where the "Free to Play" identifier actually means Free to Play and not "Free to Play (But good luck having fun or getting anywhere without purchasing the added in game items)"
There isn't even a  donation button on this games main page. This game is 100% legit FREE .
And that's just to start.
If you're curious about the gameplay, it's exactly what Max Payne 3 Multiplayer was supposed to be but failed so horribly at implementing. You roll around, jump over obstacles, dodge enemy fire, slide up and down stairs, bust through windows, all in attempt to successfully make the most intricate kill as you possibly can. Why? Because this game doesn't keep track of kills nor deaths. There's no accuracy notices or kill/death ratio comparisons. You score points by killing people in the most action packed means you can think of. You can stand in a corner the entire match, not die once, killing anyone that comes close to you, and you will still lose. Your points for kills are increased by achieving the kill while performing stunts. If somebody falls off the edge of a building on the skyscraper map, you can jump off right behind him and have a free fall shooting match to try to get the kill before hitting the ground. There's a leaderboard that keeps track of the Daily, Weekly, and Monthly top scoring players, but other than that there isn't anything at all to fuss about. This game focuses on what video gaming was initially developed to be about; Having Fun! And you will. Trust me.

Well if you didn't believe the review scores, let me put into words just how good this game is. There will be negatives believe it or not.
You see, dear reader, when a game is being developed compromises must be made because money is finite. So we end up with games with good stories and crap gameplay or vice versa. This is not the case with Half-Life 2. All aspects of the game are almost equally good to one another and to other games from 2004 (hell even 2017).
Positives:
+ Delightful characters. Well written and designed.
+ Very good gameplay. Weapons are responsive and it's nice and satisfying when you use them.
+ Very atmospheric! Seriously, the designer(s) have purposfully used a communist style architecture so you'll get the dystopian feel. There's a level where the horror is nailed much better than dedicated horror games! This is Half-Life 2's strongest aspect - the atmosphere.
+ There is a lot of diversity (when this word was associated positivley) into the game. You'll be on the run, being almost defensless, you'll be a resistance fighter, you'll drive a boat through toxic wastes, you'll go on a journey with a car visiting abanddoned (or not) settlements, you'll play a pseudo platforming if you don't want to get eaten, you'll see how horror should made in a infested village, you'll be a beastmaster commaning deadly animals.. The game bleeds of effort. (The different stages are not chronological to not spoil).
+ The story is nice and mysterious. There's philosophy and morality. You have no choice but this game isn't about choice. You're a listener and receiver. Few FPS games have such intriguing story.
+ The A.I. is good so you'll be challenged. They use tactics.
+ The gravity gun and physics as a whole. The gun is fun and practical to use. It encourages creativity and freedom. Physics makes the game feel much better. Object react to you and it's fun to blast enemies away. Note the game came out in 2004 so this was a big deal back then.
+ The sound is very subtle and it does a great job at amplifiying the feelings of the current situation. it's atmospheric. Just like the rest of the game.
Negatives (you didn't believe me did you?):
- When you've recruited enough followers they'll start getting pretty annoying when they block you from exiting rooms. For instance if you enter a room to explore, all of them will follow you in and it will become a cluster♥♥♥♥ at the door. They won't move because they are following so you'll have to push them or you'll have to get deeper into the room so they'll make space for you to exit. But most room you enter aren't that big so you'll have to push. Note this isn't that big of a deal. You'll start getting followers towards the end of the game and only on some levels so this is a minor problem.
- Another problem is that the dialogs between NPCs' are unskippable so if you do multiple playthoughts or want to speed throught the game you'll be annoyed. A minor problem, especially for first timers.
- Lastly, except the gravity gun and the crossbow the other weapons are kinda standard. Pistol, submachine gun, shotgun etc. You have a pulse rifle with a neat secondary ability but still.. Considering the positives of this game I feel bad for mentioning this :(
Neutrals:
+/- The driving sequences can be seen both as good and bad. For some this might be an awesome example of diversity of gameplay, for others it might be an inconveniece.
+/- It has puzzles. Again some might feel this is just annoying and unneeded padding, for others it might be a good time to use the gravity gun.
+/- Silent protagonist. Many (including myself) consider this lack of feature to actually deepen the game because you can easily project youself into the character of Gordon Freeman. Others might find it dull and weird their character hasn't uttered a word all game and has no personality.
As you can see the game isn't perfect but it sure is close to it! The negatives are minor inconeviences while the positives encompass big aspects of the every video game. The quality of those aspects, at the time, were better than other dedicated games at just one aspect. Hell some if them are rivaling even todays' games.
Half-Life 2 is a game which shows effort, dedication and quality while sacrificing almost nothing in return.
Thank you so much for remastering this amazing franchise. I really wish more childhood favourites would be remastered.

A decent hold'em poker game, where you can win four items of Team Fortress 2 game (which is not of any interest for me) and listen a hilarious in-game chat of 4 fun characters: Max from Sam & Max series, Strong Bad from Homestar runner, Heavy from already named Tea Fortress and Tycho from Penny-Arcade(dotcom). All of them are lovable. It could be very relaxing, dealing cards, and listen idle, yet clever chat of those four. For some time, at least.
Game have only one downside: once you heard all the lines characters were going to say... and win all 4 items from them... it is getting bleaker. Losing colours and taste. And if you're an achievement hunter... well, I wish you the best of luck. Achievements in the Poker Night are very logical and good ones, but some of them are connected to winning the hand with certain combination. And yeah, to made complete of this game, you need to get a straight flash.
Well, again, good sides:
1) Proper, enjoying poker. If you set difficult level at hard, it will be quite challenging. No, you'll not win every hand with all-in tactic, like some other reviews said. You gotta try to be a good player. A cool and smart one.
2) Not only you'll be playing poker with worthy opponents, but they'll be entertaining you in the process! And every of them has a different behavior, which you'll need to learn for make sure you're winning.
3) From those of us who are playing Team Fortress, the items you'll win should be a good reward to play a night or two in poker.
Bad sides:
1) No matter how clever and fun are the lines from all four your opponents, they are limited. And after you heard them all, in all combinations... it is not so fun anymore. And even beyond that point, sometimes, there are lines which feels out of order. Like when Heavy guy is folding cards before you, and then starting to banter you with something like "In Mother Russia you're quit when you're dead". C'mon, man, you're folded too!
2) So the game wears off... but if you want it with complete achievements, you need damned staright flush! And that's a bummer. Chances to get that combination... not high.
3) Finally, there are some stabilty issues, especially when you're trying to change skins of background. So after several attempts to change something, I decided to stick to the main theme, the reason of stability.
I have two marks: "Khorosho!" (8/10) if you are playing for the items and not for long. And 7/10 - if you're collecting achievements and getting bored with all those repeating lines again and again.

Hack and slash your way through hordes of enemies and try not to wear out your mouse buttons in Grim Dawn, a Diablo-style combat RPG. True to the genre, this game features frantic attacking, potion guzzling, spell button mashing, loot finding, quest-solving action. This time around it’s about stopping some mysterious invading force known as the Aetherials as your standard unwilling unassuming hero-to-be. Throughout the game you will also meet various factions struggling against the invading threat and choosing to assist them will open up new quests, items, and other rewards.
Grim Dawn stands out from other Diablo clones in that it has a great amount of class and build variety. Not only can you choose a single starting class, but you gain the option to expand into a second, dual class which changes your title depending on the combination. For example, I chose the occultist and nightblade classes, which granted me the combine class of witch hunter. Advancing in each class and unlocking new skills requires spending points in its mastery tree at the bottom of the screen. You can further expand on your repertoire by restoring shrines scattered across the game for devotion points used in the constellation system where star systems are completed to grant the player new passive abilities and statistic increases. Of course you also have 3 core stats (physique, cunning, spirit) that you can raise by one point every level (skills by 3) and they have their own effects on player statistics and armor/weapon requirements. Finally, the game allows you to re-allocate points for everything except your core stats and mastery points for a very nominal fee.
The overall story, graphics, and music of Grim dawn are fairly simple, as they should be, and the challenge is good enough for your typical sword and board or caster-spam builds. In fact, this game may be a bit on the easy side unless you pick a paper-tiger style build focusing on high damage with low health and resistance. Speaking of resistance, the game features ten (10!) different types of damage! Consequently, until you have reached higher levels and factional reputations and received certain augmentations and other gear, it will be impossible to have a loadout that gives you wide enough resistance coverage to significantly reduce all damage types. Basically, there will be areas of the game that you will breeze through, followed by areas where you will die over and over again before making any progress. Thankfully there is the handy portal button that allows you to drop a town-portal wherever you want at no cost, which remains even if you use it multiple times (e.x. after dying).
So is Grim Dawn worth playing? If you enjoyed Diablo 2, were bored by 1, and hated 3, you’ll probably like this game a lot. If you’re more into simplicity, a la Diablo 3, you may be turned off by all the extra resistance and point allocation systems. Either way, it’s worth a look-see for anyone craving some dungeon crawling, mouse mashing action.

This game was great in the beta but subsequent patches really turned this game into a waste of your money. Unit balance has gotten better over time but this game was ruined whtn the vehicle caps were drastically reduced. Playing with lots of infantry wouldn't be so bad if squads that took 10+ minutes to become veterans could survive late game insta-gib attakcs.  The addition of later generals were a cash grab and put the nail in the coffin for this game as it became pay to win.
If you can get it for under $10 I'd say it would be a good pick if you are a WWII period fan or just love to collect RTS games. So now that you can get the game for 10$... I am not sure that you should. They completely ruined the OKW with the december 2017 patch.  Company of Allies would be a better fitting title.
On the bright side they did finally remove a few cheap tricks (soviet demo charges cant be placed in cap zones for easy mode squad kills) but after 2 years? I think it was a bit late.
Relic came out with a balance patch this month that makes the Axis into a complete joke faction. The reasoning for such nerfs were things like " The Elephant is too effective." To make a long story short (too late?) the design of the game balance for a very long time was that the Allied infantry push back the Axis early game and that Axis armor pushes back the Allies late game.
Catch phrases like this are really quite troublesome. The problem with this type of statement is that the Elephant is designed to hard counter one of most favorite soviet tactics: SU-85 spam.
You are damn right the Elephant ruins that tactic! That's the point of that doctrine unit. The problem overall is that CoH2 had a really neat idealistic asymetrical balance. But rather than using a different tactic people just cried until the other side's units got nerfed (so that they could blindly run their favorite build order with no variation).
The Elephant gets utterly hosed by guards/AT guns. It is one of the few heavily armored units that is weak against an infantry rush. It also has trouble vs super heavy mortars.... if only there were a soviet doctrine for those.
What I loved about CoH2 was that the doctrine system they gave us allowed for extremely tactical and intelligent play (assuming you had most of the good commanders- but that is another story). You were shooting yourself in the foot if you spam SU-85s when you load into a game and see the enemy has an Elephant commander available.
What you are supposed to do is push the enemy hard as the soviets (allied strategy really) in the early part of the game so that he thinks he wont ever reach the Elephant.... so he will pick another commander. You might even be required (/gasp) to pick an early general to push the German player so hard that he cannot wait and must pick a commander who can help him now.
What I see overall is that many people never learned how to push their enemy into making that kind of decision. And that lazy style of play is why Relic nerfed the Elephant.

I brought COH2 when it first came out, and being a hardcore player of the first game i had very mixed feelings with the way number two was put together, let me try to explain. This is still most definatly a COH game first and formost, tactical infantry and tank based comabt useing cover, fog of war and suppresion; essential all the things that made the first one epic. They even refined many features like adding weather and the ability for infantry to hurdle cover, more commander options aswell as an (argubly) more defined role for airpower. Relic sknows how to make a good RTS.
Whats the bad side i hear you shout then? It's to do with scope. Im not exagerating when i say the war on the Eastern front was by far the biggest in Europe, but the problems with it are that it was fought primarily between just the Russians and Germans, which means you esentialy lose all opportunites to include the other Allied factions, the British, Americans and even the possiblity of factions like France and Italy dissapeared fast. This causes a (perhaps unforseen) consequence of the game being more streamlined and 'dumbed down'. Not to mention there was so much potential when they implemented the new commander system, what about unlockable lease-lend units like the Matilda and Churchill III Russia had access too? The game simply Could not capture either scale or scope aswell as it had the potential too. Don't even get me started on the whole 'pay for units/camo/opperations approach' relic have going atm, honestly its just a cash grab.
All in all it's still an excelent play and i do recomend it if you can look past that your not going to get much else other than pure Russian on German RTS game, with a decent campaign, but if you can look past the slightly dated graphics COH: Allied Assault is where you want to be going for online play.
(Post American update: Ironically my biggest problem with COH2 was the lack of variety of units, and while the dlc price for Americans is a bit steep it adds MUCH needed diversity to online play, the US faction has a nice selection of units and fits nicely inbetween the previous factions, with a good selection of commander units to boot. also recent changes to the way skins and commanders unlock make playing COH 2 much more fun and easy. No more worrying about unfair pay to win scenarios with overpowered commanders.)

Epic music and destruction fireworks are set to portray a clash of giants composed of men. They die and win battles of unspeakable ferocity. It's like a whirlwind on a storm dancing as you tell it to.

And you exist there, expressing yourself as a force to be reckoned. Every bullet, grenade, shell is you backlashing the possibility of annihilation. Could we ask more of a game?

I dabbled with Far Cry 2, but played Far Cry 3 and 4 extensively. I'm not sure why the idea of wandering around in the woods with primitive weapons appealed to me, but I admit that I've wanted to play this for a long time. The last sale lured me in. I'm glad that it did.
In the earlier Far Cry games, you sometimes had to travel in the wilds, but I never felt at home there. It was always "space" between the locations where the real game happened. In this game, the wildlands is where you eventually find yourself at home, and hanging out in villages is the "space" between where your adventure happens. It is a neat twist, and I have been binge playing this game since I bought it.
The story missions and how they advance things along is very well done.  You have two storyline enemies to choose from, and they are very different from each other. They are both a nice addition to the adventure, but unlike other Far Cry games, they do not feel like they are the game. They are just something else added that you do while you are "out there" adventuring.
Crafting and gathering are both necessary, and there are times that I have to go gather resources in order to further a goal. This hardly ever felt like a grind, though. It felt more like I was going into "Tarzan Mode", traveling in locations where the resources were, exposing myself to all kinds of possible adventures.  There are a number of quests kicked off by discovering locations that are actually nicely done. Though the depth of, say, Witcher 4, is missing from the sidequests, they can offer up another area you are supposed to infiltrate for one reason or another.
Stealth is rewared, but never required, and the ways to accomplish a mission are numerous. After taking over an area, I often found another way that I could have come in that would have provided different advantages than the one I had previously found.
There are a variety of mission types. A few offer some comedy relief, but if you are immersed in your character and don't want the comedy, it soon becomes apparent which missions they are in. The only mission type that I didn't for much were those where you were some kind of "spirit of the Elephant". I eventually did these for the XP, but they just weren't my thing. Otherwise, everything has been a lot of fun.
The "little adventures" that you run into while in "Tarzan Mode" are repetitive, but the repetition is fun because it you gain skills often and want something to try them out on.
Though I'm tempted to add more, I don't want to provide too much because the surprise in the game is a lot of the fun.  I definitely recommend the game.

The first time when you go back at your starting point, you ask yourself what you did wrong. Then the second time, you feel the game is just playing with you nerves and just want to finish it as soon as possible and forget it.
Really, Alan Wake's American Nightmare should be played only to see how an otherwise great licence can crash and burn due to unwise design choice.

Aaaahhhhh..... FTL. For many that does not mean anything, but for many Steam users out there, it means Faster Than Light. FTL is a very unique Roguelike with heavy focus on micro-managing and multi-tasking. In this game, you control one of 10 possible ships in order to deliver important information to the Galactic Federation Base that is crucial for stopping the Rebels. As a roguelike, the map will always be randomly generated every time you start a new run, and you can get many new weapons and systems every run as well. Despite being released back in 2012, the game had a patch in April 2014, adding many new features to the formula.
Despite the amazingly high difficulty (even on "easy" mode), this game is truly worth a look. The graphics and gameplay maybe are not too engaging, but the true feel is majorly on how you utilize the resources that you're given. And after 256 runs (out of which 2 were victories ^^' ), I can definately say that this is one of the best games in the genre.

Having grown somewhat disenchanted with the current RPG market options, I was hesitant to purchase anything new, but Grim Dawn has succeeded wonderfully in recapturing some of the greatness of ARPG's of old.
Calling it the spiritual successor of D2 does an injustice to both D2 and Grim Dawn, but I can certainly see why the comparison has been made. Grim Dawn carves its own path into the genre with a beautiful and expansive world to explore, and a very well-defined sense of its own artistic aesthetic direction.
There is a ton of class, skill, stat, and item augmentation options to choose from to satisfy even the most veteran of Diablo 2 fans. If all of this wasn't enough, the writing team has done a great job putting out some of the best writing in the genre in recent memory. Good writing is hard to come by in gaming these days. I actually really enjoyed reading the notes and scribbles found throughout the game - something I rarely do for want of interest.
If Crate can manage to remain grounded and fill in the void where Activision-Blizzard is currently lacking, all of us old school RPG'ers might be in for many years of great gaming to come.
Take note, Crate: You've got a great team across the board, and your pricing is excellent. Don't let yourselves fall by the wayside once greater success comes.

I have played all the TY games (when they were originally released) and I really enjoy all of them. Are they are as expertly crafted as mainstream platformers like Mario Galaxy? No. But they are fun little games with a lot of crazy charm.

The PC is lacking in 3D platformers, so I love that they have been porting the TY games. Even if it weren't a small market though, I would still recommend the TY games because they are just relaxing fun. You can tell the developers put some heart into the game.

I dabbled with Far Cry 2, but played Far Cry 3 and 4 extensively. I'm not sure why the idea of wandering around in the woods with primitive weapons appealed to me, but I admit that I've wanted to play this for a long time. The last sale lured me in. I'm glad that it did.
In the earlier Far Cry games, you sometimes had to travel in the wilds, but I never felt at home there. It was always "space" between the locations where the real game happened. In this game, the wildlands is where you eventually find yourself at home, and hanging out in villages is the "space" between where your adventure happens. It is a neat twist, and I have been binge playing this game since I bought it.
The story missions and how they advance things along is very well done.  You have two storyline enemies to choose from, and they are very different from each other. They are both a nice addition to the adventure, but unlike other Far Cry games, they do not feel like they are the game. They are just something else added that you do while you are "out there" adventuring.
Crafting and gathering are both necessary, and there are times that I have to go gather resources in order to further a goal. This hardly ever felt like a grind, though. It felt more like I was going into "Tarzan Mode", traveling in locations where the resources were, exposing myself to all kinds of possible adventures.  There are a number of quests kicked off by discovering locations that are actually nicely done. Though the depth of, say, Witcher 4, is missing from the sidequests, they can offer up another area you are supposed to infiltrate for one reason or another.
Stealth is rewared, but never required, and the ways to accomplish a mission are numerous. After taking over an area, I often found another way that I could have come in that would have provided different advantages than the one I had previously found.
There are a variety of mission types. A few offer some comedy relief, but if you are immersed in your character and don't want the comedy, it soon becomes apparent which missions they are in. The only mission type that I didn't for much were those where you were some kind of "spirit of the Elephant". I eventually did these for the XP, but they just weren't my thing. Otherwise, everything has been a lot of fun.
The "little adventures" that you run into while in "Tarzan Mode" are repetitive, but the repetition is fun because it you gain skills often and want something to try them out on.
Though I'm tempted to add more, I don't want to provide too much because the surprise in the game is a lot of the fun.  I definitely recommend the game.

For what it is, this is a fun game to stomp around in. I'm sitting at about 99.7% completion right now, with about 50 hours or so in the game (internet connection here isn't stable). I played thorugh FC3 and FC4 with my brother, and we really enjoy playing this series on the couch, swapping the controller back and forth every now and then. This title does have a lot of the same elements to it as the previous entries, but that isn't necessarily a bad thing. The scrounging for plants and resources for crafting actually makes sense in this environment, and don't get in the way too much while playing. The difficulty isn't terribly high on the normal settings, and it won't be long before you find yourself sprinting off of cliffs and smashing cave men's skulls with your ludicrously powerful clubs.
Fun aside, the storyline just isn't terribly engaging. The cast of depraved characters who compose your village offer you things to do, but honestly the why of it really doesn't enter the picture. You trot off and murder your way through what feels like a veritable clone army of brutish Neandertals to accomplish your objective, then head home for an underwhelming thank you. This basically repeats until you finish that questline, then starts over for the next group.
Your Wenja brethren probably should have been naturally selected out of the gene pool, they are absolutley terrible at being primitive humans. I didn't find myself caring about the poor saps who need to be rescued, and with the rate they are killed off by virtually EVERYTHING that calls Oros home I'm glad. Basically every side quest has you assisting them in some way, seeing the successful completion notification pop up, then witnessing their untimely demise by either a wave of thuggish cave men or some incredibly deadly predator, usually within seconds of them thanking you and walking away. I can't decide if this is intentional on the part of the devs to give you some sense of urgency when doing the side quests, or a side effect of bad AI programming. The programming thing is evident at times, as you can watch the "predators" run around and simply kill everything within their "territory" mindlessly.
To sum up:
Storyline, not so engaging. Sad, since FC4 was actually really good at making me hate then forgive the BBEG in that game
Visuals, damn impressive. Watching a croc mutilate someone bent on crushing my bones is incredibly satisfying
Audio, also impressive. When night falls and the forest comes alive, you often find yourself cowering behind rocks and tress until the sun comes up (until you become a Neolithic super-soldier, that is)
Fun factor, fairly high. Overall, even without some sort of driving plot to keep you going, I still found running around with a spear and club very satisfying. It's a nice break from the typical vomiting of FPS games I usually find out there. I give it an 8/10, because it was fun but I really wish their was more of a storyline there.

Overall, this was a pretty fun game.  Sucked up way more time for me than I thought, but that's what happens when you have multiple endings and playthroughs to do!
Why was this a fun game?  Well, the story is... okay, not groundbreaking or anything like that.  The combat system is decent (you have the option to equip a super powerful sword from the beginning with some included DLC: I took full advantage of this because... I don't have time to grind out levels to accomplish stuff.  I recommend doing this, but you can choose not to: if so, you'll spend much more time grinding out things like levels and materials).  For a lot of the achievements, there is a lot of pure grinding.  The music, I enjoyed a lot.  And for those who have played other Neptunia games, there is a LOT of recycled material (dungeons, music, characters, fighting system, ect.)
The reason we play Nep-Nep games is for the characters and their interactions: this game starts off a little slow with this, but as you continue on and get more characters, the interactions become better and funnier, to the point that by the end there is pure comedic gold happening.  Other Neptunia games are a little better at this, but this was still a good experience.  Getting the different endings and watching the interactions was probably the best reward this game had to offer.
If you HAVEN'T played a Neptunia game at all, just try one (probably the first game is the best to pick): if you like it, try the rest: if you don't, don't get another one!
And, if you read any other review and hear talk of the Conquest Ending... let me put it this way: the rest of the game is the typical Neptune experience: fun, funny, lighthearted, goofy, cute, ect.  The Conquest chapter & ending was like reading a strong, emotional Visual Novel with Nep-Nep characters: I went from simply chuckling and laughing at everything beforehand to remarking 'Oh crap, did that just happen?  ****, what are they going to do now?  They really ARE doing this!  Oh, NO WAY, she did WHAT?'  If you can handle strong, emotional stuff, that ending is well worth it.

*This review will contain some spoilers for the story of Alan Wake, as well as some gameplay spoilers for American Nightmare. Read at your own disgression!*
Alan Wake´s American Nightmare is a spinoff-title to the original Alan Wake. While it shares a lot of similarities with its predecessor, there is a notable amount of changes and new stuff that one should be aware before considering playing it, as these changes and additions will decide whether this game works for you or not.
The story takes place within an episode of the TV show "Night Springs" (basically the Twilight Zone of Videogames). Alan, still trapped within the Darkness of the Lake after the end of the first game (and its DLC, to be more precise), has now been trapped within one of his own stories, by none other than his doppelgänger, Mr. Scratch. Caught in a loop of endless repetition and constant torment by Scratch, Alan has to find a way to "break the circle" and return to the real world before his doppelgänger has completely overtaken his "real" life.
The gameplay of American Nightmare, at first glance, is basically the same as it was in Alan Wake: You run around in comparatively small, open areas, defeat Taken, collect manuscript pages to fill in story details, and solve some (very easy) puzzles or try and reach a certain spot to advance the story, while occacionally watching TV, listening to the radio and talking to a handful of people. This all takes place on three maps: A Gas Station/Motel in the middle of the Arizonian Desert, an Observatory, and a Drive-in Theater. While each map is quite distinct from the others, you also have to revisit each map several times over the course of the game. While this is explained and justified quite well within the story, this still means that two-thirds of the campaign are repeated content (minor changes notwithstanding). Thankfully, the actual gameplay is good enough so that one can look past it.
American Nightmare, gameplay-wise, improves on both Alan Wake´s enemy design and weapon selection. While the regular Taken are still the bread-and-butter of your combat enemies, there are also various new enemy types that demand some different strategies from the usual "shine your light on them, destroy their shield, and then shoot them". This includes Taken that are immune to your flashlight and instead split into smaller versions of themselves, Taken that flee by transforming into bird flocks, and Taken that throw "Darkness Grenades" into your direction, but keep their distance, among other enemy types. To counter them, Alan now also has access to a much larger arsenal, which gets unlocked the more manuscript pages you collect, so even if you don´t care about the story at all, you should still keep your eyes open for them. The new arsenal includes pistols, a SMG, an Assault Rifle, a Combat Shotgun, a crossbow which ignores the enemy shield, and a Nailgun, among others. Some stuff from Alan Wake also makes a return, like the flaregun and the flashbangs, but they have become quite a bit weaker, no longer insta-killing anything, but rather destroying their shields quickly (which is still useful, of course).
The gameplay in general is alot less "survival" and much more action-orientated. You will pretty much never run out of ammo or flashlight batteries, individual enemies are alot less threatening than they used to but appear in bigger numbers, and there is alot less general "creepiness" in wandering around the desert (though that may just be me). The game, in all fairness, also doesn´t try to be a horror game, unless you count the psychological "threat to your very existence, a doppelgänger overtaking your life" angle. In that regard, your occasional encounters with Mr. Scratch are fun, he´s quite a cool and fun, if decidedly hammy, villain, but there´s unfortunately no fight against him, or any boss fight at all, for that matter, which feels like a wasted opportunity, given the more arcade-y gameplay.
Once you´re done with the campaign, there´s also an Arcade Mode, in which you have to survive a certain amount of time on various maps while fending off enemies, raising your combo meter (by killing enemies and evading their attacks) and getting enough points to earn stars and unlock new and more difficult maps. Its quite fun (and more difficult than the main campaign ever gets), but probably not something that you will play for more than a few hours.
Overall, I personally would recommend American Nightmare, especially if it´s at a discount. If you liked Alan Wake overall, but disliked its gameplay, you will probably like it. If you didn´t like Alan Wake or aren´t interested in the franchise at all, I would still say that you should check it out, but the game will probably not change your overall opinion on the series.

Hello,
Rating this game out of 5 stars. I will point out each pro and con to this game as I have played every class up to this point, Node wars, as well as the PVE and story quest line.
Overall this game eats up more time then its worth putting into for those that lead jobs that working eight to ten hour days. The skill gap for a player to catch up in late game is extravagent to the point a player is willing to set down the game and move on. Having playing BDO for some time learning the enhancement process, grinding value of items and money, as well as fishing or other oppurtunities to grab scrolls to repair armor, the amount it takes to go from a +15 article of gear to PRI is on the verge of 3 to 4 hours of straight gameplay and grinding. Noteing that this is just the basic tier of gear. This is a con of the game- Gearing- more time is spent gearing at end game then it is actually enjoying the other end game features of this game. If you love spending hours upon hours of upgrading gear along with the extravagant cost it takes.
A Pro to the game- Combat system, easily learned and easy to get to define combo's no matter the class. A few hours grinding as you level will give you a better understanding as well as simply reading the abilities that come with the class. Its fluid and its not a tab target/ lock on target system.
A Con to the game- Class Balance, classes are not easily balanced as some do out shine others in small scale fights or one vs ones. Though this game is more for large scale combat, more one vs ones take place then the more notable node wars that come with the GvG territory. This area needs a ton of work though it is hard to balance large scale pvp with smaller scale pvp.
A Pro to the game- GvG Node wars. It is a fresh take on MMO Large scale open world pvp, massive scale battles that require each class and skilled person to think to over take or defend a node. Its the greatest experience one has to offer, but its good to be geared or tag along with a geared group for these. Enjoyable all around.
A pro to the game- Energy and node system. Being able to invest in the area you grind in to increase drop rate is an excellent Ideal in the game. The higher the node level is, the higher rate things drop including the lower rate items such as weapon stones or yellow border items. Though which requires energy to invest in, all things come at a cost right? Energy is used in about every thing, think about using energy to gather, it is an external resource that lets you gather for crafting or, guessed it, invest in the nodes to increase the level of the node, Now a con in the energy is that you must explore, read, gather knowledge of npc's and monsters to gain energy, but on the bright side energy level is the same across all characters.
Another Con in the game is contribution points, it is another form of way to crafting as well as buying housing or extra slots for storage in the city you are currently in or like to stay in whether its the far west or the far east. The only way to get them is log in daily click the reward button level for one hour or simply do quest daily or start new characters and do the story line. It is time consuming and virtually not worth the grind to get every single house in every town, however you do need them to connect nodes, to other towns.
Warehouse system- A con, they are not shared through each town that you visit if you put your stuff that you need far east and need it far west, you have to travel all the way back east, then pick it up or ship it as you head all the way back west, it would be great if storage was centralized and shared across all towns, howver storage does allow you to store currency and is shared across family.
Lore is a con- especially for RPers a lot is left to the imagination and what goes on in the realm of BDO, its to conflicting in many patterns and allows for many things to take place that really shouldn't, though from that angle many can see it as a plus in this aspect, this is a take it as you see it or leave it matter and most likely only effects those that tend to Role Play in MMO's.
Story Quest line can be a pro and a con- it is quick and leveling is extremely fast till you hit the mid fourties, simply only doing the story quest line leaves you in the proper area with your level as long as you save the side quest for later, However it doesn't offer too much of a story and the replay value of it is literally none. One would be better off reading a fantasy book that has more detail per page then the entire BDO main quest line.
If I had to overall rate this game in a system of 1 to 5 with 5 being the best, factoring in all things, I would rate this a 3.5 out of 5.

Having grown somewhat disenchanted with the current RPG market options, I was hesitant to purchase anything new, but Grim Dawn has succeeded wonderfully in recapturing some of the greatness of ARPG's of old.
Calling it the spiritual successor of D2 does an injustice to both D2 and Grim Dawn, but I can certainly see why the comparison has been made. Grim Dawn carves its own path into the genre with a beautiful and expansive world to explore, and a very well-defined sense of its own artistic aesthetic direction.
There is a ton of class, skill, stat, and item augmentation options to choose from to satisfy even the most veteran of Diablo 2 fans. If all of this wasn't enough, the writing team has done a great job putting out some of the best writing in the genre in recent memory. Good writing is hard to come by in gaming these days. I actually really enjoyed reading the notes and scribbles found throughout the game - something I rarely do for want of interest.
If Crate can manage to remain grounded and fill in the void where Activision-Blizzard is currently lacking, all of us old school RPG'ers might be in for many years of great gaming to come.
Take note, Crate: You've got a great team across the board, and your pricing is excellent. Don't let yourselves fall by the wayside once greater success comes.

So, Poker Night At The Inventory, the game where you play Texas Hold'em with a rabbit, 2 out-of-the-ordinary people, and... whatever the hell Strong Bad is
Seriously though, this game is amazing, I absolutely love it.
I assume the majority of us got this game for the tf2 items. If you are one of those people, or you're a fan of Sam & Max,  Homestar Runner, the Penny Arcade webcomics, or a poker player in general, I'd recommend this game to you in a heartbeat.
The story is as simple as who you play as: you are known as "The Player", a silent poker player who's arrived at the inventory to play poker with 4 other fellows. The Inventory is a secret poker place hidden from society in case those "in charge" decide to essentially ban Poker for a second time.
There you have it, that's the story: Nothing more, nothing less is known about you; the rest is playing some number of games of Texas Hold'em with the Heavy (tf2), Sam (Sam & Max), Strong Bad (Homestar Runner), and Tycho (Penny Arcade webcomics) for stakes of $10k.
Now onto the aspects of the game:
Graphics [9/10] - The graphics are their own personality, likewise the characters' models match their respective traits
Assets [7.8/10] - I run a fairly average computer with a lot of memory left, yet I run at somewhere between 30-40 fps ingame
AI [9.8/10] - The ai of the game is, I feel, unbelievably realistic
Soundtrack [10/10] - The soundtrack is stupendous, I love it: I listen to this whenever I need think music playing
Atmosphere [10/10] - Between the soundtrack, the dialouge from the characters, the game looks and feels amazing and almost believable to be sitting down playing poker with these characters
Overall score [8.7/10] - The big killer for me was the fact that the second game runs much more smoother, despite having more stuff going on: other than that, this game would've gottten a 9.6/10

FTL: Faster Than Light is a top-down, real time strategy video game created by indie developers Subset Games. In the game, the player controls the crew of a single spacecraft, holding critical information to be delivered to an allied fleet several sectors away, while being pursued by a large rebel fleet.
The player must guide the spacecraft over a number of sectors, each with planetary systems and events procedurally generated in a roguelike fashion, while facing against rebel and other hostile forces, recruiting new crew, and outfitting and upgrading their ship. Combat takes place in pausable real time, and if the ship is destroyed or the crew lost, the game ends in permadeath, requiring the player to restart.

-Deadlyness of weapons: Can you imagine a machine gun shooting at a group of infantry right in front of it, in the open, and not killing any of them for 10 minutes? Hell, this game helps you out. TY 2 is significantly different from its predecessor, but is still a fun game in its own right.  However, it's not perfect either.  I only encountered 2 somewhat major issues with the game.
Firstly, in the main game, I saw and talked to someone in a sewer area, and while in this area, the echo effect applied to the voices was a bit overkill making it hard to understand what the character was saying, especially without subtitles, and this effect stuck around for a bit even after I had exited the sewer into the outside world!
Secondly, the Cart Racing game. While I find it an interesting distraction from the main game, the controls could definitely use some work, especially when powersliding.
In fact, in the game's current state, the powerslide is not only cumbersome, but unnecessary, as when you turn your vehicle normally, you don't appear to lose any speed as in other Kart Racers such as Mario Kart or CTR.
And when you do powerslide, the angle you turn at is practically 90 degrees, almost invariably sending you into the wall.
Still, the rest of what I played of the game has me very excited for the full release!  For more of my thoughts, please check out my "Work In Progress..." episode on the game!

Pros: The atmosphere is still just delicious. There are still some memorable setpiece levels, particularly the remote observatory. They've brought back some of the original Alan Wake enemy types and added some interesting new ones, fixing one of the biggest weaknesses of the original game (lack of variety in enemies). The basics of combat are the same, but again they've thrown in a few new weaponry options. Overall the gameplay is a slightly more arcade-y than the first game, which I didn't think I would like. Indeed, the run-and-gun nature would have been terrible in the first game because that game was setting up a tense, scary mystery. Here, with a bit more fast and slapdash story, the casual firefights make more sense. Finally, I thought that the climax was pretty good both gameplay and story wise.
Cons: The writers play fast and loose with the story, frenetically bouncing back and forth between dumping huge amounts of exposition and explaining nothing at all. The extent of the powers possessed by both the protagonist and villain is pretty unclear. Spoiler alert: the game's main portion is spent in a time loop, playing the same levels three times with only minimal differences in the gameplay. The only interesting feature of this time loop is that some characters have memories of the last loop, and thus know what's coming - this is semi-interesting but the general idea was probably done better with the future-dated novel pages in the original. For a short game, it sure made itself old news fast by replaying the same sections of the game. It's also pretty damning that after playing the same storyline three times, it still didn't really stick with me. When I think of this game in five years, I'll remember the setpieces and level design, which like I said, are great. I won't be remembering a damn thing about the game's story because I'm not sure it was written to be remembered, just to create an excuse for a more arcade-y game starring Alan Wake. On gameplay, the amount of guns has increased, but the amount of creative uses of light is down a bit, which is a shame, because how damn fun was that rock and roll stage? An arcade mode with challenges was added, which I played briefly but it didn't really hook me in. Not that the combat wasn't fun, but without the story, I didn't see much point in just playing Alan Wake combat without an Alan Wake story. Your mileage may very on that. If you like that challenge-map type of add-on I don't think this is a particularly bad one, the challenge-map games just aren't my thing.
Conclusion: If you're on an Alan Wake kick, this isn't at all a bad or offensive game. But in comparison to its predecessor, most of the things that made Alan Wake brilliant are gone, replaced with a thrown-together, repetitive script and an arcade mode. My thumbs down is a gentle one, because there's a lot of redeeming qualities, but I would recommend just skipping it unless you got it free with the first game.

Dying Light is a great game. It's one of the best open world zombie games that's built on this fantastic parkour system and a big variety of weapons to slaughter the undead. It's fun, intense, and even a bit scary at times (especially if you're a new player).
There's many positives to this game. The two vast open areas of the Slums and Old Town are detailed and has a lot of exploration in them. It's fun to run around these areas with the fantastic parkour system. The parkour in this game is easy to pick up, and it makes this game unique compared to other open world zombie games. There's 4 player co-op so you can bring a bunch of your buddies along with you. There's plenty of main missions and side missions, and some agility and power challanges to participate in, and they're all playable in co-op! There's many weapons to choose from with many blueprints and upgrades to make them more badass. There's a leveling system where you gain XP for doing just about anything, so you always have a sense of progression, and your character always feels like he's getting stronger. Speaking of your character, there's a decent amount of outfits to decorate him with. There's a dynamic day and night cycle, and nighttime makes this game much more intense compared to day. Sometimes, I prefer to play at nighttime. The graphics are great, supporting NVIDIA HBAO+ and Depth of Field, and it looks great. I can pull off a consistant 60 FPS on my 960 4GB on High settings but with no View Distance. Lastly, there's official mod support. Yes, OFFICIAL. There's a Steam workshop to download a bunch of custom maps from, and you can go on the
to find a decent amount of mods to install, although it's a bit weird how you install mods. It took me awhile to figure it out. You can even run mods on co-op if your buddies have the same exact mods you have, and mods don't disable achievements (like some other AAA games).
The characters are pretty weak. Rais feels like a bad knockoff of
's Vaas, and everyone else is pretty lame. You never care that much about your teammates. Me and my pal would skip all the cutscenes pretty quickly because they can sometimes be pretty boring. The story on paper isn't actually that bad, but it's executed poorly through the weak characters. I have one minor negative with the parkour system, and its how you can't wall run. I think the parkour would've been pretty fluid if you could wall run. Nighttime is WAY too short. I think I heard it's like 7 minutes long compared to around 60 minutes in the daytime. It's ridiculous, as the nighttime is awesome! I run a
that tweaks a bunch of things, including making nighttime the same amount of time as daytime, so it's not that big of a deal for me, although it was on Xbox One.
Dying Light is one of my favorite games of all time, next to Skyrim. It stands strong along with other great AAA titles because of its gameplay and parkour, and it's a worthy title to have in your library.
