Alan Wake's American Nightmare has the same mechanics as the previous Alan Wake title, but almost everything else has changed for this one. (The game takes place in an episode of Night Springs written by Alan Wake)
First of all, the game is way easier and provides you ammo refills every 100m so you never really need to conserve ammo, except maybe at the end of the game. The spooky aspect is gone all together, making the game more action oriented, with ALOT of combat. The game is basically the same campaign 3 times (because you're in a time loop) but it manages to mix it up somewhat, even though it gets repetitive. The dialogue is less appealing than in the original and sometimes the character models of the NPC's you meet are really ugly. Lastly, the flashlight is now godly: it recharges almost instantly and you barely ever have to pop in other batteries.
In conclusion, I would recommend this game if you really want to play everything from the Alan Wake series. The game stands fine on it's own, but with the weight of the first one, American Nightmare delivered something completely different, which isn't necessarily a bad thing. I would say it's a good game, but not a very good Alan Wake game.

Alright, so this review might be a little biased due to the fact that I loved Alan Wake and am currently foaming at the mouth because of the new emergence of details on there possibly being an Alan Wake 2 in development very soon. However, I'll try to keep it fair.
If you have never played Alan Wake, you will most likely quit this game after 5 minutes, then come back and fall in love with it. That's what happened to me with the first Alan Wake game. However, there are some notable differences between American Nightmare and the first Alan Wake. For instance, you will never struggle to find ammo or batteries for your flashlight in this game. And if you do, you're doing it wrong. Remedy set out to make this short semi-sequel of Alan Wake with more of an arcade feeling than the previous game. Also, the entire campaign takes place in an episode of an in-game fictional TV show called Night Springs, which is playing on a TV in a hotel room that Alan's friend Barry is asleep in. This is unlike Alan Wake because Alan Wake had 5 "episodes" of gameplay if I remember correctly. Also, there was no true narrator in Alan Wake. There is in this game, and the narrator even gives Alan a cool nickname: The Champion of Light. And Alan's alternate, dark personality, Mr. Scratch, is coined as the Herald of Darkness. Basically, the entire goal of the campaign is to stop Mr. Scratch from turning the world into the dark place he wants it to be. His ultimate goal is to stop the sun from ever rising again. As the champion of light, you set out on a mission against the dark side of yourself to ensure that the sun indeed does rise and the world can be restored to its natural self.
The gameplay mimics the exact same style of action as the first Alan Wake. You are Alan, a horror-crime genre writer, armed with a flashlight, and any guns, flares, and flashbang grenades you can find. When you encounter a Taken individual (the poor souls taken by the darkness of Mr. Scratch), you have to rid them of the darkness before you can deal any true damage to them. This is done by focusing your flashlight on them, throwing a flash grenade at them, or putting a flare down/waiting for the unfocused ray of your flashlight to break the darkness. The game is filled with many jumpscares, much like the original Alan Wake. You may find yourself looking over your own shoulder in real life after you turn around in game and there's a lumberjack with a sickle stalking you from two feet behind. When in doubt, throw whatever throwable item you have equipped; it will solve a lot of problems in your life. The plot twists within the story are also very interesting. I won't spoil anything of course, but let's just say you'll find yourself in the same place more than once.
I absolutely recommend this game to everyone, but especially to people who have played Alan Wake or just want to try something different from the meta of the modern video game industry. This game features a lot of the concepts that were supposed to be/will be in Alan Wake 2 (incase anyone other than me is excited about that). I give it a 9/10, but only because it honestly is not challenging if you have played the original Alan Wake. I might have died 2-3 times in 7 hours of gameplay with completion of the story. You should also check out the arcade game mode if you actually enjoy the different combat style that this game features, like me. Buy it and play it. But don't be surprised if you beat the story in 5 hours.

TL;DR: Not recommended, Telltale get your♥♥♥♥♥♥together.
I don't actually have a problem with games that don't feature any relevant gameplay, as long as they have a redeeming quality. In the case of these visual novel-likes that quality is usually that the player can make choices that affect the story in some way. Now Telltale has never really been known for meaningful choices, even though they like to pretend that is the case. This game however is honestly the pinnacle of laziness.
Virtually none of your choices matter in any way. Dialogue options very often play out the exact same way, no matter of what you chose. You can be truthful in a particular situation but the character you were talking to will still react as if you lied to them, just because the devs apparently couldn't be bothered to record some additional lines for the situation. Same goes for the "big" choices. You can choose to do something and well, that's the way it will turn out. Then you can try out the other option and choose NOT to do the same thing and well... too bad, because it will happen exactly the same way regardless. Sure, Telltale never actually made it so that you could REALLY change the story and have fundamentally different paths but at least in earlier games like TWD choices would at least somewhat affect the story for an episode or two.
Actually exploring different paths in this game is a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥as well, as it doesn't let you skip scenes and only has checkpoints for rewind about every 30-40 minutes, which aren't even tied to the different characters' segments.
The writing is also rather lazy. They tried very hard to appeal to fans of the television series by just showing them things they already knew. Be it by having as many actual characters from the show as they could get in the game or by pretty much exactly mirroring the Stark family with the main "cast" of the game.
Always wanted to experience John Snow's story for yourself? Well, you can now, with this brand new proxy character who fulfills exactly the same function and meets the exact same people! Ever wanted to be Sansa? We have one for that too! ...
That being said, the game still has some moderately enjoyable, if not terribly original, characters and moments.
I can't really say that I'm not getting
enjoyment out of it and there's still something mildly appealing about seeing the same story play out with a couple of different touches (e.g. a character being snarky rather than broody or a♥♥♥♥♥♥rather than the nicest guy at the wall). Still, I would not recommend buying this, or any future Telltale titles for that matter, as it only encourages their incredibly lazy approach to making games these days. If you have to, buy it on sale.

Rebirth 2 exceeds in it's more serious story and it's characters, but falls apart in everything else.
The gameplay in battle is relatively the same from the first game, the only differnce is the additon of a fourth party member. Honestly, they didn't really need to change the battle system up too much, it's still as fun and enjoyable as it was in the first game. One problem that was apparent in Rebirth 1 was it's tiring grinding, unfortunately Rebirth 2 has this same problem, but somehow makes it even worse. It's very noticable when your trying to go after the different endings in the game which have their own specfic requirements, it just ends up repeating quest in the Guild, over, over, over, and over again. It's at its absolute worst when your trying to 100% this game *COUGH COUGH* 100 Million Credits achivement. *COUGH COUGH* May I also add, that in order to 100% this game your going to have to replay through the main story mutiuple times, like 5 or 7 times to be exact...Trust me, you will get sick of this game if you play through it back to back, so I recommend you take small breaks. New to this game is the addition of Stella's Dungeon, a real time RPG minigame, where you send Stella to explore a dungeon in real time and find items that can help you on your adventure. Sounds cool right? Well... it just ends up with you praying to RNG Jesus for Stella to make it out of the dungeon alive, since you don't have any control over what she does, i'll admit it's a pretty cool concept, but it can definitley use some more work, I would of liked it if you have more control over what Stella brings into the dungeon, because solely relying on pure luck is just stupid.
One of Rebirth 2's strengths is in its incredible story! If you didn't like how Rebirth 1's story was not taken seriously, then have no fear since Rebirth 2's story is more serious, with a few jokes sprinkled throughout of course! Instead of following the CPU of Planeptune, Neptune. You follow her younger sister Nepgear, as she journeys throughout Gamindustry to save the other CPUs, while stopping the notorious ASIC group from making people lose faith in the CPUs. There are 4 endings this time around, all of them are pretty entertaining to watch, but the one that gets the most attention is the Conquest ending, and it's definitely worth getting if your craving for dark and emotional ending, trust me, the Conquest ending changes a man...
One of Hyperdimension's greatest strengths is its characters, every character in my eyes, has a distinct personality and great character design that make their personality pop even more, aside from RED, every side character has a purpose to join you on your adventure! (I mean seriously RED just comes out of fricken nowhere!)
Overall, Rebirth 2 is still a pretty great game despite it's flaws, but from the amount of grinding and the amount of times you have to beat the game in order to get everything, this game can get tiring really fast, something that never occured when playing through Rebirth 1. If you enjoyed Rebirth 1, you'll have a good time with this game no doubt, but for people that are new to the series, this a good starting point to the series, since Rebirth 2 does a nice job introducing new poeple to its own world. Plus Rebirth 1's story is not really cannon, so techinally the story starts here.

I thoroughly enjoyed this season of Game of Thrones because of how Game of Thrones it felt.  What makes it even better is that all the TV show characters are actually voiced by the actors and actresses who play them (might seem obvious but I was surprised that it was just sound-alike actors filling in).  The story is very believable in the realm of the TV show, taking place during some key events during the end of Season 3 and the beginning of Season 4.  As an avid fan of the show it was fun to see other points of view for these events.
There are lots of arguments that your choices don't matter in these games...and they're pretty true.  The story is pretty much set in stone as to how it will play out.  Your choices might make minor changes to the details of how things went down, but history has already been written as it was.  This game seems to be worse than other Telltale games, but I enjoyed it just the same.  What is important about the choices you make is how it shapes your interaction with the characters and the world.  By choosing a different interaction from the next person, your playthrough of the game is just that much different.  It's the details that make this game what it is.
Overall the game is a lot of fun.  Your choices might not matter much in regards to the story, but that story is very enjoyable - especially when it reminds you that this is a Game of Thrones story where there's no such thing as actually winning in any scenario.  It's also a unique perspective from what were given in the show in that you get to see the world from the perspective of a house that's really not that important in comparison to the ones we're used to dealing with.

Game Of Thrones Telltale is a six episodic season that focuses on the newly introduced Westeros faction called House Forrester and whats happens to the house after the events of the Red Wedding. During the playthrough you will play as many as five characters that are related to House Forrester. Along your journey you will encounter GOT characters from the T.V show that you will interact with (Which is Fun To See The Game and T.V Show Intertwine With One Another).
Game Of Thrones: Telltale is an (sort of linear) heart wrenching story that was created more for GOT fans than Telltale fans. The quicktime events are okay and the art style/graphics are acceptable at best. If you enjoy the Game of Thrones T.V show, I recommend this game. But if you do not watch the show and just like Telltale games in general, I must warn that that more of your decisions in the game (Compared to other Telltale Games) do not really matter and that the game actually sort of reflects the decisions made in the T.V show itself.  But the story and characters are still interesting enough to keep you playing until the very end. But don't expect a great ending that will give you all of the story's answers. I enjoyed the journey through Westeros and I honestly cannot wait for season two.
GOT Fans: 7.5/10
Just Telltale Fans: 6.5/10

If you are a fan of the Game of Thrones series or a veteran of Telltale, then this game is sure to disappoint.
Never before in a Telltale game have I felt that my decisions and strategies mattered so little, no matter what you do, "kill X over Y," "send A over B" the same conclusion is reached. This game desperately wants to be a sprawling tree of alternate stories but at the same time is confined to a protective stake, forcing it back into the shape the writers intended it to be. This extremely on-rails game is only made worse by the sporadic plot holes and alternating personalities of the characters between episodes, most likely due to the writers changing their minds in between episodes (this is why you finish a game before you release it, especially one like this).
These issues only became worse and worse as the game progressed with the first three episodes mostly covering all of their bases and allowing to some degree, meaningful decisions that deeply impacted the story while the final three episodes were just absolute messes. Characters disappear for entire episodes for absolutely no reason (and don't give me that "oh, they're just not important to the story in that episode" bs) or just disappear entirely, major plot points in early episodes end up not mattering at all, alliances are completely ignored, countless loose ends with that finale, and so much more.
Edit: Almost forgot, plot armor is everywhere until the final episode where like half of the characters loose it, many for no reason (why did you sacrifice yourself? Q would have been fine, all you did was die to provide a motive for their upcoming act which is something the writers should have been building up to, not waiting until the last minute [sorry, this game made me really mad in some places]).
All in all, I recommend just playing this game once without worrying about consequences or politics or whatever, rewind if you'd like if you regret a decision but really it doesn't matter, the same outcome is likely to be reached. Episodes 1-3 are all a 6/10, episodes 4-6 are a 4/10, 4/10, and 3/10, respectively.

Almost two years later(?) of the release of this, additional factions and campaigns, and a few patches, this has gotten better. Other than that I probably wouldnt play this at all. I hope they make more mods to make the game more interesting than what it is. If I could mod games, I would mod this into CoH 1 version 2.
So to sum it up, I recommend this game because it does have mod support, and it is CoH (fanboy til the end). But man, I wish they could have done without all the watered down DLC. Major turn off for me.

The original UFO - Enemy Unknown has been voted to be the best game in history, in many occasions. This lacks maybe a hundred things we still had in the 90'ies, but still manages to be an addictive and enjoyable game. I'd recommend it, especially for the new players, who won't miss being able to:
-Send aircraft anywhere, anytime, just in case or when suspecting alien activity
-Manually track down a UFO that was lost from radar
-Send multiple craft pursuing one UFO
-Send Skyranger to follow an UFO too big to shoot down, and attack it if it lands
-Shoot UFOs into the water to avoid taking care of the mess
-Building bases where ever you want, even on poles
-Buying ten rocket launchers and giving them to ten troops. Then leveling everything. Civs, too
-Equipping everyone with 2 pistols, or any other stupid thing that you could ever imagine
-Ordering troops to open fire on a building you suspect having enemies in, then finding some corpses
-Carrying a stunned Chryssalid to the evac zone, fearing it's gonna wake up and kill you all in one turn
-Throwing a gun or magazine to a friendly who's all out
-Dropping all your weapons because you know this guy's going under alien control in no time
-Missing a shot, accientally hitting something else in the process
-With above, killing 3 enemies with one burst, of which only one you knew of

-Miss with a grenade, landing it next to a friendly

-Get smoked so bad your troops pass out. Same for aliens
-Having more attributes, like throwing accuracy and strength
Let's see if the X-COM 2 delivers anything from this list of awesomeness. UFO - Enemy Unknown continues to be the best game ever, for the shame of 20 years of game industry.

Gameplay is similar to the last Far Cry, consisting of several more or less interesting kill/escort etc. sidequests, decent main story (as far as stoneage goes), and the whole leveling skills and all that. If you liked that, you will enjoy this. Though not if you miss guns. I know I don't.
You're some sort of beastmaster/stone age hero tasked with rebuilding a tribe (including the village), and helping them against two other tribes. One tribe consists of warmongering cannibals, and the other of psychopatic pyromaniacs. Your weapons include one and two-handed clubs, spears, bows, slings and some situational items. You can tame about a dozen beasts with varying strength/speed/stealth stats and have one of them accompany you permanently (switch anytime). With the right skill you can mount some of them. Then there's a huge owl you can use for reconnaisance and the occasional kill.
The plant/stone gathering is still part of the game, and necessary to upgrade your items, as well as the different village huts. Night does bring out wolf packs and other predators, so be cautious. Lastly you can ignite most weapons and use them as light source, or to ignite the environment, animals and unpleasant fellows.
There are various difficulties and game modes, including one "deadlier nights"-mode and a hardcore mode (you die - game over).
TL;DR:
Far Cry in the Stone Age. Tame and ride wild beasts. FIRE. And cannibals.

I've come to learn that "full controller support" means "full support for certain controllers". In my case, my no-name brand USB controller worked for 80-90% of the game, but the game would require me to use the mouse instead of the right analog stick for anything that required aiming. And using the mouse would make the game think I switch to mouse and keyboard controls, so it'd tell me to mash the Q key when I should mash the A button. This was a constant issue, and any combat sequence required me to be prepared to switch my right hand from the buttons to the mouse at a moment's notice.
Even if I had played without a controller, or a fully supported controller, there is no fun to be had with the quicktime events. You have one button to push or mash, one prompt at a time to deal with. You have no combat options. This might be a Telltale standard, but 1) how is it any fun when you have no control over the outcome? and 2) the way the game makes you replay the scenes if you failed the QTE is contradictory to the core idea of your choices mattering. Why should my physical actions be outside of my agency and not have any consequences? Frankly, the game would be more fun if it were just dialog options. No walking around "exploring", no quicktime events, just dialog choices.
The story is the reason you should be interested in the game, and also the reason you should dismiss it. I overlooked two things when I bought this blindly:
1) This series of 6 episodes is not a stand-alone title. A sequel is being made. This means that there is no conclusion to the story. Just a vague sequel hook.
2) As tied in to the show as this game is in terms of visuals, music and voice acting, the game focuses only on its own made up characters. This would have been fine if they had introduced some concepts or lore from the books, or any minor characters that weren't in the show. But they don't, and the game feels completely disconnected from the Game of Thrones universe.
If you're still curious about it, read synopses on the Game of Thrones wiki. It's faster, doesn't have annoying QTEs, and it won't fool you with false promises of choices that matter.

As has become the norm for Telltale, Game of Thrones is another superb narrative, fueled by very difficult decisions.
One thing will become painfully, brutally clear the moment you start playing: this is NOT a power fantasy. I'm under the impression many people come to the game expecting one, and are sorely disappointed. Even by Telltale standards, the choices you'll face in Game of Thrones are absolutely gut-wrenching. By playing this game, you'll most likely learn something new about yourself, about how you react under pressure, about what you truly value when push comes to shove, about the prices you're willing to pay. And I am very glad that Telltale had the boldness to craft an experience like this, one that to the best of my knowledge no other developer has taken a risk on.
A few players take issue with the fact that - with few exceptions - your choices don't seem to alter the general structure of the story, but they thoroughly change the flavor and characterization of everything. Even fully understanding how it all works under the hood, I was never under the impression they were meaningless, very far from that.
Lastly, if you're wondering how faithful the game is to the franchise, I'd say very. This is Game of Thrones through and through, both in general feel, as well as the finer details.

If you buy this game, I have just one recommendation: under no circumstances, replay anything or look anything else up about it on the Internet. Do a single run through, never change your decisions and you'll feel like you had an amazing Games of Thrones experience. If I had done that, I'd probably be recommending this... at least for the sale price I bought it for.
I'll keep this as spoiler free as possible: the main shortfall is that your choices do not really matter much. Play it smart, play it stupid, play it silent - it ultimately doesn't matter. The people the story needs dead are still going to die. Yes, some details can be different, but the story itself won't change at all. And if the story isn't going to change, the only real say you get is on minor details that can be sacrificed without compromising where the story is going. Certain characters are doomed to die and some of their deaths are shocking (as you would expect from any Game of Thrones experience), but when you find out there's no better way you can play, no different plot arch you can take that can save the character, it cheapens the main selling point of this game.
You can't really influence the game or choose how it ends when the only things that are influenced are minor details. I wound up spending 12 or so hours to be able to choose between only 2 endings for your characters - both of which are usually a choice between horrible or just merely unrewarding.
Overall, if it goes on sale for under $10 again and you're a big Game of Thrones fan, pick it up - you won't have buyers remorse. If you are looking for a true choose your own adventure kinda experience and hope your decisions can truly shape the future of a Westeros House - look elsewhere. House Forrester's fate and nearly all its members are pre-determined.

Let me preface this review with the fact that this is my first serious review for a video game. I also want to mention that I am no stranger to dungeon-crawling games such as Grim Dawn, but I do tend to have my interest in these games fizzle toward the middle of Act 2.
Grim Dawn is an interesting case for me. On one hand, it has a skill tree that is probably the most intuitive and easy to mess with tree I've ever used. On the other hand, the game is bogged down by dissatisfying combat, especially where animations are concerned, an uninteresting story, and a bland, dark, dime-a-dozen post-apocalyptic fantasy/steampunk world.
I can feel the love and passion of the devs as I play this game, especially when it comes to character building, and I really think that this is one of the few true successes that have recently come out of early access, but I can't bring myself to like this game as much as i want to. Every new character I start, I can barely get past act 1, and afterword, I just get bored and want to fiddle with a new combination.
Do I recommend this game? Absolutely. Maybe you'll see something in it that I don't, and have a grand old time with it. I want this game to succeed, if only to see more projects and games of this genre pop up, because this is a truly lacking medium.
Please give this game a buy. The skill tree alone is reason enough to play it, and maybe you'll fall in love with the world along the way.

I normally play RTS games to comp stomp, one reason being that I know I'm not as amazing as the majority of players, so I like to fight the computers.
The main problem with comp-stomping on this game, is the fact that even on easy difficulty, they're so difficult it's not even fun, ever.
Now, I'm not going to say to make the AI like Command & Conquer easy, where the enemy turtles with the first five buildings available in the game, and probably send the weakest unit in a pitiful attempt to kill you once in a while, because that isn't fun, I agree.
But when you make it so damn difficult to beat an AI even on Easy and Standard, all the fun is completely drained, and you find yourself questioning why you wasted £15 or more on this game.
Coupled with the fact you have to pay for commanders, which most of which have the same skills multiple times, it's not like they're all unique ways of playing, makes me wonder, why couldn't of they just stuck with giving each side one of 3 preset command strategies?
I mean, seriously, what's the deal with that...?
THEN, to add insult to injury, they've gone and made the entire game just domination from most FPS's, let me state that I hate domination, I've always been a, 'it's not over till you've destroyed their last unit' kind of guy.  So, the fact I don't even have an option to do that, unless I make a friends only custom match just upsets me even more...
It's a shame really, because I enjoyed the first game, I also loved the way the British played differently to the other factions.  It completely fitted the way I played the game, with movable bases to help push forward where ever it was safe.  That's all gone, no way whatsoever of playing like that...
Also, the really good wave defence co-op mode from the first isn't here, which, if they had that, I would probably recommend this game, because I love to defend rather than go offensive.
It's a shame really, the game looked so promising, and Relic just failed to deliver what I, and probably quite a few of the playerbase wanted.
Just to clarify, if you're into the PvP part of the game, I can't comment on that, it's not really the part of the game I enjoy, I'm basing this being a casual RTS'er, who wants to waste a bit of time fighting a challenging AI, than to struggle and get frustrated everytime he plays.

Dying Light is a great game. It's one of the best open world zombie games that's built on this fantastic parkour system and a big variety of weapons to slaughter the undead. It's fun, intense, and even a bit scary at times (especially if you're a new player).
There's many positives to this game. The two vast open areas of the Slums and Old Town are detailed and has a lot of exploration in them. It's fun to run around these areas with the fantastic parkour system. The parkour in this game is easy to pick up, and it makes this game unique compared to other open world zombie games. There's 4 player co-op so you can bring a bunch of your buddies along with you. There's plenty of main missions and side missions, and some agility and power challanges to participate in, and they're all playable in co-op! There's many weapons to choose from with many blueprints and upgrades to make them more badass. There's a leveling system where you gain XP for doing just about anything, so you always have a sense of progression, and your character always feels like he's getting stronger. Speaking of your character, there's a decent amount of outfits to decorate him with. There's a dynamic day and night cycle, and nighttime makes this game much more intense compared to day. Sometimes, I prefer to play at nighttime. The graphics are great, supporting NVIDIA HBAO+ and Depth of Field, and it looks great. I can pull off a consistant 60 FPS on my 960 4GB on High settings but with no View Distance. Lastly, there's official mod support. Yes, OFFICIAL. There's a Steam workshop to download a bunch of custom maps from, and you can go on the
to find a decent amount of mods to install, although it's a bit weird how you install mods. It took me awhile to figure it out. You can even run mods on co-op if your buddies have the same exact mods you have, and mods don't disable achievements (like some other AAA games).
The characters are pretty weak. Rais feels like a bad knockoff of
's Vaas, and everyone else is pretty lame. You never care that much about your teammates. Me and my pal would skip all the cutscenes pretty quickly because they can sometimes be pretty boring. The story on paper isn't actually that bad, but it's executed poorly through the weak characters. I have one minor negative with the parkour system, and its how you can't wall run. I think the parkour would've been pretty fluid if you could wall run. Nighttime is WAY too short. I think I heard it's like 7 minutes long compared to around 60 minutes in the daytime. It's ridiculous, as the nighttime is awesome! I run a
that tweaks a bunch of things, including making nighttime the same amount of time as daytime, so it's not that big of a deal for me, although it was on Xbox One.
Dying Light is one of my favorite games of all time, next to Skyrim. It stands strong along with other great AAA titles because of its gameplay and parkour, and it's a worthy title to have in your library.

If you played Dead Island, this game may or may not be for you depending on how you played it. I LOVED Dead Island but I always felt that it was too slow moving. The combat could've been faster, and the movement especially, but I liked the looting, the skill trees, and the enviroments. I was younger so I never paid much attention to the story. But for some reason, this game, it's story, was near perfect to me. The combat was faster, the parkour mechanics are some of the best that I have played (aside from the Mirrors Edge series), and the RPG mechanics felt more organic. I played the main game and was somewhat unsatisfied with the ending, just because it was a cliffhanger, in the sense that there was still more to be done. Most questions were answered so they didn't mess up there. The Following expansion added tons more content and built upon the previous story. I am not one for spoilers so I will leave that to those who decide to actually play the game. But I will say that the choices throughout the expansion are very impactful, and it adds closure to the story, in my opinion. The Following was one of the best pieces of DLC I think i have ever played. I was much more enganged with this game than Techland's previous zombie game, Dead Island. If you are on the edge of buying this game, do not hesitate. It is well worth the money. The amount of content you get is astounding, and it offers lots of replayability, especially with Co-op and The Bozak Horde DLC.

Disclaimer: I have never played another Civ game except of a few minutes of Civ III.
I find Civ V an excelent turn based strategy game where every turn feels crucial and must be given as much importance as the last in order to come on top of your opponents, be it the AI or other players.
You do not need experience in other Civ games to understand how to play it but if you did not have experience with other turn based strategy games then it might be a bit difficult to adapt to the genre with this as your first such game. There is a lot of complexity and mechanics revolving around the gameplay but even if you start a new game without viewing a guide, slowly and steadily you can be learning everything by yourself without even doing the tutorial, speaking of which, it is not that good as it bombards you with a lot of information in the form of walls of texts. Should you have any  enquiry, there are fanbases and wikis available online as well as an in-game wiki.
There is a lot of content in the game, even more so with 'God and Kings' and 'Brave New World' expansion packs. I highly recommend getting the two expansion packs, and if your budget affords it, the dlcs that add new civilisations into the game as well.
You can have great fun while playing with AI controlled civilisations over a span of difficulties and world types and there are a lot of achievements that you can try to unlock. The customisation of worlds is very detailed and thus you can start your first game in an easier difficulty, should you wish. The AI is well refined making offline experience enjoyable.
Multiplayer is the only thing that I, have trouble with. I can play with some friends without any problems, but with others it is impossible as the game will either crash, disconnect or be glitchy in general with units disappearing and stats resetting. If he host, though, can keep a good connection with everyone else indepentantly, then multiplayer with friends should be fine.
All in all, I had, and still have, great fun with this game which once every so often drags me back after a time of break in order to try out a new civilisation in a different setting or start a new multiplayer session with a friend of mine. It is very refined and a must-play if you are really into turn based strategy games.
PS: If you enjoy this game, then your sessions will last for as long as you say that the next turn will be your last turn x)

If you've already played Rebirth 1, you'll notice that the gameplay mechanics are basically the same: grinding, high replay value and reused dungeons from the previous game. I also had massive fps drops everytime the enemy's guard broke, which didn't happen in Rebirth 1 (both played on PC). One new thing they added is Stella's Dungeon, a "waiting" minigame where you send a chibi to look for items in already discovered dungeons while you do other things.
As for the story, the protagonist is not Neptune but Nepgear, but she's somewhat depressive, negative and has a personality complex. The main plot is also darker than one would expect of this series, especially the conquest ending.
Still, it has the Neptunia feeling to it with the addition of a decent story and good gameplay. A bit weak for a Neptunia game but it's a good everyday comedy JRPG visual novel. Take in mind that the events from Rebirth 1 aren't related to this one, so it may be a bit confusing at first, but you'll get the hang of it.

Whether you played the original Half-Life or not, Half-Life 2 is great to play either as a sequel, or even as a jump-in point for the franchise. In all honesty, the first game is good, but it isn't very important, story-wise. I'm sure there are YouTube videos that sum up the plot in a minute, and do so without talking very fast, because it's a short and simple story. Then again, Half-Life 2, though a bit more complex, isn't heavy in the plot department, either.
Half-Life 2 is primarily about going from A to B in a variety of locations that are varied enough to keep things interesting while maintaining a cohesive and atmospheric world, conveying more about the world based on how it looks than what people are actually saying. The developers were clever enough to have each area have slight differences in gameplay, so one area might have you on the run, while the next might be medium-paced fire-fights, and the next might be a vehicular section with a few stop-offs, followed by some dialog and plot progression, and then some creepier, more horror-like gameplay, and so on and so forth.
Even when gunplay becomes on-going at times, you will generally get a new gun or something to make it interesting, or something else will be going on that keeps it fresh. It's a very clever game that persists in quality despite being about 13 years old this year that I'm writing this. The gravity gun has been emulated so many times in other games because it was so popular, and there is a nice variety of firearms, all of which you can carry at the same time, so none of that modern two-weapons-at-a-time-for-realism BS.
The characters aren't many, but the few there are work well enough. Most of them are just okay in my opinion, but Alyx Vance is the best. She's probably my favorite companion in a video game. If there's one I like better, I can't think of him/her/it. She is friendly with a great attitude, and enjoyable facial expressions and dialog.
I found the vehicular sections - especially the driving one - to be pretty enjoyable. It's a rather freeing sensation, and adds some size to the world you're in. Driving along to progress and hopping out of my car to complete tasks I couldn't while in it then hopping back in again allowed me to fulfill my childhood dream of a game taking that aspect I first saw in Blaster Master on the NES and using it in a game that didn't♥♥♥♥♥♥me off.
This is a good and memorable game, and I definitely recommend it. You can probably get it for five bucks on Steam sales by now, and it's well worth that. Don't forget to play Half-Life 2 Episode One and Episode Two if you haven't done so already. They're quite good as well.

This game fixes a lot of the criticisms I had of the first game, but it does have its own problems that may make you want to avoid it. I know it's long, but please, read this review to the end. I DO recommend the game, but with an important caveat.
Positives first: the story writing is leaps and bounds better. While the first game felt like it was just giving the player a tour of Gamindustri, this one feels like an actual struggle against the forces of evil, an actual adventure. There were silly moments and tense moments, stupid moments and clever moments. I was very impressed by the scene in Chapter 5 where (don't worry, this isn't really a spoiler), rather than jump straight into combat, Uni and Brave the Hard first try to talk out their ideological differences. This was incredible! The developers were clearly putting time and energy into these characters' personalities and the dynamic between them. They were adding depth where the first game wouldn't have.
That said, it's not perfect. Underling's motivations don't make sense in the True Ending, and some of Nepgear's actions (okay, a lot of them) seem inconsistent in the Conquest Ending. Sometimes the tone of the story shifts too drastically, jarring the player. Some villains get too much screentime (cough cough Underling), while others are criminally underused (cough cough Four Felons).
As for other good things about the game, you can now have four party members instead of three. This opens up strategy considerably - for instance, suddenly it doesn't feel like such a waste to have Rom in the party as a dedicated supporter. We get more Coupling and Formation skills than before, encouraging the player to try out new setups. Furthermore, there's a new Plan - Symbol Attack Gains - that, when coupled with Destroy Symbols, makes grinding much easier. More on this later.
Another big complaint about the first game was how gratuitously and shamelessly they reused assets. It still happens in this game, but to a lesser degree. You'll see more unique enemies and more dungeon types. It was very welcome, as I really didn't want to see the same stupid tulip in every other dungeon.
Now for the negatives. This game has nine endings. NINE. One of them is actually just a stub for five of the others, but that still means that to get 100% CG completion, you have to complete - at minimum - eight playthroughs. You can only really start affecting the ending in Chapter 5 (though Chapter 2 can help guide you onto the Conquest/Holy Sword path), so the majority of your time in this game will be spent flying through the first four chapters as fast as you can (my record is two hours). It gets repetitive and boring, and by the third or fourth time, you'll know those chapters like the back of your hand. The pain of being unable to skip cutscenes really shows here. Sure, you can fast-forward, but that still takes too long. Walking through dungeons, waiting for bosses to get within attacking distance, and going through FIVE LEANBOX CUTSCENES IN A ROW is a chore every time, and I found myself wanting to do just about anything else.
But it only gets more agonizing once you reach Chapter 5. Not only are endings affected by Share levels, but they're also affected by Nepgear's Lily Ranks and even what characters you have available. Lily Rank grinding and Share grinding are an absolute nightmare, even with the aforementioned Symbol Attack Gains. Sure, grinding is easier than it used to be, but there's more of it. To make matters worse, some dungeons are exclusive to the True Ending. So if you notice on a later playthrough that you don't have enough Red Blocks to add stronger enemies to Panan Jungle, well, you'll have to either go back to the True Ending (which means another two hours of nonsense) or hope Stella bothers to bring you some in her minigame. Oh, and did I mention that Colosseum enemies drop now items that you can't get anywhere else? At an extremely low rate? Most of which you need multiple copies of for Plans?
Additionally, it's very clear that they put more effort into some endings than into others. The True Ending was exciting and felt like an adventure, while the Normal Ending glosses over what should be shocking and emotional moments and the Conquest Ending is the very definition of wasted potential. (Yes, it was shoddily-written. Don't fall for the hype.)
And now for the big negative, the thing that could have very easily turned this into a negative review: the translation. As an aspiring translator and a fellow human being, I am personally offended that someone, somewhere, looked at this translation and said, "This is professional work and definitely not the worst thing ever conceived by a human mind." I kid you not - and I'm saying this with 100% seriousness - Google Translate would have produced a far superior game than IFI's translator did. I've gone into specific criticisms of the translation in other places, though if you're curious, say the word and I'll launch into my rant on Steam, too. I found the translation unbearable, completely ignoring the text and instead listening to the Japanese voice acting. You'd think that you could just change the interface to Japanese, as the store page has screenshots of that, but you can't - at least, as far as I know. Regardless, English-only players are nowhere near as lucky.
There is, however, a fanmade translation patch, complete with a community guide for installation. I haven't used it, but from the screenshots I've seen, it appears to be a substantial improvement over what IFI gives you - like that's hard to do. If it weren't for the fact that this patch exists, I could not recommend this game to you in good conscience. I would have hit the thumbs-down and torn this game to pieces. Yes, for all the praise I gave the game, the translation is so bad that it outweighs all of it. It consistently misses the spirit of the game and the points the developers were trying to make. If you do decide to get this game - and I think you should - then please do yourself a favor and use the fanmade translation patch. Saints Row IV is an over the top, open world over the shoulder shooter set in a virtual world similar to the Matrix. After quickly becoming the president, aliens take over the planet and lock everyone away in their own virtual world. The city is the same city from Saints Row: The Third, but now since its a virtual world, its always night and everything has neon lights like Far Cry 3: Blood Dragon. It plays the same as previous Saints Row games or any over the shoulder shooter, but with a big new addition, super powers. It might be the same town, but you play it completely different. Why steal a car and drive, when you can run faster than any car and super jump up tall buildings to wall jump even higher. You won't spend time on the streets, but on top of buildings as well. You'll even get magical powers like telekinesis, fireballs and ice to dispatch enemies. These spells replace the throwing items like grenades. Each spell has a cool down, but its infinite.
To start, you're the same character from previous games, which is to say yourself. Your own customized character that I created a drunken 80s rock star with a mustache and a gritty accent. You can even chose Nolan North as a voice. The entire crew from the previous game is back and you'll need to save them from their own virtual Hells. This is where the game pulls from the past history of the franchise and puts a nightmarish spin on them. You'll get to hear some of the franchise's greatest cameos like Neil Patrick Harris and Mila Kunis. Not to mention Kyle David plays himself as the Vice President.
The game walks the line between over the top comedy and action with great gameplay. Comedy games never really hit home for me, but this one managed to strike a chord. The humor isn't like the sexual comedy of Saints Row: The Third. Instead, there's some excellent parody of other games, like a Metal Gear Solid mission, complete with box crawling and shooting 2 lights when 1 bullet would take out a guard. Even movie parodies like a Ghostbusters 2 giant energy drink can fighting a giant statue. The entire game is its own version of the Matrix movie. You get rescued like Neo, into the real world on a spaceship where you're free to hop into the virtual version of Steelport or romance some of your crew. Its all part of the comedy. The licensed 90s music really heightens the experience and really clinches some of the moments. Climbing a rocket headed for space, you'll hear Aerosmith's "I don't wanna miss a thing." Visiting a club full of blow up dolls, you'll hear "Insane in the Membrane" from Cypress Hill.
Its not just visual gags and parody. The dialog is another strong point.  I think that because the characters are less distracting and gimmicky, the dialog stands out that much more. Your crew feels believable, while still making fun of one another and themselves. I felt they're still a big crazy family / street gang / presidential cabinet.
The story missions offer a diverse array of activities. You won't just be fighting and shooting. As an example, you'll first hop in a car to get to a location. Then fight your way through corridors, fly a spaceship, man a turret, walk around in a giant suit of power armor and finally face a boss. The game really keeps it fresh doing things unique for the story missions that you won't find out in the open world.
In the open world there is a lot of side quest fluff that you can complete to control more of the city. Things like street races, assassinations, vehicle theft, super jump accuracy, and a fight club to name a few. You can liberating areas from aliens by taking out three points and then a central point in the middle. You can get more cash by owning businesses around town. Instead of buying these, you participate in puzzle mini games. You get a specific amount of pieces, then place them on a grid of 5x5 and connect the left entry point to the right entry point. Fail and the police come. When you own businesses, the money accumulates and you collect it by going into your phone / PDA. I am happy that you don't have to go to each location to collect the cash.
Since this is an open world game, you'll be doing a lot of the same things over and over again, but in different areas. The game raises the difficulty with each success that you have. You start out facing mere aliens, but then it soon escalates into orbs that shield the aliens, hover bikes and even portals that need to be closed before new waves of enemies come in.
Committing a crime will get the police called on you. There seem to be four tiers of police that come. To get your wanted level to go down, just hide from them until it cools down. The cops aren't the only ones after you. With such super powers, the police felt irrelevant. Fighting dozens of aliens, I'd notice one cop trying to get me. Its just another enemy to face I guess.
For the most part, enemies can be quickly dispatched with guns, melee or magical powers, but the bosses are quite the challenge. These bosses are big agile creatures called agents that have force fields. To disable these shields, you need to use a super power and then shoot them. The shield regenerates of course. Sounds easy doesn't it? Well they adapt quickly, move out of range, leap tall buildings, throw cars and shoot red laser orbs at you. When you're hit, you rag doll, but the game has a recover button that puts you back on your feet again without wasting time. Other bosses do the same and you can fight them across entire city blocks. There are easier bosses in story missions, but those bosses feel more like part of the silliness and not part of the challenge.
The super powers can be upgraded by touching conduits. For the most part, the conduits are blue lights on top of buildings. Some are in walls you need to freeze or in the ground you'll need to pound. Its just an extra thing to collect and the rewards are nice, but its nothing you're forced to do. When you get each super power, the game loads up a training program to properly teach you how to use it. These are pretty basic and quick.
On top of super powers, you have abilities, perks that unlock when you level up from experience. You buy the perks with money and its things like dead pedestrians leave health, 25% more ammo capacity, take less damage from small arms fire and much more. Its all just something to spend your oodles of money on. If that wasn't enough you can visit gun shops to upgrade your arsenal. There are even unique upgrades like explosive pistol ammo and acid bullets. Its all a silly joy to play. Then during the story missions, you find alien weapons like a dub step gun and a bouncing laser.
This is a fun game. Fun to watch, fun to hear, fun to play. The story missions stand out from the rest as enjoyable. While I did get tired of the open world fluff, I'd still stop in the middle of a mission to liberate a part of the city. They were fun diversions, even the puzzles to buy or own the stores could have been their own game. The superpowers made the good gameplay even deeper. I'm shocked that the developer could fit all those powers onto a controller!

Game of Thrones is one of the more weaker Telltale games and only players who have watched up to or past season 3 of the show will benefit from it. One of it's biggest problems is it's pacing as I found myself bored through some segments, more specifically the segments that take place in King's Landing. It's as exciting as watching the Dorne arc in Season 5 of the show as it lacks the excitement seen in the other story arcs. It's incredibly slow and a slog to get through.
Also in typical game of thrones fashion, it's important to not get too attached to characters or hoping for complete resolution. It doesn't care and any choices you make only slightly alter instances. The ending is already laid out, it's just a matter of choosing path a or b to get there. Basically, you may think that your decisions are very impactful but the game has an illusion of choice. If you want a telltale experience that has satifying conclusions or are more on the up beat side, it's not here. A game that is like that would be Tales from Borderlands
I reccomend this ONLY to the Game of Thrones enthusiasts who can get this on sale. If you haven't read the books or at the very least watched a little bit of the show, just don't. It's much better to start with those first and if you want a little more, I'd almost suggest watching a playthrough or looking at wiki's, I will say that the events that take place in this game feel like they contribute very little to the grand scheme of things considering that the two waring houses are very small and barely metioned (or maybe not at all) in the show.

Platformers really need a unique hook to do well these days, and Snapshot certainly comes through on that front. It's the only one I know of offhand that has a camera gimmick central to its puzzles aside from Camera Obscura, and this is certainly the more pleasing to the eye of the two. First impressions only get you so far, though, and once you dig into this one not even solid gimmicks or graphics can save it from its fatal misstep.
The aforementioned camera dealie is that your little robot dude can take pictures of the world that save the items he snaps in them. He can then load the picture back into reality, rotating it to fit whatever the situation calls for. Pictures also capture motion, so if you snap a flying crate, it'll still be speeding through the air when you bring it back. It's an excellent setup which I'm sure already has you mulling over the infinite possibilities for clever puzzles. So with 120 levels to work through, along with stars to collect and hidden objects to find, you've got a quality mix, right?
You would, if the levels weren't designed by a sadist. Snapshot has one massive flaw, and it's the level design. Not five levels in, you'll start encountering death spikes that force you to start the whole level over. There are no lives and no checkpoints, so even on the larger sprawling levels, one error can cost you a lot of time. Worse than that, many of the puzzles in the game can be rendered impossible to solve, forcing a restart of the level. This is because many levels like to make you stack objects to scale tall walls or shafts, and then continue using those items later in the level. Of course, if you fall back down after moving your items to the top, there's no way to get them back. The very first level involving springs is very easy to ruin if you do any exploring whatsoever.
I want to say it's a shame, but honestly all Snapshot has going for it is the picture gimmick. The graphics are clean and cute but nothing special. There's no story to speak of, or if there is it's locked behind dozens of aggravating levels. And from what little I was able to see, the camera isn't even used to the fullest despite the endless potential it carries. In the end, puzzle platformers come down to their level design and if it's crap, nothing can save it. Surely there's already another platformer out there that uses the same or a similar system to greater effect. And even if there isn't, Snapshot certainly isn't worth braving just for that.

I normally play RTS games to comp stomp, one reason being that I know I'm not as amazing as the majority of players, so I like to fight the computers.
The main problem with comp-stomping on this game, is the fact that even on easy difficulty, they're so difficult it's not even fun, ever.
Now, I'm not going to say to make the AI like Command & Conquer easy, where the enemy turtles with the first five buildings available in the game, and probably send the weakest unit in a pitiful attempt to kill you once in a while, because that isn't fun, I agree.
But when you make it so damn difficult to beat an AI even on Easy and Standard, all the fun is completely drained, and you find yourself questioning why you wasted £15 or more on this game.
Coupled with the fact you have to pay for commanders, which most of which have the same skills multiple times, it's not like they're all unique ways of playing, makes me wonder, why couldn't of they just stuck with giving each side one of 3 preset command strategies?
I mean, seriously, what's the deal with that...?
THEN, to add insult to injury, they've gone and made the entire game just domination from most FPS's, let me state that I hate domination, I've always been a, 'it's not over till you've destroyed their last unit' kind of guy.  So, the fact I don't even have an option to do that, unless I make a friends only custom match just upsets me even more...
It's a shame really, because I enjoyed the first game, I also loved the way the British played differently to the other factions.  It completely fitted the way I played the game, with movable bases to help push forward where ever it was safe.  That's all gone, no way whatsoever of playing like that...
Also, the really good wave defence co-op mode from the first isn't here, which, if they had that, I would probably recommend this game, because I love to defend rather than go offensive.
It's a shame really, the game looked so promising, and Relic just failed to deliver what I, and probably quite a few of the playerbase wanted.
Just to clarify, if you're into the PvP part of the game, I can't comment on that, it's not really the part of the game I enjoy, I'm basing this being a casual RTS'er, who wants to waste a bit of time fighting a challenging AI, than to struggle and get frustrated everytime he plays.

I have to say, in early access I was extremely disappointed in this game. I loved Titan Quest and had high hopes for Grim Dawn. Unfortunately, when I first started playing, the loot felt lacking and the skills just didn't feel like they had that "umphf" that is necessary for an action rpg. However, after it's full release, I gave it another shot, and my opinion of the game was completely changed very quickly. If you had the same experience as I did initially, or you have heard some bad reviews of the game from the past, I employ you to try it out, because I seriously doubt you will be disappointed. The loot is cool, the action is fluid, and their are neat concepts that haven't really been explored in an arpg that I have seen.
One example of these concepts include the relationship bars associated with each allied and enemy factions, giving you shop perks for the allies, and more difficult spawns for the enemies, as the bar increases. Another example is the Devotion point system that gives an entire extra layer of character building, as diverse as the duel-class trees. These Celestial ability options allow you to place points into a large selection of passive properties that are part of mini skill-trees that, when completed, give you a passive skill that you can attach to your main skills. This allows you to get eruptions of fire, or healing, or poison spikes, or life-stealing, or a huge array of other effects that can be added to the skills you are already using. The campaign is very long and there is a great amount of side content along with hidden areas that add to that play time. All in all, this has become one of my top favorite arpgs by far.
Plus, if I know how this company works, they are only going to polish things and add quality-of-life improvements to the game with the expansion, much like they did with Titan Quest. From what I have seen from them, they are always bettering themselves, keeping the parts that are great, while fixing the bad and adding features to the good, always resulting in an improved experience. I am extremely excited for the coming expansion for a number of reasons.

I am suprised with this game.  I waited until it was on sale because it seemed risky to pay full price for "far cry without guns".  It is actually really good.  The player movements are more refined in some ways than even far cry 4, and you feel more agile.  The forest environment is really beatiful, and the hunting in the primal setting actually fits with the game, whereas in far cry 3/4 it seems out of place to me.  Shooting with the bow takes more skill than guns because you have to lead and elevate, and deal with less ammo and slower rate of fire.  The survival mode is really fun.  Definitely a risk worth taking for Ubisoft; a much more interesting twist on a franchise than others such as assassins creed have to offer.  Many of the things you do in regular far cry actually make more sense in a primitive time period.  Also really nice to have a day/night cycle.  On survival expert mode, primal is more immersive to me; gotten so used to far cry even on hard that it seems easy by comparison.

While the tactical options are not that polished than it's predecessor's, it's still insanely good fun. The buyable DLC commanders are muddied the water a bit, but as the vanilla commanders are more than adequate for most of the situations, I can let it pass. Note: My review is set to change as more updates come out, please beware that the game is not 100% polished yet.
TL:DR - Buy the game if you are a fan of the series but also platformers and collectathon type games. It runs well and plenty to do for what you pay for.
+ Runs smoothly (for the most part)
+ Bigger world
+ More puzzles
+ Keyboard & Controller support
- Racing
- Cutscenes
- Random slow-down
- No check-list
- Biting Issue
The game runs well, for a game larger than Ty 1 I expected it to run kinda slow due to it being not 100% polished but it runs very well. Only in minor areas has the game just slowed down for no real reason but has quickly fixed itself. I believe the loading gates are to thank for this and they don't seem to drag on as much as I remember they used to do.
Not really much to put for what is good about the game other than it runs well, more to do and explore. It is a nice upgrade from Ty 1. It is fun, the charm is still there, it feels like a more better world due to the towns and other characters being involved.
There are more puzzles, some which are harder than others to solve (looking at you Volcano!) but still enjoyable. You are getting your money's worth in game-play but also in memories for those that grew up playing the series.
---------------------------------
Now, my issue is with a few things, or nit-picks.
Firstly Ty will often face left or right randomly after 3-4 bites of a spy egg breaking your combo. This can be an issue for some collectables or area's.
There is no check-list (yet) of what collectables you are missing from which map which can be annoying when finding picture frames but due to some other power-ups it is not a big issue as after all it is quite fun to explore the new maps you are given.
The voices in cut-scenes are too low and can rarely be heard, many are having this issue and the developers have said they will be sorting it :).
The races in the game, are complete frustration. Around 3 races are fine, no issue but the final 4 races is where you see an issue. The A.I suddenly speeds up without a power-up, cut corners perfectly and tend to auto-aim at you. It is pure luck with some drifting skill and short-cut usage to complete some of the maps. It will take a few tries but you will see the pure luck involved such as the A.I attacking each other or even getting stuck on a turtle they didn't before so you could steal the win. But this issue is back from the platform version so just a heads up on how annoying they may be for some users even to this day.
Again most of these are just nit-picks. Some of the collectables are a pain to get due to perfect pixel jumps are needed but the game is not fully done and some bugs and such are being found and solved by the developers which I thank for their quick response on certain issues.
The developers are active in fixing any new issues found and are proven to be more than one-off's as well as the community's input on certain parts of the game.
Keep it up developers~

Been playing Dying Light for a while now and I am impressed with how much better Dying Light is to its predecessors. Below I have made a tidy review for you to read.

XCOM: Enemy Unknown is nothing like I've ever played, nor really thought about playing, and it has successfully piqued my interest in this particular genre. It is a tactical turn- and squad-based shooter from an isometric view. I believe it is like Fallout: Tactics and Valkyria Chronicles, based on what I have read of them, but I have played neither and can't really comment on them. I did play Final Fantasy Tactics and it's progeny, however, and this feels like dark souls dabbled with that. This game is just plain brutal until you learn how its mechanics work, which is just what a good tactical game should give you.
Let's start with the story. An alien race is in the process of invading Earth, with First Contact coming shortly before the opening mission of the game. The XCOM project is created to rally most of the first world nations to join forces to fight off the alien threat. You play as the commander of this particular project, where you answer to a Council of Nations (which apparently only has 1 member, since only 1 person ever talks to you) and have some American guy from your job downtown in a Christmas sweater advising you, as well as a French/German lady and your grandpa as subordinates to talk to when you want to customize your squad. Your base is basically from Fallout Shelter where you can see all of the individual rooms, including a barracks, research lab, engineering bay, and situation room. Long story short, the story is just kind of there. It gets some progression, but in my opinion it neither hinders nor helps the game that much.
On to the actual gameplay. You start out being able to deploy a squad of 4 soldiers, with upgrades to improve that to 6, and several different specialization options: Heavy, Assault, Support, Sniper, and a sub class of Psi that can be unlocked latter in the game. The game takes place on a grid-like layout, with cover and patience being heavily emphasized. Whenever an enemy sees you (e.g. you run up 6 tiles and there sits a Sectoid), they get a move turn while it is still your turn, meaning that if your last character reveals some enemies, he is about to get absolutely destroyed. This game has very little mercy, as most of the enemies deal outrageous amounts of damage relative to what your squad has available when fighting them. As they have access to space travel technology far superior to ours, they most definitely have weaponry far superior to ours, and only when you are able to research how to use the alien technology are you able to level the playing field and not get 2 shot by the basic enemies, but then the game gets progressively more difficult. You thought a Thin Man spitting poison on you from half a map away was bad? Try having a muton berserker cover half the map in a single turn, and then getting another move every time you shoot him, while being able to instantly kill almost anything that you can throw at him.
Squad management is absolutely crucial to being successful in your attempts to save the world. Snipers hang back, Heavies tote the heavy ordinance, Assaults go barreling in, Supports provide a little bit of everything, and Psis are there for you to use inefficient abilities in order to advance the plot (at least that's what it felt like, the nuke is always 5 damage, side effects don't do anything even at normal difficulty, 2nd level doesn't seem to be any good, telekinetic barrier might be good but I took Mind Control b/c in theory it can swing the tide of a fight but 17% is only going to save you in Dota). Found a sectopod? Send in the heavies with their double damage against mechanical units. Had a bunch of floaters just pop up? Have an Assault charge forward with Run and Gun to take one out on a really long run while giving vision for your Snipers to continously blast to smithereens. Snipers really feel like the key cog in keeping casualties to a minimum, as they can kill units from a safe distance, generally with a high rate of success and, when they get high enough level, can do it multiple times per round with the In the Zone Colonel Perk. All of them are necessary for certain junctures, these are just some examples (and I didn't find all of them because I *only* played on normal difficulty).
There are also different types of scenarios that can occur, whether as a part of story progression or from game management. There are terror missions where you have to try to save as many of 18 civilians as possible from aliens that absolutely hate their guts (the civilians are also bullet magnets and seem to have a 100% hit rate regardless of how much concrete and steel is between them and whatever is shooting them). You can shoot down a UFO and have to raid it for supplies, finishing off the survivors of the crash. Similarly, a UFO can land and you have to wipe out the crew. Alien abductions serve as the random encounters, as you have to choose one of several nations to go help, each of which offers to aid you in some way, from money to scientists to a new soldier for combat. There are also some "go find this person and escort them to this place" missions, which aren't nearly as bad as typical escort missions since you actually have control of them. Right before I played the final mission, I had to go defuse a bomb, so I have no idea how common that type might be. Either way, there are enough things to do that it won't get stale, but the most common ones have scaling difficulty, making it really hard to get more training for your newer squad members.
Between missions, it is your job to not only manage your small army of soldiers, but also to keep all of the nations on the council from getting absolutely obliterated. If their panic level goes high enough and stays that way for long enough, then they will withdraw from the XCOM project, reducing your income potential and removing the possibility of getting the bonuses from that continent.
Overall, I felt like XCOM: Enemy Unknown did a great job of doing what it set out to do. It is a tough and punishing tactical game, but really rewards those who are patient and able to get the most out of their available abilities. The story wasn't great, but it didn't hinder the game. Voice acting, graphics, and music were more or less the same, not great, but not bad either. The ever evolving list of enemies kept throwing new wrinkles into the game, and ultimately made this quite a satisfying romp that makes me terrified for when I eventually attempt the Classic Ironman run. I give it a 8.5/10, and hope that the next game expands a bit more on the current 4 class system, hopefully makes Psi more fleshed out, and maybe makes the Alien side playable (I didn't play multiplayer and don't plan to, so I have no idea if that is even possible).

When 14 year old me came home from school to play this game for the first time, I was setting myself up for disappointment. I was naive. Half-Life 2 was the first game I ever got excited for, the first game I followed extensively before release, and my expectations were... ridiculous. In every other alternate universe, Half-Life 2 did not meet those expectations, and I became jaded much too early. But somehow it not only met my expectations, but perhaps even surpassed them. This was, and still is, Valve's masterpiece.
It’s hard to describe how amazing this game was when it came out. It seemed to be the best at.. everything. The gameplay was crazy fun. So many possibilities in this game! Like using the gravity gun to attack the enemy with the environment around you, punting grenades back when they’re thrown at you, cutting zombies in half with a saw blade and setting them on fire, driving vehicles, pinning enemies to walls with a crossbow bolt, smoothly guiding rockets at gunships while they desperately manoeuvre to shoot them down... and so many other things, it felt like anything was possible. It was a phenomenal game mechanically, and at the same time so familiar, so intuitive, and so easy to pick up. The physics were something else. We’d seen ragdoll effects and moveable objects before, but nothing close to as real and dynamic as Half-Life 2 provided. It opened whole new doors to immersion, and player interactivity with the environment. It surpassed every other game with its world building, its tone and atmosphere, its animations, its iconic sound effects combined with subtle but excellent music, its pacing and level design, and I could go on...
There were of course some things in this game that weren’t perfect, and with age, they stand out more. The AI is not very good. Particularly the friendly AI, which is most evident in levels near the end of the game where you constantly have a group of them following you. They are generally pretty useless and have a tendency to get in your way at the worst possible moments. The airboat and the buggy are pretty awkward to control, and as genres have merged together more in recent years, lots of first-person games have vehicles in them, so they are no longer an interesting novelty either; though the sections were you use them are still great fun. The physics puzzles can get old quick, and from today’s perspective they aren’t impressive, so they’ve aged quite poorly. Anything else I could mention though would be pure nitpicking.
But almost all the great things I mentioned aren't impressive now right? (which I should note, you owe Half-Life 2 for) So what does this game have to offer that modern games don’t? Well, this game might not amaze anyone now, but it does remain an extremely solid, highly polished and well-designed experience; which should be clear for anyone to see, as long as they care to look. It’s still one of the gold standards in world building, pacing, and level design. Its mechanics now might seem simple and quaint, but sometimes simple is best. So many developers today cram as much fluff as they can into a single game, that many games have little focus, little drive, and hardly any heart. In a time when the art of linear level design has been pushed to the sidelines, and "huge open world" has become a necessary baseline for almost every game series (whether it warrants the change or not) Half-Life 2 can still be a breath a fresh air - if you’re looking for something more focused, that knows exactly what it wants to do, and succeeds in those goals at almost every single turn.

In this puzzle platformer your a robot that has to get to the level exit by taking and placing objects. You take objects by taking their picture and replace them by untaking their picture. You can collect stars along the way, take pictures of special objects and try to beat the fastest times.
There are 100+ levels and they are divided into groups of 3. Each group introduces and highlights a new object. Most of the objects only make appearances in their group of 3. The first level of each group are the shortest with the second and third being progressively longer. Collecting the stars and special objects also adds quite a bit of length to a level. There are no checkpoints, So most failures require you to redo the whole level.
Which objects to place where is the meat of the game, But that is pretty obvious most of the time. The puzzle aspect comes into play most when figuring out how to get things into or out of no picture taking zones. Again not that difficult. The hardest part of the game is when you have to perform some mid-air photography acrobatics. Which can get quite annoying as you'll have to play the entire level over again just give it another try if you fail. It presents itself as being a casual game, and for the most part it is, But it has these areas that require patience and persistence.
It's an OK game, best played in short sessions. I went for the extra stuff and got them all up until the last 5 or 6 levels. At that point a failed jump was crashing the game making it very hard to figure out what to do next. So I skipped the rest and just finished out the game at 81% complete.
