"When you play the game of thrones, you win or you die", except in Telltale's game, you lose everything anyway.
There's a lot of problem with GoT and I wouldn't talk about choices lacking consequences, because in my opinion great writing is way more valuable than any kind of branching storyline, but before getting to the real interesting part, you gotta slog through hours of irritating plotlines that make no sense. The best parts of the game IMO are episode 1, episode 5 and episode 6. Episode 1 because it sets a nice introduction to house Forrester and manages to get you to know crucial characters very fluidly. Episode 5 because of Asher, and Asher's storyline is the most interesting one of all, and it also has the most difficult choice in the entire game. Episode 6 because, well, its closure and pretty epic even though it still let a lot of loose ends away.
Is it worth it though? Because before being able to play the best part of the game, GoT slaps you in the face with 3 other episodes full of bad writing, pointless storylines, illogical scenarios and overly tragic plot. The first storyline that fell apart first is Mira due to HUGE intervene by characters from the show. Her story revolves around Margaery Tyell, Tyrion and Cersei Lannister so much that after the first episode, "Mira's Adventure to Take Back Freedom for Family" became "Mira's How To Survive While♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥Off People At King's Landing". Her story is pointless from episode 3 and onward, and finally she doesn't affect the outcome of Ironrath at all aside from eliminating a few Whitehill troops.
Ironrath is probably the most irritating storyline I've ever seen in any game from post-TWD Telltale. It constantly puts all Forresters into dead end, it absolutely has no sense of hope, it wants to nail you on a wood board and makes you watch a dolphin getting murdered in cold blood. It feels like the writers just took the meme "everyone dies" and applies it to the Ironrath, no, that is not the point of Game of Thrones at all. The story is ruined the moment when Ramsay ♥♥♥♥ing Snow with a thicker-than-ice plot armor put his foot in Ironrath hall, he exists just to ♥♥♥♥ up the story and create unnecessary shock value, his appearance shows that Telltale DOESN'T ♥♥♥♥ING KNOW HOW TO WRITE A VILLAIN PROPERLY. They want you to hate yourself for playing it, and you either die or making some honorable gesture before dying. Instead of painting a morally grey picture, GoT became a Final Destination movie where you advance and check the clock to see when and where characters die.
I don't know why, but Gared's storyline makes me hate the Night's Watch. IDGAF about Jon Snow and he's my favourite character in the show. The Forresters is more important than any vow, and the fact that everything you say, either hiding the truth or being honest to Jon doesn't affect the outcome anyway, makes the Night's Watch feel like it was just shoehorned into the game so that Gared can waste time and find more people that will be killed later.
The best part of the game is Asher's storyline because he's legitimately a well written character. He's light-hearted, a good fighter (equal to many good fight scenes), his relationship with Malcolm and Beshka is well thought-out and natural, and I can't get enough of his cheeky grin. However, for some reason the writers decided to turn Daenerys into a ♥♥♥♥♥ before Asher, and she completely flips you out, and I'm pretty sure Daenerys in the show will never do that to people who obey her.
Ultimately, GoT feels like a long series of tragic stories that try to push the Forresters into the end. It relies too much on shock value and death over real dramatic moments. The TV series does not revolve around any particular character, so why would the game feel the need of having characters from the show, especially since aside from Margaery and Cersei, they just appear to either♥♥♥♥♥♥you off or make no impact at all? Why did Telltale decide to put the game into the Bolton's doghouse where there's absolutely ♥♥♥♥all will happen, instead of taking somewhere else in Westeros? In the show, characters are punished because they made a mistake. In the game, you are punished because ♥♥♥♥ you we told you so, have fun feeling bad because for something you absolutely didn't do.
But hey, at least Rodrik got laid. At least, please Telltale, don't mess season 2 up. Until then

The make-it-up-as-you-go deckbuilding gameplay is sooo much fun and constantly forces you to make tough decisions about whether you should take risks in order to upgrade your deck, or try to take safer routes and plan for the long run. No matter your progression strategy, the game will always throw a good dose of random events that will stir things up, forcing you to improvise as best you can.
This seamingly random mechanic is extremely well balanced and polished (especially for its early-access stage) and every run is challenging, but always feels fair, because ultimately, how you play your cards decides how well you fare.
The game currently features two characters, that have significantly different playstyles and deck compositions. This gives the game yet another layer of variation in the sense of replayability, since you have to adapt new playstyles for each character and their deck-sets.
As an early-access title, there is already plenty of content and polish as for the value of the product... And there is SO, SO, SO much potential for future content. A third character is in the works and I can't wait for the update, but beyond that, the game and its universe have amazing potential for growth! Additional cards, new enemies and bossed, more events and relics... Even expanding the spire itself to new heights! I truely hope that this game continues to grow in content - even when it reaches its post-release state. I don't know about the developers' DLC-police, but I would gladly put my money in it, to keep the content and universe of this game growing, and growing, and growing!
To the devs, thank you for this gem, and for anyone who's still reading this, just buy the game and start playing already! :)

I have to say, in early access I was extremely disappointed in this game. I loved Titan Quest and had high hopes for Grim Dawn. Unfortunately, when I first started playing, the loot felt lacking and the skills just didn't feel like they had that "umphf" that is necessary for an action rpg. However, after it's full release, I gave it another shot, and my opinion of the game was completely changed very quickly. If you had the same experience as I did initially, or you have heard some bad reviews of the game from the past, I employ you to try it out, because I seriously doubt you will be disappointed. The loot is cool, the action is fluid, and their are neat concepts that haven't really been explored in an arpg that I have seen.
One example of these concepts include the relationship bars associated with each allied and enemy factions, giving you shop perks for the allies, and more difficult spawns for the enemies, as the bar increases. Another example is the Devotion point system that gives an entire extra layer of character building, as diverse as the duel-class trees. These Celestial ability options allow you to place points into a large selection of passive properties that are part of mini skill-trees that, when completed, give you a passive skill that you can attach to your main skills. This allows you to get eruptions of fire, or healing, or poison spikes, or life-stealing, or a huge array of other effects that can be added to the skills you are already using. The campaign is very long and there is a great amount of side content along with hidden areas that add to that play time. All in all, this has become one of my top favorite arpgs by far.
Plus, if I know how this company works, they are only going to polish things and add quality-of-life improvements to the game with the expansion, much like they did with Titan Quest. From what I have seen from them, they are always bettering themselves, keeping the parts that are great, while fixing the bad and adding features to the good, always resulting in an improved experience. I am extremely excited for the coming expansion for a number of reasons.

I had originally played American Nightmare after having finished Alan Wake in May of 2013. However, I was getting pretty tired of the combat system and seeing it repeated without a lot of variety didn’t do much for me at the time. The story’s changed tone didn’t help either. Back then, all I had finished was the first cycle of levels and decided to quit it early. I did review both Alan Wake and American Nightmare then too, where I slamming AN for being a subpar experience. It’s a mistake I’m not proud of but I’m glad to correct it now. So, I’ve completed this nightmare and have my complete thoughts on it. Admittedly, the same issues I had with it back then haven’t changed much. Except for the combat I suppose. This is another review where you have to ignore the Steam rating and read the words to find out my overall feelings for it.
Alan Wake: American Nightmare is the semi-sequel standalone that Remedy published several years after the release of the original Alan Wake. Released after they stopped working on Alan Wake 2, AN was meant to take the ideas and setting that they had crafted for a demo of AW2 and publish something out of it. When it had become clear to Remedy that the time wasn’t right for a sequel, American Nightmare was created instead while the studio went to its other announced projects. Is this the last word for the Alan Wake series? That seems to be the indication so far but it's entirely possible that Remedy could return to the series. I hope they do because this nightmare ends the series on a rather sour note.
American Nightmare plays out like a schlocky episode of the Twilight Zone. Alan Wake is fighting against a new threat from the darkness, Mr. Scratch who looks and sounds like him. Alan finds himself in Spring Falls (AZ) where things don’t seem quite right, he’s being unusually stalwart and the Scratch is over-the-top silly. There’s also this constant narration from a guy that sounds like the narrator from the Twilight Zone who uses the pronoun game way too much. Alan has to figure out what’s going on in order to defeat the trap set by Mr. Scratch.
American Nightmare lacks a lot of what made the game so tense and didn’t replace it with anything outside of a wider variety of weapons and enemies. Gone are the claustrophobic battles and limited ammunition. Ammo can be found all over these new wide-open spaces. Alan has clearly embraced his role as a warrior of light and I’m ok with that. However, the side effect of this embracing is that the tension of the previous game has been largely muted and it plays out like a fairly standard third person shooter. The major change to combat is the new weapons you can use. Assault rifles, combat shotguns, SMGs and hunting bows just to name a few. They work and sound reasonably good, if a little uninspired. They don’t really add anything to change the combat which is a little disappointing. I mean, we’re talking about a battle between light and darkness. I would have loved to see weapons that could use light or change the battlefield in some way. Instead, light weapons are still the flares, flaregun and flashbang grenades as before. The same tactic of shining a light on the taken till the darkness is gone and opening fire remains. A slightly strange change to the mechanics is that simply shining an unfocused flashlight on taken doesn’t peel away the darkness like it did before. You have to focus the flashlight on each and every one of them. This doesn’t really change the tempo of combat all that much but I felt it was worth noting.
The story plays out after the events of Alan Wake. Alan finds himself in the town of Bright Falls, AZ, in a world where his writing has power. He finds himself fighting against his evil counterpart: Mr Scratch. Who looks and sounds exactly like him except that he’s evil. Mr Scratch has trapped Alan in a time loop with the intent of wearing him down and eventually defeating him. Thereby allowing Mr Scratch to take over his life in the real world. Worse, Alan lost some of his memories and the key to defeating Mr Scratch once and for all. Alan must survive in the trap long enough to piece together a message he sent to himself that will allow him to set a deadly trap for Mr Scratch instead. Which the trap is killing him at a movie theater when the right conditions are met. Once that’s done, Alan apparently is reunited with his wife, Alice Wake. Where the two share a hug and kiss and the story ends. It’s actually kind of anticlimactic.
Alan Wake goes for a fairly realistic style that’s less punctuated with the bright lights and dark shadows of the previous title. However, instead of animated in-game cutscenes that the original title did, they go with live-action cutscenes every time Alan Wake and Mr. Scratch “interact”. It’s weird to see it used and I’m not convinced it works. I’m also not convinced by the setting of Arizona’s desert, as it feels way too bare in contrast to the Pacific Northwest’s forested and hilly areas. Side note, there are some awkward animations with facial expressions and body movement that’s bizarre to watch when the characters converse. It’s not enough to ruin the experience but it looks really dated by current standards.
American Nightmare has some serious problems that seem to stem from its limited budget. It’s missing a lot of what made Alan Wake a good experience, that underlying current of tension is all but gone. The story, writing and acting is schlocky as hell. What some of the characters say sounds weird and Alan Wake seems to be indifferent to most of what’s going on around him. Furthermore, Mr. Scratch fails to be an interesting villain, feeling like a side character most of the time. Probably the most egregious issue is the game making the player repeat the same levels three times. While they don’t have you repeat the exact same dialogues and actions, the repetition is still there and it isn’t interesting. Combat does get some changes but most of it is the inclusion of high powered weapons. Otherwise, fights are mostly set in big open areas where enemies can be seen for miles. It loses the tension fights had in AW and settles for a mostly mediocre third person shooter. Should you pick it up? I can’t decide. There’s nothing actually wrong with AN from a story or game mechanics perspective, it’s just not as good as Alan Wake. There are better titles out there worth checking out in comparison. So, my suggestion would be to think on what I’ve said and see if the change in tone is worth checking out or not.

To be honest, I played Ace of Spades: Battle Builder when it was on it's last legs. Ace of spades was a phenomenal game, I would play for hours and not get bored, the game always ran smoothly, it was fun, it wasn't repetitive, but it just died.
Then Jagex thought, You know what? Lets make AoS 2. They made this. I'm not saying Block n' Load isn't good, believe me it is, but AoS was way better, smoother performance, more choice loadout wise, more based on constructs rather than traps, no absurdly long respawn times. BnL has all of those. The core gameplay is the same, but it just isn't quite as good.
It is too class based, so it feels like a TF2 clone where you can build more than sentries. Within a class you have no choice in weapons, but you can choose different blocks.
In essence this game is AoS 2, but isn't as good as it should be. It is still plenty of fun, but It could easily be better.
Overall I give it a 7/10 because of loadout restrictions

Disclaimer: I have never played another Civ game except of a few minutes of Civ III.
I find Civ V an excelent turn based strategy game where every turn feels crucial and must be given as much importance as the last in order to come on top of your opponents, be it the AI or other players.
You do not need experience in other Civ games to understand how to play it but if you did not have experience with other turn based strategy games then it might be a bit difficult to adapt to the genre with this as your first such game. There is a lot of complexity and mechanics revolving around the gameplay but even if you start a new game without viewing a guide, slowly and steadily you can be learning everything by yourself without even doing the tutorial, speaking of which, it is not that good as it bombards you with a lot of information in the form of walls of texts. Should you have any  enquiry, there are fanbases and wikis available online as well as an in-game wiki.
There is a lot of content in the game, even more so with 'God and Kings' and 'Brave New World' expansion packs. I highly recommend getting the two expansion packs, and if your budget affords it, the dlcs that add new civilisations into the game as well.
You can have great fun while playing with AI controlled civilisations over a span of difficulties and world types and there are a lot of achievements that you can try to unlock. The customisation of worlds is very detailed and thus you can start your first game in an easier difficulty, should you wish. The AI is well refined making offline experience enjoyable.
Multiplayer is the only thing that I, have trouble with. I can play with some friends without any problems, but with others it is impossible as the game will either crash, disconnect or be glitchy in general with units disappearing and stats resetting. If he host, though, can keep a good connection with everyone else indepentantly, then multiplayer with friends should be fine.
All in all, I had, and still have, great fun with this game which once every so often drags me back after a time of break in order to try out a new civilisation in a different setting or start a new multiplayer session with a friend of mine. It is very refined and a must-play if you are really into turn based strategy games.
PS: If you enjoy this game, then your sessions will last for as long as you say that the next turn will be your last turn x)

When 14 year old me came home from school to play this game for the first time, I was setting myself up for disappointment. I was naive. Half-Life 2 was the first game I ever got excited for, the first game I followed extensively before release, and my expectations were... ridiculous. In every other alternate universe, Half-Life 2 did not meet those expectations, and I became jaded much too early. But somehow it not only met my expectations, but perhaps even surpassed them. This was, and still is, Valve's masterpiece.
It’s hard to describe how amazing this game was when it came out. It seemed to be the best at.. everything. The gameplay was crazy fun. So many possibilities in this game! Like using the gravity gun to attack the enemy with the environment around you, punting grenades back when they’re thrown at you, cutting zombies in half with a saw blade and setting them on fire, driving vehicles, pinning enemies to walls with a crossbow bolt, smoothly guiding rockets at gunships while they desperately manoeuvre to shoot them down... and so many other things, it felt like anything was possible. It was a phenomenal game mechanically, and at the same time so familiar, so intuitive, and so easy to pick up. The physics were something else. We’d seen ragdoll effects and moveable objects before, but nothing close to as real and dynamic as Half-Life 2 provided. It opened whole new doors to immersion, and player interactivity with the environment. It surpassed every other game with its world building, its tone and atmosphere, its animations, its iconic sound effects combined with subtle but excellent music, its pacing and level design, and I could go on...
There were of course some things in this game that weren’t perfect, and with age, they stand out more. The AI is not very good. Particularly the friendly AI, which is most evident in levels near the end of the game where you constantly have a group of them following you. They are generally pretty useless and have a tendency to get in your way at the worst possible moments. The airboat and the buggy are pretty awkward to control, and as genres have merged together more in recent years, lots of first-person games have vehicles in them, so they are no longer an interesting novelty either; though the sections were you use them are still great fun. The physics puzzles can get old quick, and from today’s perspective they aren’t impressive, so they’ve aged quite poorly. Anything else I could mention though would be pure nitpicking.
But almost all the great things I mentioned aren't impressive now right? (which I should note, you owe Half-Life 2 for) So what does this game have to offer that modern games don’t? Well, this game might not amaze anyone now, but it does remain an extremely solid, highly polished and well-designed experience; which should be clear for anyone to see, as long as they care to look. It’s still one of the gold standards in world building, pacing, and level design. Its mechanics now might seem simple and quaint, but sometimes simple is best. So many developers today cram as much fluff as they can into a single game, that many games have little focus, little drive, and hardly any heart. In a time when the art of linear level design has been pushed to the sidelines, and "huge open world" has become a necessary baseline for almost every game series (whether it warrants the change or not) Half-Life 2 can still be a breath a fresh air - if you’re looking for something more focused, that knows exactly what it wants to do, and succeeds in those goals at almost every single turn.

Let me start by saying that as with a large number of the reviews I have seen for this game, I liked FTL and think that it is a great game, but cannot recommend it to a friend. If it was on sale for a couple of bucks I might say grab it to play on a lunch break or on the train. That is about the amount of time it takes to play the game through a couple of times and come to the realisation that there is nothing to build towards and nothing left to see. Imagine playing a game, having fun and just starting to get some gear and put some points into the things you like and then the game ends and you have to start again. That is FTL; lots of potential but not much there. The gameplay and tactical variety are excellent but the randomness of each event and playthrough along with the truncated, rushed nature of the game ultimately leave you feeling disappointed.
You are on a mission to reach a friendly base to deliver information vital to destroying the enemy while being chased by their fleet. To do this you have to navigate your way through 7 sectors, each of which are made up of around 25 waypoints. You have time to visit roughly 10 waypoints or so before the fleet starts to catch up and you have to warp to the next sector. Finally you reach the 8th and final sector, deliver your information and attempt to destroy the enemy flagship. Each waypoint you jump to generates a random event. You might find nothing but empty space or you might encounter an enemy to fight or a store to buy weapons, ship mods or crew members.
Often you have a choice how to deal with the situations that come up, for example you might discover a damaged ship asking for assistance. In this case you will be given options such as inviting them aboard, sending your crew over to assist repairs, scrapping their ship for parts or just leaving. The outcomes to these choices can be unpredicatable; if you choose to send your crew over to help the ship might blow up and take one of your crew with it. If you invite them aboard it might only be to discover the whole thing was a trap and have them sabotage your ship before beaming back to their own and suddenly find yourself in battle at a disadvantage. Or everything might go smoothly and they pay you handsomely for your efforts. You choose whether to roll the dice. Depending on what kind of crew and ship mods you have, special options may be available such as remotely repairing their ship with a drone or teleporting them aboard safely. These specials options are highlighted in blue and always have a positive result.
There are a number of different weapons and technologies that allow you to defeat the enemies you face in a variety of ways. This is where the game shines. You can just straight up fire lasers and missiles at the enemy until you turn them into space dust or you can take a more tactical approach. For instance you could use shield bypassing missiles to blow up the enemy shield generator and target their weapons array with your lasers for a safe victory. You might use ion weapons which disrupt shields and systems to disable them and teleport your crew onboard their ship to engage the enemy in hand-to-hand combat or just focus on heavy shielding and send drones out to fight the enemy for you. You can start fires on the enemy ship and blow holes in the bulkhead.
All the flavours of the rainbow are available in terms of combat in this game and if you had more time to play around with the different approaches and it weren't entirely a matter of chance as to which ones you come across, the game would be be infinitely better. As it is you might set out with a plan in mind of how you want to kit out your ship and which weapon combinations you want to use and just never come across the ones you are looking for or find anyone selling them.
On my second playthrough I started with the Engi ship which utilizes drones and ion weaponry. At one stage I found myself in combat with the first enemy I had fought that had two layers of shields. I had two ion weapons and was able to disable their shields and one other system and slowly let my combat drone ping them down. My drone station along with half of my other systems got destroyed by missiles and with half of my ship left open to space I was stuck disabling their shields and weapons but unable to warp out or do any damage. An idea struck and I started alternating one of my ion cannons between firing at their weapons and their oxygen systems. After a while I figured it wouldn't work and was about to restart the game when a message popped up saying their crew had suffocated and I was able to scrap the ship for more loot because it was still in one piece. 'This game is awesome' I thought to myself and decided to playthrough again, focusing entirely on ion weapons and get rich capturing all the enemy ships intact. On that playthrough I never found a second ion weapon. I decided to try a build using fire weapons and a teleporter with rock crewmen who are immune to fire, I found a single low level fire weapon but no rock crewmen and no teleporter.
In the end I played dozens of games, unlocked the various ships and won the game a number of times using different combinations. After 23.5 hours played I looked back and thought 'what a waste of time'. The game is random to an annoying degree and I personally found myself playing it again purely because I never felt satisfied, even when I won. I never felt that I had gotten to play it the way I wanted to. Even when you get the weapons you are looking for, space spiders eat your pilot, just because. Ship in distress needs help making repairs and you have a crewman with maximum repair ability and max engine skills, decide to help and your gunner dies. I really like some of the ideas behind this game but it is too short, too rushed and way too random. If you are just looking for a game to replace solitaire then FTL is the game for you. Otherwise I really would not recommend it.

Very addictive and *potentially fun* game, and I don't mean "the game has potential/will be good after updates". I mean every single run can either be extremely fun and satisfying or absolutely pointless and frustrating. Almost EVERYTHING is RNG here. That's what makes this an extremely difficult game to give a solid recommendation for.
Your starting hand is basically a few bad cards (which you can only upgrade/replace or get rid of IF you get lucky) and how far you will get will entirely depend on how lucky you get during the run. Which cards and relics you get (or don't, and which ones you can get rid of), which enemies you encounter, which skills they use in which order and the cards you draw in which order. It's ALL RNG. And as it is with RNG, you can either get lucky and have a blast, or get absolutely destroyed by bad luck and have a frustrating slog through the level with no real chance to get anywhere.
Where in other games, tactics and better planning/skill can make a huge difference, in this one it mostly comes down to luck. Skill and knowing how your cards play off each other will still make a difference in the fights, so an experienced player will *potentially* avoid bad situations, but even an experienced player can and will get shafted by bad luck, and often. The chances to actually finish a run (at least in the Early Access Version) are extremely low, you basically have to build a death star by the end and have a good deck that works well off each other, and hope to not get countered by anything on the way there or get oneshot by a ridiculous enemy combo.
But at the same time,that is what makes it so addicting. The best game I can compare it to in terms of "feeling" is Binding of Isaac. It's the exact same feeling you get there: "Just one more run."  "I just need this now..." "This next item will save the run."
And it gives you the same sort of satisfaction when your "build" actually works out. You will mow down enemies left and right and snowball out of controll...IF you get that far, and if you then don't get countered by something even stronger.
As you can probably tell,this is an incredibly difficult game to simply "recommend" or "not recommend". If the game was just a bit more centered around skill and planning and toned down on the hard counters and RNG, I would recommend it without question.

The constant deletion and reproduction of content experienced playing Snapshot feels like the perfect counterpoint to its almost schizophrenic eagerness to continually replace mechanics, too insecure with the ideas its putting forward to ever spend long enough on any given one to actually develop it into more than a one off curiosity. The only constant is your ability to copy certain objects and then place them elsewhere in a level, but Snapshot treats its core mechanic as a novelty, one I quickly grew aggravated with as I attempted to work with its unwieldy interface.
Basic movements are already stiff and awkward, making rudimentary jumps hazardous and unpredictable, but trying to frame and position objects while avoiding obstacles at the speed you're often forced to is agonizing. I was constantly falling onto hazards and screwing up puzzles because I wasn't able to move my frame quick enough to grab an object, and this only becomes worse the longer you play as the game abandons any notion that it understands the weaknesses of its interface.
Nearly every chapter brings with it a new concept for you to work with, be it magnets or fireballs, but they're so briefly utilized that Snapshot is never able to build any sort of mechanical vocabulary. I never knew what I could or couldn't do or how different items interacted with one another because Snapshot never tells you, and spends so little time using any of its ideas that you're constantly going through tutorials and then being told the thing you just learned is irrelevant beyond your immediate puzzle. Snapshot's kitchen sink approach to game design also completely abolishes its difficulty slope. As it has to continually stop to tell you how something works, it creates a series of levels that vary erratically in challenge, some obnoxiously difficult while others only ask you to press right and jump. Completely a challenging puzzle only to have it followed up by one that was almost insultingly easy made it feel like my time was being deliberately wasted. Snapshot has more ideas than it has levels to hold them, so it forces you to spend needless amounts of time within a single level so as to make it appear as if whatever mechanic its currently using has any place in the game.
And a handful of them are kind of cool, but they're buried deep in a game that's too busy trying on clothes it doesn't fit to notice the parts that work. Even if it had, I have little hope it would have had any more luck utilizing them when Snapshot's foundation struggles to hold itself together during even the simplest moments. Retro Affect has stuffed their game to the point of breaking with content, but it seems to suggest even they realized most of what's here needn't be, as you can see the ending after less than half the game is actually finished. It's a silver lining I quickly took advantage of, but hardly something to recommend a game over.

CoH 2 is not a bad game. It's just not a very good one. Like a lot of people said, it just doesn't offer much in the way of new over the original. The snow/freezing mechanic is more annoying than interesting and sometimes doesn't work well. If a groups of soldiers is warming by the fire and one of them is just a little further away he will freeze to death, and requires micromanagement to stay alive. The cinematics/cut-scenes are incredibly lame, and voice acting is bad. There is a lot that can be said and remembered about the Russian struggle against the Nazis, and it's sad that CoH 2 does such a poor job at it. Did CoH 2 try to do this? Absolutely. But the result is very mediocre.
The tons of expensive DLC which doesn't go on sale when the core game goes on sale is insulting to me as a fan of the series. Half of this stuff should have been given to players for free.
Still, CoH 2 is still CoH. I recommend it. There is still plenty to like here. Great battles filled with desperation, great units, wonderful graphics. We should praise CoH 2 even if it's only for trying, because there's so few RTS games these days. This game may not be worth it's original asking price, but it's definitely worth it's current sale price, and as time goes by it will definitely be worth ten bucks.
I gladly paid for this game, because I want to support the devs(not encourage them toward mediocrity) and I hope thanks to my support and other people like me, we can expect an expansion which will make this game better in all the areas it's lacking. No need for CoH 3!!! Just make this one better! It's not too late!

Pay to win, pay for convenience, pay for cosmetics, pay for inventory space, pay for everything.

You will be simply known as the Player, a newcomer to the secret poker club known as the Inventory, taking part in five players tournaments against four memorable characters from different franchises, not only in the video games industry, but comics and video series as well. You will play against Max from Telltale's own Sam & Max franchise, Strong Bad from Homestar Runner, Tycho from Penny Arcade, and the Heavy from Team Fortress 2, characters that have absolutely nothing common, yet still manage to lighten up the mood at the poker table. Poker Night's magic comes from the conversation between those characters, which consists mostly of jokes and references, and while some were meant to be little easter eggs for fans of a particular franchise, most jokes appeal to a generic audience, making them hilarious even if you're not that familiar with the characters. A short introduction to each of your adversaries would've been welcome to familiarize the player with their background, but instead the game chooses to introduce them to you as you play via dialogue, which feels authentic to a poker experience, but ultimately falls short on how much information you will actually get. Nonetheless, the jokes are what make Poker Night at the Inventory a fun experience more than anything else, but unfortunately the amount of dialogue doesn't go on forever, and one or two hours in, the game will run out of new dialogue and start repeating itself over and over again.
There's no surprise or twist in here, what you actually play is poker, Texas Hold'em to be more specific, and that is another big reason why this game will become boring within a few hours; Texas Hold'em is the only thing you can play, and while it does work flawlessly and the game nails its table presentation, you will always play the same game, at the same location against the same adversaries, which does become boring quite easily. What will keep you playing, are the special items that each character will bring to the table as buy-in after a few rounds, giving you the opportunity to win them if you eliminate that character from the tournament; each character has one of those, making it four in total and winning those items will unlock them in Team Fortress 2, which is a nice thing if you play Team Fortress 2 as well. Even with that in mind, you can easily win those by playing a few tournaments which shouldn't take more than a few hours, and after that poker is the only thing that can bring you back, but then again, if poker is what you're here for, there are much better poker games out there. There are two difficulty levels, Normal which is the casual way to play Poker Night, allowing even the players who haven't played poker before to stand a chance by following the tutorial, and Hard which is the way to play if you really want an authentic poker experience, as the AI will become more aggressive, start bluffing and generally play smarter. The lack of additional popular poker modes such as Omaha Hold'em or Pineapple is what makes this game become boring so easily, as even with all the work put into making Texas Hold'em feel authentic, it's still the same game over and over again.
Poker Night at the Inventory isn't a visual masterpiece, but it holds on among other titles of its generation, and what really matters the most, the characters look amazing and authentic to their universe, while still fitting well in the Inventory's background. The animations are okay, but they do become repetitive as well after a while, and the visual effects, while kept to a moderate volume stand out well in the environment.
The dialogue is what matters the most in this game, and the best part about it is that all the original voice actors for those characters are here to voice them in Poker Night, with Gary Schwartz voicing the Heavy, Matt Chapman voicing Strong Bad, William Kasten providing the voice for Max and Andrew Chaikin voicing Tycho Brahe. The soundtrack fits the mood of the Inventory perfectly and the sound effects for card flips and chips movements feel authentic, making your poker experience enjoyable, even when the dialogue starts repeating itself.
It doesn't take more than a few hours to win all four Team Fortress 2 unlockables, which is probably where most players will end their business in Poker Night at the Inventory, but if you do decide to stay for a little longer, there are a few aesthetic unlockables such as new tables or decks, but apart from that, there is nothing else to see or do.
Poker Night at the Inventory is a fun thing to play for a few hours, which is more than enough considering its price; if you're a fan of one or multiple characters featured in this game, you'll have a great time hearing their dialogue, but if you're here for a lasting poker experience, there are probably better options out there.

This game is fun and challenging although the final boss can be quite frustrating at times, but it's overall, a fun experience and definatley a challenging one, I give this game a 9/10 just because I think the final boss needs a slight nerf. Snapshot is a fun puzzle platformer, with charming visuals and sound that seem halfway between fairy tale and Saturday morning cartoon. Controls are simple and mastered without fuss, based around moving, jumping, and (of course) taking photos and "printing" the objects they capture back into space. Gameplay is calm, and the puzzles are not difficult, more often requiring a bit of extra thought rather than expert button mashing.
For gamers who are addicted to achievements, Snapshot offers plenty of medal chasing: 40 levels of 3 puzzles each, with each level having 3 additional challenges (collect all stars, collect all objects, and run time) to complete. The game can be completed without completing all challenges, or indeed all levels, but the tempation to replay to 100% the game is strong.
The one big downside (mostly for those 100%'ers out there) is a bug in Steam achievements related to completing the game. There are achievements relating to percentage completion, and lower levels (e.g. 35%, 55%) do not unlock when completing the game with a higher-level achievement (e.g. 75%). That said, the game is definitely worth a look for puzzle solvers young and old.

With those things included this game would be legendary.
Instead, this is simply my favorite game this year and I'm glad I gave it a chance.

Just a quick intro: I haven't played the game as much as I'd have liked, because I had a time I went off it for no reason. I have poured thousands of hours into other ARPGs.
The multi-class system GD uses is the same as in Titan Quest and in fact, many of the mechanics spawn from TQ too.
There are 6 (soon to be 8 with an expansion?) distinct classes that all have overlapping benefits to each other, though some are more optimal.
The 6 default classes being:
Note, several of the classes have what is called an Exclusive skill near or at the end of their trees, however, the Demolitionist and Nightblade lack said type of skill.
The classes are fairly unrestrictive as to what weapon type you can use with them, but some skills do require something specific to be equipped.
You cannot undo a class selection once you've invested points into the mastery bar, but you can refund any points you've spent on skills within a class. You cannot refund skill points invested into the mastery bar itself.
This means that the class/mastery choices are quite important, but the actual skill choices can be freely changed, as the cost is relatively low, especially once you are higher level. Note: The cost does increase the more you respec, although I can't provide any numbers here. Generally you shouldn't be feeling the need to respec dozens of points.
A character is, as far as I know, limited to level 85. Every level you will gain 3 mastery points, i.e. points to spend on your skills, and 1 attribute point. After level 50 you only earn 2 mastery points per level. Found this one out the hard way, myself.
In most zones of the games, monsters will scale up to your level, up to a limit. For example, if I am level 62 in normal/veteran difficulties, MOST monsters will only go up to 40, not giving me XP/Rep.
However, some specific end-game zones in normal/vet will still have monsters scale up to my level or nearer to my level, such as 52/55.
And I do still find myself going back to veteran difficulty to farm iron bits and rep from bounties and stuff like that.
- The base difficulties, veteran having increased spawns and the like.
- Starting mostly from level 40-50 onwards. Increased mob density and reduced resistances by 25%.
- Starting mostly from level 70, as far as I am aware. The mob density is higher and resistances are reduced by 50%.
You can cleanse up to 50 devotion shrines for the same amount of points. Many of them require only components to be cleansed, but some spawn waves of enemies. Either way, the shrine will give randomised one-time loot when cleansed.
Devotion points are like class-less specialisations, and require a lot of strategically invested points to get to the really big devotion constellations. They also have some lore in their descriptions, which I personally find fantastic.
Again, this system works mostly like in Titan Quest. Items have several rarities; Common, Magic, Rare, Epic, Legendary. Items are also divided by type: Heavy, Regular and Caster.
Common items will have no level requirements, regardless of where they were acquired, but all items have some stat requirements, so that does translate to a level or other equipment requirement anyway. They are plain items.
Magic items are
and will often have 2-4 modifiers.
Rare items are
and will have many modifiers, most of the time.
Epic items are
and have fixed rolled modifiers, with their values being variable. They are the equivalent to uniques like in Diablo 2. They can also be set items.
Legendary items are
and tend to be very very good at something specific, such as boosting chaos damage, for example.
There is the special case of monster "infrequent" items that are items unique to specific monsters, such as Cultist codexes or Ghost weapons. These will roll up to Rare quality.
These are small items acquired from reps and from drops respectively, used to improve any given item, apart from relics. Augments are specific on what they do based on the faction they're from, which will have items for sale with similar properties on them. Augments make an item soulbound, due to the faction rep required to get them in the first place; this means you can't trade them to other people or to your other characters.
Components will most often drop from monsters and will be partial; they can be combined into a complete component for a more powerful effect, and weapon components will usually grant a skill. They are the equivalent to socketable items from other games like Diablo 2, except the items don't need to have sockets or anything like that.
Crafting can be used to make random or specific items, the random items scale with the level of the crafting character. There are several smiths that each provide different minor bonuses to most crafted items.
Specific item recipes are most often acquired from factions and include things like components made from other components. Skeleton keys are a special consumable item used to enter the end-game dungeons, of which there are a couple.
Some epic and legendary quality items can be crafted too.
Generally monsters fall under certain types, such as Aetherial, Beast, Human, Ch'Thonic, etc.
Some items provide bonuses against specific types and generally the enemies feel like they have enough variation.
Bosses feel worth going back to for a bit of a guaranteed loot spill, and enemy "hero" monsters will generally "loot-explode" too. Personally I think this idea was done much more appropriately in GD than in Diablo 3, where it was a hyped feature, long ago.
Sorry, I don't have a lot to say on monsters.
Reputation can be gained with several of the factions by killing monsters of the types stated in their faction profile but reputation (and some minor rewards) can be gained from bounties for each faction, too. Generally the loot reward on a bounty will be from killing a special monster.
Factions will provide equipment that can be expensive but that can be considered part of a fixed item progression, so they are good if you want to dedicate time to the faction that has items appealing to your playstyle.
This equipment will generally fall under certain level tiers, depending on the faction and the level of reputation, but the tiers will mostly be: 30-35, 45-50, 70
At certain rep levels you can buy items that increase rep gains, but these items don't stack with one another or themselves. 50% is the first one and 100% is the second one, but the 100% rep bonus item can be given to your alts too.
Factions provide a lot of the crafting recipes too, including recipes for rare components.
Personally I really love playing my Witchblade (Soldier+Occultist) as a Ch'Thonic faithful.

For the most part Tropico 4 is one of the first management games I've played in a while. I had a pretty massive gap with the my last really intense period of playing games from this genre involving Rollercoaster Tycoon and Theme Hospital, man those were some great games, then in the last few years I flirted with Football Manager before getting Cities in Motion and Tropico 4. What really drew me into Tropico 4 though is the theme and world that it built. While doing such world building isn't unique in management games, the world that Tropico 4 had built was. I was just really intrigued by the fact that you could attempt to embody some of the worst dictators in human history like Francois Duvalier or become a revolutionary like Fidel Castro or really be anything in between. I don't doubt that the reason behind this draw I felt to the game was my love for history and politics, so I'm pretty sure that anyone who has similar leanings is going to be drawn into the game much the same way I was.
Tropico 4 isn't a game for everyone though. Hell, this entire genre isn't for everyone. At the end of the day the entire management genre is just spread sheet management and its your affinity with the world and theme the developers work on that is the reason you actually engage with it. All I can say for certain is that I really like the game, I enjoyed the use of real dictators, the work that was put into the music and art in the game and the fact that game as a whole doesn't take itself serious with all the characters in the game and its campaign being caricature of various historical figure. But I can definitely see that anyone who has no political or historical interests just won't find this game interesting at all and would lean towards another management game based on their interests.

After a hard start I must say, that the game at the current state is what it should have been when it came out, however, I do not wish to punish this great game, after a lot of improvement and care from the developments side of listning to the community and improving it, I wish to recommend it.
This review is from a Multiplayer Perspetive.
At the games current state to me it seems most of the negative reviews are aimed at things where it does not feel similar to the first Company of Heroes.
It is not Company of Heores 1, it is Company of Heroes 2. Even though it is a sequal, the pace of the game and how the units work is more dynamic in terms of how the game unrolls when playing it, compared to the first game. This is not a bad thing. The first game focused a lot of having a "line" you could push forward and hold. Here it is more fluid. You use different combinations of units to take control and counter your opponent for control over Victory Points and ressources through engangement, instead of fighting a "front line" war, which were more the case in the first game.
Both the Russians and Germans have strenght and weakness that follow each other equal very well from start to finish, making it quite balanced.
A debat about one being more overpowered only comes down to what you chose to counter your opponent with, and more importantly, how you chose to counter this way of playing, his battle to take control over key points on the map, how you can harrash him to focus on different objects, and interrupt his stratigical plan of winning the game.
The debat about the different Commanders you can buy is still a bit unclear, whether or not it is "buy to win". Some do offer a harder challange to counter, but far from impossible, however, I would not say it is "buy to win", since they do not offer all-defeating abilities with no or very little weakness.
It is a game where you must learn strenght and weakness of the units, and how they support each other through your way of playing, to counter your oppenents stratigical plan, and units, to gain control and dominace over the map.

This game's difficulty is like playing a game of solitaire. you have a higher chance of winning than losing unless you understand the mechanics of the game. but even after understanding the mechanics, the game can still be difficult and doesn't only require skill to win, but also, a bit of luck. I highly recommend this game to anyone who wants a strategy game with a lot of challenge involved (because let's be honest, "strategy" games nowadays tend to hold your hand throughout the whole thing and tend to be easy most of the time). And don't worry about getting bored of the game. the more you win, the more ships you unlock, thus unlocking, more ways to play. Each ship is different and in order to unlock a new ship, you must beat the game on any difficulty with the last ship you unlocked. some people may say that this "forces you to play in a way that the game wants you to". This is not the case at all. It's more like the game is guiding you through each ship so that you don't get used to other ships as you play. This game is fun and challenging although the final boss can be quite frustrating at times, but it's overall, a fun experience and definatley a challenging one, I give this game a 9/10 just because I think the final boss needs a slight nerf. Unlike the other Kyle Pulver game I've played, Offspring Fling, which I absolutely loved, I can't say the same for Snapshot.  A unique and interesting concept quickly tires itself out and becomes bland and repetitive.
With around 120 levels it's a game that really overstays its welcome.  Each set of three levels introduces a gimmicky twist to the gameplay- I feel safe with saying gimmick because all but the most fundamental of them are promptly thrown out the window and never seen again.  There is no cohesiveness to the design that brings all these scattershot elements together into something greater.  A lot of them are poorly implemented, frustrating to use, or just plain boring anyway- if you do happen to find a mechanic you like, you'll probably never see it again.
A broader problem is that it's supposed to be a puzzle game, but has failed to puzzle me in any way.  I've rarely been stumped on how to approach a problem; instead it all seems kind of obvious.The only real difficulty I've had in finishing a level is from frustrating deaths due to a combination of insta-kill falls/spikes, the poor mechanics mentioned above, and the lack of checkpoints in levels.  A lot of the levels take far too long and offer far too much room for mistakes to not include any sort of checkpoint.  I wouldn't speak too highly of the level design itself either.
Unless it's something you're receiving in a bundle of some sort and just want to try out for a little bit, I cannot recommend Snapshot at all.   A lot of potential seems wasted with such a unique core mechanic behind it.  It is an exercise in frustration rather than problem solving; repetiveness rather than innovation.

It's not that Telltale Game of Thrones is BAD per se--trust me when I say that I love anything Game of Thrones. I would recommend picking this up on sale if you really like GoT and feel you need this experience. In fact, it's got the hallmarks of a good game:
+Solid Voice Acting (show characters in-game are voiced by their actual GoT cast members)
+Plot fits neatly into GoT's overarching story
+Telltale's quality pedigree
But all that can't really make me recommend it to you, beloved review-reader. Let me start by explaining a bit about the game. It takes place immediately after the Red Wedding, and if you don't know what that is, this game will be very confusing to you. In that sense, it is for Game of Thrones fans (obviously). You are tasked with overseeing the fate of the fictional "House Forrester", who were once one of the sworn Northern Houses of the Starks. Simple enough.
But where does it fall apart, you may ask? Well, I suppose it's probably from the very concept. This is a Telltale game, which means that it is essentially a glorified visual novel. There are no high-octane sword fights where you are in control of your character; you do not engage in what one might call "gameplay" like you would want to in a GoT game adaptation. It's just sitting back and watching, occasionally clicking a button or two. It misses the opportunity that video games provide to create immersion or interactivity. In addition, the game putters through and crashed once or twice for me despite its simple graphics and non-intensive gameplay, which still strikes me as very odd.
The story-telling is okay, but not up to the par of the books or shows. Your choices may appear to matter greatly during your first playthrough, but if you are foolish enough for a second one, you will see very clear cracks. Your choices don't matter outside of the promise of a second season of the game, which feels cheap to me. As it is now, the game's plot is unsatisfying and unable to hold itself up on its own merits without this "second season", which is sad. Your actions are pointless--your involvement in the story practically meaningless.
In the end, Telltale does do good work. Walking Dead Season One was great, and it held up well on its own merits even with setting up a sequel, which GoT fails to do. The Wolf Among Us was interesting but weaker than Walking Dead, in my opinion, as was Walking Dead's second game season. Maybe it's just me--maybe I'm "Telltale'd out", as it were--but the charm of Telltale's story-telling and game mechanics is growing lost on me. If there is a season two, I don't imagine I will be playing it at all.

Overall, I found that this game still had what I'd always loved about it, and what I'd always loved about Quake. That's great.
But, a fair amount of changes have been made which, it feels like dumb down the core experience of the game, or more so that which the now larger community of players will be experiencing. Some of these changes, I could say I do not agree with, and that would be true. The addition of loadouts and Press-to-Keep-Jumping mechanics, amoung other things, have diminished the skill gap within the community, and, for the most part, this is a positive, but I've myself am not completely keen on the learning curve being brought down so dramatically.
What I should really get at, though this review is far from complete, is that this is still Quake, the same game we've loved  for years. Sure, iD may have changed quite a lot over the years, but their company and what they've done for video game is still deeply rooted in the hearts and minds of gamers the world over.

It would be hard for me to talk about American Nightmare without touching on the original Alan Wake, because it very much feels like DLC that got spun into its own game. Alan Wake's strengths were its story, pacing, and graphics. The combat was a bit of a toss-up between decent and monotonous, depending on who you asked. American Nightmare is a shorter, weirder story told across three mostly open areas that you visit multiple times. The visuals are still sharp, but lose a lot of the atmosphere that Alan Wake had... the open desert just doesn't have the same creep factor as the dark woods, at least not as it's shown here. Dialogue is pretty snappy and clever, but it's propping up a story that really adds nothing to the themes introduced in Alan Wake.
So the main draw is the combat, and to its credit, it's a little more interesting than in Alan Wake. Enemy encounters are varied in makeup, and there are some new foes like ones that split if you shine light on them and creepy jumping spider things. All the original weapons are here, along with new additions like a nailgun, uzi, and carbine. You can unlock weapon cases with additional weapons by finding manuscript pages scattered around which encourages exploration, but honestly as large as the areas are, there's not much to find. Enemies only appear as you follow the main plot, and the game showers you with ammo and flare, more than enough to handle any situation. I tried playing on the harder of the two difficulties and the battles were still a breeze with all the resources I had, but I could be killed in just two hits which led to some frustration with unlucky hits at the ends of long fights.
There's an arcade mode similar to the mercenaries modes in Resident Evil that's pretty fun, assuming you like the combat. And that's really what American Nightmare boils down to, did you like the combat in Alan Wake? If so, this is for you, but don't come looking for the atmosphere or story of the original.

TL;DR: The familiar flashlight-shooter horror game makes a comeback but demoted to an action shooter.

Alan Wake is back. This time around he's seasoned and armed to the teeth, steeled by the Dark Place he has been trapped since last time. Consequently,
builds heavily on the original game's story. If you haven't played it expect to be confused by what's going on. In fact I'd recommend one to play (link!)
before
to be able to understand the story, if only because of the nice references.
Having played the original game ensures that you will fully understand the story. Alan Wake is very literally the superhero of his own story, somehow constantly knowing what to do when the player is left perplexed by all the peculiar events. In the story Alan is trapped in the Dark Place and wants to escape. He has a plan that is revealed bit by bit.
The ominous Mr. Scratch, introduced briefly in
, has become the villain, a malicious manifestation of The Dark Presence. He will appear from time to time in random TV screens to taunt Alan. None of the rest of the characters make come-backs (well, unless you count the radio show host). In fact, there are only three other characters to interact with. Their acting feels too cheesy and out-of-place, and it's weird anyway that there are so few people around.
The play area is also lot smaller than in
: only three (albeit rather big) maps contain the whole story in nine chapters that slyly recycle the same areas. While it makes sense for the story, it makes one think that it was done so because of low budget.
The radio shows and Alan's notes are still there and they are cool and I felt they were approximately of the same quality as in
. Graphics and sound are similar quality to the original.
Alan's confidence actually eats the atmosphere: the ominous mood of the original
is almost completely missing. The Taken appear out of no-where but there's nothing building up tension, and usually they are easy to dispatch because there's ammo and supplies basically everywhere.
is then sort of an action version of
: the Taken (i.e. the enemies) are more aggressive and numerous, and there are several new weapons from crossbows to automatic shotguns. A few more enemy types have been introduced, some of which need to be dispatched without light. They are all fine additions to the enemy roster.
To the joy of the lovers of the curious combat system an Arcade mode has been included. In the Arcade mode you have to survive 10 minutes of Taken waves of increasing strength. You build up a combo multiplier by successful kills and not getting hit and try to reach as high a score as possible. For a change, it gets fairly difficult and it's easy to run out of ammo. Your skills will be tested especially in the Nightmare mode, in which there are no longer separate waves or pauses: instead the Taken appear continuously making the action very intense.
Much shorter than
, the story lasts just a few hours and I managed to even get all the achievements without guides in 10 and 1/2 hours. The story has practically no replay value unless you missed some of the notes (in which case you can choose to replay individual chapters). Arcade mode has some interesting challenge achievements and there you can fight for the highest place on the global leaderboards if that's your thing.
I think
is an okay sequel but it pales in comparison with the original. Get it if you liked
but wait for a sale.

One of my favorite games of all time, XCOM: Enemy Unknown successfully combines deep tactical gameplay and RPG elements into a single, glorious package.  Due to recent extraterrestrial attacks, the XCOM Project has been activated and you have been appointed as its commander.  Your duties include directing the initiative's research, sending order to the engineering department, selecting and hiring the best soldiers for the job, and commanding said soldiers in battle.  You'll also be building and modifying satellites and aircraft to provide intel and defense against the alien threat as well.
As the war progresses, the alien invasion forces will become increasingly dangerous.  New alien types with more advanced equipment and abilities will show up throughout the war to catch XCOM offguard.  Fortunately, this is where your research department tips the scales in your favor.  After eliminating an enemy threat you will acquire alien materials and corpses that your scientists will be able to study.  Common results from these studies include new gear options for your soldiers, additional aircraft and air-based weaponry, new facilities to build in your base, and more that will further your cause.  I was always very excited when my research resulted in a new piece of gear based on alien tech that was significantly more efficient than what I had previously used.
In addition to improvements to their gear, your soldiers will gain promotions as they acquire experience in combat.  Each of the four classes has a unique tech three that they will progress down as you see fit.  Each rank allows you to choose one of two options that will offer new abilities to use or passive buffs to the unit's overall efficiency.  One Heavy soldier may be built around specializing with his rocket launcher, another might be entirely focused on maximizing their machine  gun capabilities, and a third might have a combination skills from both skill lines.
There are two other aspects of XCOM that I feel need to be mentioned in addition to the standard mechanics: Second Wave and Long War.  Second Wave is a menu full of options that is unlocked after having completed the game once.  These drastically change the mechanics of the game and include changes such as a semi-randomized skill tree for your units where one, or potentially both, of their options for a particular rank offer skills that are not usually allowed to that profession.  For example, you might have an Assault trooper who has an advanced talent with medicine that is capable of healing their allies for significantly more health, an ability that is usually Support-only.
Long War, on the other hand, is an unofficial mod created by players who saw the opportunity to futher improve an already great game.  Though there are plenty of mods out there, none that I have seen can come close to comparing to the ambition shown in Long War.  I won't go into the details here but I find that it improves almost every aspect of the game for me.  If you're interested, read more on it here:
There are very few people that I wouldn't recommend this game to.  The variety of difficulty options makes it an enjoyable game whether you're a more casual player of if you're a hardcore masochist (I'm looking at you Impossible/Ironman).  The mechanics are great, the atmosphere is fantastic, and everyone who I've spoken to who has played has had numerous stories to share that are a lot of fun to hear.  Just remember, you'll be losing a lot of soldier that you've customized grown attached to.
Now stop reading and save the world from the alien menace, Commander!

Alright so I played this game quite extensively, and I can safely say that almost everything that can possibly be wrong with a game manifested itself as a flaw in this game at some point in playing it.  There is a TL;DR at the end.
Let's start on a technical standpoint:
The game balance was awful.  The early game was very item reliant, and unless you grind to ridiculous proportions or use the overpowered DLC items they throw at you right at the beginning, you will have to use a LOT of items in certain fights.  There is one fight in particular very early on where you have to fight two bosses in a row where I had to use somewhere around 15 revival life fragments.  Once you are able to get life rings, the games stops being item reliant, Compa becomes useful again, and the difficulty is comfy with no need for grinding.  However, this is short lived as once you unlock EXE moves the difficulty becomes a joke, and everything is♥♥♥♥♥♥easy.  In the whole story there was only one boss that I felt accomplished after beating (and it wasn't the one that I used 15 life fragments, that one just made me mad).
The game had various performance issues, in almost all parts of the game.  Dungeons would have framerate drops when you're walking around them, the game occasionally crashes when you access HDD (this is pretty rare, but it has happened to me 3-5 times so it is worth mentioning), the game sometimes fails to load the models and then crashes shortly after, the game sometimes fails to load the backgrounds for the visual novel parts, and again crashes shortly after, sometimes you softlock the game when you try to skip text.  It was overall a disaster really.
The sound balance was really awful.  The overworld music in particular was blasting loud, while the battle music and dungeon music relatively quiet.  Compared to the other problems, this is somehow only a minor complaint.
The animations for the specials of the CPU candidates (the main characters of this game) are in some cases a little awkward, and in other cases badly modeled to the point of being uncomfortable to look at.  In particular, Rom and Ram's specials where they stab the staff into the ground tilts their backs at impossible angles and it isn't pleasant to look at.  The camera in Uni's EXE drive attack zooms in and out inappropriately and ruins it as well, and one of her specials is just her holding the same exact pose the entire time while the background moves and a very lazy beam comes out.  I think these animation problems all existed in Re;birth1 as well, but they were optional end game characters in that game so it was overlookable, not anymore.
The sprites of the enemies, while not reused as much within its own game, are still reused quite heavily.  Additionally, almost every conceivable enemy in Re;birth1 besides Arfoire herself is reused.  Including re;birth1's FINAL BOSS, which appears as a regular story boss, and later a regular field boss.  Additionally, several important story bosses are just recolors of sprites from re;birth1.  And I don't mean regular story fights, I mean story fights against important antagonists, whose sprites are just reused and recolored sprites.  Very lazy, although somehow less lazy than the first re;birth.
So that covers the technical standpoint.  Which leaves just some more abstract criticism:
There are 9 different endings, that to see you have to go through very tedious movement of shares through repeatable quests and raising lily ranks through tedious farming.  And despite there being 9 different endings, 6 of them are exactly the same, just with a cutscene of nepgear talking to a different group of people at the end.  1 of them is unique, although it is a kind of ending that most people who would want to play this game wouldn't want to see.  And the last 2 are also the same, just with a different means to get to that same ending.  The 6 different endings could have easily been condensed into one ending with 6 cutscenes after, instead of 6 endings with 1 cutscene each, and the game would have been a bit better for it.  The other 3 can stay as they are, even though two are more or less the same, leaving a total of only 4 needed endings.
In the game you unlock a sidegame called Stella's Dungeon, and it takes far too long to accomplish anything in that game without cheesing it by changing your PC's clock, or by buying the DLC and building the plans to make it easier.
Speaking of plans (blueprints), building the plans in this game is a nightmare.  You have to go on very long chains of adding enemies to dungeons so that you can make the plan to change a dungeon, so that you can make the plan to change another dungeon so that you can...  ...   ...   ...   and finally so you can just make a credit booster that isn't even that helpful.  This process was much less extreme in re;birth1.
You have to go through over half of the normal game about before you can finally add Uni, Rom and Ram (the main characters that are on the cover along Nepgear) to your team for good.  When I finally got those 3 in my first run, my team was average level 38.  When I finished the game that run my team was average level 50.  In re;birth1 it takes a while too to recruit the other CPUs, but it's still quicker than here and the reasoning behind it is better than "ram is a brat and uni is too tsundere to join".
The subtitles, particularly for Neptune, are very bad.  This can be fixed by downloading a patch, you have to go out of your way for it, and if you use English voices the voices will still say the bad lines of course.  To clarify, it isn't that I don't like what they are saying, it's that the translation does not accurately portray what is being said, and makes Neptune more hyper-active and obnoxious than she is intended to be, and makes her lines where she says semi-serious things into complete jokes as well.
There are less optional dungeons, so you're more or less forced to just continue the story a lot of the time.  The excitement of exploring a new optional dungeon that you unlocked hoping to find some secret good equipment is gone.  There are a few optional dungeons, but they mostly involve the previously mentioned awful plan building with chains through previous dungeons to unlock.
I could say more negative, but I think I've written enough complaints at this point.  Now for the important part that nobody will actually get to.
If you're a fan of the Neptunia Series, despite the massive wall of text that I just wrote complaining about this game, you should still probably buy it.  If you're someone who should buy it, you know who you are.  If you have any doubt whatsoever, don't buy it.  However if you do, I would definitely advise just searching for the cutscenes of most of the endings online, and only actually playing to see the:  Normal End, True End, Holy Sword End, and Conquest End.  The others are a waste of time.  Very important also, you should wait for the game to be on sale.  This game is not worth anywhere near the 30$ price tag on it.
One final clarification, I drew a lot of comparisons to the first re;birth in this review.  I am NOT a super fan of the first one, so I am not biased towards it or anything.  I only made these comparisons because as the sequel it should be expected that the good are kept and the bad are fixed, which was not the case.
TL;DR:  The game is broken in several senses of the word.  It would be in very few people's best interest to buy this game, especially for the price tag.  If you are someone who should still buy it anyway, you likely know who you are, you can still buy it and you will still enjoy it.

Conclusion: If you are a die-hard GOT fan and need something to satisfy your hunger for more Thrones, this game might do the trick. I would suggest any GOT fan to buy this game while on sale. Just make sure you go into it with tempered expectations.

This game's difficulty is like playing a game of solitaire. you have a higher chance of winning than losing unless you understand the mechanics of the game. but even after understanding the mechanics, the game can still be difficult and doesn't only require skill to win, but also, a bit of luck. I highly recommend this game to anyone who wants a strategy game with a lot of challenge involved (because let's be honest, "strategy" games nowadays tend to hold your hand throughout the whole thing and tend to be easy most of the time). And don't worry about getting bored of the game. the more you win, the more ships you unlock, thus unlocking, more ways to play. Each ship is different and in order to unlock a new ship, you must beat the game on any difficulty with the last ship you unlocked. some people may say that this "forces you to play in a way that the game wants you to". This is not the case at all. It's more like the game is guiding you through each ship so that you don't get used to other ships as you play. This game is fun and challenging although the final boss can be quite frustrating at times, but it's overall, a fun experience and definatley a challenging one, I give this game a 9/10 just because I think the final boss needs a slight nerf. Honestly, I understand why so many people are giving this game a bad wrap. The choices that you make really dont mean much until perhaps the final hour, but even then I can only think of maybe 3 choices in this entire game that may actually effect anthing.
However, to just leave it at that and call this game a failure is overlooking the game's saving grace. That is, this game left me feeling every emotion I was meant to feel: it made me hate characters what I was meant to hate and it made me cry by the end by my sheer attachment to the characters in this story. Heck, it even made me feel giddy the few times where things were going good (looking at you, Elena). This game made me think, several times in fact, "this feels like Game of Thrones", and as a person who has seen the entire series and owns all the books, I can say that that is a good thing.
And yes, I know that the choices are practically insignificant. I was well aware of that going into this game, but whatever I expected was nothing like what I got: a damn good GoT experience. So, yes, I'll admit it: I have fallen in the false trap that Telltale oh so famously sets, a trap meant to make players believe that what they do is significant when in reality that couldn't be father from the truth. I admit it, and am able to move past that to see all that this game has to offer as a narrative experience that truly made me feel, and I would say that is well worth the price, especially on sale.
