I read the negative reviews that complained that you get the a bad ending no matter what you choose.  I still was interested in taking a look at this game.  So I waited until it was on sale.
I haven't played long yet, and I doubt I'll play much more.  I have three main complaints so far.
My first complaint:  There's a lot of really dumb action sequences where the game requires you to quickly tap, press, and click, quickly alternating between the mouse and keyboard.  Which seems really dumb.  It's forcing a action-y gameplay element onto a game that is clearly not an action game.  I just never liked games that were like "Press this aribitrary button now....or you have to redo this part!"
Second Complaint: I don't understand why almost all the decisions are timed.  This is a real pain for me because this game doesn't always perform top notch on my machine, so my mouse sometimes just doesn't want to move where I want it to move on the screen right away.  I guess the idea is to imitate a split second decision...but that backfires because you don't have a bunch of equally bad multiple choices in most situations in life...which brings me to my next complaint
Third Complaint:  The characters you are playing often don't seem very creative or intelligent.  Often you'll think of a much better solution immediately than the two, three, or four you're given.  It's annoying to both have these choices forced upon you in a "roleplaying game" and on top of that have a limited amount of time to choose which of the equally dumb and short-sighted responses you want.
On the plus side, if you wait till it's on sale and don't pay much for it, it can be fun to just play along and see where this regardless-of-what-you-do tragic story takes you.  But think of it more as a graphic novel with annoying video game elements than a video game with graphic novel elements.

Dying light is excellent at mostly everything it does. I beat the main game several months ago and enjoyed it quite a lot. Now I am playing through The Following and I feel compelled to review this game. Since I'm not someone who is terribly concerned with stories in games, especially action games like this, I will mostly be focusing on visuals and mechanics in this review.
Visually this game is a treat, assuming you have a machine capable of handling it. I'm playing on a PC with a GTX 970/i5 4690k/16gb RAM. Most settings at high with only the gameworks options, motion blur and chromatic aberration turned off. Game runs beautifully smoothe. I can't remember the last time, if ever, the framerate noticeably dropped below the acceptable 60 fps.
Mechanically this game also performs very well. Considering so many different elements are working together in Dying Light, I feel it manages to do almost everything well. Whether you're doing parkour, driving your buggy, or slicing zombies with one of the many wonderful melee weapons, you rarely feel like your character is awkward to control. The inventory management, however, can feel a bit fiddly at times. Eventually you accumulate so many weapons and crafting items that the game starts to feel more like Fallout 4 than a zombie action FPS.
To be honest I don't remember many of the details of the main game's story and I haven't completed The Following so I can't tell you whether it's any good or not. But I can promise you won't be disappointed as long as you're not expecting some mind-blowingly awesome and original plot.

I didn't have fun for long with this game. It feels just like it lacks a lot in gameplay, as things are just greatly difficult to accomplish and in the beginning you just depend on your luck if you want to get far.
It's biggest sale point, the randomness of events is... not really that big. Yes, there is a variety of things that can happen to you, but it seems to like there isn't really that much variety.
You always follow a specific basic path, which then has several options of what could happen to you. Sometimes, you can make the decision, like jumping or fording a river, which basically means having the chance for a random event, like having to dodge bees or asteroids. The other decision will have you... dodge... boulders.
If you play it and then die and play it again, you will soon realize that there isn't really that much variety in what will happen to you. And, because the game sometimes just throws undodgeable obstacles in your way, faster than a human being could possibly react to, dying will happen to you a lot.
Also you seem to be very limited in what you can do. The weapons, which the game will not really let you choose to fire it or conserve it, always have very limited ammo. You have, if you coun't all the party members, 12 points of health, from which the game sometimes RANDOMLY decides to take a quarter away. You either heal from (quickly appearing) health pickups or from random events.
The game has a real good soundtrack though, and the design is mostly nice to look at, the sound effects also appear to be fitting and they don't get annoying.
The text "scrolling", which is not in your hand, even on the fastest setting, was still too slow for me. Why not let me decide when to skip the text?
In conclusion, the game has some sort of variety and the random events are funny at first, but they get old quickly. The gameplay doesn't have much variety, where I would really have appreciated to put more effort in. It doesn't cost a lot, so it doesn't really hurt to try it out, but I for myself, did not pull a lot of enjoyment out of it.

Lost Castle is a really good blend of Beat 'Em Up and Rouge-lite. It's very similar to Rampage Knights, only less punishing. Less punishing in a sense that you can actually beat it without losing your mind, it's not easy by any stretch of imagination.
This is a very satisfying action game. You play as a treasure hunter, who gets trapped inside a haunted castle and has to fight his way through five levels and when you die, you can buy permanent upgrades with souls of your defeated foes. On your way you pick up new weapons, trinkets, armor, sacrifice health for crit/damage bonuses, drink potions with permanent effects and get pets. Understanding gear is crucial for your survival, wrong item or potion will very likely lead to your untimely demise. Playing with friends also increases your odds of survival. This game has up to 4 players coop.
One thing I'd like to mention, there is no dodge mechanic built into the game outside muskets. But fear not, from what I've experienced, jumping works just as good.
You have choice between both melee and ranged weapons. I prefer ranged weapons, but some melee weapons like the spear are really good as well. Each weapon has a unique special ability, which can range from useless to essential. They can provide additional damage and also buffs and healing(very important!). My personal favorite is a musket, that creates black hole, which sucks up and murders everything and a holy scepter, which creates a healing pool, which allows you to save highly important healing consumables. You really have to experiment in order to find weapon class, that fits your playstyle the best.
When it comes to consumables you have quite a few. Food is used to replenish your health, potions are a bit of a russian roulette, what may be a healing potion can also be a potion that damages your health. There is so much variety of effects both good and bad. At first you cannot tell them apart, but upon drinking them and discovering what they are, their name will show up (for the duration of the run). You can also find amulets, which provide additional firepower and summoning items.
Like I said there are 5 levels in total. At first you'll probably die at the second level, but as time goes, you'll progress further and further. Speaking of progress, there is no backtracking, if you leave an area, it'll be blocked off. Which CAN be a big deal, because at times you'll come up to forks in the path- one path leads further on and the other contains treasure or shop. There is no way of telling them apart outside of a certain skill, which isn't reliable 100% of the time. So in another words, don't leave anything behind, you won't be able to get back. And don't feel too bad about not finding your secret treasure, because clearing a room will get you a guaranteed treasure chest.
When it comes to graphics, you may notice this game is very cartoony. To the point that your character may at times resemble a Funko Pop figure. But it fits the silly tune of everything that is happening and there is actually a lot of detail put into it all.
Engaging enemies can be tricky, each level has enemies, which will make you pull your hair out. And even the lesser enemies can be a problem when paired with tougher ones. Or ones with ranged attacks. Or landsharks. Or when the room also has traps. If you don't have a weapon that's beefy enough you can run into a room, where you'll be swarmed with skeletons and die. You may think running away may save you, but the usual effect is you'll attract other enemies and end up in a bigger mess than you were in previously.
Boss battles are epic. And hilarious at times. Will you fight a Goblin King? Or will you fight a giant slime, which murders said Goblin king?
Well you better hope you beat them, because you'll unlock more equipment options for future runs. Also if you succesfully complete the run, the game doesn't just start over, you'll also unlock new bosses, which means new equipment and higher difficulty.
All things considered, I cannot find much wrong with this game. Far from it actually. It's a rougelike, sure. You'll die a lot, sure. But usually the death is a player's fault and you come back stronger. This is one of the most accessible rougelikes I've played so far. It's not as punishing as many of other rougelikes tend to be, which is only a positive in my book.

So... A lot of the reviews for this game are either focused entirely on the multiplayer aspect of the game, are in broken English, or both. Well, I've only played this by myself, I think my English is fairly decent, and I have things to say.
At it's core, Lost Castle is a side-scroller rogue-lite game, where you clear rooms of enemies in a randomly generated level map for their money, items, and souls. I'm tempted to make to comparison to Rogue Legacy, but while both games are rogue-lites, have permadeath, and have you spend a currency on upgrades when you die, they're sufficiently different for the comparison to be... not that great. The similarities ARE there, but I'm not here to talk about Rogue Legacy. I'm here to talk about Lost Castle.
I may not have spent a lot of time in the game - only 2.6 hours at the time of this writing - but I had a lot of fun with it. I find the gameplay both challenging, and fun. I'm a fan of the upgrade system, and I'm definitely a fan of the items, from the health restores, to the passive upgrades, to different weapons having different special abilities, even how some armour will provide extra bonuses if you're using a specific type of weapon.
If you're only concerned about the multiplayer, other reviews seem to agree on it being pretty solid, but for the loner at heart, this game is still perfectly enjoyable, and a game I will definitely be returning to.

HOUR COUNT: >20 on Xbox 360, 1.5 on PC
TL;DR: A nice little Xbox Live Arcade game, but not quite as good as the original game.  Also, it's a little short.  Arcade mode can add a lot of replayability.  If you're not sure, just pick it up on sale, preferrably as the Alan Wake Franchise so you can get the amazing first title.
--
Do I recommend it?  Only if you liked the first, or want the arcade mode.  Still rocking those fight-with-light mechanics, still fighting them darkness zambies, just more of the same-- which, trust me, isn't a bad thing!  It's a four to six hour standalone DLC campaign taking place after the events of the first game, and possibly the closest we'll ever get to a sequel (since Remedy's in deep♥♥♥♥♥♥and leaning on the success of Quantum Break).
I went ahead and took the game for a spin in arcade mode, and the port is excellent.  Easy 60 FPS with very few dips to 48 while maxed out at 1360x768, R9 280 and Pentium E6600 with 4GB of RAM.  32-bit users welcome.  Much less CPU-intensive than the original game, and much more optimized for 60 FPS.  Vsync can cause a few strange issues with mouse sensitivity, though.
The DLC campaign has about two hours of fresh new levels, then goes back to repeat itself three times.  Don't worry; you only cross over some of the centerpieces of each level, and you keep getting exposed to new parts of the levels you haven't visited before.  It's definitely a good campaign, and while it isn't on par with the original (as very few games are), it'll keep you playing for the duration.
Mechanically, it's good ol' Alan Wake.  The only change is that you can't just aim at them to burn their shields away.  This time, you HAVE to be boosting your flashlight (right-click) to wear down their shields... which makes combat a little more tense, since your magical shieldbreaker now has limited ammunition.  The dodging mechanic also seems to be a little more responsive, and enemies don't throw♥♥♥♥♥♥at you nearly as much.
Arcade mode was done well, though it could be better.  You start with a 9mm and flashlight, you have an ammo box that comes back every three minutes, a few lights to replenish your health, and you've got 10 minutes until sunrise.  There's also weapons around the map, and a few weapon cases that can only be opened if you collected x number of manuscript pages during the campaign.  You get tons of enemies thrown at you with several variations, and you need to get the highest score you can by avoiding damage and taking out enemies.  Get a high enough rating, and you can unlock the next mission.  There's 5 or 6 stages, and a Nightmare variation (more enemies, constant spawning instead of wave-based) for each.
Is it worth $15?  Yes, but it's not the best game out there.  My recommendation's to save up and buy the Alan Wake Franchise bundle, so you can get both titles.  If in doubt, wait for a Steam sale.

Like the other series in this game the game story is told via visual novel (however you cannot change the outcome of story in this) and it is pretty nicely done altough not all dialogue is voiced. Story itself was a little bit letdown from first Neptunia but i still got engaged in Hyperdimensions story which is funny and unique, though it has those typical JRPG tropes (and yes, there is a lot of fan service).
Much of time is being spent in world map and you can access all the shops, characters, dungeons, etc. from here. This game offers pretty decent variety of sidequests accessible from The Guild which are nice variety to just blatant grinding (which you will do anyway).
Combat is same as in other games of this series which is real-time dungeon crawling until you encounter an enemy and then it switches to turn based combat. You can have four characters on the field (one more than previous version) and four more waiting for support. Combat is very well done in JRPG standards and joy to play (even the grinding is not that bad).
There is also sort of minigame added with Stella's Dungeon where you can send him to collect loot for you. But there is also the catch that she can die there and you lose all his equipments. Graphics fit nicely in this games style (and that style is amazing!) and animation deserves an praise too. Sounds and music are fitting and good but nothing extraordinary.
If you have played Hyperdimension games and liked it then this is a no-brainer purchase for you! :]
For others, if you like JRPG's and all the baggage that comes with it (good and the bad) i can recommend this also as this (whole series actually) is better than most JRPG's out there with great battle system and other nice elements like crafting, stella's dungeon, The Guild, etc. And Hyperdimension series nice own humor and unique storyline still remains here :]

The narrative was interesting, although it becomes a little repetitive -- if you don't know what I mean, you'll see. It's not at all bad, but didn't leave me particularly inclined to have another go at the game's story. The arcade mode is fun, challenging, but wasn't something I'd spend days playing.
American Nightmare is not the sequel to Alan Wake, but it's still more Alan Wake which was more than I could ask for. If you're interested in returning to the Dark Place and spending some fun hours shooting up some Taken - have at it.

The definition of wasted potential.
And I enjoy games with rewarding grind so it's not due incompatibility with the game genre.
PRO:
Nice combat. Nice graphics. Nice world. A very original blend of management and action. Features rich.
BAD:
They all blow those good things for the decision to force the player to extreme, daily, AFK intensive, not fun, not rewarding grind.
And this seems to be done for a simple strategy in mind: annoy the player until he pay money for in game items to ease the suffering...
So what you have to expect is:
-Long AFK "play" is require. So keeping the game in system tray while processing.
-"Events & Reward" generally are about being online 5-6h a day at least, daily attendance, repeat every day few fetch/produce/kill quest.
-Pay for in game items. The game is absolute hell if you do not pay. In particular, small inventory, overweight, unnecessary travel for to perform small chores, manual looting of the hundred mob/hour you kill... will drag down the play experience.
-Absolutely uncalibrated grow. Rushed early level advancement, and grind hell after liv 56.
-Uncalibrated PvE. Let's clear this. You are not rewarded to go to challenging  zones. This game is made to kill armies of mob, very fast. And it's fun for a while. However this means that you need to go in zones where you outgear and outlevel the enemy, and stick to those areas killing the same mobs for hours, days months. Otherwise, it become exponentially longer to advance, in a super grind game not a wise decision.
-PvP... is fun only when you duel someone of you same level/gear-level. In those rare occasion is rewarding challenging and require skill. But is a rare condition being extremely gear based in the extreme majority of case you outgear or be outgeared making the fight too easy and not rewarding for the stronger, and annoyingly hopeless for the weaker.

-Weak and butchered story. Story is fragmented. Mostly because accelerating the grow in early level. You will solo kill in 2 hit "cooperative Bosses". You will encounter block and jumps in the story... as part of the story was cut off, put as optional, moved to a later part of the game... the narration as result is a complete mess. So basically the main story  and 1-50 level growth is a long tutorial.
-RNG. Everything is random. That it makes sense or not. This give a “slot machine” feel to all the game. Luck worth more than skill.
Loot? RNG, ok. Even if a bit exaggerated. You can get in few kill what other grind for month to get if you are luky.
Gear Enchanting? RNG, with damaging/destroying resources, so be prepared to blow month of grind worth of material in a try to upgrade something .
But they extend this to things that don’t make any sense. For example in the desert you get A debuf that require to drink water. Nice. But is RNG. So sometime you can travel in the desert for 30minutes without getting the debuf… and sometime you can get it every 30 seconds. For my travel route in the desert, 20 minutes on cammel I drink from 0 to 30 water bottles. -_-

This game is extremely fun and addicting. This is a small mix of League of Legends + Minecraft + TF2, with it's own unique mechanics. There is a small bit of a learning curve, but you can learn it very fast.
Pros
-Fun and addicting
-Not pay2win
You pay for skins, you can pay for heroes, but still get them for free. Perks are also buyable, but only with the free currency.
-A ton of maps
Of course, some are better than others.
-Each game is different
You build and fortify your base, so each game will be different.
-Not region locked
If your friend is from EU and you're from NA you guys can still queue together, unlike a fair amount of games.
Cons
-High queue times
During weekends and afternoon weekdays the queue times are short. But other than that they can be a bit long, and you will run into the same people a lot. They are also a lot longer for players just starting out so you don't run into people who stomp you.
-Unbalanced
The game is a bit unbalanced for sure.
-Ranks
Your rank can only go up, not down. This removes the stress from the game, but rank is less skill and more grind. They are fixing this soon (maybe) with a new ranked mode.
Overall, I for sure recommend this game. It is a ton of fun

So... Another Zombie Apocalypse has landed. As an avid fan of this genre, I had to satisfy my curiosity, when it went on sale.
The short version:
- 1st person exploration, in urban (and rural) environment, with both fixed and static storylines, sandbox-style play (with crafting, but without building-aspects). Melee plays a large role, but ranged and environmental weapons are present too.
- Decent campaign mode. Pretty good coops-mode, and various Zombie-modes and participational MP-aspects present. And the ability to turn those things on and off.
- Good alround graphics and physics (aside from a bug or glitch, here and there. But nothing too aggravating, given the complexity of actions possible.
- Horror, blood and gore is definately present lol. Dont go into the nights, unless you know what youre doing!
- Story and acting is pretty good (havent played the extra content yet, though).
- Similarities to other games: Fallout 4, Mirrors Edge, Max Payne, Mad Max: Fury Road, Dead Island etc.
Long version:
The game is definately well produced, afaik. The gameplay is relatively easy to jump into, but hard to master optimally (untill you got all your skills and bling weapons ofc!).
I had great fun playing the first half of the game. Its easy to just jump in, and have some casual fun, and if youre into grinding, thats possible too. Easter-eggs are there for the picking, and the content keeps coming, if you like all sorts of gamestyles, vanity-gear and such. But its not needed to play, really.
The FPS is pretty good and the system for Coop etc. seems well designed, so far.
Ive had a little trouble with some Parkour-elements, that seem to be a little broken, in some areas, but its not too much, imo.
After a little while, it does get a little monotoneous, the environment, but as you discover more areas, and start looking at the DLCs and extra gamestyles, Id imagine that will help keeping the game fresh.
Over all, its a pretty good game, with more potential for the future. I bought it on sale (24 EU) and thats definately a good price for it. I MIGHT have bought it at full price, but Im sort of borderline on that, still. Lots of other games takes up my attention too, so Im spreading my gaming-funds so I can afford more titles, in my STEAM-library :-)
The game for me, is NOT a title, that would make me dump all other games (even for a while). After a few hours of gameplay, Id assume people would love to play something else, for a bit lol. The heads-smashing and visuals (as mentioned) does get a bit boring, after playing too long. But thats ofc subjective. I sure love to jump in, still, once in awhile, when I need to hit something hard lol.

Civlization V is one of the few games that stay engraved in your heart foverer. I still remember the time that I was playing Civilization IV and was expecting Civilization V to come out in a few months. It was a great period of time, of change, of magnificence. Some of the most beautiful and inspirational games were released between 2001-2012. Civilization V was released in the dusk of the Golden Age, but this was the most beautiful time for the gaming industry, a time where the advancement and combination graphics and gameplay were at their peak, and new ways to approach each game design had been brought up successfully, as the old ones had been mastered. Civilization V was a revolutionary game, a legacy that lasted six whole years, having been loved by both critics and the audience.
There was something unique about Civilization V when I firstly played it. I was anticipating the game, but I could not buy it on its release date due to financial problems. When I eventually played it I was stunned, and loved the texture, the music, and the gameplay was immersive. The unit formations and the map design were excellent. The UI was beautiful and as it can be noticed, each DLC adds a different and more artistic touch to it. The Complete Edition is beautiful and all its DLCs are worth the money, but only on sale. The two exapnsion packs improve gameplay and Gods and Kings brought the original game to its peak. Brave New World changed it significantly, bringing new features that were missing from the original one, creating a new ascpect for future gameplay, as it can be seen for Beyond Earth.
Civilization V is a wonderful game. It has passed the test of time and has created some of the fondest memories I have in the Gaming World. It is a treasure of strategy, knowledge, as it allows you to learn facts about the history of man, and above all it is a piece of art. It will always be remembered and will be always the one that make us continue playing for one more turn.

A fun little indie platformer. To beat each stage, you'll need to take snapshots of objects, manipulating them so you can reach the end.
Taking snapshots makes items disappear, and pasting them back into the world causes them to reappear for you to use. Momentum is preserved in the snapshot, so items flying by will continue flying by when pasted back into the world. You are limited 3 snapshots at any one time.
The game rates your performance on four criteria: finding and taking a snapshot of the hidden item (and taking them to the end of the stage, which means taking up one of your three snapshot slots), whether you beat the stage under par time (you've gotta be FAST), whether you collected all the stars in the stage (which are slightly attracted to you, making collection a touch easier), and whether you found all the stars in the chapter (each chapter consists of three stages).
This rating system makes the game addicting and very replayable. Each completed level's progress is saved upon completion, allowing you to immediately retry a particular stage to perfect it.
The artwork is beautiful and colorful. The game is highly polished quality. I highly recommend this fun little game.

On the surface, this game seems to be your regular Hack and Slash game. But it is much more.
It is built upon a foundation that Titan Quest provided a decade ago and it's no wonder people consider Grim Dawn to be the "spiritual successor" to the former. It runs on the very same engine and many things were carried over from Titan Quest, such as dual classes and parts of the crafting system.
In terms of character development, Crate Entertainment is miles ahead of both Grinding Gear and Blizzard (and probably every other developer). Grim Dawn features a dual class system, which means you can actually choose two character classes. You can choose your first class on level 2, and upon reaching level 10, a second class can be chosen. I didn't like it at first, I quickly learned to love it, as it gives you so many possibilities. Level-Ups actually feel rewarding and it really feels like you're "building" your character. It's glorious. Naturally, you get attribute points and skill points to spend when you gain a level, but there also is an extra layer of character development called "devotion". Now and then you come across shrines that have to be "cleansed" to get "devotion points". These points can be spend on a star map of sorts. Some people seem to compare this to Path of Exile's giant skill tree for some reason, but it's actually quite different. Devotion points are spent to unlock stars in a star constellation. Each constellation is aligned to an "affinity", so your first point is spent by choosing your affinity, which determines which constellations you can spend points on. Every star provides passive bonuses, like increased damage, resistances, armor, attributes, things like that. Once a constellation is complete, it grants an affinity bonus which unlocks further constellations to spend points on, and so on. This "devotion system" can massively improve your character, and in many cases even define it.
The crafting system is rather interesting. And it's great. The blueprints and materials required for crafting items can usually be found dropping from monsters or in chests. However, the interesting thing is that even crafting materials can be crafted! Some of the materials needed to craft items can only be acquired by crafting, and some items require other items, so things can become rather complex and crafting an item often isn't as easy as it seems.
The land of Cairn consists of beautiful, detailed and carefully crafted levels. And it has everything. There are dark swamps, snowy mountains, ruined cities, grim dungeons, barren wastelands, infested farmlands, and much more. The areas are also rather big and there are lots of secrets. Even after playing through the game several times, I sometimes find things that I never saw before.
And the lore! Holy crap, there is so much lore and background story in this game. You could spend ages just reading.
The only negative thing I can find about this game is the lack of voice acting. So far, only NPCs related to the main quests are voiced, everything else is text only.
My love for this game goes deep, and I haven't had this much fun playing an ARPG since Diablo II (and to be honest, Grim Dawn feels more like a proper successor to Diablo II than Diablo III does). This seems a bold statement, but I think Grim Dawn is without question the best modern Hack and Slash game at the moment. It just crushes the competition and I can't wait for the expansion.

I've been playing bdo ever since Korea had it in open beta. The game is definitely worth the $5 for the adventure, but the little issues like the Karma system and performance issues in cities along with the RNG is just not worth it. Don't be deceived by the people who put in reviews and you see thousands of hours on their playtime. Endgame is you, literally AFK lifeskilling in order to make silver to enchant your gear. The game is advertised as a PvP game but it's simply a PvE game with PvP added into it. You are punished for open world pvp. You lose karma for kills you get on other players and once you go negative, you are no longer able to go into cities due to the guards attacking you and if you end up dying you lose enchantments on your gear if you are negative. If you want to enjoy the game, you'll need atleast $30 for pets or else you won't be able to grind efficiently seeing how picking up loot is incredibly slow and tedious. By the time you finish picking up your loot with other players without pets, the mobs will have already spawn. There is a weight system but that can be fixed by purchasing more weight. The costume bonus isn't that much, it only gives a 10% exp bonus. The only content this game has to offer is Grinding mobs with friends and a pvp event called node wars. Don't even bother playing without a Value pack, once you use a value pack (Freemium subscription) you won't want to play without it. Without a value pack you dont get the full value of any items you sell on the auction house. The Auction house is also a mess. If you want to start working on getting endgame gear. Yes you can buy it from the auction house, but it's an RNG system where it randomly picks one person that is able to win the bid. It took me months to get a full set. It also gets to a point where you can have so much ingame currency but you won't be able to do anything with it, because the rest of the game is too dependant on RNG.
tl;dr Your typical Korean RNG mmorpg, has a lot of issues that still need to be fixed. Only worth the money for the adventure because you'll get your moneys worth out of that.

For what it is.. this game is the best MMO on the market IMHO. Hands down, best looking world, fantastic character customization, none better for sure. Like many MMO's, there are pro's and con's of course. The game world is absolutely insanely massive. You will never run out of quests or things to do. PVP is on par with others in the large scale wars, again, pro's con's, PVE is great although a bit easy IMHO. It's a great time burner, and if you willing to invest say $50-100 you will get all you will ever need for years of gameplay unless you want total hardcore mode.
Folks know the grind, and yes its a VERY grindy game. But there is lots to make up for it. The entire game is built around being AFK friendly and has one of the best "AFK minimize game and do other stuff" options.. you know.. for people with a life, family, work, etc... That alone is a deal maker IMHO, as i can leave the game on while im at work or sleeping and make some progress/coins!
Gear, yeah, RNG sucks, and fail stacks and repeat fails is discouraging for anyone, even infuriating make you want to kill a puppy type of suck, but also lets mention, hell you really only need 1 set of good gear for 10 characters if you have em. You can easily swap gear to an alt and steamroll stuff. Coin is easy for the most part to make, so if you hate the RNG, simply buy it off the market place, although not a guarantee, its doable for sure.
If you are looking for a game to play for 1 or more years at a lesuirely pace , or hardcore if you so desire, then this game is for you!! Pick it up on sale if you can, and get the best package available, as the 2x 30-day packs are worth it alone as well as the free pet.

I was originally skeptical of buying a $16 indie game, but it turns out that it was WELL worth the money.
Slay the Spire is when you take all the elements of a roguelike, RPG, and deckbuilder, and mash them together. A lot of times when you mash genres like that it doesn't come out too good or it has extreme flaws that make it underwhelming and boring. This game doesn't have that feeling. It doesn't feel unfinished, it doesn't feel bland, it doesn't feel too easy or too hard, and most of all it doesn't feel like an early access money-grab.
This game was fantastic. I beat the game in 16 hours and while there isn't many rewards for beating the game, I still have more cards and relics to unlock for future playthroughs. I will for sure be revisiting this game whenever updates come out.
Honestly, Slay the Spire is one of my top 5 roguelikes of all time. Probably the best one to come out in 2017 too next to Dead Cells.

You follow a small northern house: the Forresters as their good pacific lives turns into a messed up dispute with the Whitehills and Ramsay Bolton.
Every choice you make has an impact on the outcome of the plot, or so they said... Your choices don't really affect the ending, no matter what you do! I get that this is not a "and they lived happily ever after" kind of story, making justice to GOT's fame of being unforgivingly cruel, but it is really frustrating... It's not a bad game, the characters are interesting and I have hopes that the second game will be better, but I felt a little empty in the end.
Do I reccomend it? Yeah, it is still a good game (but kind of overpriced).
Will you end up crying and hating yourself? No doubt.

I've never written a review before but this game deserves one. I got the enhanced edition on sale and it was a steal. The main game is outstanding, the parkour actually made me feel sick and sweaty climbing towers! A testament to the graphic quality, you feel hundreds of feet up and stomach churns. The main story is quite short but there's so much to do it doesn't matter. Its funny in places and dark in others. The night is genuinely scary and you can easily find yourself frantically seeking shelter as night approaches. The zombie killing is satisfying with an excellent crafting system - i guarantee you'll feel genuine joy getting King upgrades. You can weight your weapons inventory with your favoured type...me its machete and sickle, others prefer the heavier two-handed weapons. The zombie types are varied enough and taking down a Volatile is satisfying cos it aint easy. Gameplay is easy to grasp and after a slow start as you begin to upgrade your skills and weapons, you can use a combination of stealth and slaughter to reach your goals. It also has plenty of secret areas and access. The Following expansion is also excellent with the addition of driving available and some extra content like special military crates for exceptional buggy upgrades. In short a well-made highly addictive game...hence my 600 hours playing overall! If you're squeamish about heights or get motion sickness you might want to avoid this...but it would be your loss. The best thing about it is even in normal mode its not that easy, you will have plenty of epic fails :). Enjoy!

Dying Light seems like another zombie game and just by looking at the basics it is. However, it’s such a well-made, feature rich and captivating game that dismissing it as just a zombie game would be a disservice.
The city of Harran is in crisis. Zombies are roaming the streets and the whole place has been quarantined. The player takes a role of an agent whose mission is to infiltrate the city and find some data about the incident. The basic premise is nothing special, but i like the tone: While there are some good news, this is not a game where the player is saving everything. Many of the missions have gruesome outcomes and unavoidable deaths. While not anything mind blowing, i liked the story elements.
Movement is key in Dying Light, be it running jumping, sliding or climbing. The game has an exellent parkour system, which lets you climb on walls etc. with ease. Since zombies mostly roam the streets in great numbers, running on rooftops is the only way to get anywhere alive. This is one of the things that sets Dying Light apart from other games. It’s often preferrable to avoid enemies, instead of taking them on. Playing changes dramatically depending on the time of day. Daytime is when zombies roam the streets in hordes but as they are slow, it’s easier to survive. Night time goes into full survival mode: Amount of zombies is reduced dramatically but instead Volatiles hunt at night. These are extremely fast creatures which can climb and run faster than the player. They are lured by sight and sound, so sneaking is the only way to stay alive. The difference in gameplay truly is like night and day.
Another really striking thing is the city itself, which is divided into two large areas. The Following adds also a huge countryside to the game. While the streets don’t have NPC characters minding their own business (for obvious reasons) the amount of detail in the environment is staggering. Every house is littered with trash, furniture, clothes and all sorts of things which make the place look really lived in. There is also some exellent environmental storytelling, usually about the last desperate moments of some poor souls life. These kind of things are everywhere and the sense of wonder stays strong. I feel like i’ve only seen half of the details, which speaks volumes about the lenghts at which the developers went to flesh out the world.
Places can be searched for supplies which are then used in the crafting system. It lets players to create their own weapons, bombs, healing items etc. All upgrades are found as blueprints which gives a recipe with various requirements. These then must be acquired from the city or bought from shopkeepers. For example nails can be added to a baseball bat to make it even worse for the zombie in the receiving end. The list of recipes is long but there were a lot of which never got used since better ones were available. As the player levels up, better basic weapons become available. Also the weapons have limited durability and will eventually break so there is a constant need to get new weapons and materials.
The game features a leveling system, which is divided into 4 (5 in The Following) categories: Survivor, which is leveled by completing quests, Power by fighting, Agility by running and jumping. The Following adds driving to the mix. Last are Legend levels which open after any one of the previous three has been maxed out. Skills gained by these levels make a lot of difference to the gameplay. By the end of the game you can use grappling hook, run indefinitely, fight without getting tired and with added moves and so on. At no part of the experience can it be called easy though. On the middle difficulty every zombie group is potentially lethal and Volatiles are always a serious threat. There are also gang members who have guns and also are to be taken seriously. Game seems to scale the enemy difficulty which keeps the player on his toes. Some of the experience is permanently lost upon death and the penalty is quite hard on later levels. So there is plenty of difficulty for those who seek challenge.
There are a lot of missions, side missions and challenges to complete so content-wise the complete edition is really worth the asking price. There are also multiple difficulties, a new game plus etc. The legend level system has some 250 levels which is an insane amount and will take ages to achieve.
Biggest issue that i have with the game is the enemy AI. They are as mindless as is to be expected, but there appears to be an set amount which are ”active” in an area around the player, while others just stand around. Let’s say there is a marketplace with about 40 zombies in there. It looks impressive but only about ten of those are actually reacting to the player (coming towards etc). After you kill one, another one becomes active and so on. It’s clearly a system resource saving limitation or something along those lines. All of the zombies present can be killed though, but the limitation is too obvious to not effect the experience. This makes setting traps also kind of useless, since luring a large group into places just doesn’t work.
That aside, technically Dying Light looks really good and runs suprisingly well. It also never crashed or even stuttered while loading or anything. Really solid game. Especially the lighting deserves praise. It gets absolutely pitch black during night and sneaking around with just a flashlight is really atmospheric. I completed the game with an Xbox360 controller and it mostly works well since absolute precision is not needed in a melee focused game.
Also, and this is a big thing, the whole game can be played seamlessly in co-op with up to three friends! It works wonderfully and while players must be doing the same quest, they are free to move about in the gameworld. Only indoor sections and talking parts need all players and there is a handy teleport system to get the players where they need to be. Mechanics are not built around co-op though, so you are not tasked to turn a valve at the same time, but while other player is turning, it’s good to have someone watching the back. It’s one of the best co-op experiences ever and a blast to play!
Despite it’s clichéd setting, Dying Light is a remarkable game that deserves a lot of praise. It’s a tense single player experience, awesome co-op game, notable in it’s open world and also solidly made. None of the mechanics are the best of their kind in gaming, but come close second or maybe third, which is suprising given how many different mechanics there are. Recommended!

I've spent a lot of time on this game, and I keep coming back to it. It's a challenging, engaging game, no doubt about it. It's easy to get hyped up on XCOM 2 (ETA: less than a month as of review), but this game has charm. Sure, stuff like forced failure in the form of abductions and unusual glitches mean the game isn't perfect. But no game is.
It's hard to describe the feeling I get from playing XCOM, because it is like no other game I've played. It's not forgiving. RNG will get in the way every day. Your soldiers will die. You will cry. But you will get up, and try again. You will get better, and try again. And you will strike at increasingly higher difficulties, hopefully achieving the venerable I/I run. The fact that this game pulls no punches means that every action, every death, and most of all, every victory, means something.

Strategy games not your kind of thing? This game will change your mind. It's an extremely fun turn-based strategy game with a cool cinematic action cam (that you can disable if you don't like that sort of thing or if you want to speed up the gameplay a bit). There is also a little bit of "base management", where you decide how things operate at your HQ. It fits into the larger theme of this game where choices have consequences. While the game can be challenging, it is definitely not hard to learn. Throughout my entire playing, I never got bored of it because as you progress throughout the game, you get new weapons, new enemies, new abilities, etc. and have to adjust your tactics correspondingly. I only have the base game and no DLC, and I've barely touched the multiplayer (only played a minute or two before I remembered I had to go to work, this game is that addicting!), and I would still nonetheless highly recommend it. I heard the Enemy Within DLC adds a lot to the game.
Some minor issues I have with this game is that the user interface seems to be designed with consoles in mind. The camera control is a bit wonky, especially when the camera is backed up against the edge of the map or it's really high up. You can pivot your camera 90 degrees but this only allows 4 different rotations of the camera. Since XCOM 2 is being designed with a focus on PC, these shouldn't be a problem. The text is too big, and generally this isn't a problem UNTIL information boxes that can't fit all the text have it slowly auto-scroll down after a time limit (and they don't let you scroll yourself). Also, another problem with the large text info boxes is that they sometimes get in the way "free-aiming". Things like grenades, rockets, and Rift. An example would be this picture:
You can't see the blue mouse arrow but it is approximately in the center of the circle. Unfortunately, that's overlapping with the text box. Not just that, but "free-aiming" can get very difficult to control some times. My recommendation is to just move the mouse slowly.
Sometimes you can't see how my red health bars enemies when you're selecting a(n) enemy to fire at and they list hit chance and crit chance. Can be a minor annoyance when you're trying to select the enemy with the most HP to shoot at, or the least or just any certain amount.
Trying to finely control elevation can be difficult. I'd say 99% of the time the higher you are, the better (unless doorway arch is blocking your view), but at times I can either choose a fairly low elevation to hover at with my Archangel or Hover SHIV, or go around to the very top of the building (so that you're standing on or hovering above the ceiling), which is definitely not what I want.
Selecting teammates who are hovering through clicking on them can be quite difficult (i.e. Archangel armor or Hover SHIV)
There also seems to be the rare line-of-sight issue, where you clearly have a direct shot at your enemy but the game doesn't think so, see these 2 pics:
Also, sometimes this game tabs out and switches to my desktop. Not much of a problem because I can switch it back but hopefully this gets fixed in XCOM 2.

First off, let me lay it all down on the table so those who are steadfast with their opinions on this particular title can disregard me right off the bat. The most I've seen of the show was around the first half of the first season, as my interest fell on the books rather than the show, so I stopped watching. Thankfully, for the most part, the Books and the Show are 1:1 in terms of story, the show not really deviating too much from the novels. So I was able to jump in with virtually no confusion as to the events and the world that envelops them.
In short, haven't seen much of HBO's
, but have read every volume of
. I was worried that it would suck, as most people. Telltale has earned my love with Season's One and Two of the
, as their method of storytelling is rather superb. Regardless, I went into the first episode relatively neutral, with leanings toward the game sucking elephant♥♥♥♥♥♥
♥♥♥♥. Telltale's done it again...
There's nothing better than delving into a world that has been fully realized to a ♥♥♥♥ing "T". Every single character, be it their mannerisms, physical characteristics, past, interactions- EVERYTHING feels real and believable, aligning with the books (and the show I suppose) perfectly. This game earned major brownie points with me by actually creating a major plot event, that we only got to see a fraction of in the books, at the VERY ♥♥♥♥ING BEGINING. Going through it initially, for a fan, it feels like a dream. Telltale managed to represent the show, and by extension, the source material amazingly. Westeros is as cold, political and unforgiving as it has ever been.
You follow the exploits of the small, old and noble House Forrester, bannermen to House Stark and Lord's of Ironrath. In the midst of the War of the Five Kings, the story centers various members of the house, stories spanning from the North, the Wall, the South and Essos. No qualms can really be given, I found everyone of the characters that was focused on to be engaging and believable. Choices you're forced to make have the capacity to have real gravity, the illusion of branching choices holding very well on your first run through.
Unfortunately, quite a few of the decisions you  have to make can be INCREDIBLY contrived. At least sixty percent of the time, out of the two choices given, you could imagine several better, much more logical solutions; or when you deliberately avoid a certain action, only to have the character carry it out regardless. In these moments, you feel less like the actual character and more like some invisible ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ giving advice on a course of action. It's annoying and occurs way more than it should.
The game, graphically speaking, is passable. Though with each passing game with a so called "stylized" look, I can only help but point out games that look FANTASTIC and are also stylized. BioShock Infinite, Overwatch, Dota 2, Wind Waker- point is, this variant of the look feels like a copout. It was fine in 2012, but dragging that same look into 2014 doesn't look good. It makes you look lazy.
Also, most of House Forrester is just a carbon copy of House Stark. While largely remedied by them being put into vastly different positions, you can't help but mistake a few for their Stark counterparts. Some of them even look the part for christ sake. Its unfortunate and a lost opportunity to actually create new characters.
Some minor bug bears I have are with Ramsay Snow and the last episode. Ramsay is a prevelant character in the books and show, having yet to suffer dire circumstances in either the books or the show thus far, so he might as well be invincible. Maybe he's in on this fact, as he operates with wild abandon,  as non of his actions will come back to bite him later. Plot armor if you will. The ending on the other hand, was just ♥♥♥♥ing weird considering the rest of the season. Magic was something that was more subtle and obscure in the books and assumedly the show, adding to their mystery. Here, it seems odd and very, VERY bombastic. The payoff is decent, but the magic aspects leave you a bit bewildered.
Still, I thoroughly enjoyed the game the whole way through. The aforementioned negatives would leave me hesitant to recommend to a non fan, but then I think about the world, choices that do matter, and the non templative characters, I happily point fans and non-fans alike toward this title. It has its fair share of problems, but they fail to overshadow the fun, engaging aspects, Its a good time that I would recommend wholeheartedly.

On the surface, this game seems to be your regular Hack and Slash game. But it is much more.
It is built upon a foundation that Titan Quest provided a decade ago and it's no wonder people consider Grim Dawn to be the "spiritual successor" to the former. It runs on the very same engine and many things were carried over from Titan Quest, such as dual classes and parts of the crafting system.
In terms of character development, Crate Entertainment is miles ahead of both Grinding Gear and Blizzard (and probably every other developer). Grim Dawn features a dual class system, which means you can actually choose two character classes. You can choose your first class on level 2, and upon reaching level 10, a second class can be chosen. I didn't like it at first, I quickly learned to love it, as it gives you so many possibilities. Level-Ups actually feel rewarding and it really feels like you're "building" your character. It's glorious. Naturally, you get attribute points and skill points to spend when you gain a level, but there also is an extra layer of character development called "devotion". Now and then you come across shrines that have to be "cleansed" to get "devotion points". These points can be spend on a star map of sorts. Some people seem to compare this to Path of Exile's giant skill tree for some reason, but it's actually quite different. Devotion points are spent to unlock stars in a star constellation. Each constellation is aligned to an "affinity", so your first point is spent by choosing your affinity, which determines which constellations you can spend points on. Every star provides passive bonuses, like increased damage, resistances, armor, attributes, things like that. Once a constellation is complete, it grants an affinity bonus which unlocks further constellations to spend points on, and so on. This "devotion system" can massively improve your character, and in many cases even define it.
The crafting system is rather interesting. And it's great. The blueprints and materials required for crafting items can usually be found dropping from monsters or in chests. However, the interesting thing is that even crafting materials can be crafted! Some of the materials needed to craft items can only be acquired by crafting, and some items require other items, so things can become rather complex and crafting an item often isn't as easy as it seems.
The land of Cairn consists of beautiful, detailed and carefully crafted levels. And it has everything. There are dark swamps, snowy mountains, ruined cities, grim dungeons, barren wastelands, infested farmlands, and much more. The areas are also rather big and there are lots of secrets. Even after playing through the game several times, I sometimes find things that I never saw before.
And the lore! Holy crap, there is so much lore and background story in this game. You could spend ages just reading.
The only negative thing I can find about this game is the lack of voice acting. So far, only NPCs related to the main quests are voiced, everything else is text only.
My love for this game goes deep, and I haven't had this much fun playing an ARPG since Diablo II (and to be honest, Grim Dawn feels more like a proper successor to Diablo II than Diablo III does). This seems a bold statement, but I think Grim Dawn is without question the best modern Hack and Slash game at the moment. It just crushes the competition and I can't wait for the expansion.

TL;DR: the "de facto" best Star Trek style spaceship commander simulator, in a "rogue-light", addictive and challenging gamplay, with undeniable charm, an impressive atmosphere, and absolutely stunning soundtrack. Multiple ships, ship systems, weapons, crew races and their abilities, all expanded upon with the FREE Advanced Edition, provide a variety of play styles and endless replayability.
As soon as that music starts, it gets to you all over again: you're in someplace special. FTL is a lovely game. In FTL you control a medium-sized spaceship and its crew carrying vital data to the Federation fleet. You are being pursued by the Rebel fleet and must stay ahead of it by doing FTL jumps between beacons of each sector and from sector to sector until you finally reach your main fleet. Problem is, it's an hostile universe out there, and you'll never know what you'll encounter on the next beacon...
In the beginning you can pick between multiple ship types (that you unlock as you play), each with different crew compliments of different races and system types that will make for different play styles. The meat of the game plays as a strategy real-time (pausable) "rogue-light", where you control your ship and crew from a top-down view, and you need to manage which crew member mans which ship system (engines, shields, weapons, helm, etc etc) for a better performance, manage when and how to fire weapons and also manage the allocation of power to each system. Crew members of different races have different bonus: some repair systems quicker, some provide extra power to the room they're in, some are excellent fighters, some are immune to fire, etc. You don't have power for everything, and also depending what systems/weapons you have and your crew type, you have to adapt and optimize your strategy and approach to your encounters.
And you'll encounter a lot: other ships, some hostile, some friendly, some you're not quite sure; there's even mini-quests and mini optional "story arcs" that you can go on. Not only that but also dangerous asteroid fields, nebulas that interfere with your shields and sensors, suns that burst out flares and set your ship on fire. Each "run" will make for a different tale of your adventure. The real-time battles, despite being pausable, are usually pretty tense. You'll mostly be trying to damage or disable enemy shields and damaging their systems, such as shields and weapons, until you destroy their ship. Or you can beam up a boarding party, kill everyone and take control of the ship, or you can bypass their shields by hurling missiles or beaming up bombs (limited supply of these), etc, etc. Or you can just run for it if things are too hot. And the best thing is, the enemies can do the exact same things! Battles will damage your systems, breach your hull, ignite fires, and that's where you'll need your best managing skills to keep things under control on the heat of battle. And sometimes things just happen too fast, you were not prepared, and you're blown into oblivion and have to start from the beginning. It's an unforgiving universe... After each battle you win, you can get random upgrades but you'll mostly accumulate scrap, which can be used to upgrade your ship's system and go to stores to buy consumables (like FTL jump fuel and missiles) or weapons and systems, or even recruit more crew members. You'll need scrap badly, but how far is it reasonable to go and risk potentially lethal encounters on its pursuit?
Between that and much more, like controlling blast doors and managing oxygen supply in case of a fire or breach, or also venting rooms in your ship to put out fires or choke intruders to death, FTL manages to be the most complete and realistic spaceship simulator, Star Trek style, that I've ever know, despite its 2D, top-down, pixel art style. You can only "save&quit", if you lose, you have to start from the beginning. Some "runs" will go better than others, it always depends on your ability to adapt and optimize your play style to what crew, ship and systems you have, but it also depends a bit on being fortunate enough on finding a really good upgrade or weapon after a battle or on a store. That can be a bit frustrating, but that's just what it is, if you don't have what it takes to survive, you won't. You'll learn a lot from your mistakes, and after finishing the game, you'll realise that you couldn't have done it if you hadn't learned so much. So it rewards you for your failures and efforts.
The soundtrack is just absolutely brilliant, one of the best in my memory, being part charming old-school style 8-bit tunes, part dreamy sci-fi space sounds, it provides a unique atmosphere that immerses completely. The overall style oozes charms and tender care, despite being a very challenging and unforgiving game.
With the addition of Advanced Edition, completely free, bringing more races, more ships, more weapons and systems, and also more encounters, the game has an impressive amount of content that can get you on it for dozens of hours. If you like space sci-fi strategy games, particularly commanding ships Star Trek style, this is for you. If you get frustrated easily with a challenge, maybe approach it carefully, but you'll be missing out.

Some time ago I was recommended the Hyperdimension series, which led to me getting my hands on Hyperdimension Neptunia Re;Birth1, which I thoroughly enjoyed. Fast forward a while and I end getting my hands on this one. Despite being skeptical about trying the first game of the series, that didn’t happen with the second entry because I knew what I was getting into.
First of all, the story in Re;Birth2 doesn’t follow the events of the previous game, at least not at full extent. The game takes place in Gamindustri, a world which is divided into 4 different nations - Lastation, Lowee, Leanbox and Planeptune - each with their own CPU (Console Patron Unit) presiding over it. Prior to the start of the game, there was a fight between the 4 CPUs and Arfoire, the antagonist of the game, which led to the CPUs being sent to the Gamindustri Graveyard. Your journey starts 3 years after this last fight, when IF and Compa, both friends of the CPUs, go to the Gamindustri Graveyard in order to save them. Of course, not everything goes as planned and they end up getting ambushed while attempting to save their friends, only managing to save Nepgear, Planeptune’s CPU younger sister. After saving Nepgear your task is to save the rest of the CPUs in order to restore order to Gamindustri and defeat Arfoire once and for all.
As with the other games in this series, the story is told as if you were playing a visual novel. You can’t change the way the story unfolds, at least during these parts of the game. You’re just pressing a button to move to the next piece of dialogue. As with the previous game, not every piece of dialogue is voice acted, which is somewhat of a bummer for me, but even more so, I’m not finding the plot of Re;Birth2 to be as interesting and captivating as the one from the first iteration of this series. In terms of writing and its depth, it’s competent, nothing of extraordinary but it does offer a lot of fan service, even if sometimes it feels like a bunch of clichés.
As it was already mentioned, the game has a visual novel component, which is to deliver the story through dialogue, and then it has the actual gameplay part of it, most of which is composed of turn based combat. You’ll spend a fair amount of time on the world map and other places accessible from here, such as shops, dungeons, the guild where you can take quests, talk to different people, craft and sell items, among other things.
You’ll be spending your time either doing the main story quests, which will either have you speaking to someone or going into a dungeon after something or someone. You might also spend some of your time doing side quests for the Guild to level up your characters and/or increase the shares of one of the Gamindustri nations. Depending on the characters you choose for your party, and the equipment you get, you may or may not need to grind in order to be able to progress through the main story quests.
Eitherways, grinding is not that much of a hassle if you come to it since enemies respawn some time after defeating them. In terms of combat, it’s pretty much the same as most of the rest of the games in the Hyperdimension Neptunia series. You walk around in the dungeons in real time and you trigger the turn-based combat when you engage an enemy or touch it. During each turn, combat range is represented by a circle around each character which represents the space in which you can move and attack from. When attacking, you can use physical, magical attacks or various special combos, as well as healing items.
There’s also a new addition to the series, which is Stella’s dungeon. This is a small mini game in which you send Stella to dungeons to get loot for you. However, if she dies she will loose the equipment she had equipped but you’ll still keep what you’ve got up until then.
All in all, Re;Birth2: Sisters Generation sticks to the extremely solid and enjoyable JRPG formula of the previous game, despite that in terms of plot it isn’t as interesting and captivating. The dialogue remains rather cheesy with a lot of humour while, at the same time, providing a lot of fan service.
The recycling of assets in dungeons (e.g. textures and layouts) is still a problem but that hasn’t kept me from enjoying what actually matters in these sections, which is the combat.
If you’re a fan of the Hyperdimension Neptunia series I’d say that this is a no brainer and you should get it. If you’re new to the series, this is a good entry point since it ignores the events of the first game, so take your pick.

is a post-apocalyptic real-time strategy adventure. You are Brad, an easy-going road warrior whose life gets turned upside down when your village is attacked by gangsters while you and your friends were away on an escort mission.
: The setting is obviously inspired by the
universe as your characters drive metal plate-reinforced, machine-gun mounted cars, trucks and dune buggies, gameplay being an instantly-recognizable
style for moving your units and attacking other units. You control a set amount of characters, which can dismount their cars to enter buildings, turrets or other vehicles you encounter. Your main character and a wacky assortment of other "heroes" will level up as they acquire experience from battle. Missions will usually have multiple objectives, and exploring the map of any given mission may uncover sidequests. In-mission story is told through series of dialog, while cut-scenes in-between missions will take the form of comic book panels. The story isn't too bad if perhaps cliché, but it's covered with humor about how sex and alcohol runs the degenerate lives of some of the characters.
: Control is pretty awful and void of any fluidity, pathfinding is a total mess, and vehicles will constantly bump into each other, stop for no reason, get stuck in obstacles such as terrain or blown up enemy cars, drive backwards, and lose any semblance of formation whenever you give orders to multiple vehicles. This makes the gameplay excruciatingly frustrating, testing your patience as you painstakingly try to progress from one mission to another. I cannot stress enough how the unresponsiveness can ruin an RTS. While the story was ok, the writing itself is pretty terrible, filled with typos, misspelling and the worst cheese you can imagine dialogs to have. Graphics show their age, lacking any modern resolution. Yet, even with the lack of high resolutions, the minimap is so small that it's barely usable in any tactical way.

Desert Law is a RTS game released in 2005. As such the graphics are dated and the engine is not the most robust around so this should be taken into consideration.
It is an isometric game, with single-player mode only, a funny (sometimes overdone) story, in a post-apocalyptic setting. Fallout meets Mad Max, kind of thing.
Gameplay:
Contrary to most RTS games around, since the inception of the genre, this one does not feature base-building. What has come to be a key component of the genre.
That in itself, at least to me, is refreshing. The game plays in typical RTS fashion controls with the exception of not having the ability to add units one by one to a group using a modifier key (usually shift). Everything else as far as controls go is like every other RTS.
What is new on the table is the use of vehicles. Your units can enter and exit vehicles (and buildings) and can survive if their vehicle gets blown up. A unit switches their active actions menu depending on if they're on foot or in a vehicle.
The game has a funny backstory that you get to watch in between chapters, in the form of a comic book and there are funny, sometimes to the point of absurd, dialogues inside the campaign missions as well.
The story, as far as I've seen, is full of cliche and sexual innuendo. It is funny enough though that it works for me.
Worthy of note is that the engine feels quite clunky. One may think that it's only reasonable in this time and age, the game is 17 years old, by the time I write this, but there have been older games of the same genre with more responsive engines (a wink to Dune here).
The pathfinding AI routines are also not very advanced. Prepare to micromanage and use the pause button a lot. Not only to think about your strategy but to correct pathing as well.
Graphics:
The game is dated 2005. With that in mind, the graphics are not bad at all. Notice though that there is no support for resolutions higher than 1280x1024 and although there are widescreen resolutions available, the game is not really made with widescreen in mind.
Music/Sound Design:
On this department it is doing ok. The music sounds good and so do the effects. Nothing special though and always minding the fact that it is a game released in 2005.
Pros:
-Interesting twists on the genre.
-Nice comic style story.
-Funny.
Neutral:
-Humour may appear sexist to some. If you are easily offended by sexist stereotypes you may want to avoid it. Also it is quite wacky.
-It is an older game and it shows.
-Single-player only. Some may like that, some may not.
-No base building. Same as above.
Cons:
-Engine and interface feels a bit clunky.
-Pathfind could be A LOT better.
Conclusion:
It is a decent game which perhaps did not age very well. If you are a fan of RTS games, wacky humour, or refreshing twists on the genre, go for it!

This game. The epic stories of my warriors, written in their crimson blood, a sacrifice to safeguard the future of humanity, will inspire generations to come. The alien threat has been pushed back but not beaten, and we stand on the brink of some of the greatest choices that humanity will have to face.
But that's a story for another day, today we remember the brave warriors who gave their last full measure of strength to defend us:
My men were tired. The aliens had landed and we were doing our best to hold them off. There were 6 of us. Myself, a colonel, I was the experienced leader of our team. The other 5 were all armored in white, identical in their helmets and armor, their laser weaponry the finest we could develop. Major Bartley, Major Lambrix, Sergeant Kuznetov, Major Blaskowicz, and Corporal Donovan were there names.
We were outnumbered, outgunned, and outmaneauvered. And then 2 Alien walkers appear. They set up, and we feel a shroud of doom surround us. We know our fates, that many of us will die. We keep fighting. 3, then 4 aliens attack, and we kill them. I faintly hear the sound of the walkers, their weapons primed. I watched in horror as Bartley is sniped by a Muton. Corporal Donovan, our medic rushes over to give him first aid. Then an explosion. When the dust clears, Bartley, Donovan, and Lambrix are all dead. Kuznetov, Blaskowicz, and I shoot wildly, trying to retreat back to the ship. Blaskowicz is quickly sniped, leaving him down but alive. I tell Kuznetov to revive him. Out of the darkness, a plasma bolt catches Kuznetov in the stomach. He crumples over, the blood staining his white armor. He's still alive. I begin to rush to his aid, and then see the walker again. Is my fate going to be the same as that of my other teammates?
I turn back towards the ship, and start running. I can hear Kuznetov still screaming. I keep running, and the sounds of battle slowly fade...
I left my men to die so that I could live. That is the bleak truth of it.
This game made me realize that I'm a selfish coward who sacrifices my men to save myself.
10/10 would desert my men in their hour of need again.

Alan Wake's American Nightmare can be considered a short sequel to the first Alan Wake game as it picks up directly after The Signal and The Writer episodes.
In general, the shooting mechanics and movement feel more crisp and smooth, there is an expanded variety of weapons to use, although most of them function similarly. (Mainly being: High Damage Single Shot, Low Damage Machine Gun or High Damage Shotgun Shot)
In the first game, Flashbangs and Flare Guns used to be the ultimate weapons as they can easily clear all enemies in an area. This is not the case in the sequel. They are only able to take out some weak enemies while their main function is to disable enemies and clear off the darkness.
The story component is short, about 1/3 the length of the original Alan Wake.
However, there is a Arcade mode which puts you in 5 distinct settings and challenges you to score as many points as possible through defeating enemies and maintaining your streak by avoiding damage.
If you enjoyed Alan Wake, this sequel is great fun. Just take your time to explore the areas and listen to the dialogue for a more detailed understanding of Alan Wake's world.
If you did not enjoy Alan Wake, this sequel will not interest you much unless you would really love to try out the improved shooting mechanics and the new enemy types.
If you are thinking about playing either, Alan Wake is a better introduction to the series.

Have you ever wanted to save the world from an evil darkness hell bent on taking over your life before destroying everyone and everything it possibly can? Then this might be the game for you.
Once again you take on the role of Alan Wake and his fight against the encroaching all powerful darkness. Blow away every evil being that wonders into your crosshairs using a large array of weapons, one that would make any gun enthusiast dance with glee. My favourite happened to be the nail gun, simple but deadly. Also the unique ability to use the beam from your flashlight to weaken your foes is back once again, something that I really enjoyed from the original.
The gameplay is very similar to the first title but this time it has a more arcady feel to it, especially with a score attack mode running parallel to the main story. It does add a lot of gameplay value but can be very repetitive continually killing the same sets of enemies over and over again.
As for the story itself, it carries the same dark humour as many other of Remedies titles even using the Twilight zone styled Night Springs as the main way to convey the story. The game is not overly long and does feel repetitive in nature, mainly due to using the same levels over and over but given the time bending storyline that is not surprising. I didn’t get bored at all and had a real desire to find out what happened to our hero in the end and whether or not he would have his happy ending.
If you have played and liked the original then this is a must buy especially if on sale, if not just to complete the story arc from the first game. If you are new to the series don’t start with this one, but buy the original as it is a phenomenal game.
