Video Review:
Grim Dawn is an isometric action RPG in the spirit of Diablo. The premise is as it usually is in games like this. Explore a world with scaled locations and enemies, kill as many as things possible, loot as much stuff as possible, complete the game, and start NG+ to continue trying to max out your character.
What makes Grim Dawn so special is that it has the most in-depth character customization I have ever seen in an action RPG in my entire life. You get stat points which allow you to boost your stats. You can customize your gear, upgrade your gear with special materials, and have two different weapon loadouts. You get to pick from several classes and use hundreds of skillpoints to upgrade active and passive abilities between them in any design you’d like. After that, you get to pick devotions which are these branching talent paths that unlock passive bonuses and chance activation skills to help make you stronger. Combine that with a very simplistic and easy to learn and master combat system revolving around occasional abilities and and clicking to essentially hack and slash, and you have a very fun concept; especially since you can play cooperatively with friends. And this is a small note, but you can’t respec stat points. So if you make a bad choice or click the wrong button, seeing as the buttons are right next to each other, you’re stuck with it.
The story of Grim Dawn is more engaging than I expected from an ARPG. It starts out with your character almost dying by hanging due to possession by the aether which is essentially a interdimensional spiritual energy with a form of sentience. You were saved because the energy left your body to escape death since apparently it can’t survive if you die. The game then immediately contradicts itself by making you fight several aether-possessed corpses and sends you on a journey to defeat the invasion of the aether while building up safe zones by choosing to help persons that can prove useful that you meet in the wilderness or not.One especially cool thing is that the game actually allows you to make choices. These choices only really have cosmetic effects and no real effect on gameplay though. For example, you can choose to save and arm some persons you meet in the wilderness to help you fight the aether. But you never see them again, the enemies do not decrease, and literally the effect of your choice amounts to zilch.
The gameplay has its own problems too. For one, nothing gets marked on the map and you’re not allowed to place your own markers either. Combine that with how level 15 areas can have level 25 dungeons? You’ll likely miss a lot of content unless you take the effort to keep physical notes telling you where everything is. Most quests don’t even get marked on your minimap so to complete them you really just have to run around and explore every nook and cranny. This is a very degressive design choice that makes you feel like you’re playing a game from the early 2000s back when quest tracking wasn’t really considered as important. The game allows you to craft bridges and blow things up too in order to access more content. But none of that gets marked either so unless you have a very good memory, or draw your own map then you’re gonna forget where most of these are never actually ever access that content.
Another problem is that the enemies don’t feel different. No matter what they are, how they look, or what attacks they have? The game feels like you’re fighting the same easy to kill enemies over and over with the exception of legendary and boss units that have some debuffs and buffs that they can cast that regular enemies don’t. This makes the game feel very repetitive and more like a chore. You’ll probably zone out while running around killing these things because no matter what you run into in this game? There’s nothing that can really kill you or even close unless you run into an area that’s five levels above you at least. And even then only really the area boss stands a chance at killing you.
The graphics and sound effects are about what you’d expect from an ARPG. They’re nothing to brag about. But they’re decent. My only complaint about them is that the game has a strange fog that makes things hard to see at the edge of your vision. It’s the same kind of fog that pops up in other games when the quality takes a dip due to an incapability to render that far. But considering Grim Dawn is isometric, the fact that this fog is here makes no sense. Is this game really incapable of delivering a clear crisp isometric image? It appears to be that way; even on max settings.
Overall Grim Dawn is a very fun concept and something that I wish was more fun than it is. There’s just so many bad design choices here that made me have to struggle to keep playing the game. It just wasn’t fun after the first few hours. Grim Dawn is a repetitive, boring, and poorly designed chore. There is no challenge, no organization, and really just no engaging entertainment to be found here anywhere outside of the character customization. I give it a 3/10. It was very badly designed and its production value was very low. Don’t waste your money on it.

You control the fate of House Forrester, an ancient Northern house fiercely loyal to the Starks, now struggling to survive in the wake of the Red Wedding where the Boltons and Lannisters have seized power. Central characters include a squire forced to join the Night's Watch, a son exiled to Essos and a daughter serving as hand maiden to Lady Margaery in King's Landing, all of whom are in a position to aid their house in some way depending on your choices.
Having played the game twice,  I'm still not entirely sure how much of an impact your choices actually have. Especially since there's going to be a second season, it seems some of your choices might only matter later on. That said, still worth playing for the story and the Game of Thrones feel.

You'll realize how far the Online FPS genre has fallen in its pursuit of the lowest common denominator when you play this 20 year old game and it shows you things you've never seen before, game types you've never heard of, and speed that will humble you.
Playing Quake, you begin to see that modern online shooters have leveling systems and gear grinds because most players are already experts when they play their first game. The grind is a way to keep people playing when they have no other reason to play. Quake doesn't need the grind because the progression happens with you instead of your gear: You need to actually practice to get better at this game. And that is a lot more fun than grinding to unlock the next gun in some gear tree.

Have you ever wanted to save the world from an evil darkness hell bent on taking over your life before destroying everyone and everything it possibly can? Then this might be the game for you.
Once again you take on the role of Alan Wake and his fight against the encroaching all powerful darkness. Blow away every evil being that wonders into your crosshairs using a large array of weapons, one that would make any gun enthusiast dance with glee. My favourite happened to be the nail gun, simple but deadly. Also the unique ability to use the beam from your flashlight to weaken your foes is back once again, something that I really enjoyed from the original.
The gameplay is very similar to the first title but this time it has a more arcady feel to it, especially with a score attack mode running parallel to the main story. It does add a lot of gameplay value but can be very repetitive continually killing the same sets of enemies over and over again.
As for the story itself, it carries the same dark humour as many other of Remedies titles even using the Twilight zone styled Night Springs as the main way to convey the story. The game is not overly long and does feel repetitive in nature, mainly due to using the same levels over and over but given the time bending storyline that is not surprising. I didn’t get bored at all and had a real desire to find out what happened to our hero in the end and whether or not he would have his happy ending.
If you have played and liked the original then this is a must buy especially if on sale, if not just to complete the story arc from the first game. If you are new to the series don’t start with this one, but buy the original as it is a phenomenal game.

It's a fighting game, it's pong, it's expressive, it's a party game, and I never would have bought it if I wasn't introduced to it at a party, because trailers have a really hard time capturing why it's so much fun.
The gameplay lives off a wide array of mechanics that are all accessed by basic movement keys and 2 more buttons. Different characters don't only have unique special abilities as showcased in the trailer but also subtle differences in the way they move, their hitboxes and the angles in which they hit the ball.
At first, the game is just enjoyable without having any clue of what's even happening, but once you play more you get an idea of how high the skill ceiling actually is. To become a master, you don't only need high knowledge of/experience with the characters and perfect reactions, but also the ability to read, surprise and outsmart your opponent.

This game in my opinion, is the the perfect rogue-like. FTL is brutal, unforgiving, and you will love every second of it. FTL is a strategy rogue-like that sets critical decision making at the forefront. The game forces you to make decisons that could potentially end the game for you. Do you take in crazed man, hoping he will assist your crew? Part of the beauty of this game is the same decision could have multiple outcomes, forcing you to decide if a risk is worth it. Combat involves carefully deciding what weapons to power and what to keep powered down. Prioritizing which enemy system to attack is crucial, as the wrong move could end in game-over. However, after every run, you learn more about the game and it's mechanics, and you learn what works and what doesn't. Every crushing defeat is off-putting, but the promise of a better run keeps you coming back for more. The game's replay value is huge too, as every run is different and there are plenty of ships to unlock, each with their own strategies. In addition the soundtrack is kickass too. 10/10 would die a thousand times

As someone who has never played Far Cry games before, the "more of the same" does not apply. I find this game extremely immersive, although I feel like I am playing with Adam Jensen 12000 years ago (same voice actor for the main character), which is not a bad thing at all, I like his voice.
Music, sounds, visuals, how the animals move, etc. (with the limitations of AI obviously) all contribute to creating a fantastic environment. If you burn an animal while hunting it, it will slide and set fire to the ground it slid onto... not that I like to burn animals alive, but if they come attack me while I am minding my business then I have no choice but to defend myself. But then you realise, wait a minute, that tiger was scared of fire, is this game going to be realistic and let me scare other animals away? And it does, you just point your fiery club towards them.
You get to tame animals, craft everything you own, build your village - I am guessing these are the elements that players of the previous Far Cry games feel are more of the same. As I said, being the first Far Cry game for me, I find this all very rewarding.
All in all, it's a beautiful, immersive experience, I highly recommend this game.

If you're into the Blitzkrieg or Sudden Strike series you might take a look at this one.
is pretty much Blitzkrieg set in a post-apocalyptic world with all those crazy vehicles minus the strategic factor of the previous Blitzkrieg games.
In every one of these 29 missions you basically control a bunch of armored dune buggies, Hot Rods or armed trucks and let them charge into hordes of wasteland punks. A handful of the stages are stealth missions, where you guide a story character through deserted ruins. All in all quite a good mission and level design if you ask me, especially the desert maps with all the details look pretty nice. Gameplay on the other hand is always relatively straight-forward and not too demanding.
Instead of Blitzkrieg-typical briefings, the missions are interrupted by cheesy comic cutscenes that illustrate the quite shallow story. But still the story lacks sympathetic characters or interesting twists, so don't expect too much. What also differs Desert Law from the other Enigma engine games is the use of hero units. If only one guy from your bunch of "heroes" dies during combat, it immediately leads to failure. This can be quite frustrating, as your heroes bite the dust pretty often in hectic firefights.
The Good:
+ Detailed maps
+ Atmospheric soundtrack
+ Cool vehicles and units
+ Pretty good mission design
+ About 10 to 13 hours of gameplay
+ Upgradable hero skills
+ Comic cutscenes
The Bad:
- No support for resolutions higher than 1280x1024!
- Heroes die too fast and lead to failure of mission
- Not really interesting story or characters
- No multiplayer
The Ugly:
-- Nothing really...
To put it in a nutshell, I especially recommend this game to fans of the Blitzkrieg/Sudden Strike family. If in addition you like the post-apocalyptic setting too and if you forgive Desert Law's minor problems, you'll have a pretty good time with this game.

A nice single-player only strategy game. Desert Law will differently appeal to Mad Max fans and fans of post-apocalyptic fiction. There is no base building, resource gathering or micro-management. It is a budget game and it shows, but it is a great little distraction for just $5. The graphics, although out-of-date are still very nicely detailed. They are 2D isometric with 3D vehicles and they also have very nice weather effects. Even without any multiplayer you are still getting a lot of content for just $5 as Desert law has a long campaign of around 30 missions of different varieties.
Gameplay is good but the only big major problem I had was that if a story character dies, it is an automatic mission failure. This can be sometimes frustrating because enemies can take out your vehicles and characters pretty quickly if they all target one in your group. So sending out your non-character units to the front of your convey is a must for success, which can be annoying because there is no option to change the types formations of your units like there are in other strategy games. Despite that issue the gameplay is still fun if you are able to overlook those major faults.

An Option to actually Guard an Certain Direction and thus having Full or even Improved Accuracy because the Soldier Expects an Enemy to come up behind an Corner would be Great and Solve this.
Same for Pathfinding as an Option to tell your Soldier which way to go would Help alot to make him move without entering someones Firing Zone.

The Game is Horribly Bugged and Unfinished.

Place 5 of the Annoying XCOM Bugs.
Managing your Soldiers is a Pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ They constantly do Random Resets of stuff you Assign to them be it Outfits or Equipment. This is really annoying because it results in you needing to always Check through them to make sure they actually kept the Stuff and Outfit you gave to them.
Place 4 of the Annoying XCOM Bugs.
The Pathfinding for Firing Arcs is utterly Horrible. Your Soldiers as well as the Enemys often Shoot through Walls and whatever other Objects or move through them like they dont Exist.
This not only causes alot of very Strange Pictures of Enemys being Killed on the other Side of an Entire House with the House not taking any Damage but rather being Ignored by the Guys entirely.
It also causes alot of Mistakes you will make when Positioning or moving your Soldiers. Because the Soldiers you assumed to be entirely Safe from Enemy Fire will suddenly be Shot and Killed through an House or other Stuff.
Place 3 of the Annoying XCOM Bugs
This also goes the other way around of Course. Sometimes despite there is nothing to Block your Fire.
Yet you just cannot shoot at the Enemy because something is Considered to be in the Way.
And as you cannot take back Moves and cannot see Beforehand if your able to Fire at an Enemy from there. This not only Results in you sitting there and wondering why the Heck Cant I fire at this Enemy which is clearly in my Range and Firing Zone. But it also means that your often Forced to Reload an Game to Undo your last Move because you Put your Soldier next to an Enemy he was Supposed to Kill and cannot Fire at him.
Resulting in that Enemy Of Course moving the one Extra Field away to pass that Invisible Magic Wall and Massacre your Soldier.
Place 2 of the most Annoying Bugs in XCOM.

AAAAND Place 1! The most Annoying Bug in XCOM
Sometimes Doors and other Pathways Bug out in a Match becoming Invisible Walls that you cannot Pass.

Civlization V is one of the few games that stay engraved in your heart foverer. I still remember the time that I was playing Civilization IV and was expecting Civilization V to come out in a few months. It was a great period of time, of change, of magnificence. Some of the most beautiful and inspirational games were released between 2001-2012. Civilization V was released in the dusk of the Golden Age, but this was the most beautiful time for the gaming industry, a time where the advancement and combination graphics and gameplay were at their peak, and new ways to approach each game design had been brought up successfully, as the old ones had been mastered. Civilization V was a revolutionary game, a legacy that lasted six whole years, having been loved by both critics and the audience.
There was something unique about Civilization V when I firstly played it. I was anticipating the game, but I could not buy it on its release date due to financial problems. When I eventually played it I was stunned, and loved the texture, the music, and the gameplay was immersive. The unit formations and the map design were excellent. The UI was beautiful and as it can be noticed, each DLC adds a different and more artistic touch to it. The Complete Edition is beautiful and all its DLCs are worth the money, but only on sale. The two exapnsion packs improve gameplay and Gods and Kings brought the original game to its peak. Brave New World changed it significantly, bringing new features that were missing from the original one, creating a new ascpect for future gameplay, as it can be seen for Beyond Earth.
Civilization V is a wonderful game. It has passed the test of time and has created some of the fondest memories I have in the Gaming World. It is a treasure of strategy, knowledge, as it allows you to learn facts about the history of man, and above all it is a piece of art. It will always be remembered and will be always the one that make us continue playing for one more turn.

After finishing Snapshot, I can say its greater quality is the superb level design. Although the entire game being built around the use of the camera, the levels still bring something new until the very end. The first few levels can be a little repetitive, you practically just uses your camera to move boxes around, but after that the game introduces new objects  (disappearing clouds, fireball throwing flowers, elephant trampolines and many others) constantly, just giving you enough time to learn how to use them before introducing something new. The majoraty of the objects are used only in a handful of levels before being dropped for something new, keeping the game always fresh. The game is very easy if you finish the level without completing any secondary goal, so I recommend to go after the secret objects and the stars for maximum enjoyment.  The graphics, although simple, are a delight to look at, evocative of the 16bit era platformers: they are exactly how you remember them being at the time, not  pixelated and low resolution as they truly are.  If you try to complete secondary objectives, the game will give you at least 10 hours of fun, more than enough to justify the $10 price.

Video Review:
Grim Dawn is an isometric action RPG in the spirit of Diablo. The premise is as it usually is in games like this. Explore a world with scaled locations and enemies, kill as many as things possible, loot as much stuff as possible, complete the game, and start NG+ to continue trying to max out your character.
What makes Grim Dawn so special is that it has the most in-depth character customization I have ever seen in an action RPG in my entire life. You get stat points which allow you to boost your stats. You can customize your gear, upgrade your gear with special materials, and have two different weapon loadouts. You get to pick from several classes and use hundreds of skillpoints to upgrade active and passive abilities between them in any design you’d like. After that, you get to pick devotions which are these branching talent paths that unlock passive bonuses and chance activation skills to help make you stronger. Combine that with a very simplistic and easy to learn and master combat system revolving around occasional abilities and and clicking to essentially hack and slash, and you have a very fun concept; especially since you can play cooperatively with friends. And this is a small note, but you can’t respec stat points. So if you make a bad choice or click the wrong button, seeing as the buttons are right next to each other, you’re stuck with it.
The story of Grim Dawn is more engaging than I expected from an ARPG. It starts out with your character almost dying by hanging due to possession by the aether which is essentially a interdimensional spiritual energy with a form of sentience. You were saved because the energy left your body to escape death since apparently it can’t survive if you die. The game then immediately contradicts itself by making you fight several aether-possessed corpses and sends you on a journey to defeat the invasion of the aether while building up safe zones by choosing to help persons that can prove useful that you meet in the wilderness or not.One especially cool thing is that the game actually allows you to make choices. These choices only really have cosmetic effects and no real effect on gameplay though. For example, you can choose to save and arm some persons you meet in the wilderness to help you fight the aether. But you never see them again, the enemies do not decrease, and literally the effect of your choice amounts to zilch.
The gameplay has its own problems too. For one, nothing gets marked on the map and you’re not allowed to place your own markers either. Combine that with how level 15 areas can have level 25 dungeons? You’ll likely miss a lot of content unless you take the effort to keep physical notes telling you where everything is. Most quests don’t even get marked on your minimap so to complete them you really just have to run around and explore every nook and cranny. This is a very degressive design choice that makes you feel like you’re playing a game from the early 2000s back when quest tracking wasn’t really considered as important. The game allows you to craft bridges and blow things up too in order to access more content. But none of that gets marked either so unless you have a very good memory, or draw your own map then you’re gonna forget where most of these are never actually ever access that content.
Another problem is that the enemies don’t feel different. No matter what they are, how they look, or what attacks they have? The game feels like you’re fighting the same easy to kill enemies over and over with the exception of legendary and boss units that have some debuffs and buffs that they can cast that regular enemies don’t. This makes the game feel very repetitive and more like a chore. You’ll probably zone out while running around killing these things because no matter what you run into in this game? There’s nothing that can really kill you or even close unless you run into an area that’s five levels above you at least. And even then only really the area boss stands a chance at killing you.
The graphics and sound effects are about what you’d expect from an ARPG. They’re nothing to brag about. But they’re decent. My only complaint about them is that the game has a strange fog that makes things hard to see at the edge of your vision. It’s the same kind of fog that pops up in other games when the quality takes a dip due to an incapability to render that far. But considering Grim Dawn is isometric, the fact that this fog is here makes no sense. Is this game really incapable of delivering a clear crisp isometric image? It appears to be that way; even on max settings.
Overall Grim Dawn is a very fun concept and something that I wish was more fun than it is. There’s just so many bad design choices here that made me have to struggle to keep playing the game. It just wasn’t fun after the first few hours. Grim Dawn is a repetitive, boring, and poorly designed chore. There is no challenge, no organization, and really just no engaging entertainment to be found here anywhere outside of the character customization. I give it a 3/10. It was very badly designed and its production value was very low. Don’t waste your money on it.

Deck-builder Roguelite Dungeon Crawler game.  If that doesn't sound like bliss to you then I don't know what would.
Having beaten it with both classes now I can say it's a good time, deckbuilding feels fun and rewarding and the game seems to have a good overall level of challenge.
Pros
+The deck-building is deep without being overly complex.
+Synergy is easy to spot, can be hard to pull off.
+Unlocks keep adding new cards and trinkets to the game, so it continues to feel fresh after multiple playthroughs.
+The different classes feel very different from each other, having different varieties of cards they can obtain.
Cons
-Only two classes so far.
-Could use a little more variety in enemy and "?" encounters.
-Sometimes turns play themselves, if you only have enough energy for certain plays or enough energy to dump all your cards.
-Can feel a little bit short since there's three areas so far.  Would be great to take broken decks further.
Neutral
=Variance can keep the game fresh, it can also just completely screw you over.  Sometimes you just want to abort a run two encounters in.  Or if you end up drawing only blocks during an enemy's buff/debuff turn.
It's still in early access.  As of this writing I do recommend it and feel it is worth the asking price as-is.  As always, it might end up changing, hopefully for the better but buyer beware.

I have recently been comparing GD with Diablo 2 and Diablo 3. I have all three running on the same machine. I really enjoy both D2 and GD. D3 I do not enjoy, for some reason they took away the character customization, and it seems like everyone ends up with the same character at endgame. GD has excellent character customization, and is way better at that aspect of the game than D2  and D3.
Things I like about Grim Dawn. Character customization spend your points the way you want. Skill points, attribute points, and devotion points, plus cool gear specific things to change the way you play your character. D2 has good customization as well. D3 character customization for some reason I don't like it, not enough choice in my opinion.
GD has a really large world. Lots of cool places to explore, plus secret areas. D2  had a decent size world and fun stuff to find. D3 looks great, but I literally have only died once by accident when my wife was talking to me. Both Grim Dawn and D2 you can die and die badly. Crafting is very well thought out in GD. D2 also had decent things to do craftingwise with the Horadric Cube. D3 has a decent crafting set up as well.

I am looking forward to the GD expansion! Inquistor and Necromancer to add to the customization with dual classing is gonna be cool!

It's sometimes really hard to find a bounty target.

The world is so large it's easy to get lost.

TL;DR: the "de facto" best Star Trek style spaceship commander simulator, in a "rogue-light", addictive and challenging gamplay, with undeniable charm, an impressive atmosphere, and absolutely stunning soundtrack. Multiple ships, ship systems, weapons, crew races and their abilities, all expanded upon with the FREE Advanced Edition, provide a variety of play styles and endless replayability.
As soon as that music starts, it gets to you all over again: you're in someplace special. FTL is a lovely game. In FTL you control a medium-sized spaceship and its crew carrying vital data to the Federation fleet. You are being pursued by the Rebel fleet and must stay ahead of it by doing FTL jumps between beacons of each sector and from sector to sector until you finally reach your main fleet. Problem is, it's an hostile universe out there, and you'll never know what you'll encounter on the next beacon...
In the beginning you can pick between multiple ship types (that you unlock as you play), each with different crew compliments of different races and system types that will make for different play styles. The meat of the game plays as a strategy real-time (pausable) "rogue-light", where you control your ship and crew from a top-down view, and you need to manage which crew member mans which ship system (engines, shields, weapons, helm, etc etc) for a better performance, manage when and how to fire weapons and also manage the allocation of power to each system. Crew members of different races have different bonus: some repair systems quicker, some provide extra power to the room they're in, some are excellent fighters, some are immune to fire, etc. You don't have power for everything, and also depending what systems/weapons you have and your crew type, you have to adapt and optimize your strategy and approach to your encounters.
And you'll encounter a lot: other ships, some hostile, some friendly, some you're not quite sure; there's even mini-quests and mini optional "story arcs" that you can go on. Not only that but also dangerous asteroid fields, nebulas that interfere with your shields and sensors, suns that burst out flares and set your ship on fire. Each "run" will make for a different tale of your adventure. The real-time battles, despite being pausable, are usually pretty tense. You'll mostly be trying to damage or disable enemy shields and damaging their systems, such as shields and weapons, until you destroy their ship. Or you can beam up a boarding party, kill everyone and take control of the ship, or you can bypass their shields by hurling missiles or beaming up bombs (limited supply of these), etc, etc. Or you can just run for it if things are too hot. And the best thing is, the enemies can do the exact same things! Battles will damage your systems, breach your hull, ignite fires, and that's where you'll need your best managing skills to keep things under control on the heat of battle. And sometimes things just happen too fast, you were not prepared, and you're blown into oblivion and have to start from the beginning. It's an unforgiving universe... After each battle you win, you can get random upgrades but you'll mostly accumulate scrap, which can be used to upgrade your ship's system and go to stores to buy consumables (like FTL jump fuel and missiles) or weapons and systems, or even recruit more crew members. You'll need scrap badly, but how far is it reasonable to go and risk potentially lethal encounters on its pursuit?
Between that and much more, like controlling blast doors and managing oxygen supply in case of a fire or breach, or also venting rooms in your ship to put out fires or choke intruders to death, FTL manages to be the most complete and realistic spaceship simulator, Star Trek style, that I've ever know, despite its 2D, top-down, pixel art style. You can only "save&quit", if you lose, you have to start from the beginning. Some "runs" will go better than others, it always depends on your ability to adapt and optimize your play style to what crew, ship and systems you have, but it also depends a bit on being fortunate enough on finding a really good upgrade or weapon after a battle or on a store. That can be a bit frustrating, but that's just what it is, if you don't have what it takes to survive, you won't. You'll learn a lot from your mistakes, and after finishing the game, you'll realise that you couldn't have done it if you hadn't learned so much. So it rewards you for your failures and efforts.
The soundtrack is just absolutely brilliant, one of the best in my memory, being part charming old-school style 8-bit tunes, part dreamy sci-fi space sounds, it provides a unique atmosphere that immerses completely. The overall style oozes charms and tender care, despite being a very challenging and unforgiving game.
With the addition of Advanced Edition, completely free, bringing more races, more ships, more weapons and systems, and also more encounters, the game has an impressive amount of content that can get you on it for dozens of hours. If you like space sci-fi strategy games, particularly commanding ships Star Trek style, this is for you. If you get frustrated easily with a challenge, maybe approach it carefully, but you'll be missing out.

Let's get this out of the way first: I used to read and watch ASOIAF/Game of Thrones and I'm not a fan. However, I do love Telltale games and this is a story I feel they did right by.
Telltale did a great job keeping up the GoT theme of "no character is safe" and it really makes you feel the urgency in every character's desperate situation. There is a surprising amount of child death/murder, kidnapping, and a lot of horrific things that happen to children (and adults). These things tend to pace themselves out when you watch or read the series. From my experience with the Telltale community however, people tend to binge whole episodes (including myself). I'm going to suggest against that this time because the game may be about the same length as one season but Telltale packed 2-3 seasons worth of content into ~10 hours. Some of the brutality got so horrific, I had to take long breaks from the game between chapters just to give my stomach time to unwrap itself.
If you're a fan of Game of Thrones, this will be a great addition to your library; it's a terrific supplement to the HBO show. I'm still not a fan of the ASOIAF series but it did surprise me in that it illustrated Telltale's (successful) efforts in keeping true to the series.
7/10

So let's talk about Black Desert Online.
I've only played for three hous so far, and was just trying to figure it out. basic controlls are the same as any MMORPG, and quests are mainly the same. "go here, collect this, kill that" but where it stands out is in the way combat works, you don't press a hotkey to cast an assigned attack or spell, there are combinations of keys. for example: "press q + f" and there is combo attack, the way combat works is new, and has you actually doing something and trying out different combinations!
Then we have the small price you pay to play, and I mean 10 euro isn't that much considering you pay 15 euro per month to play World of Warcraft (which is what I used to do), but for this game you only pay once, and that's it. there are microtransactions that make the game a bit easier, but nothing that really changes the way you play.
another amazing concept that I have not yet seen in MMORPG'S is the guild war system, every town is under control of another guild, and these guild can fight with each other. then there is a Node system, that i quite honestly haven't figured out yet. but for the three hours that i've played it's been great.
There is a great build up story line quest that will probably keep you questiong for a few hours, and then there are, as always, A lot of side-quests, and life skills (Fishing, alchemy, crafting etc.) to spend hours in. there are rewards for leveling up to certain levels and rewards for total time played (with the highest time needed for a reward being 10,000 hours, so there is a lot of grinding going to be needed for that)
Class system is the same as any MMORPG, there are different classes that can wear different weapons, and i'm mentioning the weapons as gear isn't as prominent in this MMORPG as it would be in others, where armour is a prominent feature and is obtainable through many quests. quest rewards in BDO are mainly things like herbs, meats and potions, and sometimes a weapon.
For the 3 hours that i've played this game so far I'm recommeding it, as it's really much fun, and i'm probably going to be playing this a lot, even though I should be studying.

This game has fun combat and an interesting "life-skill" system which lets you develop your own little resource gathering and crafting systems.  You can "invest" in land and in town buildings using contribution (which is gained from questing).  Land can be used in many different ways, from passive resource gain to advanced multilevel item crafting, to simple player housing.  This game does have many issues, however.  Firstly, the game was developed in such a way that you must use microtransactions if you want to be competitive whatsoever.  Without costumes or auctionhouse maids the game slows down significantly, and ♥♥♥♥♥ on your efficiency just for the sake of making the micros more appealing.  The loot system is the biggest red flag in the microtransaction department.  The loot system in this game is the same as the loot system in goddamn maplestory.  Every monsters body must be individually looted...unless you pay for the pets, which are 10 bucks each.  Each pet can only loot so often however, and even spending 10 or 20 dollars on pets wont net you a huge increase in your monster looting speed.  You have to get three pets at once, and even then you cant pick up all the loot from the monsters you kill.  The only way to make sure your pets get all the loot is to upgrade pets.  The way you upgrade pets is by fusing two pets together, and its not even guaranteed that you will get an upgrade.  Pets get up to level 4, so assuming you want maximum efficiency, you have to buy a minimum of 12 pets just to pick up items at the same rate you kill monsters.  without pets you spend literally half your time looting bodies and half your time fighting, and it reallllly hurts the grind.  Which brings me to the second problem of this game, which is the really wonky exp curve that makes the game into a super grind.  You can get to level 51 very easily, but then the exp needed to level grows exponentially, taking hundreds of hours of pure monster bashing to gain one level.  It can get to the point where 200 hours of grinding gives you less than 10% of a level.  The third major issue of this game is RNG gated gear advancement.  There is literally no skill involved in getting better gear, all of the skill in the game comes into play when you are trying to acquire the currency for RNG upgrade attempts.  A player could spend 100 billion upgrading and end up with WORSE gear then they started, while a new player with no money can get lucky and make incredible gear pieces for almost nothing.  Lastly, and this is probably the worst part of the gameplay (the micros are the worst part in general), is the sheer time requirement for many basic things.  The game has no fast travel whatsoever, so you have to ride horses EVERYWHERE.  The travel time in this game is ridiculous, 90% of your time will be spent afk riding horses to places you need to go.  Another time waster is the necessity of AFKing in this game.  If you dont leave your game on 24/7 you are losing out on HUGE amounts of wealth every day.  Your workers dont work, and you cant craft anything unless you are online.  There are also many arbitrary wait times, such as on crafting or on horse breeding.  Overall, I think this game has a lot of great systems, but the microtransactions and the "grind" (literal time wasting garbage) really make it feel like you cant compete without no lifing AND spending 20-30 bucks a month.  The game can also get very boring since all the different types of crafting have the same gameplay, and there are no instanced dungeons in the game whatsoever.  No raids or instances for late game;  late game amounts to grinding for cash to get better gear for grinding for cash.  This game feels like the combat of Tera combined with the life skilling grind of Runescape.

Don't let my low play time mislead you. I've been playing the hyperneps for a good long while, on console and PC, including the original releases. This one is arguably my favorite one, even if the main character is a bit lacking. Like virtually every Hyperdimension Neptunia, this is a mix of VN and aRPG. That means watching a story unfold and listening to dialogue occasionally interrupted by a dungeon crawl or boss fight. There are plenty of dungeons to explore, and plenty more to add through the "remake system", though in true hypernep fashion, many use the same palette (cave, snow fields, factory, etc.) with only the spawns, drops, and transition points changing. Then again, the appeal of this series is the humor, characters, and story, not the wandering around. Likewise enemies tend to be cut/paste recolors/resizes, though it makes sense in a way since the series is a parody of the game industry as a whole.
Combat can either be a grind or a breeze with the occasional challenge depending on your gear and how much you've grinded. On the one hand there are cases where not much grinding is needed to advance. Other times, you better be ready to start farming mobs and field bosses. As a general rule in a dungeon, if there is a save point, USE IT. It might just save you 30 miniutes or more if a boss shows up and wipes the floor with you.
The story/characters are good, more in depth than previous entries to the series. Players who have played reBirth I, disregard all events that occured in said game. They never happened. Everyone (aside the new characters) has already met through various other circumstances. The story of this one centers not on the CPUs, but their sisters: the CPU candidates (sorry nep, you aren't the Main Character so stop saying it). They have their own distinct personalties from their sisters and interactions with each other and the other characters. The story as a whole is good, with little rushing chapters or self cancellation. There are also multiple endings to get, as usual with most JRPGs, including a "Bad End" (conquest ending). My advice: if youre looking to get (or avoid) a certain ending, look up a guide. The requirements tend to pile up.
Overall, fans of JRPGs should be able to enjoy this (and the other reBirths as well). If you want a game that is light hearted and has characters that don't obey the fourth wall, then this'll fit the bill, as will any Hypernep game.
Suggestion: if you have to money when buying this game, but the DLC with it. its an extra five bucks for more options in the Remake System, extra weapons, coliseum battles, a headache preventor for the Stellas Dungeon minigame (the feature thats replacing the scout system from previous games), and boosts the level cap to a whopping 999.
Bigger suggestion: USE A CONTROLLER. trying to play any hypernep with a keyboard/mouse will result in urges to chuck said implements out nearest window in frustration.
Personal opinion: Can never have enough nep. And for the love of Nep DONT DO THE CONQUEST ENDING. I'm still crying inside from that. And I did it a year ago on PS3. Either do it before you pick a favorite girl or not at all.

What would happen if first person perspective Assassins Creed parkour and open world exploration met the undying popularity of zombies? Dying Light that's what.
It takes a Borderlands-esque nod in the weapon/loot system department, with a sprinkle of survival-style weapon durability for repairs to ensure you keep upgrading and mixing up your arsenal. While the infected do have a mildly annoying habit of randomly spawning just out sight while you're busy knee deep in blood and guts of their compatriots, the overall experience is a barrel of laughs and makes for some very entertaining gameplay.
This does not even touch on the expansion "The Following" where you apparenty get an offensive buggy to plough through the mutated undead. Quite reminiscent of Farcry's vehicles if you ask me, but what Techland borrows from others it successfully and seamlessly integrates these elements into the game's overall formula.
If you are not into another player being able to mess with your single player expereince however, you may want to turn the night time zombie invasion option off. A human player will spawn in as a special zombie (with its own experience and skill tree to boot) and the survivors will have to destroy its nest while the Night Hunter attempts to kill them. Nevertheless, maybe when you unlock more of the survivor skill tree it may be fun to dip your toes into this for some player versus player action.

Definitely not a copy of Dead Island! In fact this game is so much different than dead island that both these games cannot really be compared. The only thing I can see is copied are weapons and fighting system.
But I am going to compare these two titles in my review anyway - to prove my point. So what is the difference between DL and DI:
- In Dead Island you just smash through zombies (normally no more than 10 at one go) like knife through chunk of butter. After certain level you do that that without much of a struggle (okay you will die here and then if you are getting lazy and cant be bothered to look around) - In Dying light you get hordes of zombies +100 and you will just die. On lower levels and with bad weapons you can really defeat maybe 2-3 at once. Most of the times you stay on buildings or quickly run away - so the play style is completely different
- Oridinary zombies in DL are slower, more sluggish but also more durable and harder to kill - they also quickly give up running after you forgetting all about your presence - they are more easily to be manipulated and tricked. Zombies in DI are often quick and will chase you for some time
- In Dead Island you roam through never-ending day with the same enemies over and over again - In DL you get nights that are pretty scary and so much more difficult with different types of enemies
- Dead Island is type of an easy-going comedy-like zombies survival game, whereas DL is a bit more serious with horror elements. Dialogues are a bit more witty and not that stupid
- Map - in Dead Island you get an island with a main road to which the car is restricted and few rivers that are connecting settlements - IN DL you get a proper city to discover with interesting places and the safe zones
- You have a proper lockpicking in DL - in DI you just get the lockpicking skill that will instantly open chests
- Skill tree in DL is completely different with 3 independent level system (survival, power, agility) that are leveled up on their own with pretty interesting skills. In DI skills are not that much interesting at all;
- You have parkour in DL
-  Interaction with NPCs and dialogue is realistic in DL; In DI NPC are really bland
- You can fight humans in DL and not in DI
- You can sleep in DL and not in DI
- Most of the side quest in DI are really dull \
- Both games give you good experience in coop, but DI seems pointless and very boring on Single player. DL is great on Single Player and can scare you in places (especially during the night)
What I did not like about DL or in what fields DL is lacking for me:
- A bit too longish mandatory tutorial with a lot of jumping
- Weapons are loosing the durability within seconds (steel pipe can last only ~30 hits)
- You need a skill to throw weapons (What? - its not a rocket science to throw a wooden plank at a zombie)
- You cannot talk or interact with most of NPCs - you can do only with the meaningful ones who are part of main story line or have side quests for you. Even the trades haven't got anything to say to you, you just go straight to trade window.
- Dialogue choice and more game choice would be nice, but I understand that the stress in this game is on survival rather than RPG
What I liked:
- Pretty much everything else I have seen so far.
All in all I think Dying Light is so much superior over Dead island (but I still like dead island r and enjoyed playing it with all the shortcomings) and can definitely be recommended to anyone who likes zombies and/or survival and/or open world games.

If you're buying a game for the story don't expect anything here, as it's nothing new in gaming before. Basically it's like this:
World falls apart, crazy bad guys tries to convince everyone chaos is the way the world should work, there's the beta female character, bad guy captures you, leaves you instead of killing you, yells your name at the top of his lungs as you escape and kill his guys, and the ending is nothing but an action pressing sequence.
Now if you're buying the game for the fun gameplay, this game doesn't hold back at all. Hard mode is recommended (or Nightmare if you're that insane) since normal feels to easy in this game. You'll find yourself struggling to kill any zombies at all with the poor weapons you have at the start of the game and will have to repair them over and over, but eventually that fades out and you realize that's how the game SHOULD work with such weapons until you get crazy, lighting rod swords and the such that mow through zombies a ton easier (but your weapons will still break a lot, as they should and all you'll have to do is repair them or make another one) until, of course, you fight the much harder, more difficult zombies.
There's the giant ones that might as well be walking tanks, the runners that can swarm you if you're not careful, etc. and my favorite - the scary ♥♥♥♥ing ones at night time. The nighttime mode is what truly makes this a new zombie experience (as well as the parkour but we'll save that for later) giving you a sense of hopelessness the first many hours of the game. At night many of the zombies will transform into these terrifying, powerful, faster creatures that will hunt you down no matter what if they find you, forcing you to sneak around the best you can until you get to a safe zone to escape the horror. I wasn't expecting this game to scare me so much since dead island was no where near like that for me.
So if they find you, or you get into a mess with tons of zombies surrounding you on the streets, what do you do?
Parkour.
Running is your best thing to do in this game in nearly all of these situations, and being able to jump onto the building and run along the roof tops will save you from the slow, day time ones besides a few runners. At night however, it'll be more than just climb a building and run a tad bit. The evil ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s at night will chase you everywhere until you get away, so using the environment to get around is all you can do until you escape into one of the said safe zones and you'll have to be quick minded as well to make the perfect movements during these runs. One wrong move and you're dead.
One thing I have to say though - I haven't touched the DLC at all yet, so the story might have a huge improvement in The Following DLC, I don't know. I also don't know if the gameplay is still as good, or even better, or sadly worse. I'll update this when I've played the DLC.

Saint's Row IV is, of course, the fourth installation in the San Andreas-like Saint's Row series of sandbox games. Due to running out of ways to expand the traditional, GTA-like theme, Volition has instead chosen to dramatically transform the gameplay, somewhat resembling Batman: Arkham ____ or the Acrobatic / Super Speed movements from DC Universe Online.
I had found Saint's Row the Third to be slightly disappointing as it didn't offer much new in comparison to Saint's Row 2's dramatic improvements over the original game; Saint's Row IV is pretty much the opposite.
The leader of the Saints has somehow managed to become the President of the United States and, being a moron, has quickly turned the country into a flying circus. It's his rotten luck that cartoon-British space aliens choose to invade during his term.
He is trapped in a simulated facsimile of Steelport, the city featured in Saint's Row the Third. Fortunately, the nerd hacker girl Kinsie manages to contact him and begins helping him go totally The Matrix on everything in the simulation.
Saint's Row IV's primary gameplay change is the ability to acquire superpowers, because it's a computer world and you can do that. Very early in the game you get Super Sprint and Super Jump, which once sufficiently upgraded will render all vehicles moot and pointless for the majority of gameplay (except that the Boss can't use firearms while in midair.) Over the course of gameplay you will acquire other powers such as blast attacks and who knows what else. However, these powers can't be used in any mission taking place in the real world, which are played much more similarly to Saint's Row the Third.
Because the goal of the space aliens is to torture kidnapped humans, the Boss's simulation attempts to keep him from having fun. This means that there are no safehouses or any notable Saints presence, and that the usual mechanics of district control, raiding enemy headquarters, controlling stores, etc. are portrayed as attempts to seize control of or damage the simulation. It goes so far as to change "killing people" to "deleting subroutines" and other such jokes.
Also, the game heavily implies that the entire story is actually just a movie the Saints have produced due to their extreme popularity and fortune. This is good because the story would otherwise have very little potential for a Saint's Row V for reasons that become obvious as soon as you unlock the Ship.
All in all, Saint's Row IV is a great entry in the series, and is somewhere between The Third and 2 in terms of awesomeness.

So, i have jumped right into multiplayer and got a match with 2 random people, cus there was noone else around even despite sales days + 4 players coop patch (game is abandoned by players). It was sort of fun for the first 20 minutes, i figured out controlls and stuff pretty quickly. But our session was 80 minutes long and we were clearing levels very fast, so i cant call it 'funny' to spend so much time on a single run. And we havent even finished it. What you can see here is some random levels, random mosters and random items to pick up. By defeating bosses you unlock new permanent items in dungeon and by killing emeies you get exp to level up between runs. Thats all positive sides of game, now to bad part...
There is few definitions of difficulty. The REAL one presents in Spelunky HD, where no matter how well you know the game — it will find new ways to kill you every time. Even after spending more than 100 hours i still die in different ways and it gives a smile + lots of fun. In Lost Castle death feels like something annoying and booring, cus you realise that will have to spend way too much time to get back to where you was before. All enemies and levels look similar, there is no much varietty in weapon choises, items or spells. Monsters hit hard, kill fast and jump onto you ferociously, sometimes not even giving breather time (stun locking you on a single spot).
Each new level present monsters that have new unavoidable attacks, so you have to use ranged weapon to deal with them. But you cant use two set of weapons for this. Moreover, some monsters counter any ranged shots. As you should already understand, that leads to 100% death in most cases when you meet new monster or boss, so you have to start over. Also small enemies like to swarm you with numbers and just spam with attacks... If you try to outrun them, you will probably wake up even more enemies around and they will definetly join the hunt. You are a victim and you will suffer alot.
Is this a hard game? Not at all — its annoying and unforgiving. One attack can chop 33% of your life, some also stun you, slow or kick around so you lose control of hero. Most of the time there is no way to counter enemy actions and the only thing you can do is tediously deal one single hit, than run away few steps, than deal second hit and again run away, repeat... This is not a definition of 'fun' battle, atleast for me. It feels like game is moking you down and it actually is moking you! Its because game expect you to have all skills maxed from get go. Only than you will have strong damage and armor to outstand enemies. Unfortunatly, farming experience by repeatedly dieing is not interesting.
So, i expected REAL cooperation between players, but, this is one of those games where just adding few extra people to the roaster is all it can bring. Seriously, there is nothing you can do together with your mate, no special combo attacks, no traps, no bosses that require proper team actions, just nothing. You also forced to share potions, items and coins which often leads to one player being strong inside the group and other 2-3 are just garbage meat bugs. Oh and there is also quite a lot of coop bugs, not really gamebreaking, yet annoying enaugh. Also, since there is so few players around, you will morelikely end up playing with high ping and this is not the type of game where you can allow yourself to lag with 200 ms delay.
Not present. There is upgrades system, but mostly it adds stuff that you suppose to have since start. The only unexpected part of the game is ending where you can see "Jets'n'Guns" poster, as that game is BEST scroller in the world since game industry was born. Heroes in Lost Castle does not posses any special class abilities or perks, they are just nameless clones. Bosses arent new as well, they are just big guys with few attacks: some goblins, dinos, plants, etc. Among traps i seen spikes, boulders from celling, fire and pits. Nothing really interesting.
I expected more. While Lost Castle isnt a bad game, its also isnt a good one. In terms of content id rather play Has-Been-Heroes. For difficulty ill gladly give few runs to Spelunky HD and for coop fun its better to get Cloudberry Kingdom. There is no humor, no deep mechanics to play with, no real cooperation between players. The upgrades system is very short and basic. As for making builds, its also not a worthy game to stick with. To be honest, i cant find any single positive side to buy Lost Castle. In 2017 there is an ocean of good indie games, like Dead Cells, Piece Death, Battle Chef Brigade, Forager, Hand of Fate 2 and other. All those games contain FUN element, humor and unique style. I can continue list of goodies for a long time with some additional City of Brass, Volantia Kingdom etc. Yet Lost Castle is just a normal game without anything special. Why would you buy just 'ok' game while there are so many good ones and even some epic ones like Subnautica? 2017 is also year of coop games, and dam, there are a dozen of great ones to choose from (just take a look at fkng Tormentor X Punisher - youll love it).

Before I begin, let me start with a little introduction. I've read every ASOIAF book released twice, I've watched the show 3 times through(Including the horrors of Dorne in season 5 with it's "Bad kitty" debacle), and I frequently read/discuss the books. I love the series to death, so when Telltale announced they were making a game set in the show's universe, I was excited.
Episodes 1-4 were legitimately solid, but then everything went off the rails in Episode 5. The reveal of the traitor was stupid in who it is, with any reasonable attempts at their justification being drowned out by their "allies" planning to kill us. Ramsay Snow's plot armor allowed him to do whatever he wanted, and the way it was handled in Episode 5 is just baffling. Screw his 20 good men, Ramsay can just murder everyone by himself.
Episode 6 continued this departure by being 4 months after the last part(When GoT had released on a 6-8 week schedule before), having exactly zero resolution that was remotely satisifying instead preferring to plant stuff for a second Season that 7 months after the 6th episode still has nothing concrete. Rather then have any sort of interesting ideas for the characters, or using their 6 episodes to paint a story similar to the Starks that ends in ultimate tragedy, we instead get a mediocre plot that has no stakes.
When you play the Game of Thrones, you either win or you die depending on your actions. This game fails to grasp this, instead making the Game of Thrones seem more like a Charade of Choice.

FCPrimal is really a great game. It has an exensive open world full of content to explore, immersion is incredible and the game is very fun. But it has its flaws.
- Great graphs, nothing less than expected for a FarCry game. There are great places, including many rivers and lakes and waterfalls and a pretty peak.
- Big Open World. The map is very extensive. I believe that's the maximum a single player game should be. For more than that I'm happy to pay for a expansion or wait for the next game.
- A loving world. It doesn't happens around PC. There are lots of stuff happening for their own, like humans gathering resources, predators hunting, Uldam lurking, etc.
- Many small random quests, where we must save humans from predators and Uldams.
- The world is extense and open and filled with content. Definetely we don't feel in an empty world. There are animals, resources and people all around, and many fixed orange quests to do and places to explore and special items to find.
- Immersion is incredible, I really feel like a hunter stalking cross the forest to hunt animals and enemies.
- Beat AI is very bad. It is VERY common in narrow passages to have best in front of me locking the way. I'm forced to look around and send beast elsewhere to free the passage then call it back.
- Beats are unable to cross rivers. That's ok, but then they bug out and don't respawn after we cross the river. Farther in the game we have very strong enemies and we rely on beasts to fight, and we may face some threats just in river border, and best is nowhere! I'm forced to stay long minutes on river border just waiting for beast to unbug and spawn back.
- Sometimes, even when beast is close, it bugs out and don't fight. Some predator or Uldam is attacking us and we need beast to tank, but beast just stays there doing nothing.
- Sometimes we choose to not fight and just flee, that's usual in mammoth areas when they anger and berserk on us. But again beast bugs out and don't flee, even when we command them to follow they stay there trying fight!
- After a kill (animal, Uldam, etc), beast just stays on top of the body. There are some cool animations of bigger beasts carrying the body on their mouth, but I wanna loot the body and am unable to. When I hold E, instead of looting, I get a beast petting animations. That's very annoying! Again I have to send beast somewhere to be able to loot then call it back.
- Some loot and heal animations take too long. While they are running I completely lose control of my char, I'm unable to walk or attack. If some enemy comes close while I'm looting or healing, I'm unable to defend myself or fight back until the animation is done.
- In other times, heal animation fails to happen. I'm being attacked, beast is properly tanking, I'm fleeing and trying to heal. And heal just doesn't happen, for long seconds, I hold Ctrl while running and nothing happens, which leads me to getting killed. Or my beast is injured and I just stay in front of it with E hold waiting for heal animation to happen, while enemies are around attacking.
- Game fails to save. Even when pressing F5 and seeing the save animation, when game crashes and I load it back it wasn't saved.
These issues are very annoying and a shame for not being fixed. Still the game is worth the time to play it.

I don't do a lot of reviews but if a game that I think deserve recognition it would be Black Desert Online. To summarize it up for you readers it has everything you want in a mmorpg game. If you want to grind then great for you, if you want to explore the world and learn the lore there is that too. What about the lazy people or casual players? Well if you don't have time then you can just AFK since their is profession such as horse training, fishing, cooking, and processing. There is also daily attendance reward plus free silver from npc everyday. The developer spent a ton of time developing a system that allows you different path to reach end game or making money differently. Here are a few pros and cons about this game:
Pros:
Beautiful graphics
Great combat system
Lifeskills
Alt character friendly
Huge world
There is always something to do
Node wars
Great support team
It's only $10
Great RNG system (enchanting, market, drop, etc..)
Different variety of combat class
Great character customization
Cons:
Not all content in KR server are in EU/NA (such as P2W items and new release content)
The world is huge but several grind spot are not optimize well, which cause high level player to invade low level player areas
Poor swimming mechanic
Toxic community
Not enough karma penalty for players
Lack of content in high level area (Valencia and Port Ratt) also point back to lack of fair grind spot
Lack of beginner tutorial system
That's all I can really think for now. Personally, the game give you a immersion of the world where it doesn't hold your hands and makes you want to go explore and feel it out for yourself. Making this game one if not the best mmorpg currently and you won't find anything like it trust me because I quit MMO a long time ago because they are too repetitive and boring. Also if you read any bad reviews about this game please look at the hours these people had played because BDO requires at least 1000hr+ to really fully understand 80% of its mechanic. P.S. It's not a true P2W game.

Take the elements of Alan Wake, then shove MORE ACTION in there. That's basically this game. Fun story and traveling back and forth through time though.

*Best MMO I've ever played. I am a huge fan of MMORPG's and am usually biased toward Japanese productions. However, BDO completely made it to the top of my list.
*Some reviews complain about complexity. This is the best part about the MMO. There are guides online but never enough to make you a clone through walkthrough.
*WARNING: Everything below lv30 is basically tutorial. You won't feel much difficulty under that.
*The devs put in the best of details, such as allowing players to auto-journey and having a journal ingame.
*Sweet sweet freedom. You get to choose your job and goals. There are plenty of quests of all kinds, but you are not forced to do them (except maybe 1 for leveling to lv50). Chat filter could be turned off. Nowhere do I feel parented by admins.
*Well-balanced leveling. It takes only a few days to get into world boss hunting mode. However, it's still a challenge to reach the level cap. The challenge is enjoyable.
*Best of the open-world MMO category. Unlimited potential for the game. You can invest for fun in it and not be afraid of it shutting down in a few years, because the world map can continue forever. Developers are constantly adding new modes. This game feels like multiple games. Honestly, even the character creation by itself could be a separate program.
*Stunning graphics. I used to complain about the visuals of the player while riding the horse, but it turned out to be completely accurate! The developers matched the posture perfectly with that of horse racers.
*Relaxing music. I basically study with this game on. With the UI turned off, it's like a live wallpaper engine with different music themes.
*Guild battles are realistic. Some complain about trouble identifying individuals during the guild battle... yet that's the most realistic part. Unglorified, historic battles were not completely organized. Organization is a skill. Learn it and appreciate the opportunity of a higher potential ceiling.

Yes
-If you played & enjoyed "Alan wake"
-If want a continuation of the story
-if you enjoy a shooting zombie game
-if you can get it cheap... I would say, $5 or less
No
-if you have not yet played "Alan Wake"

All right, I’ve played this game long enough to review it, and I’ve to say it has gone above expectations for an old school hack’n’slash where rng changes the playstyle in every game. Drawings and artwork is relatively simple but detailed, offering a good presentation, particularly bosses in their intros (it’s boring in the long run but they aren’t long or tedious and they can be skipped).
Pros:
-Game is fairly optimized, loading quickly and fps doesn’t drop even with a big number of enemies on screen even in old laptops.
-Characters, attacks and bosses, plus response to controls are completely fluid and they don’t ever give a jarring feeling.
-Game’s OST is correct, doesn’t repeat too much and does its function.
-Game’s difficulty and item upgrades is relatively gradual, enough to avoid unexpected big gaps (except in the final level and optional rooms filled by enemies) even if rng is unfair sometimes with rooms and gear.
-Despite rng has an active role in the game, skill is needed too and I believe both are balanced out.
-The big amount of weapons and armors can create a wide variety of playstyles (I guess those can be used better in coop mode) in every game, since there isn’t any class and skills are based entirely on the weapon.
-Bosses attack pattern are well defined and they don’t act erratically.
Cons:
-General options have some sort of bug and they can be reset every time you close the game.
-Item location isn’t well defined and some of them can be hard to pick up, especially when there are several of them close to each other.
-Game compendium has some minor bugs.
-Despite the wide variety of weapon types, they aren’t correctly balanced and this makes some of them are ditched in favor of others (at least when playing solo). I’ve tried all of them in different games and areas.
-Nightmare mode is completely unbalanced respect normal and finishing a game to the end without a good rng is a titanic task, it’s a shame because is a must-to to see the game’s true ending. It would be perfect as an optional mode for those seeking a challenge.
Due to some net errors and to the fact I’ve been unable to find friends to play this game with; I can’t speak about coop experience.
8/10, it’s a great game for those who wish to have a good time and have an old computer.

The gameplay is a simple but satsifying if you like to grind. The main gameplay areas are simple, mini-dungeons loaded with enemies to encounter. The combat itself is a weird hibrid of real-time that just sort of works. It consists of moving characters based on their alloted movement points per turn turn-based stratagy style to get them with attack range of enemies. Then you attack with a unique system that allows to chain together three attacks of your choosing from your characters pool of equipted techiniques.
There's also basic item crafting as a means to unlock certian things for the store and a unique system that allows to "burn" buffs of various levels to CD items that are equipted to your characters to affect general gameplay or their own stats.
The story itself is told through visual novel style cutscenes and navigation done on a world-map. So you could describe the whole thing as a visual novel and a simple RPG mashed to together. It avoids art-style clash by sucessfully pulling off very animated looking models even in the 3D gameplay sections. This is achieved through simplified designs and high-quality, yet simple and cartoonish/colorful texture work.

After 9 runs and almost 12 hours of play, I can happily say I can recommend it.  It's challenging, different enough on each playthrough, and is as much a puzzle as it is a turn-based card game rogue-like. There's a good amount of content here. 50 floors over 3 levels.  Each level has a series of interconnected paths to take, ending in a boss.  Unlockables for each of the currently 2 (3rd not available yet) characters that are released just from playing as them (Points earned based on floor completion, enemies killed, money available, bosses killed, etc).  A run can vary from 15 minutes(loss on first level) to ~2hours depending on how well you do (My fastest won run was 1hr 57min).
Completionists take note that some of the achievements are hard to come by.
Overall it's close to worth it's current price tag and more content on the horizon.  So, if you pray daily to RNGsus, like card games, enjoy games you can play to kill time or play casually, or just looking for something a little out of the ordinary, give Slay the Spire a shot.  You'll probably get a least some enjoyment out of it.

Probably the best way to describe Slay the Spire is by calling it a procedurally generated Roguelite card game with a heavy emphasis on drafting and deck building.
The game starts with you having access to only one class, "The Ironclad" a mixture between a Warrior, Berserker and Demon Knight. You later get access to another class, "The Silent", essentially your Rogue/Assassin type character. There are plans to release a third class eventually, I haven't researched this but I would presume it would likely end up being some sort of Mage or Wizard.
There are three stages which have you navigate through a series of, "event-nodes" ala FTL or other similar games. Mega Crit manages this in an interesting way though in that they allow you to see the full map at the start of each stage, but only the basics, "Here's a basic monster fight, here's an elite monster, here's a shop, here's something more secret", this allows you to strategize and plan ahead to mitigate RNG and balance the risk vs reward of each of the paths. This is something I personally greatly appreciate.
Combat is surprisingly deep for an early access title and even if it didn't evolve an increble amount into release and only added class(es) and random events it would be more than adequate for a budget title. Both you and the enemy can manipulate battles in various ways and strategy is definitely rewarded over just, "playing what you can afford" and ignoring card effects and enemy abilities. Enemies have various interesting abilities, especially bosses, who can have various effects that can punish you for playing too many cards, dilute your deck with cards that have various negative effects or just take up your draws, or that become ever more powerful as the battle goes on thus punishing slower decks.
Deck building is handled in an interesting way in that for every basic monster encounter rewards you with various goods but also a choice of 1 of 3 class cards at the end of battle. There is nuance in how you should approach this though as a bigger deck isn't always better, each turn you draw a new hand of cards and when your turn is over you discard any cards you didn't play. What this means is you draw through your entire deck very quickly sometimes and when you have finished drawing through your deck your discard pile gets reshuffled into your deck. This leads to interesting deckbuilding as you choose a card not only based on if it fits into a current or future strategy but also based on the fact that it'll cause you to be less likely to draw every other card in your deck multiple times. The make-up of your deck can be small and focused, large and diversified and everything in between, one of my Silent runs made Hearthstones Miracle Rogue decks look incredibly tame in comparison.
As a small side note, while you can't carry over any aspects of one of your completed runs over into the next there is some run to run progression via card unlocks which can then appear in future runs. This adds variety but may make getting specific combos trickier in the future.
Pros:
- Deck building, strategy and intelligent play are rewarded and boy does it feel good.
- Aesthetic suits the game very well and beside a few missteps here and there which feel out of place (Corpse Explosion, Rest Screen as well as a few other examples) it looks damn good.
- The game already has rather good replayability and could easily be improved exponentially with just a few additions, some of which are already planned, such as the additional character. With a few more stages as well as more Relic and card additions this is the kind of game I could see myself playing a few times a week for the next few years, if not more. Right now it is slightly more barebones, but as an Early Access title that is expected.
Meh:
- Music isn't awful, but it could definitely be better. I haven't gotten to the point of muting it yet but some of the loops, especially the one for the main menu are beginning to grate. This is coming from someone who doesn't really mute music in games too. Hopefully this gets some love as time goes on.
- Current UI both for the main menu as well as in-game isn't bad but could definitely use some improvement.
Cons:
- The game is too easy. I'm sure some will argue this point, but I won my first playthrough and am sitting at a 6W, 4L record. Some of the losses were potentially winnable but I bailed on due to frustrating RNG, likely if I played through the two runs I bailed on I could have at least one more win. This coming from someone who's only knowledge and frame of reference for the game is the first two episodes of Northernlion's LP and this being a Roguelite deckbuilder convinces me the game is too easy. Maybe as I unlock more cards it'll add to the difficulty as I won't be able to achieve the combos I want as easily, but if so then it's annoying that the difficulty increase is going to be tied to watering down the card pool as opposed to a traditional difficulty increase.
- Despite the game being too easy there are also some questionable decisions surrounding the difficulty, two examples off the top of my head: If you don't make it to the first boss during a run you miss out on the bonus choices at the start of your next run added via three random choices. This seems to be a decision made to combat people rerolling into OP starts, but this is short sighted as this a single player, non-competitive game, who cares if someone is cheesing it? This also creates a situation where good players gain additional power every run when they likely don't need it and those doing really poorly are punished when they likely need the help the most. A second example would be encountering a first stage, first fight Thief, where given poor enough draws you can reach a situation where if you don't play overly aggressive and lose 40 HP or more you can risk losing half your starting gold when he runs away.
As a final warning if you dislike any form or facet of RNG impacting your chance of winning or losing, this isn't the game for you. It is a Roguelite card game and at its heart that means there will be variance. However, I found games like "Binding of Isaac: Rebirth" to be much more frustrating when it came to RNG and if you were good at it you could win most runs, I expect this to be similar. I fully recommend this game and am eagerly anticipating further content updates and even DLC in the far future as long as it's worthwhile and content updates get pushed until then.
