First of all, I would like to point out: Much of these negative reviews come from people with a very small amount of hours into the Game, so for those looking for an honest review (with experience), feel free to look upon my hours.
I have given Black Desert Online a Positive Review for the following reasons:
1. It is very well listed (on ANY Steam Game) what requirements your PC needs to have good performance.
And Black Desert Online is no different. And what do you know, they listed it properly. So if you happen to have any issues, you may need to minimize the amount of crap on your PC by Uninstalling Games or Programs that you don't use anymore. If you STILL have any issues, it's more than likely you are on a poor quality Internet Speed.
2. BDO has a very nice looking Game & Environment. There is plenty of different Flora, Fauna, Character Customizations, & Monster types. The Environment is pretty large, well-defined, & in some areas it is purposely desolate. (such as the desert.)
3. Combat is great! You can go with your Numbers for certain attacks (like most MMO's out there) or you can do movements + attacks for those 'specialized attacks'. (Basically put: Combos Attacks work off of the same Attacks you could use either the number keys for or certain button presses.)
4. Yes, any Armor & Jewelry is wearable even at Level 1. Main & Sub-Weapons are the same way. Awakened Weapons however, you must be Level 56 for & have completed a specific Quest for your Character-type. The ONE THING that I would like changed here is the ability to use any Weapon (Main, Sub, or Awakened) on any Character ... but I highly doubt that'll happen. So if you like a certain weapon-type, you'll be stuck to a certain Class or Gender. (Depending on if you're looking at Awakened or not.)
5. Crafting: Yes, all MMO'ers know of the Crafting that MMO's have. I actually like BDO's version over most others (example: Rift, Dungeons & Dragons Online: Stormreach, Lord of the Rings, & many others) because you can focus so much on one Type at a time & can really get some good use out of them too. Most MMO's, you don't really get a good use out of a Crafting Skill (Tera-I'm looking at you), until you're playing a second, third, or whatever Character later. But in BDO, it's beneficial very early on. Also, there's not really a 'need' for a Gathering Alt or Crafting Alt ... just a lot of Bank Space!
6. Extra benefits: To put this one simply, there are added benefits to simple things you can do while AFK or even Offline. For instance: You can cast a fishing pole into the water & literally walk away. After 3m with a fish on the line, you will automatically begin auto-fishing (and will re-cast on your own). Another example is: you can hire workers to gather for you at locations that you own, whether you're online or not. And a final simple example: By running around in a town or city with a Trade Pack on your back & eating food at the same time, you are Leveling your Breath, Strength, & Health ... which gives you a Bonus to Stamina, Carry Capacity, & Hit Point Pool. So not just 'Gear' can help you!
7. Environment: The Environment alone has it's own 'life' in BDO. It Rains, it's Sunny, and believe it or not ... there are also Hurricanes on the open Ocean that you could run into as well. These Hurricanes won't likely kill you, however they do tick away a tiny bit of Health every so often.
-----
The 'Cons' to BDO that I would have to mention are pretty basic now-a-days anyways.
1. Most of the Chats are Cancer. Maybe not always, but quite a bit of the time. However, some people do make Chat worth it from time to time, if you have a real question. (Thanks to any of those people that may read this.)
2. Having to Purchase (with real money) Inventory Slots & Weight Capacity, after a certain point, just to be able to carry more, is a joke. (Although I have bought them for my Characters that I'm currently playing ... but what a rip off.)
3. Sailing Skill is broken & has been since Day one.(Not a big deal, but wow .... still not fixed.)
-----
I hope this may help any of you that may be looking to get Black Desert Online for yourselves or for a Friend that may be interested in it. I've played A TON of MMO's & this would have to be my #2 out of all of them that I played. If my #1 picked hadn't have literally died & shutdown it's servers, I'd probably still be there.
~Good Gaming All!
P.S. I use the Explorer's Package. Enjoy!

A fantastic strategy game with a crowd of tough decisions that actually matter in the long run, to the extent of permideath of squad members as well as an unforgiving resource management system.
Being an aging strategy fan I regretably never played the original UFO Defense, and or other  X-Com lineage. So other than a love for Blizzard games and growing up on the Comand & Conquer series I had very little forgame insight on this title and the overall metagame of winning a war in this gritty alien invasion setting.  So, I come as a game lover with fresh eyes to this already beloved franchise.
First things first. Do Not go into this game thinking that it requires a lot of research and study or over analyzing to have fun or find entertaining. My first couple hours were spent getting my squads wiped in various trial and error fashion, but I was having a blast the whole time learning the ins and outs of this broader combat engagement. Sneaky and surgical attacks require more patience and even more nail bitting strategy where as grenade throwing, rocket launching brute force gets the job done with a serious penalty to your earnings and many supply opportunities will be wasted. Alien autopsies as well as the even more valuable alien interrigations bring some of the games best scientific upgrades, so playing it smart is more than worth the patience and impossible if you blow your enemies into bits on the battefield. Base management is just as emersive and brutally savage as the edge of your seat combat gameplay. You find your self mapping out the activities and goals of so many defferent facets of your effort against the alien onslaught. From basic resource managemnt such as power, supplies and gathering the multiple government funding required for researching and funding scientific projects that will give you an edge in combat as well as gaining access to further research all the way to customizing your individual squad members down to their genetic code. In fact, with so many options and strategies it can come off rather overwhelming at first. This is the beauty of the game, learning by experimentation. I have never had so much fun trying to barely keep up with a games tremendous challenge. You are always a step away from failure in all the directions this game takes you, but with so many paths to choose.
PROS --
*Emersive war campaign with a great story and interesting characters.
*Strategic decisions that matter, to a make or break game over affect.
*Character customization and gameplay makes it feel like being 8 years old playing with action figures.
*Very satifying progression as you get better the enemies get tougher and more dangerous.
*Fairly long for a strategy game campaign, and thats definitely in a good way.
*Nothing beats the feeling of successfully finsishing a mission without losing any troops.
Cons --
*Steep learning curve. You Will die..... a lot.
*Graphics can seem a bit out dated at times but never felt cheap.
*You may give up before the game tells you to. It's a daunting task to save the world.

Company of heroes 2 has taken all of the good things that made CoH 1, refined them, and then added yet even more.
Whilst the campaign came across as a repetitive and numbing, this game truly shines in its "Theater of War" and Online skirmish modes.
Battling it out with your friends in Online Skirmish has never felt more visceral and intense. Explosions shred the ground, as vehicles collide with battlefield obstacles, sending broken props flying in all directions, whilst gunfire and mortar fire ring out from every direction. Overall, visuals and battlefield sound fidelity are superb, serving to draw you into the tense, ceaseless atmosphere throughout the course of the battle.
The theme of asymmetrical warfare that was evident in CoH 1 has made a triumphant return, allowing a whole host of fun abilities, commanders, and units to play around with in battles.
AI pathing and vehicle controls have been significantly refined since CoH 1, allowing faster response times and greater freedom of movement throughout the map. However there are still a few issues when controlling large groups of forces, as often times these blobs can bottleneck, causing a degree of frustration.
Theater of War allows the player to play solo, or cooperatively, along the course of World War 2 on the Eastern front, spanning from the initial invasion of the Soviet Union in 1941, to the fall of Berlin in 1945. This mode allows for an interesting historical look at the game, whilst meeting your demands for action, chaos and challenge!
Whilst there is a slightly steep learning curve for those new to RTS, and in particular CoH, I can guarantee that if you stick with it, you'll not only be able to stand a chance against some of the better players, but you'll also have hours upon hours of high destruction fun.

TL;DR - 8/10 Pros: Dynamic character development, superior graphic/voice acting quality, Lots of things to do.
Cons: Basic storyline, repetitive side missions
Although the storyline is somewhat basic in nature, I did find myself pleasantly surprised with little twists here and there that made for an exciting rush just when I was starting to feel monotony was about to set in. Where Far Cry Primal lacks in its story line (unlike it's predecesors) it makes up for with significant attention to character development. Your tribe mates really come to life with stellar voice acting, interesting back stories, and pleasing attempts at realism with their design. There is no lack of side quests to do on your way to complete Main Story Quests, or after the main part of the game is finished, however be warned there are only a few categories and eventually they can become repetitious. That being said they are offered in different scenery despite being a standardized quest type which makes it feel much less of a drag, and can compell you to finsih them region by region. There are also instant adventures that appear while exploring that make it worth while not to utilize the fast travel feature all of the time. Overall Far Cry Primal was to me a very pleasing game. I found myself "hooked" being able to invest upwards of 5+ hour at a time without having realized that much time had passed. The pros far outways the cons in my opinion and I would recommend this as a purchase, and if on the off chance its price tag is not in your budget I would HIGHLY recommend snatching it up the second it goes on sale, if it ever does. solid 8/10.

First off, i must note that i've never watched the Game of Thrones TV show, so i'm reviewing this game from a somewhat blind point of view. Many reviewers said that this game is one of the worst games that Telltale Games produced. And you know what? That may be the case, but i still enjoyed it and i can say that this is by no means a bad game. I may have been a little lost during the first episode, but i quickly managed to catch up with this universe and this particular story. And that's good. It may use a license, but it still managed to entertain someone who never watched the show. I liked the overall story, maybe half of the characters (which isn't really a good thing), and even QTE fighting was fun. If you watch the show, you may enjoy it more, or quite the opposite: that i don't know. But perphaps the biggest criticism that this game has is the illusion of choice. Most choices do mean little and some lead to plotholes, and there's a few that actually matter, especially towards the end. To be honest, this is an issue with most choice-based games out there, but from what i've played this issue is bigger in this game. But don't let that disappoint you. Even with all the criticism i truly enjoyed this game, and i can recommend it but not at full price.

Crate Entertainment have made a line in the sand with this title. Grim Dawn is hardly unique (Diablo similarities will inevitably be pointed out), but its hacky-slashy goodness is very, very well constructed. The principle of "break thing to advance" effectively constitutes not only the core but also the seeds, flesh, and stem of this particular apple, and yet it provides so many interesting ways to break said thing.
The... for lack of a better term, theory-crafting-friendliness... is one of the biggest draws. Most like-minded titles - Gameloft's Dungeon Hunter franchise comes to mind - have minor to moderate complexities in character creation and development; stat points and active/passive abilities complement each other. In Grim Dawn, the player has stat specializations and abilities that are specific to their class. They will also have a second class to choose, a wide array of equipment to create and customize which will bring its own set of passive/active abilities, a totally independent set of "constellation" perks that are unlocked through exploration rather than level-grinding, and the ability to conditionally reallocate skills for trying out alternatives to one's current build. It is not a game where one can simply spend a weekend and get the feel for one's favorite mechanics - it is a massive and carefully built system.
Aesthetically, Grim Dawn also has much to recommend it. Between sound, light, and model design, it presents a world where the player is both a birth citizen and an intruder. Things go bump in the night, and - at least in the author's opining - trips to a previously-visited village often manage to remain unsettling even when a peek at enemy levels shows there's nothing to objectively worry about. The refuse of human civilization is everywhere and volumes are spoken without even picking up the snippets of lore diaries and documents scattered about, from the places where mass graves are not even totally covered to an abandoned baby carriage found near a ruined town square. It gives breath to a place where it makes sense for people to use iron as a currency and all that implies. Given how the story usually serves as a limited framework in which a hack-and-slash RPG's campaign waypoints are mapped out, Grim Dawn's tale-telling is neither revolutionary, nor merely meeting par.
There is also a peculiar quality which might be considered weakness or strength, circumstantially. Namely, whereas other hack-and-slash kinds of titles involve a good deal of active survival via dodging, blocking, warping, etc., Grim Dawn's combat provides no "innate" means of defense other than a potent regeneration capacity. If one gets caught in a cluster of tightly-knit foes, survival does not mean just leaving the area - it often means cutting a way out of the enemy formation. There are relatively easily accessible means of defense, but they have a different mechanism than in many other ARPGs of this style. As a prime example, equipping a shield allows the player to block, but this is done automatically with an attached refresh period. Other times, the player must use class- or equipment-bestowed skills like creating a wall of knives to prevent enemy attacks (and yes, this is as awesome as it sounds) or keeping foes at a distance with caltrops. For those who've gotten used to reflexively hitting dodge-roll as a get-out-of-danger technique, it provides a distinct change in pace.
In summary, Grim Dawn is like going out to take a horseback ride and discovering that the mount in question is actually a pegasus with a dog's head and flightless ostrich wings - its nature is somewhat self-evident, and it differentiates itself from its brethren in largely cosmetic ways, but the changes really shape its character and provide an interesting game with quite a lot to recommend it.

I don't get all the bad reviews concering " A lack of substance and story ". The game is set in 10,000BCE. What do you expect? I think they did very well working with what they had. They wanted to keep the game as real as possible, with still having a bit of fun (taming the beasts, and certain weapons).
I personally really enjoyed the game. There is a lot to do once you upgrade your skill points and collect all the villagers. The side quests are just as fun as the main quests. The graphics are lovely, and despite many saying there isn't a story line, there is a lot of substance once you start doing side quests. Finding out what really happened to your village, what your village was like, their philosphies - it's actually quite nice.
I love the ability to upgrade your weapons, and there is more than just a 'bow'. The more villagers and XP you gain the more you can unlock and upgrade, and upgrading certain weapons can make them into completely new weapons.
The only thing that makes me a bit annoyed is the lack of certain things. Stamina bars, under water, no real way to track your XP for SP. So you can't really farm out what missions youd like, no telling when you'll get. Also, I find the ranks on missions are completely backwards. A mission that says 'Easy' is propably going to take you an afternoon of cursing and rage quitting before you finally complete it, while the 'very hard' missions take me 10-30 minutes.
All in all, I recommend this game. It's really fun.

Oh XCOM, how I both love and hate you. I've never even beaten this game, even though I've probably had 6+ attempts to run through it. I'm trying out the popular Long War mod now, because it adds a lot of depth/ character/ difficulty to the game but I have no idea why I'm even doing that, since I can't even complete the base game. It may have something to do with the fact that I insist on playing on Ironman mode, I like the idea that of having to live with my decisions but it just ends up being a horribly masochistic choice to make...
XCOM: Enemy Unknown, and it's exemplary expansion, Enemy Within is a reboot of an old, venerable turn based strategy franchise. I've never played any of the old XCOMs, and die-hard fans will say this is a casualization of the franchise, but I found this game to be amazing, and definitley very tactically deep. Essentially, you are placed in charge of a top secret military organization that is formed, funded, and supported by every major nation on the planet, activated with... you guessed it, when ALIENS ATTACK! The game does a phenomenal job of making you feel outgunned and outmatched, you truly feel like you're fighting a desperate war where victory seems literally impossible. If you play on the harder difficulties especially with Ironman, you'll bemoan the loss of your troops and the failure of your actions.
Most of the game is spent in a tactical top down view of combat with aliens. Pretty standard fare, similar to the Fire Emblem series with more ranged weapons, but in between missions you spend time at a secret underground base where you build laboratories, factories, and research/ interrogate alien species to help you better fight future battles. A shadowy group of country representatives known as The Council funds you and critiques your mission performance, however, you don't have enough resources to respond to every attack around the world all the time, so you have to pick and choose which countries you want to keep from "panicking." If a country "panics" they'll pull out from funding you, giving you even less resources to choose from. This leads to an interesting moral choice, similar to the old Atari game Missile Comand where you have to protect cities from getting destroyed. Should you try to save every country, or just focus on a few, and forget the rest? The Enemy WIthin expansion allows you to augment the ever living♥♥♥♥♥♥out of your soldiers, leading to amputations/ enhancements that lend better combat abilities but also make you feel as if you are losing your humanity. In my opinion, since we are all getting lasered to death by aliens anyway, of course I would augment the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of my soldiers to give us a chance, but it's up to you, really.
XCOM: Enemy Unknown is one of the best strategy games on PC and you should probably own it already, but if you don't, pick it up if you like Fire Emblem/ Independence Day or if you enjoy strategy titles in general. I love that since this game was so difficult, the canonical ending of the game is that we failed. WE ALL FAILED, GUYS, THE ALIENS WON! XCOM 2 appears to show an earth dominated by the aliens due to a complete failure of earth's defenses, and in that game, we'll get our second chance at finally completing the game. Can't wait to lose again!

I recommend this game but be warned: it has bugs and glitches.
Pros:
+Its fun and addicting, turn based, tactical, strategy game.
+There's a lot of game (good value), that will keep you wondering what happens on the next turn. (I've come to expect this from Firaxis.)
+Critical thinking and management game -- you manage your XCOM base, and depending on your performance, you either keep or lose nation (members) for your XCOM project.
+Interesting plot, and CGI/voice acting isn't too bad.
+It's really cool when you're tasked to capture an alien. You have to critically think of strategies to keep your troops alive and not get hurt while they attempt to do this.
+The best strategy is, if you can employ it, rather than letting your troops take damage, which requires them time to heal, try to find a way to never let them get hurt in the first place. I found by playing with this as my priority, it seriously has helped my overall strategizing. Sometimes you can't help it.
+It's a lot of fun just blowing the hell up out of some important building, and getting paid for it because aliens are present. Having to use rockets on a particular office building, or having to use grenades next to vehicles can make some spectacular explosive displays.
Cons:
-Though I have never seen it crash to desktop, it has completely froze on me, usually right at the start of the AI's turn. I can move the mouse but the UI doesn't come back.
-I don't know what it is about the Berserker Muton but whenever this particular unit has a move, the game gets severely choppy; I guess it's because the camera anchors to this unit and it causes slow down/staggering.
-I have lost a troop due to it getting it's foot stuck in the floor. I literally have had to fight an entire mission down a man, not because he was dead, but because I couldn't move him because he was glitched for some reason.
-I have had to reload missions simply due to mis-clicking on a tile for a troop to move to, and have him going to some other tile. Sometimes, the isometric perspective doesn't work best, especially when you're going through an alien base or a large alien ship (like a supply ship), and you have multiple levels to deal with. This creates havoc for the already problematic unit placing tool.
-Other note on the unit placing tool: it's glitchy. Attempting to move a unit to a particular location on a floor could have the floor or roof intervening on your placement, right at the time you're about to click, thus placing the unit in a bad position. It just seems to cause the floor or roof to disappear by "flickering" on and off and is extremely annoying. I've had to reload games due to this.
-Probability chance of getting a hit or being hit seems to be off by a mile at times. I don't know what it is, there's just something wrong when you go to take a shot, like say, a Sniper with a 98% chance to hit a target and he misses. Crap like that has me uttering bad words... Sometimes I wonder if the % chance to hit even makes sense in this game because I really don't think it does. I have missed enemy combatants with 85-98% chance to hit and it blows me away that when they make the same moves, they never miss. You'd think that a troop that is aiming at an enemy combatant would have the same chances as the enemy combatant in terms of hitting. Sometimes, it feels like 50/50, regardless what the aiming tooltip has to say.
-Some annoyances in regards to the back and forth motion of the camera; as it zooms to whichever unit's turn it is, so you can better plan your move. Personally, I don't care about the presentation so much, especially after I'm hooked after 15 hours of gameplay; at this point, all I want to do is just play. But it's so annoying when you want to take your move and the screen is bouncing around from enemy to friendly because it has to do it's little "focus" effect, where it centers the camera right on top of the unit whose turn it is to move. Very annoying, especially when you already know where you want to throw the grenade/launch a rocket, then you click the button on the unit for it, and it goes back to focusing/centering on the unit again, so you have to find again, the spot for launching said rocket/grenade to. And then misclicking at this time can have terrible consequences -- especially if you're not intending it, you'll have to reload your game.
-I found the mini cinematics, such as watching your troop fire/throw a grenade/run to a certain location to be pointless. Deactivating them doesn't seem to speed up the game, now you just wait the 3-4 seconds instead of seeing a little cinematic, in place of watching the cinematic, as if the cinematic is playing in the background.
-Would be nice if it let you customize the individual settings for like say, map scroll speed, if whether or not it will focus/center the mouse on every action for every troop (actions being grenade toss, rocket launch), the area of map scrolling (how close the mouse has to be to the edge for the map to move left or right, up or down). If whether or not you can go with a more basic tile selecting tool because the one in the game, as it is now, is very glitch and feels resource demanding (is slow in later levels, when there's a lot going on).
-There have been times when I lost units that have been standing next to a vehicle, that doesn't appear to be on fire, but is actually on fire. But I wouldn't know it until after it explodes. Very annoying to discover this. I have determined that the tiny little fire on the inside of the car window, that is visible at any angle, indicates the vehicle is on fire.
-The difficulty of the game ramps up incredibly, especially after you're able shoot down a UFO that is known for taking out satellites. It becomes incredibly important to capture any alien you come across, and sometimes, they're incredibly strong. It only makes you wonder how can you possibly budget to have the best gear for your men and at the same time, have enough funding to launch all the satellites you need for all the members of your XCOM project? For instance: going against the Red Mutons that have plasma laser guns is an extremely bad idea, if all you have is carapace armor and less than plasma sniper rifles, since these guys can hit you at an incredibly long range, for a lot of health damage, and don't take much damage themselves.
-Snipers seem to be so important after just a little while. They have incredibly useful talents, such as being able to target foes that are visible by other troops. I find bringing at least two to every mission to be detrimental, while Support is okay, as long as you don't use any variation of the shotgun, and run&gun ability is totally stupid, except in situations where it means you have completed a mission or saved a fellow troop -- otherwise, it's just an excellent way to lose a troop; and Heavy is terrible at long range, and will miss just about every time, but is awesome for the rockets it can launch, as well as the suppression ability -- detrimental for catching aliens. So, I think there's some balancing issues with the classes and how they come together.
-Some abilities can't be lived without and some are totally pointless.
I know, I bellyached quite a bit but it's the little things that kill in a game like this. Honestly, the game is quite fun and playable, as long as you can put up with all of it's frequently occuring glitches.

This game, while it does have a large amount of fan service, has other qualities that make it a worthwhile game to play. The game itself is fairly easy once the combo system is mastered and each character's skills are explored to the fullest. There is a welcomed increase in the variety of dungeon environments and map designs when compared to Re;Birth 1. The gameplay is fairly straightforward, the story is decent, and each of the characters have their own unique personalities that shine through in the dialogue. This game has many humourous moments portrayed through its dialogue as well. The characters are all unique and many of them are super cute! Character development is evident in the main characters and in the events found in each city that allow some interaction with the side characters. Many potential endings exist in the game, allowing for some replayability to try to experience each ending. The English version has only a few typos which I think is acceptable for a game that was translated from Japanese.
As for the cons... I know that this game was designed to have exuberant amounts of fan service, but I didn't like the fan service and I didn't buy the game because of the fan service. I was able to just skip most of it though. The remake system was a bit of a let-down for me since I missed out on a dungeon unlock that could only be found in a hidden treasure in one specific dungeon. Thus, I lost the ability to fight many of the stronger monsters and find many of the crafting items in later dungeons. Stella's Dungeon was lackluster since I finished the game in just a few days. Another con for this game was that the acquisition of the Gehaburn sword DLC at the beginning of the game basically made the game "ultra easy mode" if it was used. Don't use that sword if you want this game to have even an ounce of challenge to it.
In summary: Get this game if it is on sale! Whether you like fan service or not, this game has other elements that make it enjoyable regardless. Alongside the other games in the Hyperdimension Neptunia series, this game is one of the most unique games in my entire library. Approach this game with an open mind and you won't be disappointed.

TL;DR:  I liked the game even with its flaws, and is totally worth the money I paid for.  Considering that I'm a pirate, that's saying a lot (though, if you take into account the fact that I bought it during a sale that included Re;Birth1 and Re;Birth3. . .).
If you played Re;Birth1, don't expect continuity; the game itself admitted this fact.  Still, it's a nice game and is better in terms of story compared to Re;Birth1 -- even
it's still the same "save the world from the villains", it's still enjoyable -- due to the many endings that you can get.  Yes, the main plot is still the same "save the world from the villain", but doesn't every action show  Of course, that's not necessarily a nice thing as by the fourth run, things start to get repetitive enough that you're pressing the "Skip" button to skip through the dialogues.  Unless you're not a completionist, in which case, playing through the game just to see the True Ending, Conquest Ending, Holy Sword Ending, and Normal Ending is enough to make the game worth your money.  As a side note, get the Conquest Ending as your first ending, because it's a rather grim ending, and the other endings will make you feel better (I'm weird, in that I think that I have to make up for what I did in order to get the Conquest Ending).
As a pirate, I found some of the anti-piracy message to be slightly offensive; but nothing I couldn't tolerate and rationalise.  I especially love how they managed to make a game revolve around piracy and not make it insufferable like most propaganda they throw at you when it comes to piracy.  The story, while somewhat lighthearted, can make some fine points about philosophy, life, and things you wouldn't really expect from a story about anthromorphic game consoles and video games.  There were touching scenes that made me cry, there were scenes that made me shake my hand in anger, and there were scenes that made me laugh my heart out.  Even though I used the "Skip" function, the scene where the true CFW Brave faced the party for the last time is the one scene where I used the "Auto" function instead; it's that good (to me, but YMMV).
The characters are distinct enough that they don't feel like complete carbon copies of each other (with so many characters available in the game, it's unavoidable that some have similarities with each other).  That said, other than the main characters that you unlock via story progression, the extra characters required for the True Ending aren't as fleshed out, which makes them kind of redundant as requirements for the True Ending.  The extra characters had better roles and usage in Re;Birth 1, whereas here, they seemed to have only been shoehorned for the sake of including them.  There seemed to be some extra content packed into the international version (or so I would assume, based on how they were unvoiced and how they had some sort of a retcon-ish feel to them) that made some of the gameplay easier and a little richer in terms of side character development, but I'm not quite sure.
Since I usually set the BGM at 60%, SFX at 70% and Voice at 100%, I kind of didn't notice whether the sound was good or bad, but hey, that's me.  I only listen to the Japanese audio (because it's way better than the localised content), so I have no idea whether or not the English voice acting was good or bad.  If you understand Japanese, some of the localised dialogue would seem off, but that's understandable, as you need to have some level of understanding of both Japanese and Japanese pop culture to understand the original dialogues and their references. The gameplay is simple enough that you can master the basics by the second battle, but formulating winning strategies on your first playthrough will take a bit more than just knowing the basics.  The game also includes a "Fortify Enemies" option if you don't think that the game was challenging enough, or a "Weaken Enemies" option if you're just looking to view the stories without too much grinding.  One of the major changes made to the battle was the fact that unlike Re;Birth1, there is no equipment that nullifies status ailments that you can pile up as you go through the game in multiple playthroughs, keeping the game somewhat balanced even in an NG+ situation.  If you used the DLC however, and reach levels exceeding 500, you're going to find that even the last boss will be a cakewalk.  Of course, it's not easy to reach level 500 and you'll have to either grind like crazy, or use cheats (but that sort of takes the fun out of it).  One tiny annoying thing about the game mechanics however, is how you obtain the endings.  You need to manipulate Shares (in-universe, faith becomes quantifiable and are known as Shares) by taking quests and there will be a lot of repetitive quests that you have to do in order to get all 9 endings (yes, there are nine endings).  The Colosseum will make this a little easier to do, but the battles are difficult if your team is not properly geared and leveled.
If you made it all the way here, then go buy the series and experience the awesomeness that is the Neptunia series.

Back in 1998 Valve debuted with Half-Life a FPS game changer. The long awaited Half-Life 2 was released 2004, nearly 16 years ago and you can see the significant development in the characters and AI  – adding facial expressions and player interaction, the graphics and physics – shader based technology and incredibly realistic environments with water fluidity, buoyancy and mass related items etc .
OK, it is not up to today’s graphic standards for current FPS as it can be glitchy in parts, some of the movement can be a little frustrating, but it is 16 years old, still a ‘Classic’ and will continue to be one of the Legendary  games in FPS history.
The Half-Life series has a massive following so it is worth checking out the Steam Half-Life Community, especially for the fan based mods which are out of this world, as well as the News Links for current updates, yes updates there is still a strong following today with a recent look at the development of the HL2 Water Levels without an airboat.
Overall an overwhelmingly must have game for all Steam users, so much so I personally think HL should be gifted to account holders when signing up for Steam!
Now the final question is and has been for many years, how much longer do we have to wait for Half-Life 3?

You know I actually thought this game was going to be fun, and it
.
, once I reached the awakening level (which I can't remember what it is atm because of how hard I wiped the memory of this game from my brain) I realized how many fundamental things that make every MMORPG fun are missing from this one. It's almost as if they spent 50% of their resources on stuff that REALLY doesn't matter like the insane amount of different underwear you can purchase for your favourite waifus and extremely provocative lineup of outfits for each character. When I say "this game is missing a lot of fundamental things that make MMORPGs fun" I'll give you this clean and simple example; think about an MMO without raids, boss rushes, missions, dungeons or pretty much anything involving a challenge of any kind aside from PvP. All you get to do most of the time are the same basic, boring♥♥♥♥♥hobbies that people who love to chat and listen to a podcast do when they're completely bored aka fishing, trading, RIDING A ♥♥♥♥ING HORSE BACK AND FORTH just to level it up etc. I know there's people who are all about that, and trust me so am I to a certain extent, but I like jumping into action for loot honestly.
I appreciate the fact that they at least made a huge effort with the crazy amount of move sets each character has to offer  so that you can use them in battle to mix your opponents up and not just rinse and repeat the same keys over and over like most of these games. The combat doesn't work like it does in most traditional MMOs which is literally the only thing that actually got me to play this game. Yet somehow people have found "meta" within some characters meaning that despite the devs adding a ton of options to choose from in terms of characters and their movesets, only some of them will be "destroying" others when it comes to PvP and it won't be because they're more skilled than you.
I apologize if this review is very bland and not so descriptive, but what I'm trying to say is that you really shouldn't waste your money on this game. No I'm not talking about wasting 10 bucks, I'm talking about the pay2win pets and other small things that don't necessarily boost your level progress by that much but certainly end up getting you more loot therefore earning you more money therefore buying you better gear because you payed about 20$ on a virtual PET that only picks up loot. Yeah you heard me, 20$ CAD (15$ or something in USD, which I still find stupidly overpriced). Don't even get me started on how ridiculously priced the outfits are in this game...

I've played and enjoyed pretty much all the TellTale games but this one is easily bottom of the list for me because it falls into all the traps TTG usually sidesteps.
The game very closely follows the formula TTG established with Walking Dead and it's become stale.  I have nothing against that formula in theory, but we all know now what to expect from the "every decision you make matters" bit and it's not good enough to base your entire game around anymore.  A good story can help you gloss over that but GoT doesn't measure up in that regard either.
Typically TTG does a great job of taking an established world and building out their own characters that feel completely at home there but wholly unique and fleshed out (like in Tales of the Borderlands).  But here, all of the main characters feel like a  carbon-copy of the Stark family and their story arcs.  "Oh look, it's not-Jon-Snow doing very Jon-Snow things in that area Jon-Snow usually hangs out in.  Riveting"  Despite TTG's usual adeptness at honing in on what makes a franchise special, it's closer to one of those licensed movie games you'd pick up a decade ago where you literally play out all the things you saw  in the movies.  Because...I guess we just wanted a crappier version of that experience.
I'm actually not sure who this game was made for since those with more knowledge of the show are more likely to be frustrated when they can't use that knowledge to avoid incredibly bad decisions in the game.  It will be like "Do you want to ally with this character?" and the whole time you're going "No, get the ♥♥♥♥ out of there! ♥♥♥♥♥♥is about to go down with them!!!"  while the game just plows forward regardless.
The TellTale engine also really shows it's age here.  Often when you see the close up of a character, the background looks like an Impressionist painting - a collage of abstract colors that bleed together.  When you have a higher res model jabbering in front of something straight out of a Monet exhibit, it's just a visual mess.
Finally, the ending.  No direct spoilers here, but after I hit the ending I was livid for days later.  It felt like a complete waste of time, like 4 of the 6 chapters didn't even need to exist.  What had I accomplished?  Why did I need to see half the sub-plots presented?  I felt absolutely robbed of a decent story because some exec prematuraly commisioned a second season and TTG was too lazy to make the game conclude properly.
I will not be buying Season 2 of Game of Thrones.  It will be the first TellTale game I refuse to play.

Like a SimCity with a story, Tropico 4 follows a Central American dictator as he rises against the odds to bring his country to the front of the world stage. Following from the 1950's to the 1990's, you watch the world evolve, and your own island country grow.
Game play comes with 20 missions, each on an island, that only repeat the island a couple of times, to return to it depending on what is going on in the story. Also, the better you do on previous islands, the more benefits you will have on future ones. Buildings are placed individually, but can be 'stamped' if you have enough money to afford multiple copies. The game is actually kind of difficult, as you have to balance the economy by creating industry, tourism, and agriculture; balance the defense by creating an army and keeping relations with the US, USSR, China, and "The Middle East" (Evidently a country lead by one man in this game.); and balance the interior of your country by regulating education, police, policies, and happiness.
I highly suggest the DLC "Modern Times" as it adds several new missions and islands, as well as a bunch of new buildings, events, policies, etc. The other DLCs seem so small in comparison.
All in all, I give the game 7.5/10; Definite replay value, and if you don't like the narrative story play-through, you can always play in sandbox mode.

Not that I am really invested in the story or the decisions I've made thus far, but just the fact that this game seems to not give you much of a resolution in the long run. I am well aware that the television show does favor relentless brutality of killing off characters, but here the set up is just peculiar. The game opens up with several subplots similar to that of the television show, and introduces several houses of characters completely native to this game. So far, I've grown really attached to the Forrester family, but I should know better because, it goes south from there! Some other chracters from the television show give fans that warm fuzzy feeling of confort or discomfort based on whether or not you have read the books or followed the show. What irritates me is how they put your chracter in situations where you would think you can create an outcome parallel to that of the show seeing how some involve already established chracters. The problem is that the writers did not agree and make it seemingly impossible for you to create a new possibility to change the direction of the series. In other words, your decisions are
. That's right! Not one of these serious choices you make benefits that story all that much seeing how the game ends with a resounding cliffhanger that seems unwaranted. I also don't appreciate how in some hostile encounters where the dialogue decisions take place you have little to no time to react. I feel like other games made by TellTale had a much nicer pace and narrative to their stories. Here, it feels rushed and I tend to forget specific details that are not brought up again until the next episode becuase there is so much going on at once. My friend and I played through one of the episodes and interacted with this one character where he wanted to show her up by shooting a rabbit with a bow and arrow. The game didn't give him my time to adjust his shot since the controls completely changed up on him but having him hold down the left mouse button and release. The graphics are about on the same level as The Walking Dead games, but that's its only saving grace. Hardcore fans of the books and/or television show will get some entertainment out of the dialogue and interactions with the show's characters, but even then it is not enough for me to recommend anyone this game.

Diablo was the first butt-kicking RPG that I ever played. Diablo II was a decent sequel, but never quite lived up to the glory of the original. Diablo III was a complete and utter disappointment, driven by idiots who worship money and have lost all focus on (or just have no clue) what makes a game so special - the immersion, thoughtful crafting of a world, gameplay that focuses on reinforcing the experience and truly memorable music to boot - not serving excuses to make more money, using psychology to manipulate and drive specific/desired behaviors or touting bogus ideas veiled with empty intent (ie 'pillars of design') that wreak of online-only-DRM.
Having said such, Grim Dawn does not rest on selling you ideas and what potential it might have, but actually delivers on an experience - a game that has depth, immersion and fun. This game brings back those feelings of adventure and wonder, set in a dark world that really gets you wanting to explore and reveal it's story and, though I draw comparisons to Diablo (a ground-breaking & genre-defining game), it is clearly time to move onto something that has a future - free from the greed and soulless, un-meaningful creation that has come to define Blizzard. Crate Entertainment have truly crafted something special here and it is apparent that the devs actually understand what makes a game fun - I would not be surprised to discover that every single one of the devs actually play their own game - and it is clear that much careful and considered thought has been poured into this game.
In short, Grim Dawn is an epic RPG in its own right and it is a franchise that I definitely look forward to seeing more of in the future.

It follows the Telltale style, if you're familiar with it.
The story so far is very Game of Thrones with much drama and excitment. The game is very fun.
Where it falls flat is the Telltale engine. The controls are awkward and not fluid. I was originally using mouse and keyboard, but was unable to determine if I was supposed to move my mouse or use WASD, so I quickly switched to an xbox controller.
The "choices matter" argument follows with this one as well... Choices don't actually affect the story. It affects the dialogues. With that said, it's not a bad thing, though affecting the story would make better replayability. I think if you're going to go with a system that doesn't care what you actually choose, you should not bother informing the player of what the NPC thinks.
For example:
Having the game say, "he will remember that." then killing the NPC moments later is useless.
I'd rather just go along with my choices and see the dialogue change naturally than being informed that something I said stood out.
So, like I said... Very good story. I do recommend it, but the formula needs to be worked on.

Diablo was the first butt-kicking RPG that I ever played. Diablo II was a decent sequel, but never quite lived up to the glory of the original. Diablo III was a complete and utter disappointment, driven by idiots who worship money and have lost all focus on (or just have no clue) what makes a game so special - the immersion, thoughtful crafting of a world, gameplay that focuses on reinforcing the experience and truly memorable music to boot - not serving excuses to make more money, using psychology to manipulate and drive specific/desired behaviors or touting bogus ideas veiled with empty intent (ie 'pillars of design') that wreak of online-only-DRM.
Having said such, Grim Dawn does not rest on selling you ideas and what potential it might have, but actually delivers on an experience - a game that has depth, immersion and fun. This game brings back those feelings of adventure and wonder, set in a dark world that really gets you wanting to explore and reveal it's story and, though I draw comparisons to Diablo (a ground-breaking & genre-defining game), it is clearly time to move onto something that has a future - free from the greed and soulless, un-meaningful creation that has come to define Blizzard. Crate Entertainment have truly crafted something special here and it is apparent that the devs actually understand what makes a game fun - I would not be surprised to discover that every single one of the devs actually play their own game - and it is clear that much careful and considered thought has been poured into this game.
In short, Grim Dawn is an epic RPG in its own right and it is a franchise that I definitely look forward to seeing more of in the future.

I recommend this game. Here's why.
1. It was a good sequel to Alan Wake.
2. It succeeded in making me care about the side characters.

With that said, here's a few things to keep in mind.
Alan Wake's American Nightmare is considerably shorter than the original. Assuming you've got some skill, you can Perfect this game in less than 20 hours. The original would take about 35-40. Because of the plot mechanics, you might feel like you're retreading content, which makes a somewhat short game, feel small. Lastly, this game lacks a lot of the pop reference that made the original so fun. The only thing that remains are the radio broadcasts and the TV Show.
If you already own Alan Wake, and feel like you need more, this game is a must. If you don't, you should stop reading this, and buy both of them.

I'd like to give Grim Dawn a positive review, but sadly its strengths are outweighed by a lot of weaknesses that kinda ruined the game for me. As the overall reviews are positive, I'm going to focus on the things I didn't like:
Although Grim Dawn has an interesting class system which gives you the opportunity to create many different builds and unique combinations, the game itself never made me feel like I need to explore its possibilities. I played as a Pyromancer – basically a witch wielding dual pistols with lots of fire and poison stuff going on – and apart from a heavily upgraded fire strike (which is the standard left click attack) and a self-heal ability, I did not use anything from any skill tree. I simply didn't have to, because I was shooting down every enemy including bosses on sight. So I just grinded through the whole thing holding down the left mouse button and occasionally pressing the right one. Sadly, the game was over before I got myself enough skill points to at least unlock some of the more powerful abilities.
Same goes for faction reputation, components to upgrade your gear, devotions, etc. I didn't even have to look into any of that. Didn't grind any reputation, didn't upgrade my gear, didn't put any effort into a useful distribution of my devotion points, still was easy af. Of course I'm aware that the game has difficulty settings that would require me to look into those things, but where would I draw the motivation from, if the first playthrough felt so dull? Even on Diablo 3's standard difficulty I had to check for cool gear, use newly acquired skills/runes and so on. Not to mention that I didn't find the design or generic story of "This fantasy world is threatened by some ancient evil and you as the chosen one must slay thousands of enemies to save us all" compelling enough to give Grim Dawn another go.
Also, the loot distribution system is extremely unsatisfying. Shortly before beating the final boss I found a better pair of gloves to replace the ones I found at level 12. Most loot was extremely useless and I rarely found anything to go with my build. In addition, the visual impact of new equipment is reduced to a bare minimum. Almost all armor pieces look the same, even rare pieces. My character pretty much looked the same during my entire playthrough. Is it too much to ask for that after slaying literal tons of monsters and preventing the apocalypse my armor's covered in skulls while my shoulder pads constantly emit lightning bolts?
Lastly, I felt that there was not enough feedback in terms of story progression. I never knew for sure how far I already got, which is why the end came very surprising to me and felt rushed.
For hardcore fans of complex character builds and massive grinding Grim Dawn might certainly be worth a shot, but if you're a little more on the casual side and just want to equip your avatar with increasingly powerful gear that also looks badass, this game is probably not your cup of tea.

My continued love of all things Nep continues, as I have completed Re;Birth2, having recieved the normal ending.
There were a couple of strange technical issues.  Screen tearing was pretty awful, and nothing I did could fix it.  My old system, (GTX 650ti, AMD FX 6300) crashed on the very first battle, but since my upgrade earlier this year (AMD R9-390, i5 6600k) I experienced no such crashes.  In the end I simply learned to live with the screen tearing.  Oh yeah, and every time I would start up the game, the controller wouldn't work until I went into the menu and switched the control scheme over to mouse for some reason.  More of an annoyance than a game breaker though.
Re:Birth 2 was a lot like Re;Birth 1.  Most assets are recycled, but I expected this, so I was okay with it.  This time around the game focused on the CPU candidates; Nepgear, Uni, Ram, and Rom.  The writing was still top notch, but I think this was a weaker game having earlier completed Re;Birth1.  It was a bit shorter too, and I got to the end after about 20ish hours.
Stella's Dungeon was an unexpected and neat feature.  Basically you send Stella and her cat off into dungeons after picking her equipment, and she does so in real time.  You could be in the middle of a scene or fight, and you'll get a notification that Stella's exploration was successful, or if she met her untimely demise.  Success means earning unique items and plans.
Overall, I would recommend this game, especially for fans of the series, but I won't fault you if you opt to skip it.  Personally, I'll be moving straight away to Re;Birth3, which I've heard is the best of the three, so I'm pretty excited about it.  Still, I enjoyed my time with Re;Birth 2, and I'm glad I played it.

2/5 Story
4/5 Gameplay
3/5 Graphics
3/5 Music
4/5 Replay Value
Overview:
FTL is simple, straightforward, and terrific. The story is a fairly basic space age theme. You control a ship, there are different races throughout the galaxy with a variety of technologies, weapons, strengths, weaknesses, etc... and of course the game features plenty of space battles. The wonderful thing about this game is the way it takes those same basic features we've seen before and does something different with them. You control the crew of your ship not just your ship.  You specifically assign your crewmembers to the consoles for piloting, weapons, shields, etc... all of the important technologies of your ship. You have to battle fires, and hull breaches, boarders, weapon damage, and sometimes even mind control or hacking. FTL is unique in the way it handles the same old space battles we've all been playing since the first Star Trek and Star Wars games. It isn't just shoot until the enemy dies. You have to play smart, conserve resources, upgrade when possible but carefully.
Story:
I feel bad trying to give this game a rating on story because it is not really meant to have much of one and actually manages to convey details of the universe pretty well just by way of gameplay.
Gameplay:
This is the meat and bones of this game. Gameplay is nearly perfect. Battles are tactical, interesting, and fun. The game is difficult but not impossible and exploration although not flashy or exciting uses elements of randomness that really makes it feel like exploring. The random encounters possible in FTL also offer an element of choice. Do I defend the colony from pirates or accept the pirates bribe to leave quietly? None of the decisions carry the weight or long term consequence of games like Mass Effect, but than much of the charm of FTL is the simplicity.
Graphics:
This game uses very simple straightforward graphics for the races, ships, guns, etc... Enough to know exactly what you are looking at without getting distracted by flashy bits or confused with what actions are occuring because of too much complexity. The backgrounds, however, are gorgeous and very very well done.
Music:
This is always the hardest category for me. I am not an avid music fan myself hardly even listening to music at all. However, the game music was not overly repetive or annoying and it seemed to fit the game well so I have no complaints against it.
Replay Value:
Highly replayable. This game is simple to play, complex to master, quick, easily stopped and picked up again later, contains unlockable ships and achievements you want to work towards, and is just generally a perfect replay game.

It is difficult to get noticed on Steam these days. To rise above the deluge of releases, you have to be a cut above the rest in a market where being a "7/10 okay" game is almost no longer acceptable because of the sheer amount of choice we have.
Slay the Spire, along with Dead Cells and Darkest Dungeons, is one of the most fun games I have ever played in Early Access. I will go as far as saying I haven't had the "one more run" itch this badly since I started playing Binding of Isaac.
The central gameplay loop is move up the spire in an FTL-fashion. You usually have a choice on which path to take after each encounter. Each encounter type is potentially game-making or breaking. A merchant may have a card or relic you really need, or help you prune your deck of cards you don't want. Elites are powerful combat encounters that can give you a relic, a passive item that changes how your character fundamentally works a lot of the times. Even normal combat encounters are important because you always get at least one card from winning.
There's an insanely rewarding feeling when you finish the game your first time. When you get the right combination of cards and relics, you are absolutely devasating to enemies. The right combination of relics could give you +10 block each turn
for example.
Like any card game, even ones in full release, there are fringe cases where you're not entirely sure how an interaction will work. For example, when I crunched the numbers for the above, I thought I always would get it, but I'm not sure how it interacted with dexterity modifiers and a lot of times I wasn't calculating the number correctly. Luckily, I always err'd on the side of caution.
More annoyingly, there is a persistent flashing graphical bug. Not sure what causes it, but it causes your screen to flash at random intervals. It isn't game-breaking, but very annoying. If you watch a Northernlion LP, you can see what I"m talking about.
I bought this game after watching a guy play it on Youtube for five minutes a few days ago and have pumped out 11 hours from it already even though I work a full time job. Its just very relaxing to play, but also challenging.
For $16.00 and the promise of additional content, the game definitely feels worth the price to me. I suggest you watch first impressions on Youtube if you're undecided.

Tropico 4 is a great, in-depth look at how to manage and run a city and its economy. It differs to that of SimCity and Anno as the economy and the needs of the citizens are of great importance to succeeding; imagine running a Sim household translated to city scenario, with the different aspects of society affecting citizen happiness. It's very humourous and can be considered a great introuction to the city building/simulation genre. With the addition of the multiple factions in the game, including the rebels and foregin powers, you further have to micro-manage your expenses and make sure the right people are pleased. The game did teach me about the numerous factions which can be approriated to real life such as nationalists, commuinists, capitalists, loyalists etc, which adds, for lack of a better term, political realism to the game.
You really get a hands on feel to what commodities are being produced, where you are generating money, and where you are losing it, with the aid of an Almanac displaying the numerical statatics of your city for easy referral. You dont feel seperated or alienated during the city building process as you are constantly being advised by the numerous, quirky characters, especially your loyally passionate, animated PA, and you do feel like your actions are being counted on which adds an additional layer of immersion. The soundtrack is EXCELLENT, albeit short (which therefore means you can hear you favourite track again shortly :D), with catchy jives and upbeat tempos as the tropican culture is captured perfectly and you do really feel like El Presidente amongst all the exotic instrumentation. The tutorial could have been further in-depth with explaining certain features as I had to resort to googling some aspects, but overall the campaign is great and it feels very rewarding when your exports return an enromous profit bringing you out of debt :P.
The way in which the campaign is structured with individual missions means you can schedule and pace your gaming time, instead of wondering when the end is in sight. The different avenues of money-making, i.e. the numerous exporting commodities, means you can differ your stragety each time you play a mission, without routine-like, repeting methods. With the specific, analytical nature of the gameplay, you aren't looking at expansive, sprawling cities and skylines, so this game does create an attractive niche in the genre without detracting purpose to playing other mainstream city building games. I havent played the dlc campaigns yet, but in addition to that you get more outfit options for your avatar and decorations,  I wouldn't count them as must-have additions, the campaign dlc would probably be sufficient. I'm really keen to check out Tropico 5 now and see how it differs and what new features are implemented. Grabbing Tropico 4 (presumably the Steam Special Edition) for under $10 is well worth it, no buyers remorse. Overall, I rate this game 4 out of 5 spainards.

Okay, time for a review. The short of this one is: It's light hearted enough to warrant purchase, even at full price.  Now onward to the meat of the review!
You've got 4 "goddesses" who rule over their lands and are fighting to be the One True Goddess.  Then we get a new player, and things go completely out of whack.  The story itself isn't original, but the execution of the premise is nice.  The biggest gripe I would have about the story is that most of the character dialogue is presented in the "light novel" format, which means you watch the characters' still portraits engage in a lot of talking for you to hear/read.
This is probably one of the worst things about the game.  Your sprite moves from place to place, and you can even select locations from a list.  While travelling in the overworld, you're essentially a safe person, so it's a good way to sit idle.  When you find a dungeon (or you could think of them as a "monster zone" since some of them are outside and it feels weird to call a forest a dungeon), you also get some platformer elements: jumping, running, monsters to avoid or attack and loot to acquire.
Combat is very turn based.  A queue is generated with all the characters and monsters, then we each get our turn.  Combat is nice in that you can plan your moves, and set up defenses, but sometimes it still falls to RNGeezus to win.  Unless you're completely overpowered for the monster, or have managed to get an opening attack on them.  I would say that the majority of fights can be solved with the right combination of basic attacks and the proper usage of a weapon.  Your basic weapons will have some cleave/AOE usage that will them hit multiple folks, so you can annihilate everyone in one character's turn.  And for the times you can't, there are backup characters or spells!
This is one of those subjective judgements, but I'll stand by it.  Each of the goddesses have their own personality, and FEEL like people to me at times.  At other times, they're tropes.  I have to admit that given I knew I was playing a game, seeing some of the goddesses display characteristics I can identify in myself or my friends was comforting.  The character development was mostly focused on Neptune, but since she's the hero for the game, maybe it was intentional.  I would point out that she doesn't get that much growth throughout the game, sadly.
Some of the best graphics are used in the combat sequences and the few full videos.  After that, the dungeons have some nice touches, and the overworld is the worst part of this package.  BUT I would point out that the game itself is 4 years old AND originally created for the PS Vita, so they likely did the best they could under that system's limited abilities.
Very well suited, but a tad repetitive like most games.  I will say it got points for taking me back to my older 8- and 16-bit game systems.  You can't beat nostalgia factor sometimes for a game.
You can buy or not buy some of this.  The characters added via the DLC are VERY overpowered, making some of the early challenges almost a non-issue.  But they're also cheap (with the exception of the artbook, I think the actual game-DLC is less than $5) which adds some value.
Overall, the game isn't perfect (but what game is?) but it does have its value.  The story isn't too dark, and makes enough fun of itself that you can find yourself enjoying a little escape from reality.  I have a bunch of screenshots from the funnier comments saved to my drive, and replayed the game occasionally JUST to find those triggers again.  I'd almost recommend it as a full price buy, and I'd certainly recommend the deluxe package on any discount over 20%.

City building and management simulator with a (tongue-in-cheek) twist - you play as dictator of a banana republic, some imaginary Carribean island nation of Tropico. This doesn't automatically make you a malevolent ruler, although the option is very much on the table. But you can be quite a benevolent leader, too, to avoid social unrest and having to create a police/martial law controlled state.
Usually though, you'll play as a mix of both tyrant and quite legitimately democratically elected el presidente, swaying in one way or the other depending on how much actual support you currently have from your population (and there's a whole bunch of factions to appease, with often contradictory goals and beliefs, but you're going to focus on the most numerous ones, with most voters, won't you - politics, yo).
While thematically quite distinct and lighthearted (dousing in cheerful latino music accentuates this), and generally comedic - the game is very much competent at what it does, simulating the needs and wants of your population down to individual people, quite organically punishing you for wrong choices by collapsing your economy and/or throwing you into a bloody civil war.
Campaign makes you go island hopping, trying to build up individual islands of your nation, playing to their individual strenghts, so Tropico is the best nation ever in the entire world... but things of course inevitably but suddenly go south to comedic effects. Campaign missions have their unique predetermined goals and events, however otherwise play mostly like a sandbox game, and there's of course actual sandbox mode as well to keep you rolling.
By now, at least gameplay wise, you'd maybe rather look at Tropico 5 which mixes things a bit more with multiple eras/stages of development, but this doesn't suddenly make Tropico 4 any worse or its campaign(s) no longer distinct.
As for DLC business - there's plenty here in Tropico 4, and you definitely do want Modern Times which is a big expansion with its own campaign and new versions of many buildings. Other DLCs however aren't as crucial, but surely can provide some nice buildings like plantations* for more efficient agriculture or cement factory for quicker construction and resource-free export commodity, and there's always some new trait on your leader to select (this tweaks gameplay in some fashion, like more love from some faction or more efficiency in some area) and some specific mission to reinvigorate your desire to develop one more island rather than going pure sandbox again trying your own goals. It's just that for what they provide, they kind of seem individually quite pricey.
(*sometimes new stuff may imbalance original campaign missions a bit, like I believe there was a mission with an island which was supposed to be agriculturally challenged and even disabled farms for you.. but didn't disable plantations (oversight?) so you could still start growing plants if you desired - not like your people would die of hunger otherwise unless you imported lots of food - you still could've had cattle ranches, it's just the mission was supposed to make you focus solely on industry rather than agriculture or tourism).
Once again, a great game by Telltale!

A cautious reccomend.  I'd if the setting is interesting to you, get this game on a sale. The idea of a prehistoric game has been approached many times, FC: Primal approach is a bit more grounded than you'll find in a survival game like Ark. You won't be stalking any tricerotops in this game, because  well, that is more of fantasy than reality.  The game isn't a hard shot for realism either, you will find a beavy of "far cry" powers similar to other games in the series. You will also take on a more beast master role, forming a relaitionship with wild animals which you tame and then can employ in your quest.
The main quest of the charecter is making a place for his people, the Wenja. The conflict comes not just from other wild animals but in primary antangonists the Udam, another tribe fighting for supremecy of a fertile valley known as Oros. The game does insert a moral level in that the Udam are cannibals which I guess is okay but I could have done without. Not that cannibalism is something I'd find out of place, but I don't think was needed as a motivation to fight the "bad" guys. Just fighting for resources and territory is enough motivation for me, and could have added a layer of complexity that's missing from the fairly straightforward narrative.
On the functional side you'll find the return of crafting, and harvesting of resources has been turned up to 11 vs FC3/4. You will be gathering lots of raw material. The game does grant some concessions in giving the option to remove search animations in this repatative task.

This is hands down my favorite ARPG on the market today.
Character development options have multiple layers and allow players to create quite a few builds that can be successful. Also, it's friendly both to those who like to mod and make god-like characters, as well as those who like to "bootstrap" each character through solo self found play. It also has a mini-game called "crucible" (separate DLC, very inexpensive) for those who like taking on waves of enemies. In addition, Grim Dawn has well thought through rogue dungeons that players can take on when they feel ready.
The main drawbacks to the game have to do with limited multiplayer and limited documentation. Multiplayer is doable, but it's not as accessible and easy as it is for multiple other ARPGs. Also, you need to persevere with the game for a while to see how deep it is and to see how many reasonable options there are. There is online information available, but it takes time to work through it.
Overall, though, Grim Dawn is easily worth the price being charged.

This is one fantastic game. This comes from a D2 and PoE fan.
There is nothing crazy new in this game and you have played a lot of games like it. Having said that, what this game does is takes a lot of the great aspects of other games and combines them into one great game that also supports gamepads. The typical plays on character classes are there with your melee/ranged/caster builds and then allows you to half-class D&D style. Each class has a ton of abilities/passives and even 3 people with the same dual class can have wildly different builds. There is also a "devotion" skill/passive tree that is a map of constellations that you can level up that adds a third layer to your build. I have spent hours just making character after character, experimenting with different crazy build ideas I get and seeing which would be fun and viable. I'm not much of a min/max guy, but I do love crazy custom builds!
The gameplay itself is really fun and plays a lot like diablo 3.5, if there were such a thing. You run around blasting baddies with a plethora of abilities and weapons, while gobs and gobs of loot spring forth from corpses. Loot is very random so farming for specific pieces is a bit rough but that's why I like to make so many guys, I have a guy for every item I find!
I really wanted to like D3 and I did play quite a bit, but lack of gamepad support and a terrible original game left a sour taste in my mouth. This is the diablo 3 we should have had from the beginning, instead of that misdirected mess that it was. These days I am left without a desk, using my tv as my monitor from the couch, so gamepad support is a big deal for me. It is not perfect and one might say a bit clunky, but the gamepad works in the UI pretty well. It works perfectly in movement/combat, albeit the auto-targeting leaves a bit to be desired. My main complaint would be the fact I can't do the equivilent of a shift+LMB to transfer items quickly into storage.
In final, this game has taken a lot of my time. It is a blast to play solo and it only gets better with friends. I got it on sale not knowing what to expect but it is easily worth full price. It is a fantastic ARPG and it has gamepad support. Buy with confidence.

Everyone recommends Path of Exile for those who were disappointed by Diablo III (honestly who wasn't?), for me personally PoE just wasn't good. That being said Grim Dawn should be the game for those still looking for a good ARPG; massive map with a good amount of content (both main quests and side quests) and a really good skill tree.
There's a total of 6 classes in the game each having a decent skill tree, but the cherry on top is that as you progress you get to choose 2 of 6 classes. So essentially you get to build your character via 2 skill trees and it doesn't end there, there's also the Devotion passive skill system which is massive. Earning Devotion points is done via shrines and not as you level, making the grind more enjoyable. Points have to be allocated to your characters attributes  such as strength, intelligence etc as well.
From what I have experienced so far, the world map is pretty big with a ton of quests. You get your usual main quests with side quests as well as bounties. Similar to Torchlight II that has a "fame" system Grim Dawn has a system where your standing with a particular town or group of people determines if you are eligible to do bounties for that particular town and also allows access to rare items via a NPC in the town.
Overall, Grim Dawn has a great level up system concerning skills and attributes, good amount of content in regards to quests and bounties. If you love ARPG games and the grind that comes with them, Grim Dawn is a good consideration.
Bonus: Devs are great, the Ashes DLC is more an expansion than an actual DLC with a lot of good content added.

2/5 Story
4/5 Gameplay
3/5 Graphics
3/5 Music
4/5 Replay Value
Overview:
FTL is simple, straightforward, and terrific. The story is a fairly basic space age theme. You control a ship, there are different races throughout the galaxy with a variety of technologies, weapons, strengths, weaknesses, etc... and of course the game features plenty of space battles. The wonderful thing about this game is the way it takes those same basic features we've seen before and does something different with them. You control the crew of your ship not just your ship.  You specifically assign your crewmembers to the consoles for piloting, weapons, shields, etc... all of the important technologies of your ship. You have to battle fires, and hull breaches, boarders, weapon damage, and sometimes even mind control or hacking. FTL is unique in the way it handles the same old space battles we've all been playing since the first Star Trek and Star Wars games. It isn't just shoot until the enemy dies. You have to play smart, conserve resources, upgrade when possible but carefully.
Story:
I feel bad trying to give this game a rating on story because it is not really meant to have much of one and actually manages to convey details of the universe pretty well just by way of gameplay.
Gameplay:
This is the meat and bones of this game. Gameplay is nearly perfect. Battles are tactical, interesting, and fun. The game is difficult but not impossible and exploration although not flashy or exciting uses elements of randomness that really makes it feel like exploring. The random encounters possible in FTL also offer an element of choice. Do I defend the colony from pirates or accept the pirates bribe to leave quietly? None of the decisions carry the weight or long term consequence of games like Mass Effect, but than much of the charm of FTL is the simplicity.
Graphics:
This game uses very simple straightforward graphics for the races, ships, guns, etc... Enough to know exactly what you are looking at without getting distracted by flashy bits or confused with what actions are occuring because of too much complexity. The backgrounds, however, are gorgeous and very very well done.
Music:
