I wanted to give this game a more than fair chance, before writing a review. Their are some interesting concepts that I feel if they truly look into them and fix some issues could have something here...but in all this is a game that has amazing potential but every time you think it gets close to sealing the deal...it just stays out of reach of it.
World bosses....I have always been a fan of World bosses in MMORPGS, and World PVP. I think it introduces a fun dynamic within the worlds that they clearly spent a ton of time building for us to play in, and I never understood why devs would instead relegate them to nothing more than mere loading screens or social hubs. Throw a world boss or open up some interesting pvp dynamics outside of instances to keep players engaged. This game has one of the largest worlds I have come across that is beautiful animated and rendered...only to be suckered into horrible optimization and lag when it comes to world boss encounters. I have tested this on multiple pcs and it isn't because of my low mid tier rig, but because their servers are unable to handle x amount of players in a certain area at certain time. Which leaves you outside of these encounters at times running into horrid fps lag while running through heavily congested areas. This was tested all with lowest settings on. With how these World bosses have mechanics that insta kill you in a game that will penalize you for dying by losing % of xp, unless willing to buy in game shop with real world money item, only makes people think that the true focus for devs is to milk as much money out of you instead of guarunteeing a good experience.
Lack of diversity in gear, truly makes one of the largest immersive aspects of MMOs fail here. They have less options than WoW has when it comes to Xmog, (Xmog by the way is a micro transaction). Even outside of that, their really isn't any variance with gear. This could be for 2 major reasons. 1. Makes it easier to balance for pvp since this is a HEAVY pvp reliant game. 2. In order to make the game more profitable they spend less time developing new peaces of different aspect gear.
Another issue I have with this game, is you really have to listen to the Tier system for PVP. Certain classes just wont perform and thats not cause of skill, but because they are just poorly balanced. Which leads you to the WoW PVP dilemma...and something I saw a former guildie do, with each PVP balance patch they would level that Meta's OP PVPER. I see it in this game just as heavily. Although gear outside of weapons is usable across all classes, weapons are where this game will make you hurt when it comes to alts.
Node Wars, and best farm spots are pretty much for top tier guilds only...during prime time and then some. If you aren't able to get into a top tier guild in this game, be ready to be ganked...and ganked....and ganked by those who are just that much better geared than you. Because gearing relies heavily on your ability to farm at the most efficient points in game. With a game world this massive there are really only a few spots that allow you to amass enough drops to afford gearing yourself for end game pvp.
DP is broken. It doesn't apply enough to make focusing around it worth while. Its best to build a glass cannon and focus on comboing the enemy dead.
The game overall...is just not fun. Unless you can get into a guild that has the membership to compete with top tier node guilds, or just other guilds in general you will spend more time playing possum and finding low efficient grinding spots hoping to catch up when the truth is you never truly will...and if you happen to get favor from the RNG gods...it won't last because without a solid group and guild to back you, holding onto anything worth while will be impossible. Its best to play for 30 days, take a month off and then get back to it to keep access to the olvia servers. This is a game that desperately needs to up their servers in order to placate the rapidly growing steam community...giving us access to olvia in the guise that its a "growth" server that will let us catch up is a farce. we can get to 58.9999 and get a gs clost to 300 sure...but no guild worth its mettle will look at you until your in the mid 300s, or low to mid 400s.

Think a dedicated PvE hearthstone. You can see what the opponent is going to do on its next turn and you can react accordingly to block damage, exploit breaks in combat, buff your character, or debuff the enemy. You have a resource called energy that determines how many cards of varying values you can play that remains static at 3 by default but can be upgraded by finding relics FTL style. Relics can be bought, found randomly, or earned by beating mid-bosses. After every combat you are awarded a choice of 1 of 3 cards which you can use to theme a deck. The deck building is strategic and engrossing, but a little unbalanced at the moment of this writing. Some deck combinations work much better than others, i.e. barricade ironclad or shiv/poison silent, in most situations. Overall, the gameplay is extremely solid and the main reason I keep coming back to this game.
The game only has about 4 tracks and they are all on pretty short loops. It honestly began to get on my nerves the first few hours of play and I had to mute the game and put on my own music. The soundtrack is probably the worst part of this experience as it is right now.
The game is nice to look at. The enemies, characters, and backgrounds all have a Dark Crystal vibe to them which I find awesome. There's a few small details in the enemy art that I am still finding by play. For instance, the Lagavulin mid-boss is found sleeping but if you wait around you can see his one eye darting around inside his shell on the turn before he wakes up. The player characters in particular are inspired, I've never really seen heroes that look like the silent or ironclad. They are visually interesting and well designed. The only thing is that the animations are pretty rough. Usually when enemies or characters take an action they just shift forward and shift back to where they where standing. This part is being actively developed at the time of writing, the developer was making changes to this over the last few weeks for several enemies.
Yeah, this has taken up a lot of my christmas holiday time and I enjoyed every minute of it. The hours pretty much melted away into oblivion playing this game. Not only is the game fun in its current state, but it is being actively improved on with balance and content patches coming in weekly like clockwork. There's a third character being introduced at some point in the near future and new relics and cards being introduced very frequently. I'm looking forward to see this game get some polish over the next few months and see where MegaCrit takes it. If the developer is reading this, excellent work! You've made a fan out of me.

I had no idea what to expect with this. At first, I thought it was going to be an overrated, cringey, fanservice-filled game that wasn't going to be worth putting time into. But, I was pleasantly surprised with how entertaining it was.
Hyperdimenion Neptunia Re;Birth1 is a turn-based JRPG that parodies not only other JRPGs, but the game industry itself (the in-game world is named Gamindustri, even). It centers around the four goddesses of Gamindustri, each representing a major game console. Neptune, the personification of an unnamed SEGA console, is the main character. She is locked in battle with the other three goddesses for control of Gamindustri: Noire (personification of the Playstation 3), Vert (personification of the Xbox 360), and Blanc (personification of the Nintendo Wii). The other three goddesses gang up on her, and she comes crashing down to Earth with a pretty bad case of amnesia. There, she meets the nurse-in-training Compa and the adventurer IF, and sets off on a quest for
her lost memories.
The gameplay is rather simple, with a combo-based combat system that has enough depth to not be completely braindead but doesn't take a whole lot to grasp. What is strange about the combat in this game is that your active party is only three members, as opposed to the standard four for the JRPG genre (the size increases to four in Re;Birth2). This, combined with a couple unique mechanics, sets the series a little bit apart from other titles in the genre. Each of the goddesses can change from their human forms into goddess form using Hard Drive Divinity (HDD...very funny...), which ups their stats and gives them a visual/voice change. Additionally, there are "coupling" and "formation" skills, which require specific arrangements in your party to perform.
VIsually, HDN Re;Birth1 is nothing special. If anything, it can get repetitive: the game reuses a LOT of assets. More often than not, you will be traversing through the same dungeon layout and graphics, just with different treasure and stronger enemies, which can get on people's nerves. The battle animations are pretty fluid, and some of the characters' signature abilities look pretty, so not all is lost in the graphics department.
Musically, the game doesn't have a very large amount of variety (only around 20 music tracks, which is pretty small for a non-RPGMaker JRPG), but the music applies pretty well to where it plays. The game is for the most part very lighthearted and comedic, anyway, so it makes sense that a happy and carefree tune can make an accurate setting for most of the game.
A mechanic unique to the Neptunia Re;Birth series is the remake system. You can collect objects referred to as "plans", which are blueprints to change things in the game. Plans can have a wide variety of effects, such as increasing drop rates/exp gain rates, changing the enemies/items in dungeons, allowing you to break the damage limit, and many more special effects. However, these plans require materials in the form of monster drops in order to utilize, and with the sheer amount of plans in the game, you'll need a LOT of drops.
My one slight complaint about the game is its grindy nature. The leveling curve in Re;Birth 1 is awful - there will be a boss fight that, if you fight every monster spawn once in each dungeon beforehand, will demolish you unless you are about ten levels higher or so. It requires a lot of grinding in terms of items and experience to complete, which can be a large turnoff to some players. I found the grind in this game not too bad, especially with plans to increase item drops and experience gain, but it can still be a real chore to get levels and gear at times.
Re;Birth1 surprised me with how enjoyable it was to play. I can't say with confidence that it truly was a "good" game, but it was certainly entertaining and worth the price (on a sale, of course). If you are one who doesn't mind a tropey, silly JRPG full of grinding and fanservice-y CGs, then the Neptunia series makes for a very good time-killer, if nothing else.
If you like deckbuilding games, as for video games, this is the best you can get right now.

Honestly, I took a big risk with the Neptunia serie, since I bought the all the games with their dlc (except the last one) without knowing the game and if I would like them or not.
And honestly, I regret nothing and I'm ready to do it again if I had to.
The game is very simple, half JRPG and half visual novel.
The turn based combat system is simple but enjoyable, and I think this is the best thing who could describe the game overall: simple, but enjoyable.
The character are easily lovable (I think this is the strongest game's attribute) and the sens of humor of the game is just great, it have a lot of real world's references and no respect for the 4th wall (they even joke about the fact they break it all the time) it made me laugh a couple of times.
The game have nice features.
Replayability (multiple ending).
Side quests.
A large crafting system.
A "colosseum" where you can fight mobs and gain cool stuf.
The "share" system, who influence the power of some characters (CPUs)
Character customisation.
New game +
Of course, even if I love the game and the serie overall, It's not perfect.
Assets are often recycled, weapons, dungeons, monsters, musics...
The musics are nice, but most of them tend to be easily forgetabble. (That's just my opinion, this point stay pretty subjective)
The game suffer of some balancing issue, some points are too easy or too hard, and some characters become quickly useless.
Can sometimes be grindy. (Even if personaly it don't bother me and the grind can be skiped)
But the game is so enjoyable overall that you easily forget negative points.
It's a simple and nice enjoyable journey.

Overall rating: 9/10
By far my favourite city-building sim of all time.
I actually bought this game because I had heard a ♥♥♥♥-tonne of♥♥♥♥♥♥about how awful the new Simcity was, and I was really craving a Simcity-like game. After playing Tropico, I don't think I could go back to playing Simcity ever again.
Tropico is more or less what Simcity would be if it had a nonsensical, but fantastically humorous storyline. You play as El Presidente, ruler of some island, and the game takes you through a bunch of different and ridiculous scenarios. Describing them would spoil the fun of you finding them out on their own. In the meantime, you have to keep everyone happy - be it the religious group, the nationalists or the environmentalists, which often requires a delicate balance in where you spend your hard-earned dollars.
As for the gameplay, the learning curve is just about where you want it to be. You have a lot of leeway in the earlier missions and the objectives are relatively straightforward, whilst the later objectives can be a little frustrating and even unfair. There was one mission in particular where after playing for hours and completing the initial objectives, I was told that the next objective had to be completed by a certain date - this date had already passed, and I instantly failed the objective. I was... miserable, to say the least.
Unfortunately (or fortunately, depending on who you are), once you get the hang of the game and know what you're doing, things become a little bit too easy. Without trying to spoil anything, I'll just say that some forms of income are much easier to obtain than other forms, which creates somewhat of a conundrum - you WANT to diversify your city because it's more fun that way, but it requires more work for it to be successful.
The graphics are pretty standard for a modern game, although the Caribbean-inspired music was stuck in my head for quite some time.
Overall, I'd most definitely recommend this game for anyone that likes city-building simulation games (be it Sim City, Rollercoaster Tycoon, Theme Park, etc).

Okay, before I get into what I think of Far Cry Primal, you need to know where I'm coming from.
This is the first Far Cry game I've played. I play a lot of Bethesda games. I loved Skyrim, Oblivion, Fallout 3. I liked ESO a fair bit too and in all fairness- it isn't as bad as I expected. I've enjoyed Rage, Fallout NV and Fallout 4... though FO4 was a major disappointment as I was expecting more roleplay and less never ending, boring, tedious, pointless "radiant" quests.
Suffice it to say, I like a good open world, first person RPG.
Then first question I asked before I bought Far Cry Primal is "does it have "radiant" quests?". I know it isn't a Bethesda game but still: I'm now more and more worried that modern games are gonna go right down the sh!tter as "radiant" quests seem to be a thing now. But alas I digress.
FCP DOES have some "radiant" quests. To aviod them, ignore the yellow markers that randomly pop up and don't talk to random villagers. Talk to the characters in your village, sure, just not the one or 2 unnamed randoms. And DO do the random yellow marker pop-ups, they take a minute and get extra peeps. Extra peeps means more exp.
The fun in FCP is NOT from the story line. The story lines are cool an all but there's not loads. Also, everyone speaks in some made up language with subtitles. There's one guy who fancies himself as an inventor, is thick as pig sh!t and sounds like an American hick who's intentionally half ar$ing his lines. It's actually kinda funny. As is watching him suffer. You'll know when you meet him.
The most fun to be had, if you're sadistic like me, is with animals.
...no, not like that. Sicko.
Commanding an upgraded "Owl of Doom" (as referred to by me), and the never-ending stealthy "death from aboves" hasn't yet got old. Neither has dropping bees on people. And charging through the land on the back of the uber Sabre Tooth face munching beast of doom, munching and spearing cannibals and pyro human sacrificers is a laugh too.
My favorite thing to do in the game was capturing bonfires and villages.
In summary, the game's okay. Buy when on sale. Will be fun, won't be epic. Still playable.

WORTH IT. This game is a sci-fi roguelike, mixing choose-your-own-adventures, strategy, and action. I can't put my finger on what exactly about the game draws me in. Maybe it's the combo of turn-based plus action in the same game? Not sure.

I mean.. there's some good ultraviolence and depth in this game.
It's quite polished and the graphics are great.
The music is great!
For a game developped by a small team of about 10 people.. wow!
But.
At its core, this is a walking simulator for nerds.
A completionist's wet dream.
You have to literally go everywhere and click on everything.
Ever wanted to find Backtracking Heaven? This is it.
Movement speed is caped at 135% and movement skills are few and pretty much unusable.
It all feels slow and tedious.
But bulls and spiders can accelerate faster than NASA's latest space shuttle or straight out teleport to be on top of you in a split second. Can I have the same ability pls?
Most of the time it's a walk in the park.. only everything dies around you.
And the park is an endless self-similar maze..
I feel like I've seen this before..
Mr Skeleton, have I seen you before?
Are you the same skeleton?
Oh, you are THE Skeleton, the one I've seen in 5 trillion other games.. oh OK.
I imagine a creative meeting at Crate Entertainment. Morning. The coffee machine works today, so everyone feels energized and creative.
- Sooo... Skeletons?
- Nonononono.. better! Cowboys!
- It's fine guys, c'moan.. cowboys.. AND skeletons!
- Wait, guys, wait. Guys! I've got it! Cowboys....shooting skeletons!
OK.. End game. There is none. There's not much to do aside from walking slowy from A to Z, 3-4 times, and then farming some areas.. There are a few ugly rifts/instances I don't care much about. And that's that, the space is, or at least feels really limited.
I think this is why everything is so slow. Small world, filled with details, and you better cover all or most of it.
It's like.. Hey, we worked so hard to put 10000 places to click on, you better click on all of them, and make us happy.
I did. Maybe they're happy. But I'm not.
Should I go into the bugs? Neah. None game breaking. Just enough to annoy me.
Except for one. When you run out of Aether some of your always-ON abilities get toggled OFF. And then you discover you've been strangely underpowered for a while.. maybe when it's too late. That's probably not a bug, it's a feature. Either way, no thanks. I want abilities that are always ON to stay always ON.
GD is definitely a solid, polished game, it's got a fair amount of depth in the Skills, Gear, Upgrades department.. some good number-crunching for the nerdy types. More than your average Diablo clone. The lore is very Diablo-ish, it probably tries to offer people a true, modern Diablo experience. Maybe that's why it's so unoriginal and unimaginative. But the atmosphere is great and the art is great. I'm sure a lot of people try out new builds again and again.. and find it fun, and don't suffer brain damage.

Lethal League is easily my favorite indie game of all time. It mixes an excellent blend of skill and experience into a game that is deceptively simple looking. Getting better at the game gives you a great sense of accomplishment as you go from helplessly spamming the swing key in your early days, to predicting the angle in which the ball will bounce off the walls and positioning yourself to intercept it before it even leaves your opponent's swing.
Supported by a tight and friendly community, people can ask for practice or advice from people with far more experience than them.
The only downside of the game is the cost and player count, which are not mutually exclusive. While you can still find players, it takes a few minutes rather than a few seconds from the glory days of the game. This can potentially make it harder for new players to get in, as they may have to choose whether to continue to play against someone who destroys them or potentially wait for 5+ minutes in a queue. It can be hard to justify a $14 purchase on a game where getting a fair, fast match isn't guaranteed. However, the game goes on sale fairly often.
Despite these risks, I think that a purchase of Lethal League is one that somebody with a competetive spirit owes themselves. Even if you cannot find a game using matchmaking, it shouldn't be too hard to find someone willing to play in the multiple steam groups for the game.

Greyfox is a short story-driven "RPG" that carries an interesting concept with good potential. I was ready to be hooked onto the game's story, I took time to think about what were supposed to be huge decisions, I thought about the consequences of my life-changing choices and then... I was disappointed.
A $1.99 RPG Maker game that offers something uniqe and is worth taking the time to review is commendable in the first place. I may not have loved Greyfox but it had an interesting idea and I hope that the developer can learn from the game's development process and grow with it. I'm also kinda impressed that I was able to play using a controller without any issues.
I pledge not to have spoilers in my reviews, but you can probably see my one-hour play time and my disappointment with the story progession and get a few ideas. Contrary to most RPG games, Greyfox has no combat, skills, or character levels and is entirely story-driven. There's no problem with a game being designed that way, but you would hope that the story, the entire point of the game, is wholesome. Greyfox's story seems to have been cut way too short. Your choices revolve around people you know very little about and then the game ends immediately after you make your choices. The two biggest parts of decision making - 1. What causes you to make your decision and 2. The reprecussions of your decision - do not exist! The only incentive to making choices is to try to get all of the game's achievements. If I didn't even know that "important" character's name 30 seconds ago, how am I supposed to decide if they should live or die and why would I care about what happens as a result?
Aside from that, the game is as basic as can be. I won't knock it for being simple, but it's worth mentioning that there's nothing else to consider outside of the story.
There seems to be a theme or a moral around what the story is trying to say, but I can't make it out. Not because it's cleverly cryptic, but because it doesn't make sense. I can't say much more than that without spoilers, so I'll leave that thought to those who play the game.

I desperately wish I could recommend this game, I really do.
This is one of the first MMO's I've played where they've deviated from the "hotkey combat" that's become the norm these days, and replaced it with a skill based combat system. And damn, I enjoyed the hell out of the combat!
Bu-u-u-ut, after a while, the lustre of the shiny combat mechanics start to dim down a little bit, and you start noticing the, uh, rest of the game.
The first thing I noticed was the bare-boned explanation on how things worked. I had a pretty difficult time figuring out how crafting worked, since it involved gathering levels and connecting nodes and renting workshops, and hiring workers for said workshops.
The game explained this to my by saying; "See this guy? You can hire workers from him. See this things on the map? You can rent them. Mmkay, have fun now!"
Second thing that bugged me was that the quests were BORING AS ALL HELL.
Go here, kill 20 of X creature, and bring back 20 of X items. Buy hey, we'll mix things up a little and make it so that you may or may not get the item after every kill.
And since there's usually like 15 other people trying to kill X creature in an area, you usually tend to get PK'd by territorial players if you're above the PvP threshold level.
Third. I bought the Traveller's Package to get the extra stuff in it, but I failed to read that said stuff like extra inventory and bank space expires after a month. Oh and that thing you used to dye your armour? Yeah that expires too, and your armor reverts back to its original colour.
Kind of my fault for not reading it all properly, but come on, it's kind of a d**k move.
Fourth is the goddamn marketplace. To buy something, everyone clicks the "Bid" button and all your names gets chucked into a hat. If your name gets pulled out, congrats, you get to buy the item. Too bad if you're unlucky though. I spent around 30 mins trying to buy a pair of boots one time, and then I find out that manually upgrading them with your black stones was equal to burning money, and that I should have bought the fully upgraded version to begin with. And surprise, surprise, there's more people trying to buy the +15 version of said boots, so I had to settle for my poverty +5 boots instead. That's if there's anybody actually SELLING said item, that is.
TD:LR
- Game offers poor explanations on how to game.
- Coma inducing quests
- Expiring 'Package' items that really shouldn't.
- Lottery marketplace & broken enchanting system.
Extra notes
- Character creation is amazing; you can make the best waifu ever.
- Cosmetic outfits can cost up to $30 or so, which is way too expensive.
- Nodes needed for crafting
- Bank space isn't shared across all cities. Forgot something on the other side of the map? Enjoy the ride back, beetch.
- Not really the game's fault, but high levelled groups/guilds hog good farming areas, and if you try to intrude, you better be prepared for some PvP, coz a fight is GOING to happen.
Like I said at the start, I really wish that this game was better. The combat is amazingly fun and the graphics look fantastic. But everything else is either needlessly complicated or ridiculously boring.
Oh and there's energy points. Like what is this, a mobile game?

Half Life takes this Aliens invading earth story to a whole new level its not so generic its really well put together and you feel like you are a part of a resistance that is trying to free this world from the evil combine , you play as our good ol' friend Gordon Freeman (i think thats how the name is spelled , please correct me if i am wrong)  as you try to start an uprising against the combine after earth has been invaded by them , that is after the cascade incident the combine watched waited as XEN invaded earth , but they began their invasion after xen's ruler Nihilanth has been defeated by Freeman , no where is gordon freeman during the combine invasion , he is in deep space. yes you heard me right he is in deep space after he got a deal with the mysterious gman , years later after earth has been invaded you are awoken by the gman once more to fight for your world as you meet up with your old friends from black mesa , after you destroy the Citadel and kill Dr Wallace Breen (i belive he is still alive ) you take down the citadel's portal to stop them from getting reinforcement , after that you are set the secure and destroy the Borealis which is a ship that has some unknown technology on it , but before you do that your friend Eli Vance which is the leader of the resistance gets killed by a type of soldier from the combine known as The Advisor. the story remains uncompleted for the lack for a third game , but overall its an amazing story with an annoying Cliff hanger but it has a great atmosphere.

A brief nightmare...
Alan Wake's American Nightmare is a third person shooter developed by Remedy (Max Payne and Alan Wake creators). It is a standalone game, set in the 'Alan Wake' Universe. You play as Alan Wake, a writer who has gotten stuck in a television series called 'Night Springs'.
The plot doesn't have a significant impact on the original story. Continuing (if somewhat loosly) after the orignal game (specifically the DLC 'The Writer) American Nightmare tells a the story of Alan facing off against his dopple ganger Mr Strange in the fictional country town of Night Springs located in Arizona. There are manuscript pages which serves as an insight on what happened to the characters from the orignal Alan Wake, after the ending (although since the manuscripts are found inside the TV show it is debatable whether the events actually happend outside the TV world or not).
Audio is quite good. Aside from some forgettable character's, the majority of the voice acting is great at instilling personality (especially Mr Scratch). Weapons sound decent like the orignal game. There are also some rock music as well which sound great during tesne fights. At non-combat moments, quiet music is played to instill a spooky atmosphere (although not as effective as the in the orignal game).
Compared to the original 'Alan Wake', this game has a stronger focus on combat. Like the previous game, you need to shine your flashlight at enemies until the 'shadow dissapears from them before you can damage them with bullets. You can sprint longer than in the previous game as well as removing darkness from the taken faster as well.  There is a variety of weapons available including the familiar ones pistol, carbine, shotgun, flares, flash grenades, to new ones like crossbow, double barrelled shotgun and nailgun.  You only start off with a pistol and flashlight and you need to either find new weapons or unlock them from trunks. Weapon trunks only open when you have collected enough manuscript pages. Unlike the previous game, ammunition is plentiful and is regained through red containers attatched to walls, which also replenish themselves over time. There are also a few recognisable enemies such as the flying objects and the standard goons. New enemies include bird guys (switch between human and bird form), chainsaw guy and spiders (which all have unique attacks). Other parts of the gameplay involves moving around and collecting/activating items to move the plot. There are only 3 areas in the game rest stop, observatory and outdoor cinema area (which compared to the original game is quite small). The areas are split up and not connected like the previous game. You will also go through these areas three times (which can feel a bit cumbersome), although with some different encounters to spice things up. Another issue is that the game is quite short, taking only 4 hours for me to complete (just campaign) compared to the orginal Alana wake, which took 18 hours.
There is also a survival mode available. You start with only one stage and you need to collect stars to unlock new stages. Stars are earned based on your score at the end of the stage. To increase your score you need to kill off enemies (which are basically the guys you faced in single player). Enemies come out in waves. At the start of the stage, you only have a flashlight and pistol. New weapons are scattered around the area as well as light sources (which serve as auto-healling). You also need to be awar of your score multiplier which: 1.gradually decreases 2. increases for each kill or successful dodge and 3. Reuces to zero when you get hit by an enemy.
If you like more Alan Wake gameplay, namely combat, than get this game. If you wanted a game which is similar to the original Alan Wake ,ie. focuses on plot, you will be dissapointed.

Honestly, this game is pretty fun while you're playing it.  Every choice feels important, even if a lot of them just provide different paths to the same conclusion.  The exception is when big characters from the show come around.  As a fan, it's cool to see them and helps the world feel more authentic.  But the interactions with them feel forced, and ultimately hurt the story.  Part of the fun is the whole "anything can happen at any time" suspense that you get from Game of Thrones, and interacting with show characters is the complete opposite.  You as a show-watcher know what is going to happen to them, which drives home the fact that your interactions with them don't really matter.
But all that would still be fine if not for the ending.  For all the story this game spends hours building up, the ending resolves practically none of it.  It's a huge slap in the face that basically amounts to "What happens next?  Buy Season 2 to find out!"  Cliffhangers are something you can get away with on a TV show.  In a game like this, they just make the whole thing feel unfinished.
For a story-based game, I thought there would be at least SOME story resolution.  Maybe in Season 2, but I'm not holding my breath.  Don't waste your money.

My first review with around 248 hrs of playing the game and I can't recommend the game enough for F2P!
Pro's:
- Cool cartoony graphics
- Excellent replay value; fun, daily challenges, etc
- Well balanced; In the situations where each team is well matched there are supply drops and 'block busters' which can seriously shake up the pace of the game, and as the game goes on the block busters have more powerful effects.
- Tactical unique defenses and offenses; hardly any game is the same as the last.
- Great variety of characters to play, although it does take a while to earn enough gold to buy them all
- Nice to earn gold to buy characters/ perks, I enjoy earning a game currency and have purchases to work towards
- Dynamic fully destructable evironment which can have a big impact on how a match plays out
Con's:
- You get the very occasional troll/ hacker, about 1 in every 100 matches for me and it absolutely ruins the match when this does happen, and no ability to votekick.
- The occasional connection issue I get with the master server; I get days where I can't play 5 minutes of the game without losing connection to the master server, the game just freezes and then kicks me out saying I'm idle.
- Be prepared to feel the need to log in every day to complete your daily's whilst you don't have all the characters or level 3 perks you want.
If a votekick was added and they fixed the occasional connection issue I get with the master server, it would the best F2P game I've ever played.

TL;DR: The game is worth buying but tends to freeze after 4+ hours. If you don't mind go for it.
I like this game.
I enjoy the turn-based combat, I enjoy the dialogues (not as much as rebirth1 but eh), and there isn't really any grinding needed (by the time I'm satisfied I've cleared the dungeons, I tend to be overlevelled for the story bosses).
An additional party member gives a lot of flexibility.
The Lily rank requirements based on one character for the endings are kind of annoying but they fit into the story so whatever.
However I can't recommend this game unless you tend to have high patience for bugs and can remember to save at every single opportunity.
-Noticeable delays every time you break guard on an enemy (Not such a big deal, and you can repack rebirth1's assets into this game's assets to fix it)
-Crashes when loading into dungeon saves (Fixed by running in winXP compatability mode)
-Rarely there are missing textures on models and the dungeons (Aside from looking really spooky, Falcom didn't seem affected by the black abyss on her face)
-Chance to eternally hang when loading assets. This is the big one. That was INFURIATING. Basically you ♥♥♥♥IN MURDER your best friend, one CPU in front of her little sisters, then you swiftly proceed to murder them as well while they're in tears and sobbing, and then you murder your own sister. Does this sound like a Neptune game to you? Because it doesn't to me.

Mr Skeleton, have I seen you before?

I imagine a creative meeting at Crate Entertainment. Morning. The coffee machine works today, so everyone feels energized and creative.
- Sooo... Skeletons?

Even after our success in defeating the aliens, I still have PTSD. The events of Operation Secret Giant still haunt me.
Our squad was cutting-edge, outfitted with the best weaponry and technology of any military unit worldwide. The MEC had been a sterling success, and our sniper, this deadeye Chinese gal, had been fitted with advanced genetic augmentations. With a string of successes behind us, it was no surprise we got cocky. We felt invincible. We were like comic book super heroes.
Our squad was investigating a small fishing village in Europe. We met no resistance initially, which was unsettling. As we extended, we saw movement. A large fish, hanging from a hook, was shaking. We knew something was wrong.
Not before too long, Chrysalids were ambushing us from the bellies of caught sealife. We were surrounded but we had the problem under control. It was clear the Chrysalids were coming from a source. They were typically found in small numbers, but this was nothing short of a horde.
A ship which had spilled on the shore was last place to be investigated, and the clear source.
We we're ambushed, and overwhelmed. Our weapons were getting them, sure, but not fast enough. And Chrysalids are damn fast. Our sniper, our best soldier, was the first to go. And with her, our sense of invincibility.
This Russian guy, our support. Brave man. Fast runner. Central came on comms and told us that the Chrysalids were spawning on mass from inside the belly of a whale. Said the whole area needed an airstrike or Europe would have a serious Chrysalid problem on its hands. The Russian, no hesitation, made a beeline for the comms system on the other end of the ship. Meanwhile, my squad's getting torn apart. I took the rear, and I was just far away enough that I had time to make a decision.
I could fight. Or I could run like a coward. I ran. They chased me relentlessly.
The Russian was fast. He managed to call in the air strike, no problem, whale was toasted. But fast as he was, he couldn't outrun that many Chrysalids. He made it a ways from the ship and got pinned down by about three of them. I was the only one left.
I was a heavy. My armor wasn't designed for running like that. By the time I made it aboard Big Sky, I collapsed in a heap.  As we took off, I watched the fishing village burn up in a hellstorm.
I like to think that my cowardice that day, that guilt, is what drove me to success. When I became colonel, and squad leader, I had the whole world counting on me. When we drove them back, when we destroyed their leader, I knew that all the deaths along the way of my squadmates, and friends, had not been in vain.

I've read several reviews and rather than repeat them, or even give a synopsis of what the game is about, I'm going to focus this short review on a couple of the particulars that I found to be worthwhile enough to underline for prospective buyers.
Things I wanted to call out:
- Main storyline is dark fantasy, but with guns.
- Probably 35-40 hours of game play, especially if you work in the side quests.
- The leveling system is reminiscent of TitanQuest, in that your character ends up as some combination of two classes. With 6 overall to choose from, it's not a TON of options, but there are enough (at least 15 combos) to make the gameplay different.
- Over-the-top finishers that explode enemies into the air. After 70+ hours, that still hasn't gotten old.
- Respec-ing for a different playstyle is easy and affordable.
- Repeatability is low-moderate. The main storyline doesn't really scream "Again! Again!" I can imagine the differences in gameplay between single-player and multiplayer are enough to entertain those into this type of game.
- Large variability between the challenge of regular mobs vs. unique / bosses. This can lead to potion spamming, kiting for minutes while minions chip away at enemy health, and general dissatisfaction with the game.
- While gear swaps occur frequently in the early game, once you've found one or two items that really work, very few will get upgraded. This is because the shops have crap for sale, and the crafting option is completely and utterly random.
Final verdict
Despite its rough spots, Grim Dawn is still the best Diablo clone I've played so far.

Let me tell you a story about a man named Sam Song.
Sam Song was just a regular recruit at XCOM HQ. His first mission was to go help with data retrieval on an EXALT cell. "It's going to be an easy mission", Central thought, they had dealt with an EXALT mission before, and the squad rhat was going was mostly veteran soldiers, along with a rookie to train.
As they arrived on the scene, it was very quiet for a few turns. No enemies in sight. But as soon as the squad made it to the roof of a building where the encoder for the mission was, it started to go to♥♥♥♥♥♥
First, our Sergeant Sniper got dropped by an unfortunate crit. XCOM always prepares in case of a soldier death, no biggie. Every turn thereafter, more and more EXALT members rushed in, and Sam Song's squads firepower was not enough to staunch the flow of incoming enemies.
One after one, Sam's allies dropped dead trying to protect the encoder and later the transmitter to ensure that the mission would not fail. In the end it was up to Sam and the covert operative for the mission. The covert op was some form of miraclemaker, as they would not get hit by conventional fire. A true soldier to the end. Never forget Sam Song.

I've been a long-time lover of the X-COM franchise. My dad owned every game in the series with exception of Interceptor, and I've played all except that one and The Bureau (for now). This was, and still is, a wonderful addition to the franchise that made every leap and bound it needed to into the new generation of gamers and systems.
Now, the biggest part of the game is going to be the tactical battles: manuevering your squad into position and wasting the aliens. Learning to use every class is a must, otherwise you will be destroyed. Trying to remember each perk you gave your soldiers is difficult, but this is aided by the fact that you can check soldier info any time to remind yourself. Certain perks can completely alter the way you play each soldier, so knowing what your team is defficient in and what they excel at can make tough firefights into cakewalks. And when you lose a soldier, you really remember losing that soldier. In the later missions especially, losing even one man can dramatically change how you fight and can make some fights nigh impossible. Don't be afriad to retreat. Better to lose one man and run than lose six Colonels because of stubbornness.
The basebuilding takes a decidedly more backseat role in this game. Build powerplants, build a repair bay, build your labs, research, etc. is all very simple and easy and there is very little room to mess anything up. However, make sure you have enough room set aside for satelites in the beginning, it will help.
I found the difficulty of the vanilla game to be far too easy, so I switched over to the Long War mod, and I can tell you that it is just as hard and just as worthwhile as everyone says it is. If you liked the original but want more challenge, get the Long War mod and thank yourself.

Slay The Spire is more fun and addicting than it has any right to be. You choose a class (only one at the beginning, 2 others unlock after meeting certain requirements) and make your way through the dungeon, ala Darkest Dungeon. You can pick the path you want to take through the dungeon with each room having a symbol on it representing what you will generally find in it. Depending on what path you have chosen some rooms are unavoidable, though at some points you will be able to pick from a diverging path. Each room will either have an enemy encounter, an elite enemy (read: harder enemy. More risk but also chance of better loot than base enemies) encounter, a loot chest, a campfire (to rest/heal or upgrade a card) a random story-like encounter that may give you a random upgrade, or a merchant. Each of these has different strategic value depending on what you need at the moment.
As you play through dungeon rooms and fights and loot chests, you obtain and/or upgrade or remove cards from your deck. Combat is accomplished by playing cards determined by your draw each round, that can damage your enemy, buff yourself, or debuff your enemy. The progression and card obtaining/management are a ton of fun as you get cards that totally change your playstyle or upgrade cards to enhance/reinforce your style. It is all very fluid and the gameplay is, in my opinion, quite deep although I do not have much experience with card games outside of maybe 10-15 hours of Hearthstone, so I may be naive on that point. As you can see, I'm not a big card-deck building game kind of guy, which is why my enjoyment of Slay the Spire came as a bit of a surprise to me.
The graphics I enjoy very much. While they don't blow the doors off, I find the game to be quite pretty and the basic animations of playing cards and dishing out attacks get the job done with a simple sort of charm. The audio, while never making me jump out of my seat also never got in the way of enjoying the game, and I never got bored of it or annoyed by it, which is a solid plus, there.
Even if you aren't too into card deck building games, this has enough charm and simple logic to the mechanics and card synergy and competition that you can jump in and learn fairly quickly how to maximize your effectiveness with a given hand or deck. I really love playing through this game, and have beaten it (so far only 3 full dungeons before the end boss) once, completely, already. The only thing I really wish would change about the game is it's length. It would be cool if, for instance, after you beat the vanilla 3-dungeon crawl and accompanying bosses you could play an endless mode, or they would simply add more dungeons to the play through.
The only negative is I wish there was more of the game to play, and that is a pretty resounding positive review.
I give Slay the Spire, as it stands in early access no less, a very solid 8.5 / 10. More fun and addicting than it has any right to be, and I have enjoyed every minute I have spent playing, and will continue to do so.

This is a tough game to review on a recommend it or not scale. It falls somewhere in the middle. My take, is if you enjoy the books/show you'll probably enjoy the game as well. But be prepared for the typical misery that comes from watching your favorite characters fail at what they try to accomplish by doing the "right" thing and possibly dying as a result.
There are choices to be made, but few of them really effect the story all that much. The graphics/animation are on the low end for today's modern games. Lets face it your here for the characters and story, and it's done reasonably well and gives a decent portrayal of what it would be like to live in one of the lower lordlings houses in a GOT type universe.
The lower level aristocracy obviously doesn't wield the power of the Lannister's, Targaryaen's, Starks, Bolton's, Baratheon's, etc so there's really not a lot of pull to turn events. Look what happened to the those families in the books/series and they're several levels above the Forrester clan you play in terms of power. The pieces in play are always moving so be prepared for the unexpected. Sometimes maintaining your integrity can mean giving up your life or the lives of your loved ones.
Many of the series characters appear briefly. Some stray a bit from actions you would expect knowing their character traits, but it didn't bother me much. It might for others if they expect everyone to be exactly the way they are portrayed in the series. I think of the game as a bit different animal from the tv series, just as I think of the tv series as a bit different from the books.
It's reasonably short, so you may want to pick it up on sale unless your someone who wants to play through several times to see how things change when different choices are made. Each episode was maybe 2 - 4 hours gameplay for me.
Overall I enjoyed playing it even if things didn't always work out for the Forresters the way I'd hoped. It's an interesting side story in the GOT world.

After finishing this game I was left with a depressed feeling that made me feel like I hated Game of Thrones and wanted nothing more to do with it, and yet, I now want to play it again and see if damn me I can make it feel better?!
The main reason for this is the story felt like it pulled you in, from the characters, the choices, the very way you want things to work out, to the utter despair when you feel that hard work you just put in could all just blow up in your face, and you have little power over it.
The voice acting also added to the story no end, and without the voice acting being as high quality as it was my feeling for the game might have been less than it is because of my first negative on the game.
And while the story was utterly amazing, and just breath-taking (and damn depressing and frustrating) there were some elements that made me feel somewhat disappointed in the overall game.
The primary thing is graphics. I understand that Telltale does "artistic" graphic styles and utterly applaud them for doing so, but when the graphics make the game hard to watch or just feel sloppy or unfinished it pulls you out of the immersive story and instead back into the fact the game is just very ugly. Whoever came up with the idea to do "electronic artistic filtering" on the background should rethink their idea for next games and keep it out of it (which I believe they have not done - and I am hoping they never do for Game of Thrones 2).
The choices you make only matter.... a little. Now I fully understand that it is impossible to make a fully open game where all choices matter, but in game of Thrones there are certain things where you just have no control no matter what you do. The frustrating thing there is that you go back to the same place over and over to try different ways only to find out very painfully you can't do anything to make a difference.
Now in saying that, Game of Thrones was a interactive movie, but a number of the choices had a very strong impact on the way the story was told, what characters were doing what, and who was main to the story and who was outside.
And to be honest the negatives nowhere outway the great feeling Game of Thrones gave me and the rage of emotions it force feed me. The game was just amazing an experience that I can't wait to have another run through (once I have let it rest a moment), and see what happens if I pick another direction or style of dealing with something.
For a game that I was originally Not Interested in, I bought it on special and found that the game was far more than I expected and was a railroad of real emotions I never thought I would feel.

So Grim dawn doe a nice job scratching the Diablo 2 itch. The combat is fast and furious with an array of of various abilities over it's 6 classes.
For an indie game it looks pretty good. All of the abilities are pretty well animated and have a nice pizzazz to them. The character models themselves don't look like anything special, but it doesn't detract from the experience. The story while interesting and enjoyable isn't something you'll talk especially among other RPG's. The faction system exists and is kind of a neat trick but the game seems to funnel you into being on the side of a few of the factions and against some others without much agency as to which one you're going to side with.
Part of what makes this game enjoyable is the ability to select two classes and fuse together their abilities and talents for devastating results. It really opens open the way you build your character.  I'll say the first "act" of the game is probably too easy as the only time I died was at the final boss, but the difficulty curve does jump back up to something a little harder shortly there after. I enjoy that there are no town portals that you have to use in order to get back to town. The game is as all loot based ARPG's can get a little long as you grind away and the enemy variety is good but not great.
Overall it's a fun time. Final Grade B

American Nightmare is quite different from it's predecessor in crucial points and not always for the best. Therefor, the pros and cons rely a lot on comparison with Alan Wake.
Pros:
+ Collecting manuscrpit pages now has a clear benefit that was absent in it's predecessor.
+ New cool enemies.
+ Intelligent AI, the enemies try to surround you whenever possible.
+ Loot and pick-ups are well marked.
+ Plenty of ammo.
+ Open world.
+ Battery change is quicker than in Alan Wake.
+ Usage of real actors in cut scenes.
Cons:
- From visual point of view it's a step back from Alan Wake.
- This sequel feels more like a game. It's predecessor had such a high standard of realism that it felt more life-like.
- The graphics are worse than in Alan Wake.
- Bad dialogues.
- Bad characters and voiceover.
- Feels like it was done before the main game.
- You couldn't choose weather you wanted to leave an area.
- Switching weapons is hard in the middle of a battle.
- Less atmosphere = enemies weren't that scary.
- I thought there'd be a final battle thing, it never came.
Verdict:
American Nightmare often felt raw, it's state of completion rushed. Several of the choices that the developers made leave you thinking what they had in mind. So, it's not the Alan Wake you think you'd get after what they had done previously. Nevertheless I recommend it, after all we are talking about an Alan Wake game.

I’m assuming that most people playing this game played the original so I’ll focus on comparison between the two titles.  The major difference between the two games is that AW:AN has a stronger focus on combat, with more weapons and more enemy varieties than in the original game.  I found that I enjoyed it more than the original, mainly because the variety of different enemies kept things from becoming as repetitive (as did a shorter run time).  The thing I liked was that a few of the new enemies weren’t just killed in the same way as every other enemy in the series so alternate strategies had to be used.  As this game focuses more on the action, the horror has mostly been taken out of the game since batteries/ammo are easily replenished.  The original AW had a more interesting story, but the story in this game has some neat ideas and a gimmick that keeps things fun and engaging.

Great Turn-Based Game. A must have if you like sci-fi, strategic, base building game.
Rating: A
Pacing: The game mechanics are great, once you get your head around how it works it goes fast. On the other side it starts to be annoying to not being able to fast-forward movement, when no enemies are around. Also the camera can get annoying at times. (Always moves to the targeted unit, making it annoying when you know where each units must go.)
Game Depth:
There is a lot of mechanics into the game, but easy is user friendly. When you move on difficulty you'll have to add what to build, research and improve your strategy.
Controls:
The controls are simple and intuitive, point and click. The camera can be annoying ig you want to get on the edge of an elevated position, just make sure the square you want to move your unit to is highlighted before clicking. If it's not, change the camera's angle.
Story:
There's not much story into the game, it doesn't mean you can't make one while playing it! (e.g. Story for your units). The main story are the sequence main of events happen, and meanwhile you go destroy UFOs and aliens that your scanner picks up.
Gameplay:
Through out the game, I had a good time eliminating threats and trying to not lose any member of my squads. I did lose quite a few rookies and squadies (11) with 2 colonels (last mission), which made me sad. You can get attached to your higher ranked units because you've done many missions with them. Near half way of the game I started to make a story for members of my squads. So when the last mission with my Psionic Support Col., Sniper Col., Assault Col., Assault Maj., Heavy Col. and Heavy Major, my sniper(male) was with my psionic(female)... One heavy got gunned down near the end, my sniper was killed by the boss... Which made the finally more enjoyable. So if you find that doing mission over and over gets boring, make up a story! Let's start with a personal experience.
So back in October-November 2015, when I started playing, I was amazed by this game, by how addictive it was. Wow, an actual team-based PVP version of minecraft. I used to play it over three hours a day, after school. Eventually, after around 150 hours, I decided to play this game at a competitive level. I met new people, squaded with them, TeamSpeaked with them, it was fun. Until the matches started becoming somewhat repetitive (there was only one gamemode).
Eventually, my closer friends left this game, one by one, not only because of the crappy matchmaking system, but also because of the poor optimization.
By then I was still playing to Block N Load, I even built a new PC for the sole purpose of playing this (poor optimization, as I mentionned above).
But then, I quickly realized, about a year after I started playing, that this game didn't have such a bright future. Playerbase declining, updates taking forever to be released, nothing being done with the bad optimization, bad matchmaking, etc.
So yes, I did stop playing actual matches, and instead started messing around in custom matches with my remaining friends. But that got quickly boring as well.
Somewhere at the beginning of 2017, I quit the game. There was only one developer left on the team, and the playerbase wasn't getting better.
_____________________________
I still have to give this game some credit though, as it was my introduction to PC gaming.
In conclusion, this game can perhaps still be fun for some new players, but once you know every aspect of it, it gets boring.

It's a korean developed mmorpg that is pay to win, where the player can do stuff, from killing monsters to sailing into the sunset, or tending to a small garden farm whilst managing a whole network of
workers that ask beer or certain food as salary.
As of now, I have over 400 hours playing the game, and I am not sure I can certainly say that I know more than 40% of the game.
The game is very vast and it keeps on growing. As of now, there are 14 classes, which some are gender locked to male or female, but in the future the opposite sex counterpart will be added, for example Striker's female version.
When you begin the game you will have to rely on the black spirit and the quests nearby, you won't have the need to participate in parties with someone until up to level 50 when pvp starts, but even the chances of encountering someone who pks are slim.
Some dialogues and voices are translated from korean to english are off, but that won't be a big problem.
Black Desert encourages you to take it slow, and be creative most of the time, but also patient because it takes a while to get somewhere in the game, like gathering knowledge and contribution points from npc quests take some time. =)
Of course, making money is up to you as well, because the top players keep their methods to themselves due to the fact that some players once updated their ways of making money and that method got used by alot of players and flooded the marketplace with the items they made from that method. :P
(pst, there are alot of events that may help you get some cash, for starters)
It's worth getting your lifeskills to high levels, as you will get rewarded with something useful when doing so, compared to some other games that did not do that. ^.^
For $10 / euro it's very much worth, but if you are patient you can wait for a sale to come and buy it then.
You can also make a trial on the official site . For 7 days you will be able to play Black Desert for free and see for yourself if it's the game you'll play. :)
Update : I have over 780 hours, I can easily say that I feel like I just started playing for the first time, the feelings of excitement and curiosity , as well as amazement when I discover something totally new.
The gear progression is easy to learn, and pretty difficult to master, luck plays a role in skill as well.

The Game's setting is good. You get to meet and talk to a few of the main characters from the show, as well as see some beautiful landscapes that weren't detailed in it.
You also have many QTEs and action in the game, so you won't just sit back bored with just the mouse in hand clicking from one scene to the other.
The point where this game fails, is the choice system. Telltale has gone against their own motto "This game is shaped by how you play it. your choices matter" in such way that is painful to play it. You won't have much joy in it, as no matter your choices, the worst will happen. The game becomes a choice of "who you want less to die"; you can't save someone without some else dying; you can't reach mutual agremeents with someone, just deals that suit them and dishonour you/your house; If you start to like a character, the game will make its best to drag him in the mud then kill him... and so on. Telltale tried to keep up R.R. Martin's way of writing, but failed miserably by creating too few good outcomes, and too many bad ones (even the good outcomes come at a high price).
Final Point: Personally, I hated this game while I was playing it. It had a few moments that nearly brought a tear to my eye (like a certain song at some point in the game), but apart from them I really felt unrewarded, angry and empty, ending up finishing the game just for the achievements. It might be a good game for some, but I am the type of player that gets attached to charcters and always go for the Paragoon Path; but here, I didn't had justice, I couldn't save people, and I got rewarded only with misery in the life of the characters.

After years of loving and enjoying this game and many recommendations to friends, I feel like it is time to make a full on review after my latest playthrough of the series.
The only proper way to start this review is to give my background with the Half-Life series. I first found out about this game in 2011 after playing though Portal and Portal 2. I got the game late one night and immediately fell in love after a few hours. I loved every second of this game (except for a low point I will mention later). After playing this game, I played the episodes and later went back to play HL1.
Now for a proper review:
Story: Incredible. The opening of this game scared the s h i t out of me the first night I played and left me troubled to sleep. Beyond that, the game's basic story, while a simple "kill the dictator" story at it's base, has so much going on in the background with the mystery of what the combine are, to the betrayal, to the unique and interesting side characters and aliens, this game has it all. A single shortcoming storywise is the strange worship of Gordon Freeman like a god. For some reason everyone knows exactly who Gordon Freeman is, even before he starts the actual revolution, and it's kinda strange. Final Score: 9/10
Gameplay: Very Good. This game plays like a normal FPS, and that would make sense considering that the original Half-Life innovated the FPS as we know it today. The thing that propels (get it) this game out of the area of average is the Gravity Gun. It's so fun to be able to grab any objects you can find and fling them at your enemies. One thing that majorly drives this portion down though is one section of the game: Nova Prospekt. I personally believe that this is the weakest section in any HL game, and it's gonna drive this score down a whole ranking, from an 8 to a 7, just because of how boring it is. The most entertaining thing you can do in this portion of the game is take a friendly turret with you through the whole thing. Otherwise, the gameplay is pretty great. One more complaint though: Flashlight being tied to your oxygen/ sprint meter. This was a really dumb idea, and even a step back from HL1. Glad to see that fixed in episode 2. Final Score: 7/10.
Finally, Presentation: Great. Graphically, this game looked absolutely stunning compared to most games from 2004, and its graphics still hold up today. The game lacks any graphical fads of the time (like lens flares from the 2010s and such things) and this helps to keep it looking good today. The hud is very effective without taking up too much space, or having anything unneeded displayed. The fact that they toned down how often the suit talks works very much in this game's favor, as it was kind of annoying in HL1, having it speak every time you collected a suit battery. The whole asthetic within the city is great, and has a very distopian feel without seeming copied from other works. Each section of the game has it's own specific feel, and it really makes this game feel like a journey. Overall, the game is presented very well, and was revolutionary for it's time in that respect, but it still holds up today. Final Score: 8/10
Half-Life is probably my favorite video game series, and while I'm sad that we haven't seen a conclusion to the current story arc, I trust that when it comes out it's going to be incredible. I'm glad that Valve is a company that takes time with their games, and works to make sure that their games are not only really fun to play, but leave a lasting effect on the games industry as a whole. I hope that the new game comes out soon and does really well so that the rest of the triple A companies will realize that taking your time on a game does work. Anyway, with that rant over, my final score for
Half-Life 2 is an 8/10. This is one of my favorite games ever, but it's obviously not perfect.

Now, we're getting back to some familiar territory in the Freddi Fish series. I only played Missing Kelp Seeds once, and barely touched Haunted Schoolhouse until I actually saw the ghost. But Freddi Fish 3: The Case of the Stolen Conch Shell and I have a personal nostalgic connection.
So, like all my other nostalgic ties, let's take this one and burn it to the f***ing ground.
I will be honest, this is probably the best Freddi Fish game money can buy... I mean, unless you spend an a**load of money developing an unofficial Freddi Fish 6 that's so damn good, it would even be considered by Yahtzee Croshaw to be the best game of 2025.
The reason I enjoyed Freddi Fish Tres so much more than the last two entries was the environment. It's no secret that Freddi Fish 1 had a creepy world that the oddly-cartoonish creatures stuck out like sore thumbs in. And while Freddi Fish 2 was a step in the right direction, the actual environment and fish didn't mesh well. But Freddi Fish 3 has probably the best-matched backgrounds to fit these cartoony fish characters. It's bright, cheerful, and colorful almost everywhere (barring the downed plane and red chasm where the bully-crab kid lives). But the tropical island really fits in with a cheerful kid-friendly color palette of Freddi Fish.
I also like how this is the first entry where those two incredibly thick sharks and their mob-boss, The Squidfather, have been reduced to "Wanted" posters in a jail cell. I hated those three so much. Now, the actual mystery is concealed until the very end. It's up to you and your wits to determine who the thief of the Conch Shell is.
However, where my praise ends is where the gameplay focuses on you finding three golden horns for the conch shell, so that way Luther's uncle's dog, Salty, can sniff out the perpetrator (even though he could just as easily find a trace with one, but whatever). The actual "crime solving" comes down to the very ending where you find a vital clue that fits into these Usual Suspect types, and you can achieve 1 of 6 endings. The gameplay itself only shifts when you have to find the various golden horns. The 6 endings are totally random. In my 1.2 hours of gameplay, I played about 5 times, but only got 3 of the possible endings. So if you have enough patience, or you're a toddler, you'll have plenty of time on your hands until you get all the different endings.
This particular Freddi Fish, while probably the best in the series thus far, is still far from earning a recommendation from me. "Why?" you must be asking. "Is this guy just a d***?"
No, you silly s**. Just look at my other Humongous reviews. The only three games I consider worth playing to anyone who likes good game design and clever jokes are Pajama Sam 1 & 3, and Spy Fox 3, because of their truly unique style, fun characters, and memorable little stories. Freddi Fish still feels like it's made towards the obviously younger demographic of children than Pajama Sam and Spy Fox are. It feels too safe. Too friendly. But it's, by no means, a bad game. It's worth playing if what I described earlier sounds fun to you. And I'm giving this Freddi Fish entry a 6/10.

Did you like Diablo 2? Then you will like this game too. It has better graphics, many more skill combinations and characters development, itemization and so on.
If you are new to this kind of games, then the game goes like this: ... click click (entering a huge crowd of mobs with your character) ... click click click click click click click click click (bang, boom, hack, slash, lots of graphical effects of skills, blood, flying bodies everywhere, now it's just you standing among all the dead bodies) ... click click (picking up drops) -> rinse and repeat, neverending fun.
Pros:
- Lots of skill combinations, classes, character builds.
- Balance of characters and skills. Actually the developers are still updating the game and tweaking skills or other aspects of the game when players find a way to abuse them. There is also going to be a new expansion later this year with 2 new classes!
- Noob friendly - you can undo points assigned to skills, so you can use different skills at the beggining of the game and then assign them to different skills if you don't like your character or you want to try something else without being forced to reroll your character (of course it has some limitation, you cannot change from a mage to a melee character easily)
- Nice environment and different areas
- Story. I know, for this kind of games the story is not important and you don't have to read anything, but I actually liked the storytelling, the characters you meet, the bits of diaries you find along the game and the reason why you are so strong and why it's you killing mobs and trying to "help" others.
Cons:
- Devotion system. I really hate it. I mean, it's a great mechanic that allows you to bend your character to whatever you really want and it's basically something that gives you endless possibilities, but man, it's SO OVERWHELMING. So overwhelming that it kind of discourages me to make new characters and try all the variations. If it at least had some kind of filtering, searching box or something that would help you to plan your build, but no, it's just an endless, huge screen of stars without any hints what effect would benefit your character. Even for theorycrafting out of the game in various tools it's not much easier.
- Some game mechanics are obviously (maybe intentionally) superior to others. The most obvious are the resistances. It doesn't matter how strong your character is or how good your build is, if you don't have high resistances, you're gonna die. And of course, if you maxed out your resistances, then you don't need any special equipment and you will be fine in most areas. Maybe it's a restriction for combining superior armor sets with superior jewelleries - so you have to give up something and just wear a plain ring with some resistances in it - but it just does not feel right. Especially with the fact that the game *is* properly ballanced.

Even though it's against popular opinion I'm afraid I'll have to be honest. The Far Cry games ia a series that I always had a problem enjoying. Now granted, I haven't played the first two but I jumped on the band wagon when number 3 came out. I figured this was one of those situations where the first two games far surpassed it's sequel as some games do. For instance, the first Zelda game was highly endeared whereas Zelda 2 was very hit and miss. To my surprise, 3 was just as well received if not better received than the first two games and 4 hit high as well. I just didn't understand! The game was sloppy, the story was exempt of interest, the characters lacked personality... well... besides the antagonists, and the game play was uninspired. People all swarmed for this game though and I never understood why. Was it the open world sand box elements? The fact that while dull it did bring interesting game play mechanics? The veterancy this game has? I don't know. Like I said, I know this is unpopular opinion but I never understood why this game was considered fun. So why get did I buy Far Cry Primal? Strangely... There are a lot of games I consider bad. Naturally, if a game is really bad I wouldn't dare play it unless there was incentive to. These games had no incentive but strangely I found myself desiring to play them to completion. Having beaten Far Cry 3 and 4 without knowing why I even wanted to keep playing a game I didn't particularly like made me wonder what was it that possesed me to do so. So naturally I bought the next in the series. So my reason? There is none. While I don't think it's fun... I guess I must somewhere deep down enjoy it in some way. Maybe that's the answer I've been seeking? So why am I saying all this? To emphasize my bias to this game... And to show the sincerity I mean when I say the following: Far Cry Primal is amazing.
Slight spoilers ahead:
You'd think going back to a primitive age after constantly being given a repretoire of munitions would leave you wanting more. Yet not once during my entire play through did I think "Boy I would like a more vast armory of weapons" or "A machine gun would be most endearing." There's something about getting to the base core of aiming gameplay, where you can't just rapid fire your way through a crowd and hope the spray and pray element would reap positive results. Now you actually have to focus on proper melee and arrow accuracy so combat is a legitimate practice. Storyline is abrupt as always but far more satisfying in one major regards. You actually get legitimate boss fights. I cannot stress how happy that made me. In the past Far Cry games I never got to fight any of the major bosses. This left an empty void in me. Why let an antagonist plague your life throughout the entire game only to have a cut scene plot element essentially eliminate them for you? I built up this strong desire to destroy them and you won't let me do that? This game finally did it semi right and actually lets you fight your main antagonists. I said semi, because the other games really built them up as villains while this game you encounter them maybe once or twice. Not much for dramatic build up. Regardless, satisfying to actually be the one taking them down. The pet mechanic by far is the strawberry on the cheesecake. It's so satisfying to have a reliable pet by your side who will viciously fight for you, get in your way when you need to loot things, stand in the way of your arrow shot, block your paths to caves, detonate traps you yourself had set.... Yeah they do more bad than good but you'll love them regardless.
There's just something far more charming about this game that the others could never achieve with me. I know it's a personal opinion but you know what? It's because it's my personal opinion that I feel it should be more valued. Now hold on, I didn't mean that in a conceited way. All I meant was I came in with the notion of absolutely detesting this game. I wanted to resent it with every cell of my body. I wanted to hate this game for being terrible. But I cannot say that without being a liar. I loved this game. It managed to turn around that strong personal feeling I've had with its predecessors for a long time. That should show that this game is strong enough to appeal to even those who wanted to hate it. Naturally though, to really get your moneys worth you'll have to do as much side content as possible. Otherwise I'd wait for it to go on sale if you're more of the main plot type of person.
I give Far Cry Primal an 8/10

Slay the spire is the best roguelike i've ever played. It's dessign is in a single word: Elegent.I know elegent gets thrown around a lot, but it truely is.
The core of the game is the fact that it's a deck building game. You start off with a simple deck of basic skills, and as you progress you get the opertunity to add more cards to the deck. The cards you add are more powerful than the basic cards, but the more cards you add the less consistant your deck becomes (more cards means it's less likely to draw the card you want). At what point do you stop adding cards? How valuable is removing a card from your deck?
The camps could have been simple rest stops, but instead you're given a simple choice - Do you stop and heal up, or do you use them to upgrade a card in your deck. Healing is rare, but upgraded cards will provide power through the rest of the spire.
And the events. My favourite event is a simple chose 3. Remove a card from your deck, Upgrade a card from your deck, or replace a card in your deck with a random card. I've had games where every single option has been valid. Sometimes I need to remove a card that's been slowing me down. Sometimes I just needed that extra upgrade. Sometimes, transforming one of the weak basic cards into a random power card was - while random - an effective way to buff the deck while maintaining consistancy.
Then we get to combat and actually playing the decks. While the base decks tend to be pretty simple to run effectivly, as the game progresses and your deck develops, the combo's become aparent. Playing you cards in the right order matters. Also the card pool is wide enough to develop multiple valid stratagies. Agressivly beat down with attack cards? Or max defence with a slow and steady damage over time poison that will eventually win? How about a bit of both. You can even build a combo deck that just cycles through itself forever dealing damage.
God dam this game. I love it.
