Probably the most philosophical RPG game.
You play as a new arrival in the small town Greyfox, but mysteriously you can choose the fate of the town's inhabitants; by waking up in their bodies, living a day in their life and ultimately perhaps ending it.
- The power of a God - Normaly you'd fight numerous enemies, find a magical sword and kill the villain to obtain this power.
Original story - dealing with a tough moral question.
Cheap Prize - base-price 0,99 and I even got it cheaper on sale.
Trading Cards.
This game is really short. It took around 3 hours to finish all endings; and that's by playing it over 3 times.
So it became really repeating.
But you get what you pay for and the price is cheap. - also if they added more inhabitants, it'd probably just be too much.
No replay value.
Since you know the stories it's like if your history teacher started every morning session telling the same old war-story.
Till this day I never understood why history was put in the morning, few students was mentaly awake so early.
The involvement of the inhabitants' lives could perhaps be better, it's difficult to get involved with them living only a little of their life. - Something more about their childhood, actions and persona could help.
A game which comes with a fresh touch to the RPGmaker collection, original and reflective story. However the execution of it could have been better, you're still left with a feeling of something missing (perhaps because it's so short).
But compared to so many cliche RPGmaker games, I'd recommend this.

Overall, the second installment of the COH series is a disappointment. The first game was such a classic. I felt it really revolutionized the genre of RTS, allowing for a unique gameplay. I'm not much for rushing/spamming strategies, so the original COH was a challenge, in that I was always pushing for resources, not allowing me to remain in my comfortable "turtle" style of gameplay. It never felt overwhelming, or too hurried, but rather just generally rushed, like a pitched battle would.
The second edition has not changed all that much from that recipe. There are some neat whiz-bang things like cold, and ice, and the ability to jump obstacles. However, these do little to add to the authenticity of the game. Instead, they just clutter up your decision-making with additional selections to be made each time you want to move a unit. Now, rather than selecting a squad and advancing to a location, I find myself micromanaging each squad. Sprinting from fire to fire to keep warm, or ensuring that they assault over walls rather than going over them keeps me from focusing on the big picture. Trying to manage three separate forces in a winter map? Good luck. You'll be hard pressed to track a few units, let alone forces spread across a map when a snowstorm blows in.
As far as balance is concerned, Soviet conscript doctrine seems to be vastly overpowered. The ability to produce nearly 3 units in the timeframe makes playing as the Soviets far too easy and against them far too difficult, on any setting. The Germans cannot keep up with the Soviet onslaught, and as a result are very dissatisfying to play. Perhaps this is true to life, but it certainly makes for an unappealing faction in this game.
The Command Loadout function is probably intended to help with this... but I've not been able to understand it. I cannot determine what I'm changing, what the changes are affecting, and how they will assist my game. There seem to be far too many options, many of which appear to be cosmetic (do I really need to pick from 5 different camouflage patterns, none of which do anything to help conceal my equipment and Soldiers?) and of little value.
The graphics appear to be exactly the same as the original COH, though what can you honestly do with tiny little figures? I won't fault the maker for that.
Overall, I'm under the impression that Relic took a great game that was becoming a bit stale, slapped a new face/ generals on it, cluttered the UI, made it more difficult to control the battlefield, and ensured that anyone just coming into the Series will be thoroughly confused. Not worth the money I paid for it at all.

Company of heroes takes a step further and finally makes a game around the Eastern Front (Western if your Russian). Like any other RTS game it has the basic Single-player (or story mode), Multiplayer, and not to mention the new theater of war mode. The single player is only centered around the red army. Sadly, it doesn't feature any type of German point of view. CoH2 does feature German (and Russian) point of view in the new theater of war. Which is kewl and all but majority of the theater of war is DLC. Multiplayer, is well multiplayer. And just like the last CoH it features a reasonable skirmish mode (which lets you play as the op Germans yaaay). Another new cool feature are the generals, instead of sticking you with three old boring doctrines they give a plethora of different sets of tactics to use. But a large amount of the generals are sadly *drum roll* DLC. More game changing Features would be the abilities to give small but effective bonuses to your troops,tanks,and ect.. Another new installment is being able to customize vehicle skins. In a nutshell I am pretty satisfied with CoH2 but what really brings it down is the DLC, but you still can have enjoyment with it. So i give it a 7.5/10. 8/10 if you have the money for the bundles or the DLC. Which is at most is like $12. And I have gotten the case blue bundle which I thought could've been a tad cheaper but was alright.

Lost Castle is a simple but entertaining game. It is semi-rogue-like. Allow me to explain: you create a profile, let's say it is Save Slot 1 (there are about 10 open slots from which to choose - I don't know the exact number and don't feel like checking). Whenever you begin playing this game (whether in singleplayer or multiplayer), you select the profile (i.e. Save Slot 1; Save Slot 2; etc.) you want to load for that game. This profile (i.e. Save Slot) gets stronger over time and does not get erased unless you opt to delete it. Once you have selected the profile you would like to use, you choose the appearance of your character for this particular run of the dungeon. Appearance has no in-game influence; it is purely cosmetic. Having selected your appearance, you begin the run of the dungeon with this character. The starting abilities of this character are determineed by the aforementioned profile you are using. As the character goes through the dungeon, they acquire new items/buffs/etc. that make this character (for this run only) stronger. The character also collects souls. Eventually your character dies a horrible death in one manner or another. At this point, all acquired items/buffs/etc., along with the character's selected appearance, dissipate into nothingness. You are left with a screen asking you about how you want to distribute the souls you collected. These souls are used to unlock different abilities that make your profile stronger. Next time you do a dungeon run using that same profile, your character will be stronger in accordance with the new benefits you have unlocked for that particular profile (but, again, the new character will not possess any of the items/buffs acquired during the last dungeon run). I hope that makes sense.
In any event, the game has a lighthearted, fun sort of feel. Some of the monsters can be frustrating to fight, but they are all interesting and each has unique abilities (e.g. you have slow monsters, fast monsters, charging monsters, acid spitters, casters, melee, buffers, teleporters, etc.). Maps are randomly generated, which keeps it from getting too repetitive going through the same types of dungeons over and over. There is also an adorable dinosaur that you can find - aaaand an adorable dinosaur costume. New items are unlocked as you beat new bosses.

Alan Wake's American Nightmare is the shorter expansion pack style follow up to the previous entry - Alan Wake. Utilising a more arcade-y gameplay style this time, the game features shorter stage style locations with a heavier focus on combat and a vastly expanded collection of weaponry. The gameplay is much smoother this time around to make the fights feel more fluid and energetic, this does detract from the eerie atmosphere somewhat, with Alan feeling more powerful than ever (to be fair he would be pretty battle hardened by now though) and the enemies being easier to take down it is hard to feel overwhelmed, which does detract from the horror side of things. Storywise the game features a less intricate plot - The general overview is the doppelganger of Alan created from the ending of the first game - Mr. Scratch - is on the lose and attempting to destroy everything important to Alan and he must stop him before that happens. Overall Alan Wake's American Nightmare is a great bite sized action thriller with plenty of replayability.

In the first ten minutes of Alan Wake, you are pursued and consumed by an unknown dark force, showing how it's an atmospheric horror/thriller. In the first ten minutes of American Nightmare, you blow up an oil well with a satellite, showing how it's not while still being an awesome game.
This stand-alone expansion to Alan Wake simplifies many elements of the original while making a few adjustments here and there. Now your flashlight regenerates faster and only needs one battery to fill up, but in exchange the only way you can burn darkness off of enemies is to focus your light on them. You're given a great many more weapons, but in exchange your flashbangs and flare gun don't do as much damage as they once did. There are only three levels, but they're expansive and more open ended, plus there's a manuscript radar so you aren't poking around every edge of the map looking for the last couple pages. It all works pretty well, mostly to play up the Survival-esque Arcade mode where you have to hold off waves of Taken for ten minutes. Or as long as you can in those ten minutes in Nightmare mode before the Taken smear you across the room. Speaking of Nightmare mode, it's also unlocked from the start this time, though it felt a little underwhelming. I don't know.
On the store page it's recommended to someone interested in starting out the Alan Wake series, but there are tons of post-Alan Wake spoilers in the manuscript and dialogue that it's hard to really say that. The simplified action gameplay is easy to pick up and fun, but the spoilers hurt the original game. So it's hard to start on this game if you plan to play the original at any point. American Nightmare plays as an interesting epilogue to the rest of the original series and its DLC.
While it may become repetitive, sadly, American Nightmare is still a solid recommendation for rocking what made the original game great and tackling a different genre simultaneously, while still holding the feel of the original.

Since there's a lot to manage and watch, there's the option to pause in combat and micro manage the weapons and systems you have. Though you have to be careful to watch whats going on with your ship and the attacking one.
The game is randomized with a number of events, though not very numerous. The shops are random too, offering different crew members, systems, and weapons. Using scrap, you need to make decisions on what to upgrade and what to purchase, and what you need for the future. If you don't have much of a variety, you might get overwhelmed in the future.
Be careful of the choices you make becuase they can either help you or hinder you, sometimes saving your ship and sometimes being the end of your little journey. The outcome of many events sometimes depends on the upgrades, systems, crew, and weapons you have. Luckily like mentioned above you can pause combat, if you are stumped in battle and need to re-think your strategy.
It has its downsides, though if you don't mind them, you'll like this strategy game. When you begin, you might end up going through a streak of losing and bitter battles. Chance does play a part in this game, maybe a bit or quite a lot depending on your experience. It helps to plan out along the way, with goals of what needs to upgraded and what you need to buy.

I am an avid GoT fan with my Fiancée and having bought this game on Humble bundle, yet hearing negative things from fellow fans, I had been steering away from it, but finally deciding "It can't be that bad" I booted it up.
My initial and only one over-arching complaint strangely from me, is graphics, there's a weird ''aura'' which goes around certain objects and characters which make it look weird, also their attempt at re-creating the main-theme introduction to Game of Thrones in the engine seemed extremely sloppy like they handed it to the new interns to do at 5minutes notice, I personally would've thought just editing the ORIGINAL theme to add the one new place shown would be a smarter and slicker idea, but I digress.
The characters are extremely loyal to form, Having bumped into notable characters already they act how I expected them to and gave me surprises I should've expected. As with all TellTale games it does the whole "(x) Will remember this" which often makes you worry about your decisions, but I often found what I've been doing so far feels right. The game will also often make you 'chose a side', usually between being an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ or being a wuss bag, or ♥♥♥♥ing over one party in lue for another (as to be expected from a 'pick your own' adventure). The inclusion of the new house, one which is never seen within the series, but within the game comes across as a major player, does feel relatively natural, you can feel happily emerged in the GoT universe. It creates this illusion of being involved with the main/major events, whilst not actually having your players do anything which would make the original storyline any different. As I said previous, characters which exist in the actual series (Noteable ones being Cersi Lannister, Tyrion Lannister and Ramsey Snow) are extremely true to form, not just because they're using the real voices, but because they have been written to act as they would and you have to try and use a knowledge of how they are within the series to keep them sweet or♥♥♥♥♥♥them off (I found that even though I am on the latest ep of GoT (at this point season 6, episode 3) I found that characters still threw me off guard in a very typical way to their character. Without spoiling too much, it made Episode 1 feel like a true GoT series,
The QTEs are relatively natural, only really appearing during battle scenes to make them come to life and feel more interactive, they're also not too difficult, I think I've only failed 2 QTEs when I've just hit the wrong key or been distracted.  I usually find that QTEs can ruin a game but TellTale is very clever in integrating them into the 'right' moments, not overly relying on them whilst not leaving them so far removed from the gameplay it sneaks up on you and ruins it.
Overall this is a very, very fun game to play if you enjoy GoT and generally fancy getting lost in a story. The characters are awesome, the way it tells the story is awesome and the use of... let's just say, 'colorfull language', is extremely true to form as GoT tends to be full of the C, B and F words.

At the end of the day, Grim Dawn is just another Diablo-style ARPG, but it's also a very good Diablo-style ARPG.
As you would expect from one of these games, the story is "meh, whatever" (although there are some interesting side stories scattered throughout), the gameplay is really repetitive, and the music might as well not ever be there.  Typically I reserve these kinds of games for times when I'm listening to podcasts or watching Netflix because they don't actually require a whole lot of mental effort on the part of the player (don't even consider setting the difficulty below Veteran if you want at least a little challenge from the game).  And while I'm a fan of the very obvious nods to Lovecraft in both the lore and the aesthetics, it's not exactly integral to the experience - most of the time it just feels like generic "dark fantasy", a la Diablo 2.
The one thing that really attracts me to these sorts of titles is the character building, and that is where Grim Dawn really shines.  When you create your character you choose one of six classes, as you would expect, but at a certain level you unlock the ability to choose a second class, essentially giving you access to two different skill trees.  Beyond that there is a third system called "Devotion", which gives you the ability to choose any number of dozens of different mini skill-trees (represented as stars in a constellation) which give powerful stat bonuses and, more importantly, new skills which modify the effects of your main skills (for instance, my Occultist character has a poison grenade skill, which I've modified with a 'devotion' skill that causes poison spikes to shoot out of the ground around me every time the grenade is used).  In addition to these skill systems, these are also plenty of items and item enhancements which provide even more skills to use in battle so long as they are equipped.  Needless to say, these systems provide and absolutely absurd level of character creation for you to play around with.
All-in-all, Grim Dawn is highly derivative (as all games in this genre are), but it provides fans of these games a lot of meat to sink their teeth into.

This game is weird. It actually feels like the Far Cry 3 DLC Blood Dragon, in a way; it's Far Cry, yet it's not. For the most part, it's pretty good. It's fun, the mechanics are familiar, the world is beautiful. It feels like it hand-holds a little less than the previous titles, so if you haven't played any, it may be a little tricky to start, but it's nothing mind-boggling.
However, I am glad I waited for a sale, because it certainly doesn't measure up to a mainline title in terms of value. The writing in Far Cry has never been good, but at least it was memorable and often funny; here, it's BORING and completely forgetable. This is made worse by the fact that everyone speaks in fakey caveman speak with subtitles. In a real foreign language one doesn't speak, the inflection and finer points still come through, but in a fake language, it has all the subtelty of children speaking (especially being cavemen who ARE practically children). Blah blah ME MAD NOW blah blah. I can't name a single character in this game except Dah, because duh, and nothing has made me laugh at all in this game, no Vaas, no Pagan Min, no Huxley, no tongue-in-cheek item descriptions (they did have a cameo of an established character that is actually a little amusing, but I won't ruin it). In fact, there are no descriptions of practically anything, you find a new place and it's just there. Why? What for? Who built it? What's it's purpose? Nothing, no emotional investment at all. And some of the scenes make the previous games look genius by comparison; I could understand those protagonists trying not to immediately kill everyone they see, but this guy is a warrior caveman, why is he bumbling into traps and letting tiny ladies push him around? The setting is just cavemen tribes at war. Your tribe is no better than the others, but hey, they wear green and your evil enemies wear red and blue, clearly you deserve to win. Also, the collectibles? No explanation. Literally, there's not even flavor-text for ANY of them.
As for gameplay, it's mostly okay, but it's obvious they rejiggered their existing system to fit the new setting and it's not quite right. Stealth is harder; tagging is harder and not even available for a while, it's harder to see even when you do tag (the shadows or outlines are far less noticeable), and the natural setting makes sneaking around generally very difficult (fewer corners and buildings and more randomness). Also, of course, there is no sniping, and your only consistent long-range weapon is the bow, which has never been that great either. This makes most combat into melee contests, which is a bit hard in first person, losing sight of the enemy, getting turned around, etc. There are only a handful of weapons; you can "craft" upgrades to them, there's alot of crafting in this game, but they don't feel meaningful, it just makes your club hit harder. It's really shallow with limited choice. Your other main weapon are animals; for one, you get an owl. You can "look through his eyes", so to speak, to survey the area, which is great, but you can also divebomb and kill enemies with 100% accuracy. Yes. To get that stealth bonus, just keep summoning your owl and insta-killing everything but heavies. There's a cool down, but it's less than I've spent in previous games lining up shots with a .50. Otherwise, you can tame animals to fight with you. The system is easy and there are several animals. Oddly enough though, you start with a mid-range choice, instead of at the bottom of the ladder. And it's easy to quickly get the best generic companions (there are a few quest-specific recruits as well). There seems like depth to the system, but no, get a Sabretooth and never look back. Your companion is immortal, although he can be laid out temporarily, and you can order them to attack, to stay, to sneak, even to sneak attack sometimes. It's cool, but like the rest of the combat, you quickly realize that this is it. Also, there's a...well, detective vision from the Arkham Batman games here, where everything is portrayed in a washed-out, high-contrast view where everything you can interact with (vines to climb, treasure, enemies) glow yellow. It's really annoying and ugly, but you'll probably use it all the time because it's just so useful, and sometimes literally required.
So how does the game play overall? It's okay, mostly running around the map taking out guys either by animal or by running up and clubbing them to a pulp. There's just less emotion, less fun, fewer options. You can craft alot more upgrades, but they are still mostly just "carry more spears, carry more arrows". Not having the gun system, where you had to carefully weigh and balance your load out, makes the game really shallow; you can sleep in a tent located every 500 feet, so you literally never feel like you never have to go back to camp, never sell any inventory (there is no such inventory, no money, no trade), never buy ammo, nothing. You get into a groove early on and it never changes with new weapons or new enemy types. The characters, the quests, the collectables, the plot, the locations, the animals, NONE of them have any meaning or even humor. You learn how to kill things then you just keep killing things, there's not even a central narrative, just fight the bad guys. It's fine for what it is, a game where you run around and beat things to death, and sometimes ride a mammoth into battle, it has that awesome 80's feel like (as I mentioned) Blood Dragon did, if not so overt, but it's really very shallow and lacks any kind of replayability or even different play styles, unless you count "a little stealth" and "no stealth" as different enough. I've played the previous games several times; I don't think I will ever again play this game after I wrap it up in a day or two, because it basically feels like one 40-hour DLC. I'd say it was over-priced, in the end, probably worth about $40. Oh, and the DLC for it? Completely not worth it. Seriously. One group of people I would recommend this game for are the hardcore gamers who like challenges; you can turn off all the help this game has, make your character far easier to kill, and even activate a perma-death option. If you thought beating Devil May Cry without ever getting hit was fun, well, here you go. All in all, it's a fun game to play once, but I'd wait for a sale.
Edit: I completely forgot to talk about the leveling in this game. It's actually better than previous games, I think, at least it makes more sense, with different people teaching you different skills (the hunter, the fighter, the inventor, etc). There are more trees, so you don't feel locked into learning useless low level skills to get to the good ones quite so often. What I don't like, however, is that you stop earning experience when you need about 35 more points to max out the skill tree. Why? Because the rest of the points are rewards from quests. But not story quests, or quests for your characters, or anything with a purpose, no, these are just completely random people you stumble across who go "Go save some people from that camp over there!" and you kill a few mooks, done. And there are several DOZEN of these. All of the game's other quests, as well as the randomly spawning events (like in Far Cry 4), are already kind of repetitive, now they want you to do dozens of utterly meaningless kill-quests just to finish leveling up. This is just a lazy way to add more content and try to incentivize you to do it. Fortunately, there are several skills you can ignore without even feeling it, so I didn't actually care when this happened to me and I figured out what they expected me to do. What a cop-out.

I loved Alan Wake. However I was skeptical coming into American Nightmare and rightly so. I'd call AN a spin-off rather than a sequel to Alan Wake given its slightly brighter color palette and more action-oriented gameplay. The story, as well, while having some connections to the original it doesn't have the same amount of effort put into it and seems to only be there so that there's something to call a story.
However, the game itself is not delluding itself that it's something that it's not. I feel this was done consciously to give Alan Wake fans a quick fix of what they liked while I suspect a sequel is in the works. But therein lies the game's biggest caveat: It's a game for Alan Wake fans. People coming into the series with American Nightmare will find themselves confused and lacking valuable backstory information, no matter the game's good intentions and attempts to bring everyone up to speed.
The graphics are doing new and interesting things with color and lighting in this new western desert setting as opposed to the gray and blue of the Rocky Mountains' nights in the previous game, but the soundtrack seems to fall short this time, lacking the storyline integration that made the first one great.
All in all in spite of all this I had fun with Alan Wake's American Nightmare and I'm giving it a thumbs up, but with a footnote: For fans of the series.

This game is wonderful - 10/10
Graphics - 9/10 The art style is made up of wonderfully nostalgic 2D images, with a typical over head view of the action the players point of view has been tested through time in the RTS genre and cannot be faulted. Sound - 10/10 The sound is also pretty nostalgic for anyone who played games before the mid 90s, the melodic theme is catchy and non-invasive while the sound effects are exactly what you'd expect, the lazers. bombs and shields all sound perfect.
Gameplay - 10/10 The quick paced gameplay is exhilerating, managing your crew is vital and tense strategic decisions arise regularly in combat on each playthrough. The inclusion of a pause function is vital to your survival as when the more intense battles take place every second is vital! The very inclusion of a pause function makes the game much more accessible to newcomers of strategy. A save upon exit function (no going back to your save if you die) reflects the games Rogue-Like roots.
Overall - 10/10 This is one of my favourite games, it's hard there is no sugar coating it, but oh so addictive!

Greyfox is a non-combat adventure RPG with a focus on exploring the area and talking to people. The premise of the story is that you stay at a hotel in a retirement area, where you meet a mysterious woman. Then you dream about her, and she makes you experience a day in the life of four different elderly people. As each person, you walk around the town exploring, and eventually have to decide whether or not to let them die.
The provocative premise of the plot makes the story sound better than it is, while the delivery feels somewhat non-chalant. The character graphics are better than in most RPGMaker games, but there are few reasons to consider this a high quality game. There is one bug in particular that causes the game to freeze if you talk to someone. Just one, to be fair (but save often).
At about 30 minutes playtime, and a price of $1, you won't cry over your lost time or money if you purchase this game, but be aware what you are getting, and that there may be other titles that are more to your liking.

I think the most telling statement about this game is that many reviewers have put hundreds of hours into this game, and, in the end, leave a negative review.
I believe Black Desert Online is good at what it set out to do:
Exploration is excellent. Movement alone feels satisfying, and one can jump, climb, swim, or even backflip through some majorly appealing scenery. Nothing quite beats the feel of Spanish Guitar opening up through your speakers as you race through the badlands and into the desert on the way to find some rumored location. Learning things by talking to npcs, reading books, and finding locations is well rewarded through leveling up energy, which is useful in a variety of tasks.
Roleplaying is pretty darn good as well. Higher levels of play almost always lead to guilds, where it is easy to find a community that shares your interests. Character looks are highly customizable. The wide array of useful lifeskills allow a player to engage in the world in meaningful ways outside of combat. The property system made me feel very attached to certain cities, while quests gave me insight into the lore of the land and its people.
However, this game does falter in a major way, and I think it is end game content. While player-driven content such as guild conquest sounds impressive, the successes in this game are temporary at best. Achievement ends up hiding behind long grinds, and becomes less and less satisfying as you realize you do not have incredibly much to use the power on.
Do I think this means you should not get this game?
No. I think this is very well worth the price point.

If you're interested in Hyperdimension Neptunia Re;Birth2, chances are you already played the first game from the Re;Birth series, liked it to some degree and are looking for more. Gameplay wise, Re;Birth2 offers just that. It's practically the same game as its predecessor at the core, with a few minor chances.
Compared to the first game, Re;Birth2 has a better presentation, it looks more refined and polished. The gameplay is exactly the same with just one change - you can now bring one additional party member to the field, for a total of four.
Unfortunately, the content seems to have taken a turn for the worse. The characters and the story look less involved and more superficial than before. The goddess candidates aren't quite as fleshed out as their elder counterparts were.
The main antagonist for the first half of the game, while never particularly menacing to beging with, keeps recurring time and again to the point where nobody could take her seriously anymore. Granted, the previous game didn't really have a threatening villain either, but seeing the same character try for another round after a dozen failed attempts to sabotage us, one can't help but wonder what's going on in their heads. Similar levels of incompetence are displayed by the heroines, who manage to let their enemies get away with it each and every time, despite outclassing them on several levels.
The leveldesign (more specifically, the copy-pasted dungeons), one of the biggest drawbacks of the predecessor, has been improved quite a bit, but ultimately it still leaves to be desired.
On the other hand, Re;Birth2 is much more linear. While about half of the dungeons in the previous game were optional side content, this one barely offers more than a handful, which forces you onto an almost completely linear path. However, Re;Birth2 does have multiple different endings, and some dungeons are restricted to chapters only accessible by certain endings. Which, unfortunately, brings me to another point: materials from these dungeons are required for certain "Stronger Enemies" Plans, which in turn drop materials required for other Plans, and so on, to the point where almost half the items and Plans in the game are gated behind dungeons only accessible in one particular ending.
Except for the seemingly obligatory early game roadblock, which you'll meet much sooner than Blackheart in Re;Birth1, the difficulty looks very consistent, with another exception in the form of one incredibly difficult encounter during one of the endings, which can be very tough even for overleveled parties. Overall I found the difficulty to be slightly lower than in Re;Birth1.
About the localisation... as someone who places great importance on accurate translations, I'm just going to pretend it doesn't even exist. Fortunately, there's a fan-made retranslation patch available. Unfortunately, while it applies some much needed improvements, it's far from perfect. If you understand some japanese, you'll notice that what the characters say and what you read is often quite different.
In conclusion, if you're looking for another dose of cute girls doing cute things, you'll find it here, and the gameplay is practically the same as in the previous game. But most of the content Hyperdimension Neptunia Re;Birth2 has to offer seems to be a level below its predecessor, which makes it an overall slightly less enjoyable, but still fair experience in my opinion.

I bought this in early release a few years and never really tried playing it until the last two weeks. It's a great successor to Titan Quest: Immortal Throne, and has a similar dual-class option.
A few things I like:
The story. Grim Dawn is entirely original (though a little Lovecraftian imo) and has a lot of lore in the game. It's the first game that I can remember actually reading the "Lore pages" you loot in certain areas. I found myself reading dialogue for quests, talking to random people in town, exploring every map, etc.
A great soundtrack. Very dark and forboding. Usually I turn off music on day 1 for games and play my own in the background. In Grim Dawn I did not. It fits the theme very well.
Character customization. Customization is pretty incredible through skill builds, devotions, and items. I've seen so many theorycrafted ideas and made a few of myself. I'm still pretty new here and have been consulting the forums for ideas. There are six masteries (classes): Soldier, Demolitionist, Occultist, Arcanist, Shaman, Nightblade. You pick your first mastery at level 2 and then can choose a second one at level 10 or later (I didn't choose one for a few characters until level 20 or 30 because you cannot change it later).
There's also the Ashes expansion which adds two more masteries: Necromancer and Inquisitor. That will total 8 masteries in the game which given the dual classing aspect means there are a LOT of options (28? I'm bad at math). It will also increase level cap from 85 to 100 and continue from the existing story. An "appearance"  (I think it's called an Illusionist) vendor is also coming which will allow you to set gear you've collected and customize the armor your character is visibly showing, which I think is pretty rad. I look forward to making myself some level 100 character who is clad in lowbie leathers!
Also the Crucible DLC is fun, especially co-op with a friend. It's kind of like a tower defense mini game in an ARPG and you get loot for your characters to use in the standard game. You have a wave multiplier that continues to go through 10 round segments at which time you get a breather before carrying onward. You have a timer and have to kill each wave before it ticks to 0 or you lose your multiplier. It's pretty challenging and frantic trying to kill everything before time runs out... it really makes you hesitate every 10 rounds and go "should I play it safe cash out now, or try for another 10 to get even greater rewards?"
Anyway, what I'm trying to say here is that I believe that Grim Dawn is a high quality Action RPG and I would highly recommend giving it a shot.
Update: The DLC Expansion has released and is totally worth it!

What a game this is, even though it is a breakaway from the traditional Far Cry persona it is excellent. I completed the game some time ago and still go back to collect achievements on a regular basis, it is one of those games that you want to do just that. That being said, it won't be long until I return for a full play through and this is why.
It amazes me how this game received so many bad reviews (essentially from day 1), I agree it deviates from the 'Far Cry' norm but that I think in this case is a bonus. The reason I say this is because the game has similarities but is very different overall especially because it is not your typical 'FPS'. Mainly because there isn't a gun or slab of C4 to be seen so you then need to become accustomed to using 'Bow's and Arrow's' and Spears etc. Plus, you have to collect the necessary items to craft same (as well as everything else in the game) as you progress.
This might seem a bit of a chore at first, but you will get used to it and as your village grows in population so will your available resources that you are able to acquire even when away from your village and from various collection points around the map.
You will gain many skills as you go by doing numerous missions that help to improve all your capabilities and also give you things to do other than the standard gameplay. Characters are great and very interesting and individually unique in many ways. This varies from being tough and aggressive to downright funny, my favourite side mission character is definitely 'Urki'. Without giving anything away he is the craziest guy in the place and fantastic personality that breaks up the seriousness of it all.
The setting and graphics are outstanding and the whole game is very open world with a considerably well laid out map, your only means of transport are 'Shank's Pony' (on foot for non-Australians), or you can ride certain tamed animals to get you places or help fight battles......Unlike previous FC games Motor vehicles of any description are obviously in short supply!
You will find at times that things seem to be happening too slowly, I did as well but before you know it a new mission or objective will show up and all that will change, (happens more so earlier in the game rather than later I feel).
I have nothing negative to say about Primal as to me it was great experience and one to be re-played multiple times in the future. This includes the fact that there is no Multiplayer or Co-Op, a bone of contention to many. The fact that this is a 'Single player' only game is one of its strengths, I personally am tired of paying the same for games that have small amounts of SP content and are mostly designed around MP. For me they are poor value and steer clear of them as much as I can. Luckily all FC games have great SP content and for that (especially with Primal), I commend Ubisoft for a great and very playable product.
Details of gameplay have been deliberately avoided so as not to spoil, but should anyone want help or further information just ask and I would be happy to offer assistance with any matters that may arise. I have uploaded a number of videos which will also offer some insight if you are interested which can help with completion of some parts of gameplay.
I rate this 9/10 and would love to see a DLC released in the near future to extend an already great game. Let's keep our fingers crossed.
Be certain your system can handle all that is required by this game as well before you buy and that your OS and GPU (Video Card) etc. are set up correctly and capable to run this.

PROS
- Every experience is randomized, so you solve the case differently

CONS

- Freddi still comes off as condescending to Luther, but not as much as other games I've played...This could be a pro depending on your personality but sometimes Freddi is a little too self-righteous for my tastes. She'll look at me when Luther does something wrong, as if I should chastise him too. Well, sometimes, we all just want to reach for shiny jewels, Freddi. Accept human/aquariam nature
- Horse Fetters isn't always the culprit :(
- The price is way too high
This is my favorite of the Freddi Fish games. I love that there are so many culprits and they all have different motivations for stealing the conch shell. It's definitely too expensive for what it offers, but I got these on sale for about $2-3, so I suggest waiting for them to go on sale again. I feel like the different playthroughs are interesting in how you get different golden pipes for the conch shell, so if you're the kind of person who likes playing well-thought-out children's games, I definitely recommend this as I feel like the game doesn't automatically assume you're a child, especially given the ending sequences for each of the culprits.
If you ever feel like you want to solve a mystery that doesn't require too much thought, play this. It's a different culprit every time and as far as children's games go, it still reigns supreme in my book. Freddi Fish and Luther still got nothing on the Pajama Sam universe, though.

American Nightmare is a perfect extraction of all the mistakes which kept Alan Wake from greatness, distilled and reconstituted as a sequel-spinoff. These aspects are certainly improved from the source game, but they're just not enough to sustain a new title.
The soul of Alan Wake had been that proper horror element, scrambling through the haunted forests where the shifting shadows distorted the world. The game had trouble building out the experience as a game, however, which resulted in the horde of generic enemies haphazardly and often infinitely spawning to line up and die while you fumbled along the pathway. While the story and atmosphere were fairly well-executed, the gameplay dragged down what could otherwise been a classic game. In American Nightmare, there is no darkness, shadows, distortion, or horror. There are, however, enemies lining up to die en masse.
On the positive side, this iteration does improve on the meager combat mechanics of its predecessor. You're no longer limited to one type of handgun or three samey types of long guns. There are a pretty nice selection of arms this time around, from a semi-automatic pistol to a nail gun to a full-auto shotgun to a crossbow. Unfortunately, these are not always well-balanced. Of particular note is the crossbow, which eliminates enemy defenses and one-shots all but the largest of opponents on Nightmare difficulty. Oh, and you can carry 25 bolts, and there are refilling ammunition stations all over the place. So where Alan Wake's Nightmare mode had you scrounging up whatever ammunition you could find to down the bullet-sponge big guys, you hardly have any reason to change weapons. There are also a greater variety of enemies, but they're not always inventive. The final opponent to be introduced is just an 8-foot-tall hulking hillbilly with a concrete saw. It's a step forward, but I hesitate to say that it reaches the threshold for "good" combat. Enemies aren't all standing around eating bullets while you slowly die of boredom this time, but the AI doesn't stop them from infinitely staggering in place around just the same. All of the same strategies apply, but there are just more enemies with more unique mechanics this time. It's undoubtedly an improvement over Alan Wake, but it's not something I'd go out of my way to play.
The game takes place in Night Springs, Arizona, which you will likely recognize as the Twilight Zone parody program in Alan Wake. There are only 3 fairly small locations which can be explored in their entirety in about 30 minutes. Each of the locations are entirely self-contained with little more than a comic-book to bridge the gap. American Nightmare totally lacks the great sense of place that made Alan Wake. The story concerns the existence and fate of Mr. Scratch, Wake's doppelgänger, but the game doesn't have much to offer beyond that. There are new manuscript pages to find and read, but they're not even telling a story. Instead, they're basically codex entries, describing this enemy or occasionally just telling you what you have to go do. The voice acting is often pretty terrible as well, especially where the poor stand-ins are juxtaposed with familiar voices as on the radio program. There are also more live-action video cuts, but they are worse than ever, always making me wish that it was just done in the game's engine. It just seems like nowhere near the same care was put into making American Nightmare a whole experience. Even if you're just curious to see more of the Alan Wake universe, this has little to offer.
And that's really the problem. Though the game improves on the gameplay of Alan Wake in many ways, it loses all of the things that made Alan Wake a worthwhile experience. The story is irrelevant, the environments are dead, and the game's style is more pulp than horror. It does put forth a noble effort toward rectifying Alan Wake's mistakes, but I can't recommend what comes out to, at best, an average shooter with a banal trappings.

I REALLY have no ♥♥♥♥ing idea why I decided to go through with playing this game, I guess just for the little bit of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ humor I get from playing a game meant for kids about a decade or so younger than me. Let me tell you about Freddi Fish 3.
It's not a bad game for kids. It really is not, but there are still defining flaws, some of them are issues with the entire franchise I've found.
On the positive side we have that this game allows for a lot of exploration, but not too much, just enough that a child can wrap his/her mind around the environment, which you have to do to gather up the dirt on the suspects so that you'll know who stole the golden pipes at the end. It's a fun little meander through a bouncy, colorful aquatic environement, and while I feel the pixelly graphics look and feel very dated; I didn't mind it one bit playing this game as a kid.
On the negative side we have... well the gameplay. At times doing the stupid chores that this game throws out gets horribly dull, especially when you figure out it leads to nothing but a minigame or nothing but an extra feature. (I'm looking at you, Carnival.) Although I might be thinking too adult here, as I do know Children can be very easily distracted but still very entertained by extra features and minigames, but I myself, even as a child got a little peeved when I found out doing work was for naught.
All in all, it's a neat little game, a little short, a little dull and a little dated, but it's not bad. It has extra features like the minigame, the organ that makes cow sounds and watching Luther go through "The Terrific Tumble Tubes" that make the game feel a bit more lively. It's still not a perfect kid's game, but it's okay, I enjoyed it as a kid, I just don't think I'd play it again.

Pros and Cons
Pros:

- Interesting enemies
- Real sense of progression
- FTL-like but an RPG with cards and one person to look after
- Each enemy has a different strategy against you
- probably more, but this is just a quick review after a couple hours
Cons:
- mini bosses seem to show up randomly (there isn't really a set time to fight them, with some paths avoiding them and some have 4 or 5 in the way
- potions seem to be overkill or too little too late. There isn't much reason to use them
- current seems to lack content, however, as I said, it's EA, so more will be added.
- The choices tell their consequences to explicitly (maybe a way to turn that off, idk yet)
TL;DR
Slay the Spire is a fun FTL/Rouge-like RPG with fun enemies in turn based, card driven combat with good progression and more pros than cons.

I’m writing this review from the perspective of a fan of the Game of Thrones Series (I’m current on the show and books), and a first time player of a Telltale Game.
Let me start off with what I liked about the game.  I need to give them props for not cheaping out on the voice acting.  The game has some main characters from the show, and they are voiced by the real actors.  Those characters being Tyrion and Cersei Lannister, Jon Snow, Margaery Tyrell, Daenerys Targaryen, and Ramsay Bolton.  It’s fun getting to interact with the familiar characters, and the game does a good job of recreating the personalities of each one, with the exception of possibly Margaery who seemed pretty bland.
Regarding the gameplay, it’s a Telltale game so the gameplay is obviously very decision/story based.  The game follows 4 plot lines, all of different members of House Forrester (Bannermen of House Stark).  The different settings being King’s Landing, Ironrath (the seat of House Forrester), The Wall, and Meereen.  Although there are 4 separate plot lines, they all have a similar goal in mind, which is to save House Forrester.  As I played through the first few episodes, I was given the false impression that what I did in one storyline would affect another.  But after awhile I began to realize the 4 story lines are very separate, and very linear.  But I still had hopes that at the end, the 4 paths would converge and the decisions I made on each path would affect how good the ending would be for me.  That however was not at all the case.  Only 2 of stories come together at the end and guess what... what I did in both didn’t really matter.
Regarding the plot, the reason I and many others love GoT, is because it doesn’t always have a cookie cutter happy ending, and it keeps us guessing.  That being said, GRRM knows that there needs to be a balance of highs and lows so that you appreciate each one as they come.  But this game dwells in the lows from the get go, and you are only ever given the occasional ounce of hope before it is immediately crushed.  At the end of the game I was left feeling that through all my efforts, I had accomplished absolutely nothing.  And worse, there was nothing I could have done about it.
Tl;dr: “Game of Thrones - Telltale” where the plot is super depressing and the decisions don’t matter.

I bought this in early release a few years and never really tried playing it until the last two weeks. It's a great successor to Titan Quest: Immortal Throne, and has a similar dual-class option.
A few things I like:
The story. Grim Dawn is entirely original (though a little Lovecraftian imo) and has a lot of lore in the game. It's the first game that I can remember actually reading the "Lore pages" you loot in certain areas. I found myself reading dialogue for quests, talking to random people in town, exploring every map, etc.
A great soundtrack. Very dark and forboding. Usually I turn off music on day 1 for games and play my own in the background. In Grim Dawn I did not. It fits the theme very well.
Character customization. Customization is pretty incredible through skill builds, devotions, and items. I've seen so many theorycrafted ideas and made a few of myself. I'm still pretty new here and have been consulting the forums for ideas. There are six masteries (classes): Soldier, Demolitionist, Occultist, Arcanist, Shaman, Nightblade. You pick your first mastery at level 2 and then can choose a second one at level 10 or later (I didn't choose one for a few characters until level 20 or 30 because you cannot change it later).
There's also the Ashes expansion which adds two more masteries: Necromancer and Inquisitor. That will total 8 masteries in the game which given the dual classing aspect means there are a LOT of options (28? I'm bad at math). It will also increase level cap from 85 to 100 and continue from the existing story. An "appearance"  (I think it's called an Illusionist) vendor is also coming which will allow you to set gear you've collected and customize the armor your character is visibly showing, which I think is pretty rad. I look forward to making myself some level 100 character who is clad in lowbie leathers!
Also the Crucible DLC is fun, especially co-op with a friend. It's kind of like a tower defense mini game in an ARPG and you get loot for your characters to use in the standard game. You have a wave multiplier that continues to go through 10 round segments at which time you get a breather before carrying onward. You have a timer and have to kill each wave before it ticks to 0 or you lose your multiplier. It's pretty challenging and frantic trying to kill everything before time runs out... it really makes you hesitate every 10 rounds and go "should I play it safe cash out now, or try for another 10 to get even greater rewards?"
Anyway, what I'm trying to say here is that I believe that Grim Dawn is a high quality Action RPG and I would highly recommend giving it a shot.
Update: The DLC Expansion has released and is totally worth it!

Like the game before it, Rebirth 2 tells the story of four CPU goddesses and their fight to save video games.
The story is set in an alternate universe from the original. The angle of the four fighting to decide best console is dropped to focus more on their war with piracy. Also unlike the first, the subtlety is dropped: the villain is the embodient of piracy, sin, and destruction, and the evil organization seeks to fill the world with bootlegs and illegal downloads. When the game begins, the CPUs are subdued and held captive. Without the four to protect their lands, their sisters, fittingly inspired by handhelds, are forced to take up the cause.
The game itself is very much a sequel. Much of it remains unchanged, if only because Rebirth 1 was inspired by its sequel, but much more focus and polish has gone into the game. The game's humor and quirkiness remains intact, and even more self-aware than before, even eager to lampshade the younger moe cast and take shots at the otaku fanbase. The world, art, locations, and enemies are reused from the older game, but a good number of new environments and monsters are added. The music just as strong. The grind is also lessened from before, particularly if you invest in the DLC and get some helpful bonuses off the bat.
The battle system still involves choosing between attacks that focus on reducing enemy guard, dealing heavy HP damage, or building a combo meter for special attacks. Characters have unique techniques that drain their SP (MP) or powerful attacks that drain a certain amount of the combo meter. A notable change is that the party limit is now four, allowing for a larger meter and more combination attacks between certain members.
The Remake sytem also returns, allowing players to craft recipes that add new items to stores or dungeons to the world map, alter dungeons, their items, and the monsters within, or even add new characters to the party.
A new function is Stella's Dungeons, which allows you to assign an NPC to expolore dungeons you've discovered. She can find new items for herself or you to use, or possibly fail and lose everything (without the proper DLC, anyway). The exploration is done in real time, which can be annoying for players who don't want to toy with their computer's clock.
However, while the game itself is sound, the port is not. FPS drops when Guard Break triggers are common (check the guides for a fix), cutscenes can lag, loading can sometimes be Iffy, and many report freezing around a certain Castle. Most of these issues are minor or only seem to affect the minority, so you'll probably be safe. Probably.
Overall, if you enjoyed the first game, you'll enjoy this one, too.

With a dark and (at times) serious Nep, SG induces a lot more feels than the first Nep in the series.  Although some of the content i.e. Dungeon design is taken directly from the first Nep, there is never really a time where that matters as new Neps are introduced frequently throughout the first half of the Nep - which certainly keeps the player entertained.
Truly at the Nep of the game - the personification of the CPU Candidates is absolutely stunning.  Compile Heart's aesthetics and character design are really what the fanbase Neps in the series and they definitely delivered in this second title.
-Uni is the Sony PSP
-Rom and Ram are the Nintendo DS (loli twins for the dual screens is pure genius!)
-Nepgear (Nep Jr.) is based on a fictional Sega handheld
The girls are adorable, and the Japanese voice acting is the best I've Nepped in the series.  Particularly Uni as she embodies a stereotypical Tsundere, which is totally nailed!
Ultimately, this Nep has the unique trait of being able to "de-stress" my day and consistently make me Nep.  The amount of cuteness in this game is overwhelming at times, as are the beautifully rendered still-frame Neps (well, sometimes things jiggle in them)... these are breathtaking and often add a great deal of feels towards the characters.
If you've considered getting into the Hyperdimension Neptunia series, I highly recommend this as the first Nep to pick up.  Re;Birth1 doesn't actually have a plot that impacts the main story arch in Re;Birth2 and Re;Birth3.
I believe playing SG first, and thus as the CPU Candidates (little sisters) instead of the Goddesses themselves will offer a greater reward and satisfaction, so feel free to skip Re;Birth1 and jump right into Sisters Generation for the main arch of the series.
If this title happens to be on sale and you enjoy anime, this game will not disappoint!  Additionally, you may find you replace every verb with Nep after having played this series!

I've literally alt-tabbed out of the game mid-session just to write a review about how very well executed and refreshing this game is. No, it isn't perfect, no game ever has been. However, the developers have done something that is far gone in today's gaming industry ; they branched into a different path. Instead of milking the same old formula and boring people to death (Just Cause 3, anyone?) they took a brave step, a polar opposite of the game's typical main structure of guns, vehicles, explosions and one mastermind kingpin bad guy.
Instead of doing that well-known Far Cry move again, they managed to take what made the game so great to begin with, and kept that recipe the same, while adding these deliciously brilliant new spices. You don't mess with the colonel's recipe, but you sure can build off of it. And that's exactly what they've done.
Rather than your typical guns-ablazing, almost-invincible-after-two-hours-of-gameplay "adventure" game we are used to now, FC: Primal throws you into this dazzlingly beautiful untouched world, before the menacing societal evolution of mankind came into place. And even though they speak gibberish long gone by now, I can't help but feel much more emotionally invested in this game's few shallow characters. Something about their instinctive and primal (yeah i said it) nature is much more vitalizing to experience than your hum-drum love interests or best-friend facades, you have raw connections relying on survival, and the trust of your fellow man to not beat you senseless with a bone-tooth club while you're asleep and steal all your Dhole meat.
All in all, my praise aside, FC: Primal has something to teach damn near every developer out there:
Try something new. Do different. Make your own trail. And in an ironic yet iconic way, the game does this both in execution, and in the entire point of the game itself (after all, you're a caveman slightly smarter than the rest, with a mild spiritual connection to animals...ergo, you're evolution happening in the moment!). I'd suggest this over any far cry game for the simple fact that it's a trailblazer and it does so with gusto.
Thanks for reading.

Black Desert “User Interface Overkill” Online
TL;DR: Great game with way too many interfaces. Still a must-have.
Black Desert online has a very appealing look to it; graphically seen it’s certainly one of the most beautiful MMORPGs I’ve ever played, but there are just so many options and pop-ups and tabs and more tabs, and sub-tabs with options, that it makes this game sometimes just too frustrating to even consider starting up.
I feel I really have to be in the mood for an endless UI of which I probably understand around 5% by now after having played the game for approximately 8 hours. I don’t know how or where to properly store money (which unfortunately took up about 99% of my inventory of which I sold almost everything only to find out it was the amount of silver that was wearing me down), and asking for any advice in the chat is utterly pointless as your message will disappear within 5 seconds because of “market-and-guild-quest-spams”. For a game with so many players online every single day of the week – no matter what time of the day – this has got to be one of the least social games I’ve ever seen. Then again, nobody takes the time to call you a noob either, so… that’s nice?
Admittedly this has got to be one of the most beautiful games out there with this many options which you can buy for only 10 bucks; I just wish the UI would be easier to understand, and the game in itself more obvious to how things actually work so I would feel like firing up this game every single day of the week. Unfortunately many evenings I see Black Desert Online in my Steam Library and think: “Nah, too much of a hassle.” This is a shame as – to be honest and not thinking about the UI and too many pop-ups and tiny menus on the screen – this game has awesome combat!
Whereas many similar-looking MMORPGs have the “distance fighting” with the ring around your target, Black Desert really gives you the option to fight properly. If you’re up close to an enemy whilst fighting it with a sword, but you make a move to the left while your opponent side-steps you: you miss! That’s what combat is supposed to be like. Not some sort of “roll of the dice” on hit or block, but actually some expertise with the controls; remembering your special moves and combining those with your regular moves at the right moment.
So is this a game you should have in your library? I think you should. For only 10 Dollars you have a sweet looking game with tons of options. If you are the kind of person who’s good (or patient enough) with User Interfaces you might even get a bigger kick out of the game, but I wouldn’t know. If you’re a player like me and just occasionally log on to do some mindless Imp-slaughtering and basically just travel around the amazingly detailed world, then you’ll get a lot of fun out of your 10 bucks, too.
Even though the ridiculous amount of different screens and options often pisses me off rather than encouraging me to figure out how all these options work, it still is a game I gladly start up for an hour or so from time to time.

During the late 90’s/early 2000’s Humongous Entertainment released an absolutely fantastic stream of “edutainment” point and click adventures for children. These titles focus on a range of light academics including basic geography, basic to upper elementary level mathematics, logical thinking, critical thinking and puzzle solving, topped off with reinforcement of good manners and polite social etiquette. At the lower end of the age spectrum, they may require some adult supervision and supportive guidance, but there is no better series of games for a child’s first venture into PC gaming.
I remember almost nothing about Freddi Fish 3; upon replaying it, some snippets here and there came back to me, but there were also locations that I swear I never saw. From my experience over a decade later, I think The Case of the Stolen Conch Shell is a great entry in the Freddi Fish franchise, but your child's engagement may vary depending on their personal interests. To it’s credit, the solving of a mystery is a great way to develop logical thinking, deductive reasoning and to a strangely competent extent, the ability to read emotional and behavioral clues. Buy the Case of the Missing Kelp Seeds first and if that goes well, consider picking up Freddi Fish 3.

If there's ever any time that you watch some sci-fi battle from Star Trek or Battlestar Galactica, and you've wanted to be in charge of a ship rather than merely a pilot... this is the game for you! You can redirect power from one system or another, send crew to man stations or repair hull breaches, and decide whether to go for the enemy's life support or weapons systems.
This isn't the high explosiveness of dogfighting, this is the struggle to stay one step ahead of an enemy while you balance between rebuilding your ship and upgrading systems to keep yourself alive. You have the option to pause the game and assess your situation, and even issue orders in the same manner as you'll find in the Total War series (the game's paused, you issue orders, and you can unpause to see them in action)
The game has only gotten better with the free DLC that's encluded. You can turn it off if you want to play the orginial, but a load of new features and mechanics are available to further enhance this simple-concept-but-difficult-to-master game.

So, I bought this game for a couple of bucks during the last summer sale, and I have been hooked after I really started getting into the game.
You start off as a small federation ship somewhere in space in a time where there is war between Rebels and the Federation. As you play along you make your way through sectors, upgrading your ship's shields, engine, weapons and many more aswell as recruiting new crew members on your way.
You have a certain amount of Fuel, Missiles and Drone parts which you can use to help you on your journey. Sometimes at beacons on your journey you will get to fight other ships, using Weapons and Drones, and after you defeated them, you will earn resources (Fuel, Missiles, Drone parts), scrap which can be used to upgrade your ship and maybe even weapons or drone scematics!
If you aren't doing too well resource wise, you can still visit a shop and buy some using your scrap. Also in these shops you can purchase new systems for your ship, for example Cloaking, Drone control besides weapons, drone schmeatics and arguments for your ship.
Something which also is a lot of fun, are the randomly generated events which occur on your jounrey. Based on what decisions you make, you can lose a crew member, gain one, get a lot of resources, take damage to your ship and many more.
Solid 10/10, must pick up if you like tactic based rouge-likes

First, the Tropico series has not really progressesd much in gameplay and mechanics, so every Tropico release has always felt like a slight upgrade instead of a whole new game. And fans can live with that, as generally "if it ain't broke..."
Second, the value of this game assumes one of two paths;
1) you have been a fan of the series and are considrering T4 as an affordable upgrade to T3, or
2) you've never played Tropico of any flavor and are wondering where to jump in.
For Tropico fans:
Like 1-3, T4 doesn't change a lot of game mechanics. You get a new concept, ministers, which add a little bit more complexity, and you get several new buildings that allow a slightly different late-game strategy, these really become intriguing in sandbox mode (and you need all the DLCs, as expected). BUT, the downside of 4 is the graphics. No really, I have a nice rig and don't expect Steven Spielberg CGI graphics in a game like this, but T1 was better than this. How does it matter? Because you really need to see what you are doing in any build sim, and the graphics on T4 look like 16 bit Sega Genesis stuff. It truly sucks. The additional buildings and the building upgrade mechanics introduced are nice for the numbers nerd, but really the average sim-fan will be like WTF? The strategies you will use overall haven't changed since T1, and T4 doesn't really give you much more to work with, so if you have T3 or are deciding between T3 and T4, unless the price is no object and you have to see for yourself, stay with T3 and wait to see what T5+ may bring. If you are just a Tropico junky like me, the price is still cheap, go ahea, and see if you don't feel the same way. I had to try it to believe, and sure enough, it is true. T3 is the better Tropico.
If you have never played Tropico:
Look for the entire Tropico bundle with T3 and T4. It is on sale as well. play T4 first. Then step backwards to T3, give it a whirl, and you will also wonder why they didn't just release a further T3 DLC with some new buildings. It is that much of a let-down. Or just get T3 with the DLC, you'll wish you did in the end.
PS: T4 requires a separate account login to kalypso, if you are like me you hate this stuff. T3 does not. T3 wins hands down.

I've been a QUAKE fan for longer than I can remember. I played it as soon as I could operate a key board, which is far younger than I should have been. I recall playing QUAKE II when I was as young as 5 years old.
Since then I've developed a love for shooters, especially ones that demand respect through a combination of taxing your reaction times and your guile. So it's understandable that QUAKE III is one of my favourite games of all time. In a digital age, it stands out as a strangely "analogue" game: it has plenty of heart and depth and is truly a work of genius.
So when I first heard about QUAKE LIVE, an updated and revamped version of QUAKE III, I was beyond happy. Two accounts and probably 4 years of on and off love has lead me up to its controversial patch (which includes a load out system- which works excellently by the way) and now Steam release.
Let me just put it out there that is my favourite incarnation of the game. It's smooth, beautiful and all the fat has been trimmed off it to create a modern and interesting shooter.
Its skill ceiling is high: so high in fact that if you're new to QUAKE or to arena shooters in general, then expect to be schooled for your first few games. But practice makes better (not perfect: there's always room for improvement on those flick rails and your strafe jump!) and soon you'll be landing "impressives" and nailing people with precision mid-air rockets.
It's a tonic for needlessly complex military shooters like Battlefield and Call of Duty. All there is are guns and ammo, health kits, power-ups and 8+ dudes trying to pwn each other. All this makes it greatly refreshing and interesting
But don't let this fool you: QUAKE is a game comparable to chess in its complexity. Knowing what to do to out-smart opponents, knowing how to get around maps quickly and knowing when to run or to fight it out are thing that can only be learned through doing. You'll love every second
So overall, QUAKE LIVE is a blast from the past, but one that is forward thinking. As a lover of the genre and the series, I recommend this with every fibre of my being. It's tough, fast but most importantly fun as hell.
Oh, and it's free.

I tried really hard to like this game. I was a big fan of the original and I had high hopes for COH2. Unfortunately the game has been taken in a direction I'm not particularly impressed with. Here's a run down of how I feel and why.
1. It's really COH1.5 instead of 2
Despite the claim of a new game engine, alot of the existing models have been reused. Everything looks same-ish with the Germans, even the animation of the pioneers looks overly familiar. I would really have liked to have seen individual units with slight differences ala Total War. It really feels like an expansion rather than a stand alone sequel.
2. Too much monetization
As soon as you load up the main game screen, it is literally filled with cluttered menus and windows that are essentially adverts urging you to cough up for skins and doctrines. Sure none of these things effect gameplay balance but just the sheer amount of DLC and the re-use of models from COH is a constant reminder that you have only purchased half a game.
3. Everything is bigger, louder and more explosiony
The bangs are bigger, the action is more frenzied, and units die much faster. This style may suit some people but it makes replayability boring for me as I go through the exact same motions each time. Maybe I'm getting old but I find the faster pace takes away from the strategic side of the game. All the bells and whistles in the world just don't make the game the same level of fun as the original is.
4. Doctrines have no personality
So many more doctrines but really, all the abilities are re-hashes of what existed in COH. There is nothing new here.
5. FPS style upgrade system doesn't make sense
Seriously, why do I need to be forced to play through the game to unlock all the little aspects  that make up the game as it was intended to be played? Shouldn't I want to play the game on its own merits? Shouldn't the fact that the game is fun be motivation enough to play it? The upgrade system makes playing the game a grindy chore for me.
Sad to say, COH could have been great. I don't know who is responsible, but its obvious to me that this sequel was more of a money grab than a true sequel, the same way that the sequel to Supreme Commander, although a decent RTS in its own right, couldn't hold a candle to its original. I've put about 400-500 hours into COH, I've barely played 10 hours of COH2 at this point. I just can't bring myself to play it when there's so many better options to occupy my time with.
