Very similar to the first game in the series. Does some things better, while other areas remain largely the same.
The characters are still adorable and endearing, but the main cast has grown a bit this time. This gives the characters more room to play off of each other, and some more growth overall. Even the villains get some characterization, though nowhere near as much as the main gang.
Levelling, abilities and equipment are identical to the first game, and the gameplay is also the same. Many monster designs and some dungeon designs are re-used, but there is also a fair amount of new stuff.
The main story has nine endings, and the last two chapters are only available on the "true ending" route.
The amount of side-content is staggering, ranging from extra accessories to equip, to a string of post-game dungeons and coliseum fights. This gives the game a huge amount of replayability and makes New Game + feel worth it.

The skinny: if you don't care about the world and just want to kill mobs because you're done with Diablo and♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off and PoE, this is pretty good. If you're like me and actually want the world to make sense and have some measure of depth, don't waste your time.
The world of Cairn, to which the eponymous apocalyptic event occured, is fairly bizarre. It seems as though the designers had this deep hankering for a game with demons, unknowable abominations from beyond the stars, (this time with CRYSTAL GEM aesthetics!! (no, they're not here to save the day)), magic, kings and emperors, skellingtons, cowboys, witches, shamans, an iterent, persecuted race rather like the Romani, (indeed, the devs chose the name Rohwari, or Rovers, colloquially) cultists in service to the aforementioned demons, zombies, as well as an entirely original pantheon of deities, all at the same time. Spoiler: it doesn't work. Not remotely.
That wouldn't be a bad thing, if the writers had a vestigal at best understanding of how religion and faith works, and at worst are from the /r/atheism cadre of thought. The supposed "good" deity, insofar as he is the deity of light, order, and mercy, is called Empyrion, of all things.  And the faction that represents him, are, of course, religious extremists. The dog whistle here is for antitheists- "Even the "greatest" of the gods, named after empiricism itself, has evil followers!" That isn't in itself a black mark against the game, but for that to be the game's chief foray into questions of faith, is something I'd expect from a flash game on Newgrounds.
That said, the game looks good. The enemy design is on point, especially the demons you meet in the latter part of the game, and the cosmic horror monstrosities (I hasten to say eldrich because that refers to something else, in game). Some of the places you visit in Cairn are deeply memorable, but many others are simply not, or, worse, cut and pasted from somewhere earlier. This dulls the impact of some of my favourite areas.
Almost all the place names are limp, and seem to be cribbed from the "Fantasy Place Name Generator 9001"- Homestead, Devil's Crossing, Wightmire, Arkovia, Asterkarn. Others, like Darkvale, barrel into the territory of "I am 13. Dylan Klebold and Eric Harris are my heroes. I watched shoveldog and laughed. I DEMAND TO BE TAKEN SERIOUSLY!"
Furthermore, the world lacks any nuance. We are told that the Rohwari are considered petty thieves by many, but we're given no evidence. All but nobody says that they are, the game just tells you so. We're also told that they're good boys who are pacifists and who will never go to war due to their shamantic, animistic religion- yet like any other faction they're perfectly willing to pay you to kill things for them.
The "Death's Bannermen" former penal batallion, now ex-Imperial Fist (since the empire collapsed) and Humanity's Last Hope!! wants you to murder a witch due to supersititons, but they're never detailed further than "witch bad". Surely it would be better to perhaps cooperate with the witch, to set aside differences for the good of humanity?
In the third act, the game lets you choose between the religious extremists who I mentioned above, who've drawn their inspiration from a Tempar-style monastic military order, and The Order of Death's Vigil (yes, seriously), who are necromancers (also horribly persecuted). The former want to purge the world in healing fire. The latter want to ressurect the dead to aid in the reconstruction. And there isn't room for two of them in this 'ere Cairn.
Every rivalry, every character, every faction is contrived. Conflict is forced. The Aetherials, whose colour is (guess what?) electric-teal-green, aka Otherworldly Pigment #12, are in this world because something something long before humans something something perfect time to take it back, something something kill/enslave everyone. The Cult of C'thon are a comically, ludicrously evil blood cult who want to bring blood and obsidian demons into this world. Yet they seem to have a near-endless supply of members, parents and children, who have willingly signed up. That there are that many amoral, sadistic anti-natalists in Cairn is shocking. A cult that all but straight-up tells you that it wants you, so that it can drain you of your blood should not, in any situation, receive such a large number of adherents. Nobody has credible motiviations outside of survival.
And yet when you look past all this, there's something of an interesting world hiding in the cracks. I like the Devotion system, whereby you gain bonuses and abilities by alloting shrine points into constellations, making up some basis of a symbolic order. But that's all we see of it. I love it when worlds invent their own swear words. Taff, for instance, in Thief, is deeply charming. Here, the word is slith, meaning, well, I'm sure you can guess. Slith, ingame, are tribalistic snake people, the Frankenstinian results of man Dabbling Where He Ought Not To. They come out of holes in the ground, called slithholes. It's great. But then it goes away and is barely mentioned ever again. That's another common thread in this game. None of the plots, side quests, or characters have personality. Legendary items are only legendary insofar as they have good stats and a cool name. The reason I'm so hard on this, is that if you're going to spend about 80 hours per character in a world, it better be a place worth exploring.
But none of that is what you're looking for in an ARPG. You want Combat! Blood! Violence! Cool abilities that cater to your inner Timmy. That, this game has in spades. The Mastery system, where you pick two classes and make your build from there, is a handmedown from the sperm donor of this game, Titan Quest (that is, post the collapse of IronLore, some of the devs who worked on Titan Quest wanted to make another ARPG and did so). It's a handmedown, yes, but it's inspired, and pretty fun.  The two other inherited traits from TQ (and also, therefore, from Diablo 2) are the resistance system, here fleshed out further, (there is fire, and burning damage, cold and forstburn, etc, and a whole pallette of resistances and corresponding ways to deal damage) and the loot system- Common, Magic, Rare, Epic and Legendary, in increasing order of scarcity and Ability to do Cool Stuff. It's a delight to find your first Epic weapon, but the joy soon dulls. Ibid for Legendaries.  The combat is satisfying in the same way that a kebab is, at 2am, after the 5th beer of the night: great in the moment, something you find unsubstantial and feel disgusting about in hindsight. This is probably a problem endemic to ARPGs, due to the skinner box nature of the underlying mechanics. That said, I kept coming back to it, time and again.
So if you want a game for this summer that has enough depth to fool you into believing that there's something there, and is otherwise near mindless clicking- here it is. Come and play.

Ah, lovely. My first negative review, for the first game I've ever bought that I will certainly never finish. After 20 hours with this game, I'm putting it down and never touching it again. Seems fitting.
I really wanted to like Far Cry Primal. I really, really did. I was so excited for this game when I first saw gameplay back in late February. Honestly, the concept seemed so fresh and engaging: you're a hunter from 10,000 BC who also has the ability to tame beasts? A lush open-world environment to explore? Armed with nothing but a spear, bow and arrow, and few other additions to your limited arsenal?
Sounds beautiful, dynamic, and challenging... but that's not what I ended up getting at all. But first, let's talk about what I liked.
The enviornmental graphics were absolutely stunning. It's meant to be a lush, harsh environment, and that feeling was definitely nailed. Vegetation and trees felt dense, sometimes it was genuinely hard to see because of how thick plant growth was in certain areas. The fantastic lighting also deserves some recognition. Sunrises and sunsets seemed so, so real, and after being in a cave for some time, it really did take some time to adjust to the light again. It really was the most natural and fluid part of the environment. Other devs could actually take notes from Primal's incredible use of lighting and shadows. When I made it to the northern regions, it felt decidedly different, and the atmosphere actually felt colder and even more unforgiving.
And getting to see that northern environment for the first time was pretty much where Primal's wow factor ended for me.
On the graphical side of things, everything besides the lighting and nature environments was unfortunately, subpar. Particularly, I noticed a downgrade in texture resolution where animals were concerned, as well as with any close combat. I felt pretty damn embarrassed for the devs any time I looked at an animal for too long, or did a takedown/clubbed someone... there's no other way to say it, the textures were just bad. Which, like, come on Ubisoft, if you're gonna have a game where the visceral close combat and animals are the most exciting features, wouldn't you think to make sure that's where your textures are the strongest? Yikes. There was no depth or detail in the fur of every animal I encountered. I'm not even asking for NVIDIA HairWorks, just... give fur and hair details! It seemed so flat and lacking in detail that you had to wonder if it was drawn on. It was really jarring to go through this beautiful world and feel like I was playing a game from last gen as soon as I got too close to an animal or decided to fight an enemy tribe up close.*
And there's no redeeming this title with gameplay either. While combat could have been absolutely incredible and intense within such a dynamic concept, it becomes so stale so quickly! While some may relish the challenge of being limited to a spear, bow and arrow**, and a few other traps and weapons, I found it considerably limiting. Not because of the amount of weapons I had at my disposal, but rather, because of the quality of them and what I could do with them, and how they impacted the predictability of every combat scenario I got into. I've played other games with limited arsenal, so I don't know what happened here, exactly. It just felt really empty.
And the same can be said for the objectives and the main story (which I obviously didn't complete). While one could argue that most quests/objectives in a game are based upon a fetch and carry formula, or something similar, that formula is usually expanded upon and kept dynamic and fresh throughout hours and hours of gameplay (i.e., The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt), so that the fetch and carry formula never completely reveals itself in quest after quest after quest. Futhermore, when this is excuted well, even if you notice the rehashing and reuse of the formula, you still don't care, because each quest is so unique, dynamic and engaging!
...when it's done well. And Far Cry Primal really didn't do it well. Essentially, as one of the survivors of the Wenja tribe, you are tasked with bringing all of the Wenja together, defending them, and taking control of territories across the map (indicated by outposts or bonifires), which sounds exciting but... that's it. That's the game. Every single objective or quest can be broken down into either a) track this animal and kill it or b) kill everyone. There are variations on this theme, but not enough to keep you engaged. Not enough to make you care. And while the developer updates and behind the scenes videos seemed to showcase the high level of love and care put into this game (with two languages being designed specifically for it), it just really wasn't apparent as I put more and more time into it.
And that just about sums up my experience with Far Cry Primal. My first 2 hours with this game were admittedly stunning. The environment captivated me, I felt so immersed in the world, and taking my first outpost and bonfire, taming my first beast and riding my sabertooth tiger for the first time - it was all truly breathtaking. But after 10 hours in, I felt like I was forcing myself to enjoy the game. It just wasn't exciting anymore. I even tried upping the difficulty and turning off the minimap to give myself a more immersive and authentic experience. When doing this with other games, it has breathed new life into them, gotten me excited to play them all over again. But Primal still remained stale, offering nothing new, again and again and again. And once I realized that was all there was to this, I couldn't play for another minute.
Hey, maybe you really love copy and paste gameplay that is reptitive to a mind-numbing degree. If so, Far Cry Primal is the game for you! If not, however (and I really hope not, because lord knows we deserve better from AAA games that cost $60 - I mean, come on, it's 2016 for crying out loud) please do yourself a favor and go pick up a game more worthwhile. I'm not going to say go get The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt... but... love yourself and go get The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt.
Even if you don't get The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt, you deserve better than this game. Frankly, after putting 20 hours in to Far Cry Primal, trying and failing to love this game, I can say that I feel extremely disappointed in Ubisoft for wasting so much potential. We as gamers deserve better games. We as gamers deserve better gameplay. We as gamers deserve titles with far better attention to detail. We as gamers deserve better than Far Cry Primal.***
*My complaints about textures are well founded and well earned, as for the majority of my gameplay I played Primal with my graphics set to Normal, upping them to High about halfway through my playthrough, just to see if the textures were that sloppy simply becaue of my settings. But no... they really are - just like the rest of this game - that damn sloppy.
**Yes I know you can shoot more arrows at one time, there are various weapon upgrades and improvements, etc. etc. etc. Didn't change anything for me there.
***As Far Cry Primal was my first experience with the Far Cry series, please feel free to comment below if you still think I should give Far Cry 3 or 4 a try, and let me know why.

Poker Night is a decent poker game with mediocre AI and a bunch of memorable characters whose banter will keep you entertained for a few hours. Still, if you can, skip it and play the even better sequel.
What can one say about a poker game? The computer deals you cards, and you try to win against a set of pre-determined AI players, that’s it.
As for the skill of the opponents, it’s standard. They don’t cheat, but usually play the check/fold/all in game, making it a bit hard to play against them intelligently; bullying is almost always the best tactic. They aren’t terrible, but you can always tell you are playing against bots.
So, why is this game better than any other poker game? Because of the writing: your opponents are characters from video games (and a comic strip that deals with video games), and they constantly interact with each other in well-written, humorous banter. There are hundreds, if not thousands of lines of dialogue, so it’s hard to get bored.
Still, there is one reason I wouldn’t wholeheartedly recommend this game, one large disadvantage it cannot overcome:
that is superior in every aspect.

FTL: Faster Than Light is a "tough" video game that focuses on being "hard". In this game you play the role of a space ship who's job it is to ferry your crew through 8 hubs called "sectors" in order to reach the end and fight the multi-formed demon ship, much like other JRPGS. Along the way you have to keep your crew alive, because despite your ship having the ability to fire weapons, open doors and turn every system on or off by itself, it still needs a human to actually move from one place to the other. Whilst traveling through the sectors you get to choose which circles to move to, you can't move freely about the game in any way. Each circle has the chance of being a spaceship encounter, which you will fight the majority of, a random dialogue option, which is often the choice between killing a crewmember of just doing nothing, or a shop, which will never have what you want. Along the way you can make many friends and enjoy the finer side of getting killed by something you couldn't have possibly prepared for.
FTL: Faster Than Light is an exercise in gambling. The game has so many events of chance in it they should have called it RNG (pause for laughter). Sometimes you will be able to steam through all 8 sectors using the starting equipment, and never having to buy new weapons since the game will give them to you. Other times you'll be unable to fight a single ship with your equipment and the game will never give you the opportunity to buy what you need. Sometimes the very first enemy you encounter will destroy you, having been generated to be the perfect counter to whatever ship you happened to start that run with. At times you'll have encounters that go on for ten minutes because both you and your opponent keep dodging each other's attacks. I've always wanted to play a flash game featuring two majikarps splashing at each other.
FTL: Faster Than Light is a difficult game in the same way that roullette is a difficult game and is fun in the same way that Russian roullette is fun. Much like Christopher Walking in Deer Hunter you'll be very upset at the situation you're in. At the price of only ten dollars (or whatever this goes on sale for) you can experience all the fun of making a bet on Red and Black simultaneously, only to have the ball land on green, which happens to be neither red nor black, this means that you lost your bet. I guess if you really want to experience the feeling of throwing money away ten dollars isn't that steep a price.

I really want to like this game. I've put 11 hours into it so far and I intend to put more in even still. Gameplay is easy to pick up and get into but deep enough to enable lots of customization.
However, the game - presently - is just filled with unfun mechanics and enemies. One shouldn't have to cross their fingers and hope they don't encounter X content, lest their run end. One shouldn't need to avoid Elite (miniboss) enemies like the plague because their rewards are poop and they'll bring you to ruination unless you're lucky enough to have a perfect deck.
There's a lot of really good content in Slay the Spire, but there's even more that should just be outright gutted from the game. Hence the negative review. The game is really just a big noob trap, as a big chunk of content is just better off outright avoided.
Pros:
Lots of possible playstyles to develop
Good soundtrack
Lots of intriguing risk/reward choices, as every Roguelike should have
Cons:
A plethora of enemies specifically made to counter certain playstyles. You win if you don't happen to find one that counters your deck, you lose otherwise.
Game is entirely RNG based. Even in classical Roguelikes, some level of determinism was present and heavily appreciated. Here? Not so much.
~40% of the cards are actually good.
Very slow to start new runs, making future playthroughs less and less appealing.
The Verdict?
Game with great potential but littered with things that just aren't fun. Pick it up on sale and give it a whirl, but I cannot recommend it in its current state at full price.

If you are a fan of roguelikes (like dcss and nethack) you will enjoy Slay the Spire for its permadeath, procedural generation and general difficulty level. Slay the Spire isn't a roguelike, but it makes its runs feel as diverse and and interesting as the best of them. Slay the Spire also has light progression mechanics, with runs rewarding points going towards unlocks of new cards and relics for your character to find in runs. The unlocks are usually a little more nuanced than the basic cards and artifacts, but all of them feel balanced and equally useful. The game respects your time and I haven't had a run yet where I felt like I was unable to use the resources provided to me to build a good deck. Further, the game is highly transparent and gives you the option to see your deck, draw pile, discard pile, enemy intent for the next turn, and the risks of choices in '?' encounters.
If you are a fan of deck building games, you will enjoy Slay the Spire for its incremental, piece by piece deck building and mangement. The game presents you with meaningful choices and is clear about the risks and consequences of your actions. Decks can be built big, or small, full of common or rare cards, and focused around different aspects of the combat, such as status effects, damage reflection, self-sacrifice, and others. I haven't played the second character yet, but I imagine that her options are similarly diverse.
If you are a fan of games with deep mechanics you will enjoy Slay the Spire for its rich interactions between cards, artifacts, monsters, and the player. The game rewards experimentation, and the way artifacts and enemy encounters are designed allow for many varied approaches. Artifacts can make changes to the way you play, from small (like increasing the damage vulnerable enemies take) to entirely gamechanging (randomizing the cost of all cards played, but giving you 2 extra in each hand). These artifacts stack, combining to create a huge variety of possible builds. There are also potions to support your character in combat with various effects. If you like Binding of Issac, I'm sure you'll find a commonality in this game.
If you're worried about early access, I've found myself still finding new cards, relics and encounters at 10 hours in, and like I mentioned earlier, I still haven't touched the second character. The developers have been putting out regular updates with new content, features, translations and balance adjustments, and there are more scheduled as well. There is also a third character and respective set of unlocks in development. The developers are active in engaging with the community both on the community forums and on their twitter @megacrit .
I think this game is well worth the $15 for the amount of challenging, well thought out content I've played so far. The level of polish is also fairly high, with some only some minor tooltips lacking transparency. Highly recommended.

I've been playing this for a while and this game does have its moments were this game is fun to play.  However, micro transactions kill any replay value that this game has and DLC seems to be a dull after thought.  The fact that Commanders cannot all be unlocked through achievements and medals earned within the game and instead bought with real money, kills the notion that being smart on how to use your units result to getting the best commander waiting until you reach maximum command points and then unleashing a counter attack to deal the final blow.
The bulletins are also completely useless as most of ones that I typically use are decreases in spawn time.  Not only is the pay to win multiplayer is bad, but the units themselves are unbalanced.  Even though you typically have a lot of variety in tanks and halftracks, most players rely on particular units which seem to be overpowered.
The single player has no shred of heroism within it as each scenario makes the soviet army more like criminals than heroes.  Not for one single moment do you feel a sense of a particular group of Russians as a band of brothers as most of the time, they are killed off within cut scenes.  Compared to first Company of Heroes, this game is a bad sequel to the first as it doesn’t show any effort in displaying the true courage of the soviet army at that time.  Even the DLC for the first Company of Heroes gave a little curiosity into playing each one.
As a fan of the series, this 2nd version of it is not recommended even to hardcore players.  You will encounter more than once people picking the same commanders that are bought, with the same bulletins, fighting under the laggy conditions of the servers that host these games.  If you truly want to play this game, wait until Steam has a discount under 60% or more so that way you can get all the commanders and DLC at the actual price of the game rather than paying double.

The skinny: if you don't care about the world and just want to kill mobs because you're done with Diablo and♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off and PoE, this is pretty good. If you're like me and actually want the world to make sense and have some measure of depth, don't waste your time.
The world of Cairn, to which the eponymous apocalyptic event occured, is fairly bizarre. It seems as though the designers had this deep hankering for a game with demons, unknowable abominations from beyond the stars, (this time with CRYSTAL GEM aesthetics!! (no, they're not here to save the day)), magic, kings and emperors, skellingtons, cowboys, witches, shamans, an iterent, persecuted race rather like the Romani, (indeed, the devs chose the name Rohwari, or Rovers, colloquially) cultists in service to the aforementioned demons, zombies, as well as an entirely original pantheon of deities, all at the same time. Spoiler: it doesn't work. Not remotely.
That wouldn't be a bad thing, if the writers had a vestigal at best understanding of how religion and faith works, and at worst are from the /r/atheism cadre of thought. The supposed "good" deity, insofar as he is the deity of light, order, and mercy, is called Empyrion, of all things.  And the faction that represents him, are, of course, religious extremists. The dog whistle here is for antitheists- "Even the "greatest" of the gods, named after empiricism itself, has evil followers!" That isn't in itself a black mark against the game, but for that to be the game's chief foray into questions of faith, is something I'd expect from a flash game on Newgrounds.
That said, the game looks good. The enemy design is on point, especially the demons you meet in the latter part of the game, and the cosmic horror monstrosities (I hasten to say eldrich because that refers to something else, in game). Some of the places you visit in Cairn are deeply memorable, but many others are simply not, or, worse, cut and pasted from somewhere earlier. This dulls the impact of some of my favourite areas.
Almost all the place names are limp, and seem to be cribbed from the "Fantasy Place Name Generator 9001"- Homestead, Devil's Crossing, Wightmire, Arkovia, Asterkarn. Others, like Darkvale, barrel into the territory of "I am 13. Dylan Klebold and Eric Harris are my heroes. I watched shoveldog and laughed. I DEMAND TO BE TAKEN SERIOUSLY!"
Furthermore, the world lacks any nuance. We are told that the Rohwari are considered petty thieves by many, but we're given no evidence. All but nobody says that they are, the game just tells you so. We're also told that they're good boys who are pacifists and who will never go to war due to their shamantic, animistic religion- yet like any other faction they're perfectly willing to pay you to kill things for them.
The "Death's Bannermen" former penal batallion, now ex-Imperial Fist (since the empire collapsed) and Humanity's Last Hope!! wants you to murder a witch due to supersititons, but they're never detailed further than "witch bad". Surely it would be better to perhaps cooperate with the witch, to set aside differences for the good of humanity?
In the third act, the game lets you choose between the religious extremists who I mentioned above, who've drawn their inspiration from a Tempar-style monastic military order, and The Order of Death's Vigil (yes, seriously), who are necromancers (also horribly persecuted). The former want to purge the world in healing fire. The latter want to ressurect the dead to aid in the reconstruction. And there isn't room for two of them in this 'ere Cairn.
Every rivalry, every character, every faction is contrived. Conflict is forced. The Aetherials, whose colour is (guess what?) electric-teal-green, aka Otherworldly Pigment #12, are in this world because something something long before humans something something perfect time to take it back, something something kill/enslave everyone. The Cult of C'thon are a comically, ludicrously evil blood cult who want to bring blood and obsidian demons into this world. Yet they seem to have a near-endless supply of members, parents and children, who have willingly signed up. That there are that many amoral, sadistic anti-natalists in Cairn is shocking. A cult that all but straight-up tells you that it wants you, so that it can drain you of your blood should not, in any situation, receive such a large number of adherents. Nobody has credible motiviations outside of survival.
And yet when you look past all this, there's something of an interesting world hiding in the cracks. I like the Devotion system, whereby you gain bonuses and abilities by alloting shrine points into constellations, making up some basis of a symbolic order. But that's all we see of it. I love it when worlds invent their own swear words. Taff, for instance, in Thief, is deeply charming. Here, the word is slith, meaning, well, I'm sure you can guess. Slith, ingame, are tribalistic snake people, the Frankenstinian results of man Dabbling Where He Ought Not To. They come out of holes in the ground, called slithholes. It's great. But then it goes away and is barely mentioned ever again. That's another common thread in this game. None of the plots, side quests, or characters have personality. Legendary items are only legendary insofar as they have good stats and a cool name. The reason I'm so hard on this, is that if you're going to spend about 80 hours per character in a world, it better be a place worth exploring.
But none of that is what you're looking for in an ARPG. You want Combat! Blood! Violence! Cool abilities that cater to your inner Timmy. That, this game has in spades. The Mastery system, where you pick two classes and make your build from there, is a handmedown from the sperm donor of this game, Titan Quest (that is, post the collapse of IronLore, some of the devs who worked on Titan Quest wanted to make another ARPG and did so). It's a handmedown, yes, but it's inspired, and pretty fun.  The two other inherited traits from TQ (and also, therefore, from Diablo 2) are the resistance system, here fleshed out further, (there is fire, and burning damage, cold and forstburn, etc, and a whole pallette of resistances and corresponding ways to deal damage) and the loot system- Common, Magic, Rare, Epic and Legendary, in increasing order of scarcity and Ability to do Cool Stuff. It's a delight to find your first Epic weapon, but the joy soon dulls. Ibid for Legendaries.  The combat is satisfying in the same way that a kebab is, at 2am, after the 5th beer of the night: great in the moment, something you find unsubstantial and feel disgusting about in hindsight. This is probably a problem endemic to ARPGs, due to the skinner box nature of the underlying mechanics. That said, I kept coming back to it, time and again.
So if you want a game for this summer that has enough depth to fool you into believing that there's something there, and is otherwise near mindless clicking- here it is. Come and play.

Alan Wake's American Nightmare is a game that folluws up on the succesfull "Alan Wake", starting it's story where the DLCs of the latter left of. So you should definitely play the original first, because of spoilers and because that is still better.
But is Nightmare good as well? I'd say yes, but for different reasons than the original. Where Alan Wake had a story of horror, confusion and mystery, in Nightmare this is simply not possible anymore, since the player (or at least the Protagonist Alan) already knows what is behind it all. So the game has to go into a different direction.
Nightmare has a good and fun combat system, great soundtrack (that raises some of the moments in the game to nothing short of awesome), an interesting story that fully embraces the new possibilities now that Alan knows what is going on, and most importantly one of the best villains in Video Game history: Mr. Scratch. Said villain appears on screen only as a real human played by an actor, who does a marvellous job at looking like the perfect psycho killer. With superpowers. And an army of unholy monsters.
Admittedly, the game's world is not that large and the game doesn't take that long to complete (except if you really like the combat and get into the arcade mode), but if you happen to get it on sale, for say under 5 bucks, you should give it a try, especially if you liked the original.

American Nightmare is a follow-up to Alan Wake, which for the record I found surprisingly enjoyable, if decidedly corny. Originally a short DLC game on consoles, it was developed on a limited budget that really shows. But the way they used that budget is clever.
To spoil mildly, this game involves you replaying a series of events a la Groundhog Day, so if the idea of repetitive content really bugs you, you may want to stay away. But the way it handles each loop is clever, with surprises I didn't expect and and awareness of it all that works, and so I'm generally willing to forgive them using that premise to squeeze extra playtime out of a relatively small environment. Game play for the most part mirrors Alan Wake, though there's a bit more of an emphasis on the gunplay, but with the standard survival horror need to conserve resources when possible. It's decent, but the same issues come back - it's a bit repetitive, and Alan can have trouble with camera angles, but he has more firepower and tricks this time around, which mitigates it slightly.
Like its predecessor, it uses light well as a mechanic, particularly towards the end, and offers up a cheesy b-movie 90s horror feel obviously inspired Stephen King's Dark Half. The ending just kind of trails off much like Alan Wake, which may frustrate some. It's not for everyone, and I feel like my recommendation is more tenative than that for Alan Wake itself, but if you enjoyed Alan Wake, this is worth taking for a spin.

As much as it might look like I'm just trying to be countrarian leaving a negative review for Half Life 2, I do genuinely think that HL2 shows its age, and not in a particularly good way. So before you click that thumbs down, please hear me out.
Half Life 2 was released in 2004, and it was most likely the biggest thing to be released that year. It was quite good looking, it told a story better than most FPSs up until that point (although an FPS trying to tell a story was hardly unique), and the physics was darn impressive. So darn impressive that Valve wanted to take every opportunity to show us its physics engine.
For a game released in 2004, HL2 is not a terrible looking game.  Sure, it can't compete with modern games, or even Crysis (released 3 years later), but through a consistent art direction, and graphics that are still modern enough as to not look blocky, HL2 is not a bad looker. There's not a whole lot to say about the graphics other than that. Some enemy design is genuinely really good though, and the animations for everything looks smooth.
The sound is quite alright as well. We don't get any really satisfying gun sounds, like the shotgun from DOOM, but all the weapons do at least make appropriate noises. The sound of certain enemies are also quite well done. One of the best parts of the games sound design is the chatter between the enemy soldiers (called the Combine). They tell you what's going on, and this helps convey the feeling that they're working as a team, trying to take you down. It's a small touch, but it adds a lot to the game.
Somehow after defeating the enemies in Half life 1 you find yourself on a train, going into a city. No real explanation is given, but a lot of things happened when you were gone. (How long were you gone? The game does not tell you that either). But somehow the city and its surrounding/the country/the world (the game does not really tell you...) has been taken over by one of your colleges from Black Mesa (where the first game takes place), and he's now the dictator. Somehow aliens & humans have been crossed (or something like that... again, the game is short on details), and these hybrids now form the army/police, and keep the population in check. And it's of course up to you to deal with it, and help overthrow the ruler. Along the way you meet a few friends from Black Mesa, who also made it out (one for every friendly character model from HL1), and there's an underground resistance movement who you run into, and help through the game. And everybody loves you. Every friendly character in the game who's given more than 2 lines, except for one, seems to have heard of you (how?) and think that you're going to save them. Then there's Alex, the daughter of one of the characters from HL1, who really thinks your great. She tells you that, a lot. She's never met you before, but you're amazing. And while she's given some things to do in the story, her main role is to tell you what an amazing person you are, and how great you're doing.
I can't help but think that this hurts the story, the way everyone worships you. It does not feel believable, and if the game did not play it so straight, I would almost have thought that the developers were trying to poke fun at the whole wish fulfillment aspect of playing games.
HL2 is really stuck between two eras of shooters. We've got the older style of fast movement, health pickups and lots of guns, combined with the more modern style of very linear levels, punctuated by set-pieces and story segments. And the game loves interrupting the flow of the gameplay by just having you wait for an NPC to say what they want to say, so that they then can open the door for you (very much like in the post Modern Warfare Call of Duty titles).
The actual gunplay is fine, though not spectacular. All the guns feel alright, but there's only really one "gun" that feels special, and that's the gravity gun. All the other guns feel standards, we've seen them before, and we've seen them done better in other games. The gravity gun though, that one is really fun to use. It does what you would expect from a gun like that, it lets you pick up items, and throw them. These items can be exploding barrels, sawblades or just simple crates. And you get it early, which is always a boon, as too many games put their most fun toys at the end of the game.
The level design is, for the most party, very linear. You go from point a to point b, with no real room for diversions, other than looking under some stairs to find some extra ammo. There's nothing inherently wrong with a game being linear, but it should not "feel" linear, and HL2 feels very linear. And to make matters worse, HL2 has a gimmick for almost every level, and these levels are far longer than their gimmicks can support. The two vehicle sections in particular are just painfully long, but the zombie level, the level with the ant lions or the level where you get to have a squad with you that keeps bodyblocking you are also far longer than they should have been. These gimmicks would have been fun, had they've been used for a shorter period of time, and possibly spread out a bit more (so you could have multiple short vehicle sections, instead of two very long ones).
HL2 has puzzles. Physics puzzles, because Valve wanted to show you how cool their physics engine was. And in 2004 it really was very cool. In 2017 (at the time of writing this review), they're not. They're simplistic, and the fact that the physics engine is not spot on can make certain physics puzzles a bit more annoying than they should have been.  And on a minor note, HL2 really makes you appreciate ladders in modern games, because these are just annoying.
HL2 was a game that was very impressive when it was released, but it has aged poorly. Far worse than Half Life 1. The way the game won't let you open doors until certain NPCs do it for you, the trite puzzles, and the overly lengthy sections that relies on specific gimmicks (granted, this was something people complained about in 2004 as well, in particular the vehicle sections) does make it a game that's hard to recommend. Pretty much everything HL2 does, other games have done better. But HL2 is an important game, it pushed the FPS genre forward. It did lay the foundation for games like Call of Duty: Modern Warfare and the glut of modern FPSs that followed. These games are not quite my cup of tea, but playing HL2 these days really make it abundantly clear where a lot of the design comes from. The source engine has also been used to make some really good games, like Portal, Vampire: The Masquerade: Bloodlines, The Stanely Parable and so on (and some not so good games, like Postal III), which most likely would have never seen the light of day without HL2. So I'm thankful for this games existence, I just don't think it's has aged particularly well.

A short review, but necessary.
Turn based games are not my thing. Generally speaking, modern/ futuristic games are not my thing. Games with permadeath are
.
With all that said, I could barely get away from my machine playing XCOM. I enjoyed everything about it - from the tense moments where you hoped you hadn't stepped a square too far and cost yourself a good soldier, to the dawning realisation that you should've built an extra satellite because the month's almost over and China's in full panic.
My main criticism is probably that the early game can feel incredibly difficult if you've never picked this or anything like it up before, and it's quite punishing to lose multiple countries in the first few months because you can't afford to field a good team whilst planting satellites everywhere. Later on, when your team's decked out in Titan and Archangel armour, and you're picking enemies off across the map with a squadsight sniper, and you've realised your mistake and coated the world with eyes-in-the-sky, you'll feel you can almost close your eyes and take home a win.
I haven't taken on Enemy Within yet (mind control was the bane of my life in Enemy Unknown, and from all accounts it gets worse there), but I'm already set to preorder XCOM 2 based purely on 1 campaign run. You won't regret picking this up!

I don't even know where to begin. Should I start with half the characters never affecting the story? Or canon characters from the Tv series showing up just so they can make a cameo even if the story suffers from it. Game of Thrones game by Telltale starts off by introducing house Forrester, a noncanon house made for the game. If you are a fan of the books or Tv series you can immediately see the resemblance to House Stark in House Forrester. Many of the characters in House Forrester are mirrored versions of characters from House Stark. While the characters themselves aren't bad they lack a certain amount of importance in their own game. Every character is overshadowed by canon characters making appearances and pushing the story. To make matters worse every canon character is invulnerable and unmovable in the game. Which is absolutely frustrating as canon characters seem to push the narrative more often than noncanon characters. One will always know how a scene will play-out when one of the canon characters is involved.
Let's jump into the story shall we. The Forester house is a banner-man house for the Staks. It is implied in the story that the Forresters are a lesser house which means they aren't vying for the Throne but just to keep their house in order. This is a great place to set a story in the Game of Thrones universe. Instead of having to have a hand in the major players the story can explore the houses that have to deal with the fallout of the great house feuds. Unfortunately, that isn't the case in fact the Forester house is noticed by every single canon character that it becomes ridiculous. How the hell is the Forester house even on the Lannister radar? Why the hell would the future Queen select her personal handmadien be from such a small house? Why do all the canon characters know about House Forester? Well how else are they going to get screen time in a game they really have no place in being. The game sacrifices it's own story so canon characters can show up and throw their weight around; unsurprisingly the story suffers from it.
Normally I would jump into talking about game play but since this is a Telltale game it's more of a mini-tv series and less of a game. So I'm just going to talk about the decision making mecanic. If you have ever played a Tell-Tale game before then you know that your choice won't change the major plot. Yet, in most Tell-Tale games although the major events will always happen, how you get to them or how characters approach them is tailored to your decisions. The Walking Dead games made this work by making you raise a character, Clementine, who couldn't impact the story but absorbed every decision you made. Game of Thrones lacks that, in fact the game tries to make you feel clever but since the main events are unavoidable you just feel cheated by the whole experience. This is compounded further by the end of the game when you realize only half the characters interacted with each other and the other half were on their own little story lines that never came back to the original plot. Did I mention the game has no ending? It's just a cliffhanger that I'm SURE will be resolved when the second season comes out. I felt so cheated at the end of this "game" the least they could have done was tie up loose ends and give the player some sort of payoff in the story, but they didn't.
Go read a book instead.

+ Neps

+ Good humor, fun characters

+ Lots of cute costumes and shiz
CONS:
- DLCs grant overpowered plans and equipment
- Incredibly generic gameplay
- Poor balance, difficulty can range from 'absurdly easy' to 'impossible' at various points. The game strongly encourages grinding since levels give so much stats.
- Hardly any strategy involved, just grind levels until you start crushing every enemy
- Weak, nonsensical story
VERDICT:
If you already know you're in for (i.e. the Neps), go right ahead and get this game. If you're looking for an RPG with solid gameplay and depth, this game is definitely not for you. Like many others have said, HDN is much more enjoyable if you treat it as a visual novel rather than an RPG.

Cons:
-Could have done so much more with the game to build off of a great themed poker idea to keep players entertained, unboard and replayability.
-Got boring after the 5th tournament.  Same thing over and over and nothing new other than winning 4 in-game items that only TF2 new players would want as they have no items of real value to put into their slots.
-Conversation settings need to be turned on High in the Options menu to get the most & best conversations in the game.
Pros:
-Cards randomization feels fairly accurate to real-life, something that almost all video games & poker sites stuggle with.
-Cool poker themed game with a 'Rounder's NYC Feel.
-With the conversation settings turned on high, surprisingly there are a lot of conversations where I didn't feel bored or even heard the same conversation twice in a full gaming session, and surprisingly colorful stories that was unexpected.

Being 30 years old growing up during the arcade days, we spent like $10-$20 a day where that kind of money actually meant something of value, just on quarters in order to play 1 round on a arcade machine.  So I look at it as fair entertainment value for my money, even if i'll only play it once or twice in my life.  I knew this before purchasing it and decided to purchase it for the experience to see what it was all about and to say to myself I played it.
If u get it on an amazing $1 sale then feel free to pick it up for the exp, but you can also pass on this game and not miss out on anything in this current gaming era.

When this was first released I thought nope, not buying another far cry after 4. Four was basically a boring remake of three but in a different setting. I played 4 on the playstation when it was released, played time and time again and just could not get into it. This game recently come on sale for £25, I've been after something new for a while and with the game being pretty cheap thought I'd give it ago and if it was bad I would just refund it. OMG THIS GAME IS ADDICTIVE TO PLAY!
To start, the setting fits perfect with the gameplay and controls of farycry. Everything feels smooth, easy to use and being in first person, that caveman/ice age like era looks very cool to roam in. So what is the aim of the game? Well tbh its pretty similar to previous games in terms of objectives. You take over camps to control areas whilst upgrading weapons and carrying abilities through skinning animals and gathering materials. Obviously there are no guns in this game, so weapon catches with new weapons after base take overs are scrapped and instead are replaced by upgrading your camp which then allows for improved bows, spears etc. There are hidden areas or caves which allow for more treasures for those into 100% completion. You have a main base with a population, the more people you help and save in the wild the more you will recruit in your base that will then allow you to add futher upgrades. Certain main story type characters can be recruited which you can then gather resources to build them huts which can unlcok items and item upgrades. Its very satisfying watching your base go from nothing to 100s of people and big structures.
Animals are a big fun part of the game, more than ever before. There are a varitey of animals that can be tamed in the wild which then can follow you and pretect you from people and other dangerous animals. Ive gone from taming wolfs to white wolfs acting like a stark, to taming bears and saber tooths. This is my favourite part of the game, and it reallty makes it all believable and you become really imemersed in the gameplay.
Combat is also fun, and once you perfect the bow you feel like a f**king boss. There are varient enemies such as basic people with spears that charge, bow men, men with battons that are on fire and wear armour (pain in the asses), stealthier enemies etc. All can be killed much easier in different ways so it keeps you on your toes during combat. I should point out that i'm playing on normal difficulty and its pretty easy, may be best playing hard for that extra bit of a challenge, although on normal the game can still be challenging. Also without spoiling to much, weapons and items for combat are quite creative, wasp bombs and stone shards (throwing knives) being two examples.
To finish, I haven't really played much of the story but so far it seems good and interesting. The gameplay so far has kept me hooked so I want to stick this one out to the end.
If your curious I'd say jump on this one, especially whilst its on sale. I'd even say this game would of been worth its original retail release, its that good.

As much as I enjoyed playing Dying Light, I don't think I would recommend this game if you plan on playing it alone. It is infinitely more fun to play with at least one (up to three) friend(s). Having said that, Dying Light is a fun, exciting and thrilling zombie-parkour-survival(-ish) game.
- The parkour mechanic is fun, refreshing and usually works as expected.
- Night time is scary, but the risk to reward ratio is good (once you've levelled up a bit).
-
Even when you've progressed further in the game.
- It becomes easier to kill standard zombies, but the mutated ones are always challenging.
- You will be punished for poor decisions.
- You should play with others because your teammates can revive you, as opposed to playing alone where you die instantly.
- Grappling hook is soooooo much fun.
- Two fairly large maps to explore with plenty of side quests, collectables, easter eggs and challenges.
- Scenery is quite nice.
- Interesting interactions with some crazy NPCs.
-
- Killing zombies and thugs is extremely difficult in the beginning (especially on hard).
- Ranged weapons change everything, especially the bow and arrow.
- It's a shame that you can't infinitely repair weapons unless you exploit a NPC.
- It's very difficult to get a decent weapon in the beginning of the game, but later in the game you are showered with melee weapons and guns.
- Day time can get boring and repetitive, but night time is always exciting.
Dying Light is definitely a fun game. The parkour mechanics and running at night is what makes this game for me. However, I must stress that I would not have enjoyed this game as much if I had played it alone. It is still quite expensive at the moment, but consider picking it up when it goes on sale.

A short review, but necessary.
Turn based games are not my thing. Generally speaking, modern/ futuristic games are not my thing. Games with permadeath are
.
With all that said, I could barely get away from my machine playing XCOM. I enjoyed everything about it - from the tense moments where you hoped you hadn't stepped a square too far and cost yourself a good soldier, to the dawning realisation that you should've built an extra satellite because the month's almost over and China's in full panic.
My main criticism is probably that the early game can feel incredibly difficult if you've never picked this or anything like it up before, and it's quite punishing to lose multiple countries in the first few months because you can't afford to field a good team whilst planting satellites everywhere. Later on, when your team's decked out in Titan and Archangel armour, and you're picking enemies off across the map with a squadsight sniper, and you've realised your mistake and coated the world with eyes-in-the-sky, you'll feel you can almost close your eyes and take home a win.
I haven't taken on Enemy Within yet (mind control was the bane of my life in Enemy Unknown, and from all accounts it gets worse there), but I'm already set to preorder XCOM 2 based purely on 1 campaign run. You won't regret picking this up!

I have just finished going through this in a few sittings. At first I was a bit fatigued by the multiple characters you take control of, but not too long after, I was drawn in and cared for them and had given them personalities. I thought the story was great and the way it intertwined with events from the TV series was very smart. It captured GoT extremely well. The voice acting was superb and I was mildly fanboying when I realised they had managed to get the real life counterparts to play the roles, lending to authenticity.
There were only a few minor gripes I have and they were: sometimes the game would crash on start-up; the graphics looked too much like an oil painting and whatever filter was used made it look downright ugly at time; minimal player input (even compared to Telltale's other games I've played. Those were rather minimal complaints as I really enjoyed my time with this, making decisions was rather difficult at times and it felt like those choices carried quite a bit of weight.
If you've not seen Game of Thrones, I think you should avoid this as you would get far less out of it. Otherwise, buy it.

You will need to keep your soldiers advancing in rank, abilities, and equipment to keep up.  This is not a simple mission accomplished, but a stylish and challenging salute to the original.  This was a lot of fun and I wholeheartedly recommend XCOM:EU to any fan of turn-based tactics games.

I will write a review for this game, simply because I've seen a lot of negative ones lately.
This game is not perfect - no game is perfect or will ever be, "everyone's cup of tea." Cuz, you know, peoples like all kinds of tea.
The main issues I see complaints about:
RNG -
I have mixed emotions here. When I'm attempting to upgrade gear and it fails... repeatedly smashing me back down to a lower tier and I run out of materials and then have to wait for another week of gathering/grinding or pay out the nose to try again - I HATES IT.
However... one of the things that BDO has done very well, IMO, is looked at what were problems in other games and tried to find solutions to them. For example, for most MMO's when new content is released your previous gear that you worked so hard to acquire becomes quickly obsolete. There is a PLETHORA of random gear in most games for every class. I'm not a coder, and won't even pretend to think I know anything, but to me it seems like that would create more work/require more memory in some way.
In this game your gear can be used by any of your other toons, which is nice. So the original gear I leveled my toon in can be passed on to an alt once I replace pieces, or sold. Additionally, all of those "extra" drops that would ordinarily be used to DE for chanting mats are now used here to repair instead - I don't see an issue with the logic in that, it keeps the drops relavent.
PTW -
What can I buy to win - and how much does it cost? Can someone show me this item, are there hidden stats I'm unaware of on something? I paid 5 dollars for this game, and I'm clearly spending a lot of time playing it. So yes, I am OK with spending money to support the thing thats providing me with hours of entertainment. You can pay for convienence, I'll give you that. Honestly, if you're enjoying the game paying for items really shouldn't bum you out. If you're broke, that sucks and I'm sorry, but would you go to an arcade, a bowling alley, mini golf, whatever, and say, "You mean I have to pay to play this game?"
Actually, no heres a better one - lets say Universal opened up their doors, for $9.99 and then sold a fast pass for the lines for $X, you gonna complain? I mean your ticket was only 10 bucks, you're in the park, you just gotta wait in the line dude. Its the same thing.
The Grind -
Whats the rush? One of the biggest issues I've had in other games I've played is once I hit max level I get bored. I don't think I'm alone in this - so can you blame them for saying woah there, lets hit the brakes a little and work for this. I mean it all depends on what's important to you, where your priorities lie. You can easily get 56 in a day on a weekend, and that makes sense because at 56 the class changes significantly - so why would you want to spend days/weeks to get to that awakening and then discover you no longer like the class?
I mean if that were the case then yes, much aggro, but its not.
If you want to get to max level then you should spend all of your time dedicated to getting there, it won't take all that crazy long to get to 60. I did 56-57 in a caffiene fueled 24 hours of mahem at Bashims. I didn't even pay all that much attention to it and got to 58 a bit at a time a couple weeks later.
I'm no longer leveling my toon because I want to spend some time doing other things. Like killing bosses so I can try to get out of Heves, lul. And increasing energy - you want to talk about some annoyance OMG that amity game... klsbdkfkjfsdkbn And also because yes, to just "grind" would be no fun. But guess what, theres a ton of other stuff to do! It all depends on where your priorities are.

Serious Review:
If you don't know what Neptunia series is, it's basically about Gamindustri which has 4 land representing console companies (Planeptune(Sega), Lowee(Nintendo), Lastation(Playstation), Leanbox(Xbox)) And their respecting Goddesses. The story is basically about their jolly adventure that is filled with pop culture and other game references
For Rebirth1 (A remake of the first Neptunia game by the way)  it's about Neptune who fell down from Celestia after a free for all battle between the goddesses, now Neptune who just loss her memories must find a clue about who she is and who is behind her falling incident
Pros:
-The turn based gameplay feels solid
-A pretty good soundtrack
-Characters are memorable and have a good development
-The disc mechanic is personally one of my favorite feature, because it allows you to play many different styles of tactics (Or if you just want to grind for money and items)
-Graphics are quite nice, from the environment of a dungeon to details of characters, artwork of characters, and enemy designs. It just feels pleasing to the eyes
-Good optimization
Neutral:
-The fact that this is kind of a niche series means that not everybody's gonna like this series, some people will get turned off by the presentation of the game and some people out there will also like it
Cons:
-Again, the fact that this is a niche series also makes it fall into this category, because people might not like the humor, or maybe they don't like this kind of game etc.
-Only 3 characters can be deployed on battle with 3 supporting characters on the back supposed they got defeated, this is kinda bothering because there are some skill moves that requires 2 or more 3 characters while you wanted to use your preferred characters instead (This problem got addressed in the later games by making it 4 characters)
-English voice is limited, making some scenes devoid of english voices
Result: Personally i recommended it if you like this kind of niche series, but if you don't like it you can pass on this one

Short and sweet:
A little bit of something for everyone.
Pros
-Impressive enemy numbers on screen
-Guns and melee feel good each in their own right
-Skilltree helps you determine differing playstyles for players (stealth, crafting, combat)
-Night time presents on overarching emphasis of urgency in gameplay
-Hardcore players are rewarded extra exp for night time progress
-Combat is difficult which makes each encounter very tense
-Players can opt out of combat by focusing on movement
-Movement, attacks and manuevers all mesh very well
-Lots of creative set pieces
-Altitude feels apparent
-Graphics and style are above average
-Entirely soloable without feeling like the game was meant for more players (Same devs as Dead Island so I figured it was worth mentioning)
-Coop (Never tried)
-Play as Zombie (Never tried)
-30+ hours of content (You don't get bang for your buck like this anymore) I got impatient in the later half the game and started doing only main missions
-Satisfying story ending (So many games get this wrong I'm glad I can feel some closure in finishing a story)
Cons
-Combat is unforgiving and some setpieces have infinitely spawning enemies, game makes no indication to tell you when this happens
-UI is designed with consoles in mind
-Crafting is a pain when you want the benefits of buffs but don't want to hassle with the crafting menu or searching for resources all the time
-Story often falls flat and it's often difficult to care too much about the characters since they're mostly one dimensional and very predictable.
-Dying is easy if you don't take the game seriously, and if you die too much you will lose levels which are slow to rise.
This creates a good sense of tension but also means you can't experiment or mess around for fun without worrying about how much progress you could lose.
Neutral/Opinion
-Game is really creepy/scary at some portions, especially indoor sections where you get confined to a small area and get mobbed by zombies (this happens a lot and I was getting sick of it). In singleplayer this can start feeling very clausterphobic when you're surrounded and run out of stamina and are swinging for dear life. Consider more research if you think you might get spooked. Not the scariest game out there but it certainly manages to leave an impression.
In Closing
Honestly a couple design choices that don't jive with me as a player but the overall game is an easy 8.5 if not higher. Everything from mechanics, design, music is about as spot on as is it could be. Really think theres a bit of something for everybody here. If anyone is too scared to play the game alone they can just open up their lobby too.
Thanks for the great game Techland, hope to see more of this from you guys.

This game is way to luck based. The premise is simple, you take a premade deck (choice of 2 characters, 3rd one locked because they aren't made fully yet) and you climb the spire, taking down enemies as you go.
It would be simple enough, except that Like in most procedually generated games, RNG is a big factor, in terms of what you face. The game is NOT BALANCED IN YOUR FAVOR. most enemies do way too much damage, and you can only negate so much. Unless you get a perfect hand and deck, chances are, you will not make it to level 2, out of the 3 levels.
the cards and relics are not that good, either. Most are situational at best, and provide little relief. Gold, which can be used to buy and remove cards (Yes, you have to PAY to remove cards! makes sense for curses and such, but NOT CARDS YOU'VE ADDED), is very hard to come by, and the merchant has not only little stock, but prices in the 200s for relics, and between 40-200 for cards. You only get about 10 gold per battle, and some events give fixed amounts. that is simply not sustainable.
As for the Characters, the Ironclad lets you heal after every battle, WHICH YOU NEED, since healing is a ♥♥♥♥ing rarity in this, except for resting, and primarily focuses on attack, buffs, and debuffs. He is the more balanced of the two, But I feel doesn't have enough power to get through the game without serious tweaks.
The Silent, on the other hand, specializes in poison, and cycling through her cards fast. She is extremely frail, and it is nearly impossible to get healing for. She doesn't start with ANY poison cards in her initial deck, her HP is lower, and can easily wind up in unwinnable situations.
However, while it is possible to beat level 3 and win, you will NOT be able to get there 95% of the time.
Enemies can hit for at least a fifth of your HP each turn, if you don't get any block cards (which don't do enough, and are easily outclassed.)
Not to mention, the damage/block cards for the ironclad and silent do the same exact damage, I'd figure that the ironclad's would do more straight damage, or block more, while the silent would be like "apply X amount of poison" or "delay this much damage until the end of your next turn" and such.
The game is not balanced, and while you keep on hoping the next one is a winner (like a lootbox), Luck is stacked against you big time.

Is Dying Light a good Zombie game? Yes. Is Dying Light the best zombie game out there? Definitely not.
What you need to understand is before there was Dying Light there was Dead Island, and then the publisher authorizes another studio to make the sequels, which should have been your first clue as to how the original game goes. Now Techland couldn't let such a good zombie IP go so easily, which is why there is Dying Light. Now to be fair, Dying Light is a much better game compare to the original Dead Island. The parkour system is a must for the kind of zombie game Techland is trying to achieve, the story is much better than the original Dead Island game (which isn't saying much because the story of the original is basically nonexistence). but on the other hand still isn't all that well written or paced compared to series like the Dead Rising series. The bad guys isn't as complex (i.e: flat) or memorable like Vaas from Far Cry 3. So in summary, had Dying Light comes out before those aformentioned games then it'll probably be okay, but since all those other game comes out Dying Light will inevitably get compared to those before it and in comparison, Dying Light's parkour system isn't as good as Mirror's Edge. It's story isn't as good as Dead Rising, and the Psycho villain isn't as interesting as Far Cry's villain.
Another thing I wanna complain about is the fact that boss encounter is annoyingly predictable. Every time the game strips you of all your inventory and you'll have to use whatever equipment the game throws at you. Which I find really annoying because if I grind for a powerful sword or something, I wanna get the option to dominate the boss I fight, even if it means the game become less challenging. And I want my game to restore my inentory after I'm done with that segment. In the final boss fight, you don't even get to use your equipment because the last fight was done completely in QTE.
TL;DR:  Dying Light is a good game, but not a great zombie game. Don't get it for the full price but maybe for 50% or 75% off.

Your decisions don't matter. I expected that going into this game. This is based of an established canon. Of course you can't affect the course of the show/books.
However, this takes the pointlkessness of your actions to a new level. I was excited when I saw you were playing as characters of a lesser house. That would make sense. The game could show you some of the conflicts going on behind the scenes in the fight for the iron throne that don't make the cut for the TV show.
But TellTale didn't do that. They couldn't resist bringing in the cast from the Tv show which ultimately hurts the game. Because you already know the outcome of those character's life. It gives all the TV show characters "plot armor". Have the chance to kill one of them? Well, you know you can't. They aren't dead in the show, so you can't kill them here.
And it goes far beyond that. It's a running joke that your decisions don't matter in TellTale games. But they suceed when they create a convincing
of choice. But this game doesn't do that.
Let's say you get the mission to kill a guy. Everyone is telling you you're going to kill a guy. You arrive and start to beat him. You have a choice here. Be a sadist and really abuse him, or show restraint. Now if you have no plans for mercy, you might beat him and beat him until he's dead. But the game doesn't let you. Out of nowhere you have to let him live. And I'm not talking about some unexpected, his friends come to the rescue situation. I'm talking all of your allies are gung-ho, we're killing this guy, you start to torture him thinking, "why not? I'm going to kill him anyway." and then ouit of nowhere they go, "Actually, let's not kill him." and that's it. You get no choice in the matter.
Which brings us to the next issue, lack of continuity. As said before, regardless of your actions you're driving to a single resolution. But the game doesn't even acknowledge you actions on that road. You can permanantly maim a character in one episode, and in the next episode he'll return right as rain.
I can't recommend this game to the average gamer or even to TellTale fans. Only hardcore Game of Thrones fans might enjoy this for some of the background characters/supporting lore it adds. And even they will probably leave disappointed.

My opinion about FTL has improved since I first played it.
I rather disliked the rogue-like aspect of the game, that much of the gameplay is a roll of the dice which can easily go against you, and that the final boss is so difficult to defeat (even on Easy mode). -- The final boss can be difficult to defeat even if you sliced through every other ship like a hot knife through butter. I found these things don't apply so much if you act ungamerlike and give up easily, only playing through when things go well.

But FTL can be really fun.
It's fun to be the captain of a spaceship.
It's fun to obsolutely destroy another spaceship; it's tense to be in a fight against a spaceship which isn't vulnerable to your spaceship.
There are a vast variety of tactics available; and it's quite easy to adapt to the different strategies/tactics which different ship setups or playthroughs offer. Or, rather, being able to adapt is important (but not difficult) since playthroughs quite easily diverge.

I guess I'm a little different than some of the other posters. I LOVE this game.
Gameplay, I find to be a lot more interesting then the original. For instance, in COH2 I feel more readily available to micromanage and do tactics such as flanking, the Blitzkrieg, or a bleeding retreat. I see my Panzer Grenadiers giving chase to their King Tiger as it smashes through enemy defenses, fences, trees, anything in it's path. They pour in through the gaps created by their Tiger accomplishing massive gains. The King Tiger Advances, the only defense in his way are six peasants with rifles hiding behind a wall. The Tiger fires, the wall disintegreates. Bleeding and gasping for air the Conscripts are face down in the dirt crawling away. Running at full speed, surpassing their Tiger the Panzer Grenadiers firing their STG-44 assault rifles leap over the wall and make quick work of the remaining conscripts. They even take the time to finish off his comrade whom has no rifle, and is crawling away. On the other hand I see my Soviet sniper placed in the tree line, taking out a Grenadier from 200 yards away and hiding again before the Tiger's massive turret can wheel around. While the Tigers turret is still turning towards the direction of the sniper shot I see a T-34 on the horizon. I hear the German Tiger shout "T-34! Watch out, they always travel in packs!" As the turret on the King Tiger comes to bare on the lowly T-34 you hear the heavily Russian accented driver inside "GAS IT DRIVER!" The King Tiger hits the T-34, all the while the T-34 is still picking up speed. BAM! A collision. King Tiger has had it's main gun knocked out by a suicidal T-34 charge. Both are rendered nearly useless. The Tiger is beaten, but she can still crawl. CRACK! The Sniper team has re-appeared, dropping another Grenadier. The Grenadiers noticing their gunless Panzer is providing no protection, begin to run away. With no one to guard her the battered Tiger begins to reverse. Back over the crushed trees, the broken fences, the fire scorched Russian homes. It is too late. Two T-34s  have been created in no time by the mighty Soviet industrial tank factories encircling the far too eager Germans. Emerging from the flame kissed building alleyways the T-34s are notorious pack animals, who's only available prey is a lone wounded Tiger. With cries from each side "V ATAKU TOVARISCH!" , "FUR DEUTSCHLAND!" It is your duty for the Vaterland, for the Rodina, to drive your enemies back and secure total victory.

I'm going to be honest here that I have been doubting about the final verdict of this game but overall all points generally point into the negative direction. The game has been made with RPG-maker and that is a part that I recognised. However the effort put into the game itself aside from the RPG-maker aspects are unclear to me since I'm not familiar with the program.
Greyfox is a game about a girl, around between mid-twenties and thirties, who is sick with her job and wants to move to a town called Greyfox and live there. When she encounters someone peculiar in the bar she gets to play God and decide about the inhabitants of Greyfox who shall live another day and who must die.
I think the town itself is pretty well structured but there is not a lot to do aside from the few 'side missions' you can do before the main story unveils. You can interact with almost every object in the game with some jokes here and there but most of them are cheesy jokes. Each part of the story opens up a different part of town which I wouldn't have minded if it had a particular reason.
The main problem was to me that the story tried to pull me in and trying to let me empathise with the characters but it didn't happen even slightly. Everyone in that town is just either grumpy or close to silent there is no in between. I think the concept for the story was a good idea but the execution was off.
If you enjoy an RPG that solely relies on his story and don't care about combat in an RPG you should consider this. Even if you like story driven games you should think twice before you buy. Otherwise this is a definite no buy to you.

I am really enjoying this game.
You will quickly go from "How can I possibly lose these fights?" to "How can I possibly win these fights?" based on how well you build your deck and how lucky you are with your relics and potions. This is where you realize that there seems to be well-balanced and interesting builds that can develop (although "Silent" class can effectively be "hard mode", and I think there are some bosses they just cannot beat with the current cardset), but you have to roll with the punches on whether you get what you want to play with. If you're lucky, you'll hit what I can only refer to as a "Risk of Rain" scenario where you have so many relics and upgrades that you (hopefully) curb stomp everything if you play wisesly and carefully. My only advice is (just like any card-based game) is try to *multiply* card strengths rather than simply add complementary things together, or else you will get outscaled in the lategame.
Extra bonus points for the devs offering a few ways to "thin" your deck by removing cards you don't want. What else could you get for the adventurer who has everything?

This game is worth buying to play with a friend. Me and my brother play it and love it. It isn't a game we sat down and grinded out. It is more of a game we are playing when we don't know what to play so we hop on play a few lives then get off.

There isn't much I would change about the game but here is my biggest problem.
Ranged weapons are just to easy, it might just be me and my brother. However, we find the runs where we use ranged weapons we can clear a lot more then melee. The shield mechanic is useless most if not all the time when you get that weapon to start. I think the melee weapons should give a decent boost to HP or something, when starting with a bow, musket, or staff your health will rarely be touched. The best melee weapons in my opinion are the daggers because you essentially stun lock your enemies by basic attacking, The other is the two handed swords, just because of the range. That said the melee weapons aren't impossible to use and they are fun to play with. It just seems like there is never a reason to not give up a melee weapon for a ranged one with worse stats.
The Soul trees should be expanded or made more interesting. We didn't notice until later that the soul prices got more and more expencive as we leveled so we restarted to atempt to rush to the end since we basically invested into the early game stuff and now the later tier tree is expensive. It isn't impossible to complete. We are still fairly new to the game, but I think that the tree could of more interesting option. They had some cool perks in there that I wasn't expecting from a tier tree so the creators are clearly clever and creative. So I hope they do expand on it in the future.
Those are my 2 problems with the games, ranged is always better then melee and more option with the soul tree. Other then that the game is great in my opinion.
