After playing Alan Wake I was recommended this by a friend. That friend has lost his game recommendation priveleges.
~~
American Nightmare is essentially 3 small maps played 3 times over, doing the same things but slightly different each time. The story is presented as to be one of the episodes of "Night Springs", the Twilight Zone-alike from the first game, and narrated by the same Night Springs voice. When the game started and I noticed my flashlight battery went from empty to full in about 3 seconds, and the first gun I was given was a 9mm pistol with a 10 round magazine, I knew I was in for a very different experience.
The story is passable in as much as I was clamoring for more Alan Wake after the first game, and it satisfied that to a degree. Again, the radio shows are the star here like in the first game, filling in little details about the world and NPCs that you wouldn't otherwise get. This game uses an abundance of the live-action clips that were occasionally used in the first game, to decent effect. Overall the story is nowhere near as good as the first game due to the 'time loop' scenario restraining them from doing any real progress.
As well, the atmosphere suffers greatly from your trusty revolver and shotgun with limited ammo becoming full auto combat shotguns, submachine guns, assault rifles, and carbines, with boxes that 100% fill your ammo and batteries. It becomes a straight 3rd person shooter with a flashlight gimmick which is unfortunate. That said, the game adds a few more enemy types to make up for your increased firepower, so at least some thought went into the game here.
It seems that about half of the game's achievements focus around the Arcade portion of the game. I didn't play it because I'd had my fill of the Alan Wake combat, not thta it was necessariyl bad, but that I got plentyof it by the end of American Nightmare. If you enjoyed the combat the Arcade section is likely right up your alley.
At the end of the day, though it's a decent game, I can't recommend it personally, because as a fan of Alan Wake, this has none of why I liked the original. However, if you liked the gunplay and combat system in Alan Wake, and you're jonesing for a bit more of the story that 'may or ma not have happened' to paraphrase the game, and you can pick it up on sale, you might as well. I got some hours of entertainment, even if it wasn't a good as the first.

Alan Wake's American Nightmare Review.
There's not a lot I can say about the story without giving it away, but it wasn't as gripping as the first one. I was definitely less impressed with the overall game. It seemed cobbled together, with a lot less exploration and character development. It does smoothly resume the story however, it's just not as good. Alan is stuck in a time loop that repeats itself 3 times throughout the game. There's only 3 maps in the game. The motel, the observatory, and the drive in cinema. I was disappointed by this, as I was hoping for the continuous exploration like the first game. There were no driveable vehicles, and a lot less running through the woods to get to the next area. It's all narrated and way less decision making.
There's still the "Night Springs" TV show, but there's also Alan's... doppelganger that makes dramatic appearances on the TV. There's also still the same Pat Maine slowly revealing the story through the radio. There's a lot less dialogue and interactions Alan has with other characters.
The game has a few combat tweaks, like the default unboosted flashlight doesn't harm the Taken. I had to boost it constantly but it recharges almost instantly making it almost more effective. I think I used 1 battery the whole game. There's a few more weapons but I still kept the pistol until I could get the double barrel sawed-off, which mows down almost any Taken in 1 shot. A decent game.
Gameplay:
You can see all your stats in the upper left corner and the controls are pretty intuitive.
Of course the game might have "no point" to it, but its an acarde-style game. So the point of the game is to reach the highest highscore possible. (But have a look at the end notes)
A neat addition are the different weapons (gun, machine gun and laser; with laser definetly being my favorite) as well as the graphical indication, wheather a enemy will drop a specific item or not.
But on the hand of weapons, I have to complain about an enemy type. The little triangle. It charges you super fast, once it's close to you and damages you in the process. No problem yet. But the bad thing about this little bugger is the near impossibility to hit it with something else than the laser once it got close to you. This enemy needs a bigger sprite and hitbox quite urgently.
A missing feature is an increasing difficulty, though.... The third time playing I had no problem surviving endlessly and killed myself out of boredom after about 20 minutes.
Graphics:
Ingame you will first recive quite a shock. The main menu look like someone forgot to scale it to an reasonable video resolution. Even though the background looks nice, the buttons have quite a bad color choice as well as ugly compression artifacts. I think they could really need  an update.
Ingame itself everyting looks absolutly decent from a resolution standpoint and the enemys are quite easy to tell apart.
The background is pretty and not destracting.
The sprites on the other hand are a bit.... unique. Your own spaceship looks perfectly fine, but the enemys and neutral ships(?) could need some prettier sprites. Yust plain red is easy to identify, but not that pretty.
Sound:
Music is there and enjoyable, but soundeffect for getting hit, or hitting an enemy are missing. But even without them, it's still enjoyable.
Replay Value:
I would give it an replay value of an average mobile game.
It's easy to learn and play, keeps you busy, but isn't interesting enough for longer playing sessions.
On the other hand, it's one of these games, which you can simply fire up and play for 5-10  minutes, again, and again.

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.
Eat.

Having played a few hours each of both characters available as of this review, I'm finding this game to be a mixed bag. On the positive side, I was able to happily binge a few hours of the game at a time without feeling like I was wasting my time. The style is cool, and the idea behind the gameplay is very fun. As roguelikes go, it's one of the more fun games like this I've seen and played, when it feels like I've got control of what's happening. Which leads to the downsides.
On the negative side, though, it has balancing issues. A lot of balancing issues, in my opinion, which I hope will be addressed and fixed, because I'm having a lot of fun with it whenever it feels like things are in the player's control. The combat in the game is based on cards you can draw, and it's possible to get some decent synergy going between them and the relics in the game which give passive abilities. More often than not, though, particularly once you get to the third floor, that synergy can become null and void, as the RNG and enemy-created cards can completely break your run. Being a roguelike and card-based game, some level of that is expected, but it feels like poor balancing here. For one particularly annoying example, there have been a few times where I was having solid runs almost to the final boss, only to suddenly run into mini-bosses that flood the deck with unplayable cards with no way to deal with that issue.
Ultimately, I would recommend at least giving it a try, if you like card games and/or roguelikes. Especially if the game gets more balanced as updates come out.

can very well be one, if not, my favorite RPG Maker game. This reason is entirely personal of course, as RPG Maker games are mostly known for games filled with quests and fights.
is about being alive in a new town, where  mysteries follow every step you take.
The player moves to a new town named

Hey, I've played this game for 250-300 hours, and I've come to the conclusions that this game is really bad. Like really, really bad. I'll try to keep the review simple to the best of my ability, whilst still giving the reader and good understanding of the negatives of the game.
Getting from level 1-56 is an easy thing to do, there's not a lot of complex leveling requirements, but past level 56 it gets substantially harder, and takes much longer. for example, playing on a "returning player" server (+200% xp), as well as using xp scrolls, (around a total of 250% xp), for an hour of same level grinding with okay-good gear, only gives you about 3-5% of the entire xp bar on each level past 56, it also goes down after each level, so once you get to 58-59, you will only get about 0.5-1% xp per hour of grinding. The game is really grind heavy at higher levels, which is a big negative for me.
Pay to Win, but still a chance you can get bent over by RNG!
RNG IS ANNOYING * The game is very RNG, all the time. If you want to upgrade your armor/weapons it requires black stones (there are 2 types of stones armor/weapon stones). upgrading accessories requires another accessory of the same type. The upgrade itself is not guaranteed at all, it is a chance to proc an upgrade. When you fail, the durability of the item goes down by 10 (total of 100 dura on each item). You can repair the durability, but you need a blacksmith NPC and another item of the same type to repair 10 dura each repair.
Upgrading Items Sucks * Since the upgrading process for items is RNG, there's a function in the game called "failstacking", where you take another piece of armor, or a weapon and keep failing to upgrade it so you can boost the chance of upgrading another item. The problem with this is when you are trying to failstack on another item, to upgrade your equipped item, you have a chance of proccing on the failstack item, which removes all of your "failstacks". You have to use black stones to failstack, which gets really expensive.
Item Levels are fine, but the upgrade process sucks * weapons and armor have 20 max levels, 1-15 are the regular levels, and 16-20 are the higher levels. for 1-15 you use regular black stones, which already costs a significant amount of money in the first place because the market system is messed up (i'll explain later). levels 16-20 costs even more than 1-15 because you need "special" black stones, called Sharpened Weapon Stones, and Hardened Armor Stones. These stones cost 3-4 times as much as regular stones, and the chance that you can "snipe" them off the market, is next to nothing, because the market system is sucky, and there could be a chance that people use market bots to snipe items.
Market system Sucks * The market system in the game works by a bidding system, but the bidding system is complete RNG. When you want to buy an item, the lowest priced items have to be bid on, you can't buy anything that's listed if there's already a lower price item listed, so you can't skip the bidding process. When you bid, each person that bids is given a chance to win the bid, There could be 10 people bidding, or 100 people bidding on the same item. once a person wins the bid, they can buy the item. There is a pre-order function where you list the amount ur willing to buy, and the price for each item your willing to buy, but if somebody has a higher preorder than you, they get the item first (it's competitive) although it's not guaranteed at all, you don't get a guaranteed item if you have the highest preorder, items still have a large chance to go to the bid.
Items in Market are price fixed * The developer of the game price fixes items in the game, giving them a max price and a min price, many of the popular items are fixed to have a minmax that is the same value, such as a weapon black stone's price is min 300,000, and max 300,000. This means that items that should be much lower in value on the market, are inflated by the developers so they can have more control over the game's markets.
Grinding for Black Stones is Hell on earth * The chance of black stones dropping from enemy mobs is really low, about 1-5% chance on most mobs. This means the most black stones you can get in a day is really low as well. You would think there would be a bunch of quests that you can get black stones from daily, which is wrong. Most daily quests do not give you black stones. the only quests that give you black stones are the quests in which you recieve tokens called "seals", I did a few of them, and then they stopped popping up, and i couldn't complete any more of them. So you only have a certain amount of black stones you can get in the first place. Eventually the most reliable way of getting black stones is purchasing them through the market. Which really sucks because they cost significantly more than they should, because getting them is hard af. and they are price fixed.
Black stones are rare, and you need a bunch to upgrade armor, but it's not a guarantee because of RNG, so you could waste more than 50 black stones just to get enough failstacks to upgrade a weapon from +17 to +18. easily, getting a weapon or armor to +20 will require over 1000 black stones, it's extreme RNG just to upgrade your gear so you can fight mobs and not die all the time.
Ways to downgrade items so u can keep failstacking on them * the only way i know of to donwgrade an item so you can resume failstacking, is you have to create and alt, below level 10, and kill a horse to get negative karma, then you have to die with negative karma and your +15 armor will downgrade to +14. That's a whole lot of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ just to resume failstacking. it's dumb af.
The looting system is dumb af * There is no area loot in the game, it's done on a 1 by 1 basis, so you have to keep going around clicking your loot key to loot all the dead mobs.
The only way to speed this up is buying a "pet" which is a little companion that goes around looting for you. But the catch is, the pet doesn't area loot, it does loot by the same 1 by 1 basis. And each pet costs $10 USD. $10 USD for a pet that only picks up one loot node every 10 seconds max, you can get them to do it every 4 seconds, but that's after the pet levels up to level 30, which takes a long♥♥♥♥♥time to do. you can have a max of 4 pets at a time, so $40 USD gets you enough pets to pick up 4 loot nodes every 4-10 seconds.
$40 for a function that should be free by implementing area loot like in all the other MMOs i've played. SWTOR lets you area loot everything in a 100 mile radius for FREE!
So the game is semi-pay to win, meanig you have to invest money in it if you want to have a good time, but even if you invest money, you are still going to get F***** by RNG and waste tons of stones, which means tons of time investing in the game amounts to nothing because you can't even upgrade your items from +15 to +20 without spending almost all of your bank money in-game.
Grinding for upgrade stones is♥♥♥♥♥♥ the microtransactions are♥♥♥♥♥♥ the market is♥♥♥♥♥♥ the game itself is even poorly optimized.
I have a i5-4690k which is OCed, and a AMD r9 gaming GPU (8 gb gddr5) along with a lot of other good components, but every time I go near a city, it fails to load the cells and I get stuck in a graphical tear for about 15 seconds before the cells load.
Thank god i only spent $9 USD to buy the game, but I really wish I didn't spend $10 on that stupid ♥♥♥♥ing pet. That $10 could have gotten me something else, much more useful.

I liked the game in general.
Rate: 10\10

The game seem less like a step back, as some have said, as it is not a step forward. The graphics aren't overmuch improved and the extra detail almost makes the game look more muddy and nondescript. Think Battlefield 3 type 'realistic' pallete. This makes reading the screen harder than it was in the first game. For a RTS, being able to quickly observe and analyze the playing field is crucial. I often have to really study the screen a few seconds to figure it completely out. Also, the new engine seems less efficient than the CoH original and despite the relatively minor graphical upgrades the game is much more power hungry. Bring a powerful computer and video card to this firefight. With a AMD Phenom IIX4 and HD6850 l must turn the graphical options almost halfway down to get a solid 30 fps. The game was playable at maxed out settings but I found the frequent frame lag very upsetting.
Some have complained about the new implementation of doctrinal forces. I like them. You have a healthy number of commanders at the start with several unlockable as you progress in your rank. Others may be bought online for a somewhat immodest 4 dollars apiece. I haven't played any online opponents and I've heard complaints about certain DLC commanders being overpowered and upsetting gameplay balance. Just a caution.
Each commander has a handful of doctrinal options that vary between them. Some commanders share doctrinal options with perhaps only a couple differences between them. Some are starkly different. Having the option of choosing the commander at any time adds a nice touch of strategy as you can either get started early on the doctrinal options or hold out until you decipher your opponents strategy before locking in a choice. You are allowed to choose 3 commanders from your deck to carry in-game. This element is nice and makes for some fun fretting and fussing trying to figure out which ones suit your playstyle best.
The torrential blizzards that will ultimately kill your infantry if not in shelter or around a fire isn't as big an imposition as it sounds and actually adds yet another nice touch of strategy to the mix. Risking the lives of your men in a surprise blizzard assualt is one the enemy probably won't expect as it carries a large gamble on your side to get the drop on them.
In game physics and sound effects are stellar as ever. You'll feel the boom of explosions and the lumbering sound of tank treads crushing through the forest in high fidelity is a real treat to the experience.
To cut this short I will still heartily recommend this game since the price has dropped considerably down since release. If you owned and enjoyed the first game you will enjoy this. Just don't expect it to be leaps and bounds better. If not slightly worse for wear.

[Updated Review]
Positives of BDO:
Customization of Characters is Simply Divine.
You can't get much better than this. Each class has specific traits in terms of their default physical appearance - which makes them unique (you can alter appearance around this). Every class also has certain facial features or heights. Different hair styles can be applied depending on class, as well as default hair styles. Character Creation is super high quality and worth spending time on if that's your thing. Your character appearance isn't set in stone - you can change appearance any time with an appearance changing coupon, or a value pack that can be purchased on the marketplace with silver coins.
Community isn't too Toxic, and People are Quite Welcoming Unless you're on Valencia 6.
Guilds are extremely useful to noobs who need guidance throughout the game. I feel like they are helpful and improve your knowledge (depending on the guild, of course) but a lot of guilds are structured to cater towards new people and helping eachother improve their gear, money and goals in the game.
Adventuring and Gaining Knowledge is Rewarding.
You can gain knowledge by exploring new areas, finding new creatures and gathering new plants. All these things can increase your knowledge - granting energy or ranks based on how well you have interacted with the creature or monster. It's a chill way to explore and gain energy (which is required to gather items, play mini games and use the secret shops to buy rare items).
New Events Added on a Regular Basis.
Every new event is rewarding, and quite creative. Sometimes the event rewards simply require you to click and collect items from the Rewards Tab. Other times, you may have to cook items and pack them into a crate for a reward upon return. Sometimes they involve bosses. Others, just killing monsters. The rewards vary everytime as well, which keeps it exciting. :)
Quests are Simple and Easy to Navigate.
They are easy to navigate and will guide you directly to where you need to be, and can inform you of what you need to do to complete it. It's easy to understand and you can queue alot of them or have the option to forfeit, or hide it from your quests tab.
Variety of Things to do in BDO to Keep you Entertained.
Want to fight and kill creatures? Grind mobs - find an area suitable for you gear and you'll make money at the same time.
Want boss gear? Fight bosses - join the discord channel and keep tabs on the boss timers. Ask a friend to come along and don't forget to take health potions.
Want to kill people? Go to Val6, participate in PvP and you won't lose karma for it and won't be punished.
Want to fight friends? You can go to arenas, fight them, die and respawn for free.
Want to explore? Go exploring! Find new areas. Learn new creatures, new plants, new people.
Want to buy your own house and decorate it? The biggest houses are in Heidel (9 - 3, 9 - 4) Valencia (3 - 5) and Velia (2 - 3). If you want furniture, GO TO CALPHEON. This city has the most furniture shops.
Want to work on lifeskills? Go ahead. You can get gathering materials from material vendors for gathering. Different areas in the game have different items to gather. Items you gather can be processed by pressing (L). You can cook recipes with some ingredients you gather, but other ingredients can be used for alchemy. Can catch horses and work on training. Buy a fishing rod and go fishing. Go hunting for whales. Sell your fish to the trade manager for trade xp. Grow your own garden for farming xp and buy a sailing boat to explore the seas! Most lifeskills can be done while you afk.
There are so many things to keep you occupied which keeps the game exciting.
Lots of Gameplay for the Small Amount of Money you Invest to Buy BDO.
I've got over 1,000 hours of gameplay from a game that costed about $9.00 to buy... and afterwards you don't need to pay a monthly subscription, and it's not pay to win either. You can get pets off the marketplace if you're quick enough but they're not completely necessary. They're convenient so they're a want, not a need. Everything in the real money shop is a convenience but not necessary. It can also be purchased off Marketplace (well. most stuff).
Rewards.
Daily Rewards, Guild Rewards, Rookie Rewards and the Rewards Tab are good incentives to log on everyday and you'll make decent money from it. :))
Overall - I love how you can do so many things and set your own goals.
Negatives of BDO:
Limited Mount Options.
There's currently a horse, dream horse, camel and elephant. I'd love to see more options for mounts  that are more creative than what's currently being offered. SPECIESIST. The camels only go up to tier 1 and same with elephants - but horses get tier 8. Not fair on desert loving players. Mount customizations - there need to be more for elephants and camels.
RNG.
If you want to upgrade your gear, you need to pray to RNGesus before doing so and hope it doesn't go down a level lmao. If you're upgrading accessories... be prepared to cry when they break. Don't get your hopes up either for drops because the boss gear drops are rare.
Karma System.
Super biased and speciesist. I mean, why is it okay to kill a Baby Fogan but NOT OK to kill a horse or a baby elephant... I also think bad karma shouldn't be punished as harshly...
Bland Regions.
The game would benefit from being more creative in designing their regions. They are quite repetitive and I think each region should be unique. It really is repetitive.
Glitches.
Sooo many glitches in the game. The game developers need to prioritise these issues more importantly even though there are maintanences every week.  They may seem like small issues but it takes a long time to be addressed. For example, my person sleeps in her bed but her legs are flying off  the side! Or I'll get stuck in some weird place. My person doesn't sleep on the pillow.
Steam Achievements.
Super glitched. Some people get them. Some people don't. Mine haven't worked at all since I downloaded and they don't seem bothered to fix it at all. I've passed over 60% of the achievements and none of them have progressed for me. Game devs haven't responded.
Overall: There is definitely alot of room for improvement, however I do recommend.  Not everyone will agree with my perspective, but I do like BDO. And grinding isn't the only thing in the game. Thanks for reading!

Grim Dawn is the spiritual successor of Titan Quest, both of which are similar to Diablo. Personally, I think it's way better than Diablo and I like Diablo a fair bit.
>There's far more depth to making your character. You can choose two out of six classes and mix and match the skills from them. There are shrines hidden throughout the world that, when restored, give you points to put into constellations that give you bonus stats and abilities. There are components you get in loot that you can put on your gear to get even more stats and abilities. Then there's augments that you can put on your gear to get EVEN MORE stats.
>Tons of secret areas of various sizes. Most are just a hidden chest or something, while others are entire areas with bosses and lots of loot.
>Side quests with various outcomes that depend on your choices. Some result in bosses later, or new merchants, or diffrent rewards.
>Secret side quests. Shhhhh... It's a secret...
>Optional dungeons that open once per session so if you die that's it for that session. You have to exit the game and reload and spend another key to open the dungeon again. Lots of good loot with the thrill of semi-perma-death.
>A faction system that lets you unlock cool gear, new quests and areas, and fight new enemies.
>The main story is a little weak, but the side quests and backstory of the game is amazing.
Plus Grim Dawn is getting a expansion some time this year with 2 more classes (A Necromancer and an Inquisitor) and a bunch of new areas with story.

If seeing is believing then the developer's of Alan Wake really listened to the players.
I listed in my review of Alan Wake some of the things that caused me to have to spend 16 months slowly plodding through it. I guess I wasn't the only one who felt that way because pretty much all the issues of the first game were fixed with American Nightmare.
I am happy to say that Alan can now run like the middle aged man that he is instead of his ailing grandmother. The card driving issues have been removed entirely, because they don't let you drive in this game. And the camera issues I struggled with were less cumbersome in fights.
Along with those happy notes, I have to say I think American Nightmare is a great length for an expansion. The story is engaging and interesting, and it develops three more characters in quick order who are all unique. Well... as unique as you can get with stereotypes. But I'm not going down that road.
Out of all the improvements one did shine above all the rest, and that was the decision to have new weapon unlocks correspond with the number of manuscript pages you collect. When I found the first unlock case, I immediately wanted to search the entire map for every last page. Well Done!
In the end I enjoyed this game much more than the original, and I would say pick this one up on the next steam sale by itself.

TL;DR: Grim Dawn, another generic-feeling D2 Clone from the team who brought us Titan Quest which fills the ARPG belly, but fails to satisfy the hunger. An "ok" ARPG to pass the time which falls short of greatness.
POSITIVES:
- Full controller support (for lean back, relax on the couch, give the carpel tunnel-prone click-fest a rest and run around hacking and slashing a la Baldur's Gate Dark Alliance on original Xbox)
- Fully rotatable and zoomable camera
- Feels a bit like D2 in spots
PROBLEMS:
- Lacks visceral "FEEL." Sure you have the health bar as a visual cue, but I cannot count the times I died because I had no idea I was getting hit. D2 / D3 / PoE are MUCH MORE visceral and satisfying. Bone crunching, armour-scraping, explosions, the lot. You FEEL your character connecting hits and when he's getting hit. I rarely have to even look at the health bar in D3 or PoE. I just KNOW I need to heal, kite, or flat out run. In GD, I'm constantly checking in like a nanny on the health meter because of the complete lack of connection with the game world and what's happenning. The fourth wall is just too damn thick. GD fails to connect you to your character, and that's a BIG PART of a good ARPG. Which brings me to my next problem with GD...
- I could care less. Seriously, GD simply doesn't make me care. Not about the world, its NPCs, the story (if there even is one, I couldn't tell...it's just busy-work quests as best as I can tell), not even my own character! Yeah, I fidget about with skills and builds on level-ups, but that's about it. Compare that to D3 when I transmog equipment just to make sure my character always "looks awesome." I CARE about the alter-ego I've created in this fantasy world, even if all I'm doing is grinding for gear and running bounties. Compare also to the FTP PoE that actually makes money with people who care so much for their alter-egos they are willing to pay real $$$ for cosmetic upgrades! In GD I'm just another generic character in another generic ARPG. Torchlight and Torchlight 2 suffered from this same problem as well.
SUMMARY:
Don't get me wrong: the MECHANICS are there. All the ARPG formula boxes are ticked, and in some cases moreso (see POSITIVES, above) but there's just something missing from the execution of the final product which leaves me utterly disconnected from the game, and disillusioned with the experience.

I have strongly mixed feelings about this game. It seems like a step down from Alan Wake's deep, psychological undertones, but at the same time I'd like to see more developers take a franchise and just have fun with it in the way that Remedy did with American Nightmare. Overall, Remedy Entertainment just wants to have fun with the Alan Wake universe. I would not be suprised if the game is declared non-canon before Alan Wake 2.
As a spinoff semi-sequel to the original, it is small and doesn't really connect to the original story or gameplay 'feel' in a satisfying way.
Judged as a standalone game, it's a decent but very short story-driven action game about a guy with a flashlight running around fighting zombies.
The combat is exactly the same as the first game, but there are a few more weapons to unlock and a few unique enemies.
This game is a lot more combat focused, because the atmosphere isn't as heavy as the original and the additional firepower gives the game the ability to send about 50 enemies at you in a continuous wave without you getting axed to death within the first few seconds.
This game has major issues with longevity. The game literally has you play the same story 3 times with minor variations until you reach a somewhat climactic ending. It seems like a 2-hour gameplay experience copy-pasted to become a 6-hour gameplay experience, with a few extra explory bits here and there. Even in its complete form, it still feels short.
The story is a bit of a mixed bag. It's well-written, but too short and feels awkward when done three times over.
There are some other good points though. The recurring characters have some of the best dialogue in the series so far. Alan is as genre-savvy as ever so his second clash with the forces of darkness is enjoyable to watch. Characters from the original game have fantastic cameos that are only there to keep the plot in cryogenic stasis until Alan Wake 2, but still impart how awesome these characters are.
But best of all, American Nightmare shows you one of my favorite video game antagonists ever: Mr. Scratch. He's a sarcastic, more psychotic doppelganger of Alan Wake that shows up on TVs throughout the game, mocking you.
If you're a fan of Alan Wake and you think the game would work with a little more action, then this game is probably for you. If you enjoyed the deeper, more psychological parts of Alan Wake rather than the combat, you'll probably see this as a generic spinoff that won't help you cope with the long wait for Alan Wake 2.
Overall, I had fun, and though I don't think it's as good as Alan Wake, it deserves to be enjoyed just because it doesn't feel obligated to stay in line with the original. If it were marketed as a full sequel, I would be really disappointed, but it's about as much as I would hope for as a side project.

"Graphically stunning, Ultimately Dissapointing."
I've played all Far Cry games since the first, and most Crysis games (Not crysis 3 since it's not on steam) wiht at least 4 run thoughs each.  I'm a total Far Cry fan.  I even loved Far Cry 2.
Each game in the series adds a new element.  Render distance, Physics, Water, Fire, HDR, lighting, shadows, Improved AI, animals, cyber-dinosaurs, or open world or game concepts that makes it new, exciting, or adds depth.   Except Primal.
That's not completely true.  It does add the concepts of cold and poison gas.  Used by other FPS games better, and really so weak that it never threatened me or created the intended immediacy.  Being outdoors in Metro is SCARY..
The graphics are arguably better than FC4 (I have 7870's in Crossfire, and it looks truely amazing with the HD textures, and performs flawlessly) but not in a way that modifies gameplay or adds depth.  I'll admit this is a game where I stopped in a few locations just to look around and marvel and wonder how the devs, designers and artists did it.
The acting is actually worse,.  Using primitive-stye language was bold, but doesn't pay off.  The characters are Primitive (sic) and have no depth at all. Urki is the only character that brings anything despite that not being anything new (or anything not already done in recent disney movies..).  Just a little comic relief.  OK - I laughed out loud.  I Admit it.
There's no plot.  At least nothing that couldn't be described in detail in a single sentence.  I Won't bore you.
There's no new or original missions.  Using hunter senses is more frustrating than satisfying.
Pet animals are fun, but not new - FC4 had them too.  Most of the animals are essentially the same.
It takes away the guns.  That would be fine if it replaced them with something better or diffrent but it does neither.  There were already bows in previous games, and replacing bombs with bees is a bit naff.  Spears? - meh.
Obviously It also takes away flight; no hang-glider, wing suit, or powered flight.  That removes a full dimension from the game. What's the point of a high mountain if you can't jump off it?
For some reason it does not feel as free with regard to missions.  There's a main story line, and optional side quests that appear as you progress.  The quests will simply wait for you till you bother geting to them and maybe they will open another or other options, and maybe not.
With all of that said, it's a slick production, and a technical marvel.  I only hit some minor bugs (mostly checkpoint-type issues because I tend to wander off). Installation went perfectly, and updates have been smooth and clean.  The interface is good, the game runs well (I suspect even on moderate hardware).
I don't regret buying it, but I don't think I'll make multiple runs (partially because I don't think I could handle being pushed though the tutorial part again).  I also didn't bother with ALL of the site-quests like I usually do.  It was short (for a Far Cry game that is), but too long for me.
If it was the first Far Cry game I woud have been floored by it, but in the evolution (sic) of the series it's the most primitive step so far.
Next time, please go talk to a good book or movie author first.  Make something orginal with a new concept.  New technical trick, new storyline, new gameplay element.  Than you'll win me back.  Otherwise I'll probbaly wait for it to be in the bargain bin.

Game of Thrones is a perfect franchise to put in Telltale's hands. You are constantly making tough choices, and every decision you make ultimately feels like it was the wrong one later on. If the Walking Dead games were Telltale's masterpiece games, Game of Thrones certainly deserves to be alongside those titles.
However, at the same time, due to the very nature of being Game of Thrones, you often feel like you aren't making any headway to a better place. Everything always seems so dire, and when things get better, it always seems to get worse than before. Yes, that is keeping in line with the source material. Sadly, when you reach the conclusion of this game, the story ends, and there is no chance to make things different: You feel that it could go on. While the TV show and books still have a chance to make the ending "happy" or at least finished when the conclusion inevitably comes, the game has no promises that story will continue so it ultimately feels unfinished at the end.

Here is my chocolate mouse recipe.
Ingredients:
2 cups chilled heavy cream
4 large egg yolks
3 tablespoons sugar
1 teaspoon vanilla
7 oz fine-quality bittersweet chocolate (not unsweetened), chopped
Garnish: lightly sweetened whipped cream
Special equipment: an instant-read thermometer
Thats how we do it:
Heat 3/4 cup cream in a 1-quart heavy saucepan until hot. Whisk together yolks, sugar, and a pinch of salt in a metal bowl until combined well, then add hot cream in a slow stream, whisking until combined. Transfer mixture to saucepan and cook over moderately low heat, stirring constantly, until it registers 160°F on thermometer. Pour custard through a fine-mesh sieve into a bowl and stir in vanilla.
Melt chocolate in a double boiler or a metal bowl set over a pan of simmering water (or in a glass bowl in a microwave at 50 percent power 3 to 5 minutes), stirring frequently. Whisk custard into chocolate until smooth, then cool.
Beat remaining 1 1/4 cups cream in a bowl with an electric mixer until it just holds stiff peaks. Whisk one fourth of cream into chocolate custard to lighten, then fold in remaining cream gently but thoroughly.
Spoon mousse into 8 (6-ounce) stemmed glasses or ramekins and chill, covered, at least 6 hours. Let stand at room temperature about 20 minutes before serving.

Grim Dawn is the spiritual successor of Titan Quest, both of which are similar to Diablo. Personally, I think it's way better than Diablo and I like Diablo a fair bit.
>There's far more depth to making your character. You can choose two out of six classes and mix and match the skills from them. There are shrines hidden throughout the world that, when restored, give you points to put into constellations that give you bonus stats and abilities. There are components you get in loot that you can put on your gear to get even more stats and abilities. Then there's augments that you can put on your gear to get EVEN MORE stats.
>Tons of secret areas of various sizes. Most are just a hidden chest or something, while others are entire areas with bosses and lots of loot.
>Side quests with various outcomes that depend on your choices. Some result in bosses later, or new merchants, or diffrent rewards.
>Secret side quests. Shhhhh... It's a secret...
>Optional dungeons that open once per session so if you die that's it for that session. You have to exit the game and reload and spend another key to open the dungeon again. Lots of good loot with the thrill of semi-perma-death.
>A faction system that lets you unlock cool gear, new quests and areas, and fight new enemies.
>The main story is a little weak, but the side quests and backstory of the game is amazing.
Plus Grim Dawn is getting a expansion some time this year with 2 more classes (A Necromancer and an Inquisitor) and a bunch of new areas with story.

TL;DR: Grim Dawn, another generic-feeling D2 Clone from the team who brought us Titan Quest which fills the ARPG belly, but fails to satisfy the hunger. An "ok" ARPG to pass the time which falls short of greatness.
POSITIVES:
- Full controller support (for lean back, relax on the couch, give the carpel tunnel-prone click-fest a rest and run around hacking and slashing a la Baldur's Gate Dark Alliance on original Xbox)
- Fully rotatable and zoomable camera
- Feels a bit like D2 in spots
PROBLEMS:
- Lacks visceral "FEEL." Sure you have the health bar as a visual cue, but I cannot count the times I died because I had no idea I was getting hit. D2 / D3 / PoE are MUCH MORE visceral and satisfying. Bone crunching, armour-scraping, explosions, the lot. You FEEL your character connecting hits and when he's getting hit. I rarely have to even look at the health bar in D3 or PoE. I just KNOW I need to heal, kite, or flat out run. In GD, I'm constantly checking in like a nanny on the health meter because of the complete lack of connection with the game world and what's happenning. The fourth wall is just too damn thick. GD fails to connect you to your character, and that's a BIG PART of a good ARPG. Which brings me to my next problem with GD...
- I could care less. Seriously, GD simply doesn't make me care. Not about the world, its NPCs, the story (if there even is one, I couldn't tell...it's just busy-work quests as best as I can tell), not even my own character! Yeah, I fidget about with skills and builds on level-ups, but that's about it. Compare that to D3 when I transmog equipment just to make sure my character always "looks awesome." I CARE about the alter-ego I've created in this fantasy world, even if all I'm doing is grinding for gear and running bounties. Compare also to the FTP PoE that actually makes money with people who care so much for their alter-egos they are willing to pay real $$$ for cosmetic upgrades! In GD I'm just another generic character in another generic ARPG. Torchlight and Torchlight 2 suffered from this same problem as well.
SUMMARY:
Don't get me wrong: the MECHANICS are there. All the ARPG formula boxes are ticked, and in some cases moreso (see POSITIVES, above) but there's just something missing from the execution of the final product which leaves me utterly disconnected from the game, and disillusioned with the experience.

Grim Dawn is simply an excellent title. Bread and butter Diablo-like rpg with developers designing it with elements that have all already been seen. While this might sound bad, it's actually very good: no forced originality, no stupid supposedly inovative concepts that end up being a nuisance, simply all those tried and tested little bits and pieces we played arpgs for bundled together in one well crafted piece of work.
Game offers variety of environments, monster types, character builds and play styles. Player is offered anything from melee juggernaut to fragile hit and run rogue to ranged magic user. From snowy mountain passes to deserts. From massive charging bullthingy mobs to backline healers making your life difficult. Story is enjoyable, lore is good if grim, but doing simple runs is fun too. And then there's the crucible DLC for some instant non stop action without the need to travel. A single glance on hours played of reviewers is enough to gauge how much longevity the game possesses.
There are many old school elements in the game. For example respecing is not free, attributes can't be respecced at all while skill points can be reset at a specialized npc for a price. Meaining choices have consequences. There are hidden areas that don't appear on map and need to be recognized visually without ability to highlight them or easily notice them in some other way. This is welcome for a grumpy old farts such as myself who always holds speeches about how kids these days have it easy with running after pointers, while back in the day we used to listen to "go south, follow the river, then turn west at the big boulder and then..." type of instructions and WE LIKED IT. Well nothing like that here really since maps are relatively linear but it's still is not your typical modern holding your hand game. It demands some minimum of attention.
All in all, it's just all around excellent. If you like arpgs, get it. It's worth it at full price even, which is something I'd rarely say.

My first ever review. Here goes...
Why should you play Block N' Load? Think if TF2 had relations with a base-building game and left the child in Minecraft to do what it pleases.
Basic Gameplay:
At the start of a match you get a set period of time to build a base to protect your cubes and/or base. Using stock blocks, traps, and your own creativity, figure out a way to stop the other team from hitting your stuff. After that time period, all bets are off as you start trying to hammer on their base while stopping them from hammering yours.
Blocks take bricks, which can be mined from existing blocks on the maps. Each block has a different strength, purpose, cost, and brick return (so on and so forth) meaning the possibilities are endless if you have the bricks and time to build it.
Pros:
Truly pay for premium. Gold is earned after every match (more if you win and complete objectives you see on your home screen) and that gold can buy heros as well as perks to those heros (which is the only way to get perks. That guy with really tanky turrets, really powerful sniper shots, or seemingly infinite grenades had to earn all of them). In the meantime, there is a guaranteed three hero free rotation that features one hero from each role hierarchy, Brawn for tanky characters, Brains for base defense and support, and Skill for infiltration and sneaky gameplay. Heros themselves differ quite a bit from hero to hero too, no two heros fulfill exactly the same role in game. Speaking of which...
Hero variety: There is a sizable amount of heros to pick from, from the Italian construction worker with turrets, Tony, to a psychotic killer clown who can mess with your mind, Kreepy, to an English explorer and big game hunter, Nigel, to this game's version of Rambo, Sarge Stone, to yetis, genies, mad acid doctors, so on and so forth. Each hero has a passive ability, and activatable one, and their own unique hero block.
High skill ceiling and fair balancing. That perfect base you built last time? Don't expect it to work every time. Every hero and playstyle has its counter, whether it's the bullet hell of a Tony turret blockade being shut down by sniping and tunnelling, to even the tankiest brawn character getting outsmarted by mines.
Community input. It's got a map builder. Shameless plug, I have two maps made. If only more people went to the custom games instead of basic gameplay...
Functioning matchmaking. Don't worry if you're a noob. The game actively tries to match you up with other people at your skill level. The longer you wait though, the more chance you get some really good players, but even then, the game tries to set teams up fair, with more or less equal skill distributions.
Runs on potatoes. My laptop is kinda crap, and the game runs perfectly fine on low settings. Let performance issues not be a problem unless you are running REALLY out of dated hardware.
Con:
No kick function discovered. You will have those jerks who ruin your defenses to troll your team. As of yet, I have not found a way to kick them. This is also a very isolated occurrance, at least for me, and doesn't happen too often.
Verdict:
Get this game blockhead. Sarge Stone wants YOU to download this game, Tony's union is always recruiting, and Nigel's hunting entourage can always be expanded a bit.

I am not going to lie; I did not expect what I got out of this RPG. I got it in a steam sale with a bunch of other games or it would have been about $2 bucks to buy. What I got was something that I was happy to buy during the sale, but would have felt a bit off trying to buy it when it was actually the price it was. This is not against the creator of this game, the game had no bugs and things worked the way they were supposed to. It just felt way too simple, especially with the basic art and music.
As for these small games, I have to warn you that I may end up going into spoilers slightly but will try hard not to. The story follows a young lady as she decides to move to the sleepy town of Grayfox. When she gets there, she finds the town is full of the elderly people ‘close to death’. She meets this mysterious lady who turns the girl old and has her take control of some of the other old people in town. This is the start of the problems I have for the storyline, there is no reason for it. She isn’t against the people of that down, not that hateful of old people or anything so this lady turning her old and making her go through this seems unmotivated. The main character does not even know any of these people and she is made to choose some pretty heavy decisions for them. The second problem I have is the stories. We do get some information about what’s going on, but it’s definitely not much. I couldn’t fully feel for the character how it wanted me to which broke whatever message they were trying to put across.
If you want all the achievements, then there is replay ability to it but I mostly just skipped over the story to get the last three achievements I had to grab. Nothing else really changes.
The artwork is rather simple; most of it looking like it came in the RPG Maker that this was created on. Because of this, there really wasn’t anything that stood out except the image of the Grayfox statue. It was done well and fit in with the other assets. Design of the characters was also rather generic, being used for multiple characters throughout the game, not just the character they were supposed to represent.
The music was simple and fit in well with the point they were trying to put across, but didn’t stand out. If I heard it alone I would think it was from any regular RPG, it didn’t have anything to call its own. The only real audio cue they had for when you did something in the game was if you stepped on poo too so… ya, there was that.
Overall, the game was alright, just didn’t feel like it was fully fleshed out. There could have been so much more to it and made the story that more intense but they fell short of that goal. I wouldn’t pay the full price for the game, but for a steam sale game, it wasn’t bad at all. Give it a try if you find it on sale again.

You will love this game for awhile. Maybe even too much; however, the end game system revolves around blowing up all your gear for a small chance that one item might upgrade. This is pretty much designed to prolong the game's life. It's simply horrible and extremely unfun. I don't mind the challenge, but the entire process is seriously awful. You have to build "fail stacks" on trash items to increase the chances of the item you actually want to upgrade. Problem is, the trash items will frequently upgrade and you will have to throw them on an alt character with negative karma, have them die 10-20 times to guards for a chance that the item might downgrade. This is all done just so you can repeat the entire process all over. By the way, each fail also costs you millions and your items downgrade and have to be enhanced all over. To be honest, no one in this game thinks enhancing is fine whatsoever. I just blew up all my gear going for TET (+19), and I don't really feel that it's worth it to continue anymore. I play games for fun and this system is not fun whatsoever.
In addition, the NA/EU versions are completely out of the loop. Take Valencia for example, this is supposed to be a viable end game grind region with multiple good spots, and for Korea, it absolutely is. Korea has daily loot scrolls they're given for logging in, which increase drop rate of items significantly. For NA/EU, we don't have the loot scrolls. Why? No reason, we just don't. Thus, the only good grind spot in Valencia is Pila Ku. This means that pretty much from level 51+ you'll be fighting for a spot at Sausans or Pirates. Fun times.
This game has a lot of potential, but the disconnect between the developers and NA/EU publisher is just too much, and there are no signs of it being fixed. There are tons of other things wrong with the game like artisan memories (huge P2W) and the karma system for pvp. By the way, the base price of the game is deceiving because pets are required and eventually you will want more weight upgrades, maids, and possibly processing outfit, etc.
This game tries to squeeze money out of you at every turn. Save your time and money. Look elsewhere.

Quick review:
Should you play this game? - Yes.
Will you enjoy it as much as the original Alan Wake? - Probably not, but you'll still have fun.
-------------------------
What I enjoyed:
* Additional, powerful weapons made me feel like a one-man army.
* Excellent visual quality.
* Interesting storyline that ties into the original.
* Well-executed live-action components sequences.
* Mr. Scratch (!!!)
My critique:
I purchased both Alan Wake and the American Nightmare sequel in a bundle, so I was able to play the sequel soon after completing the original game.  Perhaps I should have given some time between the two games, because the transition between the two games was a bit jarring.  American Nightmare, despite the name, lacked much of the horror atmosphere that kept me addicted to the previous game.  It was the little things; like Alan making self-referential wise cracks about his supposedly very serious mission, the much easier enemies, and the dead-panned voice acting of the NPCs.  I did not get the impression that Alan was fighting for his life and that of his wife against an unrelenting horrific force of darkness, but rather this was just something he did that was mildly irritating.  As in: "Eh, it's a job...  BLAM! BLAM! BLAM!!!"
As for the enemies being weaker, I mean that their darkness was broken much quicker, allowing them to be killed sooner.  A large part of what made Alan Wake challenging was the time needed to weaken enemies before they could be killed.  That gamepley mechanic created many tense situations where I had to dodge an onslaught of enemies while struggling to consistently shine a light on each one, before I could even start to kill them.  This was especially tricky if I ran out of batteries in the middle of the fight, which made the eventual victory all the more rewarding.  In American Nightmare, this feature is weakened, in that I was able to break almost every enemy's darkness before they came within swinging distance of me.
Regretably, this game was also much shorter than the previous one, and I was a bit surprised when I beat it so quickly.  I literally played through the entire campaign in 5 hours.  Now, I did enjoy most of that time, but I was surprised when it ended so soon.  I am not even sure if the campaign is worth playing a second time, because I saw just about every detail available in the 3 main levels the storyline loops you through.
And regarding the games looping storyline, I did enjoy the idea of Alan continually improving his strategy on each attempt and how the NPCs started to realize something was up on the second iteration.  I was fondly reminded of the movie "Groundhog Day".  However, the third iteration did not add much more to the story, as both Alan and myself were thinking, "Uh, I have to repeat this all over again..."  Right up until the game ended (too soon), I was hoping there would be more levels and another twist to the story.  Then at the ending scene, I realized that the game's developers had cleverly found a way to make a very short game three times as long...  by making you play it three times over.
Despite all of this, I DO recommend this game to anyone who has played the original Alan Wake or is just looking for a fun action game with some light horror undertones.  I had fun playing it, which is ultimately what I am looking for in any game.

I enjoyed the original
immensely: for me it is still one of the prime examples of how an action-adventure 3rd person game can be made into an exciting and scary experience. So I started playing
with high expectancies, but quickly the game let me rather down own this.
is not really a sequel nor a prequel to the original, it's more like a standalone game on the same "universe", but on a much smaller scale, so in the end it felt like some sort of expansion pack to me, using the same protagonist, game mechanics and of course game engine.
This engine still stands firm and delivers more than decent graphics: it's great in creating an atmosphere thanks to superb lighting, something which the original game used to immensely scaring effect. Although graphics are fine in this new installment, the actual gameplay is not. It felt almost painful to see the original game's tension and feeling of being utterly desperate while fighting off the forces of darkness turned into some Rambo-like experience. In the original game, guns, ammo and the ever-important batteries for the flashlight (sometimes it was the ONLY weapon to fight of enemies) were so scarce at moments that it almost drove me crazy, but the feeling of relief and accomplishment after finally getting further in the story, was all the more satisfying for it.
uses the same game mechanics, but provides such an arsenal of over-powerful weapons, an almost endless supply of ammo and a flashlight that recharges in a matter of seconds. As a result of these changes, the entire gaming experience changed from an exciting horror adventure to a lacklustre shooter where I just blasted my way past hordes of enemies. Were it not for the obvious comparison to the original game, I'd probably have enjoyed
a bit more, especially since after finishing the story there are a number of arcade-levels where the goal is just to get as many kills and as high a score as possible. These are played on fairly large and well-developed maps, and felt like playing more natural than the story.
The story, perhaps the main protagonist in the original
, is perhaps the weakest point in this newer installment. It's made coplex in an unnatural feeling way and lacks focus. But most problematic of all, it forces the player to play through the three locations (only three!!) three times, each time "altering history" a little bit, but in the end this feels more like a gimmick and the net result is simply too repetitve a game.

So, I'm an oldschool gamer, not as much as some but more than most. Specifically, I'm an oldschool RPG gamer. Some of my fondest memories are of watching my mom or brother play the early Dragon Warrior (Quest) and Final Fantasy games (I'm the youngest so I never actually got to play till I got big enough to hold my ground). So, I have a very deep rooted love of JRPGs, I'd play Xenogears every day for the rest of my life if I could get away with doing so.
What I can't comprehend, is who are these people who like grinding for hour upon hour for material in games. Now, I can understand grinding for levels; while I think WE ARE PAST THAT POINT in gaming history, that's a time honored tradition. Why I ALSO now should need to grind for crafting material is beyond me (it's not an MMO! There is no need!). This is made worse by the fact that the combat system is semi-complex, meaning I can't just mindlessly click 'attack' I actually have to position myself and input specific combos for each encounter. This is time consuming beyond belief. Seriously, I'm in my 30's, can I please just play a game for fun for once? If I wanted to grind through things with this level of thought attached, I'd just do the things that pay me money, it's pretty much the same level of enjoyment.
So, I really want to play the game and enjoy the story, but I don't think the story is worth the investment of time and energy. If you're in your teens or are really bored then this is the way to go; if you're trying to find a good new-gen RPG then this isn't it.
TLDR: I'm a grumpy old man get off my lawn, I'm trying to play FF6 for the 100th time.
P.S. somebody please make some good RPGs. They just need decent mechanics and a good story, that's all I ask for. They've made them before! I've seen them do it!

As a roguelike deckbuilding game, Slay the Spire marries the rewarding gameplay of classic deckbuilders like Dominion and the unpredictability and thrill of classic roguelikes. I'd expect fans of both genres to find this game a slam-dunk hit; people who aren't blown away by either genre might still find the combination fun.
I consider the following the main strengths of StS:
- Variety. A wide variety of game elements are determined randomly--the map of each level, the particular enemies in a given encounter, the relics a player finds in each chest, even the cards the player can add to the deck after each encounter. Runs feel different from each other. An enemy that might be trivial to a Barricade Ironclad might prove a huge challenge to a poison Silent, and vice versa. This game is almost never autopilot--the game requires close attention and encourages the deck having enough flexibility to support multiple lines of play.
- Customizability. StS allows a variety of patterns of play. If you want to challenge high-score records, you can route yourself through as many enemies and elites as possible, bank all your gold, and memorize every enemy's pattern so you can take Runic Dome. If you want to win consistently, you can opt for safer routes with more ? encounters and merchants. If you want to win with as wacky a deck as possible, by god, you can take every Bludgeon you see or buy Strange Spoon for all your Shivs. Yes, there's a lot of RNG, but the player has a huge amount of control over the actual difficulty level of the game.
- Flavor. Wounds are temporary; curses are eternal until you find a cleric to exorcise them. Striking an enemy once with a sword does 6 damage; smashing it repeatedly in the head with a hammer does 32. Red and green cards, the factions' specific bags of tricks, can be upgraded but are only playable by one character; neutral cards can be used by anyone, but aren't endemic enough to be upgraded. Poison can't be blocked but gets cleansed naturally over time. Thieves taunt you when they steal your gold and try to run away with it. So many of the design decisions in this game, from the cards to the relics to the enemies, go a long way to creating a fun and immersive environment.
Overall, I highly recommend Slay the Spire. It's a ton of fun and it's ludicrously replayable.

Welcome to hell, kids.
No aim down sight, no ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t "+50 enemy killed", no weapon camo, no slow moving, no weapon attachments, no camping, no YOLOSWAG420 quickscope, no ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t health regeneration, no killstreaks, no noob friendly♥♥♥♥♥♥ no hitscan weapons (except machinegun and shotgun, but those are♥♥♥♥♥♥anyway), no perks, no wallrun, no OP♥♥♥♥♥♥ no titans, no vehicles, basically nothing in modern millitary shooter. If you're expecting a CoD or BF or Titanfall or any other♥♥♥♥♥♥like that, don't waste your time on this masterpiece.
So what is Quake all about ? Fast moving, strafe jumping, run-n-jump-n-gun, frag as much as possible, collect weapons and use them wisely, progression (no, not ♥♥♥♥♥♥ level mechanic, you progress from a noob to a pro) and proving your skill.

Although loadout and "hold space to keep jumping" made me roll my eyes (because only noobs can't press space repeatedly to jump), Quake Live is still ton of fun and enjoyable. If you're confident about your FPS skill, give Quake Live a try. It's fast, it feels satisfied, it runs great, it aged well and it's Quake-tastic.
Run for your life, kill for your pride. Your choice.

I'm not an FPS gamer, but this is what they should be in my reckoning. Fun, funny, made up of layers (as in "not just mindless killing"), and with ever-evolving experiences. No game is ever the same, as the developers were so keen to point out. You can play the same map many times over, but the building (and destroying) element of the game allows for infinite strategies. Of course, you have to figure out which ones are the most effective...
The heroes you can play as are diverse, with their own amusing dialogue and weaponry, and the gameplay is intuitive.
However, the one problem I have experienced is the occasional lack of teamwork. For example, the start of the game can be awkward when you prepare your base and don't know which blocks you should put down because you don't know what kind of base your team wants.
Even so, this game is a gem. I mean, what's not to like about running headfirst into the front lines with mortars blasting away, or sneaking underneath the enemy base to pop up with a surprise attack as you prepare a camp nestled in the lion's den, or perching atop towers in the ultimate sniper stake-out as you take potshots at the enemy with healing stations and ammo supplies trustily keeping you alive?
Just...download it. You'll see what I mean soon enough!

This is bit of an odd game to review and I think many people familiar with western MMO's may be a bit confused by many systems in the game.  There are many ways you can play and many ways you can pay.
But let's get one thing out of the way immediatly.  The combat in this game is incredibly fun.   I'm going to start by recommending various ways of playing and paying.  With general impressions at the end of this review.
Way 1:  Budget Fun.
Buy the game for $9.99.  Play through 5-6 classes up to around level 49ish, doing quest and having fun killing mobs.  Get about 70ish hours of game play for you 10 bucks.  That's about 20 cents per hour of enterainment.
Way 2:  Casual
Buy the game for 29.99.  (Either buy the traveler's package, or buy the base game and then get 20 bucks of pearls).  I bought the game for 30 bucks on the recommendation of a friend.  Spent 10 bucks on the base game and 20 bucks to nab some pets.  The pets are super nice for picking up loot one they get a few levels on them.  Play 3-6 class up to the mid 50s levels.  Get 100-200 hours of great fun out of the game.  Maybe also build a worker empire and craft your way into riches.  Will cost you about 20 cents per hour of entertainment.
Between Way 2 & 3 here is where you hit quite a grind.  If you can relax and have more fun, then just go with it.  To some people this is where the game feels like P2W, but if you just relax and go with it you'll get there eventually.  However if you don't long grinds, then exit here.  You got good entertainment value for your money above.
Way 3:  Subscription based MMO
Remember when MMO's were subscription based?  If you want a long term MMO to delve into I suggest playing it this way.  Buy the game for 30 bucks, then play like you are paying a sub fee.  Get a set amount of pearls each month and use them on various upgrades.   Not playing as often?  don't get pearls that month.   This is if you want an MMO to play for a few years.
Things I like:
- Very fun combat:  The character animations are great.  The skill effects are fantastic.  The combat is fluid and very entertaining.  This quite frankly is the best part of the game.  I'd recommend this game for anyone for 10 bucks just to pick up and play around with the combat.
- Excellent scenery:  The game has an excellent and detailed open world.  The areas are very well design and it feels like a real world.  The towns feel like real living towns.
- Excellent monster design:  Great monster and boss design.
- There are many different game systems you could get yourself into (combat, worker empire, 6 or 7 crafting professions, horse taming/training, merchant trader... and a few more things I've not even dug into yet.  All of the systems are simple enough to dip your toe into, but very complex underneath.  I personally love the complexity... I dislike the mentality of the last decade of MMOs that were trying to dumb down every system.
- The marketplace:  I love how the marketplace works (though I have a friend who does not).  The game uses one master regional (like EU, NA, etc) Server, but many "channels" within your region.  All of the North American channels tie into the same marketplace.  This makes the ingame economy very robust for crafters/sellers.
Things I'm nuetral about:
- The enchanting system...  While I like complex systems, it's a bit over the top.  If you are playing by my Way 1, or Way 2, it's not a problem.  But if you are playing Way 3 look into the enchanting system before playing the game.  Some people don't mind it, some people hate it.  Some people just grind silver and try to buy stuff.  Very RNG based at the high ends.
- The Cash shop, AKA is the game P2W?  The cash shop does give you advantages... in most cases these are just time based things.  You can ignore 90% of these and still have a great time with the game.  You can only get pets through the cash shop, and they are very helpful.  I recommend getting 1-2.  I can't really speak to the high end PVP, but I feel like if you are really good and have alot of time, then you don't need to spend any additional cash.  However if you are short on skill or time, then you might need it.  I haven't even scratched that yet so I'm not sure how I'll feel about it.
- The late-game grind.  The game will get grindy after level 50.  So far I don't mind because the combat is just so much damn fun... and I love managing my worker empire.
- AFK stuff... this game oddly has many things that are more effieciently done AFK.  I'm a bit conflicted on this actually.  Horse training, fishing, about 50% of the crafting, and some of the worker production is really done best to just set up a thing and let it run in the backround.  Of the 600 hours in the game I have at this point I would estimate about 400 of that is afk or semi-afk running the background while I'm doing other things (sleeping, chores around the house, yard work, grocery shopping).  So consider my review as someone who has 200 hours played and not 600.  When minmized in the system tray the game uses about 4-6 Gig of RAM.  This takes away some of the grind, but I'm still a bit conflicted with it.
Things I dislike:
- Once you reach level 50 you get kicked off the nice uncrowded "channels".  I dislike how busy the main channels are in the towns.  I recommend playing several characters up to 49, before you progress to 50 so you can stay on the nice servers longer.  I do hope they had more channels if populations continue to rise.
Basic Summary:
For the casual player the game is fantastic, fun and well worth the 30 bucks.  I could quit any time now and feel like I got my moneys worth.  I've gotten about 15 cents per hour of entertainment.  I feel like I've only explored about a third of the world and I've enjoyed all of it.
If you want a game where you rush to the end game PVE and PVP wars, then this game might not be for you (unless you have alot of cash to spend) as getting there may take a while.  If you are not a casual player you should do more research into what the end-game enchanting and content is like before delving in, though I suggest just trying it casually at first and making that descition later.  You'll still get good value out of it.  Like many popular games you'll find people who don't recommend a game despite having played a thousand hours.

Watch out for hidden costs!
Exactly a month ago I got this game, and I immediately liked it. Especially the fact that you could focus on trade and craftsmanship a lot was great. Sadly this is hardly of use in practice since everything can be bought anyways and you make more money grinding mobs than putting effort into crafting, but for people like me it's enjoyable nevertheless.
However, you get a premium package for free. Through a variety of options you can obtain several of those 7 days packages and they lasted me until today. Signing in I noticed it had expired since they offer more inventory space, more money bonus from the market (the global market, auction hall in other games, is the ONLY way to transfer goods from player to player, you cannot trade in person!) and more storage space. The effect: 96 inventory slots were suddenly gone.
Since you cannot delete items from storage and my inventory has 16 items too much in it now, my character is basically locked until i throw away very valuable things from my inventory.
Extending your premium-package for 90 days costs 4500 "pearls" which equal 45€. That's 15€ per month extra costs. Now one may say you don't necessarily need that much space but if you plan to go into crafting, you definitely do. All my city storages are bursting full of crafting materials even with the package and several tier 5 warehouses (that extend your allowance) bought.
This was an aprupt ending to my time in BDO, and despite still having a good "Money per game hour enjoyed" ratio, I can't recommend a game that desperately throws premium stuff (more packages exist aswell!) at you to make you dependent on it and then asks for HORRIFIC sums of money or you lose your standard.
PS: The only way to get pets in the game is paying 10-20€ or buying them from other players for ingame money, note though that as soon as someone registers a pet half of the server will run to the marketplace to get it, so chances to actually get one are rather slim, especially when you're in a remote area.
I knew there'd be ****** microtransactions since it's only 10€, but the premium package takes it too far for me to recommend this to other players.
Feel free to make your own opinion, especially if you are into monster grinding since for that you obviously do not need that much storage space. If you are looking for a nice crafting-oriented experience, keep looking and let me know if you find something ;)
UPDATE FROM 19.10.2017
Here's an edit with a little more detailed critique: I've overcome the initial face-to-wall blockage of running out of the packages and somewhat enough storage space ;)
Two main points of critique remain though:
1. The cash shop items are horribly overpriced. Pets are in all seriousness the most "worthy" items. A simple outfit (of which all female ones look like a Beathe Uhse showcase, though I'm sure some of them are even too ♥♥♥♥♥♥ for that ;P) already costs 25€, same price for cosmetic horse armor. I recently acquired a hedgehog that is supposed to make gathering a bit easier by granting an extra item every now and then when collecting mats. That comes in handy when trying to built a boat that requires 80.000 wooden logs (calculatory) that have to be manually gathered. It cost me 60€.
It was only available in a (heavily criticized) package for 4500 Pearls (=45€) but the thing is there's hidden costs again, since you cannot simply buy 4500 Pearls. The smallest Pearl-package that is big enough to buy the package was 6000+600 Pearls for 60€. There goes the money! Of course, I didn't need to buy the hedgehog, but I think if prices were lower, the cash shop would actually generate more revenue since digital items come at no cost for the developers and the volume of bought items would drastically increase. How often did I hear sentences like "I would buy [item] if it was [amount]€"? Too often ;)
2. The community. Okay so while the chat filter is really strict, filtering even words like "canal" because they contain blocked words, the community takes every chance to ridicule, insult or even bully other players. My personal advice is to turn all chats besides whisper, guild and party off and pretend it's a single player game with your friends ;)
In all other chats all I witnessed were "WANT TO SELL" or "WANT TO BUY", "GUILD WANTS MORE MEMBERS" and at last "ARE TRAPS GAY?", the latter reoccuring on an hourly basis with an extensive... let's just call it discussion following. Not really worth the chat space ;)
I would like to give the game a thumbs up and a thumbs down at once, I've spent more than 500 hours by now so I can't say its a bad game that I don't recommend per se. But while it's one of the most played games I have recently, its also the game with the most problems I have played. Ironically, those problems could be easily fixed within a Minute or two, besides the community of course.
I still enjoy this game.
