if you plan on purchasing this game, i strongly recommend getting the Explorer's Package (even better if the game is on sale). Most of the content which comes with the package is very useful...
+ Pet is very good for collecting loot (so you don't have to pick it up yourself)
+ Horse is decent, but you should travel around the world by foot early game to increase stamina
+ Horse flute is convenient
+ Elion Blessing is not very useful (typically used for PVP or boss fights)
+ Character slots are very good (to try out other classes and for failstacking)
+ 16 inventory slot is very good for your main class
+ Housing decoration is useless (exterior of the house looks complete♥♥♥♥♥and you can't change that)
+ Silver clothing isn't anything special
+ The value pack (VP) is the main highlight of the bundle (makes your BDO experience very smooth)
I also recommend purchasing another 4 pets for grinding (costs around $40 USD but there are sometimes 20% off sales, so ~$32 USD)
Many people complain that this game is "pay to win" (P2W). I would say that this is true,
it is nowhere near as bad as you would think it is.
Value Packs are considered P2W, due to the feature of selling items on the in-game marketplace at a higher price (~20%). There are three methods to obtain a VP: buy it yourself for $15 (30 days) or $45 (90 days), snipe it on the marketplace (Don't even try this. I've spent hundreds of bid attempts on the marketplace and have yet to successfully win a bid), or you can wait 14 days to obtain 1400 loyalties (100 loyalties a day) to obtain a 1 day value pack. A 1 day VP may seem like complete garbage, but that is all you need to sell all your "expensive" loot on the marketplace. Just stock up all your loot in a town storage and dump it on the marketplace whenever you have access to a VP. Additionally, the biggest source of grinding money typically comes from "trash" loot, which can be vendored to most NPCs.
All the other features of the VP are useful, but are in no way necessary. It only makes things more convenient.
Lots of BDO players also complain about "artisan memories" (AM). AMs basically gives you more chances to upgrade (enhance) your gear, but it certainly does not ensure successful enhancements. Personally, I have never used AMs as I find it unnecessary and a waste of money. It should ONLY be used for boss gear (and some other items), but it takes time to get the gear in the first place.
There is no way around it. YOU NEED PETS IF YOU PLAN ON PLAYING THIS GAME. Grinding is the best source of income, and pets greatly increase your grind speed efficiency. Manually picking up items is a chore, and takes around 1 second to do it. Tier 1 (T1) pets do it for you, and have ~4 second cooldown time before it picks up the next loot. Having only 1 pet is pretty much useless (you have to pick up most of the loot yourself), so do yourself a favour and buy 4 pets (Assuming you have already purchased the Explorer's Package). Do not try to get T2,T3 and T4 pets. It is gambling with real money at this point, and the reward/risk is simply not worth it.
This is really only useful for grinding or fishing. 80% of the time, the items which mobs drop are garbage and have little value, so you can just throw out the item to save inventory space (only takes ~4-5 seconds to do this). On the other hand, AFK and active fishing both require lots of inventory space to yield large sums of money, but you still get a reasonable amount of money with the default inventory space (+16 inventory space). Doing the main story quest provides you additional inventory space. You can also spend 1000 loyalties for a +1 inventory space (Not worth it IMO, +1 storage space for 400 loyalties is more useful).
This only affects the duration of your grinding sessions. You store all your trash loot on your horse so it's not a big deal. You can spend 3500 loyalties for 50LT bonus (not bad) for a maximum of 4 times for each character (e.g. increase maximum weight by 200LT). I recommend getting this with your loyalties.
These maids are not necessary but they just make things more convenient. The storage maid can store 1 item or a certain quantity of money into the closest storage bank during your grinding sessions, vice versa (20 minute cooldown). A marketplace maid allows you to purchase item(s) from the marketplace anywhere in the world (normally only possible when you are in front of a marketplace director at a town, 20 minute cooldown). You can play this game perfectly fine without the use of maids. Maids cost ~$10 USD and you can buy multiple of each with separate cooldown times.
You can buy items from the cashshop and sell them on the in-game MP, limited to 5 items per week. The maximum price of an item is $34 USD on the cash shop, and can only be sold for ~37M in-game currency. This conversion rate is garbage, and will have a minimal effect on your gameplay experience. It also allows other players to obtain cash shop costumes without paying any real money.

Once you reach level 50, PVP is unlocked for you. This means that players can kill you (and your horse/camel) when you are not in a safe zone. Other players RARELY kill you for no apparent reason (probably a 0.001% chance). Some reasons why players might "randomly" kill you is because...
+ You are taking their grind rotation (which you should never do without asking)
+ You are in the desert (PKers receive certain buffs if they kill players)
+ They really hate your class
Each class has their own set of skills which they can learn from lvl 1-55. This is known as pre-awakening. Once you reach level 56, you are able to learn a new set of skills which are waaaaaay stronger then you pre-awakened skills. This is known as the "awakened". It is important to note that the pre-awakened and awakened skills can be completely different. 99% of your gameplay is going to be on your awakened state, so you should check out some vids on youtube about class play style and difficulty. Generally, the easiest classes the play are witch, wizard, striker and warrior. More difficult classes include ninja, kuno and sorceress. In the end, just play a character which you think looks cool and fun to play.
Most of the default costumes look atrocious. You can purchase a large selection of costumes which looking AMAZING for ~$34 USD.
, you can purchase most cash-shop costumes from the in-game marketplace with "relative ease" and at a decent price, so you don't need to spend even more money.

Alan Wake’s American Nightmare is a third person shooter in the psychological horror genre.  It is a stand-alone DLC that continues the story of the original Alan Wake game.
You play as Alan again fighting against his evil alter-ego and his minions of darkness.  He still wields up to six weapons – 1-hand gun, 2-hand gun, flare gun, flares, flashbang grenades and, most crucial, a flashlight.  The flashlight is required to remove the enemy shields in order to make them vulnerable to your guns.  Ammo (and batteries for your flashlight) are everywhere and there are quite a few more guns to choose from.
The story this time around pits you against your doppelganger, created by the Dark Presence.  There are some new interesting variations on the minions you face which helps against monotony.   What doesn’t help is that the three zones that the story takes you through get re-used three times each, creating nine areas to complete the game.  They do their creative best to make things a little different each time through, but there is no way to hide the inevitable repetition.
The graphics have been slightly updated from the original.  There are some great cutscenes and the voice acting is still superb.  The real life actor playing Alan Wake has some choice scenes playing the evil twin and taunting Alan through videos you can play on various TV sets.
They have toned down the many collectibles from the first game.  There are 50+ manuscript pages to find and these provide story exposition and are required to unlock better weapons.  Likewise, there are only 12 achievements now and half are associated with the new Arcade Mode.  Arcade Mode removes the storyline completely and allows the player to try and survive the night in different maps against waves of enemies.  You can compare your scores against your friends….still no co-op or multi-player available.
American Nightmare’s Story Mode can easily be completed in less than five hours, although the Arcade Mode can provide some additional hours of fun.  Overall, worth playing if you wait for the right Steam sale.

After playing the original Alan Wake, and discovering this game isn't a sequel but more of its own stand alone title, I was ready to dislike it. However I was pleasantly surprised to find that I really enjoyed this game! Though it's not a survival horror title like the first, it does improve on some features and has some rather enjoyable moments.
RIGHT: Like the original Alan Wake, the controls, story, and combat are solidly done. Unlike the original, this is a horror run-n-gun rather than a survival. Getting around the area is simple and easy, the mini map now has a handy "?" feature that generally tells you when a manuscript page is near by, and also unlike the original, Alan has brushed up he fire arm skills a bit. The armory has increased substantially, the enemy count has also doubled as well as some having specific weaknesses or advantages, and the levels have a very.... surreal feeling. Mr. Scratch is pretty amusing and even unsettling at times, giving you a solid antagonist to focus on. There is also an arcade mode if you'd rather skip talking and just gun stuff down, and do the whole leader board thing.
WRONG: For starters, this game is very short and I hate to bring this up as a negative because the games length has to directly do with the story plot. I was able to complete it in one evening, and that is with finding all the manuscript pages. Sadly, though there are several more weapons, there is only one flash light this time around and the crossbow makes even the flashlight rather worthless. I was sad to see such a great mechanic from the first game demoted to a mere gimmick. The new weapons are also rather hodge podge, and often you will end up with two fire arms that are greatly incompatible and put you at a huge disadvantage. Unlockable guns with bigger requirements aren't often better than ones with lower requirements. For example, the auto shotgun is forty pages, and really worthless against everything but the thugs with concrete saws. So unless your target is huge and slow, you're going to spray and pray and hope something runs into your field of fire. The Uzi is five pages, and pretty much able to knock down anything big and small with relative ease.
All in all, American Nightmare is a great play on the old Evil Twin Twilight Zone shows put into game form. The mood is still creepy, the voice work is great, and controls are very well done. It's sadly not a real sequel, but should by no means be discounted as a fun little jaunt into Alan's world.

The narrative, one of the best things of the previous title, is extremely silly. A complete joke compared to the original. The game has you explore a handful of regions three times in a row, explained in the story as some kind of time cycle or trial-and-error run as Alan Wake tries to re-write his story. The areas are okay, certainly not as atmospheric as the Pacific North West of the original. The game is considerably short as well, clocking in at three hours at most (I've finished my run in 2.5 hours). As short as it is, the game actually starts to drag halfway through since there isn't any new in terms of scenery. Gameplay-wise, however, it is as solid as the previous title. The enemies are diverse and the gunplay, mixed with the light mechanic, still feels as fresh as in the original. Ammunition is less scarce so the survival aspect that was present in the original is gone (safe havens are also more frequent), though this isn't all too bad. As a standalone it is hard to recommend, though I guess it should be seen as more of an expansion or perhaps (standalone) DLC. Taking the price-tag into account, I'm giving the game the benefit of the doubt. I feel the gameplay is enough to carry it.
Bottom line is that it is a fun game to kill an evening, but don't expect this to be "Alan Wake 2".

It's a card game, so RNG isn't only a given, it's the driving force behind the game.  It's basically a card game version of the little trinkets in Binding combine with the map of FTL.  That's all it has in comon with either of them.  You don't build a deck ahead of time.  You build it as you play.  This sounds sort of fun, and it is sort of fun.  It's fun until you realize that the boss you happen to run into, or even some garbage trash encounter, is just nothing you'll ever be able to beat.
There's no saving your run in this due to clever play on your part.  You will just run into things that you have no hope in hell of beating.  It's not like you can plan your next run to beat that, because everything you get is random.  There isn't enough healing in the game, and there aren't enough cards to clear negative status effects, of which you'll be bombarded every fight.
There's way too much "you never had a chance" and not enough... fun.  You know what else is not fun?   The stupid little buff you get to pick at the start of the game, that you only get to do if you happen to get to the boss on the previous run.  It's like the developer thought, "People love unlocking things, and being able to pick something to start IS fun!  So we'll only give it to you some of the time!"
I know, I'm garbage, haven't played it enough, and you beat the whole game on your first run.  I really don't care.
I like it enough to drop in and play a bit, but not enough to recommend to anyone.  It's just too irritating.  I got my money's worth out of it, sadly it's not something I want to keep on coming back to over and over.  That's a shame.

This review is strictly about Far Cry Primal's performance/graphics and nothing else. So if you're wondering if the game itself is good, look elsewhere.
My specs are as follows:
i7 6700k
GTX 970
16 gigs of DDR4 RAM
Running the game on a 128GB SSD
Resolution: 1920x1080 (1080p)
I'll start off by saying this: crappy ports =/= demanding games. Just because you can't run a game on a toaster, doesn't mean it's badly optimized. The reason I'm saying this is because judging from the ammount of negative reviews for this game on Steam, it's quite clear that a lot of people with outdated hardware haven't really grasped this seemingly simple concept, but anyways... On with the "review".
- On the Very High and High Settings, this game is extremely demmanding, to the point where I can't really get it to stay above 60fps on Very High, using the above mentioned specs. On High however, the game runs absolutely fine, and I've yet to notice a single fps drop after I lowered my settings from Very High to High. This means that the PC port has scalability, meaning that as long as you keep lowering the settings, you're bound to find that "sweet spot", within reason of course (Anything below a 750Ti will have issues running this game at higher resolutions and keeping a stable framerate, for obvious reasons).
- I've already said that the game's demanding but how are the graphics? I personally think this is the best looking Far Cry game to date. On High, the game looks absolutely stunning. Is it Ubisoft's most impressive looking title? I'd have to say no, I still think AC Unity is Ubisoft's most visually impressive game to date, but Primal isn't that far behind, especially when you take into account how great the lighting in this game is, both at daytime and nighttime. Character models are very well detailed, as they've always been in the Far Cry series, and everything look super authentic for the time period.
- Like previous Far Cry titles, everything is customizable, from the HUD elements to Rebindable Keys. It also has a built in FOV Slider and around twelve video/graphics options. The audio part of the options menu is awful though, with only ONE master slider and no options to select between Stereo and 5.1/7.1 configurations. I thought one slider audio menus had disappeared since like, 2002... It's 2016 Ubisoft, come on!
Overall I'd say this is a damn fine port from Ubisoft. No obvious downgrades as far as I can tell (You never know with Ubisoft), and the port seems to cater to a varity of different hardware combinations, like I said, I couldn't get a stable 60fps and all I had to do was lower a few settings and there you go! No more drops, which is pretty good considering the 970 is really starting to show its age. If we're strictly talking about the performance/graphics, and you have the hardware to run it, I'd easily recommend Far Cry Primal.

The game offers great graphics and animations (this includes the huge world everything takes place in), a wide variety of creatures to both hunt and tame, many skills to learn, a great amount of different weapons and tools, many ways of combat, and last but not least: missions and quests. This is not a review, but some comments about my experience with the game. It's going to be a little long, but maybe you'll find something interesting.
It's the first XCOM I've played. Since I read it was difficult (although not as the original from the 1990s), my first playthrough was on Normal. I dont want to sound smug, but turned out it wasn't difficult at all. On the contrary: when I finished, after little more than 40 hours (took me that long because I stalled the last mission in order to get some achievements), the statistics told me I was way above average and achieved things way faster than most.
The reason for that is simple: I'm cautious. I advanced the squad slowly, almost never dashing and always staying on cover. The squad was never clustered, but the soldiers weren't very apart either, so everyone had their backs covered. And I used overwatch like a motherf***er. Overwatch is so important that a button should have been assigned for a batch overwatch, because my whole squad used it at the end of a turn. And, of course, a turn of reloading after a wave of baddies. Because of that (and some beginner's luck, maybe), I had very few deaths on this first playthrough: just four (one of them was environmental), besides the ones in the tutorial.
Another secret, one that I found by accident: a sniper with the SquadSight ability made all the difference. Sarah "Low Rider" Khoury got almost 120 kills in less than 50 operations because of that and, afterwards, of Double Tap. Thanks to those and to S.C.O.P.E., normally her shots had always more than 70% chance of hitting. My other sniper, "Vampire", won as a reward from a mission, had SnapShot and wasn't near as lethal; but he contributed a lot when his psionic abilities were revealed and he made the final mission a breeze by mind controlling several enemies.
The biggest mistake I made was not launching satellites as quickly as I could've. So I lost the support of 3 countries. I could've prevented that. Now I know better.
Edit (July 2016):
My second run was with the Enemy Within expansion. The addition of genetic enhancements and the sinister MEC Troopers made the game easier, but some of the new missions brought extra excitement, specially the EXALT operations (very hard at first) and the exhilarating attack on a ship with a
(the attack against the
was less remarkable because at that point my soldiers were way too strong). And that's the problem with this game: by the endgame your squad is so powerful that the battles become kind of boring. That's why I didn't finish this run: I had every Foundry project completed (I didn't accomplish this in my first playthrough), lots of money, satellites in all but 2 countries, soldiers full of medals (another pack of big bonuses) and enhanced genetically or mechanically and psionically... There was no challenge left.
So came the time to play the Long War mod, which I'm doing right now. At first it seemed like a very hard challenge, because on the inaugural mission half my squad of newbies died by the hand of Sectoids. But so far that was it: all the next missions turned out OK and my squad began to evolve. The only missions I had to abort quickly were the ones in which the big ship lands (the interceptors are no match for them; the battle in the sky seems way harder here), because they're full of advanced aliens, besides the generally measly Sectoids, Thin Men and Floaters.
The coolest addition is the soldier's necessity of rest after a mission, even if they're not wounded. That provokes a greater rotation of soldiers, so you can't rely on your best officers anymore. Also, the ones that manage to survive after being gravely wounded will need a way bigger period of rest. So you need to employ a lot more "rookies" (now renamed Private First Class, like the real American Army), which is cool, because it keeps you on your toes. Another difference is that it's easier to make money, but harder to gather materials (countries make a lot of requests for them and it's impossible to oblige every time); also, you need a lot of engineers to build facilities. There are other cool additions regarding research (you can study the ship you take down), which takes way more time than in the vanilla game, but I'm still fairly early in the campaign, so I'll update this log eventually.
Edit (February 2017):
Combat missions are easier now, with less rookies, even though I'm not very advanced in terms or research (still using bullets). Terror missions are the hardest (in my 1st one in this Long War run, I could only save 6 out of 18 civilians; because of that I'm about to lose South Africa), but I'm managing thanks mostly to Assault troopers with the Close Combat Specialist ability _ they're saving my bacon now, instead of the snipers; the infamous "ship mission" was a breeze this time, thanks to them (Engineers and their grenades are also very well welcome).
What's kicking my♥♥♥♥♥is the fight in the sky. The interceptors are no match for the alien ships; I have way more of them than I had in the vanilla game, but they keep being destroyed or damaged for almost a month, satellites end up unprotected and destroyed. This never happened before and I don't know what to do, I'm spending a lot of money on the fleet, but it's useless so far... I'm not complaining of the challenge, but it bugs me that the game is unbalanced; missions should be harder to keep up with the massacre I'm under.

Hello everyone, I just wanted to write this because I've seen all the negative reviews out there, and I have no idea what most of these people are talking about. I am a huge fan of the Company of Heroes franchise, and I have put many hundreds of hours into CoH1 both before and after if went on Steam. Not everything that the nay-sayers is wrong, but the amount of negative attention this game is getting is unfair to it, and I think that anyone who was a fan of VCoH should give it a chance.
First, I will say that the game mechanics are nothing but improved. Infantry AI is much better, units can no longer be run over by a stray tank and destroy entire squads. Tanks can no longer just roll over an opponent without being supported. Infantry anti-tank abilities (available on all factions core units except the Oberkommando West) will very often damage a vehicles engine, slowing it down to the point where other anti-vehicle weapons can easily take them out. Artillery is dumbed down from the first game, with only a handful of on-map artillery options available. You will not be able to park calliopes outside of your opponents base and win the game with long range barrage weapons. These are all, in my eyes, improvements and make for a more exciting, balanced game.
Navigating the game maps is slightly different now as well. A few things that stood out is how much less important bridges are. Terror doctrine in VCoH could esentially pick a bridge, firebomb it, and destroy it on demand if the munitions were availbable. Now, alternate (but less convenient) routes to the front are almost always available, and bridges can even be repaired before they are destroyed. Infantry can vault over low walls and obstacles too, which is just one more tool available to the player to get to the fight (or away from it) swifter. This also means troops can no longer be trapped on the wrong side of a sandbag wall, they can simply jump over to the other side. This is true for trenches as well, they can leap in and jump out without using the main entrance.
(EDIT-WINTER MAPS REMOVED)  While winter maps were not 100% removed, blizzard effects were removed on all maps. There are still places where you can fight in frozen conditions with heavy snow littering the ground and ice covering waterways, making new avenues for attack that are not present in summer. The removal of blizzards was a good decision on Relics part and shows how this game is still growing and changing. Blizzards allowed for very static gameplay by slowing down all units and encouraging long-range units to sit and camp, whereas the rest of the game demands that your forces be in constant motion, and the faster you can move the better.
The true line of sight concept I mentioned is also a new improvement to the formula. Units can only see what is in front of them, and can no longer draw line of sight through walls, buildings, enemy vehicles, or smoke clouds, making smoke much more useful than it was in VCoH. This makes setting up ambushes and scouting considerably more important and exciting. It is a good feeling for an enemy tank to roll around a corner, only to find out that an infantry squad and an AT gun are in extremely close proximity to it. The infantry squad will almost certainly slow the vehicle with an AT grenade or panzerfaust, and the AT gun will take care of the rest.
But not all was good on the eastern front, and the game did have the flaw of an overabuse of paid DLC. Relic has listened to its fans, and there is no more paid DLC commanders/skins/bulletins (the three prevalent multiplayer unlocks) that you cannot unlock by playing the game. Company of Heroes 2: Armies of the Western Front, unveiled a concept of "War Spoils", a stystem where players will earn random commanders, bulletins (which are static buffs for a specific unit type), and skins simply by playing for a set amount of time. War Spoils is a good idea, but it is poorly executed as the player does not have control over the drops they are getting. If you want to unlock a specific commander, it is very likely you will unlock three different commanders, four skins, and countless bulletins before you get the one you want. You also do not know how much you are progressing towards your next drop, and it does not seem to be connected to win/loss rating.
Still, this formula is a radical improvement over buying those fancy commanders. If you want to play around with new units and tactics, now all you have to do is play more in stead of breaking your wallet out. Want to unlock that German winter camo for your heavy tanks? Better go kill more Communists. Blow up your opponent in style for the low low price of... who knows how much time spent playing the game you bought! The war spoils system is nice, but ultimately I think people will still pay for commanders rather than work for them, as it can take some time. A good improvement on this system would be making it so you can choose what to work towards unlocking as well as the elimination of duplicate war spoils drops, which are by and large useless with the exception of certain bulletins, though even most duplicate bulletins do not function.
All this aside, the game itself is well worth its cost, and is definitely worth looking into for any Company of Heroes veteran, or anyone interested in real time strategy games or World War II history. Armies of the Western Front adds the OKW and American forces into the game, and both these armies bring new soldiers and vehicles (not to mention commanders) to the table, and demand new strategies from Whermacht and Soviet players to combat them. The unit emotes are all great, the sound effects are nice and authentic, and the checks and balances of the game make you end up using every weapon in your arsenal to crush your opponent, resulting in good-looking, authentic armies. The gameplay is fun, it is pretty, the auto-matching multiplayer will usually find you games in less than a minute, and the multiplayer is competitive and diverse enough to keep you coming back. I give it a 9.5 out of 10 and highly reccomend this game.
[EDIT 12/26/15] A lot has changed in this game since I originally wrote this review. I have tried to go back over it and change content as is necessary, but tried to maintain its intergrity. The biggest differences are the removal of blizzards on winter maps, the overhaul to the OKW, which was a good idea but still needs some work as of this edit, and the introduction of the British forces in multiplayer, which brought a lot of new units to the table and changed the games balance.

This is a neat little game with a simple but clever premise: Windjammers (an old battle frisbee game for Neo Geo) meets Smash Bros. It's fast-paced and the action is really fun; it's a real rush to watch the puck zoom around the room, ready to whack somebody. There are so many chances for "ooooh" and "ha, got ya!" moments with your friends - you can bunt the puck up and then smash it down, angle it off the corners, give it some speed and then trick your opponent to jump in the way, etc. You can psych out your opponents and do all sorts of tricks, but when that fails, you can just wait and see who gets hit first (which is just as fun). I also really like the art style here: it's sort of got a Jet Grind Radio vibe, like graffiti cartoons that popped off the wall and started going at it. The designs look a little amateurish, but that just adds to the flavor.
Now, I definitely think that the game is a bit short of content when you consider how relatively steep the asking price is. There are just six characters, and you can only fight against a string of AI opponents or fight against your friends/online strangers. That's it...no bells and whistles, no hidden characters, no story mode, just straight-up fighting. I wouldn't be surprised if someone bought this and felt that there wasn't enough here to justify the cost. If you're really excited about the game or you tried it with your friends and you know that it's the game for you, go ahead and snatch this up, no question. But if you're only just curious about the game, I'd say to wait for a sale or until you see it in a bundle.
I had a similar issue with Nidhogg, a vaguely similar social hour/party time fighting game which is also on Steam, because it's likewise too expensive and thin on content. I don't recommend Nidhogg, but I do recommend Lethal League because of two important differences. 1) Lethal League is just more fun, and its greater depth means that it'll have longer legs with your gaming group. There are more opportunities for tricky plays and getting creative and figuring out how to best utilize each character's special move. And 2) the netcode in Nidhogg is awful, but Lethal League's online play is really nice and silky smooth. If you want to play this game online, you'll have no problem!

During my time with this game, I have found that there are 3 words that perfectly encompass the whole of my thoughts for it. This game is short, tedious, and boring.
Allow me to explain a bit further
As far as gameplay goes... there isn't any. This is a game where you walk around using wonderful rpg maker movement, and talk to people. I can certainly understand if the developers were to opt out of having a combat system, but they need to replace it with some sort of gameplay mechanic rather than just giving me a slightly more interactive version of a visual novel. Having said if the developers had wanted to make the game better without adding anything else, honestly, I would just convert it to a visual novel. The most frustrating/tedious parts of the game was walking around attempting to figure out who I was supposed to be talking to, and this took up the majority of my playtime. When a game rely's on a player's confusion to pad out the playtime, something is very wrong. Also, the story was just kind of there, it was very boring and I didn't really care about it whatsoever.
For those of you who are actually considering this game, and don't want story spoilers as I specifically go over my complaints, don't read this particular paragraph. The story begins with a 4th wall break as the protagonist explains that she is quitting her job and moving to greyfox, which she says is a small sleepy town, but in reality it's more of a retirement home (there is only one remotely young person besides youself, and that would be the bartender). During the opening, there is a very brief section where you are asked to drive the protagonists car. This section pains me to even think about, as the car is just as slow if not slower than the protagonist on foot, and is extremely big relative to the on foot npc's (as it admittedly should be, but bear with me) making it a pain to maneuver into the parking space you are attempting to reach. This particular section does nothing whatsoever to enhance the gameplay or the story more than an autopiloted car would have, it is merely a one off section that adds to the tedium. After this, the player enters the hotel as directed and is told that they will have to wait until an empty room opens up. The hotel worker says that she told the guy upstairs that she would send him some "company" and asks if you would mind doing that for her, and also reccommends you go to the bar to wait until the room is ready. Now at this point two of my main issues with this game are found. First, the dialogue. Nothing can pull me out of a story faster than dialogue that sounds like no person on earth would actually say, and the way this is written it simply doesn't feel like a normal conversation between two people. Some of the word play is off, people not simplifying words as they would in regular speech, causing all dialogue to either sound really formal or really forced. The other issue with this game is the lack of direction given to the player. This opening section is one of the few times I have a remote clue on what I'm doing, and even with this it took me forever to figure out I had to talk to the old lady several times to move the story forward in the bar, and was left for about 15m (which in this game is a long chunk of time)  wandering about attempting to figure out what I was missing to advance the story. I won't type the whole story out here, as the complaints i've just addressed are my main irritations story wise throughout the game, but let's just say the story does nothing to pull the player in, and often times when presented with the choice to kill someone (don't ask, you really don't want to know), it wasn't even my choice as I pressed the next button thinking that would advance to bring up the menu (as it would be in most games) but instead the menu auto popped up and made me select something without even reading what on earth I just picked (I figured it out just in time for the last choice in the game (which i didn't end up caring about, but at the very least I would like to have made the other ones specifically for achievement hunting purposes).
The game is extremely short, which due to it's price isn't actually a negative, however the game could have been elongated in a very non-tedius way with the addition of actual gameplay such as a combat system or something of the like.
Even when this game goes on sale for 2 bits I wouldn't reccommend this game. Save your quarters.

Alan Wake’s American Nightmare takes the best parts of the original game (the atmosphere, the setting, the mystery, and the cast) and throws it out completely; then takes the worst part of it (the combat mechanics, which are only enjoyable against a small group of enemies) and builds a whole game around it. The end product is a shallow, outrageous mockery of the original game, which may only be enjoyable for those who like the simplest B-grade shooter titles, or just thought that Alan Wake wasn’t like Max Payne enough.
If Alan Wake was the video game equivalent of a large-budget mystery thriller miniseries that aired on prime time, then Alan Wake’s American Nightmare is like as if Syfy made the second season.
The original game featured a highly detailed and lush environments and led you through several unique and enjoyable levels. This one has three painfully empty maps with a few objects scattered here and there and buildings crammed together with little coherence. And the maps are recycled three times in the so-called “story” with the exact same objectives, but with some new type of enemies.
You can also forget the memorable supporting cast, here you have the most clichéd evil twin of the protagonist and three female supports, who are so bland and void of all character traits that you will most likely forget their names by the time you see the level end screen.
In some manner this is all explained in the intro and in the (horribly banal) narrative: the whole story is supposed to be taken as some low-budget late-night horror show with all the bad things it comes with. But the problem is: they nailed it too perfectly. It
boring and uninteresting, and in all the wrong ways.
And this leads us to the worst part of the game: it’s nothing, but a huge shooter. The weak story and the non-existent characters are only cardboard decoration to the never-ending shooting. The combat focus becomes even more painfully obvious when you see the Arcade mode in the main menu, which is exactly what it sounds like: you get dropped in an arena and must kill the never-ending wave of enemies.
The only problem is: the mechanic is the same. You still have to shine light on them for several seconds to make them vulnerable, and you still can’t shoot while doing it. So each fight is nothing but a big chase around the empty maps: you try to dissolve shields while dozens of baddies are trying to get you. Sounds fun? Probably not, because it isn’t.
Just avoid it and act like Alan Wake’s story ended with the last chapter of the original game.

Please note that I only played this for 7 hours during the Steam Free Weekend. I have not played the original CoH, but did buy it in the steam weekend sale. I have played other rts games such as all the age of empires and their expansions, command and conquer 3: red alert, Wargame: European Escalation. I played two campaign missions, two challenges, no theater of war (not included in steam free weekend. This is not covered in my review) and leveled up to level 45 in multiplayer.
Company of Heroes 2 is a fast paced strategy game mainly based on capturing points (in skirmishes). It is possible to win by destroying the opponents base, but it is far easier to simply hold the majority of the points. You can play as the Germans or the Russians.
Tactics play a big role in the game. The two campaign missions didn't really seem to have a story (maybe it didn't, I only played two of them and their wasn't really a story there.) But they focused heavily on flanking, so tactics should be a big component of the campaign. The challenges were hard, so I would recommend holding off on those until you are more familiar with the game and the tactics.
One great thing about CoH2 is the fact that you have to use multiple units. There is no one unit that is virtually invincible, and to be effective in skirmishes you have to use a combination of two or more units at any given time. For example, early in the game mortars are effective in eliminating infantry, but vulnerable if the infantry get too close. Using standard infantry to protect the mortars and take points is necessary to be effective.
If you don't keep upgrading technology, you get left behind. The game rapidly progresses from infantry to light vehicles, and from there to tanks. Typically if the opposing team brings out two tanks before you can bring out one, he has an immense advantage. It is always better to upgrade to vehicles sooner rather than later.
Russians are more advantageous in numbers in the game, the germans are more advantageous in technology and damage. (Russian infantry are typically 6 strong, with sniper squads having 2 units. German infantry are usually 4 strong, with the sniper having 1 unit) Tactics for the two are very different, causing you to have a different experience when playing as different factions.
The game is a little dlc heavy with a bunch of purely cosmetic dlcs, and dlc commanders that only offer a slight advantage of the vanilla ones. They are usually remixes of the vanilla commanders with one or two slight advantages. None of the advantages is anywhere near large enough to turn the tide of the battle (unless you have two experts playing or something)
Is it pay 2 win? Definitely not. Totally unnecessary and should have been included in the original release or for free? Absolutely.
Bottom Line: Coming from a non-original coh standpoint, the game is a fast-paced good rts with a focus on battlefield tactics like flanking and requiring combinations of units to win. While it has a bunch of pointless dlc, they aren't pay 2 win and don't really add any major advantages to the players. They should have been included in the original release, but weren't. They don't change my recommendation of the game.

I have played this game only a few hours and already am I hooked. Even on easy this game is hard, I'd recommend that you do the tutorial first. This is a 2D top-down starship strategic fighter game. The object of this game is to progress through sector after sector to complete your mission. Throughout each sector you "Jump" from location to location fighting enemy factions or sometimes getting lucky and score equipment and/or spare-parts(virtual currency). The mission is you have been given vital information to pass on to your federation that will inevitably determine it's fate. Your starship has systems that are upgradeable, all upgrades of systems require upgrades to your reactor(your ships powerplant). Combat is simple but challenging, targeting your enemy's systems such as shields or weapons is an effective strategy. Battles can last anywhere from 30 seconds to a 10 minute intense power struggle if your both evenly matched. After a while you might find the AI predictable, but is certainly doesn't render this game unplayable.
With all this said I highly recommend this game, at it's price I think anyone will enjoy it. I bought it on sale and I feel a little ashamed for paying so little for it.

The idea of a game where the player controls the outcome of the story has long been the holy grail of gaming, but as usual, in the case of Game of Thrones, reach exceeds grasp.
Telltale bills their games as interactive stories, claiming that you control the plot, and the outcomes. In practice though, this means occasionally choosing the dialogue or mashing buttons to make sure someone doesn't die (which turns out to be a pointless endeavour, since this is GoT and EVERYONE dies). It feels like I'm being given the illusion of choice, when in reality I'm being railroaded into a very small set of possible outcomes, where some events are totally unavoidable.
Worse, when I watch the TV show or read the books, it's easy to distance myself from the violent deaths of main characters. When I'm forced to participate, the game imbues me with sense of responsibility, and I feel like I'm leading all of my characters to their deaths; It's depressing.
In the Game of Thrones Game, you either lose, or just don't play.
Whatever this is, it doesn't work well as a story, and it doesn't work well as a game. Save your emotional energy for real life.

First and foremost, I think what needs to be said about this game is that it an exploration game, (Similar to To The Moon, Ib, Mad Father, etc.) that means that this is NOT a JRPG. This isn't mentioned anywhere on the store page, and saying the game was inspired by Chrono Trigger and Final Fantasy 3 definitely doesn't help prove this.
Now onto the actual game, I can't really criticize the gameplay since there's very little actual gameplay. It's just walking about, talking to people, and inspecting objects. I honestly feel that any engine, other than RPGMaker, would be better for games like this, but I guess ease of use makes RPGMaker so prevalent.
So that means what I need to critcize this game on is it's story. To put it blunty, this game feels like it was written by someone who has a very black and white view on morality. Your character decides to move to a town that's famous for an old folk's home, but you run into a mysterious lady that says you should leave. You end up going to sleep, then wake up in a dream world where your character is now old and you then see the world through 4 different people that live in the same town. You spend a day in their life and then need to decide if you should kill them or not. For the most part, everyone, expect for one person, is painted in a horrible light so you'll want to kill them.
The entire premise of the game, felt at odds with each other. The beginning has a weird magicial element to it (They never explain why a magical entity wants someone to not live in this town.), then it just transistions into normal character driven short stories, where the writing for each, with the exception of the nurse, just feels bland and boring (The nurse's story is just spastic and makes no sense.). It's on par with stuff you'd see on a fanfiction site.  Also, despite being less than 2 hours of content, I often wanted to just stop playing this and go play, or read, something else.
Then there's 3 endings. If you killed no one you get the good ending, where
If you kill atleast 1 person, but not all 4, you get the mediocre ending where
Finally, the bad end where you kill all 4 people where
Each ending ends with your character not living in the town, which doesn't make much sense, they quit their job to get away from the hustle of the city and, for some reason, moving to a town requires intervention from a magical being to make the character stop from making that mistake. Unless the character is just actually just crazy, but eitherway it's still not a compelling enough.
TL;DR: I applaud the dev for trying to make a dramatic story about moral choices, but they lacked the writing skills required to make a good story. Meaning this game's only real use is making a profit off the cards.

It doesn't matter how extensive, or interesting a game is, if the mechanics and the combat is terrible. Lost Castle is a beat-em-up style dungeon crawler, but it plays like a cheap flash, or cellphone game.
-Attacks aren't fluid, or cancelable
-each weapon has three variations of "attack" (some moves are a linear teleport, or a food drop for example)
-movement is slow and clunky, even by SNES/Genisis Standards (dodges require a weapon with a dodge for example, you cant do it implicitly, which is terrible game design)
-Even when you learn how to deal with this (I made it to the second level before I quit) the combat just isn't fun.
Mechanics are essential for any beat-em-up. If this game were Mario, the poor plumber wouldn't be able to jump very well. good luck having fun with that.
Make the combat fun if you want to make a good game. It doesn't take more than 20 minutes of gameplay to know the mechanics are horrible. When that's the case, it doesn't matter how good the rest of the game is.

When I started I didn't  really know what I was doing because the game starts of pretty quick in my opinion but after the first couple hours the "story" has much better pacing and it's very nice to just explore the world.It contains lots of content and is one of the best looking mmo's I've played in along time, it has multiple classes each with their own unique weapons attacks and play styles now I mostly play wizard but I have touched upon Dark knight and Musa/maehwa (they are pretty much the same just different genders) and I can certainly say that they are all different. Levelling is very well paced, when you level your stats will increase and you earn new moves by getting points that are earned by killing enemys similar to experience points. This isn't so much a "sequel" as a "remake" of sorts: Alan Wake reimagined for the Borderlands crowd. Whether or not this constitutes an improvement is up to individual taste, of course...
There seems to come a time in every "survival horror" franchise's lifespan when it's time to dumb things down a little...to sacrifice some of that oh-so-sacred atmosphere in favour of MORE ACTION. 'Cause after all, we video game addicts are basically just a bunch of infantile, monosyllabic EEJITS, right? We just like to kill things, essentially; and the more things, the better.
The Resident Evil series cottoned onto this, slowly, gradually, and by RE5 we'd well and truly decided to favour firepower over anything more nuanced, such as making the audience♥♥♥♥♥♥in their proverbial pants and re-check their ammo supplies every time so much as a single zombie started lumbering towards them. Silent Hill: Downpour introduced boxing-style "dodge" mechanics to a series once about blundgeoning things slowly to death with a crude "found" weapon like a piece of pipe; and perhaps appropriately so, considering we now had enemies which danced about like Cassius Clay while jabbing punches in our general direction. Nothing says "scary" like a bout of gentlemanly fisticuffs, I'm sure you'll agree.
The Alan Wake series has seen fit, for whatever reason, to escalate things to the "♥♥♥♥ art, let's kill" aesthetic by the mere SECOND game in the series, but the news isn't all bad...'cause as these sorts of games go, this is actually a good'un. But first, let's get the more negative observations out of the way, with the aforementioned Borderlands reference being a good place to start.
The graphics, while frankly gorgeous, are decidedly more "comic book"-ish a la the Gearbox game, but this is all in keeping with the tone of the piece (i.e. less moody, more cartoon-y), so let's call that a "draw" rather than a negative. Compared to the original, this game also has a much greater variety of guns and enemy types - again, some of you are probably saying "Oh, sweet" at this point - but it also has ammo in such bountiful supply that you barely ever raise a sweat over running out of said goodies, a sure-fire way to reduce the tension and thereby "scariness" of any remotely serious horror game to almost nada.
Furthermore, while the original was a TINY bit guilty of such modern-isms, this entry is SO overgenerous in pointing out where you're supposed to go next that you could easily halve the game time by just ignoring all the little extras hanging 'round the periphery in favour of making a beeline to every objective. In short, you don't NEED to explore all around, and doing so will pretty much just give you a couple of extra weapons (which aren't necessarily any "better", and which you have to throw away existing ones to weild anyway), as well as a handful of oh-so-integral "Achievements"...as opposed to the earlier game, in which failure to search around could very well mean the difference between having enough supplies or not to combat and/or sprint your way through to the next section.
One of the few Silent Hill-esque almost-clichés which the first game (mostly) overlooked was that of deja-vu. Now, I know a lot of you whiny ♥♥♥♥ers who complain about not getting enough monetary "value" out of your games often see this as a cheap-'n'-nasty way for game designers to skimp on programming fresh new locations, but I actually quite dug the way that what you essentially do in this game - SPOILER ALERT - is play a mere three locations/"maps" THREE TIMES EACH, with relatively slight variations each time.
I've read a few reviews which bemoaned this, but the truth is, not only are things somewhat "different" every time you revisit a location (it's a "time loop" thing), but the chapters also get shorter and pacier as NPCs you've met before retain enough awareness of previous encounters with you that they start helping out in ways which save both time and effort, creating a genuine sense of increasing momentum which gave yours truly, at least, sufficient motivation to finish the game in a mere three sittings (which, believe me, is much quicker than I tend to finish MOST games, hahaha).
I actually found the way the whole thing unravels to be quite interesting. (I won't go as far as to say "intriguing", but definitely interesting.) Story-wise, this game is actually quite comparable in quality to the original, it's just the STYLE of presentation which I found less to my liking. This is basically a "third person shooter", when all is said and done, while Alan Wake the first had quite a bit more to it - including tactical decisions such as when to just RUN for one's dear life rather than stand and fight - while in this one, you really may as well just stick around and take 'em all down, 'cause chances are there's plenty more bullets and batteries just five metres away from where you're standing.
Nifty story-telling, charming graphics, and great voice (and sometimes visual) acting aside, this is basically just a "run here, kill some things, pick up something or switch something on, then run back to here" kind of game...though one which fortunately doesn't overstay its welcome (yes, sure enough, the "this game isn't long enough" brigade are sure to complain, even at ten lousy dollars).
One unusual criticism coming from the likes of me, though, is that it's a surprisingly EASY game, at least on Normal mode. Maybe this was partly because I'd just come straight off the more challenging main game and its two hard-as-a-mother-♥♥♥♥er DLCs...but there is at least a Nightmare mode for me to look forward to (though I suspect that one's not going to be TOO much of a strain either, considering I only died in this one about four or five times at most. We shall see).
On the whole, however, this is a really, really good game...one which I would probably think more highly of if my expectations hadn't been unrealistically heightened by the sheer "old-school survival horror" excellence of its predecessor. Oddly enough, it almost seems to be a game targeted more at people who DIDN'T like the first Alan Wake, as opposed to those who DID! Or perhaps this was just meant to be a short, fun, trashy fill-in adventure between Alan Wake and a "proper" sequel, which one can only hope is still to grace this world with its glorious presence. But enjoy this one for what it is, for what it's clearly INTENDED to be, and Bob just might be your mother's brother.

I've almost been in car crashes, and my most constant thought was not my life flashing infront of my eyes, it was a desire for air bags, my last thoughts would have been "Get a car with air bags."

Take on Helicopters is a very good simlite simulation, the addition of an auto-menu for turning the engine on, and auto-hover, make taking off and landing with computer assistance considerably easier, but it's a real thrill to master landing without computer assistance, and one of the many joys of the game.
I've really enjoyed this game, coming from an OpFlash/ArmA/ArmA 2 and Battlefield Desert Combat helicopter flying background, it's not an incredibly detailed sim except maybe in flight model, but I find too highly detailed sims boring, so for me this game works real well.
I can see why people who are masochistic and want the super-real sim experience might not feel satisfied, or have a lust for multiplayer, if that's the case, try DCS World, or ArmA 3, and otherwise, enjoy this :)

I have to make this fairly simple and straight forward instead of a lengthy review.
Overall, positive head nod to Bohemia Interactive in this now aging title as in the words of Monty Python, "and now for something completely different".
IMPORTANT Point:
I predominantly have played this game "offline" as Steam does not detect the game activation if you modify some of the game files and I bypass the standard Steam startup, which I did so in order to ramp up the difficulty to give the flight modeling a much more realistic feel and activated the ArMA 2 modules I WANT TO RUN.
I have easily logged 300+ hours on this game.
Key Points:
1)  If you are looking for a hardcore "simulation" this is NOT your game.
2)  If you are looking for a "light" simulation game with PASSABLE aerodynamics physics for the starting helos this works.(but NOT the medium and heavy helicopters who FMs are skewed),
3)  If you have ever wanted to fly over the Pacific Northwest and Puget Sound with a helicopter, you will like this game immensely, the modeling and collison detect is better than most modern flight simulations.
4)  If you are interested in learning about the basic functionality of helicopters without flight manual complication, this is YOUR game.
Bottom line, the game itself is entertaining, the plot is a little "tired" but still fun.
The Seattle map region is EXCELLENT, with all the actual landmarks noted.
However, if you want to run this game REALLY well, you are going to need a beast of a gaming system, and not because the game is overly "complex".
The ArmA 2 game engine just was never that well optimized for this kind of "simulation" and the overall graphics close to the ground can really get ugly, and SO WISH the engine had been optimized because the modeling and collision detection is GOOD.
Never was flying a "little bird" over Seattle so much of a small guilty pleasure, especially for cheap the game is now with all the DLC packs.
You are going to need a flight control system in order to get the most out of the game.
In a pinch, you can use a Xbox 360 controller, but that unprecise when playing at difficulties at veteran and above.

Please note that I only played this for 7 hours during the Steam Free Weekend. I have not played the original CoH, but did buy it in the steam weekend sale. I have played other rts games such as all the age of empires and their expansions, command and conquer 3: red alert, Wargame: European Escalation. I played two campaign missions, two challenges, no theater of war (not included in steam free weekend. This is not covered in my review) and leveled up to level 45 in multiplayer.
Company of Heroes 2 is a fast paced strategy game mainly based on capturing points (in skirmishes). It is possible to win by destroying the opponents base, but it is far easier to simply hold the majority of the points. You can play as the Germans or the Russians.
Tactics play a big role in the game. The two campaign missions didn't really seem to have a story (maybe it didn't, I only played two of them and their wasn't really a story there.) But they focused heavily on flanking, so tactics should be a big component of the campaign. The challenges were hard, so I would recommend holding off on those until you are more familiar with the game and the tactics.
One great thing about CoH2 is the fact that you have to use multiple units. There is no one unit that is virtually invincible, and to be effective in skirmishes you have to use a combination of two or more units at any given time. For example, early in the game mortars are effective in eliminating infantry, but vulnerable if the infantry get too close. Using standard infantry to protect the mortars and take points is necessary to be effective.
If you don't keep upgrading technology, you get left behind. The game rapidly progresses from infantry to light vehicles, and from there to tanks. Typically if the opposing team brings out two tanks before you can bring out one, he has an immense advantage. It is always better to upgrade to vehicles sooner rather than later.
Russians are more advantageous in numbers in the game, the germans are more advantageous in technology and damage. (Russian infantry are typically 6 strong, with sniper squads having 2 units. German infantry are usually 4 strong, with the sniper having 1 unit) Tactics for the two are very different, causing you to have a different experience when playing as different factions.
The game is a little dlc heavy with a bunch of purely cosmetic dlcs, and dlc commanders that only offer a slight advantage of the vanilla ones. They are usually remixes of the vanilla commanders with one or two slight advantages. None of the advantages is anywhere near large enough to turn the tide of the battle (unless you have two experts playing or something)
Is it pay 2 win? Definitely not. Totally unnecessary and should have been included in the original release or for free? Absolutely.
Bottom Line: Coming from a non-original coh standpoint, the game is a fast-paced good rts with a focus on battlefield tactics like flanking and requiring combinations of units to win. While it has a bunch of pointless dlc, they aren't pay 2 win and don't really add any major advantages to the players. They should have been included in the original release, but weren't. They don't change my recommendation of the game.

This game also doesn't have many trolls, as there is not much for them to do to harm their team, lest they be subject to the working report system (yes, it actually works).

or watch the character videos in-game under the characters profile, as it greatly helps you to learn how each character works.
The community is, hands down, the best player community I have ever played with. If I ever need help, I ask either in team or all chat and I get actual responses to my questions, not some troll spamming chat with 'Darude - Sandstorm'
All in all, I rate this game 11/10, would play over and over and over again.

I suppose if they were recreating how an inexperienced person in King's Landing would be totally lost amidst the web of secrets and intrigues spun around and using them, but Mira is described as smart and a natural when it comes to scheming amongst top-tier schemers.
- I was reading a wiki with plot synopses to see what sort of bits I may have missed on my one playthrough and amusingly almost every paragraph has a sentence with the words "Regardless if you choose..., " or "Even if you choose X over Y action, Z character conveniently comes along and makes Y happen anyway."  That basically sums up the TellTale experience.
- On a technical level as well I had preceisely the same issues I had with The Walking Dead S. 1., and the Wolf Among Us: Not only did my choices matter little by design of the game, but my progress was not properly tracked and I would watch the "Previously on..." montage tell me about a bunch of decisions I never made thereby messing with the continuity of the game I held in my head.
- The game looks okay and I'm not altogether bothered by the characters who move and emote like wooden dolls, but I imagine it might distract some people.
- The unskippable GoT intro was bothersome too.  It may have been jarring change in aesthetic, but maybe they should have just plopped in the actual TV version.  The current one looks like a 1990s 3D job.
- I think a more focused approach may have been better.  Martin has hundreds of pages with which to weave his tales, but these sorts of episodic games don't appear equipped to handle so many characters and locales satisfyingly.  I'm contstantly reminded of hte Walking Dead's docus on a small group of survivors whose relationships strengthen and weaken.  As a result, while the decisions don't affect the plot that much, the decisions took on a hugely personal edge: E.g.,
- I'm sorry TellTale and co.  I know that a massive amount of work goes into these games and for what it's worth I did play it all the way through and wasn't completely dissatisfied.  There were some moments like standing up to Gryff tha really worked, but there's a lot that springs to mind crowding out the good parts.  I'd say this ranks quite a bit below Worlf Among Us, and without question below Walkding Dead S. 1.

As a diehard lover of Game of Thrones and Telltale's history of their projects, I cannot honestly recommend this game for a specific type of players with this specfic perspective - that is mine. Here is why.
Game of Thrones, is a gigantic source to adapt. I'm not even talking about the books here, only the TV series and as someone who have not read the books I don't hold anything against the series or Telltale's game adaptation because it chooses a different path than the books.
The problem is, this game is not for those who already know the TV series and invested in it deeply (the game's timeline is deep in the TV series' timeline, starts with the Red Wedding). For those who are not yet there with the TV series, it absolutely ruins a sh*tload of spoilers, but at the same time it's utterly boring for those who are well past this and watched the TV series far futher already. Remsey kills someone you happen to like in this game, you want revenge? Too bad, you know already that Remsey is untouchable and will survive no matter what, simply because you have seen months if not years ahead of the GoT timeline already in TV. If you didn't, you either don't know anyone / understand anything happening in the world of Game of Thrones because you are thrown in the middle of it, but many important stuff are ruined for you in case you start watching the series.
Now, I wouldn't be against that, but Telltale's game engine really shows how badly aged and primitive it is, because of the content it adapts.
* It worked with Walking Dead, because it came up with all new characters that we didn't and couldn't compare to anything.
* It worked with Wolf Among Us, because it's literally a living tale that is by it's nature supposed to look cartoonish.
* It worked with Tales from the Borderlands, because the original source looks exactly like that (+ TT is far better at bringing characters to life than Gearbox ever will be).
But it doesn't work with Game of Thrones for me, at all. All the well known, loved and hated characters from the TV series are like puppets made of wood, with horribly simplicistic robotic movements and emotions, and the whole wold around them as we know it, dirty, shiny of gold, warm of fire-, blood and love, dark and full of death, is just so... sterile, blank and empty here. I simply cannot get invested with the new characters either (with the exception of a few) because Telltale was(?) kind of forced to copy the idea of a family spreading across the world (e.g. Starks, Lennisters) just so they could show their version of EVERY major location from the TV series.
I can't get invested in a character if his or her every moment just screams he or she doesn't exist because that person is interesting or important, that character so painfully obviously exists only to "put someone there too, because we want to use and recreate that location from the TV series too". It's like everyone has a dozen noname unimportant relatives that are only there for the sole reason to start a storyline in the other corner of the world too, so Telltale can say "we have the Wall! We have those desert cities too! Oh and here is this or that from the TV series!", and the REAL PROBLEM is that almost everyone who are supposed to be the focus here, house Forrester, are just B tier fire and forget sidecharacters in different games. And there are many of them even, to cut the story to many tiny pieces and throw them to many corners of the world.
If you have multiple seasons of a TV series to do that, it's an excellent opportunity for fantastic world building.
If you have roughly 6x2 hours to not only try to do something similar, but copy as many of that world from the TV series, it cannot be helped but most of it will be shallow. But here it's not only supposed to do the world building here, it is supposed to build up about 15 characters for us to care about at the same time, SEPARATED to about 5-6 far away locations... it's not enough time, simple as that. And it really feels like it, because everything is so shallow, rushed and thin.
I wanted to like this game so much. I love Telltale's work, I love Game of Thrones, and I love good adventure games. And I came to the conclusion that I cannot recommend this game if:
* If you are not yet at the red wedding in the series
* If you are just at the red wedding in the series (because if you stop there to play the game, you cannot know what will it spoil for you from the series)
* If you are way past the red wedding, because most of the needlessly forced characters in the game who are (just like the locations) clearly there only to show "LOOK HE/SHE IS HERE TOO FROM THE TV SERIES! HOW COOL IS THAT" and all their lines and everything about them just feel like "desperate-forced-merchendise".
* If you don't know anything about Game of Thrones.
Now where does that leave us? I cannot find any... way, to recommend it, anyhow.
Add that the low quality engine really shows it's downsides here that weren't a problem at all with other material (first I saw Remsey I didn't even recognize him and after that he was shallow and empty too, because you know he is untouchable, and because everything the ACTORS fantasticly do in the source material, is translated here with a primitive engine that makes them... feel dead).

When I first saw people booting up
, only one thought came to mind...
(If the video is removed:  Metal Gear Awesome 2.  Grey Fox going crazy and Solid Snake's only reaction of "GREY FOX!!!")
I was looking forward to trying out
when I heard that it was on sale AND that it included the concept of swapping bodies...how can you NOT have suggestive ideas when that thought enters your head?~
Unfortunately, I was disappointed with this particular title.  I respect that this game was a beginner project and respect is also due in the fact that this game is an RPG Maker title that focuses on the narrative, but there were particular areas where the game practically shoots itself in the foot, one of which breaks the entire game.  (Do NOT give the dog treat to the guard dog from below, it WILL break your game)
It's nice to have checkable objects, but...why is EVERYTHING checkable?  This should not be a feature in an RPG Maker game.  Rule of thumb is to only have areas of interest as checkable objects.  I also heard that this game was "inspired by Final Fantasy III and Chrono Trigger"........ HOW?!  I don't see any of the influence of these RPGs even remotely hinted in this title.
The narrative is also...lacking, though I understand and respect what the developer was trying to convey.  Though it's nothing that you couldn't already learn after reading
, which this story seems to be more of a reference of and how the new age must respect the old age values.  It also gives you that "Walk a mile in my shoes" aspect as you follow disturbed elderly individuals and various stresses that plague their lives.  After experiencing their lives for a day, you are given an option by a death-obsessed elderly woman (
).  You can give in to the elderly woman's death-based suggestions or to listen to your morality which may suggest another aspect may be true.
In the end, you get one of three endings.  A good ending for being a moral person who doesn't feel the elders deserved to die, a neutral ending for giving in to a single temptation of murder/suicide or to have mercy on one soul, and a bad ending for giving in to your murderous temptations...whether they're mercy-killings or flat-out murders as "Payback" for the disturbed.
Now, I can tell that this developer spent a long time working on this title and I respect the effort that went into it.  However, it ultimately feels like a generic RPG (using many generic assets) with a relatively weak story.  To be perfectly honest, it feels like something you would expect for free or at least a pocket-change discount of 25-50 cents.   Not worth $2 (Full price) by any means.  Gameplay will take you about 60-85 minutes as you explore everything.  Speedrunning will be about 20-30 minutes.
2/10  A short, generic narrative RPG that didn't live up to satisfactory expectations.  Easy 100%.

Even though the whole prehistoric may seem like a far cry from the Far Cry series (get it?), it still sticks to the same gameplay mechanics old far cry players know and love. The game plays very similarly to Far Cry 4, but instead of guns, you have upgradable spears, slings, clubs, and bows, which, in my opinion, is a fresh new feature in the FPS genre. However, there are a few bugs in the game, which did force me to restart the game/level because I kept getting killed in the same spot (I got stuck in a tent's wall). The characters are also one-dimentional (including Takkar, the main character), and are nothing like the developed cast from Far Cry 4 (Pagan Min, Ajay Ghale, etc). However, with the introduction of tamable beast companions, you'll probably end up bonding more with your pets as opposed to your tribe.
Pros:
- Great weapons (gameplay, feel)
- Great companions (beasts, not tribe members)
- Hours of exploring in a prehistoric open-world map
Cons:
- A few bugs
- One-dimentional characters
- Repetitive and annoying hunting/scavenging mechanic
Overall, Primal is an extremely fun game that I'd definitely recommend for those who have or haven't played a Far Cry game before, or for those who are looking for a fresh addition to the FPS genre.

American Nightmare still has a similar method of storytelling as the main game, and now features a truly psychotic villain. A slightly modified HUD which has a more modern look to it. There is only 1 type of flashlight. Batteries fully recharge in about 2 seconds. Ammo is no longer scarce, with ammo boxes that completely resupply you with ammo and batteries. These boxes also replenish after a couple of minutes. Since you have more ammo, you will also be fighting more enemies at any given time. The overall game has a more action-arcade feel to it. There is even an arcade mode where you fight waves of enemies and then get a score with leaderboards support.
Bottom Line: If you liked Alan Wake, you need to get this game.
