If you liked Alan Wake you will like this, but it is more combat driven than it's predecessor.  This game basically takes the "Night Springs" parody of the Twilight Zone included in the original, and incorporates Alan Wake into it.  The story is a small continuation of where Alan Wake left off, but more of a hold over than a true sequel.
Gameplay is linear just like in the first game but gunplay is way more extensive.  The fights have many more enemies simultaneously and there are far more weapons to choose from.  Also, for some reason they took away the flashlights passive damage to shadow shields.  Now you always have to burst the flashlight to damage the shadows.  There are essentially 3 maps than you have to replay 3 times due to a "time trap".  I won't ruin the story but I never found it monotonous since the playthrough changes slightly each time.
That said, this is definitely something to just hold you over until a true sequel to Alan Wake comes out.  But fun all the same.

It runs nicely on a single 970, everything set to the max with only shadows turn to "very high".
That being said the game basically follows the same old Far Cry formula, ever since 3 came out, the game has a varied set of characters who are very interesting, while in other cases can be extremely annoying, and corny, but never to the point of making me want to stop playing, or even hearing them, they have that sort of cherishable annoyance, if i may say, to them.
The setting it's probrably the biggest difference between this Far Cry, and the ones that came before it, it's a prehistoric setting that looks absolutley fantastic, despite the complaints of the game being very similar in terms of it's graphical fidelity to Far Cry 4, i think it's completely the opposite, i can see where the complaints lay, but at the same time i think the aesthetic for the most part it's entirely different, as well as the new weather system, which works wonders in correlation with a new mechanic that allows you to set fire to your weapons... and that's it.
There really isn't anything that new, the combat's been improved, and focused to be more "brutal" considering this is the "primitive times" remember, the vehicles have been removed in it's entirety with only now some "companions" that come in the form of animals, or "beasts" as the game calls them, that can be mounted to travel through the map faster, there a lot more fast travel locations, and the map it's a lot more dense, there's a lot to do here, the problem comes from each activity, being basically exactly the same, there's a very basic formula here of just getting materials, upgrading things, taking out bad guys in the middle, rinse, and repeat, in this game i think this "formula" it's being done in an even more aggresive way than in any past Far Cry game, even then tho, strangely enough... I actually being enjoying the game, it's weird, it feels as i was eating a very trashy bag of chips and then i thought really badly of it, only for the next day to come back for more, it reminds me a lot of that episode of Sequelitis, with Egoraptor explaining the whole thing.
Despite all of this, i think Far Cry Primal it's a nice game, it's not a revolutionary game by any stretch of the imagination, but it's a game that i think does just enough for me to think it's a nice game to play from time to time, you're just supposed to be aware that buying a game like this is like watching that one terrible action movie one day just because you want something to watch, you're playing this not because you want to get something from it, you're playing this because you want to waste your time by doing the same thing over, and over again, and gaining nothing more than a virtual reward for your time. Some people enjoy that, some people don't, i think that's fair, i that's fine, if you want an open world game that actually leaves you with something, that actually indulges you in it's experience, that embraces who you are and cares for you not only as a player but as a person, then you can go and play something like the Witcher 3, it's an incredible game for plenty of reasons, but i appreciate that games like this one are part of the medium too, i like the fact that i can have a very meaningful experience like the Witcher 3 when i can, and other times i can have a silly, but fun experience with something like this.
Far Cry Primal might not do anything new, but it does enough to keep me entretained when i just want to get a crack at something, the funny thing it's that ironically, this game being as immature and dumb as it is, it also, i think, showcases the growth of something like gaming as a whole, otherwise you wouldn't be able to have something like The Witcher 3, and this, in the same room.

Lethal League is a devilishly simple fighting game where you hit a ball at your enemies. Said ball speeds up each time you hit it, making each round become real hectic real quick. Aside from the addictive easy-to-play but hard-to-master gameplay, Lethal League is also insanely stylish with some downright freaky characters, settings right out of a grungy anime, and a killer soundtrack.
I highly recommend the game because it's fun and challenging, almost like a demented virtual sport. However, I would never pay the full price for it because it's quite a sparse game. You can play matches against the computer, you can play online matches, or you can take on a 10 fight challenge where each character gets progressively harder. That's pretty much it, other than practice mode. You do unlock outfits for your characters as you play and "level up", which is a great touch. But I can't help feeling that there could have been something more to the game, especially for the price tag. The creators kept it simple: simple but cool characters, simple settings, and a very simple game. That's all cool. But then they kept it simple with the content too, providing as few modes as possible. Usually games based on short and simple events (Super Smash Brothers and Mario party games for example) offer a variety of modes to play in and also some record keeping so that you can see what exactly you did. The fact that Lethal League provides as little of that as possible makes it almost feel like you are playing the beta version of a game.
All that said, I love this game. I just think you aught to get it on a deep discount, or in a bundle. It would be awesome if the devs decided to add some content in an update, or maybe even make a Lethal League 2 which kept the core game the same but added more to the game.

Let me get this out of the way: I'm writing this review after finishing all 3 rebirth games.
The first had a light-hearted storyline and character interaction, and slightly clunky gameplay (+3 party only). Neptune was the main protag.
The second builds off of the first one in many good ways.
+ It's more or less the same gameplay, with 4 people now.
+ Attack Symbol Gains cuts down immensely on the post-game grind.
+ You get a much more stable party this time around (fewer characters leaving your party after you acquire them).
+ I thought the conquest ending was great. YMMV.
The problems are as follows:
- Still have to rely on google-fu to find item drop lists
- Stella's Dungeon can be a hit or miss time sink
- Waaaay too many endings to obtain, and they're all generally obtained by moving shares around. (which is tedious at 5% a battle via colosseum)
- Nepgear is the protag this time around, and she's really boring compared to her sister. Which causes the game to take a more serious/boring turn for about 60% of the game. IMO this franchise is not improved at all with seriousness.
- The translation is a lot more unbearable than the first one. Along with some framerate issues, I ended up having to use community mods to fix some of these problems.
- This time around there's a few sections that aren't fully voiced in JP. I don't play the English dub, but when I did turn it on, only the main storyline was voiced.
- Lots of reused assets.
Overall the gameplay gets some improvement over the first, but the story drops a few levels. I would recommend this game only if you liked the first, and want to play the 3rd (it's really good) as this is the prequel.
EDIT** Other than the content packs, I don't recommend picking up the DLCs as all they do is give you OP items for Nepgear at the beginning, which are later outshined by in-game items anyway.

I'll give Company of Heroes a 4/10 because it's not the worst game ever made, I can think of other games that are more deserving of a 0-1/10 - looking at you Big Rigs: Over the Road Racing. However, I (like many other gamers) feel that Company of Heroes 2 just doesn't live up to the expectations of its predecessor.
What has happened to the sophisticated commander tree? It has been replaced by a new commander system with no choice, except you can choose 5 different commander 'perks' before a match, then when you get commander points it'll unlock perks automatically (as each perk has a commander point requirement that, once reached, the perk will instantly become available). Okay, but at least CoH 2 has interesting concept art briefs between each mission right? Wrong. Those concept art briefs - which I, personally, loved and associated with the CoH titles - have been replaced by 30 second longish cut scenes between a lieutenant (who you never see or hear from in the missions) that is going to be executed for desertion and his old commander talking about the war - CoH 2 has replaced exciting and interesting character development and artistic cut scenes for a character you'll never see in-game and mediocre between mission cut scenes. There's almost no continuity between missions, in the original CoH you'd get a patriotic and informative brief (so you know what's going on in the grand scale of things), but in CoH 2 it's a case of; a minute cut scene that says "the Germans attacked Russia" and "they get really close to Moscow", from there on it's a case of go there, kill them, we won, fight them - then the level design and gameplay follows this pattern, so what may seem interesting and innovative to start becomes dull and representative in later missions. Yet another CoH 2 mistake is the lack of units, you'll have 2 units that you'll ever really use, your conscripts (infantry) and the T34s (tanks), that's it, you do have snipers (that for some reason only use stealth while they're in cover) and mortar teams etc but what's the point when they'll just get flooded by infantry and tanks? If you want to fight for the Germans, you better go somewhere else, because the singleplayer campaign is all Soviet - you can play as the Germans in multiplayer. Well, you can also play as the Germans in a new feature called 'Theater of War' which, basically, mini-campaigns with about 2 singleplayer missions and tonnes of co-op missions (which is a welcome feature) - but when I realized that my friends weren't prepared to pay £30 for a sub-par sequel, I was left with about 4 hours of German gameplay, max...
Well... I think I've said all that I can about Company of Heroes 2. In conclusion, I'm not satisfied with Sega's sequel on what was a milestone in real-time strategy games. It has lost its strategy and has replaced it with numbers. And has many little 'features' that'll drive you mad, like units flashing their player colour when they're clicked on and all your recruited units now start off-map so you have to wait for them to come to you. There seems to be a never ending list of what's wrong with CoH 2, it's like they got the designs and features from the original games and said "these are good, but, scrap them and let's start from fresh without taking any inspiration from the originals". Plus CoH 2, to me, seems to have been Sega-fied.

The Steam release of Quake Live has been a long time coming, more than likely years too late, but with it Bethesda had a choice in how they were going to approach this opportunity to revitalise the game and get new players in.
They could either implement the crucial infrastructure needed by all classes of players (improved matchmaking, party system, tutorials, steamworks integration, even silly things like workshop), or determine that the problem lies in the game itself and try to make it more "accessible".
Unfortunately, they went with the latter. Features such as "weapon loadouts", universal ammo packs and pip timers decrease the crucial aspect of weapon/item control (Quake's defining dynamic). On-screen damage numbers were introduced. A new weapon was introduced to fill the "assault rifle" niche, the one niche that is neither needed nor wanted... and the LG, a crucial core weapon, was nerfed to allow for the new weapon to exist.
Improvements to infrastructure could have added value to their subscription model and help vanquish the image problem that plagues Quake. Instead the misguided, destructive and cynical approach is to dumb down the game and hide the "proper" game behind a paywall (a classic ruleset is available if you subscribe...).
Quake is a strange game and always has been, and is very hard to make work in a large scale in the modern gaming environment - but this surely cannot be the way to do things.
(I have not played the Steam version yet, but have played Quake in its various forms casually for over a decade and played the update that included most of these big changes.)

I've sunk 250+ hours into this game, and it is still amazingly fun to me. I would definetly recommend trying it out and refunding if it doesn't fit your taste. But I honestly think it will. I played Titan Quest back in the day, aswell as all the Diablo Games, and I can honestly say I find this game to be one of the best ones. That's just my personal opinion though.
I'll start of with the two 'flaw' or 'problem' you might find with the game. Personally, these don't bother me, but I'll mention them to make an honest review. You only have one select model for male and female, you cannot edit these. This is an unnecessary addition, since you'll be finding loads of armor that will cover all that up. The second 'flaw' is that initially, getting into the game might feel slow. The masteries and stats might also confuse you a bit, if you aren't familiar with games like this. Let me tell you that I figured it out relatively quickly by trial and error. You can easily solve this by looking at a tips guide or a video real quick. In no way do I find these flaws to be a no towards buying the game though, but hey, to each his own!
All in all, for the price you pay (which is 25 bucks for the full game - Crucible/Loyalty DLC) it's worth every penny. The DLC is put on a discount relatively often aswell. If you can get this game at a discount (like summer sale) you'll probably pay about 12,50 or so. You get so much for so little. (the development team is a small indie team, so they're not that big) they really don't overcharge their fans at all (DLC is like 5 bucks and not necessary at all to play the main game, it doesn't take any elements 'away' and puts them behind a paywall). The DLC's are a horde-mode arena like area added to the game, aswell as another DLC, which has cosmetic items.
If you're looking for a nice game, with good story and well-developed classes with unique mastery trees, this is the game for you. Affordable, and fun to play alone, or with friends!

I had played FC 3 but i skipped FC 4. Few players from FC 4 complain about Primal primarily because of absence of modern arsenal and I agree that bow arrows don't give you the 'oomph'. But that's what this new game is all about. I welcome this completely new environment and I think it was a bold step. The OMG moments of the breathtaking atmosphere are just too many and I couldn't decide on which screenshots to showcase.
The story is linear and uninteresting except for some jaw-dropping 'dejavu' moments of the Beast Master. Yes, I think the interaction of beasts in the storyline saved the game big time! Infact, capturing outposts stealthily without you even having to infiltrate the area is fantastic. Command the owl to tag strategic positions and tame a beast to go for a kill. Or just drop 'bombs' with the owl. The owl attack has a cooldown period for added challenge.
Coming to the arsenal, you have clubs, shards, bow arrows, 'bombs', spears, slings that can be upgraded from the resources you collect in the land of Oros. I just loved spear throwing and bee 'bombs'. I really didnt use clubs in combat but they are extremely useful for a lasting fire in dark places. I have played the game on a keyboard mouse and frankly its not friendly. Slingshots are difficult to operate with it.
Lastly, I was able to run the game for an average of 25 fps on 'normal' settings on my Nvidia Geforce 940m. But extended periods beyond two hours caused bottlenecks eventhough I use a cooling pad and the temperature was kept within 91 Celsius where many other graphic intensive games run smoothly for longer periods.
Summary.
Pros.
+Great visuals
+Immersive environment and sound
+Beast master missions and taming beasts
+Discover breathtaking locations
+Stealth missions when done with only beasts
+Cave exploration
+Beast riding to cover greater distances
+Bonus Assassin's Creed eater egg ;)
Cons.
-Storyline
-Not a really good experience from keyboard mouse
-Frame rate drop for extended periods 100% of the time
-North winds 'buzz' a lot sometimes
Overall rating 8/10

When I bought this game, I've never played any Neptunia games before, and I didn't expect much.
As it turns out, this is one of the most fun games I've ever played. It has a soft story, nice characters, many classic games jokes and if you like turn-based combat, I can say this is the best turn-based combat I've ever seen in a JRPG.
Since the franchise is basically a parody of the gaming culture, the world of the game is like a digital world. Thinking about this, the game has a Plan system, where you can change the aspects of the game by gathering plans and the materials to craft them. You can add powerful monsters in dungeons,  completely change the monsters or items that spawns in the dungeons, unlock outfits, items, weapons. Increase or decrease the difficulty, jump higher, break the damage limit and many more.
That said, there are dozens of optional stuff to do, and more than 5 different endings. When you beat the game, you can start a New Game+ with all the levels and items, and trust me, I'm in New Game++ and there are still stuff to unlock, and I didn't get the True Ending yet.
Since there are ways to alter the difficulty and there are very powerful optional enemies, you can have a very good amount of challenge if you want to, but the game has some hard encounters even if you don't want to increase the challenge.
All in all, it's an awesome game, and I'm only waiting to get the True Ending to play Neptunia rebirth 3.

There are games that try to be good and succeed. There's games that try to be good and sadly fail. Then come games like this, which don't even try. Honestly I wasn't expecting much from a giveaway game but holy #nal f#cking sh#t, that was BAD. I usually talk first about the bad stuff the game has, but I don't think there's much else to talk about.
First and foremost, the graphics. I don't usually don't talk much about them but for some reason the dev (I don't think there were a lot of people behind the creation of this thing) decided it was cool to have anything that's 20 meters away from you blur in a really dumb way while also making any incomming traffic dissapear completely. The map, of which there's only one, also lacks much detail, has holes that lack textures and other weird crap you can think of. It also never went above 15-20 FPS, despite looking quite outdated.
The truck mechanics are also not something to look up to, and being a game that's all about driving trucks, you'd think they would put effort into it. Turning is extremely sentitive, controls are crap and worse of them all, the physics will fight anything you try. Hit something? Then expect your truck to, for some reason, be unable to drive forward for a few seconds, or suddenly jump into the skies for no reason. It also hurts that the camera is controlled by the mouse, which makes the first person view a pain and even worse than the third person one.
Then come the bugs. I would call it the only good part of the game but being honest here, they were only fun when I wanted to see how far I could fly with a truck by breaking the game. It gets even worse when you fly out of the map and drop down to infinity; you'll be unable to use the tow-truck option and can't get out, so you would be forced to delete any progress and start from scratch.
I've played less than an hour and I got the game for free, somehow I still feel ripped off. Developers like these deserve an award that shows in all of their steam page games which warns everone about how bad they are at actually developing a game. I even made a short video about it, you're free to watch it instead of buying the game. At least it's free, instead of being priced at 9,99€ like this horrible abomination.
TL;DR Edition: Don't buy it. Think of Big Rigs but without any possible fun that game could have ever had and filled with bugs.

Graphics
As in all Neptunia games we have gorgeous art in visual novel segments by Tsunako. In gameplay segments: adequate quality for characters and attack animations. Nothing too fancy but good enough.  Sadly ps2 or even ps one quality for dungeons. Massive reuse of assets.
8/10 for visual novel segment.
5/10 for the rest.
Sound
While all Rebirth games share most of the soundtrack, Rebirth1 is the one which uses it in the best way. From the main menu theme to normal battle themes, boss battle themes and power up music etc. You will remember tracks from this game.
8/10.
Plot/Characters
Typical Nep plot. There is some evil and plot can suddenly be serious, but for the most part it's about laughs. Various references to games, anime, manga, japanese pop culture and general humor known to fans of j-things in the form of various tropes.
Another thing is the fact that the games is the remake of the first HDN. The first HDN was expected to be a one-shot. It obviously meant that the plot feels slightly different compared to the later games and while the remake makes changes to the plot it still feels somewhat different. Not better or worse but different. It's somewhat refreshing if your played the other Nep games. Another thing is that this is the only Rebirth game which treats Arfoire as a serious character. Sure the main cast gets to laugh at her, but in this game she is treated ultimately as a serious character and gets some justice in the end.
There is also the matter of DLC and optional characters. The cpu candidates are completely optional and arrive very late to the game (if you even bother with them), they only have an introduction event and that's it. DLC characters are also another problem. While Histoire isn't a problem due to the fact the she is part of the main plot the other characters in the form of Plutia and Peashy (HDN: Victory/Rebirth3 characters) are a problem. The plot doesn't recognize that that they exist and they basically serve as p2win characters for the player in the beginning of the game. IF/Compile have proven that they CAN handle DLC characters and provide plot for them. Look at Megadimension and DLC characters from that game: Nitro+, Milion Arthur and God Eater-chan.
8/10
Gameplay
As is all Rebirth games, somewhat grindy and simple battle mechanic but ultimately somewhat addicting due to simplicity and nice attack animations.
Sadly it has it's difficulty spikes. I think everybody who didn't completely over level his/her characters will remember "that" fight with Black Heart.
7/10
Overall
If you're not allergic to Japan and want a nice character driven comedy you should definitely play Rebirth1. It's a great introduction to the series and one of better games of the series.
8-/10

A very interesting RTS that gives you something to think over. Set apart from the usual genre of RTS games, Company of Heroes 2 is an engaging strategy with a simple but effective story line. It follows the tale of a Russian soldier during WWII who has seen the horrors of war and how carelessly Russian commanders throw away thier men. Gameplay includes placing your men in strategic cover to defend a position, or placing them in cover that they can easily advance past when attacking. It also includes stealth gameplay, as you play as snipers sneaking through enemy territory. Or perhaps you would like a big, booming mission with tanks, planes and soldiers rushing past your men to take the objective, it has this too. With a little something for everyone, I would definately recommend this Historically accurate, engaging and fun game.

I don't understand why there are so many negative comments on the game, I've played Microsoft Flight Simulator X and Longbow II as well as Take on Helicopters, and all have their strengths and weaknesses, but this game felt like I was actually learning to fly a helicopter as some of the fast paced missions stumped me for a bit, but with persistence and saving at key points, it has been a very good experience.
Should I play this?:
If you enjoyment of being immersed in a good story, and upgrading the various helicopters to take on more missions, this will not disappoint.  The military sims are enjoyable, and definitely challenging, but seem to hurry past the learning to fly and focus more on combat.  There is a good mix of civilian, transport, and law enforcement/military missions which allow you to earn money and buy all the upgrades, there can be an issue if you sell a helicopter you need, so picking up extra missions is helpful.  I would do often walk around inspections of each heli before taking on a mission to significantly lower the repair bill.
Realism:
Without a doubt, this is the most realistic feeling physics in a flight simulator I've played to date.  With flight Simulator X I almost feel the helis were an afterthought addition because it lacks certain flight physics that require the constant adjustments required to keep the helicopters in flight.  In Take On Helicopters, the wind and added weight of personnel and cargo changes how the helicopters fly, the copters accrue damage and can feel like a rickety bucket of bolts, giving an impending doom feeling before they ultimately reach maximum entropy and fall out of the sky.  I had more than a few instances where I killed the Huey because I failed to properly finesse them through the trial without burying the throttle and burning out the engine.
Bugs:
Every simulator has it's glitches, I've seen more glitches in Flight Sim X than I have in TOH.  Only one instance have I seen a glitch and pressed escape, then selected skip in the menu.

I have mixed views of Greyfox.
Greyfox has an interesting story where the main characters finds themselves inhabitting the bodies of elderly people from the town of Greyfox days before their deaths.
It is an interesting and creepy idea, where your moral choices will determine which of the three endings you get.
However...
The game is very short. I got about 4 hours out of this game and that was with three play-throughs to get the different endings (minus another half an hour of tea and pee breaks...)
I got in on sale for 79p so the shortness did not bother me, but I would not recommend getting it for it's usual retail price of £6.99.
Though the plot and themes are interesting, I personally find them underdeveloped. The game had a lot more potential with its characters, ideas and moral choices.
The gameplay is a little boring too... there are "mysteries" and problems to solve but they are VERY easy which also contributes to the shortness of the game.
I don't want to say Greyfox is inhrentily a bad game but for its usual price I would not recommend it.
I will say though that is does have MASSIVE potential if its developers decide to remake or create a sequel.

“I am incapable of conceiving infinity, and yet I do not accept finity. I want this adventure that is the context of my life to go on without end.” ― Simone de Beauvoir, La Vieillesse
Greyfox is a really short RPGMaker adventure game that tries to come as an empathy simulation with the touch of speculative supernatural motifs scattered on the side. Fair warning though: pledging catch phrases like "a town with a sinister secret" and "uncover its mysteries" that we encounter in the trailer are quite the misleading advertisement here. Whether there be any sinister secret or a mystery to uncover - or not, it sadly won't be in our heroine's power to reveal in this really, really short adventure. We are just invited for a brief experience and shooed away to carry on with our lives without much explanation.
If we are to arrange a consistent outline of events; here we have a young, dumbly cheery heroine who gets bored of her daily rush in the big city and decides to move into the retirement community of Greyfox. She comes in, greeted by a townful of dull, bitter old people without an ounce of empathy left in them and struggles through some frustrating interactions. Tired by the end of her first day, the heroine is welcomed by a mysterious old lady in the local pub only, with a sarcastic yet intriguing proposition to make: What if you could live their lives and decide their fates? By the touch of this mysterious lady, our heroine is to live an ordinary day in the lives of four town inhabitants and decide their fates eventually.
Let's blurt out the truth: as far as choice and consequence games go, Greyfox isn't one of the greatest, but that doesn't mean that its trash. The game feels mysterious and deep at first, but it unravels to become quite superficial in display, limited and fractured in dialogues; and sadly rushed in its endings. On the other hand, there is also some symbolic figures and attributions to other games in the genre here and there, that may bring a brief smile when encountered. There is quite a good amount of anecdotes scattered around the little town for you to discover, alongside some interesting characters.
One primarily weak point of all display is the narrative. It is depressing, cyclical and limited in its perspective. There isn't much humor - or at least qualitative humor to lessen the burden of the subject, yet the gravity isn't concluded with a consistent argument either. The final conclusion presented by the mysterious lady about the concept of right and wrong felt a bit contradictory for my taste. Please do not go into this little adventure to come across a genuine miracle. You'll get what you pay for: a small story with one ambiguous point of view that will present you maybe something to think about. With better writing, this game could have been much, much more.
Graphics are basic RPGMaker, without a notable soundtrack or any voice acting. Character designs are somewhat curious and interesting though. The first playthrough will take about an hour - one and a half at max - and the game has 3 different endings. Going for all will give you roughly 2 hours of gameplay. Oh, and it has achievements if that means anything to you. For its current price, I think its basically fair deal. If on sale; heck, why the hell not to support an indie developer struggling to create her first game?

Black Desert Online is unlike any MMORPG that I have played. The graphics are stunning, combat is diverse, infrastructure is exciting, and the overall gameplay is something other MMORPG's should strive to gain likeness to. They truly are setting the bar for these types of games.
I particularly like this game not from a game stand point but from a financial standing. It is $10! Such a steal for a game of this caliber! Truly, this game should be a model for other MMO's out there. You don't have to bother with monthly charges in order to play such as the case with World of Warcraft. I have yet to come across an area where it required further purchases.
We are starting to see more and more games turn to this style as it allows a more broader spectrum of players to join in. The occasional gamer wouldn't want to spend a sum of money each month for a game he or she hardly plays, or at least I wouldn't. There is of course the paid currency which are called pearls. They have their own special market for fancy weapons and skins but are not necessary at all.
The gameplay of this game is far to complex to be written in one review so I recommend checking the games mechanics out on YouTube or one of the forums. The combat is truly satisfying and definetly skill based to a degree. Combat runs smoothly and the effects of the attacks are breath taking. Unlike other games where you click on your opponent and proceed to use the hotbar numbers to activate spells or attacks, each ability has a characteristic key combo. I.E. W+LeftMouseButton. Of course there are countless more combinations for other abilities.
The game also boasts an econonmy which is very intrigueing to play around with. The game has places called nodes where you can connect to from large cities and send workers to gather resources or make products. The large cities have houses which can be purchased and used for a variety of things. Factories, storage which effect how much things can be stored in the town warehouse, lodging for your workers, your own personal residence, a shipyard for constructing boats and ships, and crafting houses to name a few. All of these locations are manned by your hired workers which produce the goods which you can then sell to the market for profit.
The PVP aspect is also very nice. The nodes have a tax which goes to the dominating guild. The guild in control gets the taxes that are collected from the node. A rival guild can declare war in order to gain control of the node, thus allowing them to collect the taxes. It makes for some interesting gameplay and scenes where guild members will start fighting in the open world as you watch. Granted you might get killed!
I could go into much more depth but I'd rather much play it so I hope you find this game interesting and do go have a look on YouTube! You won't regret it!

Previously impressed with the intricate story-line, plot and themes from Alan Wake, I was anxious to get my hands on its stand-alone addition, Alan Wake’s American Nightmare. While American Nightmare takes aim at correcting many shortcomings from the original game, such as the horrid combat system, it felt as if it was missing much more.
As stated, American Nightmare supplies Alan with a greater arsenal and enhanced combat system much lacking in the first game. Unfortunately, American Nightmare steers away from the captivating storyline and supplies the gamer with a plot that is more reminiscent of an afterthought or pages of the original script that arguably, should have been left in the waste bin.
Featuring unusual level lay-out I can't explicitly describe without a spoiler, I can say it seems very much a cop out. At times I felt frustrated enough to mutter to myself, “If this keeps going on like this… I’m going to stop playing.” American Nightmare comes across less as an excellent addition to a thought provoking game, and more of an over-hyped, contractually obligated DLC. I would only recommend if you can find on sale, and were a huge fan of the original game and really feel the need to lick Remedy Game’s plate clean.

I did enjoy my time with BDO, however there are a few issues I have with the game that ultimately led me to move on to greener pastures.
BDO has a  beautiful, expansive world, interesting enemy design and excellent combat make for an exellent experience .  There's an incredible amount the player can do.  Crafting, cooking, horse taming and breeding, gathering, fishing, fighting, world bosses, PvP and repeatable quests are all available. It's a sandbox MMO so there's plenty to do if you feel like doing it.
There's little reason to get invested in the game's story, however. It seems tacked on as an afterthought to lead new players from area to area.
Endgame is also very lackluster if you don't want to PvP.  It's all fine and good whilst you're levelling up, seeing new areas, killing new mobs, but when you hit the soft level cap and you've been there, seen and done that, it leaves you with little to do save for dailies and a very slow, repetitive grind.  There are engame PvE dungeons, but they are so far out of the way and require such high levels and top tier gear that they may as well not exsist for the majority of players.
Despite the fact there is so much to do, the game does an atrociously poor job of explaining anything to the player, it's irritating to need an entire wiki and multiple youtube videos just to grasp the basics of how to play the game and how to progress.  Many essential mechanics are never even hinted at to the player or are so easily missed or dismissed as irrelevant that the player can end up gimping themselves for weeks of real time play as a result
BDO also is also like that psychotic girlfriend you used to date.  It'll demand your full, undevided 24/7 attention, even more than other MMO's and woe betide you if you aren't slaving away to please!  Even casual players leave the game on overnight or when they're at work to regain energy or to earn passive coin via fishing.  Not doing so is far more detrimental to your overall experience than you'd  think.
The game is so grind heavy you need evey single coin, every energy point, every bit of exp and consistant advancement just to have a chance at competeing and even then you can spend literal billions of silver, a months worth of grinding and selling items on the chance to upgrade a piece of gear only to have RNG dictate it blows up in your face leaving you with nothing but an empty gear slot and another months worth of grind just to get back where you were!
However the real killer for me was the community and the PvP mindset.  Simply put, BDO has the most toxic community I've ever experienced in an online game, worse than any other MMO, worse even than League of Legends at it's lowest and that's saying something.
The in game chat and naming policies are almost wholly unmonitored and unregulated.  Racism, homophobia and downright offensively degenerate garbage are mixed in with tasteless non-memes and mindless, repetitive spam. Actual questions about gameplay and mechanics are often ridiculed or ignored entirely.  The game cultivates and even encourages a bully boy mindset with unrestricted open world PvP that leaves everyone but the best geared players squabbling over scraps.
Anyone with more levels and better gear than you can and will butcher your character for whatever reason they deem relevant and you will have no way to fight back.  You simply cannot farm mobs in many end game areas of the world unless you get very lucky.  Geared players will often kill you  simply for passing through these areas in case you might decide to attack and kill 'their' mobs and take 'their' loot and exp.  Even farming resources , like cutting trees or mining rocks in the same area as another player is likely to see you casually murdered if they think they can beat you.  Don't even go afk to the bathroom whilst standing in a non-safe area unless you want a 50/50 chance of coming back to a dead character.
To compete at this level , as I said, you MUST dedicate your life to the game.  High level players have such a massively insurmountable head start over new players than unless you do no-life the game intensively for months or get incredibly lucky with drops, you will NEVER be able to compete. Or pay real money to catch up fast.
One of it's most debated points is the the fact that BDO IS Pay to Win.
I'll re-iterate that point. The game is Pay to Win.  This is NOT opinion.  It is FACT.   Many naysayers of the P2W arguement would claim the game is only pay for convenience.  Pets to pick up loot, costumes to give more exp, weight increases to carry more items and so on.  Some of these things can be obtained via the in game currency market, others cannot and in a game where every single coin and exp point is valuable, a player who spends real money for conveniences so they  can spend less time farming to earn that level or upgrade will have a massive advantage over a player who won't.
More than that, costumes and pets can be sold for silver and then used to buy top tier gear from the marketplace, gear that a non paying player may have to grind for months to obtain and still never be able to afford. Even if this silver is used to buy upgrade tems, replacement items if upgrades fail and so on, it can shave off weeks and weeks of farm time. There are also some items and services that are impossible to obtain unless real money is spent.
Even the most adamant defenders use the arguement that 'It would cost thousands to fully upgrade you with the best gear' so it's not pay to win.  However by that admission alone they acknowledge you CAN buy the best possible gear with real money if you're willing to pay for it.
This game is all about the competitive PvP scene and you CAN use real money to gain an immediate advantage over someone who will not spend money.
I myself may play from time to time in the future with friends or just to revisit old areas and level up a new character, but I will never set BDO as my main, go to MMO because of this reason and the atrocious community.
So with all that in mind, if you want to experience it, wait for a sale, spend nothing in the store, get to soft level cap (56) whilst experiencing everything that makes BDO fun ,then move on unless you decide that the rancid community, putrid attitudes and extremely lengthy months long grind that can be removed by spending real money don't bother you.

At the beginning, I found the loop repetitive, but enjoyable. I had to put some thought into my characters' strengths and weaknesses, some of the enemies were challenging, hunting down the item drops and crafting new gear was a decent enough carrot to keep me going. Then I reached the point where I had to fight the same battles dozens of times to get all the drops, and after a point none of them were useful to me. It took me 30 hours to get halfway into the game, and I was getting bored with it.
Luckily, I realized that you can hold the left shoulder button to skip all the battle animations, which made the game go about 75% faster. My strategy had turned into using only rush attacks and building enough exe meter to kill everything on the screen by turn 2 or 3 every combat. I would occasionally have to heal, which is the most interesting thing that happened for the rest of the game.
Of course, once I realized how nice it is to skip the animations, it was only a matter of time before it dawned on me that there was no good reason not to skip all the cutscenes and dialogue too, so that cut out another 20% of the game. The remaining 5% was walking around identical environments, fighting identical enemies, watching numbers go up, feeling dissatisfied about how quickly they were going up, and grudgingly doing the next thing I had to do to make the numbers keep going up. I finished the second half of the game in 6 hours.
The best thing about the game is that it ends, which is more than you can say for most games in the idle game/clicker genre, but all I got for the $6 I paid when it was on sale was 36 hours I didn't have to spend thinking about anything else. If you're completely miserable and there is no alcohol and no drugs available, there are worse ways you can numb your brain for $6. Hyperdimension Neptunia is better than huffing paint, but just barely.

Hyperdimension Neptunia Re;Birth2: Sisters Generation is a remake of a 2011 RPG game released on the PS3, and a sequel to the first Re;Birth game. Originally a PS Vita game, it was later ported to the PC and released on Steam.
Just like with Re;Birth1, it's a unique take on the idea of "Console Wars" with every console being anthropomorphised into a "Goddess". However, in this world, called Gamindustri
the four Goddesses battled the Arfoire Syndicate of International Crime, however they all lost to CFW Magic, the leader of the organisation, and together with the main heroine, Neptune's sister by the name of Nepgear, were sealed and kept in a coma in Gamindustri Graveyard. After three years of ASIC running rampant and ruining the economies of all the nations, Compa and IF with the help of Histoire manage to wake and free Nepgear, and they begin their journey to find the Mascots, other CPU Candidates (based on portable consoles), and free their older sisters.
The gameplay is basically your typical turn-based jRPG with minor tactical elements. Your characters and enemies take turns performing attacks, using abilities or items. It's rather simple to get a grasp if you played any other turn-based RPG. Outside of dungeon exploring and fighting, you can use shops, view the gallery, accept and complete quests, or use special "Plans" to add or modify existing content in the game. The difficulty feels just right - it's not as hard as old-school jRPGs, but also not easy enough that you will be bored (unless you specifically overlevel your characters for the upcoming fights, or use the horrendously overpowered
sword). The game even hands you certain Plans that make the enemies tougher or easier, so there's always some way of tuning the difficulty a bit if you want a challenge or - the opposite - want to focus on the story. Majority of the content is grind-based, however, so if you care about exploring everything, you'll have to level up your characters quite a lot. That being said, the general progression has been improved upon in comparison to the first Re;Birth game - you don't have to grind nearly as much to get past certain boss fights.
The story is quite engaging, with you traveling and exploring different lands, attempting to get the help of the Mascots to gain enough power to free the Goddesses from their prison, interspersed with jokes about gaming cliches, breaking the fourth wall, and all sorts of humor. Of course, it's full of fanservice in one way or another, but what would you expect from a game that creates Moe Anthropomorphisms of game consoles?
The graphics are good. You might notice blurred textures here and there, but it's nothing big, and it's pretty to look at. The only reason you might not like it is if you don't like anime style.
In the sound department, we get mostly electronic music or rock, with quite a lot memorable or downright awesome themes. It's definitely worth listening to even outside the game.
As far as the DLC goes, it's kind of a mixed bag. The "additional content" DLC, when all of them are purchased, introduces a lot of new dungeons and Colliseum battles, while extending the level cap from 99 to whopping 999. But, as you can guess, all of this content is purely grind-based, so if the only thing you care about is the story and not watching your characters grow stronger, I would suggest against buying this DLC. Also, there are a lot of DLCs that make the game easier in one way or another, like giving you plans that increase the EXP you gain and such.
The game also pretty much requires New Game+ in order to unlock everything, since one playthrough does not yield enough MB (Megami Bytes) to craft every Plan you can get.
Overall, this is a great game, featuring adorable, likeable characters, nice graphics, great music, interesting storyline, as well as lots of humor and content. I heavily recommend it to anyone who likes jRPGs that don't take themselves too seriously or cutesy games.

I'm dropping the game 10 hours in, after beating the first two chapters. I think it's enough to have a taste of what it is. I'm sure people who gave it an Overwhelmingly Positive rating had their reasons to love it -- here are my reasons not to.
Like many JRPGs, this game is mostly character-driven. The main character has two main traits: she's hyperactive, and she loves to eat pudding. That's it, there's nothing more to her. Other characters are just as shallow. We're playing as a bunch of dumb girls who just don't shut up, tearing the player's ears with extremely silly banter in extremely high-pitched voice. Not that it's bad by itself, but it's written poorly. It's probably supposed to be cute and funny. It's not. Don't expect Azumanga or Lucky Star level of writing. They are just annoying.
The plot is beyond nonsense. For a bit, it was cool to see a meta story full of fourth wall breaking jokes, but after a while you realize it's just a gimmick. The game throws pop culture references at you with no rhyme or reason. It's a JRPG equivalent of Scary Movie 5.
The gameplay is... Okay, I guess. It's grindy, it has some room for strategy, it's more or less engaging... Not better or worse worse than in most turn-based JRPGs. By itself, it's not bad, but you can enjoy more or less the same in games with much better story and characters.
The dungeons are tiny, ugly and very lazily made. They are just bunches of corridors with monsters hanging around.
Lesbian romance as a core mechanic is cute, but to care about characters' romance, I need to care about characters themselves. For that, again, they need to be likable, not obnoxious. And it's more teasing than actual romance anyway -- again, don't expect to read anything like SonoHana here.
If you like ultra-cheesy romantic comedy anime, you'll probably like this game too. If you don't -- beware.

I don't like JRPGs. I don't like visual novels.
This is a visual novel JRPG... thing. I love it. Why? The characters are relatable because you have to live through their struggles with them as your proxy. But why is the gameplay tolerable?
Well...
There's a sword in the DLC that totally destroys the progression curve in the game, and its ♥♥♥♥ing fantastic. No, seriously. I'm not kidding. I'm a gamer of two realms, one of action and one of story. I like multiplayer competitive games such as World of tanks, and story-driven games like Bioshock and System Shock 2. Grinding for hours and hours on end isn't something I have time for.
Very minor spoilers ahead, stuff you'll see in the first five minutes:
That DLC sword cut the entirety of the game's grindtastic feel out, made me feel like a baddass and I roleplayed (ACTUALLY ROLEPLAYED) as NepGear, the protagonist, being actually powerful enough to take on the big bad from the get-go, but she didn't have the confidence.
This actually plugs up a few plot holes, such as why NepGear was the only one to go with the other main CPU goddesses to fight the big bad in the first place. The very first cutscene in the game shows the main CPU characters being stomped into the dirt when you (probably) spent the entirety of the last game, which took me 50~ ish hours to complete. Most of that was boring slog grinding.
One has to assume that battle-hardened warriors wouldn't take a squishy newbie into such a critical battle, so therefore she must have been talented enough to risk taking her to the big bad fight. No, you can't say that it was for a numbers advantage, because they didn't take the other CPU canidates.
Its also worth noting that litteral goddesses should be able to outright crush low-level monsters and people with minimal effort, delegating other characters to support roles.
This is the first time I've ever seen DLC improve a game in such a profound manner.

Played through this with my girlfriend who enjoys the series tremendously, and I think we both found it to be mostly a flop. I have a hard time as is with most of the TellTale Games as they don't do much for me. Your decisions never feel meaningful, and you feel more like you are on the rails of someone ELSE'S story, not your own. All of the action scenes in the game are QTEs based on the same six keys, and there's no originality in any of it.
Where I feel the game could have shined, but flopped was the original stories of the Forresters. GoT is a grand, robust story with tons of lore and rich history where, quite literally, anything is possible. Instead of blending the Forresters in with that, they are given by far the most bland history and nearly zero importance within the realm. They don't ever feel like they have any presence, and none of them ever get interesting.
This is not to say the game is bad technically; it plays well (controls are easy enough, that is), looks good, sounds great, and the likenesses of characters in the show are nearly spot on. Also shout out to the VAs for coming back to reprise their role in this game. If you're looking for some fan service, or an excuse to nab yourself some sweet Jon Snow wallpaper, this is the game for you. Otherwise, give it a hard pass and spend your money on obtaining the show on DVD/Blu-Ray.

I did enjoy my time with BDO, however there are a few issues I have with the game that ultimately led me to move on to greener pastures.
BDO has a  beautiful, expansive world, interesting enemy design and excellent combat make for an exellent experience .  There's an incredible amount the player can do.  Crafting, cooking, horse taming and breeding, gathering, fishing, fighting, world bosses, PvP and repeatable quests are all available. It's a sandbox MMO so there's plenty to do if you feel like doing it.
There's little reason to get invested in the game's story, however. It seems tacked on as an afterthought to lead new players from area to area.
Endgame is also very lackluster if you don't want to PvP.  It's all fine and good whilst you're levelling up, seeing new areas, killing new mobs, but when you hit the soft level cap and you've been there, seen and done that, it leaves you with little to do save for dailies and a very slow, repetitive grind.  There are engame PvE dungeons, but they are so far out of the way and require such high levels and top tier gear that they may as well not exsist for the majority of players.
Despite the fact there is so much to do, the game does an atrociously poor job of explaining anything to the player, it's irritating to need an entire wiki and multiple youtube videos just to grasp the basics of how to play the game and how to progress.  Many essential mechanics are never even hinted at to the player or are so easily missed or dismissed as irrelevant that the player can end up gimping themselves for weeks of real time play as a result
BDO also is also like that psychotic girlfriend you used to date.  It'll demand your full, undevided 24/7 attention, even more than other MMO's and woe betide you if you aren't slaving away to please!  Even casual players leave the game on overnight or when they're at work to regain energy or to earn passive coin via fishing.  Not doing so is far more detrimental to your overall experience than you'd  think.
The game is so grind heavy you need evey single coin, every energy point, every bit of exp and consistant advancement just to have a chance at competeing and even then you can spend literal billions of silver, a months worth of grinding and selling items on the chance to upgrade a piece of gear only to have RNG dictate it blows up in your face leaving you with nothing but an empty gear slot and another months worth of grind just to get back where you were!
However the real killer for me was the community and the PvP mindset.  Simply put, BDO has the most toxic community I've ever experienced in an online game, worse than any other MMO, worse even than League of Legends at it's lowest and that's saying something.
The in game chat and naming policies are almost wholly unmonitored and unregulated.  Racism, homophobia and downright offensively degenerate garbage are mixed in with tasteless non-memes and mindless, repetitive spam. Actual questions about gameplay and mechanics are often ridiculed or ignored entirely.  The game cultivates and even encourages a bully boy mindset with unrestricted open world PvP that leaves everyone but the best geared players squabbling over scraps.
Anyone with more levels and better gear than you can and will butcher your character for whatever reason they deem relevant and you will have no way to fight back.  You simply cannot farm mobs in many end game areas of the world unless you get very lucky.  Geared players will often kill you  simply for passing through these areas in case you might decide to attack and kill 'their' mobs and take 'their' loot and exp.  Even farming resources , like cutting trees or mining rocks in the same area as another player is likely to see you casually murdered if they think they can beat you.  Don't even go afk to the bathroom whilst standing in a non-safe area unless you want a 50/50 chance of coming back to a dead character.
To compete at this level , as I said, you MUST dedicate your life to the game.  High level players have such a massively insurmountable head start over new players than unless you do no-life the game intensively for months or get incredibly lucky with drops, you will NEVER be able to compete. Or pay real money to catch up fast.
One of it's most debated points is the the fact that BDO IS Pay to Win.
I'll re-iterate that point. The game is Pay to Win.  This is NOT opinion.  It is FACT.   Many naysayers of the P2W arguement would claim the game is only pay for convenience.  Pets to pick up loot, costumes to give more exp, weight increases to carry more items and so on.  Some of these things can be obtained via the in game currency market, others cannot and in a game where every single coin and exp point is valuable, a player who spends real money for conveniences so they  can spend less time farming to earn that level or upgrade will have a massive advantage over a player who won't.
More than that, costumes and pets can be sold for silver and then used to buy top tier gear from the marketplace, gear that a non paying player may have to grind for months to obtain and still never be able to afford. Even if this silver is used to buy upgrade tems, replacement items if upgrades fail and so on, it can shave off weeks and weeks of farm time. There are also some items and services that are impossible to obtain unless real money is spent.
Even the most adamant defenders use the arguement that 'It would cost thousands to fully upgrade you with the best gear' so it's not pay to win.  However by that admission alone they acknowledge you CAN buy the best possible gear with real money if you're willing to pay for it.
This game is all about the competitive PvP scene and you CAN use real money to gain an immediate advantage over someone who will not spend money.
I myself may play from time to time in the future with friends or just to revisit old areas and level up a new character, but I will never set BDO as my main, go to MMO because of this reason and the atrocious community.
So with all that in mind, if you want to experience it, wait for a sale, spend nothing in the store, get to soft level cap (56) whilst experiencing everything that makes BDO fun ,then move on unless you decide that the rancid community, putrid attitudes and extremely lengthy months long grind that can be removed by spending real money don't bother you.

Ever wondered what it would be like to run your own island as a dictator? Well no worries! Now you can with Tropico 4.
The humor in this game is stunning and several months down the line is still making me chuckle, with obvious rips on the cuban missile crisis and similar world incidents.
Some of the humour can be taken as racially insensitive if you're completely incapable of understanding using stereotypes to comedic effect, and if you are one of these people; walk away from this game now and save everyone your ♥♥♥♥♥ing.
As with other simulation games how you handle your dictatorship is up to you, run the country into the ground, or provide free healthcare for all and tend to the happiness of your citizens!
You will have to deal with several factions, both within and without your country, with the U.S and U.S.S.R being the most threatening of the foriegn powers- mostly due to their ability to invade them should you♥♥♥♥♥♥them off too much and swing to much towards capatilism or communism (or for any other number of reasons), however unlike many other faction systems, this is intuitive and with enough effort it's perfectly possible to balance both factions and keep both happy.
Keeping your citizens needs up becomes progressively difficult as more and more people immigrate to Tropico to live under you, your excellency. But the curve is great fun to keep on top of and not so difficult as earlier sims (Sim City 2000 looking at you buddy).
Overall, this game combines great mechanics and fluid building with awesome humor, the graphics arn't the shiniest thing out there, but to be honest; they didn't need to be. With everything else I was more immursed in keeping my population happy enough to vote for me in the next election (My reign will  be unbroken!).
So in conclusion, unless you're an SJW with a stick up your tush, you'll probably love at least one feature of Tropico and the humor alone makes it worth the buy. So stop dawdling and run your island already.

Reaching level 20 takes 1-2 days for begginers.
After reaching that milestone you will be offered to purchase extra inventory & weight carrying limit boost for real cash (not a 2$ purchase but a whole 10$. For each boost).
If you don't buy extra storage - be prepared to lose a lot of time traveling to various warehouses arround the map to store items in their small limited storages. Then, of course, you need to travel back to each individual town to utilize your coins and valuables - since you can't store everything in one town without purchasing Warehouse storage boosters. For real Cash.
You will quickly realize that despite the beautiful graphics this game lacks anything that makes an MMO. Quests are for the large majority some go-fetch or go-farm-mobs for mediocre loot. Really mediocre loot. most of which gives less than 10% the xp you would get if you went and killed some mobs of your level.
Speaking of killing mobs. Be prepared to lose a fair percentage of your RNG based loot simply because you didn't have time to loot it off the ground.
Loot dissapears after barely 30seconds of the mobs death. The only way to avoid manually spamming your loot key is to purchase pets. For real cash. Each pet is arround 10$ and you need to merge two pets if you wish to have a RNG based chance to upgrade your pets Tier, and therefore its looting capacity. Each pet can reach Tier 4. Meaning if you ace your pet upgrade you only need to buy 8 pets to have four Tier4 pets. Only 80$! But from what every person i've spoken to has said; nobody aces their pet upgrades. Everyone i have spoken to has spent a minimum of 200$ on pets alone.
Just so their loot won't despawn.
TL;DR - Beautiful game but lacks a huge amount of basic components that are required for someone to have a decent gameplay, quests are nothing fun to do but rather something you finish quickly to be able to get back into the world. I would strongly recommend avoiding this Candy-Crush on steroids that tries to drain your bank account with numerous pop-ups and restrictions to basic gameplay if you don't.

TL;DR
Greyfox RPG is not necessarily a "bad" game, but it's not good either. It's not the worst rpgmaker game on steam, but it doesn't have much content to be interesting or give a lasting impression.
What I like best in Greyfox RPG is the theme. You basically control 4 different characters in the game and make choices about whether you think they should live or die. It's an interesting mechanic and idea, especially because it's unique, but that's about the best the game has to offer.
Graphics are fairly basic for this kind of game, though by no means ugly, and dialouge is just okay. Gameplay is dull though. You do little besides walk around, talk to people, and collect items. It's not a bad system by any means, but if the characters and story are bland, which in all honestly, they are, it's a bad idea to have little gameplay. Each full playthrough, if taking your time, will last about an hour or so. I did a speedrun for leftover achievements which took about 20 minutes.
I would not recommend this game unless it's onsale, and even then I'd recommend it for seeing the theme of the game (which would be great for psychologial/thriller types) or for the easy 100% or trading cards. It is somewhat misleading to call it an RPG because it gives the player a certain expectation in their mind. This game, while having an interesting concept, does not utilize it to its fullest potential. At the end especially, it tries to be deep and complex, but gives no reason or explanation why the player should care. I will say though, that the 2+ hours I spent on this game was a waste of time for me.

A fun spin-off to the original Alan Wake (though it does actually continue the same story, so you could take this as a sequel as well) that manages to lose some of the narrative charm, but improves on the combat in almost every way. The story is so so, having you play through the same three areas three times across all the acts, which got tiring after the second time through. There's an explanation for why you do it, but seeing the same areas across 6-8 hours is disappointing. On the bright side, it is less linear than the original, but that's only if you care to search for collectibles (only manuscript pages this time around).
The new arcade mode is a welcome addition, though, which has you playing through 10 minutes as waves of Taken attack your position. Most of the maps provide one position that you can abuse if you're just looking to 3 star the levels, but that's a choice you can make so I have a hard time complaining about it.
It's not Alan Wake 2, but still worth your time if you're looking for more Alan Wake.

I absolutely adore the Alan Wake series, but this one really let me down. Its narrative is related to the rest of the series, contrary to my initial reaction, and it drops some interesting tidbits about what's happening outside Alan Wake's insane dreamworld, but much of the dialogue and voice acting is pathetic (with the exception of the guy voicing Mr. Scratch and Alan). I did not like the shift in tone at first, but eventually it was justified by the narrative. That said, I really hope they return to the darker, horror-based tone of the rest of the series for the next true installment (which I fear might not come for a while). The graphics rival those of the previous entries, but the cinematics are cheesy live action video clips that are at times cringeworthy. Fans of the series who are craving to find out what the hell happened in that huge cliffhanger at the end of the first one and its subsequent DLC should definitely give this a try, just to hear the juicy hints about what actually happened. That said, Remedy needs to finally bring this story back into the real world and answer some questions, rather than keep producing hints about what is actually happening in this story. Otherwise I fear that one of my favorite tales in gaming might just fly off the rails.

Alan Wake's American Nightmare is a fun game. But compared to its predecessor, it is definitely not as good. It doesn't live up to the first Alan Wake, mainly because they didn't put as much effort into it.
On the good side of things, Alan Wake's American Nightmare presents a brand new story that is very interesting, but it is a bit of a stretch from the first game. The weapon system is fun, making you collect manuscript pages to unlock new guns. The enemies are also new, improving on the plain minions from the previous installments. They introduce an all new Arcade Mode as well, and it provides entertainment for those that have finished the Main Story. Plus the game improves on the graphics, looking better than ever.
But, there are some bad things. The story is extremely short, especially taking into account you go to the same areas 3 times. Yes, it is a part of the story, but they should've considered making it more interesting. Increasing the difficulty each time isn't going to win you Game of the Year. The story in itself gets pretty boring. Fans of Alan Wake will enjoy it more, but it just doesn't pull you in. It doesn't do very much to keep your interest, relying on the gamer to finish the game just because they paid money for it, and they should get their money's worth. The new characters (everyone except Alan) are not that enticing either; they don't make you sympathize/get attached to them. And finally, the game is easy. I beat the game in three hours. That's just unprofessional.
It may sound like I hate the game, but I don't. The story is an episode of Night Springs that Alan wrote, putting Mr. Wake in a time loop set by his dark side. Alan must perfect everything in order to defeat his evil self, or be sent back in time to relive the defeat all over again, until he suceeds. The ending is decent, and it isn't that bad of a story overall. But it fails to make an impression that rivals the previous game or any other best seller. There is some replay value, but not much. The Arcade Mode is pretty much the only reason to go back to the game.
In summary, this game is for fans of Alan Wake. So make sure you've played that one first. The game has an okay story, but some great improvement, like new enemies and better graphics, but it just isn't as good as the first.
Score: 7/10 - Good

A highly addictive game of strategy on intersecting tiers.  The immersive music is a high point, and it's also highly customizable. However, its difficulty settings can be frustrating; Normal dumbs down the AI, and the next step up, Classic, is prohibitively harder if you don't fully understand how combat plays out.
You may find yourself in a position where you can't go back to playing Normal, but can't have fun with Classic where perfect runs are ruined from units getting one-shotted out of nowhere.  But that is the point of XCOM - there are no perfect runs in war, there is only calculated risk.  It takes a lot of work to approach a suitable playstyle, and for a time, I gave up.  But it's a testament to how compelling XCOM is that I gave it another try, over and over, until I developed the necessary skills.  The game also encourages multiple runs through a generous variety of mode settings.
Faithful to its roots, XCOM is still the most fun strategy game I've ever played.  It's the ultimate game of strategy, and one I could play forever - indeed, I am already doing that on a daily basis.  Every game and every mission is a fresh chessboard, just waiting for you to sink your teeth in.

This game is an MmoRPG that is heavily focused on making money, way more than it has to do with actually fighting or leveling up. At the beginning of the game all you will do is grind until you have reached "awakening" which is essentially the point where you get to use a main MAIN weapon and unlock new abilities. The rest of the game you will spend trying to make money, or if you are in a guild, wasting time doing contracts and occasional node wars.

Don't worry it is not complicated and you get the hang of it quite quickly. The effects from your abilities feels fast, and powerful. - Visually beautiful and grand
- Roleplaying elements
- Good community

- Alt accounts are rewarded
The biggest flaw with this game is it's learning curve. I get it Mmo's have learning curves, but it is not the curve it's self that is the problem, it is that things that could easily be explained are not, and it is done through shear laziness of the developers. To give you an example, lets say you decide you want to mine gems for money. You go out, buy a pickaxe, and go to a mine where emeralds spawn. You can tell they can be mined and are ready to be mined because of a shimmer. You go over them and press "r" and nothing happens. So why can't you mine it? The game doesn't tell you, it doesn't even tell you that you can't mine it... just nothing. The reason is either your pickaxe is too low, or your gathering is too low. How could this be solved, by having a notifcation pop up that says why you can't mine. Instead you have to sift through multiple forums to find you that you need to be "prof 5". What does "Prof 5" mean? What is that referring to? And so on and so on. You will literally have to look up the most simplest tasks all the time. I could go on and on with examples of where this game fails to tell you basic information, that could be solved with 1 line of coding.
One of the only things this game mildly teaches you how to do is enhancing equipment to +15, anyways... What you need to know about that is... DONT DO IT. If you talk to anyone who has played this game, the first thing they will tell you is, anything you need you should just buy, because you will spend infinitely more trying to upgrade your equipment. You can make money from multiple things in this game, but not enhanced gear. You can sell if for a lot, but not nearly as much as if you just sold all your black stones (enhancing resource). This is probably one of the worst parts of the game, seeings as it discourages players from creating weapons and seeings as selling them will always put you at a net loss.
The market is pretty awful too. The game is full of hidden stats, and in the market there is a really big one. So pretty much any item that has constant listings will be placed on the market in bid mode. What happens is everyone goes to buy that item and you name gets put in a draw, and a person is randomly selected from everyone that bid. When I say RANDOM I say it really losely, as this is where the hidden stat comes in. Players have a better chance of getting items from the market based on a threshhold they hit that is measured by how much real world money you have spent on the game. So people who pay money for things in the store have higher priority during the bids. Due to this, if you don't plan on spending money you could easily spend an hour trying to buy 1 item. (I would like to mention here, that I heard this from several experienced players, who have put probably close to 5000 hours into this game if not more. I have not been able to confirm this from any online source, so take this point with a grain of salt.)
Speaking of paying real world money, pets is the biggest aspect of P2W in this game. You can have upwards of 4 pets at a time, and it is pretty much essential to have upon reaching high levels when you don't have time to stop and pick items off the ground. They have "maids" which do multiple things, such as buy items off the market from anywhere, without haveing to go to town. Costumes that boost your efficency while doing a profession. Camoflage which hides your name tag, which pretty much makes you completely unnoticable in pvp, especailly in group battles like Node Wars. Gimmicky underwear which gives you +1 luck. Items to make you inventory larger/carry more weight, and so on. The P2W aspect is not nearly bad as most, but there are aspects of this game which pretty much making it detrimental that you cough up some extra money. It is actually essential that you spend some money in the market... It feels like you have only purchased part of the game if you don't. In addition, almost everything costs atleast $20 or more... which is expensive for cosmetics.
Nodes, are actually an awesome idea, and Node wars are pretty fun, the problem is mainly the fact that it is designed in such a needlessly complex way, and the UI for it could be drastically simplified to the point where you don't need to spend an hour going through different versions of tutorial videos trying to understand it. Also, it is never explained how or what is required to replentish your workers - which is beer. This kind of makes this whole system fall on it's head seeings as everything comes to a grinding hault until you figure that out.
- Nothing is explained
- Enhancing is a money burning sim
- The Market is awful
- P2W is essential
- Nodes
There is plenty more I could comment on, but what I have above is pretty much the main things.
The game can be fun, but it definitely requires a special type of person to really enjoy it. It is not like most mmo's which is refreshing, and does not feel super grindy, atleast in combat. If you have a lot of free time, and don't mind shelling out more money than the purchase price, then this game might be for you. I wouldn't say this game is bad, I wouldn't even say it is not fun. This game is good, and is fun, it is just sloppy in how it is given to the player, and requires a lot of time, ESPECIALLY in a guild. I highly recommend playing this with a friend, and not by yourself. For me, this game began to feel more like a chore than an actual game. I logged on because I had to finish a contract, or because I had to feed my workers. I also felt obligated to play because of the money I had put into the game (shame on me). I feel relieved and happy that I have time to play other games, and do other things. You don't think you're not having fun until you take a break and realize how much time you've wasted to accomplish something so incrimentally miniscule.
For those who enjoy the game, more power to you, I guess I just don't have it in me.  (:

You play a young woman who quits your job to move to a retirement town called Greyfox, seemingly because you've had it with life and want to take things slow and easy. Upon moving to Greyfox, you encounter a mysterious woman who brings you on a rather unique and interesting adventure.
This isn't your conventional RPG, in that no battles are involved. Instead, this is much more like a regular adventure game, except you move around and interact using the keyboard instead of mouse. There are many different locations to check out even though the story only ever takes place in the town of Greyfox, and every location is visually a joy to process.
Almost everything (from people to objects) in this cute little pixel world can be clicked on to yield elaborate - and in many cases, humorous - descriptions. There are also many optional extras or bonuses to be gleaned from exploring as much as you can. E.g. I found it a delight to randomly dig into some seats and find cash!
Lots of instances where you must make decisions. In at least several of them, these decisions will result in a different ending. So there's a degree of replayability involved - choose different paths the next round to get different results.

Lethal League is a fantastic party game.
Fighting games are a blast, but learning all the move sets and combos can make it really difficult to just sit down and play. Lethal League, on the other hand, has a pretty simple set of controls, leaving the complexity up to the actual players' strategy.
In addition, since it supports 4 controllers, more people can crowd around and join in at once. Be prepared for things to get loud when someone manages to get an amazing volley in.
I kind of wish there were a few more character and environments available, but the current offerings are very well-done, and help keep things simple, so I'll leave it as a wish, rather than an actual complaint.
Even at current pricing, it's well worth it, but should not be missed if you see it on sale.
